Title: Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Festival begins nationwide journey celebrating a shared spiritual legacy
Content:
Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Festival, a nationwide cultural festival, was inaugurated on September 11 at the field of Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka, celebrating the timeless spiritual traditions and artistic contributions of Kabir (1398–1498) and Fakir Lalon Shah (1774–1890). The festival celebrates the influence of the two mystic figures whose teachings have shaped generations across the Indian subcontinent through messages of equality, compassion, devotion and human unity.

Organised by Lalon Biswasangha with support from the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, the festival will continue until October 30. Cultural programmes will be held every day from 5:30 pm to 9:30 pm, and the celebration will travel across all eight divisions of Bangladesh, including Dhaka, Chattogram, Rajshahi, Sylhet, Mymensingh, Khulna, Barishal and Rangpur.

Kabir and Lalon’s philosophies represent a spiritual tradition that emphasises the search for truth beyond social divisions and external identities. Their songs and teachings have long encouraged people to look within themselves, embrace humanity and recognise the connection between all beings. Through this festival, organisers aim to introduce their profound creations to younger generations while creating a space for cultural dialogue, reflection and appreciation of the region’s shared spiritual heritage.

The inaugural ceremony was attended by prominent cultural and political figures. Advocate Fazlur Rahman MP, freedom fighter and senior political leader, inaugurated the festival. The scheduled chief guest, State Minister for Cultural Affairs Ali Newaz Mahmud Khaiyam could not attend due to unavoidable circumstances. Representing the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Md Mizanur Rahman, Joint Secretary of the ministry, attended the programme as chief guest. Dinesh Trivedi, High Commissioner of India to Bangladesh, joined the ceremony as a special guest. The event was chaired by Professor Emeritus Dr Anisuzzaman, Chairman of Lalon Biswasangha.

Speaking at the inauguration, Fazlur Rahman highlighted the relevance of Kabir and Lalon’s teachings in understanding human struggles and spiritual questions. He said, “To understand the struggles of life, turn to Kabir; to understand the mysteries of the soul, turn to Lalon.”

The inaugural ceremony featured discussions, musical performances and cultural presentations involving scholars, researchers, musicians and representatives of the Kabir and Lalon traditions. The discussion panel included noted academics and cultural personalities such as Professor Dr Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Professor Dr Priyanka Gope, Dr Ahsanul Hadi, Fakir Abdul Hossain Shah, Nijhum Pankiya, Dr M K Roy and Syed Faiyaz Hasan, who shared insights on the philosophical, literary and cultural significance of Kabir and Lalon’s works.

The High Commissioner of India to Bangladesh, Dinesh Trivedi, highlighted the spirit of equality and universal humanity reflected in the teachings of Kabir and Lalon, saying, “Here, everyone is equal, an ambassador, an MP, or a common person. This equality is the very essence of Kabir and Lalon’s philosophy.”

Reflecting on the persistent relevance of their wisdom in today’s world, Trivedi added, “When sailors lose their way, they seek a lighthouse. In a world that has lost its path and peace, Kabir and Lalon’s wisdom remains that guiding light for humanity.”

The festival also served as a platform to preserve and promote the Bhabsangeet tradition, a form of spiritual music that carries deep reflections on life, humanity and the search for the divine.

Bringing together artistes, scholars, cultural leaders and audiences from diverse backgrounds, the Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Festival seeks to celebrate a shared heritage built on compassion, equality and spiritual awareness.
Author: F Faiza Ramim Faiza Ramim

Title: Exhibition on Sheikh Rabiul Haque’s 80-year creative journey being celebrated
Content:
A week-long art exhibition celebrating the 80-year creative journey of writer, painter, singer and entrepreneur Sheikh Rabiul Haque was inaugurated yesterday at the National Art Gallery of Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.

Renowned painter Rafiqun Nabi attended the inauguration as the chief guest. Painter Jyotsna Mahbuba, Kamrul Islam, general secretary of the Bangiya Sahitya Sanskriti Sangsad, and other cultural personalities were also present.

The exhibition, being held at Gallery 7 on the third floor of the National Art Gallery, will remain open until September 18.

A cultural programme and discussion on Haque’s multifaceted creative journey will be held on September 15 at the National Art Gallery Auditorium. The event will explore his contributions to art and culture across his long career.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Remembering Anwar Hossain, the ‘uncrowned Nawab’ of Dhallywood
Content:
Anwar Hossain was one of the most celebrated actors in Bangladesh. Over a career spanning hundreds of films, he played an astonishing range of characters — from heroes and rulers to ordinary villagers and morally complex figures.

He became the “uncrowned Nawab” of Bangladeshi cinema after his iconic performance as the titular character in Nawab Sirajuddaula, directed by Khan Ataur Rahman. His deeply emotional portrayal of the doomed Nawab captivated audiences, particularly during the character’s tragic death. The role became so closely associated with Hossain that audiences everywhere began calling him the “uncrowned Nawab”.

His versatility was further evident in Zahir Raihan’s landmark political film “Jibon Theke Neya”. Playing a politician, Hossain created a very different screen image. He also appeared in the film’s memorable musical sequences, including “Karar Oi Louho Kopat” and “Amar Sonar Bangla”. In the latter, his emotional expression as tears rolled down his face remains particularly memorable.

In “Lathiyal”, Hossain delivered another acclaimed performance, convincingly portraying a rural stick-fighter. His natural and powerful acting won over audiences across the country and earned him the National Film Award for Best Actor.

Although best known for his character roles, Hossain was also a leading man. He made his acting debut as a villain and later played the hero in “Surja Snan”. Across hundreds of films, he portrayed virtually every kind of character — rich and poor, king and commoner, saint and sinner.

He continued to surprise audiences in films such as Amjad Hossain’s “Golapi Ekhon Traine”, in which he played an ordinary man with remarkable sensitivity. His performance earned him another National Film Award. He also played the titular roles in “Shahid Titumir” and “Isha Kha”, further demonstrating his extraordinary range.

Some of the songs associated with Hossain’s performances became cultural favourites. “Hay Re Manush, Rongin Fanush, Dhom Furaille Thush”, featured in “Boro Bhalo Lok Chhilo”, became widely popular across cities, villages, markets and tea stalls. His screen presence in films such as “Manusher Mon”, “Bhanumati”, “Chakorani” and “Bhat De” also left lasting impressions on audiences, often through emotionally charged performances and songs.

In “Doyal Murshid”, Hossain played Hasan, an honest young man who desperately wanted to free himself from his burdens. His performance once again demonstrated his ability to bring dignity and emotional depth to a character.

Anwar Hossain died on September 13, 2013. Yet decades after his passing, he remains the uncrowned Nawab of Bangladeshi cinema — a rare actor whose range, screen presence and body of work remain difficult to match.

For his contribution to cinema, Hossain received the National Film Award for Lifetime Achievement, multiple National Film Awards and the Ekushey Padak, among numerous other honours.

Anwar Hossain was, quite simply, one of a kind.
Author: S Shah Alam Shazu Shah Alam Shazu

Title: Shanta Islam receives Lifetime Achievement Award in Canada
Content:
Once a widely popular actress in numerous television dramas and a National Film Award winner, Shanta Islam has now received a Lifetime Achievement Award from an organisation outside Bangladesh. The Federation of Bangladeshi Associations in North America (FOBANA) presented her with the honour at the Don Valley Hotel and Suites in Toronto, Canada.

Speaking to The Daily Star over the phone from Canada, Shanta Islam said, “I am extremely happy and delighted. FOBANA has given me a Lifetime Achievement Award in Canada. I feel deeply honoured.”

She said, “I have acted in numerous dramas throughout my career and have received the love of many people. I received the Bachsas Award for my performance in ‘Mayur Singhasan’ with Aranyak Natyadal. I also received the National Film Award for acting in films. However, this is the first time I have received such a major honour outside the country — and that too a Lifetime Achievement Award.”

Asked about the recognition, Shanta said, “I truly feel proud to receive this honour. I am grateful to the organisers. I would also like to express my gratitude and love to all the directors, producers, fellow artistes and journalists in my own country.”

She added, “We artistes work for the people. Alongside receiving people’s love, when an organisation or a state recognises our work, it gives us encouragement and a sense of fulfilment.”

Recalling her career, she said, “I acted in numerous dramas for Bangladesh Television at one time. I also worked in many package dramas and performed in stage productions. I became involved in cultural activities while studying at Dhaka University. I acted in several popular dramas, including ‘Rupnagar’. I also worked as a presenter for many years. Receiving this honour has brought back memories of the work I did throughout my life.”

Meanwhile, Shanta Islam is enjoying her time in Canada, where her only son, daughter-in-law and granddaughter live. She is spending time with them.

“My son’s success gives me peace and fulfilment. My daughter-in-law is like another mother to me, and my granddaughter is my inspiration to keep living. I am doing very well with all of them around me,” she said.

She added, “I have also been meeting many friends and well-wishers in Canada. I am having a wonderful time. I am especially enjoying spending lovely moments with my daughter-in-law. We go out and explore places on holidays.”

Finally, she said, “My son is extremely happy that I have received this Lifetime Achievement Award. My daughter-in-law is happy too.”

Notably, acclaimed magician Jewel Aich also received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the same event.
Author: S Shah Alam Shazu Shah Alam Shazu

Title: ‘Symphony of Life’: Exhibition reflects life through diverse artistic lenses
Content:
172 artists came together last week with 172 different ways of looking at life. Their works span landscapes, Islamic calligraphy, folk traditions, still life, abstract imagery and experimental compositions, creating a diverse visual experience under one roof.

Titled “Symphony of Life”, the group art exhibition organised by Shilpo Bangla opened at the Zainul Gallery of the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Dhaka, on September 10. The exhibition brings together artists working across different styles and mediums.

The exhibition was inaugurated on September 10 at 5pm at the Osman Jamal Auditorium of the Faculty of Fine Arts. Eminent artist and Ekushey Padak-winning Professor Dr Abdus Sattar, honorary teacher of the Department of Oriental Art at the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Dhaka, attended the event as the chief guest. Professor Kaoser Hassan Togor of the Department of Sculpture at the Faculty of Fine Arts, Shanto Mahmud, Channel i Chief Executive Producer of News, and Associate Professor Habiba Akther Papia of the Department of Fashion Design at Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology attended as special guests. Professor Dr Azharul Islam Sheikh, Dean of the Faculty of Fine Arts and Chairman of its Department of Ceramics, presided over the ceremony. Minne Art Gallery and Mahfuz Canvas are supporting partners of the exhibition.

The broad theme of the exhibition allows the artists to approach life and society from their own perspectives. The result is a collection where a quiet watercolour of a village homestead can hang beside an elaborate gold calligraphy piece, while a traditional still life may sit next to a painting of a seedling emerging from the earth.

Landscape painting occupies much of the gallery space. Rivers lined with mangroves, boats moored at wooden jetties, moonlit canals and vivid sunsets appear across the walls. Rural Bangladesh returns repeatedly in images of flame trees beside ponds, narrow lanes between tin-roofed houses and quiet village settings. Many of these works are acrylic on canvas, with soft, blended strokes giving the landscapes a gentle, atmospheric quality.

Islamic calligraphy forms another strong visual thread. One large framed work features a Quranic verse written in gold against a background that shifts from deep red to blue. Beneath the lettering, two cupped hands hold small circular images of a damaged landscape. Another work combines golden lettering with a black background and a jewelled mandala-like form. A night view of the Masjid al-Haram, glowing beneath a crescent moon and framed by an ornate arch, adds another striking piece to the collection.

Folk traditions also have a strong presence. One canvas draws on the visual language of nakshi kantha, depicting two peacocks facing each other across a lotus medallion, with decorated elephants and an intricate floral border. Another borrows the bold outlines and flat colours of rickshaw art to portray a mother holding her child. Elsewhere, women sit on a chequered mat in a village courtyard.

Some artists move further away from realism. In one unusual composition, a figure carries a teacup where the head would normally be. Another brings together dozens of small faces to form a single heart. Two whirling dervishes appear against a smoky blue background, their faces left undefined while the movement of their white garments becomes the focus of the work.

The variety extends to the mediums. Acrylic is widely used, appearing both in the flat colours of folk-inspired works and the heavier textures of landscape paintings. Oil, watercolour, charcoal, graphite and pen are also represented, while some artists have used modelling paste, gold leaf, beads and collage to add texture to their works.

More than anything, “Symphony of Life” reflects the different ways artists interpret the world around them. By bringing 172 artists into one space, the exhibition creates a collective experience without asking them to give up their individual voices. “Symphony of Life” will remain open to visitors at the Zainul Gallery until September 16, daily from 12pm to 7pm.
Author: Anika Tahsin Hafsa Anika Tahsin Hafsa

Title: Samina Chowdhury set to launch music academy for aspiring musicians
Content: After five decades in music, Samina Chowdhury is now preparing to take on a new role as a music mentor. The singer, who completed 50 years in her music career this year, is set to establish a music academy named Samina’s Academy of Music (SAM). The initiative aims to provide proper guidance to aspiring musicians of the new generation. Samina began her musical journey in 1976 when she won first place in the patriotic song category of Bangladesh Television’s children’s talent competition “Notun Kuri”. She made her debut in film songs in 1981 with the title track of “Jonmo Theke Jolchi”. She has continued to perform and release music over the years. As Samina spends part of the year in the United States, she plans to operate the academy in both Bangladesh and the US. Classes will be offered both online and in person. “The activities of Samina’s Academy of Music will mainly be conducted online. However, there will also be arrangements for those who want to learn in person. That will be available in both Bangladesh and the United States,” Samina told Ajker Patrika. She is currently in Bangladesh and will travel to the United States on September 22. She plans to return after two months, after which she will complete the remaining preparations and officially announce the academy. “Many people have been telling me for a long time to teach music. Swapon (Samina Chowdhury’s husband) also repeatedly suggested that I establish an academy. So, I decided to start teaching music,” she said. The logo for SAM has already been designed, and Samina hopes to begin its activities later this year.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Nrityanchal marks 25 years with three-day dance festival
Content:
Nrityanchal is celebrating its 25th anniversary with a three-day dance festival at Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy, bringing together more than 700 young and senior dancers across two major productions.

The festival began on September 11 with a rally on the academy premises, attended by Nrityanchal’s teachers, students and performers, alongside its directors, dancers and choreographers Shamim Ara Nipa and Shibli Mohammad.

The second day featured “Chhoray Chhonde Nrityomala”, a production centred on children’s rhymes and educational themes. More than 400 children and teenage students of Nrityanchal took part in the performance at the National Theatre Hall on September 12.

Nipa choreographed the production, while Mohammad supervised the overall programme. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid attended as chief guest, alongside Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy Director General Rezauddin Stalin and other cultural figures.

Combining dance, rhythm, education and entertainment, the production featured performances based on children’s rhymes and themes aimed at younger audiences.

The festival will conclude today, September 13, with “Nrityomalika” at the National Theatre Hall. Featuring more than 300 performers alongside Nrityanchal’s senior artistes, the programme will showcase folk, creative and classical dance.

Nipa and Mohammad will also perform a special duet during the closing programme. Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury is scheduled to attend as chief guest.

A photographic exhibition documenting Nrityanchal’s 25-year journey is also being held in the lobby of the National Theatre Hall on September 12 and 13. The exhibition features photographs and memorabilia tracing the organisation’s activities, performances and milestones since its establishment.

Founded in 2001, Nrityanchal has grown into a dance training institution under the leadership of Nipa and Mohammad, providing training and performance opportunities across several dance traditions.

The organisation’s anniversary celebrations have included programmes throughout the year, including a Bharatanatyam evening in June that recognised three dance gurus for their contributions to the classical dance form in Bangladesh.

The 25th-anniversary festival is being held with Maasranga Television as media partner and Shah Cement as associate partner.

Title: Farida Parveen remembered on first death anniversary
Content:
Channel i is marking the first death anniversary of Farida Parveen today, with two special programmes remembering the singer whose voice helped bring Lalon Shah’s songs to generations of listeners in Bangladesh and beyond.

Parveen died on September 13, 2025, after suffering from kidney complications. She was 70.

A special magazine programme, directed and presented by senior journalist Abdur Rahman, will be broadcast at 5:18pm today. The programme will look back at Parveen’s life, career and contribution to Lalon Sangeet.

She will also be remembered on “Gaan Diye Shuru”, which will air after the 7am news. Renowned flautist Gazi Abdul Hakim will appear on the programme.

Parveen began her musical career in 1968 as a singer with Rajshahi Betar, initially performing Nazrul Sangeet. She came to wider public attention in 1973 through patriotic songs before turning increasingly towards the music of Lalon Shah.

She trained in Lalon Sangeet under spiritual mentor Moksed Ali Shah. Over the years, Lalon’s songs became the defining body of her work, with Parveen developing a distinctive approach to performing the mystic poet’s compositions.

Her work went beyond the concert stage. She established the Ochin Pakhi Sangeet Academy to introduce Lalon Sangeet to younger generations and encourage the study and practice of the tradition.

Parveen received the Ekushey Padak in 1987 for her contribution to music. She also won the Bangladesh National Film Award for Best Female Playback Singer in 1993 and received the Fukuoka Asian Culture Prize in 2008.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: 83rd Venice Int’l Film Festival: ‘Woman Unknown’ wins Golden Lion, John Malkovich takes Best Actor
Content:
May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown” has won the Golden Lion for best film at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, with the Danish drama also earning Mathilde Arcel the Volpi Cup for best actress.

The film, which follows a young housemaid whose intimate relationship with a German soldier during World War II threatens her future, was the only competition title solely directed by a woman.

Accepting the festival’s top honour, el-Toukhy addressed the lack of opportunities for women filmmakers, an issue jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal had raised at the beginning of the festival.

“Thank you to the jury for this great honour — and to you, Maggie, especially for using your voice and shining a light on the lack of equal opportunities for female filmmakers in our industry,” el-Toukhy said.

She described making the film as financially, logistically and emotionally challenging, adding that she was driven by a desire to bring attention to the “unknown women of our common history”.

Earlier in the ceremony, “Woman Unknown” star Mathilde Arcel received the Volpi Cup for best actress. The film marks her first leading role and her first appearance at a film festival.

“This is my first lead role in a movie and it’s my first time at a film festival and my first time to win a film award,” an emotional Arcel said.

John Malkovich received the Volpi Cup for best actor for his portrayal of an eccentric CIA agent in Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine”. Unable to attend the ceremony as he was filming another project in Montreal, Malkovich accepted the award through a video message.

“I am humbled to be chosen for this award, which has been given to so many wonderful actors over the past 83 iterations of the Venice Film Festival,” he said, also thanking McDonagh and co-star Sam Rockwell.

The Grand Jury Prize, the festival’s second-highest honour, went to South Korean filmmaker Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love”. The drama, which follows two married couples from different social classes, will represent South Korea in the international feature film category at the Oscars.

Accepting the award, Lee reflected on the erosion of human connections and the changing meaning of labour.

“I made this film to ask what cinema can and should do in times like these,” he said.

Russian filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovsky won the Silver Lion for best director for “DAU”, a three-hour-and-15-minute film he has worked on for two decades. Khrzhanovsky dedicated the award to Ukrainians fighting in the war and to his mother, who was born in Ukraine shortly before the arrival of Nazi forces.

The Special Jury Prize went to “NAZA”, a documentary about the conflict in Gaza by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who previously worked on “No Other Land”. In his acceptance speech, Abraham spoke about criticism of the documentary and stressed the importance of confronting the realities depicted in the film.

The ceremony also included tributes to Oscar-winning British producer Jeremy Thomas, who died on Friday at the age of 77. Thomas won the Academy Award for best picture for Bernardo Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor” in 1988 and collaborated with the Italian filmmaker on several projects.

Alongside Gyllenhaal, this year’s competition jury included filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania, Hong Kong director Johnnie To, Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat, French director and screenwriter Xavier Giannoli, composer Daniel Blumberg and Italian film academic Francesco Casetti.

Title: The Difficult Bride wins Bisato d’Oro at Venice Film Festival
Content:
Bangladeshi filmmaker Rubaiyat Hossain’s "The Difficult Bride" has won the Independent Film Critics Award, Premio Bisato d’Oro, at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, ahead of the festival’s official awards ceremony.

The recognition marks another significant milestone for the film, which made history this year as the first Bangladeshi feature film to compete in the Orizzonti Competition at the Venice Film Festival.

Set in contemporary Dhaka, "The Difficult Bride" follows Zaineen, a young bride-to-be whose body begins to transform as she undergoes the beauty rituals and preparations surrounding her wedding. Blending feminist folk horror, body horror and supernatural elements, the film explores how women’s bodies become sites of family expectations, social control and desire.

For Hossain, the recognition comes at a landmark moment for both Bangladeshi cinema and her own filmmaking journey.

“I made The Difficult Bride from a very intimate place — thinking about the ways women learn to inhabit, discipline and sometimes fear their own bodies. To have the film recognised by independent critics in Venice is deeply meaningful to me. I hope the film can open a space for audiences to encounter Bangladesh not simply through its social realities, but through its imagination, its folklore, its darkness and its beauty,” she said.

The Bisato d’Oro is an independent critics’ prize associated with the Venice Film Festival and is separate from the official awards presented by the Biennale. The recognition places "The Difficult Bride" within the wider critical conversation surrounding this year’s festival.

The film’s Venice selection had already drawn international attention, with critics praising its transformation of South Asian wedding rituals into a feminist folk-horror language. IndieWire described the film as turning South Asian wedding tropes into “feminist folk horror”.

Produced by Francois D’Artemare, "The Difficult Bride" is an international co-production between Bangladesh, France, Germany, Norway and Portugal. International sales are handled by Films Boutique.

Following its Venice premiere, the film will continue its international festival journey, including its North American premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Lady Gaga welcomes first child with fiancé Michael Polansky
Content:
Pop star Lady Gaga has welcomed her first child with fiancé Michael Polansky. The 40-year-old Grammy winner and Polansky are now parents to their first baby together.

Motherhood has long been something Gaga has spoken openly about. In a 2019 YouTube video, she discussed her plans for the following decade and said she hoped to have children alongside pursuing more acting roles.

“I want to do more movies, I want to have babies,” she said at the time.

She reiterated her desire to start a family in a 2020 interview with InStyle, saying she was excited about having children and looked forward to becoming a mother. Gaga also joked about the maternal nickname “Mother Monster”, which her fans have used for years.

More recently, during a 2025 appearance on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, Gaga described motherhood as something she hoped would be her “next starring role”.

“I would like to do many things,” she said while discussing her future plans. “But what I really want is to be a mom. That’s my next starring role, I hope.”

Gaga and Polansky were first linked in 2020 after they were photographed together at a New Year’s Eve party in Las Vegas. They later made their relationship public, including appearances together around the 2020 Super Bowl in Miami.

The couple spent much of the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic together while quarantining. Over the years, they have largely kept their relationship private while supporting each other’s professional and philanthropic work.

Polansky serves as executive director of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, while Gaga has been involved in mental health advocacy through her Born This Way Foundation, which she founded in 2012.

In 2021, a source told PEOPLE that the couple had also bonded over their shared interest in charitable work, describing Polansky as “sweet and supportive” and saying the two made a strong team.

Gaga confirmed her engagement to Polansky in 2024. She was heard introducing him as her “fiancé” to then-French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal during the 2024 Paris Olympics in a TikTok video posted by Attal.

The new arrival marks a new chapter for Gaga, who has previously balanced her career in music and film with her advocacy work.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: James and Rupam Islam set to share stage in Sydney
Content:
After wrapping up his nearly two-month European music tour, Bangladeshi rock icon James is now in Australia, where he is set to perform alongside West Bengal singer and Fossils frontman Rupam Islam.

The two musicians will take the stage today at a concert at Norwest Convention in Sydney, bringing together two prominent voices from the Bengali rock scene. The event has already generated significant excitement among expatriate Bengalis, with all tickets reportedly sold out.

Rupam Islam is a longtime admirer of James and has spoken on several occasions about the influence the Bangladeshi rock star has had on his musical journey. While James is affectionately known as “Guru” among his fans, Rupam has described him as “Mahaguru”.

Ahead of the Sydney concert, the two musicians were seen chatting in a video, where Rupam expressed his excitement about performing with James once again.

“Joy Guru, Joy Rock, Amar Bangla” is the slogan for the concert, Rupam said, adding that sharing a stage with an artiste whose music has influenced an entire generation and Bengali-speaking community is always a special experience.

James, smiling throughout the conversation, told Rupam, “It’s been a long time since I saw you.” The two then tried to recall when they had last met.

Rupam remembered performing with James at a Rock Fest in Bangladesh, although there was some confusion over whether the event took place in 2007 or 2011. James eventually joked about how long it had been.

The pair also performed at a concert in Kolkata in 2024, though their interaction at the time was brief.

During their recent conversation, Rupam recalled James once promising to take him around Dhaka in his car when he next visited Bangladesh. “That never happened,” he joked, referring to James’ famously private lifestyle.

The Sydney concert will give the two artistes another opportunity to perform together, much to the delight of their fans. Before taking the stage, Rupam also touched James’ feet to seek his blessings, adding a personal moment to their reunion.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: ‘The stage means everything to me’: Tamalika Karmaker on her return to theatre
Content:
After a long break from the stage, National Film Award-winning artiste Tamalika Karmaker is set to return to theatre with Mamunur Rashid’s “Omanush” in Virginia. Directed by Jannatul Tumpa, the play will be staged on October 4. Tamalika will share the stage with actor Sayed Babu. Tamalika spent three decades performing with Aranyak Natyadal, appearing in several acclaimed productions and earning recognition for her stage performances. She has been living in the United States for several years.

Speaking about her return, Tamalika said, “To be honest, I am scared. Every time I return to the stage to perform, I feel nervous. This time too, I will be returning to the stage after many years with ‘Omanush’, and I am genuinely scared.” Despite working in television and films, theatre has always remained her first priority. “I performed on stage with Aranyak Natyadal for 30 consecutive years. The stage means everything to me. The joy, satisfaction and happiness I get from performing theatre, I do not get from anything else. The stage always comes first for me,” she said.

She added, “My love for theatre is such that I have left television dramas and films at times. I always made time for other work while keeping theatre as my priority.” “Omanush” is particularly meaningful to Tamalika as it was written by her mentor, Mamunur Rashid.

“I will take the stage on October 4 for ‘Omanush’. It was written by my mentor. I have learnt and gained a lot from him. Since I will be performing in Virginia, I will miss Mamunur Rashid a lot. I will miss my Aranyak family,” she said. Although she now lives in the United States, Tamalika said her connection with theatre remains strong. “Even though I live far from my country, I have not forgotten the stage. That is why I am working in theatre here as well. I am currently rehearsing,” she said.

The artiste is also grateful for the support she has received from fellow artistes in Bangladesh. “I am grateful to my group, Aranyak. I am also grateful to many other artistes. They have been encouraging and supporting me by sending congratulatory videos for ‘Omanush’,” she said.
Author: S Shah Alam Shazu Shah Alam Shazu

Title: BRAC Institute of Languages and The Daily Star redefine English Education for youth
Content:
In an educational landscape often dominated by rote memorisation and rigid textbook formats, a collaborative initiative between the BRAC Institute of Languages (BIL) and The Daily Star's English in "Schools (EIS) initiative" is redefining how young learners engage with language. Through the compilation and adaptation of Learn English for Success: Climb Higher (Class VI-VIII) and Learn English for Success: Climb Higher (Class IX-X) , this partnership stands as a beacon of fresh, dynamic, and deeply interactive learning for students.

Originally conceived to provide school students with accessible opportunities for additional English language practice through the pages of The Daily Star, these materials have moved beyond their original newspaper format. They have now been carefully adapted and compiled into classroom resources for both teachers and learners.

Even though the original newspaper-based initiative has concluded, its legacy endures. The rich collection of learning materials remains remarkably relevant, offering educators practical, engaging, and interactive content that integrates seamlessly into modern English language classrooms. By connecting journalism with classroom teaching, the initiative champions a learner-centred approach that encourages active engagement with language.

Senior figures at BRAC University, notably Advisor Lady Syeda Sarwat Abed and Director of the BRAC Institute of Languages Professor Shaila Sultana, envision that this publication will inspire renewed enthusiasm for innovative methods in language teaching. Above all, the initiative underscores the lasting value of student-centred, engaging resources that encourage young minds to see language not as a burdensome task, but as an engaging pathway to exploration.

Rifah Tashfia Islam is a postgraduate student at North South University and an intern at Star Books and Literature. A writer and dreamer, she is often found chasing stories and romanticising ordinary moments.

Title: Finding home, identity, and art in ‘Parsa’s Pithas’
Content:
How do you stay connected to your own culture and roots while living thousands of miles away from home? This is the question at the heart of Sumaiya Matin’s debut children’s book Parsa’s Pithas. Set in Canada, the book tells the heartwarming story of a seven-year-old girl named Parsa who, through making pithas with her mother, is able to learn more about her Bangali roots and traditions while also gaining more confidence in her ability to express herself through her art.

The book opens with the young protagonist frustrated at her inability to draw the “perfect” sky. In dire need of a distraction, Parsa decides to take a break from her school art project to instead help her mother make nakshi pakon pithas for the Bangla New Year. However, as the two begin to make the pithas, Parsa’s frustration returns when she realises that she cannot make pithas as smoothly and intricately as her mother. First struggling to make the right consistency of dough, and then betrayed by the breaking of a toothpick, Parsa struggles with a question that every artist has asked themselves at least once —does art have to be perfect in order to be good?

For Parsa, the answer to this question is found in her mother’s stories about the Bangladeshi women who first made nakshi pakon pithas. Learning about the girls in Bangladesh who made art with whatever they had—rice flower, sticks, stones, and thorns of date palm trees—inspires Parsa to jump over the hurdle of perfectionism and focus her energy and creativity in expressing herself in her own unique way rather than trying to replicate what others are doing.

It is in this intertwining of cultural lessons with a story of a young girl persevering and learning not to give up that Parsa’s Pithas achieves immaculately what every good children’s book sets out to do—act as “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” for children around the world.

First introduced by children’s literature scholar, Rudine Sims Bishop, the concept of “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” is a metaphor for the different ways in which children can see themselves and the world around them in children’s books. Mirrors signify children seeing their own experiences reflected in the books they read, windows symbolise children learning about different cultures through books, and sliding glass doors refer to children using their imaginations to enter experiences that are different from their own. Bishop argues that all three of these reading experiences are essential to the development of a growing child. What makes Parsa’s Pithas so remarkable is that it is able to do all three of these things at the exact same time.

Written primarily with Bangladeshi diaspora children in mind, the book puts to pages an experience that is not often represented in books or media. Though there are an abundance of Bangladeshi children’s books with representation of Bangladeshi characters, we seldom see books made specifically for children who are learning to navigate their Bangladeshi roots and identity while living away from Bangladesh. Acting as a mirror, the story of Parsa and her mother keeping Bangali traditions alive by celebrating Bangla New Year all the way in Canada allows children of the Bangladeshi diaspora to finally see their own unique experiences and struggles be represented on paper.

Acting as a window, Parsa’s Pithas being a book that is written in English and available on the international market, offers many children, both in Bangladesh and outside, an insight into the Bangali culture and its traditions. The stories of Bangladeshi women told to Parsa by her mother in the book, combined with the vibrant and colourful illustrations by Nesba Yousef, act as the perfect introduction to Bangladeshi history. Furthermore, by framing the cultural lessons within the narrative of a young girl struggling with her artistic expression, the book is able to introduce Bangladeshi culture and values not as something that is unfamiliar and distant, but rather as something that everyone can learn from and incorporate into their own lives.

Lastly, it is in this invitation to participate, that the book shines the brightest. Going a step further than just introducing Bangladeshi culture to readers, with a full recipe for nakshi pakon pithas and an activities section, the book invites readers not only to learn, but fully immerse themselves in the culture they just read about.

It is here also that Matin’s message of embracing uniqueness over trying to replicate things perfectly comes in full clutch. For children in the diaspora, taking part in their culture may not always look the same as what it does for children living in Bangladesh. Many of them may be working with different tools, ingredients, and circumstances. However, as Parsa learns, just because something is different does not mean it is any less meaningful or beautiful in its own right. Afterall, sometimes to keep a culture alive is to be brave and resourceful enough to make it your own.

Shanjida Nowshin Chowdhury is a lecturer in the Department of English and Modern Languages at North South University.
Author: S Shanjida Nowshin Chowdhury Shanjida Nowshin Chowdhury

Title: Out of the archives, into the feed
Content:
Open Instagram or TikTok for 10 minutes and you will likely run into him: a nervous Prague insurance clerk, dead for a century now, staring out from a grainy black-and-white photo with a quote about cages and birds stamped across it. Beside him sits a brooding Russian novelist who once faced a firing squad and lived to write about it afterward.

Franz Kafka and Fyodor Dostoevsky—two of literature’s heaviest names—are thriving unexpectedly on apps built mostly for dance trends and comedy skits.

It shouldn’t work on paper. These are writers obsessed with guilt, confusing systems, and deep self-doubt—hardly algorithm-friendly material. Yet here we are, watching teenagers highlight The Brothers Karamazov (1880) between class notes and skincare reviews. What explains this sudden revival of century-old books among young people online?

‘Burnout’ plays a huge part in this trend. This generation didn’t inherit simple, inspiring stories where the hero wins and everything turns out fine. Instead, they inherited constant traffic jams, rising heat and pollution, endless coaching classes, hyper-competitive exams, and a job market where people who were promised high salaries after studying BBA 10 years ago now face modest pay in Motijheel or Gulshan and are treated like they can be replaced at any moment.

Kafka never wrote heroic adventure stories. He wrote about regular people stuck in absurd, stressful situations they couldn’t escape. In his most famous story, “The Metamorphosis” (1915), a man named Gregor Samsa wakes up turned into a giant bug. His main worry isn’t his terrifying new body; it is how he will explain being late to work to his boss.

That is the real tragedy of the story. And somehow, it hits harder for an exhausted 22-year-old today than any big action quest could. The story was never really about turning into a bug—it was about how soul-crushing it feels to give your life away to a job that doesn’t care about you.

“I am a cage, in search of a bird.”

Dostoevsky hits a different note. Where Kafka suffers quietly, Dostoevsky explodes with emotion. His short story “White Nights” (1848), about a lonely dreamer wandering the streets of St. Petersburg, has become an unlikely hit for people feeling overwhelmed by their own thoughts. His lines get placed over slow piano music and blurry city footage, and somehow, it keeps working.

“I am a dreamer; I have so little real life that I look upon such moments as this as a dream…”

There is a strange reality worth thinking about here. This is the most digitally connected generation in history, yet surveys constantly show record levels of loneliness. Everyone is easy to reach through text and social apps, but very few people actually feel understood.

The overwhelming guilt, overthinking, and deep loneliness in Dostoevsky’s stories no longer feel like old, distant fiction from Russia. They read like entries from a private diary written yesterday. They give young readers permission to feel things deeply in a culture that often tells people to stay detached.

Meme culture deserves plenty of credit for this revival too. Classic literature usually comes wrapped in dust and serious classroom rules, which keeps everyday readers at a distance. The internet strips that seriousness away without much ceremony.

On social media, Kafka becomes “that anxious guy who hated his job and had huge issues with his dad.” Dostoevsky becomes “the guy who replays one single awkward conversation in his head for six years straight.”

It’s funny, but it’s also remarkably accurate. Internet humour makes these intimidating writers feel like old friends. Someone laughs at a joke about a man turning into a bug, gets curious, opens the book, and suddenly finds themselves deep in a story that speaks directly to their own inner thoughts. The joke acts as a welcoming front door to complex literature.

Visual style plays a big role as well—perhaps bigger than most people like to admit. The Dark Academia online trend—tweed jackets, candlelight, rainy library windows, and worn-out paperbacks—adopted Kafka and Dostoevsky as unofficial faces of the movement.

Sharing a photo of a coffee-stained copy of Crime and Punishment (1866) alongside a warm drink isn’t always just about the plot of the book. Sometimes it’s a quiet signal to the world that says: I want to slow down, and I care about deeper things than just short video clips.

Kafka’s private love letters help explain the appeal too. Letters to Milena (1952) is full of short, emotional lines that easily fit into video captions. Lines like “I am yours, even if I am not with you” look completely natural written over a moody picture online today. They offer a level of romantic vulnerability that feels refreshing in a world of quick online chats and ghosting.

Is some of this just for show? Probably. Does that make it fake? Not necessarily. It is completely possible to use literature as an online style choice and still be deeply moved by the words inside the book once you actually read them.

What stands out most is that neither writer offers easy comfort or fake happy endings. Gregor Samsa dies forgotten by his own family. Dostoevsky’s dreamer ends up more alone than when his story began. Nothing about either writer fits neatly into a social media feed built on beauty filters and forced happiness.

So, why do these century-old writers matter so much to young readers right now? In a culture, like ours, where family expectations, academic pressure, and the fast pace of city life leave very little room to feel uncertain, Kafka and Dostoevsky offer something rare: real validation. When we feel overwhelmed by high demands, strict societal goals, or the quiet loneliness of a crowded city, these books do not sell us fake comfort or easy answers. Instead, they gently remind us that feeling lost, overthinking, and searching for who you are isn’t a personal failure—it is a timeless human experience that people have been trying to make sense of for over a hundred years.

Rania Fatema Tui is a writer and master of making simple tasks complicated. Powered by iced coffee and last-minute panic, she spends 10% of her time typing, 90% staring at a blank screen, and re-reading text messages five times before sending them.
Author: R Rania Fatema Tui Rania Fatema Tui

Title: Kobitabela: a soulful afternoon
Content:
On Friday, September 5, 2026, a small crowd gathered beneath the bright summer sky, drawn together by their shared passion for poetry. Organised by Intersectional Network Bangladesh (INB) in collaboration with Circle of Sorts (CoS), Kobitabela—a poetry reading event—was hosted at the Garden Bistro, Uttara. Initiated by Asif Ahmed, guardian of CoS, Nahid Kabir, owner of Garden Bistro, and Kashfia Nahreen, founder of INB, this programme aspires to bring people together and to foster community spaces through literary events.

The programme commenced with a round of introductions, moderated by Kashfia Nahreen. 12 poets from diverse backgrounds read their expressive poems, some penned in Bangla, some in English, others blending both languages. One performer accompanied their poem on the ukulele while singing the verse. The performances underscored the significance of expanding the boundaries of traditional verse, prompting listeners to ponder the definition of poetry itself.

The concluding open-mic segment extended the programme, drawing several audience members to read their works. Two poets collaborated on an impromptu duet, captivating the audience with their verse. The evening created a space where students and professionals alike could step away from the demands of everyday life and find comfort through their shared love for creative expression.

Kashfia Nahreen is a passionate reader and writer who can be found exploring various arts and crafts while cuddling with her cats. She can be reached @the.k.atelier on instagram.
Author: K Kashfia Nahreen Kashfia Nahreen

Title: Two nights that lit Azimpur
Content:
In the Azimpur government colony of the 1970s, two occasions—Ashura and ShabeBarat—turned familiar lanes into processional corridors and classrooms of companionship.

In the government colony blocks of Azimpur, the 1970s felt like a long conversation that picked up each afternoon where we had left off the day before. We belonged not only to our own flats but to shared stairwells and open courtyards, to verandas with gossip flowing like tea, and to a playground that doubled as parliament, theatre and auditorium.

Ashura arrived with the hush of a story you don’t interrupt. The Hussaini Dalan complex lay roughly two kilometres from our colony, near enough for curiosity to tug at our sleeves. In the days leading up to the tenth of Muharram, we sometimes walked over in small groups to watch preparations: the measured fixing of banners and standards, the careful laying out of routes, the way elders explained, in low voices, the meaning of what was to come. It was a lesson given without a classroom. Even the silence of the workers felt like part of a longer recitation.

On the day itself, a grand mourning procession would emerge from Hussaini Dalan and move through the city streets. We stationed ourselves at the Salimullah Orphanage intersection, where, year after year, the procession seemed to collect and release the city’s breath. To secure a view we formed a small wedge at the front of the crowd—half strategy, half bravado—leaning forward as if those few inches would let us better understand grief carried across centuries. Chests beat in rhythm, eyes glistened, and yet the atmosphere felt protective rather than frightening, the way adults will form an invisible ring around children in a sudden rain.

If the procession supplied our solemn awe, the fair supplied our giddy hunger. The long road between the Azimpur bus stand and the graveyard would wake up like a travelling caravan, the ‘official’ oneday fair stretching, quite naturally, into a week and peaking on Ashura. It was a child’s university: you learned to bargain for toy pistols and tin cars, to press your eye to a bioscope’s small window and gasp at a parade of painted frames, to feel important holding a plastic binocular that made the world nearer by stubborn faith alone. The dhol beat from a few stalls at once as if sound itself were a banner; clay dolls sat in patient rows, their eyes permanently surprised; and a creaking nagordola—our modest Ferris wheel—climbed and descended like a lesson in bravery. Father gave me five taka and with that money I bought a bioscope and a tin car. How happy I was!

We returned home from the fair carrying a mathematics of delight. If I saved two taka on toy money here, could I add a packet of muri-murki there? If I skipped the binocular for now, would the stall still be open tomorrow? These negotiations felt like a first apprenticeship in adulthood, though our parents pretended not to notice, smiling at the way we reported our victories with straight faces. The colony community absorbed the energy of the day: khallamas compared prices as if they were recounting cricket scores; uncles developed brisk opinions about bioscope morals; neighbours tried the nagordola to show the younger ones that fear is a muscle that improves with use.

If Ashura took us into a history of courage and loss, ShabeBarat returned us to the night as a neighbour. In our colony it had a robust presence—part supplication, part streettheatre of generosity. Every home cooked halwas and sweets; ricerotis stacked high on trays seemed to multiply, as if the house itself had become a small bakery. Before the call to Magribh, families began a gentle choreography of distribution: plates travelling to the next flat and the next; portions set aside for those who slept outside our gates or simply needed the comfort of a soft, sweet bite. The flavour of the night was mercy.

But if you ask what we children looked forward to most, the answer is shamelessly simple: we were allowed to stay out all night. In groups that reshuffled like playing cards, we visited almost every mosque within walking distance, including, with a certain pride, the old Shahi Masjid of Chawkbazar. Our piety, I admit, was often a cover for adda—long conversations that circled the same topics and somehow never grew dull: the speed of a leftarm bowler, the possibility of a new cassette deck, the mystery of a classmate’s smile. We lit candles and tarabati sparklers that scribbled light on the air, our laughter briefly drowning out the night birds.

Our vigil had a ritual ending. Just before dawn we would make our way to the Tin Gambuj mosque—some three hundred metres from home—to offer Fajr. But what drew us there, alongside prayer, was an older comfort: warm tehari served on daora woven from dried jackfruit leaves. The first bite felt like a promise kept. We ate not only with our mouths but with our shoulders and eyes, borrowing warmth from each other under a sky that was just beginning to colour. By the time we emerged, the alleys were narrower, the hush clean, and the permission of the night had become a memory we could carry into algebra and homework.

Looking back, I realise how elegantly these two nights taught us about companionship. Ashura asked us to witness another community’s wound with sincerity and respect; ShabeBarat asked us to enact generosity until it felt like habit. Both made room for us, children of many flats and a few religions, to belong to a city larger than our block. The lessons were practical rather than preachy. Hold your ground at the intersection, but do not shove. Stand aside so an elder can see. Share your lanterns. Give your last halwa without counting.

We sometimes say that those days were simpler, as if simplicity were a property of the calendar. They were not. Grownups still flinched at newspaper headlines, and budgets were still a kind of puzzle. But the colony’s distances were small enough for hope to travel fast. A call from one staircase would be heard in the next; a rumour of trouble would fetch a father in sandals and a mother with a shawl around her shoulders; a plan for a midnight mosqueround would produce, from somewhere, an extra sweater for a younger cousin who insisted he was not cold.

I still picture the Hussaini Dalan preparations in the hush of late afternoon, the banners catching the smallest breeze. I still hear the bioscopeman calling out a story in a voice that had absorbed a hundred other stories. I still see the slow carousel of the nagordola tipped against the sky. On ShabeBarat I still taste a spoonful of halwa platehopped from one kitchen to the next and feel the soft warmth of tehari on daora after Fajr. When memory lines up these images like frames in a projector, the throughline is easy to read: religious in nature, secular in spirit, these occasions took private devotion and turned it into public companionship.

Azimpur taught us that a neighbourhood can be a syllabus. Ashura showed us how a people remember—out loud, together, and with beauty that does not hide pain. ShabeBarat showed us how a people feed—quietly, door to door, until nobody feels left out of the night. In the morning after, when we washed our faces and headed to school, we carried the residue of those lessons like a second skin. They have not rubbed off. Even now, all these years later, I still find myself glancing up when the air changes, as if a procession might turn the corner or a lanternline might suddenly appear, and the colony of our childhood might, for a moment, come back into view.

Ahmed Ahsanuzzaman is professor of English at Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB). He can be reached at: ahsanuzzaman@iub.edu.bd.
Author: A Ahmed Ahsanuzzaman Ahmed Ahsanuzzaman

Title: MT Hossain Institute: A fading chapter of Bangladesh’s cultural history
Content:
A crumbling building on a sprawling railway compound along Fire Service Road in Lalmonirhat town stands as a fading reminder of the region’s rich cultural history. This is the historic MT Hossain Institute, once a major cultural hub of northern Bangladesh and home to one of the Indian subcontinent’s rare revolving theatre stages.

Established in 1905 as the Pierce Institute on around 2.73 acres of railway land, the institution was renamed in 1934 after railway ticket examiner MT Hossain, whose dedication and service earned him widespread respect among railway employees.

Naming such an institution after a local railway worker during British rule was considered highly unusual, as public institutions of the time were generally named after colonial officials.

The institute’s most remarkable feature is its revolving stage, built on a circular platform with an iron rail-and-wheel mechanism that allowed scenery to be changed without lowering the curtain.

During its heyday, the institute hosted theatre productions, musical performances, poetry recitals, literary gatherings and film screenings, attracting artists and cultural figures from across the country.

Veteran playwright Advocate Chittaranjan Roy, who performed there several times, said it was once considered a prestigious venue for cultural organisations.

“I acted here many times. Today, it breaks my heart to see this historic institution reduced to a skeleton,” he said.

Cultural activist Shamim Ahmed said, “It was simultaneously a theatre, cultural centre and cinema hall. It introduced modern entertainment to the people of Lalmonirhat," he recalled.

Researchers believe the institute also played an important social and cultural role before and after Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War by fostering public awareness and strengthening community ties. However, from the 1980s onward, its activities gradually declined due to shrinking sponsored cultural programmes, the rise of television, declining public interest in theatre, inadequate funding and prolonged administrative neglect.

In 2017, a proposal to build an educational institution on the premises triggered protests from cultural activists and civil society members, eventually halting the plan. Heritage advocates have since demanded that the institute be declared a protected heritage site.

A theatre festival in 2019 and a folk festival in 2023 briefly revived activities there, but no comprehensive restoration has begun.

Architect Abeg Rahman completed an award-winning adaptive restoration proposal for the institute in 2024, documenting its historical significance and suggesting new cultural uses for the century-old building.

Sufi Mohammad, general secretary of the Sammilito Cultural Forum in Lalmonirhat, said they had been campaigning for years to revive the institute.

The Department of Archaeology says it is now working to bring the institute under its conservation programme.

As part of the initiative, the Ministry of Cultural Affairs has requested the Ministry of Railways to transfer ownership of the property before conservation work can begin, said Abu Sayeed Enam Tanvirul Islam, field officer of the department in the Rangpur Division.

Theatre historians consider the institute's revolving stage one of the last surviving historic revolving stages in South Asia, he said.

“The MT Hossain Institute was once the centre of cultural activities in northern Bangladesh. It possesses immense historical value and deserves preservation,” he added.
Author: S Dilip Roy S Dilip Roy

Title: Panam city where history still whispers
Content:
On the way to Sonargaon in Narayanganj, time seems to move backwards.

Leaving behind the bustle of the modern city, traffic congestion, and hurried lives, visitors suddenly find themselves in a quiet settlement where rows of old buildings, moss-covered walls, crumbling balconies, and shuttered windows make it feel as though history has stopped.

Once, horse-drawn carriages carrying wealthy merchants raced along its streets. Today, tourists walk those same roads through an abandoned town. The broken doors and windows of century-old buildings seem to wait for people who will never return.

Sonargaon was one of medieval Bengal’s most important commercial centres. Carrying that legacy, Panam City emerged during the 19th and early 20th centuries. Affluent Hindu merchants built their residences here, blending European colonial architecture with traditional Bangalee design.

Elegant arches, intricate ornamentation, wrought-iron balconies, and decorative windows made every mansion a marker of prosperity.

Perhaps the most striking feature of Panam City is its silence. Standing here, it feels as though even the wind speaks. Sunlight filters through cracks in old walls, weeds grow on broken staircases, and birds perch along weathered cornices, as if narrating stories from another era.

But Panam’s story is not only one of wealth. It is also a story of separation.

Following the Partition of India in 1947, residents gradually began leaving the town. After the Indo-Pakistan War of 1965, the migration of Hindu families left Panam largely deserted.

The houses that once echoed with celebrations, guests, and thriving business activities were abandoned. Over time, nature began to reclaim the city. Rainwater, tree roots, and decades of neglect have left visible scars on almost every structure.

Panam City’s main street is relatively short, yet the buildings lining both sides preserve centuries of architectural heritage. Each structure reflects a fusion of European colonial design, Mughal influences, and traditional Bengali craftsmanship.

According to Banglapedia, after the Mughals took control of Sonargaon in 1611, roads and bridges were built to connect the Panam area directly with the capital. Three brick bridges from the Mughal era still survive today: Panam Bridge, Dalalpur Bridge, and Panamnagar Bridge.

Their locations, along with the canals surrounding Panam on three sides, suggest that the area once served as a suburb of a medieval city.

Modern Panam City developed largely through the commercial activities of the British East India Company and the Permanent Settlement introduced during British rule. Sonargaon became a major trading centre for cotton textiles, particularly English “thaan” cloth, giving rise to the new urban settlement of Panam.

During the 19th century, several wealthy Hindu landlords and merchants chose the area as their residence. The brick buildings that still stand today were their homes, with the earliest structures believed to have been built in the early 19th century and later ones in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Panam continued to expand and flourish until around the end of the Second World War.

Architecturally, the residential buildings in Panam can be classified into three main types: those centred on a grand hall, those built around an open courtyard, and hybrid designs.

Hall-centred houses featured lavish decorative elements, making the central hall the architectural focal point. Courtyard houses had rooms arranged around an open, paved courtyard surrounded by verandas with arched entrances. Most single-storey houses belonged to the third category, lacking both a central hall and a courtyard.

Today, the first thing visitors notice upon entering Panam City is its extraordinary tranquility. There is no urban noise, only birdsong and the gentle rustling of leaves. That silence has become Panam’s greatest charm.

Last Friday, this correspondent spoke to a number of visitors at Panam City.

Md Anisuzzaman, a young visitor from Dhaka, said, “I’ve seen countless photographs of Panam City, but standing here is an entirely different experience. It feels like walking through history.”

Sushmita Roy, who travelled from Bandar in Narayanganj, said, “Many people don’t realise that Bangladesh has such magnificent historical sites. Coming here made me appreciate how rich our heritage truly is.”

Fazlur Rahman, who visited from Dhaka with his wife, said, “People travel abroad to explore historic cities, yet we have such an extraordinary place in our own country. If it were preserved more effectively, it could become a major attraction for international tourists.”

Local visitor Habibur Rahman, from Narayanganj, added, “I come here quite often, and every visit feels different. However, better cleanliness, more information boards, and trained guides would help visitors understand the site’s history much better.”

For many visitors, Panam City is more than a picturesque location for photography. It offers a rare chance to experience history firsthand. The weathered walls, broken wooden windows, and banyan trees growing from rooftops remind visitors that nature never leaves emptiness untouched.

The Department of Archaeology is now responsible for preserving and maintaining Panam City. Still, many visitors believe restoring the buildings alone is not enough. They said regular maintenance, scientific conservation, wider research, and improved tourist-friendly infrastructure are equally essential.

Otherwise, they fear, this historic town may continue to deteriorate.

Amirul Islam Rajib, another visitor from Dhaka, said, “There are not enough resting areas, the number of guides is limited, and there is a lack of modern digital displays or audio guides explaining the site’s history. If Panam City could be integrated with local culture, traditional cuisine, and folk arts, it could become a complete tourism destination.”

Speaking to The Daily Star, Afroza Khan Mita, Regional Director of the Department of Archaeology, said, “We have undertaken a major project to make Panam City more visitor-friendly. Once the project receives approval, we expect to introduce a range of new facilities for tourists, which will significantly increase visitor numbers.”

As plans for the site’s future are discussed, the setting sun bathes the old buildings in golden light. In those final moments of the afternoon, Panam City becomes even more mysterious.

The warm glow on the weathered brickwork creates an unforgettable atmosphere. One cannot help but imagine that, a century ago, a merchant may have returned home under this very light, children may have played along these streets, or someone may have waited for a loved one from the balcony of one of these now-silent homes.
Author: Dipan Nandy Dipan Nandy

Title: Old Dhaka’s Narinda wasn't always called Narinda!
Content:
The Puran Dhaka locality of Narinda is no ordinary area. It is home to the oldest surviving mosque in the capital: Binat Bibi’s Mosque. Established in around 1456, it stands as a strong reminder that Dhaka is much older than just 400 years as some people think.

Our city dates back to pre-Mughal times; and Narinda, with this mosque, is a testament to that.

The area is historically important for commerce. To illustrate, the pages of history shows that the English had established a factory here in circa 1735.

But the twist is that the name Narinda is technically not original, even though we have heard our fathers and grandfathers call it Narinda.

Once upon a time, Narinda was called Narayandiah, meaning, island of the Narayan deity! Over time, this evolved into Narinda, sort of a distortion of the old name Narayandiah!

Sources- "Dacca: History and Romance in Place Names" by Azimusshan Haider; “Notes on the Antiquities of Dacca" by Sayid Aulad Hasan.
Author: M M H Haider M H Haider

Title: Farashganj: The testimony of French trade in Puran Dhaka
Content:
What comes to mind when you think of Farashganj in Old Dhaka — chaos of the bazaars, loading and unloading of goods, or perhaps the elegant Northbrook Hall?

Or do you think of the French? Puran Dhaka is located thousands of kilometres away from France, but Farashganj brings it closer to us.

The word "Farash" means French and "ganj" means market, and hence, the name of the locality stands as a testimony of the French people and their businesses in Dhaka during the olden times.

In 1740, the French people had acquired permission to establish a "ganj" or market in Dhaka; the name "French Gunj" appears in a document from the year 1790.

In fact, before the famous Ahsan Manzil came into existence, the French used to have a factory in its place. Ahsan Manzil is quite near the Farashganj area.

The French had wrapped up those businesses and are long gone, but the presence they once had in our capital remains today through the name Farashganj!

Source- "Dacca: History and Romance in Place Names" by Azimusshan Haider
Author: M M H Haider M H Haider

Title: Ever wonder how the name Tikatuli came about?
Content:
Tikatuli – have you ever stopped to ponder how this curious name came to be? Probably not, because the locality is all too familiar to even pause and think about.

But that’s exactly what this series intends to do! Welcome to “Naamer Araley Dhaka,” a project where each episode will explore the origin of a neighbourhood or street name in the capital.

For this first episode, our focus is on Tikatuli.

Once to upon a time, to meet the demand of hookah-manufacturing, there was a group of artisans who used to make “tikiya” (ember or charcoal tablets). And the place of these tikiya-makers eventually came to be known as Tikatuli!

These craftspeople took their artistry to a rather high level. The products were so light and exquisite that you could light up multiple embers with just one matchstick.

A curious detail regarding all this involves one tikiya-maker. He was mockingly nicknamed “Maharani ka Beta,” meaning Queen Victoria’s son!

Of course, Tikatuli is not the only area in Dhaka that gets its name from a trade or profession. What other names spring to mind?

Keep your eyes on The Daily Star’s Facebook page, and our website, for upcoming episodes!

Source: Kingbodontir Dhaka by Nazir Hossain
Author: M M H Haider M H Haider

Title: Punashcha Dhaka: Revisiting the city’s social and cultural past
Content:
Dhaka has always been a city that returns to itself. Every alley, riverbank, and ruin seems to hold another story waiting to be rediscovered.

It is this endless wave of memories that Ridwan Akram’s book “Punashcha Dhaka: Charsha Bacharer Dhakar Samaj O Sanskriti” seeks to explore. Published by Kathaprokash, the book revisits more than 400 years of the capital’s social and cultural history, presenting Dhaka as a layered historical landscape.

The title “Punashcha Dhaka” itself announces a return. According to the author, writing about the city never truly concludes. The past often appears in small, overlooked details that have shaped Dhaka’s identity. Some stories remind us of the city’s golden past, while others trace its decline and transformation over time. Though they may sound like tales, they are rooted in history.

Akram structures the book thematically, allowing readers to explore Dhaka through different phases of its past. The chapters are arranged under sections such as Transport, Festivals, Administration, and Conflict. Through these categories, the author paints a mosaic of the city’s everyday life across centuries, its administrative structures, its cultural rhythms, and the professions and practices that once defined urban existence.

One of the book’s strengths is the historical anecdotes it brings to light. Dhaka became a Mughal provincial capital about 400 years ago, under Subahdar Islam Khan Chisti. The book revisits this period and raises curious questions about him, such as how he died in Dhaka and how his body was taken nearly 1,706 kilometres away to his final resting place.

The narrative also uncovers lesser-known chapters of the city’s history. According to the book, in 1790, foreign soldiers introduced horsecarriages for hire, marking an early chapter in public transportation in the city. The book also traces the origins of Ramna Park, which was first established during the Mughal era and has since witnessed many phases of the city’s historical transformation.

The book is complemented by historical photographs gathered from a variety of archival sources. Many come from the British Library’s collection, while others have been sourced from other repositories. These images add a visual dimension to the narratives, helping readers imagine the city’s transformations across time.

Speaking about the book, Akram emphasises the responsibility that comes with writing history. “Books live through detailed work, proper research and readers,” he explains. According to him, the task of a historical work is not only to document facts, but also to create a meaningful connection with its readers.

The author also notes that the history of Dhaka exists in pieces scattered across different sources. His effort, he says, was to gather those pieces together. “The history might be here and there, but I took the initiative to collect them,” he shares, adding that the work involved large-scale interviews and consultation with legitimate sources.

At the same time, Akram believes that historical writing must offer something fresh. “A book should give readers the taste of something new, something they may never have heard before.”

In fact, Punashcha Dhaka is not the result of a single period of writing. Rather, it is a compilation of his essays and research gathered over many years. “I did not write this in one sitting,” the author explains. “It is a collection that began many years ago, bringing together many of my writings about Dhaka’s history in one place.”

In that sense, Punashcha Dhaka works both as a collection of history and an invitation to rediscover the city. By bringing together archival sources, stories, and research, Ridwan Akram reminds readers that beneath Dhaka’s busy present lies a rich past that still echoes through its streets.
Author: J Jawwad Sami Neogi Jawwad Sami Neogi

Title: Rose Garden: a palace where legacy blooms
Content:
Hidden within the bustling alleys in Old Dhaka’s Tikatuli lies a regal architectural gem -- the Rose Garden.

Built in the early 20th century, the palace that once reflected an elite lifestyle now carries the scent of history, the echoes of political discourse, and the essence of cultural heritage.

Located on KM Das Lane, the Rose Garden now stands as a preserved heritage site and public entertainment centre.

The estate features an elegant white marble mansion exuding Greek architectural style, white marble sculptures, a field with an artificial fountain at the centre, a pond with a paved bank, and a lush green garden with rows of rose bushes, creating a mesmerising ambience of grandeur.

The ground floor of the palace consists of eight rooms, all currently closed. On the upper floor, four of the five rooms are open to visitors. Along the wooden staircase to the second floor, there are colourful glass designs that make the palace come alive in a play of light and shadow.

The palace features a large hall, which was once the ballroom, with every corner intricately adorned and the ceiling featuring chandeliers that are still ready to shine.

On one side of the palace is the Bengal Studio, where the Bangladeshi film “Harano Din” was shot.

Every day, a host of local and foreign visitors visit the Rose Garden.

Shiuly Akter, a visitor, said, “The architecture of old houses and palaces always fascinates me. The Rose Garden is not just a palace. As I entered, I felt as if I were standing as a witness to time. Its serene beauty is enchanting. If anyone ever seeks tranquillity, history, and beauty, then an afternoon visit to the Rose Garden is highly recommended.”

Rajnin Farhana, another visitor, said, “I heard about the palace since it reopened. A number of my friends visited earlier and posted photos on social media. Now I came to visit the palace and take a lot of photos.”

Monowar Hossain, a local resident, said, “I was born and brought up in this area. The Rose Garden is the symbol of pride not only for our locality but for the whole country.”

The story of Rose Garden begins during the British era in 1931, when Rishikesh Das, a nouveau riche businessman, constructed the mansion.

Once, after being humiliated at a cultural gathering at Baldha Garden, Rishikesh decided to host his own events at a grand garden house. Due to the abundance of rose bushes, the estate was named “Rose Garden”.

However, before the decoration of the building could be completed, Rishikesh went bankrupt and had to sell the property in 1937 to Khan Bahadur Abdur Rashid. The mansion was then renamed “Rashid Manzil”.

Later, it came under the ownership of Kazi Mohammad Bashir (popularly known as Humayun Saheb) and subsequently to Kazi Abdur Rakib and his wife Laila Rakib.

The mansion is deeply entwined with Bangladesh’s political history. Following the Partition of India, many significant political meetings were held here, including the first informal meeting to establish the East Pakistan Awami Muslim League in 1949. Numerous renowned politicians and leaders from Bangladesh and India were hosted here.

In 1966, the property was leased to Bengal Studio. In 1993, the Rashid family regained ownership. In 2018, the Government of Bangladesh acquired the property for Tk 331 crore.

After 2022, the building was restored and reopened on July 30 last year. Now, visitors can enter the building from 11:00am till 6:00pm. It remains fully closed on Sundays. On Mondays, it remains open partially from 2:00pm to 6:00pm. Entry tickets are priced at Tk 30 for regular visitors and Tk 10 for students each.

Afroza Khan Mita, regional director of the Department of Archaeology, said the Rose Garden has seen a steady stream of local and foreign visitors since its reopening.

“In August and September last year alone, we earned a total of Tk 17 lakh from ticket sales. Clearly, there is immense public interest. The site offers Dhaka residents a peaceful retreat while also contributing to government revenue,” she said.
Author: Dipan Nandy Sukanta Halder Dipan Nandy and Sukanta Halder

Title: Decay threatens 250-yr-old Lalmonirhat mosque
Content:
Worshippers at Nidaria Jame Mosque, a protected 18th-century monument in Lalmonirhat, are facing safety risks as parts of the boundary wall and a tin-shed veranda remain in a fragile condition due to a lack of renovation.

Declared a protected archaeological monument in 1994 by the Department of Archaeology, the over 250-year-old mosque at Kismat Nagarband village under Panchgram union has seen little visible repair work in recent years, locals and mosque authorities said.

They urged the immediate need for steps to ensure safe prayer facilities while preserving the historic structure.

According to the Department of Archaeology, the three-domed mosque was built in 1762 by Mansur Khan, son of Masud Khan, as indicated by a Persian inscription engraved on a black stone on the front wall.

The rectangular structure features octagonal corner towers and three mihrabs on the western wall, reflecting Mughal-era architectural style.
