Locals said the main structure has remained largely unchanged since its construction and has not undergone significant renovation for many years.

The boundary wall is now at risk of collapse, while a tin-shed veranda built beside the mosque is being supported with bamboo poles.

Due to limited space inside the mosque, many worshippers offer prayers on the veranda, which becomes unusable even during light rain, they said.

Hossain Ali, general secretary of the mosque committee, said the mosque cannot undertake any renovation work independently, as it is a protected monument.

“Since the mosque is under the Department of Archaeology, we cannot carry out development work on our own. We are communicating with the authorities concerned,” he said.

Imam Fazlul Karim said the mosque is architecturally significant, with thick walls and high domes giving it a distinctive character.

“Visitors from different parts of the country come here every day. Many of them offer prayers,” he said, adding that the committee has been urged repeatedly to improve facilities.

Abidur Rahman, a college teacher from Sirajganj who recently visited the site, said, “I have offered prayers in the historic mosque. The veranda and boundary wall require urgent renovation to ensure safety for worshippers.”

Contacted, Abu Sayeed Inam Tanvirul, field officer of the Rangpur divisional office of the Department of Archaeology, said any development work must follow the department’s guidelines to protect the monument’s original features.

“If the mosque committee wants to renovate the walls or veranda, they should contact us formally. We will provide the necessary guidance and assistance,” he said, adding that preservation of the heritage structure must remain the priority.
Author: S Dilip Roy S Dilip Roy

Title: Your complete map to Bangladesh’s most iconic Mughal mosques
Content:
Our country is blessed with beautiful mosques. Be it the Sultanate era mosques or the modern marvels, Bangladesh is dotted with these awe-inspiring places of worship that span many centuries. Among them, Mughal mosques are indeed an interesting chapter of our heritage.

In this holy month of Ramadan, Star Lifestyle presents to you a map of Bangladesh's prominent Mughal mosques — your essential list of mosques from this era that you should definitely visit.

We invite you to see this map, which took us about a month to create, and we invite you to visit these age-old buildings.

Along with the map, this article will give an idea about our research journey, providing you with more insights than just names and geography.

Mughal mosques combine to form a rich time capsule, but which timeframe are we really looking into?

According to the book Mosque Architecture in Bangladesh, by Dr Abu Sayeed M Ahmed and Syed Zakir Hossain, Bengal was "conquered by Mughal rulers" in 1576. So, that is the beginning.

On the other hand, we can cut off the Mughal era at 1757 if we are very strict — an obvious year, due to the Empire's collapse surrounding the Battle of Palashi that was led by Nawab Sirajuddaula against the British.

Of course, the timeframe is up for debate. To exemplify, it can be stretched to 1857, and rightly so, because there was resistance to the "new" British East India Company regime. Nazly Chowdhury and Babu Ahmed wrote in Mughal Monuments of Bangladesh, "In 1857, the Sepoy Revolt broke out but was soon suppressed by iron hands... and the rule of the Mughals in India was finally ended."

Neither the beginning nor the end of the Mughal era happened overnight.

Given this context, even though we kept in mind the 1576-1757 time period, we prioritised those mosques that are the most Mughal-inclined in terms of architecture, reputation, etc., hence allowing flexibility for a few mosques that were likely established after the 1757 milestone.

We will spare you the technicalities and details, leaving them for architects and historians. It is best to visit the mosques in person to appreciate it. And now, you have the map to guide you there!

Three-domed structures are common, although variations regarding the number of domes can also be easily found. Facades are decorative. Four corner turrets (or small towers) reinforce elegance. Inside, cusped arches, floral motifs, and views of the domes above your head will strike a chord in your heart!

However, it is saddening that many mosques of that era underwent mindless paintjobs, addition of tiles, extensions, etc. in modern times. Where such cases were severe, we dropped them out of our list.

In some cases, old structures have more or less been completely replaced by modern ones. For such mosques, the only major Mughal connection is in the collective memory of locals, history books, or the dates on the signboards. We have not included those buildings in our map as well.

Furthermore, there are several mosques that locals believe to be Mughal, but that fact cannot be ascertained from inscriptions (or lack thereof), architecture, or books of history. We have dropped most of those as well.

Therefore, this map indicates the most prominent ones that are worth visiting for the budding history buff.

You may be furious to see that very few number of mosques from the Dhaka district have made it to our map. Well, control your rage, and look at the disclaimer at the bottom of the map: Old Dhaka is home to so many magnificent Mughal-era mosques that it was not possible for us to fit them all: Haji Khwaja Shahbaz Mosque, Khan Muhammad Mirdha Mosque, Khwaja Ambar Mosque, and Begum Bazar Mosque are some of the names that have every right to be included in the map, and being history buffs ourselves, our hearts ached for this compromise.

Dhaka division posed another head-scratcher. This one had to do with the Mymensingh division. Curiously enough, this division is empty in our map! After consulting credible sources, we believe that Mymensingh's prominent mosques that are irrefutably Mughal in style, architecture, date, etc. are from the so-called "Greater Mymensingh" region, which includes places like Kishoreganj and Tangail; but in present times, they officially fall under Dhaka division!

Overcoming the many challenges throughout this journey, we have finally come up with this map. We hope it encourages you to visit the mosques and stir up conversations about the rich heritage the Mughals have left us.

Sources: Mosque Architecture in Bangladesh by Dr Abu Sayeed M Ahmed and Syed Zakir Hossain; Mughal Monuments of Bangladesh by Nazly Chowdhury and Babu Ahmed; Mosques of Bangladesh by Nymphea Publication; Banglapedia; Bangladesh government websites; UNESCO's Tentative List of "Mughal Mosques in Bangladesh".

Special thanks to Sazzadur Rasheed, architect, academician, and admin of Save the Heritages of Bangladesh for providing valuable inputs to our project. We are also grateful to The Daily Star's Habiganj and Moulvibazar correspondent Mintu Deshwara, and Sheikh Nasir, Sylhet photographer for their help in our research.
Author: M M H Haider J Jawwad Sami Neogi A Ashif Ahmed Rudro M H Haider , Jawwad Sami Neogi , and Ashif Ahmed Rudro

Title: Nawabganj: Where heritage meets harmony
Content:
A crumbling mansion rises unexpectedly along the main road of Kolakopa Union in Nawabganj, Dhaka, its grand pillars still holding their ground against time. Just an hour and a half from the capital, the riverside estate on the banks of the Ichamati is more than a relic. It is a window into centuries of wealth, memory and local legend.

This is the Kokil Pyari Zamindar Bari, a neoclassical marvel now abandoned but impossible to ignore. Its towering pillars and intricate carvings still catch the eye, even as the building succumbs to neglect.

After the zamindari system ended in 1950, the mansion served as a residence for teachers of Kokil Pyari High School. Locals recall that six to seven families once lived there. On closer inspection, the walls reveal faint sculptures, including one of Venus, the Roman goddess of love, beauty and prosperity.

Yet the history of Kokil Pyari is as layered as the walls themselves.

Who was Kokil Pyari? Locals offer two accounts.

Braj Niketan, now known as Judge Bari. Photo: Star

According to one version, Kokil Pyari was a descendant of the Bhagya Kul Zamindars of Bikrampur, who founded this estate. Around 200 years ago, Yadunath Roy acquired the zamindari from the British. He was related by blood to Radharaman Roy, the mansion’s builder. Both Yadunath Roy and Radharaman Roy were merchants, trading areca nuts, salt and saris from Barishal to Kolkata and Murshidabad.

Another account says that in the 18th century, a wealthy businessman named Brajen Roy, also known as Sudarshan Roy, constructed the mansion. Surrounded by a garden, the mansion, built with brick, lime and rods, was originally called Braj Niketan. Over time, ownership changed hands, first to an oil trader and later to a judge, which led to the mansion also being referred to as the Telibari (Oil House) and the Judge’s House.

The 500-yard premises of Kokil Pyari Zamindarbari include a Buddhist temple, the house of Shriloknath Saha, Kolakopa Ansar Camp, Ukilbari, Dasbari, Adnan Palace and the Ichamati river. Many believe all these structures were once part of the original estate.

Unofficial sources suggest that Kokil Pyari had five sons. He left his main house to his youngest son and built four additional houses for the remaining sons.

Within the premises stand two memorial shrines. After Zamindar Kokil Pyari died, his son Radharaman Roy built a shrine in the Bangalee year 1334 in memory of his father. Later, he built another shrine in memory of his mother. Both shrines originally housed sculptures of his parents. Locals say that during the Liberation War, the mother’s sculpture disappeared and the head of the father’s statue was broken. The sculptures were reportedly imported from Europe.

Adjacent to Kokil Pyari Zamindarbari is Braj Niketan, now known as the Judge’s House. Locals say that around 200 years ago, in the 18th century, wealthy businessman Brajen Roy built it as his residence. Its five elaborately decorated pillars, adorned with pieces of precious glass, immediately draw attention. Eight large windows and a central grand veranda add to its imposing appearance. Surrounded by a garden of diverse trees, the Judge’s House still carries a sense of the world it once belonged to.

Moving along the narrow road to the right of Kokil Pyari Zamindarbari, one encounters Telibari, also called Mothbari, by the riverbank. It is currently used as an Ansar and VDP camp and houses 17 Ansar Battalion members. According to local lore, it was once owned by an oil trader named Loknath, hence the name Telibari.

Telibari now being used as an Ansar camp.

Next along the riverbank is a structure called Painna Bari, said to have belonged to Madhubabu, who became wealthy by selling toddy (palm wine). Its walls are adorned with intricate carvings, and the house sprawls across a large area.

Galib Rahman Khan, a banker with extensive knowledge of Nawabganj’s history, said, “The buildings in Kolakopa are all late-colonial, dating from the late 1800s to the early 1900s. None of them were zamindar houses. They belonged to prominent businessmen, some traded in oil, others in salt or betel leaves. Most of these houses were abandoned after the Partition of the country.”

To the right along the road lies a two-storey mansion on the edge of a large pond, believed to have been built in the late 19th century. The ground floor houses several dark rooms. The building features nine domes resembling granary roofs, with the central dome being the largest. Some locals refer to this as Khelaram’s Vigrah Mandir or Khelaram Datar Kotha.

According to Syed Nurul Islam, a septuagenarian who lives nearby, “Khelaram was called a donor because he supposedly robbed from the rich and distributed among the poor. There was an underground passage from the mansion to the Ichamati river, which he used.” Towards the end of his life, he reportedly became devout.

However, Galib said, “There are many stories and myths about Khelaram Dutta’s Kotha. Putting those aside, documented history shows that it is a late Mughal-era temple, built by Khelaram Dutta himself.”

Across Kolakopa village, other old structures remain, each carrying its own story. On entering, the Shri Shri Mahamaya Mandir, built in Bangalee year 1315, stands out, where rituals are still conducted. Nearby, an old house is now home to the Mitra family, whose forebear was once a timber trader. Legend says he struggled to unload a piece of timber from a boat and was guided in a dream to bring it home, leading to the start of a worship practice centred on the timber. Locals believe dreams about it still occur.

In Baktar Nagar, Shikaripara Union, another zamindar house, Ata Khan’s Zamindarbari, is visible from across the road. The second-storey building, though now ruined, still shows the outlines of its past. Plaster has fallen away, and large banyan trees grow through the brickwork. Doors and windows are missing, and the structure appears precarious. Locals call it Sab Bari or Shaheb Bari. A mosque stands nearby.

Based on the mosque’s construction style, Professor AKM Shahnawaz of the Department of Archaeology at Jahangirnagar University said the buildings likely date to the Mughal era, though exact dates remain uncertain.

Galib, however, said a stone inscription at the mosque’s main gate shows that a woman, Foyzunnesa, built it in 1870 after inheriting the zamindari from her aunt, Janab Hasina. This suggests the mansion was likely built around the same time.

On Nawabganj’s architectural history, archaeologist Dr Shahnawaz said these settlements were established in the late 18th century, primarily by Hindu merchants who built multiple palatial residences along the Ichamati for habitation and for trade convenience. “Kolakopa and Bandura in Nawabganj are highly traditional and historically significant areas. These landmarks are important archaeologically,” he said.

Nawabganj is not only known for old architecture, but also for a tradition of communal harmony. Alongside temples and mosques, the area has several historic churches. In Hasnabad village of Bandura stands one of the most striking, Our Lady of Holy Rosary Church.

Hubert Joseph Gomes, principal of St Joseph Tutorial in Hasnabad, said, “It is the fifth church in undivided Bengal, built in 1777 by priest Raphael Gomez. It was renovated first in 1888 and again in 2002.”

“Over 1,700 Christian families live in Nawabganj. People of all religions have lived here peacefully and harmoniously for generations,” he added.
Author: Sakib Ahmed Sakib Ahmed

Title: Mymensingh a land of stories, songs and untapped tourism
Content:
With nearly 250 years of history behind it, Mymensingh stands quietly as one of Bangladesh’s most culturally rich regions, yet remains largely underexplored.

From the flowing Brahmaputra to the green hills of Haluaghat and Dhobaura, the district offers a rare blend of natural beauty, folk heritage and historical depth that could easily place it on the country’s tourism map.

The spirit of Mymensingh lives in its stories and songs. The renowned Mymensingh Geetika, rural fairs, folk music and age-old traditions continue to shape the region’s identity.

Landmarks such as the Zainul Abedin Sangrahashala, the Bangladesh Agricultural University (BAU) campus, Shashi Lodge, Gouripur Rajbari and Nazrul-related heritage sites reflect a long legacy of art, literature and education.

Qutub Shah Mosque in Kishoreganj

“The region is well known for its rich history, unique folk culture and natural beauty, but continues to face multiple limitations despite strong prospects of becoming a full-fledged tourism city,” said tourism researcher and development expert Sajal Quraishi.

“The art gallery has the capacity to attract international tourists. The BAU campus itself is a major tourist destination. Its vast area, botanical garden, germplasm centre and agricultural museum can serve as research hubs for students,” he said.

“Local foods such as the famous Muktagarha Monda also have huge potential for food tourism.”

Imtiaz Ahmed, member secretary of the Archaeological Preservation Committee of Mymensingh region, said the city, known for art and culture, was established in 1787. Despite being a 238-year-old district with immense tourism potential, the sector has not flourished due to a lack of proper initiatives and planning.

Although the region is home to many attractive locations, tourists remain largely unaware of them, he said. There are 11 officially declared archaeological heritage sites in the district, yet the present generation knows very little about their history.

According to government and archaeology department sources, major attractions in the district town include Shashi Lodge, Mymensingh Museum, Alexander Castle, Gouripur Lodge, Raj Rajeshwari Water Works and Bipin Park. Other sites include the Independence Monument; the Old Brahmaputra River and its adjacent Zainul Uddhyan; Nazrul Memorial Centres, Jatiya Kabi Kazi Nazrul Islam University and Bailor Zamindar Bari in Trishal; Atani Zamindar Bari, Maharaja Suryakanta’s residence and century-old temples in Muktagarha; Gouripur Rajbari, Birangana Sakhina’s Mazar and Ramgopalpur Zamindar Bari; pineapple and rubber gardens and Borovila Beel in Phulbaria; Kadigarh National Park and a crocodile farm in Bhaluka; Gabrakhali Park and the Ethnic Cultural Academy in Haluaghat; china clay hills in Dhobaura; language martyr Abdul Jabbar Memorial Museum in Gafargaon; and the Atarobari Zamindar Bari in Ishwarganj, a palace once visited by Rabindranath Tagore.

Kacharibari in Ishwarganj

Archaeological researcher Swapan Dhar described Mymensingh as a pilgrimage of folk culture, festivals, music and legends. He said the region’s cultural heritage has made significant contributions at both national and international levels.

The stories of Mahua, Malua, Chandrabati, Dewana Madina Pala, Kamala, Dewan Bhavna, Dasyu Kenaram and Kajolrekha from Mymensingh Geetika are highly admired in world literature, he said, adding that sites associated with these folk epics could offer a unique experience for tourists.

Dhar said greater Mymensingh could emerge as a major tourism hub, as the wider region includes many tourism-rich locations. These include the Someshwari River, china clay hills, Birishiri Tribal Cultural Academy, Chandradinga waterfalls, Komola Rani’s Dighi, Dingapota Haor, Tonk Shaheed Memorial and Ranikong Mission in Netrakona; Madhutila Eco Park, Pone Tin Ani Zamindar Bari, Gajni Abokash Kendra, Raja’s Hill and Panihata-Tarani Hills in Sherpur; Jangalbari Fort, Egarosindur Fort, Sholakia Eidgah, Pagla Mosque, Shahidi Mosque, Qutub Shah Mosque and Taljanga Zamindar Bari in Kishoreganj; and Gandhiji Ashram, Hazrat Shah Jamal (R) Shrine, Zeal Bangla Sugar Mills and Dayamoyee Temple in Jamalpur.

“Besides Poune Tin Ani Zamindar Palace, the district also has Tin Ani Zamindar Palace, Araiani Zamindar Palace and Nayani Zamindar Palace, all enriched with architectural heritage and local history. A historic mosque in Sherpur could also draw the attention of thousands of tourists to the frontier district, known for its greenery and hillocks,” said Hakim Babul, a senior journalist in Sherpur.

However, the buildings are in a pitiable state. All archaeological sites should be protected from further decay, as the palaces reflect the history and tradition of the district, said Babul, also convener of the citizen platform Jonouddhog Sherpur.

The architectural features of the palaces, including wide steps and decorated columns, reflect Greek architectural influence, he added.

Kishoreganj, too, holds strong potential to rise as a tourist zone. The Qutub Shah Mosque, a 16th-century structure built by Hazrat Qutub Shah (R), is one of the district’s most significant archaeological landmarks. A shrine of Qutub Shah (R) is attached to the five-domed mosque.

The district has developed through a blend of ancient and modern architectural traditions.

SK Rasel, a young journalist in Kishoreganj, said besides the mosque, many antiquities in the district have been listed by the Department of Archaeology.

These include Qutub Shah Mosque, Harshi Mosque, the memorial temples of poet Dwijbangshi Das and poet Chandrabati, Isha Khan’s Palace in Jangalbari, Shadi Mosque, Shah Mahmud Mosque, Saheb Bari (Sekandarnagar) Mosque and Gurui Mosque.

Locals have repeatedly demanded better preservation of these sites, he said, noting that they are among the strongest symbols of the district’s history and tradition.

Experts point to the absence of coordinated planning, limited promotion and slow conservation efforts as major obstacles. Many archaeological and cultural treasures remain unknown even to domestic travellers.

Tourism researchers and cultural activists believe a comprehensive tourism master plan, combined with heritage conservation, river dredging and private investment, could transform Mymensingh into a leading destination for cultural and eco-tourism.

Despite its promise, tourism in this culturally rich region remains largely untapped.

Mymensingh Deputy Commissioner Md Saifur Rahman said efforts are underway to develop tourism in the district.

Sherpur zamindar palace

With the cooperation of the Department of Archaeology, initiatives will be taken to develop heritage and historically significant structures, he said.

Sabina Yeasmin, field officer of the Department of Archaeology for Dhaka and Mymensingh, said the region has many ancient and historical structures that could be highly attractive to tourists if properly preserved and promoted.
Author: M Md Aminul Islam Md Aminul Islam

Title: How one family keeps the 'Tepa Putul' tradition alive
Content:
Rag dolls made from tattered saris and handmade clay dolls called tepa putul were once the few tangible belongings young girls in rural Bangladesh ever had.

Silt and clay collected from riverbeds, along with scraps found around their homesteads, were the materials village children used to craft their own toys. They kept them with utmost care in shoeboxes or rusted tin containers.

But these are stories of once upon a time. Today, the face of toys has changed, and with it, the fate of traditional toys and crafts.

With imported culture flooding the market and the aggressive rise of plastic products, even village shelves are now filled with mass-produced items.

These seemingly insignificant clay dolls, tepa putul, once found across pastoral Bangladesh, along with other artisanal items, have now become part of our lost craft heritage.

I met Subodh Kumar Pal, a tepa putul artisan, at an upmarket fair in Dhaka last year. Since then, I have followed his work, and he eventually took me to his village, Boshontopur Palpara in Rajshahi.

I am fascinated by heritage and folk keepsakes, and tepa putul is one cultural legacy I want to hold on to. Crafted by pressing raw clay with fingertips, dried in the sun, and then fired, tepa putul derives its name from the Bengali words tepa (pressing) and putul (doll), a nod to its simple finger-moulding process.

Figures of a mother and child, brides and grooms, farming families, or deities make up these rustic dolls. Unpainted and adorned only with ornamental clay markings, they are fine specimens of Bengal's folk artistry.

These crafts are not only cultural markers but also vital to the livelihoods of artisan communities.

Subodh's small family -- his son Shojib Kumar Pal and wife Bijli Rani Pal -- is the only one in Rajshahi still making tepa putul.

There are other potter families in the village, but each specialises in a different traditional craft. His neighbour, for instance, only makes Shoker er Hari or Hobby pots, decorative vessels used to store food or carry sweets during weddings and rituals.

Subodh, however, carries the torch for clay dolls. Bijli Rani has been making traditional clay dolls for 18 years and insists the craft requires a joyful mind.

"To do this kind of work, your mind must be in a good place. If the heart is heavy, the work won't turn out well. You must keep yourself happy," she says.

Her journey into mrit shilpo, the art of clay crafts, was shaped by her husband's family. Her father was a doll maker as well, though her mother never practised the craft. Bijli embraced it after marriage, continuing a fragile lineage of artisans.

An intricate doll can take two to three days to finish, while smaller ones are often made in batches of eight or ten over two days.

"The dolls that require painstaking work are priced at Tk 100 to Tk 400 depending on size, and Tk 3,000 to Tk 5,000 for the large ones. But profits are limited. People don't want to pay much for these delicate items. Only collectors who value heritage pay their true worth. Most prefer cheaper products," Subodh says.

In Rajshahi, only one family continues the craft; in Tangail, Somodarani Pal keeps it alive; in Kishoreganj, Sunil Pal does the same. Bijli says only a handful of artisans remain, though perhaps some practise quietly elsewhere. The tradition is on the verge of disappearance.

HAND-CRAFTING THEIR SURVIVAL PLAN

Sales in Subodh's village are modest, so the family relies on fairs in Dhaka, Sylhet, and government-sponsored exhibitions.

"I am gearing up for Independence Day, the Zainul Mela, and other fairs in Dhaka this December. These events are essential for our survival," he says.

Bijli and Subodh express deep gratitude to the organisers of the Zainul Mela and the Charukala (Fine Arts) authorities, who offer food, lodging, respect, and excellent sales opportunities – almost a lifeline for niche crafts.

"They value us the most. Without such fairs, our craft would have gone extinct years ago," they say.

"If Charukala stops including clay dolls in their fairs, we will lose everything," Bijli warns.

The challenges facing mrit shilpo are many. The widespread use of plastic for household items has eroded the market for clay products. Cooking pots, bowls, plates, and even matir chari – large clay tubs used for feeding cattle – have all been replaced by plastic alternatives.

Clay items are becoming rare, and their value is diminishing.

The financial strain on artisans remains a pressing issue. It takes almost three days of labour to complete one large doll. Every step is done by hand – moulding, polishing, finishing, and designing – and even collecting raw clay requires effort. River silt, once freely available, now requires payment to collect.

Most potters work independently, stocking items for yearly fairs, which remain their primary income source. Commissioned orders are rare. This raises the hard questions: how do they manage daily expenses, or pay helpers?

"The truth is, if I don't work, I don't eat. Courier services refuse to take responsibility for fragile clay items, which limits distribution and our income," Subodh says.

Clay crafts require time and artistic freedom. Electric wheels may help with larger items like pitchers or tubs, but they cannot replace the artisan's touch. Delicate work still relies entirely on hand finishing and creative insight.

Tepa putul is more than craftwork; it is a heritage skill passed down through generations. Subodh showed me an archetype of the first tepa putul made by his great-great-grandfather. The red-fired clay figure had only a pressed outline and simple dots for eyes. Over generations, intricate designs were added, shaping the doll we recognise today.

Subodh believes his son will eventually add his own creativity to this age-old tradition.

The story of Subodh and Bijli is emblematic of Bangladesh's endangered mrit shilpo. Their words reflect resilience and vulnerability. They reveal a devotion to craft despite low margins, cultural neglect, and systemic obstacles.

This tradition is sustained by festivals, a fragile network of artisans, and the stubborn persistence of those who refuse to let crafts like tepa putul vanish.

It is a way of life rooted in joy, patience, and heritage. Unfortunately, its future is threatened by rapid urbanisation and the social turmoil of the present.
Author: Raffat Binte Rashid Raffat Binte Rashid

Title: ‘Support comes from unexpected places’: Badhan reflects on Venice ordeal
Content:
Actor Azmeri Haque Badhan has reflected on the difficult experience she faced in Venice and expressed gratitude to those who stood by her after she was allegedly assaulted while attending the Venice International Film Festival.

In a Facebook post on Thursday night, Badhan wrote, “When life puts you through difficult times, always remember that something beautiful may be waiting for you on the other side.”

Reflecting on the experience, the “Rehana Maryam Noor” actor wrote, “What a long journey it has been! A journey filled with difficult moments — humiliation, harassment, physical assault and even the feeling of being abandoned by my own people. But through it all, I realised a profound truth: sometimes the greatest support comes from the most unexpected places.”

Badhan thanked the governments of Bangladesh and Italy, the Bangladesh Embassy in Italy, Italian police and the festival authorities for standing by her during the ordeal.

“When I needed help and support the most, you stood by me,” she wrote.

The actor said that when some of those close to her distanced themselves, the institutions and individuals who came forward became important sources of strength and protection.

She also expressed her gratitude to everyone who supported her, checked on her, prayed for her or simply offered words of kindness.

“I love you all,” Badhan concluded.

Badhan travelled to Italy to attend the screening of Rubaiyat Hossain’s “The Difficult Bride” at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival.

She alleged that she was physically assaulted by a group of individuals while visiting a local park with her brother and his family on Monday night, September 7. According to Badhan, some of those involved identified themselves as supporters of the Awami League.

Following the incident, the Bangladesh Embassy and local authorities extended assistance to the actor. The alleged assault also prompted expressions of protest and support for Badhan from people in Bangladesh and abroad.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: ‘One Piece’, ‘Dragon Ball’ voice actor Mike McFarland dies at 56
Content: American voice actor, writer and director Mike McFarland, best known for voicing Buggy the Clown in “One Piece” and Master Roshi in “Dragon Ball”, died on September 9. He was 56. McFarland died after battling glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. He was diagnosed with the disease in 2025, according to Anime News Network. McFarland was one of the early and influential figures in Texas-based anime production. He began his career with Funimation and later continued his work with Crunchyroll following the companies’ merger. “Mike brought so much to all of us who knew him, and to all of the anime fans that knew his work. He was an incredible talent, a good friend to so many of us, and will be sorely, sorely missed,” Crunchyroll said in a statement to Deadline. McFarland voiced Buggy the Clown in “One Piece” from 2007 until his death. He also voiced Master Roshi and Yajirobe in “Dragon Ball” and “Dragon Ball Z”. His other notable roles included Jean Kirstein in “Attack on Titan”, Jean Havoc in “Fullmetal Alchemist” and Teppei Sugo in “Psycho-Pass”. He also voiced Makoto Hyuga in the “Evangelion” film series, Sky Master in “Heaven’s Lost Property”, Goemon Ishikawa in “Lupin III: The Woman Called Fujiko Mine” and George in “Case Closed”. His more recent credits included Hiroshi Odokawa in “Odd Taxi”, Big Bad Wolf in “Date A Live IV” and E G Mine in “Trigun Stampede”.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Documentary on Gaza killings gets 25 minute ovation at Venice Film Festival
Content:
If last year’s Venice Film Festival spotlighted "The Voice of Hind Rajab", this year’s edition has turned its attention to "NAZA", a documentary exploring the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

Directed by Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the film received an overwhelmingly positive response following its premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday.

According to AFP, "NAZA" received a 25-minute standing ovation after the screening, reportedly setting a new record at the festival. The audience continued applauding the directing duo, surpassing the 23-minute ovation given to "The Voice of Hind Rajab" last year. The docu-drama tells the story of the killing of a five-year-old Palestinian girl by Israeli forces.

Earlier, as Abraham and Szor walked the red carpet towards the screening venue, spectators could be heard chanting both "Free Palestine!" and "Free Israel!" The strong response has positioned "NAZA" as a frontrunner for Venice’s top prize.

"The Voice of Hind Rajab" was similarly considered a favourite for the festival’s top award last year after receiving an enthusiastic response. However, it ultimately won the festival’s second prize, amid reports of divisions among the jury.

For years, the length of a standing ovation has been regarded as an indicator of a film’s reception at major international film festivals. AFP noted that while such ovations can be manipulated, they can still offer an insight into the impact a film has on festival audiences and critics.

"NAZA" features testimonies from 24 Israeli military insiders, including intelligence officers and soldiers, who describe their experiences during the war in Gaza and what they allege was the systematic killing of Palestinian civilians.

The film was shot secretly over three years on rooftops across Tel Aviv. The identities of those interviewed have been concealed through digital alterations to their voices and appearances.

Speaking at a press conference in Venice on Thursday, Abraham said the filmmakers primarily asked the Israeli officers and soldiers to describe in detail what they had done.

"Of course, there were other questions that arose, but the principal question was a question of detail — sketch it for us, we want to know how it worked," he said. "And sometimes just asking the question, you get answers."

The film’s title refers to an Israeli military acronym used as shorthand for civilian casualties, including men, women and children.

"NAZA" builds on investigations published between 2023 and 2025 by Israeli-Palestinian magazine 972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.

At the Venice press conference, Szor also addressed the filmmakers’ decision to make a documentary based on information that had already been reported and published.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Dhallywood’s formidable villain: Revisiting ATM Shamsuzzaman’s memorable television roles
Content:
For many, ATM Shamsuzzaman remains synonymous with the formidable antagonists he portrayed in Dhallywood. Over the course of his career, he played numerous negative roles on the silver screen, earning immense affection from audiences. During his lifetime, he received several honours, including the Ekushey Padak and the National Film Award for Lifetime Achievement.

Beyond cinema, however, Shamsuzzaman also left his mark on television, appearing in numerous dramas that earned him widespread appreciation.

Today, September 10, marks his birth anniversary. On the occasion, we look back at some of his memorable performances on television.

One of them was the immensely popular long-running series “Ronger Manush”, jointly written by Selim Al Deen and Masum Reza and directed by Salahuddin Lavlu. Shamsuzzaman played Bostani Shah, a character that became a favourite among viewers. Just as audiences remember the series, Bostani Shah remains one of its most memorable characters.

Another popular series was “Vober Hat”, written by Masum Reza and directed by Salahuddin Lavlu. The drama notably brought Shamsuzzaman and Humayun Faridi face-to-face in a major television serial. Shamsuzzaman portrayed Marem Khan, delivering a memorable performance.

He also drew attention for his role in Mir Sabbir’s long-running series “Noashal”, in which he delivered his dialogues in the Noakhali dialect.

In the widely acclaimed drama “Noiboch Noiboch”, Shamsuzzaman played an idealistic teacher navigating the joys, sorrows, frustrations and disappointments of life. One particularly emotional moment, in which the teacher is humiliated by a student, moved many viewers to tears.

The original story of “Noiboch Noiboch” came from Shamsuzzaman himself, while Flora Sarker wrote the screenplay and dialogues. The drama was directed by Salahuddin Lavlu.

Shamsuzzaman also appeared in “Shilbari”, directed by Salahuddin Lavlu and written by Brindaban Das. Centred on the lives of an impoverished Shil family in a village, the drama featured him as Upen Shil. His performance earned appreciation from audiences across generations. Brindaban Das played his elder son, while Chanchal Chowdhury portrayed his younger son.

In “Napit”, Shamsuzzaman played a village man deeply attached to trees and determined to prevent one from being cut down. One of his memorable lines was, “I won’t let this tree be cut down.” The drama received praise from audiences at the time.

He took on the role of a miser in “Ei Je Duniya”, which also featured Ishita and Tony Dias. He also appeared in the comedy “Prem Piriti”, where his character spoke in the Noakhali dialect.

In the one-hour drama “Goruchor”, Shamsuzzaman played a cattle thief, a performance that earned him further recognition. Other notable television appearances included “Ghorkutum”, “Dholer Baddi” and the acclaimed “Ponditer Mela”.

These were only some of the many television dramas through which ATM Shamsuzzaman demonstrated a range that extended far beyond the negative characters for which he became widely known on the silver screen.
Author: S Shah Alam Shazu Shah Alam Shazu

Title: Toronto film festival opens with 200-plus films and major stars
Content:
The Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) opens Thursday with more than 200 films and a line-up featuring stars including John Malkovich, Penélope Cruz, Chris Rock, Helen Mirren and K-pop star Lisa. The 51st edition of North America’s largest film festival runs through September 20, following major festivals in Venice and Telluride. Hundreds of thousands of audiences are expected to attend screenings and red-carpet events in Toronto. The festival opens with the world premiere of “Being Heumann”, directed by Oscar winner Sian Heder, best known for “CODA”. Ruth Madeley stars as US disability rights activist Judy Heumann, with Mark Ruffalo also in the cast.

Among the major premieres is “I Play Rocky”, directed by Peter Farrelly of “Green Book”. The film tells the story of Sylvester Stallone’s struggle to get “Rocky” made and establish himself as its star, with Anthony Ippolito playing the young Stallone. Chris Rock returns behind the camera with “Misty Green”, a Hollywood satire starring Rosalind Eleazar, Daniel Kaluuya, Adam Driver and Anna Kendrick. Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine”, starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell, is also among the festival’s high-profile titles. Other major films include “Elsinore”, starring Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman; Jesse Eisenberg’s musical comedy “The Debut”; and Zack Snyder’s “The Last Photograph”, starring Stuart Martin and Fra Fee.

Helen Mirren stars as author Patricia Highsmith in the psychological thriller “A Talent for Murder”, while Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz play a couple in crisis in “Bunker”, which arrives in Toronto after premiering in Venice. The festival will also feature documentaries, including “Always Lalisa”, following Lisa’s solo career and her move into acting after her work with Blackpink and her appearance in “The White Lotus”.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Stars take social media back to the ’80s and ’90s
Content:
A retro trend has taken over social media, with popular stars recreating the fashion, hairstyles and makeup of the 80s and 90s through AI-generated photographs. The trend has drawn praise from fans, while the nostalgic looks have sparked discussion online. Some stars have recreated the styles of popular heroes and heroines of the era, while others have given the period’s fashion a contemporary twist. Actress Purnima joined the trend with a photograph on Facebook. Sharing the picture, she wrote, “New trend.”

Actor Apurba posted a picture of himself sitting on a motorcycle in an 80s-inspired look. “What being an actor in the 80’s used to mean…” he wrote.

Actress Bhabna also embraced the trend with an 80s-inspired look. “Me in the 80’s — in a vintage mood, in an eternal charm,” she wrote alongside the photograph.

The mood of the era was also reflected in a picture shared by actor Tawsif Mahbub. “From some afternoon in the 80’s,” he wrote.

Puja Chery shared her own take on the 80s trend, captioning the photograph, “Just did it.”

Safa Kabir, who played Dr Irine in the web film “Chaa Gorom”, also appeared in an 80s-inspired look. AI was used to give the makeup, setting and overall appearance an old-world touch.

Actress Tama Mirza joined the trend with a retro-style photograph, writing, “Following the trend.”

Masuma Rahman Nabila has also shared photographs inspired by the fashion and aesthetics of the 80s and 90s, adding to the growing wave of retro-inspired posts by the country’s stars.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: ‘Drishyam: The Conclusion’ trailer pits Ajay Devgn against Jaideep Ahlawat
Content:
The trailer for “Drishyam: The Conclusion”, the third instalment in the Hindi “Drishyam” franchise, has been released, introducing Jaideep Ahlawat as a new police officer determined to uncover the truth behind the case that Vijay Salgaonkar has kept hidden for years.

Ajay Devgn returns as Vijay, with Tabu reprising her role as IG Meera Deshmukh. In the trailer, Meera is once again determined to expose Vijay's involvement in the death of her son, but this time she is joined by Ahlawat's SP Crime Branch Rajveer Singh Tomar and Prakash Raj, who appears as a lawyer.

Meera's pursuit has also taken a darker turn. “I don't want justice anymore. I want revenge,” she declares in the trailer.

Vijay, meanwhile, appears aware that his carefully constructed story may finally be under serious threat. He tells his family that what lies ahead is no longer a game of wits, but a game of destiny.

The film brings back Shriya Saran, Rajat Kapoor, Ishita Dutta and Mrunal Jadhav, alongside the new additions Ahlawat and Prakash Raj.

Directed by Abhishek Pathak, “Drishyam: The Conclusion” is written by Pathak, Aamil Keeyan Khan and Parveez Shaikh. It is presented by Star Studio18 and produced by Panorama Studios.

The film follows the Hindi adaptation of the Malayalam “Drishyam” franchise created by filmmaker Jeethu Joseph. The first Hindi film, released in 2015, established Vijay as a man willing to go to extraordinary lengths to protect his family after his daughter became involved in the death of a teenage boy. The 2022 sequel continued the family's attempt to stay ahead of the investigation.

“Drishyam: The Conclusion” is scheduled to release in cinemas on October 2.

The film is being positioned as the concluding chapter of Vijay Salgaonkar's story, with the new trailer setting up what could be the family's biggest challenge yet.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Mymensingh’s Zainul Udyan comes alive with Shah Abdul Karim’s music
Content:
Zainul Udyan in Mymensingh came alive with the soulful melodies of legendary Baul saint Shah Abdul Karim as the third edition of the monthly folk music programme "Bhab Taranga" was held on Friday evening.

Organised by local cultural organisation Samaj Rupantar Sangskritik Sangha, the programme aims to promote Bangladesh’s folk-rooted cultural heritage among younger generations while preserving the values of indigenous culture and the spirit of the Liberation War.

Held regularly on the second Friday of every month at Zainul Udyan, located along the banks of the Brahmaputra River, the gathering brings audiences closer to the country’s traditional Baul music in an intimate, open-air setting.

The third edition, titled "Karim Parbo", featured timeless songs by Shah Abdul Karim, reflecting his messages of humanity, equality and communal harmony.

Baul maestros Jalal Shah Chishti and Abdul Jabbar, one of the senior-most Baul practitioners in the Mymensingh region, performed alongside Baul Swadesh Talukder, Md Shahidul Islam, Md Abdul Hafiz, Md Siraj Mondal, Billal Fakir and Imtiaz Ahmed.

The singers began the evening with Shah Abdul Karim’s "Tumio Manush, Amio Manush, Shobai Ek Mayer Shontan", a song that reflects the legendary Baul’s message of equality and communal harmony. They went on to perform a selection of his songs representing different musical traditions associated with the iconic folk musician.

The performances were further enriched by traditional instruments. Md Shahidul Islam and Swadesh Sarkar played the harmonium, Alamgir Hossain Rana played the dhol, and Billal Hossain performed on the mandira. A tabla duet by Syed Arman Hossain and Emon added another layer to the evening’s musical atmosphere.

The performances drew enthusiastic applause from the audience throughout the evening.

Imtiaz Ahmed Tansen, president of Samaj Rupantar Sangskritik Sangha, said the initiative was launched to bring the messages of equality, communal harmony and humanity preached by Baul saints closer to ordinary people.

“There is no modern mechanical setup or artificial grandeur in the programme. To preserve the rural and traditional atmosphere, the artists sit on the ground by the Brahmaputra and perform their songs,” Tansen said.

He added that each edition of "Bhab Taranga" focuses on the songs and philosophy of a particular Baul saint.

“The programme is being organised to spread the simple and gentle philosophy of Baul saints while remaining close to the soil and the people,” he said.

The organisers said "Bhab Taranga" began its journey in July with a session dedicated to Lalon songs. Its second edition, titled "Jalal Parbo", was held on August 14 and featured songs by Baul saint Jalal Uddin Khan, exploring themes surrounding the human body and creation.

The third edition, "Karim Parbo", was dedicated to Shah Abdul Karim.

The audience also praised the organisers for creating a space where traditional folk music could be experienced in an authentic setting.

The organisers said Bangladesh has long been home to spiritual Baul saints whose music has carried messages of humanity, equality and communal harmony across generations.

At a time when commercial music increasingly dominates the cultural landscape, they stressed the importance of preserving these timeless folk melodies and continuing to connect younger generations with the country’s rich folk heritage.
Author: M Md Aminul Islam Md Aminul Islam

Title: Revisiting ten memorable songs from Kanak Chapa’s film career
Content:
In Bangla cinema, few voices are as closely associated with nostalgia and romance as that of Rumana Morshed Kanak Chapa. For generations of listeners, her voice has been an inseparable part of countless memorable film songs and the cinematic moments they accompanied.

Kanak Chapa’s strength lies not only in her ability to follow a melody, but also in the emotion she brings to the lyrics. Through her expressive vocals, she gave depth to the feelings portrayed on screen, particularly when her voice was used for heroines.

Today, September 11, marks the birthday of the celebrated singer. Over her long career, Kanak Chapa has lent her voice to numerous films and delivered countless popular songs. On the occasion of her birthday, here are 10 memorable film songs from her repertoire.

‘Tumi Amar Emoni Ekjon’

Composed and arranged by Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul, "Tumi Amar Emoni Ekjon" is from Shibli Sadik’s film "Anondo Osru".

‘Sathi Tumi Amar Jibone’

From M M Sarkar’s "Chawa Theke Pawa", starring Salman Shah and Shabnur, "Sathi Tumi Amar Jibone" was written and composed by Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul. The duet was performed by Kanak Chapa and Khalid Hassan Milu.

‘Tomake Chai Shudhu Tomake Chai’

Matin Rahman’s "Tomake Chai", starring Salman Shah and Shabnur, featured the popular duet "Tomake Chai Shudhu Tomake Chai". Written and composed by Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul, the song was performed by Andrew Kishore and Kanak Chapa.

‘Amar Nakeri Phul Bolere Tumi Je Amar’

Another memorable song from "Tomake Chai", "Amar Nakeri Phul Bolere Tumi Je Amar" was performed by Andrew Kishore and Kanak Chapa. Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul wrote and composed the song.

‘Je Prem Shorgo Theke Eshe’

"Je Prem Shorgo Theke Eshe" is from Mohommod Hannan’s "Praner Cheye Priyo", starring Riaz and Ravina. The duet was sung by Kanak Chapa and Khalid Hassan Milu, with Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul serving as lyricist and composer.

‘Ononto Prem Tumi Dao Amake’

From Kazi Hayat’s "Loottoraj”, starring Manna and Moushumi, "Ononto Prem Tumi Dao Amake" was performed by Ayub Bachchu and Kanak Chapa. Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul wrote and composed the song.

‘Onek Sadhonar Pore’

Mohommoad Hannan’s "Bhalobasi Tomake", starring Riaz and Shabnur, featured the popular duet "Onek Sadhonar Pore". The song was performed by Khalid Hassan Milu and Kanak Chapa and was written and composed by Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul.

‘Amar Premer Tajmahal’

"Amar Premer Tajmahal", from Gazi Mahbub’s film of the same name starring Riaz and Shabnur, was sung by Monir Khan and Kanak Chapa. Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul wrote and composed the song.

‘Tomay Dekhle Mone Hoy’

From Matin Rahman’s "Biyer Phool", starring Shakil Khan and Shabnur, "Tomay Dekhle Mone Hoy" was performed by Andrew Kishore and Kanak Chapa. The song was written and composed by Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul.

‘Jibon Furiye Jabe Bhalobasha’

The list concludes with "Jibon Furiye Jabe Bhalobasha", from Mohommoad Hannan’s "Bidroho Charidike", starring Riaz and Popy. The duet was sung by Andrew Kishore and Kanak Chapa, with Ahmed Imtiaz Bulbul writing and composing the song.
Author: Zahid Akbar Zahid Akbar

Title: Hania Aamir makes music debut with a message for her critics
Content:
Pakistani actor Hania Aamir has made her official music debut with “Pablo”, a Punjabi hip-hop track in which she addresses the criticism and scrutiny surrounding her public image.

Released on Wednesday (September 9), the song was written and composed by Aamir herself, marking a new creative chapter as she celebrates 10 years in the entertainment industry.

“Pablo” begins with a soft piano melody before shifting into an upbeat Punjabi rap. In the song, Aamir responds to people who have described her as “fake” and questioned her personality and guarded public image. She also references her popularity and the attention she receives from fans.

One of the song's most notable lines sees Aamir addressing her critics directly: “Assi hassde te tussi pichhe sarhde-sarhde. Assi chill ay te roz panga lai re ne.” The line roughly translates to, “We're laughing while you're back there fuming. We're chilling while you keep trying to pick a fight.”

Aamir also references her “Pindi attitude” and the attention it receives in India, using the track to present a confident and carefree response to her detractors.

The song's most unexpected moment comes towards the end, when Indian reality television personality Rakhi Sawant appears in the outro with a message for Aamir. Sawant praises her beauty and confidence, calls her a “lioness” and encourages her not to be affected by her critics.

For the official music video, Aamir also took on the role of director. Mohammad Mohtashim handled associate direction, cinematography, editing and grading, while Kumail Abbas produced, mixed and mastered the track.

With “Pablo”, Aamir has added music to a career that has so far largely centred on acting and modelling, using her debut single to respond to public scrutiny on her own terms.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Bono makes history as U2 named 2027 MusiCares Persons of the Year
Content:
Irish rock titans U2 will be honored as the 2027 MusiCares Persons of the Year, making frontman Bono the first artist in history to receive the distinction both as an individual and as part of a group.

The 36th annual charity gala will take place on Friday, Feb 5, 2027, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, two nights prior to the 69th Annual Grammy Awards at nearby Crypto.com Arena.

U2—comprising Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr.—becomes the fourth band to receive the honor, following Fleetwood Mac (2018), Aerosmith (2020), and the Grateful Dead (2025). Bono was previously honored as an individual at the 2003 gala.

“We are huge fans of MusiCares and the lifelines they provide across the incredible pool of talent that is the music industry,” the band said in a joint statement. “‘Persons of the Year’ couldn’t be a better title as it’s the people we’ve been so fortunate to work with, and of course our indomitable audience, that have given us the opportunity to keep making music and keep rocking the boat on things we really care about.”

Harvey Mason jr, CEO of the Recording Academy and MusiCares, highlighted the band's balance of cultural impact and philanthropy. “Their impact goes far beyond the stage,” Mason said. “Not only has their music defined generations, but they’ve been equally exemplary in their dedication to humanitarian work and using their platform for good.”

Celebrating 50 years together after forming at their Dublin high school in 1976, U2 remains the most decorated group in Grammy history with 22 wins. They are also the only act to win Album, Record, and Song of the Year twice.

Beyond the music, all four members have maintained distinct humanitarian footprints. The group campaigned against South African apartheid before securing their first record deal, received Amnesty International’s Ambassador of Conscience Award in 2005, and continues to support Music Generation, Ireland’s national music education program. Individually, Bono co-founded ONE and (RED) to combat poverty and HIV/AIDS, playing a pivotal role in creating the U.S. PEPFAR program. The Edge co-founded Music Rising in 2005 to replace instruments for disaster-stricken musicians, Clayton advocates for addiction recovery through initiatives like Ireland’s Walk in My Shoes, and Mullen Jr. has championed dyslexia awareness as a film producer.

The 2027 event marks a venue shift from the Los Angeles Convention Center to the 7,100-capacity Peacock Theater. MusiCares is also introducing individual theater seating for the tribute concert alongside traditional gala tables, opening the performance to a broader public audience. Produced by Lewis & Clark, the event raises funds for MusiCares’ health, mental wellness, addiction recovery, and emergency financial assistance programs for music professionals.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Chhayanaut hosts an evening of Tagore with Laisa Ahmed Lisa, Imtiaz Ahmed
Content:
Tagore’s songs filled the Chhayanaut auditorium in Dhanmondi on Thursday as Laisa Ahmed Lisa and Imtiaz Ahmed performed a mix of solos and duets.

Organised by Anondodhara Arts UK, the evening, titled “E Amir Aboron”, unfolded in eight sections, beginning with the two singers’ rendition of “Oi Asonotole”.

Rabindra Sangeet exponent Laisa Ahmed Lisa then performed “Modhur Tomar Shesh Je Na Pai” and “Bajao Amare Bajao”. Singer Imtiaz Ahmed followed with “Adhora Madhuri Dhorechhi” and “Modhur Modhur Dhoni Baje”.

The third section opened with the duet “Ogo Shefali Boner Moner Kamona”. Lisa then sang “Bajilo Kahar Bina” and “Amalo Dhabalo Pale Legechhe”, while Imtiaz performed “Jibone Joto Puja Holo Na Sara” and “Boro Bedonar Moto”.

The fifth section brought the two singers together for “Tumi Kemon Kore Gaan Koro Hey”. Imtiaz then performed “Tomay Gaan Shonabo” and “Tumi Nobo Nobo Rupe Esho Praney”.

Lisa returned with “Jodi Jantem Amar Kiser Byatha” and “Tomay Notun Kore Pabo Bole”, followed by Imtiaz’s performances of “Amar Bhanga Pother Ranga Dhulay” and “Jete Jete Ekla Pothe”.

The final section featured Lisa performing “Kar Milan Chao Birahi” and “Aji Jhorer Rate”. The programme concluded with “Gaaner Bhetor Diye Jokhon Dekhi”.

Imtiaz, who is based in London and works as a doctor, is also a Rabindra Sangeet singer.

Rashed Hasan, Granthana Yusuf and Laila delivered readings on Tagore’s songs during the programme.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Runa Laila’s daughter Tani calls for action against AI-generated death rumours
Content:
The daughter of renowned singer Runa Laila, Tani Laila, has urged fans to report social media accounts spreading false reports about her mother’s health, after a claim that the singer is “battling for her life” began circulating online alongside AI-generated videos and images.

Tani, who is currently in the United States with her family, confirmed in a social media post that her mother is alive and in good health. She also expressed frustration over the spread of fake news and misleading content created using artificial intelligence.

“I am truly annoyed and fed up seeing these posts, AI-generated YouTube videos and fake news being spread just to make a small amount of money,” Tani wrote. “I will personally start reporting these types of content, one by one, until these idiots stop this nonsense.”

Reflecting on her mother’s six-decade musical career, Tani also criticised those who continue to disrespect the veteran singer.

“My mother has devoted six decades of her life to serving music. Yet people continue to disrespect her in this way even now — what an utter shame and humiliation this is for us!” she wrote.

Tani further clarified that the claims about Runa Laila’s health are entirely false.

“My mother is completely healthy and alive; no one has died, nor is she on the verge of death. These are all videos and images created using AI,” she said.

Urging Runa Laila’s followers to take action against such content, Tani added, “It is no longer tolerable. Those who follow Runa Laila, please report such accounts.”

Runa Laila performed at two concerts in Australia last month. Earlier, she also performed at a solo musical event organised by the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Nirvana to receive Video Vanguard Award at 2026 MTV VMAs
Content:
Rock band Nirvana will receive the Video Vanguard Award at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, recognising the band's lasting contribution to music videos and visual culture. MTV announced the honour on September 9.

The announcement came exactly 34 years after Nirvana made its first appearance at the VMAs on September 9, 1992. The band performed “Lithium” at the ceremony, which became one of the most memorable appearances in the show's history.

Nirvana earned five VMAs during its career, including awards for Best New Artist in a Video and Best Alternative Video in 1992. The band rose to international prominence with its 1991 album “Nevermind”, followed by “In Utero” in 1993.

Frontman Kurt Cobain died in 1994, after which Nirvana's surviving members Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear have occasionally reunited for special performances with guest vocalists.

In 2014, Grohl, Novoselic and Smear performed Nirvana songs with Joan Jett, Kim Gordon, St Vincent and Lorde during the band's induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. The surviving members also reunited for the FireAid benefit concert in 2025.

It has not yet been confirmed who from Nirvana's surviving members will attend this year's ceremony or whether the honour will be accompanied by a tribute performance.

The Video Vanguard Award has previously been presented to artists including Mariah Carey, Katy Perry, Shakira and Nicki Minaj.

The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards will take place in Los Angeles on September 27. The ceremony will air live on CBS and MTV and stream on Paramount+. A host has yet to be announced.
