Title: 200 percussionists honor Nazrul's rhythmic compositions at Shilpakala
Content:
A two-day special programme exploring the rhythmic compositions and diverse musical patterns of National Poet Kazi Nazrul Islam will be held at Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy on September 9 and 10, featuring around 200 percussionists.

Titled “Nazruler Chhandataranga” (Nazrul’s Rhythmic Waves), the programme will be held at rehearsal rooms 104 and 105 of the Music and Dance Centre building under the initiative of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs.

The sessions will run from 10 am to 2 pm and from 3 pm to 7 pm on both days.

According to Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy officials, the programme will examine the rhythmic language and structures developed by Nazrul, as well as his approaches to percussion and the broader artistic possibilities of rhythmic performance.

The two-day programme will also feature collective practice involving the participating percussionists, offering an opportunity to explore Nazrul’s rhythmic ideas through ensemble performance.

The organisers said the programme aims to highlight the richness of Nazrul’s musical innovations and their continuing relevance to Bangladesh’s musical traditions.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Theatre Charonik brings ‘Kaljatra’ to Shilpakala next week
Content:
Theatre Charonik is set to stage its sixth production, “Kaljatra: Ekti Nishiddho Janazar Golpo” at Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy’s Studio Theatre Hall on September 16 at 7pm. The second show will be held at the same venue and time on September 17.

Written by Mahfuza Hilali and directed by Shyamin Sagar, the production features a solo performance by Safia Khandaker Rekha.

The play centres on Kumkum, whose mother, Princess Mahima, was a celebrated jatra performer who portrayed Sita, Draupadi and Behula on stage. After Mahima’s death, Kumkum is left with her mother’s final wish — to have a janaza.

As Kumkum tries to fulfil that wish, she encounters barriers shaped by religious rules, social restrictions and invisible structures of power. The play explores how identity, fear and social prohibitions can become barriers as formidable as physical walls.

Mahima’s stage life repeatedly resurfaces through Kumkum’s memories, bringing the characters she once portrayed into the present. Draupadi’s questions, Behula’s long wait and Sita’s trial by fire blur the boundary between theatrical performance and lived reality.

Writer of the play, Hilali said the production examines the neglect, discrimination and oppression faced by artists, particularly women artists, despite there being no reason for gender-based distinctions within the arts.

Director of the play, Sagar said the play does not seek to put any religion on trial, but instead questions the power, narrow-mindedness, fear and cruelty created by people in the name of religion.

The production is the sixth by Theatre Charonik.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: ‘Kali O Kalam’ awards honour four young writers
Content:
Four young writers were honoured at the City Bank “Kali O Kalam Torun Kobi O Lekhok Puroshkar 2025” at Bengal Shilpalay in Dhanmondi today. The ceremony began with a welcome address and a note of thanks, followed by a documentary on the journey of “Kali O Kalam”, the monthly literary, art and cultural magazine. The programme was hosted by Bengal Foundation Director General Luva Nahid Choudhury. Prominent novelist Hasnat Abdul Hye attended as the chief guest, while renowned essayist and researcher Professor Abul Ahsan Chowdhury was present as the special guest. City Bank Managing Director and CEO Mashrur Arefin also attended the event.

Writer Imdadul Haq Milan announced the names of this year’s award recipients. Hamim Kamal received the award in the fiction category for his book “Tristan”. Rafat Alam was recognised in the essay and research category for “Bangladesh Patth”. Ranak Zaman won in the poetry category for “Ei Gram Kuriye Peyechi”, while The Daily Star journalist and children’s author Robiul Kamol received the award in the children’s literature category for “Dosshu O Dui Duronto”.

The four awardees later took the stage and shared their thoughts on their work and the recognition. They were also presented with flowers. Each awardee received a cheque of Tk 2 lakh and a crest. Speaking at the event, Mashrur Arefin highlighted City Bank’s involvement in the award as part of its corporate social responsibility initiatives. He stressed the importance of supporting literature and said that relatively few people and organisations are working in this field. He also praised “Kali O Kalam” for its continued efforts to promote literature and encourage young writers.

Professor Abul Ahsan Chowdhury then spoke about the history and significance of Muslim Sahitya Samaj, the historic organisation associated with the intellectual movement for the liberation of the mind. Writer Hasnat also discussed the importance of the different award categories and suggested adding travel writing to the list. He noted that many women are now travelling across the world and producing travel literature, making the category relevant to contemporary literary practice.

The programme concluded with a special musical presentation marking the centenary of Muslim Sahitya Samaj. Noted artiste Priyanka Gope performed several historic songs associated with gatherings of the organisation.

Since its introduction in 2008, the annual award has sought to encourage young poets and writers in Bangladesh and support their creative pursuits. With this year’s four recipients, 75 young writers have now received the award.
Author: Anika Tahsin Hafsa Anika Tahsin Hafsa

Title: Mustafa Monwar’s legacy lives on as BotTala celebrates children’s theatre festival
Content:
Children’s theatre, puppetry, music, storytelling and creative workshops filled the premises of Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy as BotTala theatre production company organised the Mustafa Monwar Children Theatre Festival 2026 on August 29 and 30. The two-day festival marked BotTala’s 18th founding anniversary while paying tribute to legendary puppeteer and Ekushey Padak recipient Mustafa Monwar, who passed away on June 29. Mustafa Monwar was a beloved artist who played a significant role in popularising puppet theatre in Bangladesh and encouraging children’s participation in creative activities.

The festival featured a range of programmes designed for children, including stage performances, puppet shows, clay-making sessions, drawing workshops, storytelling and musical activities. A major focus of the event was creating opportunities for children to engage with different forms of art.

BotTala’s children’s theatre group staged “Bonnotherium” and “Dakat Halum Chitpotang” during the festival. “Dakat Halum Chitpotang” was adapted from German writer Otfried Preußler’s well-known children’s story “The Robber Hotzenplotz”. The stage adaptation was translated and adapted by Shammi Akhter, with direction and design by Humayun Azam Rewaz.

“Rather than focusing on perfection, our aim is to create an environment where children can enjoy art, express themselves and gain a creative experience,” said Humayun Azam Rewaz, director of BotTala.

The puppet show “Shobuj Desher Bipod”, presented by Universal Puppet, was another attraction for young audiences.

The event also included the launch of two children’s books by Goppo-Soppo Publication. One of them, “Boma ar Senapoti”, is the Bengali translation by G H Habib of Italian writer Umberto Eco’s anti-war children’s picture book “The Bomb and the General”. Theatre artist Samiun Jahan Dola presented a storytelling session based on the book. The other book, “Mirabelle”, is a translation of Swedish writer Astrid Lindgren’s work by Mazahar Ziban.

Several organisations and artists joined the festival with creative programmes. Cartoon People, Together We Can, Khokon Karigor, Inventors Puppet, Universal Puppet, Kaktarua Puppet Theatre and Dhaka Little Opera contributed to different segments of the event. The festival also included book-reading sessions, puppet-making activities, clay workshops and storytelling programmes.

With performances, workshops and interactive programmes, the festival offered children an opportunity to participate in the arts beyond traditional learning spaces. BotTala plans to continue organising such initiatives to promote creative practices among children in the coming years.
Author: F Faiza Ramim Faiza Ramim

Title: Nazrul’s traditional Leto Gaan staged at Shilpakala Academy
Content:
A special cultural evening featuring National Poet Kazi Nazrul Islam’s traditional Leto Gaan (folk musical theatre) and Kabigaan (poetic musical debate) was held at the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka on Thursday as part of the ongoing Nazrul Year celebrations.

The programme, titled “Nazruler Letogaan O Kobigaan” (Nazrul’s Leto Gaan and Kabigaan), was held at the auditorium of the Academy’s National Music and Dance Centre. It opened with a paper presentation titled “Kazi Nazrul Islam’s Leto Gaan and Kabigaan: Exploring the Sources of Folk Heritage, Creativity and Rebel Consciousness”.

Dr Kamal Khalid, associate professor and head of the Department of Folk Song at Government Music College, presented the paper. Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy Director General and poet Sheikh Rezauddin Ahmed (Rezauddin Stalin) presided over the programme, while Bangladesh Film Development Corporation Managing Director Masuma Rahman Tani attended as a special guest. Mehjabeen Rahman, director of the Academy’s Music, Dance and Recitation Department, delivered the welcome address.

The second session began with “Andho Raja” (The Blind King), a Leto Gaan directed and conceptualised by Dr Kamal Khalid. Saima Ahmed Liza provided overall supervision, while the Leto troupes “Nimsha Leto Dal” and “Medenipur Leto Dal” performed the piece.

The programme continued with “Kabir Lorai” (The Poets’ Duel), written by Kazi Nazrul Islam and directed and conceptualised by Jibon Chowdhury. Kabiyal Gumani Babu took part in the musical duel with Kabiyal Jibon Ure.

The performers included Jibon Chowdhury and Gumani Babu, Babul Hossain and Jibon Ure and Mamun Hossain as Sutradhar/Kayali (narrator/commentator). The Dohars (chorus performers) were Shan, Syed Masumur Rahman, Jayanta Bikash Das, Mahmuda Akter Rupa, Arbi Islam Swarna, Jannat Ara Shyamoli, Anannya Roy and Narayan Deb.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: ‘Untold Story’: A window into the emotions and memories of women artists
Content:
In our society, a man is simply a man — a protector and provider with a linear existence. Women, however, are put into similar moulds that force them to lead multidimensional lives. Thus, a woman’s heart is deeper than the Pacific Ocean — containing secrets and stories born from her social identities, the phases of her life and lived experiences with others. These narratives often go unnoticed within the patriarchal system that prevails. A group of women artists has now decided to share their memoirs through an art exhibition titled “Untold Story”.

The inauguration of “Untold Story” took place at Alliance Française de Dhaka (AFD) on September 1, 2026, on a calming evening of drizzle, as if the sky knew to be gentle that night. Frédéric Inza, Deputy Head of Mission at the Embassy of France in Dhaka, and Tanvir Ahmed, Managing Director of Sheltech Group and Envoy Legacy, attended the event as chief guests.

Curated by Fareha Zeba, the exhibition features artists Esha Ahmed, Fouzia Mahin Choudhury, Kazmin Samia, Shulekha Chaudhury, Sumana Akter and Surovi Akter, alongside guest artists Alia Kamal, Arpita Singha, Mahmuda Siddika, Rafia Mahjabeen, Rituparna Saha and Venessa Kaiser.

“Untold Story” is an exhibition where visitors can interact with the artworks, which are meant not only to be seen but also touched, listened to and felt. Zeba said she encouraged the participants to create unconventional books through their artworks, allowing audiences to interact with the pieces and relate to the artists.

Zeba’s own work introduces her practice of working on palm leaves, a technique she learnt in Odisha, India, in 2017. Her paintings are conversations between women and seeds, with both asking the same question: “Are we here to nourish the earth and its living beings?”

Venessa Kaiser presents a bold, eye-catching set of images exploring limerence — an intense romantic obsession with someone despite uncertainty over whether the feelings are reciprocated. The pages of her book resemble the shape of a human heart.

Surovi Akter creates a journey from childhood to adulthood, looking inward and embracing her feelings. Alia Kamal, meanwhile, has created a cleverly cut-and-folded book featuring portraits of her mother, maternal grandmother and herself at different phases of their lives, presenting a dialogue among three generations of women.

Esha Ahmed has handmade a chocolate-shaped quilt with her poem embroidered on it, portraying the sweetness of her childhood memories. Of her three books, the tiniest is perhaps the most endearing — filled with beads, flowers, lace and other crafts.

Arpita Singha’s work challenges archaic social prejudices sugar-coated with aestheticism. She confronts the discriminatory notion that a dark complexion brings misfortune, particularly affecting girls. Her work also connects such superstition with attitudes towards crows, nature’s scavengers that help keep cities clean.

Mahmuda Siddika’s collage, made with countless tiny pieces of fabric, presents the countryside and Sal forest through her eyes — a visual memoir of her journey home to Mymensingh.

For Rituparna Saha, the loss of a loved one forced her family members to live apart at a time when they had no home of their own to return to. Using textile manipulation, photo transfer and eco-printing alongside hand embroidery, she depicts her search for a home.

Sumana Akter’s work explores her journey through motherhood and the bond she shares with her son. Between 2024 and 2026, Shulekha Chaudhury faced fear, loss and uncertainty surrounding her mother’s battle with cancer and events in her motherland, Bangladesh. These experiences led her to create “Shodesh”, depicting both of her mothers.

Kazmin Samia explores a post-traumatic emotional state, navigating grief, resilience and healing through images, text and personal narratives.

Through hand-stitching and natural dyes on textile, Rafia Mahjabeen remembers “Panthakunja”, a five-acre park that provided shelter to people and animals in Dhaka before being affected by the construction of the elevated expressway. Around 2,000 trees representing 45 species were cut down, resulting in the loss of animal habitats.

Fouzia Mahin Choudhury offers an auditory experience in which visitors can communicate with a speeding ceiling fan, much as she does herself. Her mirror, meanwhile, portrays her gaze towards her innermost self rather than the outside world.

Ultimately, “Untold Story” is an exhibition filled with emotional depth and warmth as well as technical intellect. The exhibition will remain open at AFD until September 9, 2026.
Author: Aishwarya Raihan Aishwarya Raihan

Title: ‘Molotov Man’: The photograph that outlived a revolution
Content:
On the afternoon of 16 July 1979, in the northern Nicaraguan city of Estelí, a young man named Pablo Aráuz found an empty Pepsi bottle, filled it with petrol, lit it and threw it at the local headquarters of the National Guard. An American photographer standing a few feet away made a picture of him doing it. Somoza fled the country the next day. The dictatorship his family had run for 43 years collapsed two days after that.

The photograph is called “Molotov Man”. Aráuz, known to everyone as Bareta, has been throwing that bottle ever since.

The Somoza family had governed Nicaragua since 1937. Their instrument was the National Guard, a force the United States had armed and trained, and Washington kept backing them for four decades on the reasoning that a friendly dictator was preferable to an unfriendly election. The opposition organised slowly. The Sandinista National Liberation Front, named after a guerrilla leader the Guard had assassinated in 1934, was founded by student activists in Managua in 1961 and spent most of the next 15 years being hunted.

What broke the arrangement was a murder. On 10 January 1978, Pedro Joaquín Chamorro, editor of the newspaper La Prensa and the most prominent critic of the regime, was shot dead in Managua. Nobody believed the government’s account. A hundred and twenty thousand people came to his funeral, a general strike followed, and a country that had been quietly angry for 40 years stopped being quiet.

Susan Meiselas arrived five months later. She was 30, from Baltimore, and had studied anthropology before she studied photography. Her only substantial body of work at that point was a book about women who performed in travelling carnival strip shows in New England, made over three summers while she taught photography in New York public schools. She had joined the Magnum agency in 1976. She had never covered a war.

She has said she went because she wanted to see what American foreign policy actually looked like on the ground. Her passport and press card let her move between the Sandinistas and the Guard, a freedom almost nobody inside the country possessed. She stayed for a year. She shot in colour, which at the time was slightly disreputable for serious conflict work, colour being associated with advertising rather than with witness.

Most people remember the photograph as a silhouette of a man throwing a bomb. Look at it properly and it is far stranger than that.

He is leaning back, arm fully extended, the bottle lit and still in his hand. He wears a beret over dark curly hair. A crucifix has swung out from his chest, thrown clear by the speed of the motion. In his other hand he is holding a rifle, and that hand is wrapped in a bandage. Behind him, a few metres back, other fighters are crouched low behind sandbags. He is the only one standing.

Each of those details does something. The Pepsi bottle is an American consumer product turned into a weapon and thrown at an American-armed government, which is a joke the photograph makes without saying anything. The crucifix belongs to a specific history: liberation theology was a real force in the Nicaraguan revolution, and priests served in the Sandinista government afterwards. The photograph later ran on the cover of a Nicaraguan church magazine. The flame is small because the weapon is homemade and the building is fortified.

The bandage is the detail that stays with me. Nobody arranged it. It does not serve any argument. It simply says that his hand was already hurt, that this was not his first hour of fighting, and that the man who became a symbol was a body that could be broken.

Meiselas made the picture from low down and close in. Low angles enlarge people. Combined with the backward lean, the angle turns a man throwing a bottle into something closer to a statue. She was not shooting from safety with a long lens. The composition also depends on what she left out. There is a whole battle in that frame, and the crop pushes it into the background. A wider frame would have been a photograph of an insurrection. This one is a photograph of a man.

Within a year of the revolution, the image was everywhere in Nicaragua. It appeared on matchbooks made for the first anniversary. It went onto posters, stamps, T-shirts, brochures and woven straw rugs. People painted it as murals and cut it into wall stencils. Bareta’s silhouette became the visual shorthand for what the country had just done to itself.

Then it went further than anyone intended. In the 1980s, the Sandinista government used the image to recruit a popular militia against the Contras, the rebel force the CIA was funding out of Honduras, pairing it with graffiti reading “No Pasarán”, a slogan borrowed from the Spanish Civil War. At the same time, in the United States, the Contras were putting the same image in fundraising material as evidence of communist aggression. Two sides that were shooting at each other were using the same photograph to raise men and money.

The strangest chapter came much later. In 2003, an American painter named Joy Amina Garnett found a cropped JPEG of the figure online. She did not know who had taken it, who the man was or what country he was in. She painted him as part of a series about people in states of extreme emotion and titled it “Molotov”. A cease-and-desist letter arrived from Meiselas’s lawyer, and the internet did what the internet does. Artists around the world began posting their own versions in protest, an episode that came to be known as “Joywar”.

The two women eventually met at a symposium on fair use in 2006 and wrote a joint essay for Harper’s Magazine the following year. Their disagreement is worth reading because neither of them is obviously wrong. Garnett asked whether the author of a documentary record gets to control what that record means forever. Meiselas’s answer was that stripping the context turns a named man’s specific act on a specific day into a generic image of rage, and that she owed it to him not to let that pass without objection.

Meiselas went back to Nicaragua in 1990 to find the people in her photographs for a film called “Pictures from a Revolution”. She found Bareta driving a lumber truck, delivering timber, still a Sandinista and raising a family. He had no objection to how the picture had been used. He understood it as belonging to a collective struggle rather than to him. Later, his likeness was adopted as the official emblem of the overthrow, and a monument to him was put up in his home town.

So there are three parties with a claim on this photograph. Meiselas holds the copyright. Bareta did the thing it records. And the people who have reproduced it since, in Nicaragua and elsewhere, have used it for whatever they needed at the time. The claims are all reasonable and they do not agree with each other.

The picture is a record of something that happened. A man named Pablo Aráuz threw a petrol bomb at a garrison in Estelí on the afternoon of 16 July 1979. The same picture was also used by the Sandinistas and by the Contras while they were at war with each other, and by a painter in New York who had no idea what she was looking at. Those things are all true of one photograph.

A photograph does not hold its meaning by itself. The meaning comes from what is attached to it, and that can be taken off. It is worth keeping in mind now, when most of the images we see reach us cropped, with no caption and no idea who made them. Somebody made each of them, and somebody is in them, and both of those people usually had something specific in mind.
Author: Nafi Nawar

Title: Tigers begin Asian Games camp, hoping to get ‘adequate’ preparation
Content:
Bangladesh began their Asian Games preparation camp on Sunday, returning to T20 cricket for the first time since their full series in Zimbabwe in July. With concerns over the facilities in Japan, adequate preparation is the priority as the Tigers prepare to depart for the tournament on September 24, ahead of their opening match in the quarterfinals on September 28.

At least half of the squad, including skipper Litton Das, Najmul Hossain Shanto and Mustafizur Rahman, were present as the Tigers began their preparations. The team are still awaiting the arrival of players who recently featured in the ‘A’ team’s tour of South Africa. National team head coach Phil Simmons attended the session, while Mohammad Salahuddin, head coach for the Asian Games tournament, conducted the preparations.

“We may not have access to adequate facilities in Japan, so we have to make the most of what is available here and complete as much of our preparation as possible before leaving. We are structuring our practice sessions accordingly,” a member of the team management informed.

The Tigers will also play two practice games in Mirpur on September 21 and 23.

Bangladesh clinched the gold medal at the 2010 Asian Games in Guangzhou, China, and the feat remains their only gold medal at the Asian Games to date. The last time they appeared in the event, the Tigers won bronze by beating Pakistan by six wickets. This time, they are once again aiming for gold, having named a strong outfit featuring several senior national team players.

“The goal is to definitely go for gold medal. Given that we have not played T20 cricket for quite some time, the goal in terms of preparation is to get into T20 rhythm,” a member of the coaching staff said.

It is understood that a drop-in wicket is likely to be used during the tournament. The Tigers’ main concern will be regaining their batting rhythm after a lengthy break from the format, and batting will be given priority as the tournament approaches. Mustafizur was the only bowler to bowl at the two centre wickets during the batting session.

“We practiced on the [two] centre wickets and slabs were also used. Everyone got a chance to bat on the two centre wickets,” the coaching staff said as preparations kicked into gear for another gold-medal bid.
Author: Sports Reporter

Title: The bet that changed everything: Rybakina’s journey to world No. 1
Content:
Less than a year ago, Elena Rybakina was fighting simply to make the WTA Finals.

On Saturday, she stood on Arthur Ashe Stadium with the US Open trophy in her hands and the world No. 1 ranking secured.

The 27-year-old defeated Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 to win her first US Open title, complete a remarkable rise to the top of women's tennis and claim her third Grand Slam crown.

The journey to get there has been anything but straightforward.

Born in Russia, Rybakina was not considered a priority by the country's tennis system as a teenager. Her family could not afford the coaching, travel and other costs needed to build a professional career, and she was facing the possibility of going to university in the United States.

Then Kazakhstan stepped in.

Billionaire businessman Bulat Utemuratov was building a national tennis programme and saw potential in Rybakina. Kazakhstan's federation provided the funding and support that allowed her to continue developing, and in 2018 she switched allegiance.

It proved a pivotal decision.

Four years later, Rybakina won Wimbledon, announcing herself as one of the most dangerous players in the sport. Her huge serve and clean ball-striking made her a formidable opponent, but consistency remained elusive.

Then came a difficult period.

She split with coach Stefano Vukov in 2024 before bringing him back, only for the WTA to provisionally suspend him during an investigation. Rybakina repeatedly said he had never mistreated her, while the WTA later found that Vukov had engaged in "abuse of authority and abusive conduct". The ban was subsequently lifted after an appeal and private arbitration.

The turmoil coincided with a dip in Rybakina's results.

By late 2025, she had failed to reach the quarterfinals at any of the four Grand Slams and had needed a gruelling run of tournaments to qualify for the WTA Finals.

Then everything changed.

Rybakina won the season-ending title, beating Sabalenka in the final. A few months later, she defeated the same rival again to win the 2026 Australian Open.

Suddenly, the player who had looked vulnerable was becoming almost impossible to stop.

She arrived in New York as the second seed and left as the world's best player.

Rybakina clinched the No. 1 ranking by reaching the US Open semifinals, becoming the 30th woman to top the WTA rankings. She then beat Coco Gauff in three sets before finishing the job against Sabalenka.

What makes the surge even more remarkable is that her appearance in New York was far from guaranteed.

Just weeks earlier, Rybakina had withdrawn from the Cincinnati quarter-finals with an Achilles problem and did not touch a racket for more than a week.

She arrived in New York unsure of what to expect.

She left with a Grand Slam title and the No. 1 ranking.

"I didn't expect anything like this coming into the tournament," she said after the final.

For Kazakhstan, there is a deeper significance.

Rybakina may have been born in Russia, but the country she chose to represent has embraced her as its own. Utemuratov flew from Almaty to New York for the final, while fans back home stayed awake into the early hours to watch the biggest moment in the country's tennis history.

It was the culmination of a bet Kazakhstan made on a talented teenager who had been overlooked elsewhere.

Rybakina has since repaid that faith many times over.

From a player struggling to find her place at the top of the sport, she is now its leading figure.

And perhaps the most remarkable part is that the climb is still going.
Author: Agencies

Title: Root hails England’s response to ‘unusual summer’
Content:
England have responded excellently to an "unusual summer" marked by a captaincy change, a new coach and off-field incidents, Test captain Joe Root said after his side completed a 3-0 series shutout of Pakistan.

The 35-year-old Root, the second-highest run-scorer in Test cricket history, returned as England Test captain after all-rounder Ben Stokes retired from international cricket. Root led England in a record 64 Tests between 2017 and 2022, winning 27 of them.

Former New Zealand batter Stephen Fleming was appointed head coach in July following the sacking of compatriot Brendon McCullum after a four-year stint.

The build-up to the second Test against Pakistan was overshadowed by controversy surrounding fast bowler Brydon Carse, who was dropped from the England squad following an incident outside a nightclub in Derby.

Despite the distractions, England completed the sweep on Saturday, sealing an eight-wicket victory in the third and final Test at Edgbaston.

"There's been a lot of chaos around this series before a ball was bowled," Root said at a press conference. "At the start of the series, we wanted 3-0 and we've been clinical enough to do that.

"It's been a very unusual summer, hasn't it? That's probably a better way of putting it. There's been a lot of different things happen. We had a resignation mid-series, there has been a few off-field incidents and we've got a new coach.

"Whether you call it chaos, whether you call it unusual, whether you call it unsettling, all are fair. But ultimately, the thing that I care about, and that's most important, is what happens from that. And I think the way that we've responded to that has been excellent.

"And the fact that there's now clarity in what is expected of the group moving forward is quite evident and we build on that now."

England next host Sri Lanka in a three-match Twenty20 series beginning in Southampton on Tuesday before facing them in three One-Day Internationals.
Author: Reuters

Title: In Pictures: Litton and Co begin practice ahead of Asian Games
Content:
The Tigers returned to training today after a short break following their tour of Australia, kicking off preparations for the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Wicketkeeper-batter Litton Das will lead the team in the T20 event.

Thirteen of the 15 squad members were present at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur. Pacer Hasan Mahmud has yet to return home from England following his early departure from Kent duty, while left-arm pacer Shoriful Islam is currently on leave. According to BCB sources, Bangladesh will play two practice matches before the Asian Games.

The team will play the quarterfinals directly on September 29, facing a side that advances from the first round. The opponents and dates for the practice matches have yet to be finalised. Title: 'Gloomy times': Pakistan cricket at a new low after England humiliation
Content:
Pakistan cricket hit a fresh low during the dismal 3-0 Test whitewash in England, even if a dazzling cameo by debutant Razaullah at least ensured a tour marred by mid-series sackings ended with a flicker of hope.

Described as the worst team to tour England in the last 50 years, Pakistan's cycle of chopping and changing continued when head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling chief Umar Gul were sacked from their posts.

Seven players were expelled from the squad as the often vulnerable batting fell to a new low, failing to cross 200 in five of the six innings.

White-ball coach Mike Hesson was brought in to take charge of the side for the third and final Test, a move which failed to reverse Pakistan's fortunes.

The turmoil intensified when expelled players Mohammad Rizwan and Imam-ul-Haq were investigated by the national cybercrime agency on charges of leaking team information.

Former Pakistan captain Wasim Akram said he had predicted this free fall.

"It's a disappointing state but I could see this coming for the last five years and you can't blame one particular person and one factor because there are many," Akram told AFP.

His fellow former star Shahid Afridi described the situation as "bleak".

"These are gloomy times in Pakistan cricket," Afridi told AFP. "You don't disrespect players like this and your system is not strong."

Changes and upheaval after defeats are hardly new for Pakistan. The cricket team has had three captains and six head coaches for Tests over the last three years.

The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) has also had five different chairmen in as many years, resulting in a lack of consistent planning that has hurt the game's development.

Punishing players has often gone hand in hand with those changes.

The PCB banned then-captain Mohammad Yousuf and senior batter Younis Khan for an indefinite period and disciplined five other players, including Afridi, after a disastrous 3-0 whitewash in Australia in 2010.

The third-test defeat to England at Edgbaston was Pakistan's 16th in their last 21 Tests, leaving them ninth and last on the World Test Championship (WTC) table, the same position in which they finished the previous cycle.

Results in white-ball cricket have not been encouraging either.

Pakistan crashed out in the first round of the ODI Champions Trophy last year, even though the event had marked the revival of their hosting rights after a 29-year exile caused by security concerns.

Their Twenty20 fortunes have also gone into free fall.

Pakistan failed to reach the semi-finals of the 2026 T20 World Cup, while another campaign two years earlier ended in an embarrassing group-stage exit that included a shock defeat against an unfancied USA side.

Former leg-spinner and 1992 World Cup winner Mushtaq Ahmed blamed the decline on a lack of planning.

"We had a great number of match-winners and a strong legacy, and that is why we produced results in the past," Ahmed told AFP. "Now the decline is steep and will take time to fix."

With a flawed and inconsistent domestic system failing to prepare players for the demands of international cricket, an immediate solution appears unlikely.

"We need to realise that we lack talent in red-ball cricket. White-ball teams are okay," said Akram. "It's easy to blame the PCB chairman but when we were sleeping and not addressing the overall flaws then such a fall happens."

Meanwhile, fans are fast losing interest.

"All my four sons and I used to play in a local academy but in the last two years we all have lost interest as our team is not doing well," said Mohammad Afzal, a banker.

"Cricket is fast losing ground in Pakistan and we need strong measures to revive the glory."
Author: AFP, Karachi

Title: Zverev vs Shelton: Two very different stories behind the US Open final
Content:
Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton arrive at Sunday's US Open final from very different places.

For Zverev, this is about finally establishing that he belongs among the Grand Slam winners. For Shelton, it is about proving he can stay at this level against the best player he has faced on this stage.

The German top seed has spent years being measured against Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, the generation that has dominated men's tennis. At 29, after three defeats in Grand Slam finals, there was a growing sense that Zverev might never turn his undoubted talent into a major title.

That changed at Roland Garros. After winning the French Open earlier this year, Zverev has now reached a third straight Grand Slam final and is one victory away from claiming a second major of 2026.

Shelton, meanwhile, is entering his first.

The 23-year-old American has enjoyed a breakthrough season of his own, winning four titles across different surfaces and beating Alcaraz in a marathon quarter-final in New York.

Now he has a chance to complete a remarkable fortnight in front of a partisan home crowd of around 24,000 at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I'm in positions I've never been in before," Shelton said. "I've beaten guys I've never beaten before."

He will need another first. Shelton has lost all five of his previous meetings with Zverev.

Zverev’s road to the US Open final has not been spectacular from start to finish. Some of his opening matches were long, untidy affairs that stretched into the early hours.

But he has steadily improved.

And although he has yet to face a top-20 opponent in New York, the bigger picture is what matters. Zverev no longer looks like a player waiting for his chance.

He looks like a player who expects to take it.

"The question was always: Is Carlos and Jannik going to play all four Grand Slam finals between each other again?" Zverev said.

Their absences through injury have opened the door. Zverev has walked through it.

Now he wants to close the year with another major.

Shelton's story is different.

He is not carrying years of failed Grand Slam finals into New York. He is carrying the opportunity to win one at the first attempt.

The American had reached Grand Slam semi-finals before, including at the 2023 US Open, but this is the first time he has gone one step further.

The significance runs deeper.

Victory would make Shelton the first American man to win a Grand Slam singles title since Andy Roddick at the 2003 US Open. He could also become the first Black American man to win a men's singles major since Arthur Ashe at Wimbledon in 1975.

Shelton insists he is not overwhelmed by the history.

But his tennis suggests he is ready for the occasion.

The 23-year-old has also expanded his game. His serve remains the obvious weapon, regularly pushing beyond 140mph, but the bigger development has been his willingness to stay in rallies and defend when necessary.

His father and coach Bryan Shelton has seen that evolution first-hand.

"He's willing to suffer a little bit in the rallies, go deeper and really use his athleticism," he said.

That development was evident in the biggest win of Shelton's career.

Against Alcaraz, returning to competition after almost five months away, Shelton survived an epic quarter-final that finished at 3:34am and showed that he could withstand both the physical and mental demands of a Grand Slam run.

Now comes a very different test.

Zverev has the experience of five previous Grand Slam finals. Shelton has the confidence of a player who has spent the past two weeks discovering new territory.

That makes their five previous meetings worth little once the final begins.

Can Shelton's explosive serve and aggressive tennis disrupt Zverev before the German settles into the long, physical exchanges in which he is so comfortable? Can Zverev's experience and consistency force Shelton to play one more ball, one more point, one more game than he has been used to?

However it unfolds, both men have already changed their stories in 2026.
Author: Agencies

Title: Fixed vs fluid: The tactical battle between Carrick and Maresca in the Manchester derby
Content:
Manchester United and Manchester City share a city, a history of rivalry and the same ambition to return to the top of English football.

But under Enzo Maresca and Michael Carrick, they are taking strikingly different routes to get there.

When City and United meet on Sunday, the most intriguing battle may not be between Erling Haaland and Bruno Fernandes, or even in the two penalty areas. It could be between structure and freedom.

Maresca wants City to control games through precise positioning, clear roles and rehearsed movements. Carrick has built a United side around a looser framework, giving players positional references but greater freedom to interpret the game as it unfolds.

Fixed versus fluid. That contrast could shape the derby.

Maresca's football has strong roots in positional play, the philosophy associated with his former mentor Pep Guardiola.

The basic idea is simple: put players in the right places and reduce the number of unpredictable situations.

City's shape in possession often resembles a 3-2-5 or 3-1-3-3, with players occupying specific zones across the pitch. There are rotations, but they usually have a purpose and end with City restoring the structure.

It can make them predictable to watch but difficult to defend.

Everyone knows where the next passing option should be. Everyone knows where the space ought to be created. And because those movements are repeated in training, players do not have to invent solutions every time they receive the ball.

Maresca's view of freedom is revealing.

"If the freedom for you is that you can move everywhere, that is not freedom, that is chaos," he once said.

For City, freedom comes within the system.

Rayan Cherki is a useful example. The French playmaker has the technical quality to drift around the pitch looking for the ball, but Maresca wants him in dangerous areas when City are attacking. The instruction is not to eliminate creativity, but to channel it.

That is the trade-off with a fixed system. Individual expression is sometimes restricted, but collective execution becomes sharper.

United are not without positional rules.

Their centre-backs hold their positions in the build-up, while the deepest midfielder can drop between them to create a back three or remain alongside the other central midfielder.

The full-backs have their own reference points too. Higher up the pitch, their positioning changes according to where the wingers are, with one able to move inside while the other stays wide.

But from there, Carrick gives his players considerably more freedom.

Bruno Fernandes is the obvious example.

Starting as a No 10 does not mean he remains in the same corridor for 90 minutes. If he believes moving towards the ball or drifting into another area can create an advantage, he is trusted to do it.

Matheus Cunha has similar licence.

That movement can unsettle defenders because it forces them to make decisions rather than simply follow a pre-programmed pattern.

Follow Fernandes and space opens elsewhere. Do not follow him and United can create an overload around the ball. That uncertainty is part of the plan.

Carrick's players are essentially given a tactical language rather than a complete script.

That difference could make for a fascinating battle in midfield and between the lines.

City's structure is designed to stretch opponents, move them around and create space through disciplined positioning. United, meanwhile, will look to attract pressure towards the ball before exploiting the gaps that appear elsewhere.

The interesting question is what happens when those philosophies collide.

If United's roaming players repeatedly drag City defenders and midfielders away from their zones, Maresca's carefully constructed shape could be tested in situations it was not designed to handle.

But there is a danger for United too.

Fluidity only works when everyone understands what everyone else is doing.

A player may have the freedom to leave his position, but somebody else has to recognise that movement and cover the space behind him. A moment of hesitation can turn improvisation into imbalance.

City's fixed structure offers fewer such risks.

Their players may be easier to read, but that does not mean they are easier to stop. When the movements are rehearsed and executed quickly, knowing what is coming is one thing; stopping it is another.

That is why Maresca's approach can provide consistency, particularly with a team still developing its chemistry.

Carrick's method may ultimately offer United something different: unpredictability.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Why Chelsea keep losing control of games
Content:
Chelsea have made a habit of starting games brilliantly. The problem is what happens next.

For the fourth time in six matches this season, they took the lead but failed to turn control into victory, held to a 2-2 draw by promoted Hull City at Stamford Bridge.

Morgan Rogers gave Chelsea the perfect start in the seventh minute on Saturday, driving into the area before finding the bottom corner with a crisp left-footed finish.

The hosts were in complete control. Yet, within six minutes, they had somehow gone from one goal ahead to one behind.

Mohamed Belloumi scored twice, with both goals exposing the defensive fragility that has followed Chelsea into the new season.

For the first, Jorrel Hato failed to deal with a long ball into the area, allowing it to bounce before Belloumi finished. The second came from a Hull corner. Emiliano Martinez came for the cross but failed to reach it, and although Semi Ajayi’s header struck the bar, Oli McBurnie kept the move alive before Belloumi’s shot took a deflection off Levi Colwill on its way in.

Joao Pedro eventually rescued a point for Xabi Alonso’s side, but the bigger concern remains the same.

Chelsea have conceded in 20 consecutive Premier League games, a run that tells its own story. Opponents now have every reason to believe they can score against them, regardless of how well Chelsea begin.

They have taken the lead in five of their six matches this season. Only Luton Town, in the Carabao Cup, have failed to score against them.

There is a recurring pattern.

Chelsea dominated after Rogers’ opener, with their passing and movement earning loud applause around Stamford Bridge. Then came a stoppage while Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis received treatment.

From the resulting restart, Tzolakis sent a long ball forward. Chelsea failed to deal with it, Ryan Giles hooked it into the area and Hato misjudged the bounce. Belloumi did not need a second invitation.

The goal was a reminder that Chelsea can go from looking completely in control to making elementary defensive errors in a matter of moments.

And once Hull equalised, Chelsea lost their composure. Six minutes later, they were behind.

That inability to respond calmly to setbacks has been a recurring problem at Stamford Bridge in recent seasons, and Alonso is discovering that changing the manager does not automatically change the habits.

Chelsea even had warning signs before falling behind for a second time. Martinez had already produced a fine save to deny Lewie Coyle, while Ajayi headed against the bar.

Hull were not simply hanging on. They believed they could win.

That may be the most concerning part for Chelsea.

A team with title ambitions should not allow a newly promoted side to sense that a game is there for the taking after going behind early.

Alonso had already made one notable selection call by leaving Maxence Lacroix on the bench after five consecutive starts, but changing personnel has not yet solved Chelsea’s defensive problems.

Until they learn how to control the difficult periods of matches, the same mistakes will continue to cost them points.

That is where the optimism surrounding Chelsea needs to be tempered.

There is plenty to like about Alonso’s team going forward. They are aggressive, entertaining and capable of creating chances at will.

But title contenders also need to know when to slow a game down, protect a lead and kill off an opponent’s momentum.

Chelsea are not doing that.

A 2-1 defeat at Arsenal last week was hardly embarrassing. Arsenal are among the favourites for the title and Chelsea competed well.

But dropping two points at home to newly promoted Hull immediately afterwards is a different matter.

Depending on the other results this weekend, Chelsea could already find themselves five points behind the champions and Manchester City.

There are mitigating factors. Alonso is still building his team, and the absence of Moises Caicedo has deprived Chelsea of an influential presence in midfield.

His return cannot come soon enough.

Chelsea’s realistic minimum target remains Champions League qualification, whether through a top-four or top-five finish.

That is still well within their reach.

But talk of Chelsea going toe-to-toe with Arsenal for the title looks premature.

Before they can challenge for the biggest prize, they need to solve a much simpler problem: when they have control, they need to learn how to keep it.
Author: Agencies

Title: Messi’s stunner in vain as Inter Miami held to 2-2 draw
Content:
Lionel Messi extended his incredible scoring streak against MLS-leaders Nashville on Sunday as Inter Miami battled to a 2-2 draw in their top-of-the-table Eastern Conference clash.

Messi curled in a superb strike on 62 minutes at Miami's Nu Stadium to fire Inter into a 2-1 lead but Nashville grabbed a share of the points after striker Sam Surridge bundled in an injury-time equaliser.

The 39-year-old Messi has now scored a remarkable 17 goals in 14 games against Nashville in all competitions since joining Miami in 2023.

And Messi could have even improved his goals record against in Sunday's game between the first and second-placed sides in the Eastern Conference.

Messi saw a shot crash off the underside of the bar in the 50th minute and also saw a shot cannon off the post in the 78th minute. A late Messi effort was also headed clear by Nashville defender Jeisson Palacios before Surridge's leveler.

The result leaves Inter nine points adrift of Nashville in the race for top seeding with nine regular season games remaining.

Earlier, Nashville had got off to a dream start when English striker Surridge sprang the offside trap before burying a low shot into the bottom corner in the fourth minute.

But Miami drew level midway through the half and again Messi was involved. The World Cup-winner's wicked in-swinging corner found the head of Nashville defender Reed Baker-Whiting, who glanced in an own goal.

It looked as if Messi had grabbed the winner midway through the second half when he combined with former Argentina international team-mate Rodrigo De Paul on the edge of the area before curling a shot beyond the dive of Brian Schwake.

But Miami's failure to extend their lead proved costly as Surridge scored from close range in injury time to steal a point.
Author: AFP, Miami

Title: ‘Let’s see if Elena can beat me’: A playful challenge from the dethroned No. 1
Content:
Aryna Sabalenka may have lost her US Open crown and world No. 1 ranking to Elena Rybakina, but the Belarusian still had a joke to share -- challenging her new rival to match her 99-week reign at the top at a stretch.

Sabalenka held the number one position for a total of 107 weeks -- including the stretch of 99 straight weeks that will end on Monday.

"Ninety-nine? Well, that's amazing. Let's see if Elena can beat me in that," Sabalenka said with a laugh after Rybakina defeated her 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in Sunday’s final.

“She continue to play like that, then yeah, I’m in trouble,” added the 28-year-old.

The defeat was a bitter one for Sabalenka, ending her bid for a third straight US Open title and denying her the chance to join Serena Williams and Chris Evert as the only women in the professional era to win three consecutive championships at Flushing Meadows.

The weight of that pursuit, she admitted, made the final especially difficult.

“It’s really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat,” Sabalenka told reporters.

Her frustration boiled over twice as she fired a ball into the crowd and later broke her racket while Rybakina maintained her composure and pulled away in the deciding set.

“I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, I wouldn’t be able to say a word,” she said.

Despite the disappointment, Sabalenka vowed to use the lessons from a difficult season as motivation to return stronger.

“As experience shows, I only come back stronger, and all of these lessons this season definitely already made me stronger, but definitely going to motivate me for the next year to do better job,” she said.

The defeat marked her first year without a Grand Slam title since 2022, after she lost the Australian Open final to Rybakina, exited the French Open in the quarterfinals and fell in the fourth round at Wimbledon.

Rybakina’s victory ended Sabalenka’s 20-match winning streak at Flushing Meadows and gave the Kazakh her third Grand Slam title and first US Open crown.

For Sabalenka, though, the next target is clear: come back stronger -- and see if Rybakina can match her at the top.
Author: Agencies

Title: ‘He made a difference’: Mourinho praises game-changer Guler
Content:
Arda Guler’s introduction proved the turning point as Real Madrid regained control after a shaky start to the second half and defeated Rayo Vallecano 4-1 on Saturday to pull level with Barcelona at the top of LaLiga.

Jose Mourinho’s side looked in complete command after taking a 3-0 lead into half-time, but Rayo came out with renewed purpose after the break. The visitors launched a series of attacks in the opening 10 minutes, testing Thibaut Courtois several times as Sergio Camello pulled one back in the 51st minute.

Rayo began dominating possession and creating most of the chances, leaving Real looking increasingly unsettled. Mourinho responded by bringing on Aurelien Tchouameni for Bernardo Silva in the 69th minute, with Tchouameni and Eduardo Camavinga, who had replaced Federico Valverde at half-time, forming a more defensive double pivot.

But the game changed when Guler replaced Yan Diomande three minutes later.

The Turkish midfielder immediately demanded the ball, linking the defence with the attack and helping Real regain their rhythm. His influence was reflected in his numbers: despite playing just over 20 minutes, Guler completed 16 of 18 passes, created five chances -- including two big chances -- and registered one shot on target.

He also provided the assist for Kylian Mbappe’s second of the night in stoppage time, sealing a convincing victory that had looked far less certain after the break.

“Arda is very good, he’s got a lot of quality, he influences the team’s play in a good way and today he made a difference in terms of the stability of the game,” Mourinho told Real Madrid TV.

The victory saw Real recover from their previous LaLiga defeat by Real Betis, with Mbappe scoring twice and Jude Bellingham and Alvaro Carreras also finding the net.

“We killed the game in the first half -- that’s not easy, working like we did after the Champions League game, not just physically, but mentally,” Mourinho said of Real’s dominant opening 45 minutes.

But it was Guler’s arrival that helped ensure Rayo’s second-half resurgence did not turn into a damaging collapse.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Rybakina reigns serene as new world number one
Content:
Elena Rybakina punctuated her rise to world number one with a US Open title on Sunday, but the Kazakh star at the summit of the women's game remains an enigmatic figure.

The powerful game is there to see, but the thoughts and emotions driving it are largely shrouded -- and that's the way Rybakina prefers it to be.

"Elena is not nonchalant, I don't want to say that, but just no reaction ever," said American Coco Gauff, who fell to Rybakina in the semi-finals in New York.

"We're all feeling nerves and stuff. Now, how much of that she lets get to her, we don't know, and I think that's the strength of her. You can never see what she's feeling."

When Rybakina beat Ons Jabeur for her first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in 2022, she didn't shout with joy or flop to the grass.

She raised one clenched fist before heading to her chair.

"I'm going to have to teach her how to celebrate properly," Jabeur quipped.

But Moscow-born Rybakina, who opted in 2018 to represent Kazakhstan, says it's a tactical choice to keep her feelings in check on court.

"Well, it's a lot of emotions," she said. "I'm trying to hide it, because you just don't want to let the opponent also see your frustration when something is going wrong.

"People who know me well, long enough, they read even little changes in my face."

Rybakina has found her famous composure challenged in the face of off-court controversy.

Russian players were banned the year she won Wimbledon, and she faced numerous questions about choosing to play under the Kazakh flag when she was a little-known 19-year-old ranked 175th in the world.

"They believed in me. There is no more question about how I feel," she snapped then, and when she cemented her rise to number one in the world by reaching the semi-finals in New York she spoke proudly of representing the country that backed her pro career.

"Every time I come back to Kazakhstan, no matter which city I go, it's always so many kids," she said. "Now they play tennis, and more and more are coming to the tennis facilities. It just proves that everything is possible if you believe, if you work hard."

But tennis stardom wasn't something she dreamed of as child, Rybakina said.

"I never thought that I'm going to be professional or I'm going to be even playing on these kind of tournaments on the biggest stages.

"I was just enjoying playing tennis after school, hanging out with the friends. It was just for fun."

Now she's a three-time Grand Slam champion. She bested Sabalenka in the Australian Open final in January to claim her second, four years after her Wimbledon triumph.

The intervening years had seen her on-off Croatian coach Stefano Vukov -- who guided her to Wimbledon success -- suspended over a potential breach of the WTA's code of conduct.

Vukov was reported to have used harsh and abusive behaviour towards players, claims he denied.

Rybakina was exasperated by the allegations and suspension, refusing to pose for a photo with WTA chief executive Portia Archer after Rybakina's victory at the Riyadh Masters in November 2025.

She's had Vukov back in her corner since the suspension was lifted.

Now the winner of 14 titles, Rybakina has twice led the WTA in aces in a season and has significantly improved her baseline game, according to American world number three Jessica Pegula.

But Pegula, like Gauff, thinks Rybakina's self-control remains her greatest strength.

"Cool as a cucumber," Pegula said after falling to Rybakina in the Australian Open semi-finals. "She's so chill. She doesn't really give you anything.

"You're not really sure if she's upset or if she's excited or what it is. I think in today's game that goes a long way."
Author: AFP, New York

Title: Rishad, Aliss shine as Bangladesh 'A' clinch series in South Africa
Content:
Rishad Hossain and Aliss Al Islam shared seven wickets before Saif Hassan and Mohammad Naim hit fifties as Bangladesh ‘A’ registered a five-wicket win over South Africa ‘A’ in the third and final one-dayer in Potchefstroom on Saturday, sealing the series 1-0.

Rishad claimed 4-45 and Aliss 3-35 as Bangladesh dominated with the ball and bowled South Africa ‘A’ out for 182 in 40 overs after opting to field.

Skipper Marques Ackerman top-scored with 54 off 61 balls, while number nine Imran Manack made 43 off 53 balls to give the hosts a fighting total. Without their late resistance, South Africa ‘A’ could have been dismissed for a much lower score as they were reduced to 89-6 at one stage.

Bangladesh got off to a flying start in the chase, with Saif and Naim putting on 92 for the opening wicket to lay the foundation for victory. Saif was eventually dismissed for 61 off 53 balls, hitting nine fours and three sixes.

Bangladesh lost a few more wickets thereafter, but Naim remained composed before falling for 60 off 77 balls. The visitors, however, had already done enough to reach 185-5 in 33 overs and finish the series on a high.

Kyle Simmonds took three wickets for South Africa ‘A’.

The opening match, which witnessed only 11 overs’ play, ended without a result, while the second was abandoned without a ball being bowled.

Bangladesh had earlier lost the preceding two-match four-day series 1-0. They suffered an innings-and-413-run defeat in the opening game before Tawhid Hridoy’s unbeaten 350 helped them draw the second
Author: Star Sports Report

Title: ‘Neither guilty nor innocent’: Excluded BPL players free to play
Content:
Cricketers excluded from the 12th edition of the Bangladesh Premier League (BPL) over suspicions of involvement in fixing-related irregularities are free to play in other competitions in Bangladesh, according to Alex Marshall, independent chair of the BCB’s Integrity Unit.

Marshall, speaking to reporters in Mirpur on Saturday, clarified that his recommendation to exclude the players applied specifically to BPL 12 and did not prevent them from participating in other tournaments.

A day before the players’ auction for BPL 12 in November last year, the BCB excluded several local cricketers from the auction list over suspicions of their involvement in fixing-related irregularities during the previous edition.

The decision came following a recommendation from Marshall, who advised the board not to include any cricketers or officials who had been “red-flagged” by the board’s inquiry committee.

“The only advice I gave about not inviting people was not nine; it was a higher number, and it was specifically for BPL 12. There are no restrictions on any of the players taking part in cricket unless they are currently charged, and none of them have been charged. Therefore, they are clear to play,” Marshall told reporters.

Several of those players have since featured in different domestic tournaments organised by the BCB, while one has also represented Bangladesh in national colours.

However, when Integrity Unit general counsel and BCB lawyer Mahin M Rahman was asked whether the players had been completely cleared of the allegations, he said: “They are neither guilty nor innocent.”

Since Marshall’s appointment, the Integrity Unit has charged several individuals with breaching different provisions of the ICC Anti-Corruption Code. The latest cases were announced on September 1, when a former BCB director and two other individuals were charged.

Marshall said more names could be announced in the coming weeks.

“Some of the people who were charged in recent weeks have already accepted their charges and are awaiting their agreed sanctions.

“We’ve announced eight cases in recent weeks. There are more cases under investigation. You can expect to see some more announcements in the coming weeks.”
Author: Sports Reporter

Title: ‘Beauty of Pakistan's raw talent’, Razaullah provides ‘the missing intent’ in England Test series
Content:
A young Razaullah arrived in the northern Pakistani city of Mardan with his two elder brothers, dreaming to make it big in cricket with his thunderbolt deliveries and powerful hitting.

His brother Samiullah did not want his sibling to be a truck loader like him, and instead made sure the tall and strapping fast bowler went to the town's cricket academy on his way to play for his country.

Razaullah dismissed one of the world's best batters Joe Root with his fourth ball on his Test debut before smashing nine sixes in a sensational innings of 81 against England at Edgbaston.

The 21-year-old's fearless batting brought Pakistan from the brink of an innings defeat on Friday as he added a fighting 121 runs for the ninth wicket with Mohammad Abbas, who scored 42.

His sensational hits -- some landing in the under-construction hotel adjacent to the stadium -- caused a sensation from England's Midlands to Mardan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa back home.

"This is the beauty of Pakistan's raw talent," said commentator Urooj Mumtaz, a former Pakistan women's captain. "He batted fearlessly and entertained all those who were watching. It was sensational."

Razaullah himself admitted he wanted to entertain others and enjoy himself.

"I just had to bat, you are the ones who get to enjoy it," he said in post-match comments on Sky.

Just like his sensational Edgbaston knock, Razaullah's induction to the Pakistan team was as much out of the blue.

Smarting from humiliating defeats in the first two Tests, Pakistan withdrew seven players in a shock reaction, drafting as many new ones -- with unheralded and uncapped Razaullah one of them.

Razaullah's coming of age at the international level will inspire the next generation of players.

The unassuming young man left his remote village of Wari in the hilly parts of Upper Dir -- an area close to Lower Dir from where another fast bowler Naseem Shah emerged in 2019.

He endeared himself to everyone at the Mardan academy for his obsession to bowl as fast as Shoaib Akhtar -- the former Pakistan express pacer -- and ability to clear the boundary off many deliveries bowled to him.

"He (Razaullah) came for Under-19 trials in 2023 wearing spikes bigger than his size and with his first delivery he sent the batter staggering with his speed," Mardan and Abbottabad coach Ahmed Said told AFP earlier this year.

"I asked him not to bowl another delivery for fear of causing injury to any young and inexperienced batter."

Said recalled Razaullah always wanted the Number 14 shirt that Akhtar used to wear.

"Razaullah insisted he wanted a Number 14 shirt in the National Twenty20 Cup and was elated after he got it, albeit two sizes bigger, and we all started to call him Shobby."

Former Pakistan coach Abdul Rehman spotted Razaullah in a Twenty20 tournament in Quetta and recruited him for the Rawalpindiz team in the Pakistan Super League, where he impressed with his speed.

Pakistan selector Aaqib Javed helped his growth in the High Performance Center in Lahore, from where he jetted to England.

Razaullah's idol Akhtar was impressed with his play.

"Look at his intent and fearless batting and this was the intent Pakistan players were missing in earlier matches," Akhtar said on television.

"He is a product of the Pakistan Cricket Board's pathway, and it's now the duty of the coaches to manage him properly so that he can progress further."
Author: AFP, Karachi

Title: Workload concerns prompt Hasan’s early return from Kent
Content:
The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) has decided to cut short pacer Hasan Mahmud’s County stint with Kent, with the pacer set to return home soon to join the Asian Games camp, which begins in Mirpur on Sunday.

Hasan, who has taken 26 wickets in four matches in County Championship Division Two this season, was initially granted a No Objection Certificate (NOC) until September 27. However, after being named in Bangladesh’s Asian Games squad, the BCB changed its decision and called him back to manage his workload.

“He has been playing continuous cricket since joining County cricket around April. He played two matches, then went to Zimbabwe and played a Test. From there, he played in the Blast [Vitality Blast Men T20] and the LPL. After the LPL, he played two Tests against Australia. After those two Tests, he played two more County matches and has been bowling a high volume of overs per match,” BCB cricket operations in-charge Shahriar Nafees told The Daily Star today.

“We have the Asian Games, the tour involving Afghanistan, the West Indies series, the South Africa tour, and domestic T20 cricket. Given the amount of cricket he has played and our upcoming schedule, his workload is getting excessive and he needs a break. That is why we decided he should return.”

“When he was originally granted the NOC, he was only part of the Test squad. He is showing good performances for Bangladesh and in County cricket, which increases his opportunities for Bangladesh.

“He is returning now and will not participate further this season. They have two matches remaining, and he will go to the Asian Games, but right now he needs a break and fitness work. Considering everything, the BCB felt his workload was becoming excessive.”

Meanwhile, chief selector Habibul Bashar said the Bangladesh ‘A’ team players, currently in South Africa, who are part of the Asian Games squad will join the camp after returning home.

Parvez Hossain Emon, Saif Hassan, Tawhid Hridoy, Rishad Hossain and Mohammad Saifuddin are among those players. Bangladesh ‘A’ won the three-match one-day series 1-0 after beating South Africa A by five wickets in Potchefstroom on Saturday to conclude their tour.

“Those A team players will probably join two days later,” Habibul said.

Bangladesh are expected to leave for Japan on September 25 for the Asian Games. They will enter the cricket competition at the quarterfinal stage and face the Group B winners -- Hong Kong, Malaysia or Oman -- on September 29.
Author: Sports Reporter

Title: Nepal qualify for Men's Asia Cup 2027
Content:
Nepal's rise continues on the cricketing horizons of Asia, as the side secured a place in next year's Asia Cup, where they have the prospect of facing full-member nations such as India, Sri Lanka, Bangldesh and Pakistan.

This is Nepal's second apperance in the Asia Cup, the first came in 2023 in Sri Lanka.

Nepal elected to bat first in the ACC Men's Premier Cup Final against UAE in Bayuemas Oval, Kuala Lumpur.

Opener Aasif Sheikh set the base for Nepal's winning total with his 102 off 106, with good support from Rohit Paudel (40) and Gulshan Jha (52).

Ibrar Ahmad (4/62) had the best bowling figures for the Emiratis, but eventually the Rhinos managed to get to 313/9.

Despite a spirited start from Tanish Suri (42 off 28), the UAE innings lost its way as Karan KC (3/49) and Lalit Rajbanshi (2/43) brought key breakthroughs. Despite an unbeaten ton from Rahul Chopra, UAE fell short by 44 runs.

Sandeep Lamichhane was the Player of the Series for his 17 scalps, while Aasif was the Player of the Match for his splendid knock.
Author: ICC

Title: England survive scare to complete series sweep against Pakistan
Content:
England overcame a major wobble to beat Pakistan by eight wickets in the third Test at Edgbaston on Saturday, sealing a 3-0 series sweep.

The home team, chasing just 130 to win, were in deep trouble when openers Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay were dismissed in the first over, bowled by Mohammad Abbas.

Joe Root, England's record runscorer, edged his first ball, bowled by Razaullah, through the slips for four in a nervy start but settled and scored quickly to take the sting out of the situation.

The skipper was given a huge reprieve when he chopped onto the stumps off Mohammad Ali, only for the umpire to signal a no ball, leaving the bowler distraught.

Root, with Jordan Cox at the other end, had another let-off when he edged an Abbas delivery between first and second slip, with neither fielder moving.

But he reached his half-century off 57 balls with a cut for four and Cox matched him shortly afterwards.

England reached their target in the 25th over, with Root unbeaten on 62 and Cox 59 not out.

Root's men had appeared set for a quickfire win inside three days on Friday before debutant fast bowler Razaullah launched an audacious assault with the bat, clubbing nine sixes as he raced to 81 off 63 balls.

The 21-year-old number nine, who also took four wickets in England's first innings, put on 121 for the ninth wicket with fellow paceman Abbas (42) as England floundered.

Razaullah's heroics have changed the mood music but they came too little, too late for Pakistan, who have endured a miserable series, losing the first Test by an innings and 103 runs and the second by 194 runs.

The tourists sent seven players home after their crushing defeat in the second Test at Lord's and brought in seven replacements, with Razaullah among them.

They also sacked head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul as their tour plunged into chaos.

Pakistan made four changes to their side for the third Test and they put up a fight despite being dismissed for a paltry 133 in their first innings.

The 3-0 whitewash is a huge tonic for England, who were in turmoil just weeks ago following a series loss to New Zealand and the exits of head coach Brendon McCullum and captain Ben Stokes.

But tougher challenges lie ahead, starting with a Test series in South Africa in December and January, while a home Ashes looms next year.
Author: AFP, Birmingham

Title: Miraz continues impressive CPL run with four-wicket haul
Content:
Mehidy Hasan Miraz continued his impressive start to the Caribbean Premier League with a four-wicket haul as Guyana Amazon Warriors beat Trinbago Knight Riders by six wickets in Providence on Saturday.

Playing his second match of the tournament, Miraz returned 4-23 from four overs to help restrict the defending champions to 126-8 in 20 overs. He had taken three wickets in his first appearance, leaving him with seven wickets for 36 runs from his first two CPL matches.

The Bangladesh all-rounder made an immediate impact after Guyana chose to field. In the fifth over, Miraz dismissed Colin Munro for 26 and Nicholas Pooran for a golden duck with consecutive deliveries, reducing Trinbago to 41-2.

Miraz celebrated both wickets with his trademark ‘Nagin dance’, and he returned to strike twice more later in the innings. He dismissed Jyd Goolie for four in the 13th over before removing Sunil Narine for seven in the 15th.

His four wickets came at an economy rate of 5.75, as his off-spin repeatedly troubled the Knight Riders. Justin Greaves, who scored 35 off 37 balls, was Trinbago’s top scorer, while Akeal Hosein remained unbeaten on 12.

Guyana made a cautious start to the chase, losing Mavendra Dindyal for 19 and Glenn Phillips for 11 inside the first seven overs. But Shai Hope steadied the innings with an unbeaten 42 off 35 balls, including one four and two sixes.

Hope and Shimron Hetmyer then put the Amazon Warriors in control with a 51-run partnership. Hetmyer struck three sixes in his 19-ball 28 before falling in the 13th over, but Hope stayed until the end to complete the chase.

Miraz was dismissed for 2 off 14 balls, but his earlier spell had done much of the damage.

Guyana reached 127-4 in 18.4 overs, with Quentin Sampson unbeaten on 12, sealing victory with eight balls remaining.

The win was the Amazon Warriors’ eighth in nine matches, strengthening their position at the top of the CPL table. It was also the franchise’s 100th win in the competition.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Nine sixes, 81 runs: Debutant Razaullah’s heroics keep England waiting for clean sweep
Content:
Debutant Razaullah launched a remarkable late salvo as Pakistan finally showed some fight at Edgbaston on Friday, setting England a target of 130 to seal a clean sweep in their three-Test series.

The fast bowler came to the crease with the tourists on the brink of defeat at 318-8, still two runs behind the home side, with more than two hours of play potentially remaining.

Showing no sign of nerves, the 21-year-old launched an audacious assault, clubbing nine sixes in his 81 off 63 balls -- and sharing a ninth-wicket partnership of 121 with fellow paceman Mohammad Abbas.

His tally of sixes tied Ben Stokes's record for the most maximums in a Test innings in England, set against Australia in 2023.

Pakistan, who have endured a torrid series, were eventually dismissed for 449, forcing the match into a fourth day.

"I just had to bat, you are the ones who got to enjoy it," Razaullah told Sky Sports. "I was planning to take it longer and deeper -- 81 runs is not bad though.

"The ball was in my slot. I was eyeing that up and trying to provide support for the other batters and trying to take it as deep as possible.

"I broke both my bats and wore down my third. I have six bats, I've come prepared."

Razaullah was the last man out, stumped by stand-in wicketkeeper Jordan Cox off the bowling of spinner Dan Lawrence.

Earlier, Shan Masood scored 95 and captain Babar Azam made 76 as much-changed Pakistan passed 200 for the first time in the series at the sixth attempt.

The visitors, facing a first-innings deficit of 320, lost two wickets without scoring a single run on Thursday but opener Azan Awais and the experienced Masood took the score to 125 before Awais was dismissed by Lawrence for 59.

Masood was in sight of an eighth Test hundred when he fell to a sensational slip catch by Lawrence off the bowling of Gus Atkinson.

Azam, who missed the first Test with an injured hand, batted fluently but got a feather of a touch to a Josh Tongue delivery, with Cox taking the catch.

Saud Shakeel (29) was next to go, caught by Emilio Gay at short leg while trying to fend off a Jofra Archer bouncer, while two more Cox catches accounted for Ghazi Ghori and Mohammad Imran.

But Pakistan were not finished as Abbas joined Razaullah at the crease for their show of evening fireworks.

Razaullah showed his intent early, clubbing three sixes off Atkinson in four balls and the pair brought up their fifty partnership off just 57 balls.

Inspired, Abbas, with a previous top Test score of 29, smashed Ollie Robinson for six as England looked powerless to stop the carnage.

Razaullah reached his 50 off 43 balls with a fifth six, this time off Archer, repeating the dose the following ball to leave the England man shaking his head.

Abbas was eventually caught by Atkinson off the bowling of Tongue for 42, ending a spellbinding partnership.

Razaullah, who had by now removed his helmet to face Lawrence, launched the ball into the stands to move into the 80s in the final over of the day.

He successfully appealed an lbw decision but was stumped by Cox off the next ball for 81 as the spectators applauded him off.

His sparkling knock comes after he took four wickets in England's first innings in a debut that he will never forget.

Joe Root's side have dominated the series, winning the first Test by an innings and 103 runs and the second by 194 runs and remain likely to complete the whitewash on Saturday.

Pakistan, who have endured a disastrous tour, released seven players and sacked head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul after their defeat in the second Test, making four changes to their side in Birmingham.
Author: AFP, Birmingham

Title: Asia Cup failures rooted in weak pipeline
Content:
The meek nature of Bangladesh women’s team’s performance in the Asia Cup exposed the widening gap between Bangladesh and the growing cricket nations. The toothless campaign has even brought scrutiny on their biggest triumph, with suggestions that the 2018 Asia Cup title was a one-off rather than a sign of sustained progress.

Women’s cricket has grown rapidly in recent years, and the Asia Cup highlighted not only Bangladesh’s in-game limitations but also the lack of growth behind them, largely stemming from a weak domestic pipeline.

The inability to chase targets around or above 150 was particularly telling. It was evident again when the Tigresses fell 40 runs short of India’s 150 in Thursday’s semifinal in Dubai.

“I wouldn't say the intent was wrong, but in terms of shot execution, we probably didn't choose the right option,” batting coach Nasiruddin Faruque told The Daily Star.

While India’s approach was deliberate, targeting Marufa Akter and off-spinner Sultana Khatun, Bangladesh’s batters struggled to adapt their individual plans during the chase.
