Title: Mungdi brings hill cuisine to Dhaka
Content:
A bowl of Mungdi does not rely on thick gravy or an abundance of spices. Handmade rice noodles sit in a light chicken-stock broth, accompanied by egg, chicken, fish or prawns. The broth remains delicate, the ingredients recognisable and the flavours closer to the natural character of the food.

For many diners in Dhaka, however, even the name is unfamiliar. Tara Bikash Tripura, owner of Mungdi Restaurant, is working to change that by introducing traditional foods from the hilly regions to a wider audience.

“Mungdi is one of our traditional soup items,” he explains. “The broth is very light and does not contain many spices. It has a natural flavour that comes from chicken stock.”

According to Tripura, the restaurant serves five variations: Egg Mungdi, Chicken Mungdi, Fish Mungdi, Prawn Mungdi, and Special Mungdi. The broth remains largely the same, while the main accompaniment changes. Egg Mungdi contains a whole egg, while Chicken Mungdi is served with sliced chicken.

Each bowl also contains handmade rice noodles brought from the hilly regions. For Tripura, sourcing these ingredients helps maintain a connection between the food served in Dhaka and the places where the recipes are traditionally prepared.

Before opening Mungdi Restaurant, Tara Bikash Tripura worked for a company for around eight to 10 years. During that period, he continued thinking about establishing a restaurant of his own.

“I always had a passion for opening a restaurant,” he recalls, adding, “I had been planning it for a long time. After eight to 10 years of preparation and planning, I finally opened this place on June 15 last year.”

The beginning was difficult. As a new establishment serving unfamiliar food, the restaurant struggled to find workers and earn customers’ confidence.

“People did not trust us at first,” he recounts. “So, I started it myself along with some of my cousins. Three or four of us managed everything together.”

Gradually, customers began discovering the restaurant and learning about its menu. “Now we are in a much better position than before,” Tripura elaborates. “People are becoming familiar with our traditional food. Our customers are satisfied, and that makes me very happy.”

Although the restaurant is named after the soup, the menu includes several other traditional preparations.

One is Toja Morich Bhorta, made with boiled vegetables and chilli mash. Dried fish, onion and a little lemon are added, and the dish is eaten by mixing it with rice.

The menu also includes Chicken Laksa, made with steamed chicken, lemon and chilli.

“The chicken is steamed and then prepared with lemon and chilli,” Tripura explains. “It is a sour and spicy, salad-style item. People really enjoy it as a snack.”

Together, these dishes show the range of flavours and techniques found in the food traditions of the hilly regions. Steaming, boiling, mashing and lightly seasoning ingredients allow the natural taste of vegetables, herbs, bamboo shoots, fish and meat to remain prominent.

Running the restaurant involves more than preparing food. Tripura and his team must also explain the dishes to customers who may never have heard their names.

“At first, people ask, ‘What is this?’ because they have not even heard the names,” he says. “We have to present it to them very politely and explain what it is.”

There is always some uncertainty when a new customer tastes the food. “We feel a little anxious about whether they will like it, since they are not accustomed to these flavours,” he admits.

Positive feedback, therefore, carries particular significance.

“When a customer says the food is good, it feels like a great achievement for us,” he says. “It means we are successfully reviving something that was being lost.”

Tripura remembers a time when these dishes were more common in Khagrachari, where he once lived. He believes the growing popularity of fast food is gradually pushing traditional foods out of everyday life.

“With the rise of various fast-food items in Bangladesh, our traditional food and culture are on the verge of fading away,” he remarks.

The disappearance of a dish can also mean the loss of knowledge about local plants, ingredients and preparation methods. Preserving indigenous food therefore requires more than documenting recipes. The dishes must continue to be cooked, served and taught, while the communities behind them receive proper recognition.

“I hope more people start doing this so our heritage and culture can survive,” Tripura says.

Mungdi offers a reminder that Bangladesh’s culinary identity extends far beyond its most familiar dishes. In one light bowl of broth and handmade rice noodles lies a story of migration, entrepreneurship and cultural preservation.

Each time Tripura explains an unfamiliar dish to a customer, another traditional name enters Dhaka’s food vocabulary. Each bowl served becomes a small but meaningful act of keeping that heritage alive.

Author: A Ayman Anika Ayman Anika

Title: Recipes that keep your gas cylinder going longer
Content:
With the ongoing gas shortage, every extra minute the stove stays on feels like a luxury. The good news is that delicious meals do not always require long hours over a flame. These recipes are designed to keep cooking time to a minimum, while also keeping the kitchen cooler during the sweltering summer heat. Whether you are looking for a quick lunch, a light dinner, or a refreshing snack, these low-effort dishes prove that less time at the stove does not have to mean less flavour.

1 cup cooked brown rice

150g boneless chicken breast (boiled and sliced)

150g button mushrooms (sliced)

1 small apple (diced)

1 small cucumber (diced)

2 tbsp chopped walnuts (optional)

Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté the mushrooms for 4–5 minutes until tender and lightly browned. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper, then let cool slightly.

In a small bowl, whisk together the olive oil, lemon juice, honey, salt, and black pepper until well combined.

In a large bowl, combine the cooked brown rice, sliced chicken, sautéed mushrooms, diced apple, and cucumber.

Pour the dressing over the salad and toss gently until evenly coated. Sprinkle with chopped walnuts, if using. Serve immediately while the mushrooms are still slightly warm, or chill for 15 minutes before serving.

2 packs instant ramen noodles

2 tbsp creamy peanut butter

1 tbsp sesame oil (optional)

2 cloves garlic (minced)

1 small cucumber (julienned)

1 carrot (julienned)

2 spring onions (thinly sliced)

1 tbsp roasted peanuts (chopped)

1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (optional)

Cook the ramen noodles according to the package instructions for two to three minutes. Drain and rinse thoroughly under cold running water until completely cooled. Drain well.

In a bowl, whisk together the peanut butter, soy sauce, sesame oil, vinegar, honey, ginger, garlic, and cold water until smooth and creamy.

Add the chilled noodles to the sauce and toss until evenly coated. Divide the noodles between two serving bowls and top with the cucumber, carrot, spring onions, chopped peanuts, sesame seeds, and cilantro.

Serve immediately, or chill for 10–15 minutes for an even cooler, more refreshing meal.

300g medium shrimp, peeled and deveined

3 tbsp extra virgin olive oil

1 cup cherry tomatoes (optional)

¼ cup black olives (sliced)

2 tbsp fresh lemon juice

¼ tsp red chilli flakes

Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste

30g Parmesan cheese, shaved (optional)

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil and cook the pasta until al dente. Drain, rinse briefly under cold water, and toss with 1 tablespoon olive oil to prevent sticking. Let it cool.

Season the shrimp with salt and pepper. Heat 1 tablespoon olive oil in a skillet over medium-high heat and sauté the shrimp for 2–3 minutes per side until pink and just cooked through. Add the garlic during the last 30 seconds and cook until fragrant. Remove from the heat and let cool slightly.

In a large bowl, combine the cooled pasta, shrimp, cherry tomatoes, cucumber, and olives.

In a small bowl, whisk together the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil, lemon juice, lemon zest, chilli flakes, salt, and black pepper.

Pour the dressing over the salad and toss gently until everything is evenly coated. Chill for 15–20 minutes before serving to allow the flavours to meld. Garnish with shaved Parmesan and extra herbs, if desired. Serve cold or at room temperature.

4 slices sandwich bread (white or whole wheat)

160g tuna in water or oil (drained and flaked)

¼ cup sweet corn kernels (cooked and drained)

1 tbsp spring onions (finely chopped)

In a medium bowl, combine the flaked tuna, cream cheese, mayonnaise, sweet corn, spring onions, and lemon juice. Season with salt and black pepper, then mix until smooth and evenly combined.

Spread a generous amount of the tuna mixture onto the slices of bread. Top with lettuce and sliced cucumber or tomato, if using. Cover with the remaining bread slices and press gently.

Slice each sandwich in half and serve immediately, or chill for 15–20 minutes before serving for a firmer filling.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: The flavours of a rainy afternoon
Content:
Rain has a way of slowing life down, and making us crave comfort on a plate. Whether it's the smoky sweetness of roasted corn, the crunch of golden pakoras, or a steaming cup of fragrant tea, some flavours simply belong to a rainy afternoon. From timeless favourites to indulgent treats, these rainy-day recipes promise to make every shower a little warmer and every tea break a little more memorable.

Ingredients 2 sweet corn cobs 1 tsp chilli powder ½ tsp salt 1 tbsp melted butter 1 lemon, cut into halves and deseeded Method Combine the chilli powder and salt in a small bowl and mix well. Roast the corn cob over an open flame till black spots appear on all sides. Once roasted, brush ½ tablespoon of melted butter evenly over it. Take half of the lemon, dip it in the chilli-salt mixture and rub it all over the roasted corn cob, while squeezing the lemon lightly. Serve immediately.

Ingredients 4 boiled eggs, cut in half ½ cup chickpea flour 1 tbsp corn flour 1 tsp red chilli powder Pinch of turmeric powder ½ tsp ginger-garlic paste ¼ tsp baking soda Salt to taste Oil for deep-frying Method In a bowl, add chickpea flour, corn flour, chilli powder, turmeric powder, ginger-garlic paste, cooking soda and salt. Mix all of them. Make a thick batter by adding a little water. Heat oil in a pan. Now dip each egg piece in the batter and deep fry until golden brown on a medium flame. Serve hot with chutney or sauce.

Ingredients 1 cup chicken mince 10 pieces mozzarella cheese, cut into cubes 3 tbsp chopped onion 2 tbsp all-purpose flour 1 tsp ginger paste ½ tsp garlic paste ½ tsp black pepper powder 1 tbsp soy sauce 1 tbsp chilli sauce 2 eggs Breadcrumbs, as required Salt, to taste Oil, for deep frying Method In a bowl, mix chicken mince with onion, flour, ginger-garlic paste, sauce, black pepper powder, salt and egg yolk. Divide the mixture into equal-sized round balls and press them lightly. Cut the mozzarella cheese into cubes. Take one ball and add one cube of cheese in the centre of the chicken, close all the corners and make a ball shape. Coat the balls with egg white and then coat with breadcrumbs. Heat oil in a pan. Fry the balls until golden brown. Serve hot with tea or coffee.

Ingredients 1 cup prawn 2 slices of bread 1 large onion, chopped 2 green chillies, chopped ½ tsp garlic paste ½ tsp ginger paste ½ tsp coriander powder ½ tsp turmeric powder Salt, to taste 1 tbsp lemon juice 2 tbsp flour 1 beaten egg ½ cup breadcrumbs Few sprigs of fresh coriander leaves Oil, for frying Method Shell, de-vein and wash the prawns thoroughly. Soak the bread in cold water for five minutes, squeeze out the water, and blend in a food processor with the prawns until smooth. Take out from the blender, and add onion, ginger-garlic paste, coriander powder, turmeric powder, lemon juice, coriander leaves and salt. Mix well and divide the mixture into 10 equal portions and shape into cutlets. Dust them with flour, then dip in beaten egg and roll in breadcrumbs. Ensure that the cutlets are coated properly. Heat oil and deep fry till golden brown. Serve hot.

Ingredients 1 cup fish-roe (of any white fish) ¼ cup breadcrumbs ½ tsp ginger paste ¼ tsp garlic paste ¼ tsp cumin paste ¼ tsp turmeric powder ½ tsp red chilli powder 1 tsp chopped green chillies 1 tsp chopped coriander leaves 1 tsp chopped mint ½ cup chopped onions Salt, to taste Cooking oil (for deep frying) Method Rinse the fish-roe carefully and let the water drain away. Marinate the fish-roe by mixing all ingredients with it, except the oil. Wait until the breadcrumbs absorb the excess water from the fish-roe. Heat oil in a pan for deep frying. Take 1 spoonful of the mixture at a time and fry it until golden brown. Tip: If you want crispiness to last for a long time, then add 2 teaspoonfuls of corn flour with the mixture.

Ingredients 8 pieces of onion, sliced 1 cup chickpea flour ¼ cup rice flour ½ tsp ginger paste ½ tsp garlic paste 1tsp red chilli powder 12 tsp turmeric powder 4 green chillies, paste ½ cup chopped coriander leaves ¼ tsp baking soda Salt, to taste Oil, for deep frying Method Take chickpea flour in a bowl, add rice flour, salt, ginger-garlic paste, red chilli powder, turmeric powder, baking soda and green chilli to it. Mix the ingredients and add coriander leaves. Make a thick batter by adding water. Heat oil in a pan. Now dip onion slices into the batter and fry them in the pan. Deep-fry until crisp and golden brown. Serve hot with sauce.

Ingredients 2 cups milk 2 cups water 2 tbsp tea powder 2 lemongrass stalks, each cut into pieces ½ tsp crushed ginger 2 cardamom pods, crushed 1 stick cinnamon Sugar, to taste Method Combine 2 cups of water, tea powder, sugar, lemongrass, ginger, cardamom and cinnamon in a pan. Boil on medium heat for 2 minutes. Add the milk, mix well and bring to a boil on medium heat. When the mixture boils to the brim, reduce the heat to prevent it from spilling out, and continue to boil for 4-5 minutes. Strain immediately using a strainer and discard the tea powder mixture. Serve the tea immediately.

Title: The World Cup final match munchies guide
Content:
By 1 AM, the curry and rice you devoured at dinner are long gone, and after the national anthems are played tonight, you give up and inspect every container in the kitchen like a chubby-cheeked mouse, only to find a few stale crumbs.

But don’t you worry, because we are here to present you with easy recipes and tricks for the FIFA World Cup final, so when you scream "GOAL!", you scream the loudest.

Croquettes are a classic Spanish snack made by combining a creamy or mashed filling, commonly potatoes, meat, seafood, or cheese, into small rolls or oval-shaped portions. They are coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried until crisp and golden, creating a crunchy exterior that contrasts with the soft, flavourful filling.

Start by boiling the chicken with the ginger and garlic paste. Once cooked, shred the chicken and mix it with sautéed onions and 2 tablespoons of breadcrumbs. Set this mixture aside.

In a pan, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the flour and stir for about a minute. Gradually pour in the milk, whisking continuously to eliminate any lumps. Season the mixture with salt.

Combine the creamy mixture with the shredded chicken and chill it in the refrigerator for about an hour. After chilling, shape the mixture into croquettes. Place the croquettes in the freezer for an additional 2 hours.

Next, heat oil in a medium-sized pot over medium-low heat. To prepare the croquettes for frying, coat each one in flour, ensuring all sides are covered. Then dip them into beaten egg and roll them in breadcrumbs for an even coating.

Finally, fry the croquettes in the hot oil until they are golden brown and crispy. Enjoy!

A traditional pastry popular in Argentina, empanadas are made by enclosing a savoury filling, such as seasoned beef, chicken, cheese, or vegetables, within a thin layer of dough. They can be either baked or fried until golden and crisp. Their convenient, handheld shape and rich, flavourful filling make them a versatile dish, suitable for serving as a snack, appetiser, or light meal.

3 cups all-purpose flour

3 to 4 green chillies

½ cup chopped tomatoes

½ cup mozzarella cheese

Start by combining the flour, baking powder, and salt in a bowl. Cut the cold butter into cubes and mix it into the dry ingredients. Next, add one egg and ¾ cup of water, gently mixing until a dough forms. Knead the dough on a floured surface for a couple of minutes until smooth, then wrap it in cling film and refrigerate for at least one hour.

Heat a pan over medium heat and cook the finely chopped onion until soft. Add the garlic and stir for about a minute, then incorporate the ground beef, cooking until it is no longer pink. Stir in the tomato paste, green peas, salt, green chillies, and spices, allowing the mixture to cook while stirring occasionally. Once the mixture has cooled slightly, add the cheese.

When you’re ready to assemble, roll out the dough evenly on a floured surface and cut out circles. Lightly dab some water around the edges of each circle, then place a generous amount of filling in the centre. Fold the dough in half to create mini parcels, sealing the edges by twisting them. Whisk the remaining egg and, if desired, add a pinch of sugar. Arrange the empanadas on a baking tray and brush them with the egg wash before baking in a preheated oven at 180° C for about 25 minutes.

A fusion recipe that combines Spanish albóndigas (meatballs) with Argentinian choripán (sandwiches).

2 garlic cloves, minced

Salt and black pepper

4 sandwich rolls or hot dog buns

Cook the ground beef with the spices and onion until the meat is no longer pink. Then gently shape the mixture into meatballs. Brown the meatballs in a skillet over medium heat for 6–8 minutes. Remove and set aside.

In the same pan, sauté the onion and garlic. Add the tomatoes, paprika, salt, and pepper. Simmer for 10 minutes. Return the meatballs to the sauce and cook for another 10–15 minutes until fully cooked. Thinly slice the onion and soak it in white vinegar for half an hour. Toast the sandwich rolls. Add the cheese, spoon in the meatballs with a little sauce, and finish generously with the pickled onions.

In the end, one of the smartest game plans is simply stocking your pantry before kick-off. Keep coffee or tea on hand for a late-night energy boost, a bag of popcorn kernels ready to pop during half-time, and a few easy munchies like biscuits, roasted nuts, or dark chocolate for those nail-biting moments. If the match stretches into extra time, you will be more than glad you prepared beforehand. A little planning means you can stay glued to the screen without missing a single goal or making an emergency snack run.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: Relationships & Family
Author: Munira Fidai

Title: Adult phone addiction: A problem we often overlook
Content:
Most research over the years has concentrated on excessive screen time for children and everything it takes away from them. However, in a surprising turn of events, children between the ages of 8 and 16 are now flipping the tables on their parents, saying that phone addiction in adults causes them to overlook important family moments. Suddenly, it seems as if the older generation must do some soul-searching of its own.

Fairly concerning results came to light in a study conducted in the UK. Through responses from 16,000 people and a separate poll of 1,000 children, the research that spanned 18 months made it evident that intentional or unintentional scrolling by the parents of children under 18 chips away at precious family time.

The research shows that parents spend, on average, 88 hours (almost 4 days) on unconscious phone activity. Over this time, they miss moments that matter to their children, such as talking or playing together, family days out, and so on. In fact, 63 per cent of the children who were part of the survey believed that their parents had no idea how much time they were actually spending online.

The results of the study indicate something even more puzzling: parents of minors spend more than two hours a day on their smartphones unintentionally, 40 minutes more than an average adult who is not a parent.

This means that parents check their phones more than non-parents and often, without a concrete reason.

“Scrolling is a break from reality,” shares Shoily, mother to a 6-year-old. “It’s mindless, and that’s precisely why I indulge in it.”

Many parents like Shoily say they often pick up their phones without thinking after a long day at work, and do not realise that they may be overdoing it or overlooking their children while doing so. Often, this is not the same for people without children.

“I make it a point to consciously use my phone as little as possible once I’m off work,” says Alvi Mannan, a 36-year-old graphic designer. “My wife and I both feel like our work is heavily screen-dominated, and we opt to read books, go walking or explore cafes instead.”

Of course, there is a very evident reason for all this. Non-parents have time after work to spend as they wish.

Taking care of a young child is not a burden they have to carry, and therefore, they can see scrolling for the mindless, soul-sucking activity that it is, rather than an escape. For parents, the scenario is vastly different. Their timetables revolve around their children and, for lack of a break, they turn towards the screen. The consequences that follow such an activity are, however, more far-reaching than parents realise.

According to psychologist Inara Salim, when parents are physically present but mentally on their phones, children learn they are less important than a screen.

“Every child who has to repeat themselves because a parent was on their phone, or has to turn back from a parent without having shown them or told them what they wanted to, feels unseen, and teaches them that love is something that must be earned.”

According to the psychologist, this dent in confidence can show up as doubt in class, anxiety in friendships, and a belief that they must compete to be chosen.

“The repair is simple: children don’t need perfect parents; they need present ones. Even 10 minutes a day of phone-down attention tells a child: ‘You matter.'”

Perhaps then, the real question simmers down to what message adults are willing to impart to children. It is no more about how much time the children are spending on their phones. Rather, it is what they learn from the behaviours modelled by the adults around them. Each time a parent chooses a device over a conversation, even unintentionally, that choice becomes part of a child’s understanding of attention, love, and importance.

This in no way means that parents can never disconnect from their role or catch a break. It simply means that if adults want children to develop a healthy relationship with technology, they must be willing to be honest about their own habits first.

Sometimes, putting the phone down is more than a break from scrolling; it is a way of saying, without words, that the children will always come first.
Author: M Munira Fidai Munira Fidai

Title: Why parents should think twice before giving kids smartphones
Content:
Parents are seen handing phones to children younger than ever, with reasons like convenience, safety, and social pressures taking the lead. However, experts urge parents to exercise stronger oversight and patience as pediatric studies link early phone ownership to depression, obesity, and poor sleep.

The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, conducted on some 10,600 adolescents across 21 research sites in the United States, examined the relationship between the age when children receive smartphones and how the age of ownership relates to mental and physical health.

According to this research, almost 64 per cent of all children receive smartphones by the age of 12 and another 25 per cent by 14. This means that in the age range of 8 to 12, children average between 5 hours of screen time daily.

The study probed deeper. It looked into 12-year-olds with and without smartphones. Predictably, and in congruence with similar studies in the past, children who owned smartphones were at least 30 per cent more vulnerable to feelings of depression than those who did not own the devices.

In addition, 40 per cent of phone owners were obese, and 60 per cent of them suffered from sleep deprivation. The biggest shocker of all: the earlier the children received smartphones, the higher the chances of these issues.

Scientists caution that this is not a study that proves a direct correlation between smartphones and issues such as depression, obesity and sleep deprivation. However, some of the most crucial development that occurs in children occurs in adolescence, and pre-teens and teenagers may not have the self-control to manage unfettered access to social media, games and constant notification interruptions. This itself is enough to crowd out sleep, exercise and in-person social interaction.

According to psychologist Inara Selim, the stakes are even higher as her concerns lie beyond simply sleep loss and depression. They diversify into what happens to a child's social development when a screen replaces face-to-face interaction during these formative years.

“Social skills aren't innate; they're built through repeated, real-time practice — reading tone, sitting with awkward silences, learning how to repair a friendship after a conflict,” stresses Inara.

“A twelve-year-old is still developing that capacity; constant notifications and curated online interactions can quietly erode the learning curve before it's had a chance to form.”

To her, every hour spent on a screen instead of with peers is an hour not spent learning how to actually be with people, and that's the quieter cost behind these numbers.

For parents, this means wading into a grey area and allowing children some level of control, without compromising on their mental and physical health. In this day and age, smartphones cannot be deemed all evil and banished from their lives. The pervasive nature of technology will require them to operate on screens on some level or another, and there is no way to work around that.

Scientists have some advice for parents in this regard. They have termed this approach “dedicated oversight”. This includes delaying the ownership of devices as far as possible, enforcing rules such as limiting daily screen time, including non-negotiable screen-free times during the crucial times of the day such as before sleep or right after waking up and key parental controls such as on certain apps and sites. Parents must also encourage healthier alternatives such as outdoor play and sports and physical reading.

Psychologist Faria-A-Khair has another perspective to supplement the one above. “Children who own smartphones and are screen-dependent from an early age often suffer from inattention and hyperactivity, hampering their academic performance and rendering them unable to build meaningful connections with people around them, including friends, family members, relatives and even their own parents.”

She feels that instead of going to extremes, parents must compromise and meet children halfway.

“We need to spend time with our children,” stresses Faria. “We must build lasting connections with our children to create a sense of secure attachment for them and pull them away from screen dependence.”

Khair emphasises the importance of taking some time out to talk to kids, taking them close to nature, and arranging play dates with children of similar-minded parents. “The idea is to rebuild in children the habit of exchanging thoughts in person, and make parents the safe space of their lives, as opposed to screen time.”
Author: M Munira Fidai Munira Fidai

Title: A beginner’s guide to Gen Z dating dictionary
Content:
Our parents had a fairly simple dating vocabulary. You liked someone, you dated, and then you either broke up, or got married. Maybe there was a “prem” somewhere in between if things got serious.

Gen Z looked at this perfectly manageable system and apparently decided it needed 47 new terms.

Take pocketing. This is when someone is dating you, but keeps you hidden from their friends and family. In Bangladesh, this can get particularly impressive. You could be together for eight months and still be introduced as “a friend from university” when you bump into their cousin at a restaurant.

Then there’s fizzing, where a relationship slowly dies without anyone officially ending it. Replies get shorter, plans disappear, and eventually, both people are technically still together, but only because nobody has bothered to announce the funeral.

If that sounds bad, meet zombieing. Someone ghosts you, disappears completely, then suddenly returns weeks or months later with “Sorry, life was hectic.” Congratulations, the dead have risen.

Roaching takes the situation further. You think you're dating one person, only to discover they’ve been seeing several others at the same time. The name comes from cockroaches, if you see one, there are probably more hiding somewhere. Quite romantic.

There’s also emotional Airbnb, which is exactly what it sounds like. It describes someone who uses you as temporary accommodation for their emotional problems. They arrive with heartbreak, unload everything, feel better and check out when they’re ready.

And before the relationship can even begin, there’s the soft launch, which is posting a suspiciously cropped arm, two coffee cups or someone’s silhouette on Instagram without revealing who they are. This kick starts the guessing game on Instagram, with each friend coming up with their own theories as to who the mystery person is.

So, if someone tells you they’re “talking to you” don’t assume you understand what that means. Ask whether they’re talking, soft-launching, pocketing you, or accidentally using you as an emotional Airbnb.

You may need a dictionary before you need a partner.
Author: M Mehdi Islam Mahi Mehdi Islam Mahi

Title: How should parents react to their child's O’Level results
Content:
Ordinary Level results can feel like a verdict. For students, months of studying, late nights and exam anxiety come down to a few letters and numbers on a result sheet. For parents, those grades can bring relief, pride or disappointment. But whatever the result says, the way parents react can matter more than the result itself.

A disappointing result does not mean a child has failed at life. Yet, some parents react as if it does. Shouting, comparing their child with classmates, threatening to take away privileges, or repeatedly asking, “Why couldn't you do better?” can turn one bad result into a much bigger problem.

For students already worried about their grades, the fear of facing their parents can be worse than the result itself.

O Level candidate Assaduzaman Abrar says he feels a certain amount of pressure from his parents to perform well. “I know they want me to do well, but sometimes the pressure gets to me,” Abrar says.

His parents say their expectations come from wanting the best for their child. “We expect more from him because we know he can do better. That expectation naturally comes into play, especially when the results are important,” his parents say.

The intention may be to push a child towards doing better, but expectations can easily feel like pressure from the other side. Parents may see a good result as a reflection of their child's effort and future. Students, however, may have struggled with a particular subject, dealt with exam anxiety, or simply performed below their usual standard on the day.

That doesn't mean parents should pretend a bad result doesn't matter. It does matter. The question is what they do next.

Rafia Mondal, who recently passed her O Levels, had a more relaxed experience at home. Her parents accepted her moderate result. She noticed, however, that some of her friends had a very different experience.

“I've seen friends get scared to show their results because they already know their parents will be disappointed,” Rafia says.

That fear can create a communication gap. A student who expects anger may avoid telling their parents what went wrong. Instead of saying, “I struggled with math,” they may simply hide the problem. Instead of asking for help, they may keep it to themselves.

Parents should therefore start with a simple question: “How do you feel about your result?”

That gives the student room to speak before the conversation turns into criticism. If the result is genuinely poor, parents can then look at the individual subjects and figure out what went wrong. Was the student struggling with a particular topic? Did they lack enough preparation? Were they distracted? Or did they simply have a bad exam?

The next step should be a plan, not a punishment.

Parents can help their child set realistic academic goals, arrange extra support for difficult subjects, or change their study routine. They can also remind their child that one set of O Level grades does not decide their entire future.

Most importantly, parents need to separate disappointment from rejection. It is perfectly reasonable to expect a child to work hard. It is not reasonable to make them feel that their worth depends on their grades.

A student needs to know that they can walk through the front door with a bad result and still feel safe enough to talk about it. After all, the purpose of parenting is not simply to produce good grades. It is to raise someone who can handle failure, learn from it and try again without being afraid to tell their parents what went wrong.
Author: M Mehdi Islam Mahi Mehdi Islam Mahi

Title: The unspoken burden of being the head of the family
Content:
It sounds more like a melodramatic dialogue from some retro Bengali movie. However, whether we acknowledge it or not, in every family, there is one person who is the proverbial ‘head’. And while that title has been used and misused in fiction and movies, what is rarely acknowledged is the story from their side.

The title — head of the family — is a neat little wrapper that delivers responsibilities to you. Many people take the mantle at an earlier age; others get the luxury of waiting till their 30s or 40s.

Irrespective of the age, it is the bearing of responsibilities that makes you the head. Once you take the role, your whole world changes. Your dreams and goals change, your perspective changes, your priorities change, and most importantly, your identity changes.

“Just a few years back, when I was a student, I could think in solo terms. ‘I’ want to do this, ‘I’ want to go there. But now, that chapter is closed. It’s no longer just me. My family depends on me, so whatever decision I make, I have to think about them for everything,” said Saikat Barua, a young professional.

When we were younger, we used to see our fathers as the head of the family. He was this powerful person who could make the decisions. Everyone would ask him for advice. And the biggest fish head would always be saved for him, even after he had repeatedly said that he did not enjoy that particular piece.

It seemed like a very powerful place in the family. We all wanted to be the “head of the family”. Now looking back, it seems less glamorous.

“Sometimes I wonder if I am doing an acceptable job at all? What will my children think of me when they grow up? There are a lot of things to take care of. A lot more than I can count and a lot more than I can manage. And there are times when I really think I could use some advice from someone who has been in my place,” sighed Musfiq Fuad, who has two children and an extended family to look after.

“At those times, I miss my late father because while the rest of my family loves me, they have not been in these shoes. I think my father could tell me what to do,” he added, observing that sometimes the pressure can get to a person.

And what’s interesting is that he still does not loathe his role or the pressure. He welcomes it, saying that family will always be family.

“It’s not a burden in the proper sense of the word, but it is a conscious psychological pressure in the back of your mind that just does not go away. I try not to think about it too much; instead, I do my best and keep my faith”, he explained, adding that the pressure can be overwhelming at times, but keeping his faith in the Almighty helps him through it.

Everyone turns to the head of the family, but whom does he turn to? Or she, for that matter? Because it is even harder to be a woman and lead a family. Our society still does not look kindly towards them and often puts some sort of label on them, making their job harder as if the title itself is not heavy enough.

Everyone describes their own way of coping with the title because it is a title that comes with a heavy crown. And it comes with not just responsibilities but other ‘not so great’ feelings such as guilt and blame. Sometimes it seems like no matter how hard you try, it makes no difference, and despite all your efforts and sacrifices, you will be blamed for “not doing enough”.

Which brings us to how the people in this role cope. Apparently, the secret is patience. And it grows with experience. So does your respect for your parents as you realise they had to do it during a harder and more unforgiving time.

Sure, in many families, the title is not as prevalent as in others, but the title still exists in most families in our country. And as a new generation emerges, younger people are taking on responsibilities. If you are playing the role, do not blame yourself. You are doing the best you can, and we are rooting for you.
Author: A Ashif Ahmed Rudro Ashif Ahmed Rudro

Title: Should you replace your partner with AI as soon as possible?
Content:
As a generation, we have transitioned from “Google knows everything” to “AI is the one who truly understands me.” Although this may sound cringe and comical equally, it is what the recent data says.

Travis Butterworth, a leathermaker from Colorado, USA, made headlines a few years back when he fell in love with a pink-haired Replika chatbot named Lily Rose during the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns, eventually having a digital wedding, which was approved by his human wife, no less. Yes, that is what you can call a modern love story!

In early 2026, a 32-year-old woman named Yurina Noguchi decided to marry her machine intelligence generated partner, Klaus, whom she designed using ChatGPT after a rough real-world relationship. And these are just the two cases among the dozens.

Well, once, dating required exceptional fashion sense, charismatic communication skills with the perfect sprinkle of humour, and most importantly, a colossal dose of courage. You had to make an effort to approach someone, say something slightly unsmart, withstand the possibility of rejection, and then spend hours analysing every moment to extract some semblance of wisdom.

So, we thought we had had enough of that, and designed a much simpler alternative: the AI.

That never says anything mean or leaves you on “seen”, neither does it take an eternity to reply. No matter what happens, your chatbot is always sitting there patiently (at least as long as there is Wifi and enough credits) to listen to your breakdown, and to validate all of your feelings with beautifully structured answers, remembering your preferences from past chat sessions.

Honestly, the competition is unfair. We human beings haul around emotional baggage that seems to get heavier as we age, whereas the digital companions simply get an update every now and then, and gradually gets better at “understanding” human feelings.

But let’s pause for a moment.

Automated intelligence is, in many ways, the ultimate low-maintenance partner of your dreams. Except, there is one tiny problem. It is not your partner. That sweet, compassionate text you receive is not from someone who is thinking about you. The chatbot is probably sending an empathetic text to you, recipes to someone else, and recommending ointments for a rash to another at the very moment. Talk about commitment issues!

But in earnest, what we must not forget is that treating chatbots as a romantic partner has its own downsides as well. These are perpetually available, agreeable, and designed to be pleasant to interact with, which subtly reshape the expectations of real relationships, making the frictions and unpredictability of human connection feel unappealing in comparison.

Also, did you know that excessive time spent with a virtual assistant can deepen loneliness? Especially for people already prone to loneliness or isolation, since time and emotional energy spent on an AI relationship often substitutes for, rather than supplements, human contact.

There is also a risk of emotional dependency: the robot in your phone can not independently verify a person's situation, hold them accountable, or offer the grounded, external perspective that friends or family can.

To be true, in this era, the real reason dating is exhausting is not that humans are badly designed. It is because we are complicated creatures.

We sometimes (or often) misunderstand and disappoint each other without knowing, change our minds, and act irrationally when we have terrible days. But that is also what makes human connections meaningful. Your synthetic sweetheart can give you the perfect response, whereas a human can give you an unexpected one. And sometimes that unexpected response is exactly what you need.

But then again in all seriousness, if dating apps continue churning out conversations that begin with: “Kaman asan?” I would say the artificial intelligence certainly has a bedazzling future in dating.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: Why people keep falling for toxic partners?
Content:
If you have ever found yourself in an argument with your best friend because he or she keeps tiptoeing back into their toxic relationships and wondered “Why?” you should know that this is so widespread that even the smartest people might sometimes find themselves trapped in the loop of toxicity.

Some people consciously choose chaos in relationships because they have become habituated to it during their upbringing.

According to Abdul Hamid, a psychotherapist at the Monobikash Foundation, for these people, “The emotional environment they were raised in, or how conflict was handled at home, sets the standards for what ‘normal’ love feels like later in life.”

That means, the children who grew up in unpredictable environments, where the parent was warm one day and cold the next, as adults, they cannot register a relationship as ‘warning’ when it swings between highs and lows constantly.

However, Hamid mentions it still varies from person to person, and though family dynamics play an important role, it is not the whole story. Some children might grow up in a stressful environment, yet develop self-awareness that allows them to distinguish between calm and chaotic relationships. Ultimately, this ability depends on the cognitive functioning of the individual.

The first misconception we hold is that people with minimum self-respect would never do such. But Hamid explains that, surprisingly, self-respecting people might sometimes hope that “love” will “fix” the narcissistic attitude or mistreatment of a partner in the course of time.

More often than not, trauma bonding or the cycles of immense affection and abuse create a powerful attachment as well.

That is equally true for self-esteem as well. As the psychologist clarifies, “Someone can be entirely sure of themselves at work, negotiating confidently, leading a team, making sharp decisions; still feel completely unmoored when it comes to their own worth in a relationship.”

It is because professional confidence is built on visible, repeatable proof: you do the task and get positive feedback; but self-worth in intimate relationships is shaped much earlier, and much less consciously.

So, it is entirely possible to be a person who commands a room and still firmly believe that this particular partner is the best they will ever get, or that this level of disrespect is what they deserve. Not to mention, toxic partners often exploit this gap.

However, Hamid says, the strongest reason why people constantly fall back is quite intriguing. Manipulative partners typically make you feel like the centre of their world at the beginning of the relationship; they may even make you reliant on them for everyday tasks that you once handled easily, and then later withdraw that support. This withdrawal creates a strong desire to regain the affection you initially received.

In many cases, some might often get baffled to distinguish between a rough patch in a relationship and a genuinely unhealthy relationship. Every relationship goes through periods of conflict, misunderstandings, and stress sooner or later, which are often resolved through mutual respect, open communication, and, most importantly, willingness from both.

In contrast, a dysfunctional relationship is often characterised by recurring patterns of manipulation, disrespect, emotional or physical abuse, and excessive control even after the difficult phase is over.

That brings us to the next reason for choosing a toxic relationship again and again. Sometimes a calm, steady relationship can feel way too quiet; no dramatic highs, no big reconciliations, just consistency, and consistency can register as boring rather than as safety.

Movies and social media play the biggest role here: the intense push-pull dynamics get framed as passion, jealousy as devotion, and chaos as chemistry, while the smooth, functional relationships rarely make for a compelling scene or a viral post.

Over time, that steady diet of dramatized toxicity can quietly recalibrate what excitement is supposed to look like, so real peace starts to feel like the absence of love rather than the presence of it.

In the end, Abdul Hamid advises, walking away from relationships lacking mutual respect is more about being self-aware, and if you find yourself stuck in one, try to grow alternatives that truly make you feel good and surround yourself with family and close friends. Above all, stop seeing yourself as the person who can rectify a toxic partner, and avoid constantly feeling guilty for not trying enough.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: How solomaxxing is changing the way we look at being alone
Content:
There was a time when going alone to a restaurant made us wonder what people were going to think. Watching a movie alone felt slightly sad, travelling alone sounded like a vivid dream, and being single for too long came with inevitable questions.

However, people seem to have silently decided that none of these things are taboo anymore. Welcome to the era of solomaxxing — the art of doing everything by yourself, intentionally choosing your own company and enjoying it. The term has recently started appearing across social media all over the world, describing young people who are choosing to invest their time, money and energy in themselves rather than constantly pursuing a company.

And we can see the shift in the everyday choices. Solo dinners, cinema trips, solo travels, and attending concerts alone are no longer viewed as a sign of being "alone" or as a sign that someone has “no one”. They are increasingly becoming experiences people actively choose.

And honestly, there is something strangely beautiful about that.

Think about the last time you wanted to try a new cuisine but nobody else was interested, or there was a movie you desperately wanted to watch but your friends wanted to watch it with their partners. Or you badly needed a break from the busy life and planned a trip, but everyone’s schedules refused to match.

For years, we have been taught to cancel or postpone these little joys until someone can join us.

What if we simply went to that restaurant? Watched that movie? Or planned that trip?

Sarwat Sameen, a Bangladeshi restaurant owner, talks about solo travels and puts it beautifully, “If you want to discover yourself, understand yourself and learn to love yourself and life, then travel alone; it will teach you a lot.”

And for women especially, choosing to travel alone can carry a whole different weight. There is something so rebellious yet beautiful in that sentence. For years women were taught that travelling alone invites judgement or considered incapable of handling situations alone.

But women choosing their peace over society's permission feel less like another trend and more like a quiet act of reclaiming her own life. Sometimes solomaxxing does not always have to mean booking a flight or planning a big adventure.

Nusrat Kamal, 23, says, “I used to feel weird sitting alone at a coffee shop, but now I actually enjoy having that little time to myself. I rearrange my thoughts while having my cappuccino and observe surroundings.”

It is such a simple but relatable example of how our relationship with being alone is changing. We often assume that sitting alone means that the person must have been stood up, when in reality, they might simply be enjoying their coffee without having to make conversation.

Solomaxxing is not necessarily about avoiding people entirely. It is about learning that independence and companionship can exist together. You can cherish your family, adore your friends, aspire to have a relationship someday and still enjoy spending an entire afternoon alone.

Being alone can sometimes make us notice small things we usually miss. It can be as simple as enjoying the taste of the food silence, reading a new book while sipping coffee in a cosy café or wandering down a street without worrying about being somewhere else.

Labib Rahman, a 28-year-old graphic designer, shared, “I started going to cinema, art exhibitions, and even attending concerts alone because I realised I was missing so many experiences because I was simply waiting for a plus-one."

And honestly, I agree; we started to miss a lot of things the moment we made our plans according to someone else’s availability. That is where solomaxxing starts making sense. Why should you put something you are excited about on hold just because nobody else is available?

We are so used to a plus-one for everything that initially it feels unusual, but once we stop seeing it as sad or embarrassing, we start enjoying life on our own terms.

Being alone does not mean being sad and lonely. Being single does not mean being sad and incomplete. And being unmarried definitely does not mean sitting in some imaginary waiting room. It is simply refusing to put life on pause while waiting for someone.

If company arrives, wonderful. If it does not arrive tomorrow, that is fine too. Life goes on.

So, the next time you see someone eating alone at a restaurant with their headphones on while enjoying the food, resist the urge to feel sorry for them. Chances are, they picked the specific table on purpose and had a better evening than us.
Author: F Faria Nowshin Tazin Faria Nowshin Tazin

Title: 10 realities of moving abroad nobody warns you about
Content:
Nobody talks about what happens after you move abroad. They talk about courage. They talk about opportunities. They talk about new beginnings and fresh starts.

Nobody talks about the random Tuesday when homesickness hits you out of nowhere, and suddenly you are crying because a stranger’s cooking smells like something your mother used to make. Nobody talks about how lonely it can feel to build a life from scratch. How exhausting it is to always be adapting. How sometimes you can be surrounded by people and still feel completely alone.

Maybe that’s the thing about moving abroad.

You do not just leave a country. You leave a version of yourself behind. The version that knew where they belonged. The version that never had to explain their accent. The version that could call someone and have them at their door in ten minutes. And then one day you wake up in a different country and realise there is no guidebook for this part.

Just survival. Just trial and error. Just learning as you go.

Over the years, I have learned a few things that helped me cope when everything felt too heavy. Not because they fixed the loneliness. But because they made it easier to carry.

So, here are 10 things I wish someone had told me when I moved abroad:

Stop trying to be strong all the time. Missing home does not make you weak. It means you came from somewhere that mattered.

Call your people regularly. Not just when you are struggling. Relationships need maintenance when they are separated by oceans and time zones.

Create routines. A morning coffee, a Sunday grocery run, an evening walk. Small routines create stability when everything else feels uncertain.

Find one place that feels like yours. A café, a library, a park bench, a bookstore. Somewhere you can go when life feels overwhelming.

Cook food at home. It will not taste the same, but sometimes comfort matters more than perfection.

Build a support system before you think you need one. Loneliness is much easier to manage when you already have people around you.

Stop comparing your journey to others. Some people seem to have everything figured out. Most of them are improvising too.

Get out of the house. Fresh air won’t solve your problems, but neither will lying in bed creating twenty-seven imaginary worst-case scenarios.

Laugh at the absurd moments. One day, you will be explaining your culture. Next, you will be explaining why you cried over a particular brand of biscuits. Both are valid experiences.

Allow yourself to grow. You are not supposed to be the same person you were before you left.

That’s the whole point.

The funny thing about living abroad is that nobody warns you about the identity crisis. You miss home when you are overseas. Then you visit home and realise you have changed. You belong there. But you also belong somewhere else now. You find yourself living between two worlds, carrying pieces of both.

And sometimes that’s beautiful. Sometimes it’s heartbreaking. Most of the time, it’s both. But here’s what I’ve learned.

The goal was never to stop missing home. The goal was never to become fearless. The goal was simply to keep building a life anyway. To keep showing up. To keep making connections. To keep finding joy in small things. To keep choosing hope on the days when everything feels uncertain, because eventually the city that felt foreign becomes familiar. The streets become part of your story. The people become part of your life.

And one day, without even noticing, you realise that while you were busy trying to survive abroad, you were quietly creating a home. Not the one you left behind. A new one. One built from resilience, memories, friendships, heartbreak, growth, and all the little moments that nobody posts about on social media.

And maybe that’s what moving abroad really teaches you. That home isn’t always where you came from. Sometimes it’s who you become when you have no choice but to start over.
Author: Shahreen Rahman

Title: New cigarette prices could be your best reason to quit
Content:
The new fiscal year budget has been announced and as always, people are paying close attention to which expenses are set to rise and which might offer a little relief. While most of these changes affect our wallets, some also have the potential to affect our habits.

Cigarettes are among the items that have seen an increase in price, adding to the cost of a habit that was never cheap to begin with.

For those who have spent months or even years, telling themselves that they would quit "one day", this price hike could offer a reason to finally start. Quitting smoking is rarely easy, but if the latest price increase feels like the final push you needed, here are a few practical ways to make that decision stick.

Smokers are aware that cigarettes cost money, but they do not calculate how much they actually spend over time. Imagine someone spending Tk 200 a day on cigarettes. That amounts to Tk 1,400 a week, roughly Tk 6,000 a month and more than Tk 70,000 a year!

The figure will vary from person to person, but the principle remains the same. Small daily purchases add up to a significant amount over time and looking at that may prompt different thoughts. This money could contribute to a holiday, a new gadget, or even a small investment. Seeing the annual cost rather than daily terms can be a source of motivation for those considering quitting.

Breaking a long-standing habit can feel overwhelming, which is why many people find it helpful to focus on small milestones rather than the end goal. Several smoking cessation apps are designed around this idea. They track smoke-free days, celebrate progress through badges, estimate money saved and provide regular reminders of how far a user has come.

What makes these tools effective is that they turn quitting into a series of manageable challenges. Users are encouraged to focus on reaching the next milestone, whether that is a day, a week or a month without a cigarette. For people who enjoy tracking progress or staying motivated through goals, these apps can help to accomplish.

Quitting smoking is not only about willpower, but also about understanding the situations that quietly keep the habit alive. Most smokers do not light up randomly. There are usually patterns behind it. It could be a cigarette with morning tea, one after meals or during work breaks.

Identifying these triggers is an important step. Some people find it useful to observe their smoking patterns for a few days and note when cravings appear most strongly. Once these moments are recognised, they become easier to anticipate and gradually avoid or replace with other actions.

Quitting something often works better when something else replaces the habit. Smoking is not just nicotine for many people, it is a ritual for them.

Simple substitutes like chewing gum, mints or even a bottle of water can keep the mouth engaged during cravings. Some people also find it helpful to distract themselves with small activities, whether it is scrolling through something, listening to music or playing games.

The goal is not to find a perfect replacement, but to interrupt the loop that leads from craving to cigarette. Over time, the urge weakens when it is no longer paired with the familiar action that follows it.

Willpower alone often struggles when the environment keeps reinforcing the habit. That is why small changes in surroundings can make difference. Spending more time in smoke-free places such as cafés, libraries or study spaces can reduce exposure to situations where smoking feels automatic.

It also helps to avoid carrying extra cigarette or keeping them within easy reach. Minor frictions, like making cigarettes less accessible, can interrupt impulsive decisions. Over time, these small barriers add up and make smoking less convenient, which is often enough to reduce frequency without relying purely on self-control.

Quitting smoking is rarely a straight or simple journey. The intention may be strong, but setbacks are part of the process. A price increase alone may not force anyone to quit, but it can serve as a reminder of what the habit is costing in the long run. Sometimes, even a small shift in perspective is enough to take the first step in a different direction.
Author: M Mir Elham Bin Ahmed Mir Elham Bin Ahmed

Title: How To watch every FIFA World Cup 2026 match in Bangladesh

Title: Simple habits that can ease financial stress
Content:
If you ever felt the correct way to get rid of financial anxiety is to get rich, you are absolutely wrong. Of course, theoretically, it should work, but practically, maybe not much. So, here we present the simplest guide to shoo away the overwhelming thoughts of economic insecurity.

Financial anxiety is never solely about money. Underneath might hide a specific fear, the apprehension of being judged, not being able to retire at the desired age, or maybe not being able to fulfil one's expectations. Before you can address the problem, you need to declutter your mind and pinpoint what exactly scares you.

It is one of the quietest, yet most powerful things you can do for fixing your relationship with money. Most importantly, it does not have to be large; the equivalent of two or three weeks of essential expenses sitting untouched in a separate account changes everything. At the end of the day, the size of the fund matters far less than the fact that it exists.

Avoiding checking the accounts might make you feel safer for the time being, but avoidance triggers anxiety in the long run. Sitting down once a month and simply looking at your savings and bills gives you a clear idea of whether you are overspending intentionally or it is slipping without notice. When you know your monthly expense limits, spending stops feeling like a gamble, and it alone takes a huge burden off your chest.

Financial anxiety thrives on extremes, either “I have nothing” or “I must have everything figured out right now.” A steadier mindset sits in the middle.

Thinking about small wins is the baby step you can take, tracking one week of expenses, saving a tiny amount, and saying no to one unnecessary purchase, is undoubtedly boring, but effective.

In the end, a constant worry about finances is more about the fear of not being enough in a world that keeps raising the price of “enough”, and there is always someone ahead of you. Counting your expenses, worrying sometimes is perfectly fine, but that should not own you. And that quiet shift, where fear begins to fade just enough for you to move forward, is where real stability begins.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: How to avoid overeating during Eid-ul-Adha
Content:
Eid-ul-Adha, the festival of kindness, togetherness, and food, might leave you lethargic and regretful if you are not eating mindfully enough. You do not have to be the person counting bites on a feast. However, there is a difference between eating with joy and eating until you can barely move. By being a little more intentional, you can enjoy the celebration without any guilt.

If you skip meals and show up in the “Eid dawat” hungry, it is surely going to backfire. Have a light, protein-rich snack before heading out. A boiled egg, some yoghurt, or a handful of nuts are healthy approaches. Hence, when the aroma or perfectly spiced beef hits your nose at the dawat, you can still make wiser food choices.

If you see a table full of juicy, meaty options, yet start eating a large portion of salad, your brain might go, “Why are we eating leaves like a confused goat?” But believe it or not, this strategy helps you practice mindful eating more than you can imagine, and fills you just enough to stop you from attacking food like a lion hearing the dinner bell at the zoo.

When you eat quickly, which is easy to do in a festive setting, you can consume far more than you require before the signal of fullness arrives from your stomach to your brain, which leads to overeating.

Moreover, eating large amounts of food within a short while makes you swallow more air, which increases stomach pressure and pushes acid upwards, causing heartburn, or even rapid blood sugar surges and palpitations.

It sounds simple, but studies constantly show people eat less when they use smaller dishes, yet feel equally satisfied. Smaller plates almost naturally limit portion sizes, without much willpower. Also, your brain might signal you that carrying a huge overloaded plate during Eid gatherings is very risky, because one wrong move and you have redecorated someone’s living room carpet with beef curry.

Sugary beverages and sweets add a significant number of calories to every course. If you have a sweet tooth and a little dessert does not spike your blood sugar, you do not have to entirely skip it, take minimal servings and opt for water over cold drinks after a meal.

It doesn't have to be a long one; even a gentle 10 to 15-minute walk after a banquet can do more than you would expect. Walking stimulates digestion, helps your stomach empty more efficiently, and prevents that heavy, sluggish feeling that tends to set in after a big Eid feast. It also helps regulate blood sugar, which tends to spike after large, carb and meat-heavy servings.

The key is not to collapse onto the sofa the moment the plates are cleared, and you will likely arrive at the next table feeling comfortable and ready to enjoy the celebration all over again.

In Bangladeshi households, love comes in the form of “extra rice” during any occasion. We take it personally if the guests do not eat enough, according to us. But listening to your body is far more important than being polite.

You do not have to refuse right away, and may accept additional portions if you are feeling you could have a little more without upsetting your stomach. Also, try saying, “I’m still eating, let me finish this first,” to avoid disheartening your host; it has been proven to work.

In the end, if you do overeat, do not spiral into guilt. Even if you are trying to lose weight, one or two indulgent days will not derail your health. Just return to a normal eating pattern the next day and move your body a little. Eat with joy, but stop with wisdom.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: What else must women do?
Content:
When a woman journalist attends a political party’s event, the only qualification she should need is that she is a journalist there to do her job. She should not have to satisfy a political leader’s religious expectations before asking him a question.

Recent remarks from Islami Andolan Bangladesh Senior Nayeb-e-Ameer Mufti Syed Muhammad Faizul Karim suggest otherwise.

At an IAB press conference in Purana Paltan on September 10, a woman journalist was allegedly moved from the front row and asked to sit at the back. When another journalist asked whether women reporters should sit in the front or at the back at IAB programmes, Faizul Karim did not give a direct answer. Instead, he said women journalists should attend while “observing purdah” , according to reports by Prothom Alo and bdnews24.com.

When a journalist pointed out that IAB leaders had appeared on television talk shows with women, Faizul Karim initially disputed this. He later acknowledged that one such appearance had taken place and said the party had stopped it.

He then said women were not being prevented from working as journalists, but should do so in accordance with Shariah.

The exchange raises a question that goes beyond where a journalist sits at a press conference: does a political party have the right to impose its religious expectations on women as a condition of doing their jobs?

Women do not practise journalism because political leaders allow them to. They attend press conferences to ask questions and inform the public. Their presence is professional, not religious or an endorsement of the people they cover.

Personal faith deserves respect regardless of who holds it. What is at issue here is different: whether one person's religious convictions should shape the professional conditions placed on someone else.

Press access can depend on security, accreditation and professional rules. It should not depend on a political party’s religious expectations.

And where does such a condition end?

Can a woman stand among male reporters? Can she interview an IAB leader face-to-face? Can she sit wherever male reporters sit? Can she host him on television? If any of these depends on whether she is a woman or meets a political leader’s religious expectations, she is not being offered equal professional access.

This is not merely a theoretical concern.

On May 3, 2025, Jugantor multimedia reporter Monika Chowdhury alleged that she was forced out of an IAB press conference in Barishal because women journalists were not allowed to attend.

Faizul Karim said he was unaware of the incident. The allegation alone does not establish an official party policy, but his latest remarks make it harder to dismiss it as an isolated misunderstanding.

The concern also extends to decisions inside newsrooms.

If an IAB leader refuses to appear on a television programme with a woman presenter, an editor may simply assign a man. If women face additional conditions at IAB events, newsrooms may find it easier to send male reporters. A woman could then lose assignments not because she is less capable, but because accommodating a political party’s preferences is seen as more convenient.

Politicians should not decide who covers them based on gender. Editorial assignments should be decided by editors, not by the people they cover.

Article 28(2) of the Constitution says women have equal rights with men in all spheres of the state and public life. Article 39 guarantees freedom of thought and speech and freedom of the press, while Article 40 protects the right to enter a lawful profession or occupation.

Not every objectionable act automatically becomes a constitutional violation. But a political party seeking public office should still be judged against the principles it would be expected to uphold if entrusted with power.

That is particularly important in a country where press freedom remains under pressure. Bangladesh ranks 152nd out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index . The media already operates in a difficult environment. It hardly needs another barrier to journalism based on gender.

IAB’s political record makes the question even more relevant.

The party has sought to expand its outreach among women voters and has been organising women and female students. There is nothing contradictory about organising women or seeking their votes. The concern arises when women are welcomed as voters and organisers but face additional conditions when they seek political representation or work independently.

IAB initially submitted nominations in 268 constituencies for the 2026 parliamentary election, although the final number was later reduced to 259 after scrutiny and withdrawals. Reports on the nomination process showed that the party had no women among its candidates.

There is a difference between welcoming women as voters and supporters and treating them as equals. That commitment is tested when women seek office, question leaders, disagree with them or simply do their jobs. That is why “we are not stopping them” is such a poor standard.

The question is not whether a political leader has decided not to prevent women from working. It is whether a woman can do the same job, enter the same room and ask the same questions on the same professional terms as the man beside her.

Arafat Rahaman is a journalist at The Daily Star. He covers education and writes on governance, rights and public accountability. He can be reached at arafat.mcj@yahoo.com.
Author: Arafat Rahaman Arafat Rahaman

Title: What the economics of happiness can teach us in Bangladesh
Content:
Although the term “economics of happiness” was conceptualised over half a century ago, it continues to pose an intellectual paradox for many. I first came across it in 2014 during my Erasmus exchange semester at Poland's famous Poznan University of Economics and Business to fulfil my German MBA requirements. I was surprised to find the university offered an entire course on this fast-growing field.

In simple terms, the economics of happiness studies how money and wealth affect our overall life satisfaction. Rather than judging a country's success purely by its financial output, or GDP, the field asks what actually makes people happy. Is it health, relationships, job satisfaction, free time, or perhaps all of the above? It challenges the traditional focus on GDP by putting well-being, mental health, and social connection on equal footing with material wealth.

Contemporary experts are quietly challenging the global focus on GDP as the best way to measure national progress. For decades, governments assumed that a larger economic output naturally led to happier citizens. Yet, the contemporary realities of development tell a radically different story. While global wealth surges, it leaves behind an unsettling trail of rising inequality, chronic anxiety, and profound social alienation, even within the most affluent societies. This glaring divide reveals a fundamental truth: economic growth is merely a vehicle, not the finish line. If an expanding economy leaves its populace feeling deeply anxious, precarious, and left behind, it cannot be classified as a complete success.

This very conflict sits at the centre of the economics of happiness—a discipline perfectly captured by the famous Easterlin Paradox. In 1974, economist Richard Easterlin observed that while wealthier citizens within any given country are generally happier than their poorer counterparts, a nation’s average happiness remains largely stagnant over decades of continuous macroeconomic growth. Two powerful psychological and social forces drive this phenomenon. First, humanity adapts rapidly to material improvements—a phenomenon psychologists term the "hedonic treadmill". A pay raise or a new phone gives a quick burst of joy before quickly becoming the new normal. Second, human well-being is heavily contingent upon relative status. In an interconnected world dominated by digital comparison, individuals judge their success against neighbours, peers, and idealised digital lives. If everyone gets a raise at the same time, no one feels they have actually moved ahead, and the anticipated psychological reward of making more money evaporates.

For a growing economy like Bangladesh, this paradox is an urgent policy problem, not just a theoretical debate. The World Happiness Report 2026 highlights this reality by placing Bangladesh 127th out of 147 nations . Even though this is a small improvement from its 134th position in 2025, Bangladesh still ranks behind South Asian neighbours like India, Pakistan, and Nepal. Rather than looking only at GDP, this global index measures overall progress by tracking social support, healthy life expectancy, institutional trust, and personal freedom. In Bangladesh, low satisfaction scores are directly tied to ongoing issues like systemic corruption, high inflation, youth unemployment, and limited personal freedom.

The structural divergence between economic metrics and real life is starkly evident in our urban landscapes. Over the past 30 years, Bangladesh has constructed a genuine macroeconomic success story characterised by healthy GDP growth, expanding electricity grids, upgraded rural connectivity, and a significant reduction in extreme poverty. This output-focused model has simultaneously extracted a severe human toll. The modern Bangladeshi urban experience is defined by the punishing, hours-long gridlock of Dhaka’s traffic, hazardous levels of air pollution, skyrocketing living costs, and profound job insecurity within a massive informal economy. Traditional economic indicators capture the value of the concrete poured for new roads, but they completely fail to register the mental exhaustion of the daily commute, the toxic smog blanketing our cities, or the pervasive anxiety regarding next month’s rent. Money is still essential for poor people because a small raise directly reduces their daily suffering and hardship. Nevertheless, once fundamental survival thresholds are achieved, marginal increments in financial capital yield progressively diminishing returns on subjective well-being.

To close this gap, Bangladesh needs to change its focus from basic economic growth to building a society that values real human well-being, just like other progressive nations do. For example, the United Kingdom formally tracks national well-being, the OECD uses a "Better Life Index," and Bhutan has long used Gross National Happiness. For our policymakers, this evolution requires executing specific, localised structural interventions across the following four critical pillars.

First, urban planning must prioritise human time and public health over unmanaged congestion. Transforming Dhaka and expanding divisional cities requires massive investments in high-capacity public transit, decentralised commercial zones to reduce long-distance commuting, and the strict enforcement of air quality standards to mitigate the unseen tax on public health. Second, the government must protect workers' dignity and financial safety. Giving garment and informal workers secure contracts, safe workplaces, and fair wages will drastically lower the daily stress that causes national anxiety. Third, public health policy must treat mental health with the same urgency as physical ailments. Integrating robust psychological counselling into primary healthcare centres and community clinics will address one of the most powerful, yet neglected, predictors of human well-being. Finally, dismantling systemic corruption and expanding personal freedoms are essential to restoring institutional trust, ensuring citizens feel safe, valued, and empowered in their daily choices.

Raw economic growth can no longer be treated as our ultimate finish line. By shifting our national focus towards the human factors that enrich daily life—prioritising fair distribution, mental well-being, liveable cities, and social trust—Bangladesh can finally break free from the trap of outdated metrics. The real measure of our country's progress must be how safe, strong, and content our people feel. We must build a society that is not just richer, but deeply and lastingly happier.

Rifat Ibne Jamal is a retired military officer, currently working as the deputy general manager for a major conglomerate. He can be reached at rifat.ibnejamal@gmail.com.
