Author: AFP

Title: Rybakina beats Sabalenka to win US Open title, takes No. 1 ranking
Content:
Elena Rybakina defeated defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday to win her first US Open title and complete her rise to the top of the women’s world rankings.

Rybakina had already secured the No. 1 ranking by reaching the semifinals, but capped her campaign by claiming the trophy Sabalenka had won in the previous two years.

“It’s still so difficult to process what happened,” Rybakina said. “Too many achievements these few weeks.”

The victory gave the 27-year-old her third Grand Slam title and second of the year. She also defeated Sabalenka in the Australian Open final earlier this season.

Rybakina ended Sabalenka’s 19-match winning streak at the US Open. Sabalenka had not lost at Flushing Meadows since the 2023 final against Coco Gauff.

Rybakina earned $5.5 million, the biggest prize in Grand Slam history, and joined Sabalenka and French Open champion Mirra Andreeva as the only players with three tour titles this season.

Sabalenka, who received $2.8 million, was seeking to become the first woman since Serena Williams from 2012-14 to win three consecutive US Open titles. She smashed her racket after briefly embracing Rybakina at the net.

“I was just out there competing, trying to do my best with what I had there today,” Sabalenka said. “Not good enough.”

Although Rybakina struggled with her first serve, she consistently pressured Sabalenka with her returns. She earned 12 break points and converted three, enough to secure the victory.

Rybakina’s win was the first time the lower-ranked player prevailed in a US Open women’s final between the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds since 2000.

Sabalenka had occupied the top ranking for 99 consecutive weeks, but Rybakina will take over on Monday.

Born in Russia, Rybakina represents Kazakhstan. She won her first Grand Slam at Wimbledon in 2022 and now needs only the French Open title to complete a career Grand Slam.

Sabalenka acknowledged Rybakina’s powerful serve and ability to dictate play, particularly on the fast US Open courts.

Rybakina had struggled at the US Open in previous years, never advancing beyond the fourth round before this tournament. She also briefly stopped playing during a quarterfinal match against Iga Swiatek in Cincinnati because of a foot injury but recovered in time for New York.

“I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years, and it was never successful — nothing close to that,” Rybakina said. “It’s just incredible. I’m falling in love with New York more and more.”

Sabalenka had reached the US Open final four straight times and the semifinals six times, but her impressive run at Flushing Meadows ended with Saturday’s defeat.

The Belarusian had won both of her previous meetings with Rybakina this season, at Indian Wells and Miami, and leads their career rivalry 10-8.

Rybakina took the opening set after Sabalenka struggled with her serve and became increasingly frustrated. Sabalenka recovered in the second set, breaking Rybakina late to level the match, but Rybakina quickly regained control in the decider and completed the biggest victory of her career.
Author: Agencies

Title: Bangladesh positive to play bilateral T20I series against Nepal next year
Content:
Bangladesh is positive to play a bilateral T20I series against Nepal next year amid a packed schedule, with the two sides set to meet in a bilateral series for the first time.

Bangladesh have so far played two T20Is against Nepal, both in the T20 World Cup. However, the two teams have never faced each other in a bilateral series.

Nepal’s ambassador to Bangladesh Ghanshyam Bhandari expressed interest in arranging a bilateral series with Bangladesh during a meeting with State Minister for Youth and Sports Md. Aminul Haque last Thursday.

The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) has also responded positively to the proposal, with the series potentially taking place early next year.

“Talks are going on between the BCB and the Nepal Cricket Association. Our FTP is very packed. Even then, we are trying to find a convenient time within this cycle. If everything goes well, the series may take place,” BCB cricket operations manager Shahriar Nafees told reporters at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur on Saturday.

He said both boards were keen to arrange the series within the current FTP cycle.

“We want to arrange the series within this cycle. The Nepal Cricket Association has also made the request. We are looking at the matter positively,” Nafees said.

Nepal was recently hit hard by devastating floods. The ambassador proposed the bilateral series with Bangladesh as a gesture of support and to inspire the people affected by the disaster.

The series could be held at the beginning of next year.

Bangladesh is currently preparing for the cricket event of the Asian Games after returning from their tour of Australia.

The team will travel to the United Arab Emirates after the Asian Games conclude at the end of this month to play a Test against Afghanistan and a tri-nation series involving Zimbabwe.

The Asian Games preparation camp will begin in Mirpur on Sunday.
Author: BSS

Title: BCB Integrity Unit vows to stamp out corruption from Bangladesh cricket
Content:
Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) Integrity Unit independent chair Alex Marshall on Saturday iterated his stance on stamping out the corruption from the country's cricket.

He said the unit is working independently to investigate alleged breaches of the anti-corruption code and hinted at more corruption cases coming to a conclusion in the coming weeks.

"There are more cases under investigation. You can expect to see some more announcements in the coming weeks," Marshall said at a press conference organised by the BCB Integrity Unit here today.

He, however, declined to disclose details of the ongoing investigations, saying it would be unfair to individuals under investigation and could affect their right to a fair hearing.

Marshall said the Integrity Unit has announced eight cases in recent weeks, with seven people charged under the anti-corruption code and one declared an excluded person.

"Some of the people who were charged in recent weeks have already accepted their charges and are awaiting their agreed sanction," he said.

He explained that the Integrity Unit follows a three-category process after completing an investigation.

"If there is very strong evidence, I recommend charges. If the evidence is not strong enough to charge, people remain under monitoring and review for a period of time. Or there is no evidence and the matter is finished," he added.

Marshall clarified that the nine domestic cricketers who were not invited to the auction of the 12th edition of the Bangladesh Premier League (BPL) were not found guilty or cleared through an anti-corruption investigation.

He said the independent inquiry report, which ran to 900 pages, contained negative information about more than nine people, including foreign players, local players and other individuals associated with cricket.

"I identified all the people who were in the 900-page report who were likely to take part in BPL 12," he informed.

Marshall said he advised the then BPL governing council that some people featured in the report might pose a threat to the integrity of the tournament and that they might consider not inviting them to BPL 12.

"The only advice I gave about not inviting people was not nine, it was a higher number and it was specifically for BPL 12," he revealed.

"There are no restrictions on any of the players. They've been playing."

He also made it clear that the independent inquiry commission was not an anti-corruption investigation under the code.

"The inquiry committee was asked to do a different thing and they did what they were asked to do," he said.

Marshall said his role was to provide confidential advice to the BPL governing council and that he could not impose bans or make final decisions on player participation.

"I cannot find anyone guilty. I cannot issue any bans. I oversee investigations," he remarked.

"At the end of the investigation if I think the case is strong enough, very strong evidence, then I make a charging report recommendation to the general counsel who then consults with the president to make a decision," he added.

Marshall said the BCB Integrity Unit is responsible for all domestic cricket in Bangladesh, while the International Cricket Council (ICC) handles international cricket, including international matches played in Bangladesh.

He said the unit receives information from players, coaches, team managers, journalists and the ICC regarding suspected corruption.

The unit assesses the credibility of the information before deciding whether to open an investigation.

"People make all sorts of allegations. Sometimes a team plays really badly and we get three phone calls saying they were all out for 50, they must be fixed. But that's just an angry fan," he said.

Once an investigation begins, it remains confidential. Marshall said he had not named anyone under investigation during the last nine years, when he had dealt with more than 100 cases.

He also praised the support of BCB President Tamim Iqbal and the general counsel, saying they had allowed him to operate independently.

"You are seeing in Bangladesh proactive steps to stamp out corruption in cricket," he said.

"I think what is being done by my team and the support of the president and the general counsel is excellent and you can compare it to anywhere in the world," he added.
Author: BSS

Title: Bangladesh U-20 women’s hockey team beat Malaysia to clinch fifth spot at Junior Asia Cup
Content:
Bangladesh concluded their campaign in the 2026 Women’s Junior Asia Cup hockey tournament with a 2-1 victory over Malaysia in Hulunbuir City, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, China, on Saturday.

The victory in their final match secured Bangladesh fifth place — their best-ever finish in the competition.

The women in red and green started strongly and displayed excellent hockey from the outset, but neither team managed to find the net in the first half.

Bangladesh finally broke the deadlock in the third quarter when captain Sharika Rimon converted a penalty stroke in the 31st minute.

Kona Akter then doubled Bangladesh’s lead with a superb field goal in the 50th minute.

Malaysia pulled a goal back late in the match through Irdina Jefrey in the 59th minute, but Bangladesh held on to secure a memorable victory.

The result capped an impressive campaign for Bangladesh, who began the tournament with a 7-0 victory over Chinese Taipei before thrashing Pakistan 5-1, Kazakhstan 4-0 and Hong Kong China 6-0 to finish as unbeaten champions of the Challengers Group.

Bangladesh then suffered a 2-0 defeat to strong Japan in the quarterfinals, sending them into the fifth-place playoff, where they overcame Malaysia to finish fifth.

The result marks Bangladesh’s best-ever performance in the Women’s Junior Asia Cup, improving on their ninth-place finish in their maiden appearance in the competition in 2024.
Author: Tribune Report

Title: Miraz continues to impress in CPL
Content:
Bangladesh allrounder Mehedi Hasan Miraz produced a yet another match-winning bowling performance to guide Guyana Amazon Warriors to a six-wicket victory over Trinbago Knight Riders in the Caribbean Premier League (CPL) at Providence Stadium.

Making his CPL debut in the previous match, Miraz had taken three wickets for just 13 runs.

He followed that up with an impressive four-wicket haul in his second appearance, earning the Player of the Match award as Guyana chased down a modest target with eight balls to spare.

Put into bat, Trinbago Knight Riders made a brisk start, reaching 41 in 4.3 overs before Miraz struck for the first time, bowling Colin Munro for 26 off 16 balls.

Imran Tahir, who had set a world record for the oldest player to claim a five-wicket haul at the age of 47 in the previous match, dismissed Alex Hales for 22.

Justin Greaves top-scored for Trinbago with 35 off 37 balls, but the rest of the batting lineup failed to offer much resistance.

Miraz then bowled Nicholas Pooran first ball before dismissing Gudakesh Motie and Sunil Narine to finish with four wickets for 23 runs from his four overs. Shamar Joseph claimed two wickets as Trinbago were restricted to 126-8 in 20 overs.

Guyana lost openers Mavendra Dindyal and Glenn Phillips for 36, but Shimron Hetmyer and Shai Hope steadied the innings and guided the hosts towards victory.

Hetmyer scored 42 off 35 balls, while Hope contributed 28 off 19 balls. Guyana reached 127-4 in 18.4 overs to secure their sixth-wicket victory.

Miraz, who came in late in the innings, scored just two runs off 14 balls, but his outstanding bowling performance had already laid the foundation for Guyana's comfortable win.

The victory kept Guyana Amazon Warriors at the top of the points table with 16 points from nine matches. Antigua and Barbuda Falcons are second with 13 points from 10 matches.
Author: BSS

Title: FIFA rebuffs Morocco claim over 2030 World Cup final
Content:
FIFA said on Friday that a decision on the venue for the 2030 World Cup final would be made "in due course", after Moroccan football federation president Fouzi Lekjaa said the showpiece match would be staged in Morocco.

Morocco, Spain and Portugal are co-hosting the 2030 tournament and have already begun competing for the right to stage the final, with Madrid's Santiago Bernabeu and a planned 115,000-seat stadium in Benslimane, near Casablanca, viewed as the leading contenders.

Lekjaa said on Wednesday that the final would take place in Morocco.

"Benslimane province will host the World Cup final. Whether some people like it or not," Lekjaa said during a public meeting in the region, according to video published by local media.

However, FIFA said no decision had yet been taken.

"As communicated on 5 August 2026, a decision will be made by FIFA in due course," a FIFA spokesperson told AFP on Friday.

The comments prompted reaction in Spain, where Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho backed the Santiago Bernabeu as the ideal venue for the final.

"I would like the final to be in Lisbon, but I'm already happy that a country like ours will have at least one match (at the World Cup)," the Portuguese coach told reporters on Friday.

"If you can play in a legendary, historic stadium, where some of the greatest players in history have played, the stadium of the most important club in the history of football, then I think it should be here," Mourinho said, referring to the Bernabeu.

"If I were Benfica's coach, I would tell you exactly the same thing."
Author: AFP

Title: Razaullah’s fearless Edgbaston assault gives Pakistan a lift
Content:
Pakistan pacer Razaullah produced a stunning counterattacking display on Test debut to give Pakistan a much-needed boost in their World Test Championship clash against England at Edgbaston.

The 21-year-old walked in at 9 with the score at 312/7 and Pakistan still needing another 8 runs to make England bat again, and went on an assault, smashing 81 from just 63 deliveries.

His nine sixes equalled the record for most sixes by a debutant in a Test innings and helped Pakistan set England a fourth-innings target of 130 after being pushed to the brink.

Razaullah’s approach was one of fearless aggression, particularly against the short ball, as he took on Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue.

“I was being selective with which balls to slog, but they all seemed within range,” he said after the conclusion of Day 3.

“I wanted to take it as deep as possible. I wasn’t scared of pace.

“I wanted to punish the balls from Archer that landed on a hard length.

“There’s nothing to be scared of when you’re playing for your country.

“I was just enjoying myself.”

At Edgbaston, he backed himself against an England attack that had repeatedly troubled Pakistan’s batters during the series, which gave the home side an unassailable 2-0 lead from the opening two Tests.

“My favourite ball [to face] is the short ball. I just believed in myself.

“I thought if I played 50 balls, I’d get a positive result. And thankfully that happened.”

Razaullah’s intent was matched by the enjoyment he displayed at the crease, soaking in the reception as the Edgbaston crowd stood up to commemorate his fighting spirit.

“I enjoyed the standing ovation.

“I like to enjoy life and I was relishing the moment.”

England will begin Day 4 with the bat, needing 130 runs to make it 3-0 in the three-match series.
Author: ICC

Title: Zverev holds off Khachanov, Shelton powers past Tiafoe to reach US Open final
Content:
Top seed Alexander Zverev out-gunned Karen Khachanov to reach his third straight Grand Slam final on Friday, rolling into the US Open title match with a straight sets win.

Big-serving Ben Shelton overpowered American compatriot Frances Tiafoe in four sets to reach the first Grand Slam final of his career.

Zverev, who followed up his maiden major at the French Open with a runner-up finish at Wimbledon, saved two set points in the final tiebreaker to close out the 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) victory.

He'll face Ben Shelton in Sunday's championship match.

The German predicted an "absolutely epic" contest between the two Americans, after which he'll be out to thwart the winner's bid to become the first American man in 23 years to lift a Grand Slam trophy.

"Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true on Sunday," said Zverev, who came agonizingly close to the US Open title in 2020 before falling to Dominic Thiem in five sets.

After a somewhat inauspicious start to the tournament, spending nine hours and 26 minutes on court in laborious five-set victories in the first and second rounds, Zverev has steadily upped his game.

He needed two hours and 57 minutes to deny 50th-ranked Khachanov's bid to become the lowest-ranked Grand Slam finalist since number 54 Marcos Baghdatis at the 2006 Australian Open.

But the Russian, who fell to Zverev in the Olympic gold medal match in Tokyo in 2021, put up a spirited challenge in the second and third sets.

Unable to make any real headway in the first set, Khachanov fell a quick break down in the second.

The Russian couldn't resist a grin when he snuck a passing shot by Zverev to open the fourth game, and flung his arm into the air in celebration three points later when a forehand winner gave him his first break chance of the match.

Zverev double faulted to hand him a break that leveled the set at 2-2.

Khachanov had another chance two games later when Zverev's backhand into the net to end a 32-shot rally gave him a break point.

But the German came up with a big serve and escaped the danger as they went to the tiebreaker, where Khachanov denied Zverev on two set points with thumping forehand and a brilliant backhand down the line before Zverev closed out the set.

Neither player mustered a break point in a tense third set. Khachanov had a chance to extend the match when he took a 6-4 lead in the tiebreaker, but after a pair of forehand errors from the Russian Zverev came up with his 15th ace and sealed the win on the next point when Khachanov sent a forehand long.

Eighth-seeded Shelton blasted 20 aces on his way to a thrilling 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory on the Arthur Ashe Stadium court that sends the 23-year-old into Sunday's championship match against top-seeded Alexander Zverev of Germany.

A pulsating all-American semi-final had seen both players vying to reach a Grand Slam final for the first time.

Shelton -- who took down defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in the quarter-finals -- will now have the chance to become the first American man to win a Grand Slam title since 2003, when Andy Roddick triumphed at the US Open.

"It's a lot of emotion," Shelton said in an on-court interview after a win that was watched by a star-studded New York crowd.

"My dad, my mom have sacrificed a lot for me to be in this position today. My dad lost his mom earlier this year, and she's the reason that he was able to play tennis.

"Without her, there's no Ben Shelton standing here today. So this one is for her. And I'm gonna need you guys on Sunday to to bring the energy. I'm going for it. I'm gonna leave it all on the court.

Earlier, Tiafoe got off to a bright start, claiming the first set after breaking when Shelton uncharacteristically double-faulted to trail at 5-4.

Tiafoe held to love to clinch the first set but Shelton came flying out of the blocks to start the second.

An early break helped him into a 2-0 lead before Tiafoe responded with a break to level at 2-2.

Yet with Tiafoe's serve increasingly erratic, Shelton grabbed another break in the eighth game to go 5-3 up and then held to level.

The momentum was all with Shelton and Tiafoe had to fight off two break points before holding early in the third set.

However Shelton – who had one serve initially clocked at 158mph before it was later adjusted to 144mph -- made no mistake in the fifth game with a break to go 3-2 up.

Tiafoe needed to hold to keep the set alive in the ninth game, and a furious arm-wrestle saw the 11th seed once again save three break and set points.

Shelton though earned his fourth break point after pouncing on Tiafoe's second serve once more, scorching a backhand return down the line.

Shelton converted that when Tiafoe netted a forehand to find himself 2-1 down.

The fourth set went with serve until the 12th game, when Shelton grabbed the crucial break to seal victory.
Author: Tribune Sports Desk

Title: World Cup winner Juan Mata hangs up boots at Melbourne Victory
Content:
Spanish World Cup-winner Juan Mata on Friday opted against playing another season with Australian side Melbourne Victory, but stopped short of calling time on his career.

The former Manchester United and Chelsea ace has enjoyed a late-career resurgence and was voted the domestic A-League player of the year in 2025-26.

But the 38-year-old has decided not to play on at the club as he mulls "the next steps in his career".

He will remain involved with the Australian side after taking an ownership stake.

"I loved every minute and so greatly enjoyed everything that we achieved last season, falling back in love with football at such a special place, in an amazing city that it was a privilege to call home," Mata said.

"Now I am excited about our next chapters, believing together in the future of Australian football and inspiring the next generation of Melbourne Victory players and supporters."

Mata announced in June he would take a minority stake in Victory. The terms of the deal were not disclosed but he will become chair of their newly established football committee.

"Juan's 2025/26 season will live long in the memory of Victory fans and should be cherished by all supporters of the world's game here in Australia," said Victory's football director John Didulica.

"Everyone at the club is excited that he is part of our ownership group and, in the future, looks forward to his football intelligence leading our football committee."

Mata, who played in Spain's 2010 World Cup-winning campaign and won the Champions League with Chelsea, moved to Victory in 2025 after a season with Western Sydney Wanderers.

He also has stakes in Formula One team Alpine and Major League Soccer club San Diego FC.
Author: AFP

Title: Ronaldo takes last crack at Asian glory as Saudi teams set to dominate
Content:
Cristiano Ronaldo will have a last crack at winning the Asian Champions League when the continent's top club competition begins on Monday, with big-spending Saudi teams set to dominate.

The 41-year-old former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus superstar said in August that it was "probably my last year in football".

The Portuguese attacker has nearly won it all during his club career, including five UEFA Champions League crowns.

But the Asian Champions League has so far eluded the five-time Ballon d'Or winner.

His Al Nassr side go into the latest continental campaign under a new coach in former Tottenham manager Ange Postecoglou, who was sacked by Spurs in June 2025 despite taking them to Europa League glory.

Along with Ronaldo, the Riyadh-based outfit have proven international attacking quality in Kingsley Coman, Sadio Mane and Ronaldo's Portugal team-mate Joao Felix.

Al Nassr are second in the Saudi Pro League after six matches, behind Al Hilal only on goal difference.

The skipper Ronaldo has been in good form, scoring three times in five league games.

Simone Inzaghi's Al Hilal present a major obstacle in Ronaldo's bid to win the AFC Champions League for the first time.

Al Hilal were major spenders in the recent transfer window, snapping up Aston Villa's England striker Ollie Watkins and Brazil winger Gabriel Martinelli from Arsenal for a combined $150 million.

The format of the Asian Champions League is heavily skewed in favour of teams from Saudi Arabia, which is spending vast fortunes on football and will host the 2034 World Cup.

Since the 2024-2025 season the competition was rebranded as the Champions League Elite and the quarter-finals, semis and final are held in a centralised location in Saudi Arabia.

Al Ahli made the most of home advantage by winning the title in 2025 and 2026.

An Al Ahli side with England's Ivan Toney in attack beat Japan's Machida Zelvia 1-0 in extra time in April's final on home turf in Jeddah.

Al Nassr, Al Ahli and Al Hilal will be joined in this year's competition by Al Ittihad and Al Qadsiah, making it a bumper five Saudi sides among the 32 teams.

As in recent years, the competition is divided equally into two leagues of East and West.

Each side will play four matches at home and four away.

The biggest threat to the Saudi stranglehold will likely come from Japan -- teams from Asia's strongest footballing nation have reached the final in each of the last four editions.

There are also five J. League teams, prime among them reigning domestic champions Kashima Antlers.

Former Kashima star Yasushi Endo admitted the Saudi teams would be hard to beat.

"It's difficult for Japanese teams to be champions these days given the financial strength of teams in the West who can invest heavily in players that traditionally play in strong European leagues," he said.

"With the tournament being played in a centralised format in the West, it also makes things extra difficult.

"We cannot underplay the importance of having large fan support."
Author: AFP

Title: Man United, Bayern cruise as Como make dream Champions League start
Content:
Manchester United celebrated their return to the Champions League with a 4-0 thrashing of Sabah on Thursday, as Cesc Fabregas's Como impressed on their debut in Europe's premier club competition.

Harry Kane and Michael Olise, with a brace, both scored in the week that they were nominated for the Ballon d'Or as Bayern Munich were made to work before Bodo/Glimt's second-half collapse in a 5-0 rout.

Matheus Cunha scored his first goal of the season while captain Bruno Fernandes, forward Benjamin Sesko and centre-back Lisandro Martinez were also on the scoresheet on a comfortable night for the Red Devils at Old Trafford.

"I think it was perfect for everyone, especially our fans," Sesko told TNT Sports.

"It means a lot to them, especially when they see so many goals. I think it was great for us in general to give us more motivation for the upcoming games."

There was one moment of concern after Cunha had given Michael Carrick's team a 27th-minute lead from Patrick Dorgu's cross, as United's defensive frailties almost came back to haunt them.

But Joy-Lance Mickels headed wide for the Champions League debutants when free at the back post from less than five yards out.

The Azerbaijanis wilted at the end of the first period as Youri Tielemans teed up Fernandes and then Sesko ran onto Bryan Mbeumo's through ball before rounding goalkeeper Stas Pokatilov before sliding the ball home.

Midway through the second half, Martinez pounced on a bobbling ball that ricocheted off Pokatilov and a defender from substitute Joshua Zirkzee's backheel as United went into cruise control.

Carrick even had the luxury of bringing on youngsters Harry Amass and Shea Lacey for their Champions League bows as he sought to rest legs ahead of Sunday's Manchester derby.

"I think the confidence boost is definitely big. It's important to recover good and focus on the derby," added Sesko.

Goals from Croatia midfielder Martin Baturina, Greece forward Tasos Douvikas and Senegal's Assane Diao put Como in control against RB Leipzig.

Serbia midfielder Andrija Maksimovic pulled a goal back for Leipzig before Maximo Perrone sealed a 4-1 victory late on a dream night in northern Italy.

Kane scored for the eighth Champions League game in a row as he powered home a header from Olise's free-kick, with Bayern eventually overcoming a spirited Bodo/Glimt.

Jamal Musiala had given them the lead shortly after a goalless first half and after Kane's goal, Alphonso Davies shot into the bottom corner when Olise's corner was only half cleared.

It was Musiala's first goal since he collapsed on the pitch during pre-season due to a neurological condition.

"Scoring a goal -- pure happiness," Musiala told DAZN.

"I just want to perform well again... I just want to get back to my level step by step, playing with a sense of ease, joy, and fun on the pitch."

Olise got in on the act with a sumptuous finish seven minutes from time before Odin Bjortuft was dismissed for the Norwegians.

Olise then completed the rout with his second.

Lens twice came from behind to beat 10-man Slavia Prague 3-2 with injury-time goals from Florian Thauvin and Ruben Aguilar.

Danijel Sturm had twice given Slavia the lead, firstly just after Mikulas Konecny was dismissed and then with just two minutes remaining, but the Czechs were unable to hold on.

Earlier on, there were 1-1 draws between Fenerbahce and Roma, and between PSV Eindhoven and Shakhtar Donetsk.

Fenerbahce coach Ismail Kartal quit after the match in Istanbul, during which he was targeted by a bottle thrown from the crowd.

But his president Aziz Yildirim said he had rejected the resignation.
Author: AFP

Title: Rybakina rallies to beat Gauff, book US Open final with Sabalenka
Content:
Elena Rybakina rallied from a set down to beat Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 on Thursday and book a US Open championship showdown with two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka.

In Saturday's final Rybakina will try to deal another blow to Sabalenka, having knocked her out of the number one world ranking just by reaching the semi-finals.

"I feel like I definitely need to step my game up, serve much better than today and stay aggressive," Rybakina said of her looming clash with Sabalenka.

Gauff's bid to return to the final for the first time since she defeated Sabalenka for the 2023 title had got off to a smooth start, with the American seizing the initiative in the opening set with a break to go 4-2 up.

She held to love to take a 5-2 lead and then held in the ninth game to take a one set lead.

But Rybakina hit back with an early break of serve in the second set for a 3-1 lead and held to go 4-1 up.

Gauff responded superbly to claw her way back into contention with a break to make it 4-3 before holding to square it a 4-4.

Yet she was unable to make the most of her fightback and double-faulted in the 10th game to hand two set points to Rybakina at 15-40. Rybakina pounced on that chance to take the match to a third set.

The decisive set followed a similar pattern.

Gauff conceded a break to trail 5-3 and leave Rybakina serving for the match.

But the American broke back immediately to make it 5-4 to get it back on serve.

Again though Gauff was unable to capitalise, and a deft volley from Rybakina left her with two match points at 15-40, before Gauff then hit a wide open smash long to hand her opponent victory.

"It was such a cool third set -- I feel like I was a little bit lucky on her serve," Rybakina said. "A couple of deep returns, one mistake from her, it went quickly my way...it was a real battle."
Author: AFP

Title: Messi to buy second Spanish lower league club
Content:
Argentina icon Lionel Messi has agreed to take over Spanish club Eldense, the second division side confirmed on Thursday.

Eldense, based just in-land from Alicante, will become the former Barcelona attacker's second venture into Spanish football ownership having bought fourth-tier Cornella in April.

The 39-year-old plays for Inter Miami and retired from international duty after Argentina's loss to Spain in the World Cup final this summer.

"CD Eldense can confirm that Lionel Messi has reached an agreement in principle with the club's current owners to acquire the shares currently held by Grupo TH Soluciones, which would make him the majority shareholder of CD Eldense," they told AFP.

"At this time, the transaction is pending completion of the final legal and contractual procedures, including the due diligence process, as well as the required authorisation from the Spanish Sports Council (CSD).

"For now, the club is unable to provide details on the financial terms of the transaction or set a definitive date for its completion, as the process has not yet been finalised.

"Once the relevant procedures have been completed and the necessary authorizations obtained, CD Eldense will officially report any developments in this regard," the club founded in 1921 added.
Author: AFP

Title: Bangladesh, Nepal discuss strengthening ties through sports diplomacy
Content:
Bangladesh and Nepal discussed ways to strengthen bilateral ties through cricket and sports diplomacy when Nepal's ambassador to Bangladesh, Ghanashyam Bhandari, met State Minister for Youth and Sports Md. Aminul Haque at his Bangladesh Secretariat office on Thursday.

The meeting also focused on expanding sports and cultural exchanges between the two countries.

Ghanashyam Bhandari thanked the Bangladesh government and people for their timely support to Nepal following the devastating floods and mudslides in the country's northern region.

Highlighting the strong political relations between the neighbours, the Nepalese Ambassador said there are opportunities for further cooperation through cultural and sports exchanges.

"Bangladesh and Nepal enjoy excellent political relations. However, there is ample scope to further strengthen this relationship through cultural exchanges and sports," he said.

Ghanashyam Bhandari proposed a bilateral cricket series, noting that the two countries had not played a bilateral series in recent times.

"Especially for our people affected by the recent disasters, inspiration is needed. We request Bangladesh to organize a T20 series. Our team is fully prepared to tour Bangladesh."

Likewise, we are also prepared to welcome the Bangladesh team to Nepal,â€ said the Ambassador.

State Minister for Sports Md Aminul Haque welcomed the proposal and reaffirmed Bangladesh's commitment to using sports diplomacy to promote regional cooperation.

"We strongly believe in sports diplomacy and are already working to expand cooperation in different sports," he said.

The State Minister asked the Nepalese Ambassador to submit a formal proposal. Bangladesh would then discuss the matter with the Bangladesh Cricket Board and take necessary steps.

Aminul Haque also suggested using Nepal's geographical advantages to improve the training and capabilities of Bangladeshi athletes, particularly by creating opportunities for them in mountaineering and related sports.

The meeting highlighted the potential for closer Bangladesh-Nepal ties through expanded sporting and cultural exchanges, with cricket identified as a key area of cooperation.
Author: BSS

Title: Antimicrobial resistance: The silent pandemic
Content:
Most of us think infections come from outside invaders; harmful germs that enter the body and make us sick.

However, some microbes of growing concern are not strangers; they are long-term residents of our own bodies.

The human body is like a busy neighbourhood, home to trillions of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and viruses.

Together, they form what scientists call the microbiome. Most of these tiny residents are not enemies. They help digest food, strengthen the immune system, and protect us from harmful germs.

For the most part, we live peacefully with these microbes. But when this delicate balance is disturbed, some of our friendly neighbours can become opportunistic pathogens.

In the age of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), these once-manageable microbes are becoming increasingly difficult to control.

Take Escherichia coli ( E coli ), for example. It normally lives in our intestines and plays an important role in maintaining gut health. But if it enters the urinary tract, it can cause infection.

Until recently, these infections were usually easy to treat. Today, many E coli strains no longer respond to commonly used antibiotics.

According to a landmark study published in The Lancet in 2022, six leading pathogens collectively accounted for nearly 1 million AMR-attributable deaths in 2019, with E coli being the single largest individual contributor.

The same is true for Candida , a fungus that normally lives quietly in our mouths and digestive system. Most of the time, it causes no harm. But when the immune system is weakened by illness, cancer treatment, or prolonged antibiotic use, it can multiply rapidly and cause serious, sometimes life-threatening, infections.

Another example is Staphylococcus aureus , a bacterium commonly found on our skin and inside the nose. Many people carry it without ever becoming ill.

However, some strains have evolved resistance to important antibiotics, making infections much more difficult and costly to treat.

One of the biggest reasons is the misuse and overuse of antibiotics. Every time antibiotics are taken unnecessarily, used incorrectly, or stopped too early, bacteria are given another opportunity to adapt.

Over time, they develop ways to survive medicines that once killed them.

In a sense, we are unintentionally training our microscopic neighbours to defend themselves.

This is no longer just a concern for scientists and doctors; it is a growing global public health problem.

In Bangladesh, this problem is easy to observe in everyday life. A parent may visit a local pharmacy for a child with a fever or a common cold and receive an antibiotic without a prescription, even though many of these illnesses are caused by viruses, against which antibiotics do not work.

While this may seem like a quick solution, repeated unnecessary use encourages bacteria to become resistant.

Studies have shown that antibiotics are frequently purchased without a prescription in Bangladesh, highlighting the urgent need for stronger antibiotic stewardship and greater public awareness.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the misuse and overuse of antibiotics are among the leading drivers of antimicrobial resistance worldwide.

Resistant infections lead to longer hospital stays, higher healthcare costs, and fewer treatment options. They also threaten many of the medical advances we now take for granted.

Safe surgery, cancer treatment, intensive care, and the care of newborn babies all depend on antibiotics that work.

The answer is not to eliminate the microbes that live with us. Most are essential for our health.

Instead, we must preserve the delicate balance between humans and the microorganisms that share our bodies.

That requires responsible antibiotic use, stronger infection prevention, better public awareness, and effective antimicrobial stewardship programs.

Healthcare professionals, policy-makers, pharmacists, and the public all have important roles to play.

Antimicrobial resistance is often called a silent pandemic because it spreads quietly, without the dramatic headlines of outbreaks like Covid-19. Yet its impact could be just as devastating.

The World Health Organization has identified AMR as one of the top 10 global public health threats facing humanity. The microbes that have lived alongside us need not become our enemies. Whether they remain trusted neighbours or dangerous adversaries will depend largely on the choices we make today.

ASM Tarik Hasan is a public health researcher specializing in antimicrobial resistance and clinical microbiology.
Author: A S M Tarik Hasan

Title: They looted the banks
Content:
We've got to get this firmly in our minds that they looted the banks. As this newspaper reports : “Nearly Tk33 of every Tk100 lent by banks is now in default.”

Now, some of this is just banking. There're always some loans that go bad. People borrowed and things didn't work out. The amount of interest charged on loans reflects this, the knowledge that some will not be repaid.

So, every loan has to pay 1%, or 2%, more, to cover the 2 or 3% of loans that don't get repaid. It's just part of the business.

But one third of loans going bad? That's either the effect of a dreadful recession -- depression -- or evidence of looting. Bangladesh hasn't had a recent depression, therefore our conclusion should be that, well, you can add in the rest.

As to who “they” were or are, we can all have a good guess. But we'll not mention specific names, obviously, since libel laws do exist.

But, well, people with good and close connections with the previous political regime would be a good guide.

As to why they looted the banks, that's easier, as Willy Sutton said. He was a US bank robber and when asked why he stole from banks said: “That's where the money is.”

And if you've got political power, it's a lot easier to steal from the banks than it is from the government.

Certainly, the government spends a lot of money, but stealing tax money is still difficult. But banks exist to make loans. So, if you've political power, then you can force -- or even just “persuade” -- the banks to lend you money which you've no intention of repaying.

This does become a loss of tax money eventually, as we're finding out. Because the government that comes afterwards has to do something about those banks and those loans.

Which is what is being done and is what has to be done. As the banks have been looted, we have two, and only two, choices.

We'll stop depositing our money in banks -- as has been happening -- and that means we'll all be poorer in the future. Because what banks do, as an economic factor, is repurpose our savings into the investments that make the future richer. If we all stop using banks for our savings this will not happen.

We also have to prosecute those who took the money. Bankrupt them for not repaying. Take their businesses off them. A few in jail would be a very good idea indeed.

We also need to make sure that the political system does not determine such lending again in the future. There's no point in getting rid of one bunch of thieves just to allow another to repeat the exercise.

But one more thing. Some of those loans were just looting. But many of them -- even most of them -- were for at least attempts at investing.

We all recall the minister who tried to build an international property portfolio, right? Who bought at the peak and has been seeing the value of the properties falling since he bought?

That's the thing to really remember from this. Those in politics, or even those closely allied with politics, do not in fact know what to do with the money.

They cannot even invest free money profitably. Therefore, the new system should not only insist upon no looting but also no investing by politics, politicians, and the politically associated.

Thieves are always with us, and it's a very good idea not to give them access to our money. But politicians, the politically aligned, are also -- even if honest -- terribly bad investors. So we should also not give them access to our money.

Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.
Author: Tim Worstall

Title: The quiet strain of working mothers
Content:
Every working mother in Bangladesh endures an exhausting dual existence. In one scenario, you're juggling the pressures of a typical 9-to-5 job -- attending back-to-back meetings, receiving urgent client calls, meeting tight deadlines, and striving for career goals.

In the other world, your mind remains permanently tethered to a phone sitting next to your keyboard, quietly waiting for updates from home.

Has my baby eaten? Did he take his bath? Is he crying?

As a new mother of a seven-month-old boy, I never imagined how challenging it would be to cross this mental difference.

Motherhood is meant to be a journey of connection, yet every morning feels like a quiet tug-of-war.

Like any mother, I wish I could experience every fleeting moment of his early months without blinking.

Yet, my hands are tied. Every morning, I pack my bags, say goodbye, and leave my son in the care of my ageing mother before stepping into the office.

While I am really lucky to have family support, this arrangement has replaced one type of anxiety with another.

Throughout my workday, a constant loop of fear runs in the background: Did my mother remember to take her medicine while keeping up with an energetic infant? What if something terrible happens while I am locked in a presentation -- how will she manage alone?

This constant tension is not unique to my household; it reflects the daily reality of hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of urban working women across Bangladesh.

Relying on grandparents is a temporary patch, not a sustainable solution -- it places heavy physical strain on elderly parents while leaving working mothers carrying an inescapable sense of guilt.

The true tragedy is that this strain arrives at the worst possible moment in a woman's career.

Most of us spend 25 or 26 years pursuing higher education and building professional foundations. Yet, just as female professionals reach their prime years for career advancement, the arrival of a child creates a stark ultimatum.

Without accessible, institutional childcare, a vast number of women are forced to step away from the workforce at the precise moment they are ready to step into leadership.

This mid-career exit represents a massive, preventable leak in our country's talent pipeline.

Section 94 of the Bangladesh Labour Act mandates that every establishment employing 40 or more women must maintain a suitable room for children under the age of six.

Yet across corporations, institutions, and factories, compliance remains largely symbolic or entirely absent.

Where daycare facilities do exist, capacity rarely meets demand.

Childcare should not be treated as a woman's personal dilemma or a luxury corporate perk. When workplaces integrate safe, professionally managed, and on-site daycare facilities, childcare ceases to be an overwhelming burden borne by one person at home.

It creates an ecosystem where fathers can also take active, equal roles in daily caregiving during work hours.

If Bangladesh aims to sustain its economic growth and empower its female workforce, care infrastructure must be prioritized as essential national infrastructure. Until employers and policy-makers build safe harbours for our children where we work, our brightest women will continue to be forced out of the workforce -- not for a lack of ambition, but for a lack of support.

Jerin Tasnim is a senior executive, HR, Dhaka Tribune and Bangla Tribune.
Author: Jerin Tasnim

Title: Do not repeat the same mistakes with cybersecurity
Content:
Transparency International Bangladesh’s concerns about the draft Cyber Security (Amendment) Act, 2026 deserve serious attention.

As written, the proposed law risks repeating the mistakes of previous regimes -- vague language, unchecked authority, and broad surveillance powers had been a mainstay with previous cybersecurity laws.

There is no questioning the fact that such laws were used to silence dissent rather than protect citizens. Bangladesh cannot afford to walk that path again.

As rightfully noted by TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman: “The draft law brings three complex and distinct issues -- cybercrime, cybersecurity and people’s right to freedom of expression -- under a single law, without giving adequate attention to any of them."

Deliberate misinterpretation and misuse of our cyber laws have been weapons for the previous administration, violating the human rights of many. We must move away from vagueness in our laws that create a landscape where interpretation becomes discretionary, enforcement becomes arbitrary, and ultimately citizens become vulnerable.

When terms such as “rumour,” “misinformation,” “demeaning,” “defamatory,” and “insulting to the state” are defined loosely, authorities have the power to target criticism, satire, or legitimate political speech. Our history suggests that such ambiguities have repeatedly been weaponized by the state at the expense of the people.

Equally troubling is the proposal for a 28-member Cyber Security Council dominated by government representatives. A council structured this way risks becoming an enforcement arm rather than an independent oversight body.

No good comes from sweeping powers without accountability, combined with immunity for actions taken in “good faith.” All they usually achieve is undermining the principle that all are equal before the law.

We are not arguing that Bangladesh’s digital space must be protected from cybercrime and genuine threats, which is a given. But protection cannot come at the cost of fundamental rights.

Laws that blur definitions, expand surveillance, and criminalize expression do not strengthen cybersecurity but weaken democracy. Our digital future must be secure, but it must also be free. This is what the present administration must ensure.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: Developing nations must work together
Content:
With September 12 marking the UN Day for South-South Cooperation, Bangladesh must recognize the importance of cooperation among developing countries and actively work to strengthen its ties.

Indeed, it would not be a mistake to argue that most meaningful development partnerships increasingly lie within the Global South.

This day reflects a shift in global power, knowledge, and innovation. Developing nations now generate a substantial share of global growth, and their collective experience offers solutions far more relevant to our realities than traditional models originating in the developed North.

Bangladesh has repeatedly benefited from exchanges with fellow developing nations, be they agricultural techniques, disaster‑management expertise, digital‑governance models, renewable‑energy solutions, or public health innovations.

It goes without saying that solutions have greater odds of success when there is an exchange of context‑appropriate tools shaped by countries that have confronted similar constraints and pressures.

It must also be stated that Bangladesh is not merely a recipient, and its achievements in community‑based health systems, microfinance, disaster preparedness, and social‑protection programs have become global references for other nations in the Global South.

South-South cooperation allows Bangladesh to share these strengths while gaining new approaches to emerging challenges such as climate shocks, rapid urbanization, food insecurity, and digital transformation.

Given the importance, it is imperative that we deepen this engagement. Too often, cooperation remains limited to conferences, pilot projects, or symbolic agreements.

Bangladesh needs long‑term partnerships, ones that expand joint research, strengthen climate resilience, and reduce dependence on external models that do not align with our local realities.

The Global South’s collective future depends on how effectively its members learn from one another and build systems rooted in solidarity rather than hierarchy.

This cooperation could be a central pillar of a fairer, more resilient future for all of us.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: Protecting the hand that hurts
Content:
Picture a courtroom in Bangladesh. A woman is sitting on a bench, hiding her bruises, and waiting to testify against her own husband who beats her mercilessly.

When her name is called, she suddenly changes her original story, fervently trying to withdraw the case and convince the magistrate that her injuries were rather the result of an accident.

Outside the courtroom, her mother-in-law is standing, waiting for her to take her to the same house, the same husband, and the same violence.

This is not a rare scenario in Bangladesh’s family courts or police stations; rather, it is a pattern so common here that oftentimes the police or the court shows reluctance to even register cases of domestic violence.

Why do these women, despite years of abuse, try to protect their abusers?

To answer this question, let us travel 53 years into the past.

In 1973, four employees (three women and one man) of Kreditbanken Bank in Stockholm were taken hostage by two robbers for six days.

By the time the police were able to free them, they had grown protective of their captors, refusing to testify against the perpetrators and instead raising money for their legal defense.

Psychiatrists called this condition Stockholm Syndrome; a survival response where the victim develops sympathy, even loyalty toward the abuser who controls their fear.

Similarly, among women who are victims of abuse, a long period of intimate violence and torture produces Stockholm Syndrome in the form of fierce trauma bonding, which leads to an unintentional instinct to protect their abuser from consequences of their own.

In Bangladesh’s household scenario, this trauma bond rarely announces itself as a pathology; rather, it looks like a housewife telling her neighbours that the bruises on her face are from an accidental fall down the stairs, a mother telling her daughter to call the injuries on her body marks of a self-inflicted accident, or a young wife defending her husband’s violence as occasional outbursts of anger.

According to analysts, the main reasons for South Asian women experiencing Stockholm Syndrome are financial dependency, fear of social stigma, patriarchal society, and a conviction that suffering silently is a form of loyalty and a badge of honour for women. A woman's own family often supports this idea of protecting the abusive husband at any cost.

This is akin to the boiling-frog pattern, where researchers illustrate that when abuse towards a woman increases gradually, she can lose the ability or the willingness to protect herself or remove herself from the situation.

Based on the irrational belief that the world cannot offer her a better alternative than what she already has, she thus ends up subconsciously developing instincts to protect her abusive partner.

To make things worse, the Domestic Violence Act (2010) in Bangladesh every so often clashes head-on with the involuntary, deep state of self-preservation in women who have been conditioned to defend their abusers.

As a result, police, often reluctantly, send complaints back for domestic violence matters to be settled “domestically.”

Millions of women enable their partners to continue abusing them throughout their relationships. However, putting the onus of standing up to violence on the victims themselves is easy but, by no means, fair.

Instead, we need to ask the difficult questions here.

Why, after all, do the abused women enable their abusers? And why do they keep protecting these sadist oppressors?

A quick glance at these ill-fated women’s formative years will tell you why.

Since their early days, many women see their mothers silently suffer physical and mental torture, verbal assault, and various other forms of hostility in their own house.

These women keep hearing from their family, neighbours, relatives, and everyone else in society that domestic disputes are normal between married couples, that “purush manush ektu emoni hoy, meye der manay nite hoy” (men will be men and women need to adjust), that a woman’s real house is her husband’s house, and that a good wife should prioritize her family honour and endure her husband’s maltreatment at any cost.

The mass media these women become exposed to during the developmental period further normalizes and even glamorizes violence against women.

Many movies, dramas, and even cartoons typically characterize women as damsels in distress and men as their saviors, romanticizing toxic relationships and portraying physical violence as a sign of passionate love.

Essentially, when a woman is repetitively told that she is a nobody without her husband, the narrative gets fixated in her mind.

Sometimes this narrative can become so noxious that women even end up becoming complicit in their husbands’ crimes. In the brutal Ramisa rape and murder case, for instance, the wife of the offender actively took part in the atrocity.

While this woman’s crimes are unforgivable, have we ever stopped to think that perhaps it was Stockholm Syndrome that made her feel compelled to protect her husband?

What can be done to save these women from themselves? Do we really believe that only enforcing stricter laws against domestic violence, getting more women educated, or helping women become financially independent will solve the issue?

Admittedly, a combined effort from all these fronts will likely improve the situation to a certain extent. However, until and unless our society recalibrates its views on domestic violence and stops telling women to adjust, accept, and adapt, women will continue to protect the very hand that hurts them.

Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at BRAC Business School and Faizah Zahin is an English and Humanities student, BRAC University.
Author: Nadia Afroze Disha Faizah Zahin

Title: On the road again
Content:
My sister and her retired husband have benefited from forms of support that would be unimaginable in many countries. Assistance with household tasks, social support, and allied health services can help older people and people with disabilities remain at home and maintain a degree of independence.

Australia's aged-care system formally includes services such as social work and physiotherapy among the forms of support that can be provided in home and community settings.

Australia's relatively high wages are another part of this social model. As of July 2026, the national minimum wage is A$26.44 an hour, or A$1,004.90 for a 38-hour week,

Singapore provides another fascinating example.

I spent a couple of weeks there and was struck by what highly educated, pragmatic, and institutionally minded leadership can accomplish when it is combined with administrative competence and a long-term vision.

I visited a school whose principal had become something of a legendary figure. He had grown up poor and had been supported by teachers from religious communities different from his own. His life story was therefore a personal testament to the possibilities of education and merit.

He also played an important role in promoting the recognition of South Asian languages in Singapore's educational system.

Singapore's mother-tongue policy is particularly interesting in this respect. Alongside the country's four official mother tongues -- English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay, and Tamil -- students who meet the relevant criteria can study non-Tamil Indian languages, including Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Punjabi, and Urdu.

The principal told me about an encounter he had with Lee Kuan Yew. He explained that he had argued for the importance of allowing children to maintain a connection with their mother tongue. Lee understood the argument and gave his support.

The principal proudly showed me a copy of the letter, now framed and displayed on the wall of his office.

The episode stayed with me because it illustrated something larger than language policy. A country's development is not simply a matter of GDP, technology, or infrastructure. It is also about whether its leaders understand the importance of education, culture, language, and human dignity.

Travel in the global age may no longer give us the same sense of discovering an unknown world that it once did.

Before the internet, arriving in a distant country could mean entering a world about which we knew very little. Today, Google, YouTube, social media, and satellite television have brought much of the world into our living rooms.

But travel has not become irrelevant. Quite the opposite.

Travel allows us to test what we think we know against what actually exists. It introduces us to people whose lives cannot be reduced to statistics.

It allows us to see institutions at work rather than merely read about them. And occasionally, it offers an insight that is difficult to obtain from books or screens.

In Zadar, the sea itself became an orchestra.

In Croatia, I saw how a small country takes education and sport seriously.

Among Bangladeshi migrants, I was reminded of the distance that can exist between a country's citizens and the people who govern them.

In Australia, I saw how democratic institutions and a welfare state can become part of everyday life.

And in Singapore, I was reminded of the transformative possibilities of education and leadership.

Perhaps, then, the real purpose of travel is not to see places. It is to see societies.

These experiences have left me with one broader thought.

Countries do not develop simply because they possess natural resources, favourable geography, or large populations.

Nor does economic growth automatically produce a just, prosperous, or cohesive society.

Institutions have to be built, maintained, and protected. Schools must function. Public officials must do their jobs. Governments must think beyond the next election. And leaders must understand that public office is a responsibility, not a private entitlement.

Education matters enormously because educated leaders are more likely to understand the complexity of modern societies, appreciate evidence, learn from experience, and recognize the importance of institutions.

But education by itself is not enough. An educated person without integrity can become more dangerous, not less.

Knowledge must be accompanied by honesty, competence, humility, and a commitment to the public good.

The examples I encountered on the road -- from Croatia to Australia to Singapore -- are obviously very different, and none should be romanticized. Every society has its contradictions, inequalities, and failures.

Yet they illustrate a common principle: Development depends not only on resources and policies but on the quality of institutions and the people entrusted with them.

A country needs leaders who are educated enough to understand the world, honest enough to resist corruption, competent enough to turn ideas into institutions, and humble enough to listen to ordinary citizens.

Perhaps that is the most important lesson of travel.

The distance between countries is no longer very great. We can cross it in hours.

But the distance between good governance and bad governance, between competent leadership and incompetence, between public service and self-service, can determine the fate of an entire generation.

And that distance is not measured in kilometres.

Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.
Author: Habibul Haque Khondker

Title: Ensuring the right to healthcare
Content:
Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain’s declaration that either he or irregularities in hospitals will remain is certainly a strong statement, but the circumstances under which he said so are deeply concerning.

A surprise inspection of Mugda Medical College Hospital was conducted, where the complaints being investigated were unfortunately found to be true -- including that of patients being sent to outside diagnostic centres, despite the hospital having facilities to conduct the required tests.

This is just one example of what is undoubtedly a gross neglect of people's right to healthcare.

Government hospitals are meant to provide accessible healthcare to those who cannot afford expensive private treatment. When patients are directed elsewhere for services that are already available within public facilities, they are not only being made to spend more money, but may also be exposed to unnecessary additional steps and other irregular practices.

The minister also heard complaints about lifts not operating regularly, forcing patients and their relatives to struggle between floors. Such seemingly basic failures can become serious problems for elderly, sick, and disabled patients.

However, impromptu inspections and strong statements can only take us so far. What matters now is what actions are truly taken.

To that end, those responsible for irregularities must be identified and held accountable, while systems should be put in place to ensure such practices cannot simply return once the spotlight moves elsewhere.

This should also be a nationwide effort. If irregularities exist in one government hospital, there is every reason to examine whether similar problems exist elsewhere.

Regular unannounced inspections, transparent complaint mechanisms, proper monitoring of diagnostic services, and consequences for those abusing public facilities can help restore confidence in the system.

Our public hospitals serve millions, often under difficult circumstances. They deserve better management, stronger oversight, and greater accountability.

The minister has made his position clear. Now the health sector needs to see to it that his position is translated into lasting action.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: Keeping the city clean
Content:
It is disconcerting that in Dhaka, a city that generates more than 7,000 tons of waste every day, finding a public bin is still challenging -- a basic gap in public infrastructure that should no longer be acceptable.

The absence of bins makes responsible waste disposal unnecessarily difficult. A pedestrian carrying disposables accumulated through daily activities should not have to walk for kilometres to find somewhere to dispose of them.

While this inconvenience certainly cannot excuse littering, it does highlight the responsibility of the city corporations to provide practical facilities that make good behaviour possible.

There have been attempts before. In 2016, more than 11,000 mini bins were installed across Dhaka, but most disappeared within about a year because of theft and inadequate monitoring.

The fact that the capital is facing essentially the same problem a decade later shows that simply installing bins is not enough.

The current plan by Dhaka South City Corporation to install 2,000 heavier, more durable bins is therefore welcome -- but this time, the authorities must also ensure proper placement, regular maintenance, monitoring, and timely waste collection.

Dhaka North City Corporation, meanwhile, should move quickly to finalize a dedicated roadside-bin program instead of leaving pedestrians without convenient disposal options.

At the same time, public responsibility cannot be overlooked. Bins are useful only when people actually use them, and damaging or stealing public facilities only makes an already difficult problem much worse. Littering should not become the default simply because facilities are inadequate.

Ultimately, this is about more than waste management. Public services should be designed around the everyday needs of citizens, while citizens must also take responsibility for protecting and using those services properly. A cleaner Dhaka will require both.

The city corporations must provide the infrastructure and accountability, and the public must do its part too. Only then can keeping Dhaka clean become a shared responsibility rather than an endless struggle.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: India’s BRICS leadership could offer Bangladesh an economic bridge to recovery
Content:
Bangladesh approaches the New Delhi BRICS Summit at a critical economic moment. After years of impressive export-led growth and social progress, the country is contending with persistent inflation, slower growth, pressure on its banking sector, and subdued private investment.

The World Bank projects growth of 3.9% in the 2025-26 financial year, while the International Monetary Fund expects consumer-price inflation of around 9.2% in 2026.

Bangladesh is also preparing to eventually graduate from the United Nations’ least-developed-country category. Graduation is a major national achievement, but it brings the challenge of competing without some of the trade preferences that previously supported Bangladeshi exports.

India’s leadership of BRICS offers Bangladesh a bridge between these immediate pressures and its next phase of development. When leaders gather in New Delhi on September 12-13, India will be representing not only one of the world’s largest emerging economies but also the country with the deepest capacity to connect Bangladesh to regional markets, electricity networks, transport corridors, and development institutions.

Bangladesh is not a BRICS member, but it is a member of the New Development Bank. India played a founding role in creating the NDB as an institution capable of financing the priorities of developing economies. Bangladesh’s membership now gives it direct access to an expanding source of infrastructure finance.

The bank is already financing Bangladeshi projects in solar energy and electricity distribution. Its wider discussions with Dhaka cover bridges, railway modernization, urban transit, and maintenance infrastructure. These are precisely the investments Bangladesh requires to restore productivity, attract private capital, and create employment.

Energy cooperation demonstrates India’s role as a regional champion particularly clearly. Bangladesh already imports substantial electricity from India. It has also begun receiving Nepalese hydropower through the Indian grid, creating a historic three-country electricity arrangement.

India’s transmission infrastructure and regulatory cooperation allow clean power generated in the Himalayas to reach consumers in Bangladesh. Bangladesh gains a more diversified electricity supply, Nepal gains export revenue, and India strengthens the resilience of the entire regional grid.

Connectivity provides a second pillar. India and Bangladesh have revived railway links, expanded road connections, and increased the use of inland waterways. The operational use of Chittagong and Mongla ports is creating shorter routes between mainland India and its northeastern states. Bangladesh, in turn, is gaining new opportunities in logistics, port services, manufacturing, and regional commerce.

India’s approach recognizes Bangladesh not simply as a transit route but as an essential economic partner in the Bay of Bengal. Better connectivity increases the value of Bangladesh’s geographic position and helps link its businesses with India’s large consumer market and the economies of Nepal and Bhutan.

This integration matters as Bangladesh prepares for its post-LDC future. The country’s next stage of growth depends on diversifying beyond ready-made garments and moving into higher-value textiles, pharmaceuticals, food processing, electronics, shipbuilding, and digital services. Indian companies, technology networks, and supply chains provide a natural platform for that transition.

India is already emphasizing trade finance, start-up cooperation, resilient supply chains, and support for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. These priorities can complement the growing start-up and digital connections between India and Bangladesh. Affordable finance and easier access to regional markets would help Bangladeshi enterprises expand at a time when domestic credit conditions remain difficult.

Climate resilience is another area in which the two countries’ interests converge. India’s satellite capabilities, forecasting networks, digital public infrastructure, and disaster-management experience add regional capacity to Bangladesh’s internationally respected community-based preparedness.

Cooperation across the Bay of Bengal can improve cyclone warnings, coastal protection, resilient housing, emergency communications, and climate-smart agriculture. The NDB’s focus on sustainable infrastructure gives Bangladesh an additional route for financing projects that protect lives while strengthening economic security.

Neighbours prosper most when connectivity produces balanced benefits. Shared power networks, waterways, railways, and ports create economic interdependence that no country can build alone. India’s size gives it the capacity to initiate these systems.

Disagreements between Dhaka and New Delhi will continue to require patient diplomacy. No mature relationship is free of difficult questions. Yet the architecture of cooperation is now far deeper than any single political moment. Electricity continues to flow, trains and ships continue to move, and development projects continue to connect the two economies.

Rishi Suri is the chief editor at The Daily Milap, one of India’s oldest and largest Urdu newspapers.
Author: Rishi Suri

Title: Clock ticking on the Ganges
Content:
Between today and December 12, a narrow three-month window remains for Bangladesh and India to walk the talk on renegotiating and renewing the historic Ganges Water Sharing Treaty. Signed in New Delhi on December 12, 1996, by then Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her Indian counterpart HD Deve Gowda, the milestone 30-year agreement is set to expire at the end of this year.

The Ganges river system -- known as the Padma in Bangladesh -- is a vital lifeline for millions of people, with its basin covering more than a third of Bangladesh’s total land area.

Consequently, there has never been a more urgent need for Bangladesh to ensure that the treaty does not lapse. Anyone in Bangladesh understands how crucial this water is to local livelihoods and how damaging a diplomatic void could be if the 1996 treaty expires without a consensus on renewal or a fresh framework.

While I prefer not to be a naysayer, we are rapidly approaching the deadline with very little visible bilateral discussion. The public is largely unaware of any progress, save for a few stray news reports about technical-level talks and hydrological data sharing.

As someone who has followed Bangladesh-India water negotiations for more than two decades, I find the current atmosphere noticeably lacking in urgency and expediency. With the clock ticking down, the absence of high-level water diplomacy and ministerial-level Joint Rivers Commission (JRC) discussions raises genuine concerns that we might end the year without a fresh deal. I would be glad to be proved wrong.

This quietude stands in stark contrast to the water negotiations in the years immediately after the turn of the 21st century. In the early and mid-2000s, I had the opportunity to observe JRC meetings closely from the sidelines. I watched then Bangladesh Water Resources Minister Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, now the House Speaker, and his Indian counterpart, Priya Ranjan Dasmunsi, engage in fierce but constructive debates.

During the 36th JRC meeting in Dhaka in September 2005, they debated over the Teesta water-sharing formula. Ahmad raised Bangladesh’s genuine concerns about the diversion of Teesta water in the upper riparian region of West Bengal and India’s construction of barrages at Fulertal and Gazoldoba, while Dasmunsi vigorously defended India’s position.

Dasmunsi, a seasoned Congress politician serving in Manmohan Singh’s Union cabinet, was a Bengali born in the Dinajpur region of pre-partition India. I still fondly recall receiving a surprise letter from him in October, 2005, about a month after his visit to Dhaka. In the letter, he was full of praise for the way we gave him a hard time in Dhaka by shooting a barrage of difficult questions.

The beauty of the ministerial talks and subsequent press briefings back then was the complete absence of hard feelings; both sides acknowledged and appreciated each other’s genuine constraints, speaking to the press in a transparent manner without evading even the toughest questions.

Looking back, any water expert in India or Bangladesh can see how pragmatic it was for Bangladesh to sound the alarm over the Teesta in the mid-2000s. We later witnessed how a near-deal in 2011 fell flat because West Bengal’s then chief minister Mamata Banerjee refused to sign an agreement she felt would leave her own state thirsty.

Today, as we push for a timely deal on the Ganges to avoid a legal vacuum, another Indian state has raised its voice. Sanjay Kumar Jha, a prominent Rajya Sabha member representing Bihar, recently called on the Indian government not to renew the Ganges treaty, claiming it has negatively affected his state.

This plea carries significant political weight: Jha was Bihar’s water resources minister as recently as 2024 and currently serves as the national working president of the Janata Dal (United), making him the de facto second-in-command to Bihar Chief Minister Nitish Kumar.

The response from New Delhi was swift. India’s External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar wrote to Jha, assuring him that India would take Bihar’s interests into consideration when deciding on the renewal of the 1996 treaty. While domestic and interstate stakes are India’s internal affair, Bangladesh must take note. We cannot afford to become collateral damage to India’s internal political dynamics. If the ghost of the stalled Teesta deal proves anything, it is that internal roadblocks matter: Back then, it was West Bengal; this time, it could very well be Bihar.

Bangladesh needs to take a cue from the proactive approach of Hafiz Uddin Ahmad two decades ago. Under his stewardship, water talks were conducted in a way that took the wider public into confidence. Whatever discussions are happening today are largely in camera, with very little filtering through to the press.

By contrast, the 35th JRC meeting in New Delhi in late 2003 and the 36th meeting in Dhaka were held under an intense media spotlight. At post-talk press conferences, ministers, delegates, and water experts routinely shared outcomes with reporters, ensuring the general public remained informed. Our delegates debated at length, tackling areas of cooperation alongside major concerns such as India’s river inter-linking project, barrages, and upstream diversions at Tipaimukh, Fulertal, and Gazoldoba.

Beyond the immediate issue of the Ganges, both nations must step up political and ministerial engagement to revive the lost momentum of water diplomacy. If you ask when the two countries’ water ministers last held JRC talks, it is difficult to give an instant answer. Following those 35th and 36th ministerial meetings two decades ago, Bangladesh and India have managed to hold only two more ministerial-level assemblies. This speaks volumes about the gradual disengagement.

In fact, the last time the respective water ministers sat down for a formal JRC meeting was in 2022 -- an event that itself broke a 12-year hiatus. While high-level technical and secretary-level meetings have continued, including the 90th routine technical JRC meeting in May 2026, a fresh ministerial-level assembly has yet to be convened.

The discussion must expand beyond the Ganges alone. Bangladesh needs to swiftly revive the discourse from where former water minister Hafiz Uddin Ahmad left off when he raised serious concerns about India’s inter-linking of rivers (ILR) program.
