If upstream waters from shared Bangladesh-India rivers are diverted under the ILR project, Bangladesh will face severe water constraints in the foreseeable future.

The scale of this threat was recently underscored by official statements. In a written parliamentary reply last month, India’s Minister of State for Water Resources Raj Bhushan Choudhary said India has formulated a National Perspective Plan for inter-basin water transfer.

Under the plan, 30 ILR projects have been identified, comprising 16 link projects under the Peninsular component and 14 under the Himalayan component. While most of these projects remain at various pre-implementation stages, the Ken-Betwa Link Project has already entered the implementation phase, with a massive budgetary outlay of nearly 45,000 crore Indian rupees.

The project aims to divert 591 million cubic metres of surplus water from the Ken River basin to the water-deficit Betwa basin. Because the Ken flows north into the Yamuna -- the largest tributary of the Ganges -- such large-scale upstream water withdrawal could potentially reduce the volume of water entering the mainstream Ganges.

The consequences extend beyond simple hydrology. A 2023 study published in Nature Communications by researchers at IIT Bombay found that large-scale river interlinking in India alters crucial land-atmosphere feedback loops, potentially reducing summer monsoon rainfall by up to 12% in already water-stressed regions.

Ultimately, these upstream diversions within the Ganga basin could drastically reduce the seasonal flow of the Padma, triggering severe agricultural losses and ecological distress.

The Ganges treaty stands as a testament to the political will that has allowed these two co-riparian South Asian nations to share waters peacefully for three decades. We should be building on this legacy rather than letting it slip away.

Bangladesh and India share 54 common rivers, yet binding instruments, such as agreements or memorandums of understanding (MoUs) exist for only three: The Ganges, the Feni and the Kushiyara. The 2019 Feni River MoU permits India to withdraw a minor 1.82 cusecs strictly for drinking water in Sabroom town, Tripura. The 2022 Kushiyara MoU allows Bangladesh to withdraw 153 cusecs for dry-season irrigation.

Meanwhile, the long-anticipated Teesta treaty, drafted in 2011, remains frozen by West Bengal’s political opposition, while active water-sharing frameworks for seven other priority rivers -- the Manu, Muhuri, Khowai, Gumti, Dharla, Dudhkumar, and Ichamati -- have failed to materialize.

Time is running out. Bangladesh and India must urgently upgrade their diplomatic engagement, bringing ministers back to the table to secure not just the Ganges but the future of the Teesta and the rest of our shared river basins.

Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.
Author: Reaz Ahmad

Title: The need for mature cooperation
Content:
The reaffirmation of Bangladesh‑India cooperation following the latest high‑level meeting between Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi and Defense Adviser Brigadier General (Retd) Dr AKM Shamsul Islam is a reminder of something both nations often acknowledge but do not always act upon: When Dhaka and New Delhi work together, the entire region benefits.

From trade and connectivity to security and environmental management, the two neighbours are bound by geography, history, and shared interests. Areas of cooperation will continue to be prevalent and relevant. The challenge is to ensure that cooperation is sustained with consistency, trust, and political maturity.

The commitments outlined in the meeting are all practical necessities: Strengthening border management, expanding trade routes, improving energy connectivity, and enhancing people‑to‑people ties. What must be understood is that when cooperation falters between the two nations, it is ordinary citizens that pay the biggest price.

With that said, meaningful cooperation requires maturity -- especially from the larger economy. India, with its size, influence, and regional weight, must show restraint and understanding when grievances arise.

Bangladesh’s concerns over the past couple of years have not been irrational but have stemmed from real issues such as border incidents and delays in resolving water‑sharing agreements, among others. A strong partnership demands that these concerns be acknowledged rather than dismissed.

For cooperation to deepen, India must demonstrate that it values Bangladesh not merely as a neighbour, but as a strategic partner whose stability and prosperity strengthen the entire region.

That means listening carefully, responding constructively, and avoiding actions that create unnecessary pressure. Mature diplomacy is not measured by dominance, but by the ability to build trust.

South Asia is stronger when Bangladesh and India work together. It is in everyone’s best interest that this cooperation not only continues, but evolves with the maturity, restraint, and mutual respect that a true partnership demands.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: Talking about suicide prevention
Content:
With September 10 being World Suicide Prevention Day, Bangladesh must confront a crisis that demands more attention.

Speaking of suicide has always been considered taboo in our society, yet the reality remains that as per the World Health Organization (WHO), Bangladesh records thousands of suicides every year, with an average of about 13 people a day losing their lives. That is a deeply distressing number that must not be brushed aside.

What is even more frightening is that the true scale is likely far higher due to underreporting, stigma, and the absence of a comprehensive national surveillance system.

With women, adolescents, and marginalized communities remaining disproportionately affected, we also lack the mental‑health services needed to help people. Those that exist are unevenly distributed and often inaccessible to those who need them most.

Without coordinated action, preventable deaths due to suicide will only continue. Bangladesh’s current response is nothing if not fragmented, underfunded, and heavily dependent on NGOs. Suffice to say, it is insufficient.

Suicide is a complex issue rooted in mental‑health challenges, economic stress, domestic violence, social isolation, and lack of support systems, to name just a few of the reasons. Addressing it therefore requires a whole‑of‑society approach.

Bangladesh must therefore invest in mental‑health services and integrate suicide prevention into school and community programs while expanding helplines.

Most importantly, we must normalize speaking about mental health and suicide and destigmatize seeking help. Policy-makers must also recognize that suicide prevention is inseparable from broader social protections, from reducing domestic violence to supporting vulnerable youth.

Suicide is preventable, and Bangladesh must ensure real change, real investment, and real protection for those who continue to suffer.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: Time to clean up our polythene problem
Content:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to intensify action against the unchecked use of polythene and plastic should not be treated as another routine instruction.

Polythene bags, single‑use plastics, and unregulated packaging have been a major reason for our environmental degradation. The reality has been clogged rivers and drainage systems to contaminated farmlands and wetlands to plastic piling up in urban neighbourhoods with little to no attempt to fix any of it.

We must also recognize that the unchecked use of plastic also contributes to urban flooding, destroys ecosystems, contaminates soil, and adds to the public‑health burden.

That polythene has been banned in Bangladesh for well over two decades now, yet the ban exists only on paper, is what is particularly infuriating. Once again, we already recognize the issue and have the law in place but unfortunately, enforcement has been non-existent and plastic consumption has grown unchecked.

This lack of accountability and disregard that has unfortunately come to define our nation must no longer be tolerated and as such, the prime minister’s words must be treated as a turning point.

Bangladesh cannot aspire to be a middle-income nation while allowing polythene and plastic to undermine every aspect of environmental management.

The government must act decisively. Start with shutting down illegal polythene factories and enforcing fines on distributors. They must also ensure that alternatives -- jute bags, biodegradable packaging, and regulated plastics -- are not only widely available but are a viable alternative for the masses.

Bangladesh has long had the policies, the laws, and the public awareness that polythene and plastic damage our nation. What it has lacked is consistent enforcement and political will. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has made the call and the country must now respond with urgency and discipline.

A liveable Bangladesh will always be out of reach if polythene and plastic continue to choke our rivers and streets. It is time to clean up.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: A senseless tragedy
Content:
Bangladesh has now crossed a devastating milestone in its measles outbreak, with the death toll reaching 1,000 -- a number that represents a thousand families mourning children who should have had every chance to grow up.

Measles is, while highly contagious, also a preventable disease through timely vaccination, and that makes this tragedy even harder to accept.

The outbreak has exposed dangerous gaps in the country’s immunization system. Routine vaccination programs were disrupted during a period of political upheaval, while subsequent problems with vaccine procurement further weakened protection.

The result has been an immunity gap that left hundreds of thousands vulnerable.

It must be understood: There can be no justification for allowing political disagreements, administrative transitions, or changes in policy to interrupt essential healthcare services.

Children cannot be made to wait for stability while governments change, political priorities shift, or institutions are reorganized. A missed vaccination today can and has become a life-threatening infection tomorrow.

It is therefore imperative that the government treat routine immunization as a national priority that must remain independent from political turbulence. Vaccine procurement and distribution need stronger oversight, adequate stockpiles and clear accountability.

The health authorities must also maintain reliable records to identify children who miss doses and ensure that the missed vaccination reaches them.

The emergency vaccination campaign was necessary earlier this year but it cannot be the end of the response. Bangladesh must rebuild a resilient immunization system capable of functioning through subsequent crises.

Public awareness must also improve so that parents understand the importance of timely vaccination and know where to obtain it.

Most importantly, there must be accountability. 1000 child deaths cannot simply become another statistic in an annual health report.

Political disagreements must never again come at the cost of preventable infant deaths. In fact, no preventable disease should be allowed to claim a single child’s life because the systems meant to protect them failed.

We owe our children this much.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: Why the government should prioritize regional economic development, and now
Content:
Bangladesh has been given three more years for LDC graduation. The UN Committee for Development Policy has recommended deferring our graduation from least developed country status to November 24, 2029. The General Assembly is due to take the decision before November this year.

The Committee attached a condition in its own words, that the extension should not be viewed as an opportunity to delay reforms but should accelerate them. The question that follows is a plain one: What are the three years for?

My answer is regional economic development, and I do not mean it as a matter of fairness between divisions. I mean it as the fastest route we have to a diversified export base, to jobs at the scale the country needs them, to women's employment that does not require a woman to move house, and to growth that adds less to the environmental load we already carry.

We usually pursue these as four programs with four budgets. But they meet in one place, which is the region.

By regional development, I do not mean spreading projects more evenly across divisions. I mean treating a division as an economic unit with a declared specialization rather than as an administrative area that receives its share of everything. That has four parts: (i) each division carries a declared economic identity based on what its enterprises already do best; (ii) public investment there is sequenced to that identity instead of spread thinly across every sector; (iii) the support functions the identity needs, being finance, standards, testing, skills and logistics, are built at the cluster rather than in the capital; and (iv) one institution is answerable for the division's economic outcome and is measured on it.

The first part should not be difficult, as our productive geography is already specialized. The specialization is also sharper than our policy acknowledges. In the agro-logistics system mapping we undertook for the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands this year, we found that the top three mango producing districts account for roughly 50% of national output, and the top three papaya districts for 43%. Watermelon has been shifting into Patuakhali, Bhola, and Barguna, where the top three districts now hold around 30%.

The pattern holds well outside agriculture. Bogura carries around 70 foundries and 1800 manufacturing and workshop units. These meet some 70% of national demand for agricultural machinery and spare parts, are worth Tk500 crore a year, and employ about 15,000 people. Bhairab in Kishoreganj holds over 10,000 shoe making units across some 20 villages. The trade there supports close to two lakh people and turns over Tk15-20 crore a day.

None of this was planned. These are comparative advantages that enterprises built themselves, and no policy has yet been written to them.

Writing one would look concrete, and it would look different in each place. Rajshahi would be developed as a horticulture economy. The packhouses, hot water treatment plants and phytosanitary certification that mango and papaya exports require would be sited there rather than at the airport in Dhaka.

Bogura would be developed as a light engineering economy. It would need metallurgical testing, tool and die capability, industrial training, and working capital lines, as these are what let a foundry district move from spare parts into finished machinery it can sell abroad.

Bhairab would be developed as a footwear economy, with component supply, design services, and the standards testing that an international buyer asks for before placing an order.

Each of these is a different economy and each needs a different set of institutions. That is not what we build.

What we build is one national system, and we build most of it near the capital. Our logistics costs stand at 15-20% of the GDP, which is amongst the highest in Asia. This cost falls hardest on the production areas that are farthest from the capital. Nearly 95% of our cold storage is dedicated to potatoes.

Producers of fresh vegetables are thus forced to send their produce fast to urban markets. The highways cut travel times to those markets by 30-40%, but did not address the issue of preservation. We lose 6.0-8.1 million metric tons of cereal a year, worth $2.1-2.8 billion. A 30% reduction would save $630-850m and feed 15-20m people without bringing another hectare into cultivation.

The environmental case is not separate from this. We have little new land or water to bring into cultivation. Additional food will therefore have to come from what we stop losing.

Activities that we will require to overcome this loss would also push the frontiers for jobs. Grain spoils as nobody dried, graded, or stored it, and that work would be employment. Agriculture contributes about 11% of GDP but employs 43-44% of the labour force. Most of our workforce is thus in the part of the economy that produces the least value per worker.

Only around 12% of our agricultural output is processed. The work that would close the gap is drying, chilling, grading, packing, machining, assembly, and stitching. It belongs in the cluster rather than in Dhaka.

This matters most for women. Our garment industry brought women into waged work, but it required them to move to Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj, and Chittagong. The move cost them in the form of rent, travel, and separation from their families. Work sites at the cluster do not ask that price, as they are available where women already live and where their labour is often already offered without wages. A quarter of the Bogura light engineering workforce is already made up of women, despite the fact that it was not designed to employ women.

The question therefore is, why does economic development remain centralized? It is because we are yet to have the institutional system to support regional development. There is no institution that owns a region's economic outcome. Our Annual Development Program is allocated by ministry and by project, never by region. Nobody is therefore answerable for what Bogura's or Barishal's productive base looks like in five years.

The Local Government Division takes the largest share of the ADP and carries no economic development mandate. We have already tried the alternative of announcing sites. Of the 100 economic zones announced, roughly a tenth reached the ground in a decade before the program was cut back to five.

A zone is a site. A site with neither an owner nor a declared purpose fails to become an economy.

Other countries in the Global South have given their regions an owner, and I have watched this at close quarters in the work I do outside Bangladesh. In Nigeria, every state carries a declared economic identity. Lagos is the Centre of excellence and Kano the Centre of commerce. Those declarations came first, and the instruments were built to them afterwards, most recently Lagos's industrial policy and the state-level agro-industrial processing zones.

The declaration is what made the investment legible to everyone who had to act on it. Vietnam supplied the piece that Nigeria does not, which is measurement. Its Provincial Competitiveness Index gives every province a published score on economic governance, and provinces compete on it openly. We have neither the declaration nor the score.

Both are available to us within the current fiscal year. The FY2026-27 Annual Development Program is Tk3 lakh crore, 30% above last year. It already names region-based balanced development amongst its five pillars, with the northern region, the coastal belt, Chittagong, and Mongla named specifically.

The intent is on paper and the money is appropriated. What is absent is the machinery.

The government should declare an economic identity for each division on the comparative advantage its enterprises have already built. It should name a single owner for that identity within the Planning Commission. It should then publish a divisional measure the owner is held to.

Tk74,000 crore of this year's ADP sits in block allocation, undirected; that is the instrument. Routing it through the divisional plans would cost nothing that has not already been budgeted.

How this should be done -- meaning the sequencing, the institutional design, and the financing -- needs more space than a column allows, and I will set it out separately. What I am arguing here is the prior point: The decision to organize the economy regionally has to be taken in this fiscal year for any of that design to matter. Three years is not long for this kind of work. If we begin in the next budget rather than this one, we will reach November 2029 with the structure half built and the preferences gone.

The Committee for Development Policy was right that the extension is not an opportunity to delay. It is the time available to build in, and what we should build is regional.

Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director, Innovision Consulting.
Author: Md Rubaiyath Sarwar

Title: The invisible plastic problem we can no longer ignore
Content:
For years, the public face of plastic pollution has been easy to recognize: Bottles caught in rivers, shopping bags on roadsides, wrappers buried in rubbish dumps. But increasingly, attention is turning to particles so small that they can pass unnoticed through everyday life.

In Bangladesh, that concern has recently entered an unexpectedly familiar place: The bathroom. A July 2026 study by the Environment and Social Development Organization, or ESDO, reported that microplastic particles were detected in 26 of 34 toothpaste samples tested from local and imported brands.

The findings have prompted concern among consumers and drawn the attention of policy-makers, with the High Court ordering an expert investigation into the matter.

The study does not establish what those particles mean for human health, nor does it suggest that every plastic-containing product presents the same risk. But it has raised a larger question: How much plastic do we encounter without thinking about the material itself?

Modern packaging is built around convenience. It protects food from contamination, keeps clothes clean during transport, and allows products to travel thousands of kilometres before reaching a customer.

Plastic became central to that system because it is inexpensive, light, and durable. Those same qualities, however, create a problem when the product reaches the end of its useful life.

A bag used for a few minutes can remain in the environment for years. As larger plastic items weather and fragment, they can produce particles commonly referred to as microplastics.

That has changed the way environmental researchers and policy-makers think about plastic pollution. The question is no longer simply whether a package performs well. It is also what happens to its material after it has performed its job.

There is a potential solution. Bangladesh's apparel industry is one of the country's defining economic forces. It also produces an enormous quantity of something that receives considerably less attention: Textile waste.

Every garment factory generates scraps. Some are reused or recycled. Others have little economic value and can become a disposal problem.

That discarded material can be used to produce compostable packaging, including shopping bags, grocery carriers, apparel packaging, and mailer bags. There are already companies that have started doing this.

The conventional packaging system is largely linear. Raw materials are extracted. Products are manufactured. Packaging is used. Then it becomes waste. Circularity attempts to interrupt that sequence. Materials are kept in productive use for longer, recovered where possible and, where appropriate, returned to natural or industrial cycles.

Compostability is not simply a claim that a material will “disappear”. The conditions under which a product breaks down, the testing method used, and what remains afterward are all important parts of the scientific assessment.

This is where the recent toothpaste findings intersect with a much wider debate. The concern around microplastics is not confined to toothpaste. Researchers have reported their presence across a range of environmental and consumer settings, while scientists continue to investigate how these particles move through ecosystems and what their long-term implications may be.

But the response cannot simply be to declare every plastic product dangerous. The more useful question is one of material design. If packaging is made from a material intended to persist, then its environmental fate must be considered over a long period. If packaging is made from a material designed to compost, then its environmental fate is different.

The most important part of a package may be the part that nobody sees. Not the logo. Not the colour. Not the handle. The end. A conventional plastic package is designed primarily around its useful life. Its environmental fate comes afterward, often outside the control of the manufacturer or consumer. A circular approach tries to consider that fate at the point of design.

There has to be more to a biodegradable or compostable shopping bag. It is an argument about responsibility. What should happen to a material when its job is finished? Should it persist? Should it be recycled? Should it be reused? Or can it safely return to the biological cycle? There will not be one answer for every product. But increasingly, companies are being asked to provide an answer.

The environmental movement has spent decades asking people to produce less waste. The next phase may require something more difficult: Rethinking what we call waste in the first place. A discarded piece of fabric has already absorbed energy, labour and resources. Treating it as worthless at the end of one production cycle ignores the value still contained in the material.

The recent toothpaste findings have brought an invisible form of plastic pollution into an unusually intimate setting. That may be uncomfortable. But perhaps discomfort is useful when it makes a familiar system worth questioning.

The issue is bigger than toothpaste. It is bigger than shopping bags, too. It is about whether the materials we design today are suited to the world we expect to live in tomorrow.

For Bangladesh, that conversation has an additional dimension. A country whose economy has been built in part on textiles is now experimenting with ways to turn textile waste into another industry's raw material. That is more than waste management. It is an attempt to redesign the relationship between production and disposal. And perhaps that is where the next packaging revolution will begin.

Tarif Mohammad Khan is a brand marketing, business strategy, and communications expert.
Author: Tarif Mohammed Khan

Title: Your CV is not just a CV
Content:
A CV is usually treated as a piece of paper that helps someone get a job. We write our details, send it to an employer, and move on. But in the digital age, a CV is much more than an application for employment. It is a compact map of a person’s identity. It tells someone where we live, where we studied, where we worked, how to contact us and, sometimes, what we have been doing for years.

That is precisely why the recent controversy over the alleged sale of millions of Bangladeshi job seekers’ CVs on the dark web should worry us far more than an ordinary cyber security incident.

A hacker group calling itself Madrex has reportedly claimed possession of the CVs of around six million users of the popular Bangladeshi job platform BDJobs and has advertised the information for sale. BDJobs has denied the claim.

Yet, 148 CV samples were reportedly published as evidence of the alleged breach. At this point, neither a hacker’s claim nor an institutional denial should be treated as the final word. The important question is not who is telling the truth but whether the public has a reliable mechanism through which such a claim can be independently verified.

This is where our digital culture reveals a troubling weakness. When sensitive personal information is allegedly exposed, the immediate response often becomes a contest of statements.

One side makes a claim, another denies it, and the public is expected to decide whom to believe. But data security cannot be established through public relations. It requires technical investigation and institutional transparency.

If the claim is false, an independent investigation should establish that clearly. If the claim is true, the same investigation should determine how the information was obtained, what information was compromised, and how many people may be at risk.

The larger problem is that we continue to think of personal information as if it were an ordinary administrative resource. It is not. A database containing millions of CVs is potentially a database of millions of identities. Each individual record may contain a person’s full name, telephone number, email address, residential information, educational history, employment history, training and other professional details.

When these pieces are assembled, they become far more valuable than any individual piece of information. A criminal does not need a person’s entire life story. A sufficiently detailed digital profile may be enough to impersonate that person convincingly.

This is where the alleged CV leak becomes particularly disturbing.

A fraudster armed with a person’s professional history can design a much more convincing scam than someone who merely knows a telephone number. A fake recruiter can mention the person’s university, profession, or previous employer. A fraudulent job offer can be tailored to the individual’s career interests. A phishing message can appear to come from an organization the person is likely to trust. The victim may not even realize that the information used to deceive them came from a compromised database.

The European Data Protection Board recognizes identity theft, fraud, and financial loss among the potential consequences of personal data breaches. That understanding is important because it shifts the discussion away from the narrow language of passwords, servers, and firewalls.

The ultimate victim of a data breach is not a database. It is a human being.

A compromised database can be repaired, a password can be changed and a server can be replaced. But once personal information enters the criminal ecosystem, it may be impossible to retrieve it.

If someone steals a document from an office, we understand that something valuable has been taken. Yet when millions of digital records are copied, we often describe the incident as a technical problem. The language itself is misleading. Data theft is theft, even when nothing physical disappears from a building.

The controversy also raises a more uncomfortable question: What responsibility does an organization assume when it collects our information? When people create accounts on job portals, banks, hospitals, universities, or government platforms, they surrender information because they need a service. They do not surrender ownership of their identity.

The organization becomes a custodian of that information, and custodianship creates responsibility. This responsibility cannot end with having a password policy or installing a firewall. Serious data protection requires knowing what information is being collected and why, limiting unnecessary collection, controlling who can access sensitive databases, encrypting information, monitoring unusual activity, conducting regular security assessments, and maintaining a credible response plan.

It also requires knowing what to do when something goes wrong. Security is not a product that an organization purchases once. It is a continuous institutional practice.

The developed world has increasingly recognized this principle. The underlying philosophy is simple: Institutions that collect valuable information must also prepare for the possibility that someone will try to steal it.

Bangladesh needs to develop the same culture of responsibility. Too often, cyber security is treated as the IT department’s problem. It is not. It is a management issue, a legal issue, and increasingly a public-interest issue.

The person responsible for collecting millions of records cannot wash their hands of responsibility by saying that a technical team manages the server. The technical team may operate the system, but the institution carries the responsibility.

There is another reason this particular controversy deserves serious attention. Job seekers are among the people least capable of protecting themselves from the consequences of a data breach. Many are young graduates desperate for employment. They are already vulnerable to fraudulent recruitment, fake interviews, demands for registration fees, and other forms of exploitation. If detailed CV information becomes available to criminals, an already vulnerable group could become even easier to target.

The answer, however, is not to stop sharing information online. Modern life makes that impossible. The answer is to recognize that information has value and therefore demands protection proportional to that value.

We have spent years teaching people to protect their passwords. We now need to teach institutions to protect the information people are forced to entrust to them.

This is ultimately a question of digital dignity. A person should not have to wonder whether the information submitted in good faith to find employment will someday appear for sale in an underground marketplace.

Nor should citizens have to depend entirely on corporate assurances when serious allegations of data exposure emerge. They deserve transparent answers, independent verification, and meaningful protection.

The Madrex claim may eventually prove to be exaggerated, partially true, or completely false. That is precisely why it must be investigated rather than simply argued about.

If the claim is false, an independent investigation can restore confidence. If it is true, the investigation can help identify the breach, protect potential victims, and prevent a recurrence. Either way, the public interest is served by finding the facts.

We often repeat that information is power. But information becomes dangerous when it is concentrated in the hands of those who have no right to possess it. The real lesson of the alleged CV leak is not that hackers have become more dangerous. It is that institutions entrusted with our information must become far more responsible.

A CV may help someone get a job. But in the wrong hands, the same CV can help someone steal a person’s identity. We need to understand that difference before the next six million records become another statistic.

HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.
Author: HM Nazmul Alam

Title: Steeped in bad economics
Content:
Tim Worstall says Bangladesh's tea estates should die because they can't pay market rates for capital. He built that on a price that was, for years, not a market price at all: Whatever a small pool of buyers felt like paying that week, with no floor underneath.

In 2023, Bangladesh produced a record 102.9 million kilograms of tea, while the corresponding auction year delivered a 12-year low average price of Tk171.24 per kilogram. Then the Bangladesh Tea Board introduced minimum auction pricing.

By 2025-26, the average auction price had risen to Tk245.50, up 43% -- and total auction revenue had increased by roughly Tk562 crore, even though less tea was sold through auction.

That's a broken pricing mechanism, not a verdict on tea.

Everything else in his argument rests on that price being honest. It isn't, and the rest of this piece works out the consequences.

I come to this from both sides; I studied economics and political science, have come from a family that has grown tea for four generations, and work in venture capital for emerging and frontier markets.

I've watched capital wasted propping up businesses that should have died. Worstall isn't wrong to worry about that. He's wrong about where the disease sits.

A tea estate is not a spreadsheet

My favourite economics joke: Assume rationality. Frictionless markets, perfect information, the model hands you the answer you wanted before you built it.

That's Worstall's picture -- capital and labour gliding from tea to whatever earns more this quarter.

Bangladesh's tea sector employs roughly 102,000 permanent workers and 40,000 seasonal ones. Close to half a million people live inside estate boundaries.

These are not abstractions to me. Factories my family has run, land my grandfather planted, and my father and uncles have managed. There are names and faces I know behind those numbers.

An estate isn’t just tea bushes. It includes housing, schools, roads, water systems, embankments, farmland, factories -- none of it fungible.

A tea company is not the same as any other factory or office. It’s a strange combination of agronomy, microeconomics, political systems, and many things hard to explain in a single article, best explained over a few cups of tea and a long afternoon. Anyway, I digress.

What I mean is that an estate doesn't deserve to survive simply because people depend on it. But exit has a cost, and it lands on people, not a balance sheet.

A 6% loan when inflation runs at 8% is concessional financing. Fine. But Worstall treats a subsidy's existence as proof of what it's used for.

That doesn't follow: Bangladesh's own garment industry was built on duty-free imports, bonded warehouses, and tax holidays before it became the country's largest export earner.

Some subsidized spending is waste. Some are why an industry exists at all. A subsidy tells you nothing about which bucket you're in. The real question is what the concession buys.

Another year of losses with nothing changing is a slow bleed with a government signature on it -- fair criticism. But financing replanting, irrigation, or debt restructuring is transition capital. Priced correctly, that's how you fix things.

There's a second case for keeping capacity alive that has nothing to do with restructuring math: Import substitution. Bangladesh's domestic tea consumption has been closing in on production for years, and the country already imports tea most seasons to cover the gap.

Every estate that goes under doesn't just cost jobs and export earnings; it widens a shortfall the country then has to fill in foreign exchange.

That's not a reason to keep a terminal estate on life support. But it is a reason the value of a marginal estate can't be read off the auction price alone.

Once the Tea Board introduced a minimum price to correct that twelve-year low, the average price rose by roughly Tk74 per kilogram within two years, adding hundreds of crores in producer revenue -- without a single bush growing better tea.

When the Board pushed the floor further, buyers boycotted an auction outright, leaving more than half the tea offered unsold that day.

The price was never an unimpeachable verdict on value. It was the output of a lopsided buying process, and the buying side had enough leverage to walk away from half a season's output rather than pay more.

What the price actually measured was leverage, not tea.

Between the producers and the retail shelf sits a long chain -- brokers, blenders, packeters, whoever finally puts a brand name on the box -- each taking a cut. Ordinary commodity economics, not a scandal.

But it means the auction price captures only one point in a much longer chain, with no guarantee the margin is split fairly between growers and everyone downstream.

If an estate can't produce tea at a cost the market will sustainably bear, that's structural, and Worstall's remedy applies.

If it produces something worth far more than it's paid, but the value leaks out between garden and shelf, that's a market failure -- and closing the garden doesn't fix a market failure. Fixing the market does.

The test that actually matters

None of this means every estate survives -- that would be as lazy as Worstall's conclusion. Some will need restructuring more radical than a rate cut can provide, some need new ownership or a different use for the land. Let the evidence decide, estate by estate.

So far it doesn't look terminal: Production hit 95 million kilograms in 2025, against a record 102.9 million in 2023, the same year prices bottomed out. A sector producing more than ever and getting paid less than ever for it -- a margin problem, not a dead one.

There's a real difference between "a business with no credible path to viability should exit" and "needing concessional financing proves a business destroys value." The first is analysis. The second is an assumption wearing analysis as a costume.

The task force behind this financing paired it with replanting, export strategy, and debt restructuring. Cheap credit without reform is life support; tied to performance, it's a turnaround.

Estates that can't show a credible path shouldn't get it indefinitely. On that, Worstall is right.

The right test: Can this estate become productive and sustainable? Where yes, finance the transition and measure results. Where no, let the capital move.

Less satisfying than "things that lose money should close down." But having spent a career on the investing side of exactly this question, I'll take the answer that's actually correct.

Farhan A Rahman is the founder of Lontana Consulting, an emerging-markets advisory firm, and a fourth-generation tea planter. He is obligated to have an opinion on tea economics.

Title: Tuku urges joint action against drugs and crime in Dhaka
Content:
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin Tuku MP called for effective coordination among the district administration, police and public representatives to maintain law and order and advance development activities.

At a meeting with members of parliament and administration officials at the Dhaka deputy commissioner's conference room, he made the remarks as the chief guest, according to a press release.

The meeting reviewed the overall law-and-order situation and development activities in Dhaka district. Tuku, who oversees these activities in the district, said the elected government was working to maintain stability and implement development initiatives.

Alongside maintaining law and order, he urged those concerned to identify and resolve obstacles hampering development work.

The state minister said improving law and order was not the administration's responsibility alone. He said building a safe and stable society required coordinated efforts by political leaders, the administration, law enforcement agencies and the public.

"Drugs have become a major threat to society at present. People from different classes and professions are getting involved in it. The administration, public representatives and social organisations must play a more active role in preventing the spread of drugs," he said.

Tuku called for heightened vigilance against criminal activities in the capital and surrounding areas. He stressed the need for more active law enforcement in crime-prone areas, alongside public awareness efforts by political and social organisations.

Criticising the previous government, which he described as fascist, Tuku alleged that misgovernance, oppression and widespread corruption had pushed the country into crisis, and that money had been laundered abroad.

He said the government elected by the people had taken responsibility under the prime minister's leadership and was working to improve the situation. He added that united, responsible efforts could help overcome the challenges.

On dengue, the state minister warned that the risk could rise over the coming months. He urged public representatives, administration officials, and residents to work together to maintain cleanliness, eliminate mosquito breeding grounds, and raise awareness.

He also called for stronger regular monitoring of residential hotels, guesthouses, and other establishments to prevent what he described as anti-social activities.

"As state officials, we must perform our duties with utmost importance to the welfare of the people and the interests of the state. All administrative activities should be conducted in the interests of the state and the people, not in the interests of any individual or group," he said.

Dhaka Deputy Commissioner Farida Khanam chaired the meeting, while State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishraq Hossain attended as the special guest.

Opposition Chief Whip of the National Assembly Nahid Islam MP, Dhaka-12 MP Saiful Alam Khan Milon, reserved women's seat MP Ferdousi Ahmed, and Superintendent of Police Shamima Parveen were also present.

Representatives of law enforcement agencies, local government department officials, public representatives, and members of the district law and order committee attended the meeting.

Content:

Bangladesh Bank Director of the Supervisory Policy & Coordination Department (SPCD), Abdur Rab, and Joint Director Md Nurul Huda conducted the workshop.

They discussed the key elements of the RBS framework, practical considerations for effective implementation, and the regulatory expectations banks need to address.

Jamuna Bank Deputy Managing Director, Chief Risk Officer, and RBS Focal Point Md Shahidul Islam inaugurated the workshop as chief guest. Deputy Managing Director Mohammad Jahangir Alam attended as a special guest.

Divisional heads and senior branch heads took part in deepening their understanding of the RBS framework and strengthening the bank's preparedness to meet regulatory requirements.

Title: Banglalink offers free Friday imo calls with seven-day and 30-day packs
Content:
Banglalink has launched "Kotha Bola Shukrobare Free", offering free imo voice and video calls on Fridays nationwide to prepaid and postpaid customers subscribing to seven-day or 30-day data packs or bundles.

Eligible customers can make these calls every Friday for the duration of their packs or bundles, without deductions from their data balance, according to a press release.

Banglalink said the initiative aims to help customers stay connected with family members living abroad. The operator introduced the offer in recognition of how many customers use imo for voice and video calls with their families.

The company said Friday is an important day for family gatherings and shared meals in Bangladesh and an opportunity for migrant workers and their families to reconnect across borders.

Through the initiative, Banglalink aims to ease customers' concerns about data consumption so they can spend more time speaking with family members. The company said the offer reflects its commitment to putting customers' needs first.

Banglalink Chief Marketing Officer Kazi Mahboob Hassan said, "It is not easy to stay away from your family, thousands of miles away. The deep emotional distance that families of immigrant workers face cannot be bridged so easily, but as a 'people-first' brand, we have to try."

He added, "Friday is a sacred day of togetherness for Bangladeshi households, and Banglalink believes connectivity should bridge physical divides. This initiative is an effort to bring families close on the day it matters the most."

The offer requires no separate registration or additional payment beyond purchasing an eligible pack or bundle, inviting customers to use it immediately.

Customers can access the benefit by purchasing or renewing any seven-day or 30-day data pack or bundle through the MyBL app, mobile financial services (MFS), USSD codes, or retail outlets.

Title: Govt working to create new sports movement from grassroots: State minister
Content:
The government is working to create a new sports movement in Bangladesh by developing sports at the grassroots level, State Minister for Youth and Sports Aminul Haque said today (13 September).

The government plans to build a football or sports field in each of the country's 4,599 unions and a mini stadium in every upazila, he said at the final of the District Commissioner Gold Cup Football Tournament at Jamalpur District Stadium.

"A project to build a mini stadium in every upazila is already underway. The government also plans to establish a sports village in every district in phases," he added.

Emphasising the need to develop Jamalpur as a sports-friendly district, the state minister said steps would be taken to complete the unfinished gallery at the district stadium and turn it into a full-fledged facility.

"We want to take advantage of the renewed interest in sports in the country and further develop Bangladesh's sports sector. Our goal is to strengthen sports by producing players from the grassroots level," Aminul added.

He further said the government would develop the necessary infrastructure at district, upazila and union levels for the development of football, cricket and other sports. "Such infrastructure will encourage children, teenagers and young people to take part in outdoor sports while helping identify new talent for the country's sports sector."

Title: CUFL set to resume urea production after gas supply normalised
Content:
Chattogram Urea Fertilizer Limited (CUFL) is set to resume production following the restoration of gas supply.

As ammonia production resumed on 9 September, the factory management said urea production would begin shortly after the necessary repairs are completed.

S.M. Abdullah Al Mamun, General Manager (Commercial) of the factory, said, "The factory has been receiving the necessary gas supply for more than a week. The ammonia plant is now operational."

Liquid ammonia and carbon dioxide serve as the two essential raw materials for urea production. The restoration of the gas supply has enabled ammonia production; however, repairs to the mechanical faults in the urea plant are required before it can be operational. So, despite the initial target to commence urea production on 12 September, this has not been feasible. Efforts are currently underway to resolve the mechanical problems. If everything goes as planned, urea production could resume shortly, he said.

He said that under optimal conditions, CUFL is capable of producing 1,000 tonnes of urea per day. Therefore, once production resumes, the factory could significantly contribute to the country's fertilizer supply.

Meanwhile, an official of Karnaphuli Gas Distribution Company Limited (KGDCL) said that, following government directives, priority is being given to supplying gas to fertilizer and power generation plants.

Title: Tripura begins pilot project for 'smart border' with Bangladesh
Content:
Tripura's government has launched a pilot project to develop a "smart border" along its frontier with Bangladesh, aiming to strengthen security through technology and curb cross-border crimes, Chief Minister Manik Saha said today (13 September).

The pilot is being implemented in Sepahijala district, which shares more than 100km of border with Bangladesh, Saha told reporters on the sidelines of a blood donation camp at the Border Security Force's Tripura Frontier headquarters in West Tripura.

"A pilot study on smart border has got underway in Sepahijala district, which shares over a 100km border with Bangladesh. I heard the authorities have already floated a tender to push the plan," he said.

Tripura shares an 856km international border with Bangladesh, around 80% of which has been fenced, according to Saha.

He said some stretches remain unfenced because of difficult terrain, including rivers and other geographical barriers, as well as objections from across the border.

Indian Home Minister Amit Shah visited Tripura in June and announced plans to introduce "smart borders" by combining local administration, technology and the efforts of security personnel.

Saha said stronger border security would significantly help curb human trafficking, drug smuggling and other forms of cross-border crime.

Title: 'Let them do it, I am ready': Asif Mahmud on ACC graft probe
Content:
NCP spokesperson Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuiyan has questioned the independence of the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) after the anti-graft body launched an inquiry into allegations of financial irregularities, bribery and money laundering involving around Tk13,000 crore against him.

Reacting to the development at a press conference today (13 September), the former adviser to the Ministry of Youth and Sports said he was prepared for further allegations against him, while alleging that the ACC was being used for political purposes.

"If the government decides to arrest someone, there are many ways to do that. We have seen this being done against the BNP as well," Asif Mahmud said.

He alleged that the ACC had shown little interest in investigating corruption committed during the Awami League period.

"The ACC was formed five months later, but they have no concern about the corruption during the Awami League period. I am the first political figure against whom an initiative has been taken. However, I have already made my position clear," he said.

Asif Mahmud also alleged that an earlier complaint against him related to promotions during the BNP period had failed to gain traction.

"When they saw that it did not work, now they are bringing another one. Tomorrow they will bring another one. Let them keep doing it. I am ready," he said.

He also questioned the independence of the ACC, saying, "When we saw that the ACC had not been reformed and the ordinance was repealed, we understood what the ACC would be used for. It was used for that reason in the past, and it will be used for the same reason in the future."

However, Asif Mahmud said he had not yet received details of the latest allegations against him. "Specifically, I have not yet learned the details of what happened today."

Title: BB launches bi-annual reviews for bank MDs, CEOs; underperformers may face removal
Content:
Bangladesh Bank has introduced a new performance evaluation framework for managing directors (MDs) and chief executive officers (CEOs) of scheduled banks, with their performance to be assessed every six months against nearly 30 indicators.

The central bank issued the Key Performance Indicators (KPI) Framework today (13 September) and instructed the chairmen of all scheduled banks to comply with the new policy.

Under the framework, the board of a bank must prepare a performance plan for a newly appointed MD or CEO at its next meeting and finalise it with Bangladesh Bank's approval.

For executives already serving in the posts, the first evaluation will cover the period from September to 31 March.

The framework assigns a combined 100% weight to five areas. Bank solvency and liquidity will account for 25%, asset quality 25%, governance and internal control 25%, inclusion, customer and market conduct 15%, and profitability 10%.

The areas cover nearly 30 indicators, including the Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), gross and net non-performing loan (NPL) ratios, return on assets (ROA), regulatory compliance, anti-money laundering and counter-terror financing (AML/CFT) compliance, and outreach in cottage, micro, small and medium enterprises (CMSMEs) and agricultural lending.

Executives scoring 75 or above will be rated "Above Average", those scoring 65 to below 75 "Average", and those scoring below 65 "Below Average", indicating a need for immediate improvement.

A senior Bangladesh Bank official said the central bank could issue warnings to MDs and CEOs scoring below 65%. Depending on the circumstances, underperforming executives could also be removed from their posts.

The framework includes an additional mechanism covering six specific areas, with up to five marks deducted from an executive's overall score.

For example, an executive scoring 75.50 out of 100 initially could lose 5.08 marks for failing to meet the required benchmark in all six areas, reducing the final score to 70.42.

A Bangladesh Bank official said NPL-related indicators would cover the overall NPL ratio, the amount of bad loans, annual cash recovery from defaulted loans and the amount of loans written off.

Indicators linked to the advance-deposit ratio (ADR) will assess the proportion of deposits being lent, whether loans are being recovered on time and compliance with central bank limits, including the 85% or 87% thresholds.

The concentration indicator will examine whether a bank's major loans are concentrated among its top 10 or 20 customers and whether it complies with the single-borrower exposure limit.

The framework will also assess financial inclusion and priority lending, including CMSME, agricultural and green finance, as well as efforts to bring new customers into formal banking services.

Arfan Ali, former managing director of Bank Asia, welcomed the framework but said the review period could be longer.

"Accountability is necessary for any job. I would say the framework Bangladesh Bank has set for bank MDs is a good step. However, evaluating them every six months is very early. It would be better to make it an annual evaluation," he told The Business Standard.

He said some bank MDs had remained in their positions for long periods by maintaining the confidence of their chairmen.

"Bangladesh Bank considers their experience when appointing them. But if they are kept under continuous monitoring through a prescribed framework, it could bring greater discipline to the banking sector," he added.

Title: Iran's economic ties to Dubai hard to break despite war
Content:
In the markets of old Dubai, saffron, cumin, pistachios and almonds from Iran still fill the stalls, as if the two shores of the Gulf were not separated by war.

Last month, the United Arab Emirates announced the suspension of trade and financial exchanges with Tehran, which has responded to American attacks by targeting the US-allied country and tightening its grip on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

But in old Dubai, where Iranian merchants are firmly established, they do not believe there will be a break in the ties forged over decades between the UAE's financial hub and southern Iran.

Since the start of the war, certain Iranian products have become scarcer, and others have seen their prices soar, says Morteza Asaadi, who runs the grocery store his father founded in 1963.

Most traditional foodstuffs, such as nuts or zereshk -- small red berries used in Persian cuisine -- remain available, however.

"It's just coming. How? I don't know, but it's coming," he said.

Two wholesalers interviewed by AFP on condition of anonymity said they are still sourcing from Iran, notably via Omani ports.

"We can't export from the Emirates anymore, but we can still bring in certain goods," one of them said.

In Yasser's saffron shop, the precious spice arrives by air from Mashhad, in northeastern Iran, thanks to the resumption of air links after a brief interruption.

Dubai's Iranian community

Dubai is home to a large Iranian community, estimated at several hundred thousand people, which has contributed to the emirate's commercial development and weathered the various periods of tension with Tehran.

After the US tightened its sanctions against the Islamic republic in 2012, "those in Dubai managed to convince their partners in Abu Dhabi that the trade, regardless of the sanctions, needed to continue because it was contributing to the UAE economy," Mehran Haghirian of the London-based Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank told AFP.

In 2024, the UAE was the main entry point for goods into Iran, accounting for more than 30 percent of imports, worth $21 billion.

It was also Iran's third-largest customer, absorbing nearly 12 percent of its exports, worth more than $7 billion, according to the World Trade Organization.

Dubai is an important financial hub for Iranian businesses, with Washington accusing it of being a key node in financial networks used to circumvent sanctions.

As part of its policy of economic pressure on Iran, the United States announced new measures at the end of August targeting Iran's trading partners, and sanctioned the director of the Dubai branch of Iran's Bank Melli.

The institution nonetheless continues to welcome clients.

"We've been under sanctions for years," sighs an employee at one of two branches in Dubai.

For Haghirian, Abu Dhabi's announcement of the suspension of relations with Iran is part of efforts to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table, and is meant to show the Gulf country's alignment with the United States.

But it will not necessarily cut informal flows or exchanges between private actors, which are deeply rooted on both sides of the Gulf.

In the long run, a lasting rupture could even weigh on Dubai's economy.

"It's difficult to just suddenly cut it off and not have an impact, leave a huge chunk. That chunk cannot easily be replaced," he stressed.

But at a conference in Dubai, Emirati businessman and former senior official in the emirate, Nasser al-Shaikh, downplayed these concerns, saying that Iran is "no longer as important to the emirate's economy as it was a few years ago".

"The relationship was mutually beneficial," he conceded, but "in times of war, priorities change... National security comes first".

In his shop in Bur Dubai, Asaadi is convinced that trade will survive the current crisis.

"You see the water there?" he said, gesturing at the Gulf separating the UAE from the coasts of southern Iran.

"Water can break a mountain."

Title: 'Pathao Commerce’ launched to simplify business for merchants
Content:
Pathao has launched Pathao Commerce, an integrated platform that brings storefronts, sales channels, orders, inventory, payments, delivery, and customer communication together to help merchants manage and grow their businesses.

Bangladesh's social commerce ecosystem comprises 200,000 merchants and accounts for more than 80% of all digital commerce, according to a press release.

Built around three core merchant needs — management, efficiency, and growth — Pathao Commerce aims to reduce manual work, simplify everyday operations, and help businesses focus on expansion.

"For years, merchants have trusted Pathao to take the hassle out of deliveries and help them get their products to customers reliably," said Pathao CEO Fahim Ahmed.

"With Pathao Commerce, we are taking that commitment beyond delivery, giving entrepreneurs a single platform to manage everything from their storefront and orders to inventory, sales, payments, delivery, and customer communication. By removing the burden of juggling multiple tools, we are giving merchants greater control and confidence to focus on their customers, build their brands, and turn new opportunities into growing businesses."

Pathao Commerce brings together the tools merchants need to run their businesses. They can manage product catalogues, orders, payments, inventory, and deliveries, and create a professional online storefront through the same platform.

It also connects with third-party sales channels such as Shopify, WooCommerce and Daraz, allowing merchants to bring their existing sales operations into Pathao Commerce.

Sales, orders, inventory, and earnings update automatically, giving merchants greater visibility and control over their businesses. Pathao said this would provide a single place to manage operations that previously relied on multiple disconnected tools.

For many online merchants, completing a single sale involves switching between Facebook Messenger, Instagram direct messages, WhatsApp, spreadsheets, and delivery platforms. This often requires entering the same information multiple times.

Pathao Commerce simplifies this process through a unified chat inbox, bringing customer conversations from these communication channels together through official Meta integrations.

Merchants can view order histories within conversations and use artificial intelligence-enabled support, backed by Pathao's database of nearly 10 million unique addresses nationwide, to enter delivery information faster.

They can also generate an Instant Checkout link directly within a customer chat window, allowing customers to complete their orders and payments in a single step.

Once an order is placed, a pickup agent is automatically dispatched to the merchant's doorstep. The company immediately shares a tracking link with the customer, reducing the need for merchants to handle delivery-related queries.

The company said reducing platform switching, copying and pasting, and manual coordination would make the process from customer conversation to delivery faster and simpler.

Pathao Commerce also provides tools to help merchants grow beyond their day-to-day operations. Businesses can customise their storefronts, track sales and inventory, and use analytics to make informed decisions.

Merchants will soon be able to run sponsored campaigns directly through Meta Catalogue integration, the company said.

The platform offers secure payments, instant payouts through Pathao Pay, real-time delivery tracking, and customer trust ratings. Pathao said these features were designed to help merchants sell with greater confidence.

The company said its customer trust ratings, developed using historical data, helped keep social commerce return rates in single digits, compared with around 30% for online marketplaces in Bangladesh.

Pathao Commerce also allows merchants to publish their entire product catalogue to Pathao Shop, opening an additional sales channel in a few clicks.

Through Pathao's Instant Delivery service, merchants can fulfil orders requiring faster delivery. Businesses can also automate the service through direct application programming interface (API) integration with Pathao Commerce.

Pathao described the launch as a milestone in its transition from an e-commerce logistics provider to a broader provider of digital commerce infrastructure in Bangladesh.

The company said bringing logistics, payments, communication, and business management into a single platform would help merchants manage increasingly complex operations and pursue growth opportunities.

Title: Crude bomb blasts in Gulshan: 9 more accused sent to jail
Content:
A Dhaka court today (13 September) ordered nine more accused in a case over alleged crude bomb blasts and sabotage in Gulshan to be sent to jail pending completion of the investigation.

Dhaka Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Joshita Islam passed the order after a hearing this afternoon.

Sub-Inspector Moktar Hossain of the Dhaka Metropolitan Prosecution Division confirmed the matter.

The accused are Rehana Parvin, 43, Mohammad Saiful Islam, 52, Mohammad Jewel Sikder, 33, Mohammad Nazim Uddin, 34, Mohammad Sahed, 37, Shanto Sheikh, 28, Mohammad Harun Maizbhandari, 55, Khaled Mahmud Faisal, 40, and Mohammad Shafiqul Rahman, 50.

Earlier, Gulshan police Sub-Inspector Mohammad Ruhul Amin, also the investigation officer, produced the accused before the court and sought an order to keep them in jail until the investigation is completed.

The prosecution told the court that the accused had provided information about the incident during preliminary questioning, while their names and addresses had been forwarded to the respective police stations for verification.

The investigating officer also said the accused needed further interrogation and that separate remand petitions would be submitted.

A Dhaka court on 12 September placed 24 other accused in the same case on 10-day remand.

According to the case statement, leaders and activists of various affiliated organisations of the Awami League, whose activities have been suspended, and the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League gathered in the Gulshan Police Station area around 11:45am on 11 September.

The gathering was allegedly organised to chant anti-government and anti-state slogans, create disorder and carry out activities aimed at undermining the image of the elected government and putting it in a difficult position, the case statement said.

It further alleged that crude bombs were exploded in and around the area, creating panic among the public.

According to the statement, members of a banned organisation carried out the explosions with the alleged intention of damaging the government's image and causing damage to state property and people's lives and property.

When police attempted to disperse the gathering, the accused allegedly threw crude bombs at them.

Police later fired two rounds of rubber bullets to bring the situation under control, prompting the group to disperse and flee, according to the case statement.

Police seized five crude bombs from the scene.

Gulshan Police Station Sub-Inspector Mohammad Mahbub Hossain filed the case under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The case names 118 people as accused and includes another 80–100 unidentified people.

Title: Saad faction presses for separate Tongi Ijtema, rejects alternative venue
Content:
A faction of Tabligh Jamaat followers loyal to Maulana Muhammad Saad Kandhalvi today (13 September) demanded separate dates to hold their Bishwa Ijtema at the Tongi ground, along with several other demands.

"The date for the upcoming Bishwa Ijtema to be held by the followers of Maulana Saad at the Tongi Bishwa Ijtema grounds must be announced immediately," a speaker said while reading a written press release.

These demands were made at a press conference at the National Press Club in the city arranged by representatives of the Saad faction.

They said the Tongi Ijtema ground is government-owned and should be accessible to both factions of Tabligh Jamaat.

"The ownership of the Tongi Bishwa Ijtema ground rests entirely with the government; it does not belong to the Zubair faction under any circumstances," a speaker said.

He said the Saad faction would have no objection if followers of Maulana Zubairul Hasan held their Ijtema at the venue several times a year, but insisted that the Saad faction should also be allowed to hold its programme there.

"An alternative venue is not possible by any means," he added.

Referring to a decision of the previous interim government on 9 Feb, 2025, the speakers claimed that an official letter had allowed the Saad faction to hold its Ijtema at Tongi from 14 to 16 Feb that year.

They also claimed that no undertaking or bond was signed barring the faction from using the venue for future Ijtemas when the ground was handed over to the authorities.

Their demand comes after Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed announced on 3 Sept that the Bishwa Ijtema would be held in two phases at Tongi from 8 to 10 Jan and 15 to 17 Jan .

The Minister also said the government was considering a separate proposal from the Saad faction to hold another Ijtema at the same venue.

The speakers also demanded that the government ensure both factions can conduct Tabligh activities across the country without obstruction and take steps to resolve the dispute over the Kakrail Mosque.

The dispute within Tabligh Jamaat in Bangladesh intensified following the death of its leader Maulana Inamul Hasan, with the movement subsequently divided between followers of Maulana Zubairul Hasan and Maulana Saad Kandhalvi.

The two factions have been involved in clashes at the Tongi Ijtema ground, including in 2018 and 2024.

Title: Over 30,000 remain stranded despite slowing Padma River rise
Content:
The rise in the Padma River has slowed in Kushtia's Daulatpur, but 30,000-35,000 people have remained stranded for more than a week, with food and safe drinking water becoming increasingly scarce.

The river rose by just 1cm in the 24 hours till today (13 September), according to the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB). But the prolonged inundation has continued to worsen conditions in the char areas.

Official figures put the number of stranded people at around 30,000-35,000 from nearly 8,000 families. Local representatives, however, estimate the number to be much higher, saying at least 60,000 people in 40 villages of Chilmari and Ramkrishnapur unions are waterlogged and waiting for relief.

According to the Hydrology Division of the Pabna Water Development Board, the Padma's water level at the Hardinge Bridge point stood at 13.06 metres at 9am today.

The danger level there is 13.80 metres, leaving the river 74cm below the threshold. The level was 13.05 metres at the same time yesterday.

Ilias Hossain, executive engineer of the BWDB's Hydrology Division, said the river had risen rapidly due to upstream water and heavy rainfall, but the rate of increase had slowed.

"Water rose by only 1cm in the past 24 hours. However, it is too early to say whether this slower rise will continue," he said.

The water level also remained unchanged between 6pm on Saturday and 9am on Sunday, he added.

Despite the slower rise, prolonged flooding has created acute shortages of food and safe drinking water across the char areas.

Farmers and small-scale livestock owners are also struggling to protect their cattle, with many unable to find higher ground for their animals.

The agricultural losses are mounting as well.

Daulatpur Upazila Agriculture Officer Rehena Parvin said crops on around 1,000 hectares of farmland in the char areas of Chilmari, Ramkrishnapur, Philipnagar and Moricha unions had been submerged.

Chilli and banana growers have suffered the most, she said, warning that continued flooding could cause further losses.

Floodwater has also inundated educational institutions in the char areas, forcing 30 of them to suspend classes.

According to the upazila education office, the affected institutions include 25 government primary schools, three secondary schools and two madrasas.

Administrative and official activities at the institutions, however, are continuing.

Chilmari Union Parishad Chairman Engineer Abdul Mannan said water levels had not risen significantly since Saturday, but the prolonged inundation had intensified people's suffering.

"Government assistance will start reaching affected families in the union from Monday," he said.

Daulatpur Upazila Project Implementation Officer Shubhagata Biswas said the existing relief allocation was inadequate compared with the number of affected families.

The deputy commissioner had contacted the relevant ministry seeking an increased allocation, and additional assistance was expected soon, he said.

The existing relief supplies would be distributed by Tuesday, he added.

Based on information from the BWDB, there is now less likelihood of another major rise in the river, Shubhagata said. Water levels could remain stable for a day or two before beginning to recede.

However, he identified prolonged waterlogging as the biggest challenge.

Local residents have called for urgent supplies of food and safe drinking water and urged affluent individuals and organisations to come forward to support flood-affected communities.

Title: BB launches 'Udyog' to spur youth entrepreneurship with up to Tk20 lakh blended financing
Content:
In a major push to foster self-employment and drive grassroots economic growth, Bangladesh Bank today (13 September) issued a comprehensive guideline titled "Udyog: Upazila-Driven Youth Opportunity for Growth".

The program aims to hunt, identify, and finance prospective young entrepreneurs across all upazilas in Bangladesh.

Issued by the SME and Special Programmes Department, the circular directs Managing Directors and Chief Executive Officers of all scheduled banks to immediately implement the scheme.

The policy covers a wide array of legal ventures–including tech startups, agriculture, food processing, light engineering, renewable energy, and handicrafts–prioritising both new innovative ideas and existing business models.

To ensure funding reaches genuine and capable young creators, Bangladesh Bank established specific eligibility guidelines:

Age Limit: Applicants must be adult Bangladeshi citizens aged up to 28 years on the final date of application submission.

Local Residency: Candidates must be permanent residents of the respective upazila.

Clean Credit History: Applicants must not be loan defaulters. Any default status revealed during Credit Information Bureau (CIB) checks will result in immediate cancellation.

Furthermore, anyone who has previously taken a business loan from any bank or financial institution is ineligible.

Employment Status: Public, semi-government, and autonomous institution employees are excluded from applying.

No Collateral Required: To alleviate barriers for youth, loans under this program can be disbursed without collateral support.

The framework offers a maximum blended financing package of up to Tk20 lakh per selected entrepreneur, evaluated strictly against business requirements and proposed cost plans, according to the circular.

The funding is split equally: 50 percent bank loan (Up to Tk10 lakh) and 50 percent matching grant (Up to Tk10 lakh)

If a business needs Tk12 lakh, for example, the applicant receives Tk6 lakh as a bank loan and Tk6 lakh as a grant.

The grant and loan portions will be disbursed simultaneously into the recipient's bank account.

However, failure to repay the loan or misuse of funds will automatically convert the grant portion into an interest-free debt, recoverable under standard recovery laws.

Bangladesh Bank will nominate one Lead Bank for each upazila to execute and coordinate the program.

Any branch of scheduled banks will collect application forms. On the working day following the application deadline, branches will forward all applications to the respective Upazila Lead Bank, which will then channel them to the District Lead Bank and eventually to Bangladesh Bank's departmental offices.

A multi-stakeholder panel comprising central bank officials, scheduled bank representatives, successful entrepreneurs, industry leaders, and academics will evaluate business plans, market feasibility, and employment potential to make final selections.

Designated banks must sanction loans within 15 working days of final selection, adhering to their internal credit rules and central bank regulations.

All participating banks will also provide financial literacy training, mentoring, market linkage support, and assistance with business registrations to ensure long-term sustainability for the newly minted enterprises.
