Title: Effective local government needed to reach services to people's doorstep: LGRD Minister
Content:
Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan today (13 September) said an effective local government system is required to deliver government services to the doorstep of people.

"An effective and strong local government system is particularly important to deliver government services to the doorstep of people in a densely populated country like Bangladesh," he said.

The minister made the remarks during a courtesy meeting with Ambassador of Switzerland to Bangladesh Reto Renggli at his office at Secretariat.

State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam was present at the meeting.

Dr Moyeen said there is no alternative to strengthening local government to institutionalise democracy and ensure people's participation and accountability.

"The foundation of democracy needs to be strengthened at the grassroots level; otherwise, it will not be possible to consolidate the overall democratic structure of the state," he said.

He also stressed the need to transform the country's huge population into skilled human resources and enhance the financial capacity of local government institutions.

The minister said genuine decentralisation is necessary to effectively strengthen local government.

He said local government institutions can be made more effective by increasing people's participation and expanding opportunities for decision-making at the local level.

During the meeting, various issues, including further strengthening the bilateral relations between Bangladesh and Switzerland, strengthening democracy and the local government system, the local government election process, increasing rural women's participation in economic activities, and addressing the impacts of climate change came up for discussion.

Ambassador Renggli referred to the existing friendly relations between Bangladesh and Switzerland and expressed interest in expanding cooperation in various fields.

He stressed exchanging mutual experiences in areas such as enhancing the capacity of local government institutions, increasing accountability to people and women's empowerment.

Briefing reporters after the meeting, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam said they discussed various aspects of further strengthening the local government system and institutionally consolidating democracy.

Title: Eminent Bengali writer Syed Mujtaba Ali's 122nd birth anniversary today
Content:
The 122nd birth anniversary of eminent Bengali writer, journalist, travel enthusiast and linguist Syed Mujtaba Ali is today (13 September).

Born on 13 September 1904 to a Bengali Muslim Syed family of Khandakars in Karimganj, Sylhet district, British Raj, Ali was one of the first to call for Bangla as East Pakistan's state language on 30 November 1947, at the Sylhet Kendriya Muslim Sahitya Sangsad , according to Wikipedia.

He was a prominent activist and supporter of Bengali as the national language of the then East Pakistan (now Bangladesh).

In 1948, being the principal of Azizul Huq College, Bogra, he wrote an essay, 'The State Language of East Pakistan', which was printed in Chaturanga of Kolkata.

During that time, the West Pakistan Rulers tried to impose Urdu as the only state language of East Pakistan while Bengali was spoken by most of the people. The government of Pakistan demanded an explanation. But Ali resigned and moved to India.

Ali slipped back to India in August 1949, tipped off by a friend that Pakistani authorities intended to arrest him for his vocal support of the Bengali language movement.

After a brief stint at University of Calcutta in 1950, Ali became Secretary of the Indian Council for Cultural Relations and editor of its Arabic journal Thaqafatul Hind.

From 1952 to 1956 he worked for All India Radio at New Delhi, Cuttack and Patna.

He then joined Visva-Bharati University (1956–1964) as professor of German language and later of Islamic Culture. He lived in Kolkata till early 1972. Following the liberation of Bangladesh, he moved to Dhaka to live with his family until his death in 1974.

Ali's mother tongue was Sylheti-Bengali, but he also could speak standard Bengali, English, Russian, French, German, Italian, Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi, Gujarati, and Pashtu.

He lived in Bangladesh, India, Germany, Afghanistan and Egypt.

Alongside Natya Guru Nurul Momen and Jajabar (Binay Mukhopadhyay), Ali was one of the trail-blazers of a unique category of Bengali writing.

'Ramya Rachana' in the Bengali language, an anecdotal story-telling – often based on real-life experiences – became immensely popular, mostly because of the attractive writing style of Ali.

Deshe Bideshe, the story of his journey to and experiences in Kabul during his brief stint as professor in a college there is one of Ali's best works. Panchatantra is a collection of thoughts and short stories (some already published in 'Desh' magazine) of his days in Europe, Cairo and Baroda.

In 1972, after the Independence of Bangladesh, Ali returned to Bangladesh. He died on 11 February 1974.

Extracts from his literary works are included in the curriculum of school level, secondary, higher secondary and graduation level Bengali Literature in both Bangladesh and India, particularly in the states of West Bengal and Tripura.

He was awarded Ekushey Padak, (posthumously) the second highest civilian award in Bangladesh in 2005 by the Government of Bangladesh.

Title: Saudi pipeline outage threatens loss of 4% of global oil supply
Content:
Saudi Arabia will run out of oil stocks for exports ‌if it doesn't restart its major pipeline to the Red Sea within days, leading to a loss of up to 4% of global supply, Saudi oil buyers and traders said. A further decline in Saudi flows will worsen the global supply crunch, which has already pushed global fuel prices to record highs, spurred ​inflation around the world and sent US bond yields to the highest levels since the 2008 financial crisis.

Since drone ​attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its huge east-west oil pipeline on Friday, Riyadh has not given full ⁠details about the extent of the damage or how long the route will stay off-line.

Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying ​estimates, with one saying the damage could take as long as five to six weeks to repair, while another said it could be ​fixed sooner and could resume pumping partially while repairs are ongoing.

Saudi Arabia's government media office and energy ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. For the past six months, the pipeline running through the desert across the Arabian Peninsula has spared Saudi Arabia from the brunt of the impact of ​the wartime shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz that has crippled exports from its neighbours.

The world's biggest exporter has used the pipeline ​to reroute around 4 million barrels per day — around 4% of global supply — to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. But with the pipeline ‌out of ⁠service, Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days, according to three industry sources familiar with Saudi exports. Saudi Arabia also has stocks to supply customers for several days from Egypt's ports of Ain Sukhna on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean, a fourth source said.

Yanbu storage capacity stands at around 35 million barrels, according to industry estimates, with Ain Sukhna ​and Sidi Kerir able to store ​18 million and 20 million ⁠barrels respectively. Stocks are not full and will ultimately run out without the east-west pipeline resuming operations, the four sources said. Saudi oil supply has already fallen to a more than three-decade low in August on ​reduced flows via Hormuz and the Red Sea, the International Energy Agency said on Friday. World oil supply ​will decline this year ⁠by 5.7 million bpd, or about 6%, the IEA, which coordinates Western energy policies, said. In addition to the attack on the pipeline, Houthi fighters in Yemen who have threatened Saudi oil shipments seized an an island on Friday in the mouth of the Red Sea.

The Middle East supplied around 22 ⁠million barrels ​per day of oil before the war. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz ​have slowed to just 6 million to 9 million bpd, industry sources say.

Saudi Arabia told OPEC last week that its oil production had dropped to just 6.2 million ​bpd in August from 10.9 million bpd in February before the start of the war.

Title: Bangladesh wants to 'reset' ties with India: Humaiun Kobir
Content:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir today (13 September) said Bangladesh wants to "reset" its bilateral relationship with India after what he described as an uncomfortable relationship over 15 years under an "authoritarian, corrupt and exploitative" regime.

"We want to move towards a new relationship, which should be done through bilateral discussions, not through a multilateral forum," Kobir said while responding to a question at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"We have to get out of the India fascination. India is just another country, and Bangladesh wants good bilateral relations with it," Kobir said.

Responding to the continued focus on India, he said, "Breakfast in India, lunch in India, dinner in India - then when will you eat your own food?"

He said his earlier remarks specifically referred to India and the need to rebuild bilateral relations through direct bilateral engagement.

"What I said was mainly applicable to India. We want to build a good working bilateral relationship with India," he said.

Kobir said Bangladesh's first engagement with a country with which it wants to develop better relations should ideally be through a bilateral visit rather than a meeting on the sidelines of a multilateral forum.

"That was said only in the case of India. I never said that whenever we attend a multilateral event, we will not meet anyone," he said.

He clarified, however, that this does not mean Bangladesh will avoid meeting countries on the sidelines of international forums.

Asked about recent incidents along the Bangladesh-India border, Kobir said the government would address such issues through diplomatic channels. "We will resolve these issues through diplomatic discussions," he said.

He said Bangladesh would raise its concerns with India at every appropriate level while adhering to international law, border protocols and agreements between the two countries.

Asked about the reported review of 101 MoUs, Kobir said the agreements were being scrutinised and reviewed through the parliamentary process.

The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) will once again bring together world leaders to revitalise global cooperation, give a critical push to the Sustainable Development Goals and drive collective action for peace, dignity and equality on a healthy planet.

The State Minister said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to leave for New York on September 21 to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly and will stay there until September 26.

The Prime Minister is scheduled to address the UN General Assembly, where he will present Bangladesh's new vision and highlight the country's democratic transition and aspirations for the future.

"He will share his thoughts and vision for the future of Bangladesh with world leaders," Kobir told reporters.

"He will have a very busy schedule in New York," Kobir said, adding that the Prime Minister would hold meetings with world leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Asked whether the UN Refugee Convention would be discussed during the visit, Kobir said Bangladesh would organise a sideline event focusing on the Rohingya crisis.

"There will be a high-level discussion or meeting on the Rohingya crisis as part of the visit. It is a major priority for us," he said.

Asked about the possibility of a sideline meeting between the Prime Minister and US President Donald Trump, the state minister said such meetings are often decided at the last moment during major international conferences.

"The primary focus of the Prime Minister's visit is to address the UN General Assembly," he said, adding that details of the sideline meetings would be known in due course.

Title: Paris cheers the power of Celine Dion
Content:
Celine Dion made an emotional return to the stage after a six-year absence yesterday (12 September), overcoming high-profile health woes to ​thrill fans in the first of a series of concerts in ‌Paris.

"I'm standing on stage in this city I love so much thanks to your support and your love," she told the crowd. "The path was rocky, the road was longer than ​planned but I held on."

The star announced in 2022 she had been ​diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological condition which ⁠causes muscle spasms and left her unable to perform.

Dion seemed overwhelmed at times ​and broke down in tears during her opening number, holding out a microphone ​to the audience to help her through the bridge.

"I promised I wouldn't cry - but they're tears of joy," she said, speaking mostly French throughout.

The staging was muted and Dion mainly wore ​a series of black gowns, leaving little to distract from her obvious ​emotion at being back in front of a crowd.

"She didn't shy away from what she suffered ‌and ⁠she shared it with her audience," British fan Catherine Rushforth said as she left the arena in Nanterre on the outskirts of Paris.

Dion strutted confidently through her familiar on-stage theatrics, pulling faces and playing air guitar, and belting out ​ballads including "My Heart Will ​Go On" and "All ⁠By Myself" which made her one of the best-selling recording artists of all time.

But she opened with one of ​her biggest French-language hits "On Ne Change Pas" ("We Don't Change") - an ​apparent reference ⁠to her extended absence.

Her 16-concert residency, with a further 10 dates in 2027, has caused a frenzy in the French capital where crowds gather outside her swanky ⁠hotel until ​the early hours hoping to catch a glimpse ​of her.

"Her fight is an example for all of us, it's wonderful," said fan Julien Faruch, ​a chef.

Title: ASK demands arrest, trial of all accused in Brahmanbaria dancers' rape case
Content:
The Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) has condemned the alleged gang rape of two female dancers in Brahmanbaria's Sarail and called for the immediate arrest and trial of all those involved.

In a press release issued today (13 September), the rights organisation urged authorities to conduct a neutral and professional investigation and ensure that no accused escapes justice because of influence or pressure.

According to ASK, the two dancers were lured with a fake offer to perform at a wedding ceremony and taken onto a boat on Thursday evening (10 September). They were allegedly held hostage at gunpoint and raped in the middle of the Titas River.

ASK said the incident was a serious violation of women's safety and dignity, as well as their right to work freely in a safe environment.

"Working as a dancer or performing at an event in exchange for payment cannot expose anyone to the risk of violence or abuse," the organisation said, stressing that ensuring citizens' safety at work is the state's responsibility.

The rights body urged the authorities to ensure the victims' safety, medical treatment, psychological support and legal assistance, while protecting their identities and privacy.

It also said the incident should not be viewed solely as a crime committed by individuals, arguing that it raises broader questions about the effectiveness of state mechanisms to prevent violence against women and ensure their safe movement and working conditions.

According to police and the case statement, three professional dancers from Cumilla, including the two women, were taken to the middle of the Titas River after being hired to perform at a wedding ceremony in Sarail.

One accused, identified as 19-year-old Shanto Biswas, was arrested the following day.

ASK said women's safety is not merely a law-and-order issue but also a matter of equal rights, dignity and human rights.

The organisation called on the state to create an environment in which women can work in their chosen professions without fear or insecurity.

Title: ACC launches probe against Asif Mahmud over Tk13,000cr corruption, money laundering
Content:
The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has launched an inquiry into allegations of financial irregularities, bribery and money laundering involving around Tk13,000 crore against Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuiyan, former interim government adviser to the Ministry of Youth and Sports.

The allegations include trading in appointments, transfers, and promotions; taking commissions from tenders; inflating development project costs; and siphoning off funds.

He allegedly laundered Tk4,500 crore to Dubai, Tk3,000 crore to Singapore, Tk2,000 crore to Australia and Tk1,500 crore to Switzerland to purchase villas and invest in businesses there.

ACC Assistant Director (Public Relations) Md Tanzir Ahmed disclosed the information at the commission's regular media briefing today (13 September).

According to the complaint, the former adviser allegedly took around Tk60 crore in connection with appointing an administrator to Dhaka North City Corporation. It also alleges that Tk2-10 crore was exchanged for the appointment of each of 36 deputy commissioners across the country.

The complaint further alleges that he took 10%-30% commissions from development project tenders while serving at the Local Government Division. It also accused him of involvement in tender-related irregularities at Dhaka South City Corporation, Narayanganj City Corporation and Cumilla City Corporation.

It alleged that project costs for rural infrastructure and bridge construction under the local government ministry were inflated to embezzle thousands of crores.

The complaint also raised questions over alleged abnormal cost increases in the third phase of Dhaka Wasa's Sayedabad Water Treatment Plant project and claimed that Tk1,200 crore was added to the cost of the Sheikh Russell Mini Stadium project for illicit gains.

Allegations of bribery in recruitment, transfers and promotions at the youth and sports ministry were also brought against him. The complaint alleged that Tk10 crore was taken as a bribe for appointing Abdus Salam as managing director of Dhaka Wasa.

It further accused him of taking Tk52 crore for appointing former LGED chief engineer Md Abdur Rashid Khan and Tk65 crore for appointing Abdul Latif Khan as chief executive officer of Gazipur City Corporation.

The complaint also alleged that Asif Mahmud used government funds for helicopter travel and maintained a luxurious lifestyle, including stays at five-star hotels, a luxury apartment and expensive vehicles.

It also alleged that his father Billal Hossain and former APS Moazzem Hossain controlled contractor syndicates and collected money by influencing local administration officials.

The complaint also accused his former personal officer Mahfuzul Alam Bhuiyan of lobbying for bribe transactions and abusing his power.

The ACC said the inquiry will verify the allegations, the roles of those involved and the sources and movement of the alleged funds. No findings have yet been established against Asif Mahmud.

'Prepared for further allegations'

Reacting to the ACC's inquiry, the National Citizen Party (NCP) spokesperson said the government could use various means if it decided to target someone.

"If the government decides to arrest someone, there are many ways to do that. We have seen this being done against the BNP as well," he said at a press conference.

He questioned the ACC's priorities, saying, "The ACC was formed five months later, but they have no concern about the corruption during the Awami League period. I am the first political figure against whom the ACC had initiated such a process."

"However, I have already made my position clear," he added.

Asif Mahmud also alleged that an earlier complaint against him related to promotions during the BNP period had failed to gain traction.

"When they saw that it did not work, now they are bringing another one. Tomorrow they will bring another one. Let them keep doing it. We are prepared for this," he said.

He also questioned the independence of the ACC, saying, "When we saw that the ACC had not been reformed and the ordinance was repealed, we understood what the ACC would be used for. It was used for that reason in the past, and it will be used for the same reason in the future."

However, Asif Mahmud said he was yet to learn the details of the latest allegations against him.

"Specifically, I have not yet learned the details of what happened today," he said.

Title: Shimanto Gronthagar: Old Dhaka’s 75-year-old cultural hub fights for survival
Content:
For generations, Shimanto Gronthagar in Gendaria was more than a library — it was a cultural gathering place in Old Dhaka.

That very place remained locked for nearly a year. Neglect left the library in disrepair, damaging around 600 of the 10,000 books in its collection. The door through which generations once entered in search of knowledge had quietly closed.

On 1 September, the library's door opened again. But reopening is only the beginning. The bigger question is whether this 75-year-old institution can find a way to survive.

A library born in a home

In 1951, progressive political figure and leftist leader Nasim Ali, locally known as "Kochi Bhai", founded the library at his Distillery Road home with 50 books.

The land later came under the name of Ambika Charan Chakraborty, who left the country. The library still operates on land leased in his name, classified as "Ka" schedule vested property. During the Communist Party's underground period, revolutionary politicians including Gyan Chakraborty reportedly took shelter here.

After independence, Chakraborty reportedly refused Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's proposal, conveyed through Sengupta Nanaji, to take over the land, saying it was better kept for children to play and the library to remain.

A 1969 storm damaged the collection, including encyclopedias and Britannica volumes, while rare books scattered afterwards were never returned. During the 1974 famine, the library also housed a relief kitchen (langarkhana).

In 1973, at the Nazrul birth anniversary event organised at the library, the rebel poet Kazi Nazrul Islam and his family were present as chief guests.

Enayet Kabir, a regular reader from that era and local resident, said, "I've been reading books here since my college days. I prefer storybooks to academic books, so I used to come here for that. Even now, whenever I have time, I occasionally drop by."

Manzarul said, "I joined as a librarian in 1980 and took charge of the library the following year."

The library has long been associated with prominent figures in literature and culture. Writer and novelist Imdadul Haque Milon developed his craft in its reading environment, while theatre personality Ali Zaker and film actor Shawkat Akbar also took part in its activities.

Its supporters included Dhaka University teacher Jyotirmoy Guhathakurta, his wife and educationist Basanti Guhathakurta, and Jogesh Chandra, all remembered for their association with the library.

Later, local enthusiast Golam Mawla, known as Kayes, helped secure its permanent home. He funded the present building in memory of three family members—Nazrul Islam, Sabera Khatun and Sahara Khatun. Artist Bazle Mawla designed its historic monogram.

"Back then very few homes had televisions, and there were no mobile phones at all. Hundreds of boys and girls used to come here," Manzarul recalled.

The library was not merely a quiet reading room—it was a bustling cultural incubator for the neighbourhood's youth.

"We would take everyone on educational trips, and after returning, they had to write about their experiences—prizes were given for good writing," he recalled. "There would also be Jhumur dance, stick dance, and dumbbell exercises."

The demand for books was so high that readers often lined up outside the door.

"We have plans to build a few shops at the front. The rent income from those shops will be used to cover the library's regular expenses. There are plans to formally request book donations from the National Book Centre, the Bengal Foundation, and the Liberation War Museum to further expand the collection." Manzarul Islam Chowdhury, General Secretary, Shimanto Gronthagar

"To prevent book theft, a deposit of 200 taka was kept, which was returned when the book was brought back," Manzarul added.

Shimanto Gronthagar's former general secretary, Kazi Sultan Ahmed Token, added, "The library used to open six days a week, except Sunday. It offered more than books, with weekly dance and drawing classes. People of all ages came, especially young people. Three daily newspapers were also kept, drawing morning crowds of readers."

Alongside former officials and elders, in Enayet Kabir's memory, Shimanto Gronthagar was not just a library for borrowing books; it was a place wrapped in gatherings and memories of adolescence.

Recalling those days, Kabir said, "Back then, this was our evening gathering spot. Without TV or phones, books and friends were our main attractions. I still remember waiting hours for a favourite book and once even stealing money from my father's pocket to pay the Tk200 deposit."

From the aftermath of Partition through the Liberation War and into the 1990s, Shimanto Gronthagar remained a place where reading, cultural activity and community life converged in Old Dhaka.

Why was it shut down?

The library's financial crisis began when its annual tax bill rose sharply—from Tk7,000 to Tk60,000.

Manzarul said, "We're just a library — where would we get this money from? Even if we sold everything, it still wouldn't be enough."

Kazi said the library once ran largely on voluntary labour, but now has to pay staff and cover expenses including Tk60,000 in annual tax. "Without a permanent source of funding, it is difficult to sustain such a historic institution," he said.

Talha, a second-year student who comes to read at the library, said he had not visited for a long time because it remained closed. He used to bring his younger brother with him, who would play with other children while Talha read.

Committee members covered the library's running costs themselves, alongside an annual Tk70,000 government grant secured by Manzarul in 2020. However, the grant requires annual paperwork to be submitted to the Ministry of Social Welfare, which the previous committee failed to do.

Kabir attributes the closure to the tax burden and neglect. He said fewer people now come to read than in the past, but welcomes the effort to repair and reopen the library.

Since the reopening, he said, his wife has been bringing their child to the library, which he hopes will help the child develop a habit of reading.

Manzarul said, "When an organisation falls into the hands of an individual, it gets ruined. Those who were responsible didn't take proper care of it, and through this continued neglect, it shut down in January 2025."

During this period of neglect, road-cutting and drainage work nearly blocked access to the library. Taking advantage of this, miscreants stole electrical wires, fans, window glass, taps and a sack of newly purchased books worth Tk40,000–50,000. More than 600 books were lost in the theft.

Manzarul said the theft was part of a conspiracy to seize the land. "Many people's eyes have fallen on this land, and people are still trying to seize it. The way the theft was carried out was not ordinary," he said.

When the new committee took charge, the library was in poor condition. Manzarul said, "When I took charge and formed the new committee a year ago, its condition was very bad — nothing was there, many things were missing, many books were ruined. We started fresh from there."

Talha said he had already stopped visiting regularly before the closure because the road in front of the library was difficult to access. The theft also left the library with far fewer books, he said.

Rebuilding from the ruins

After years of neglect and theft, Manzarul returned as general secretary to revive the library.

"I'm trying to bring it to a point where, even if we're not around, the library keeps running by its own rules, in its own way," he said.

When the new committee took charge, the library was in disrepair. The restoration included five fans, a water motor, taps, a water tank and new electrical lines. Around 600 damp-damaged books were beyond repair, but nearly 10,000 new books have since been added.

Talha said that after it reopened, he came and saw quite a few new books had been brought in, and apparently more will come. He also noticed now that there's always a person present for the library's security.

Manzarul said he has personally spent Tk156,000 on the restoration so far.

Security measures are also being strengthened to prevent a repeat of the theft. The entire premises are being brought under CCTV surveillance.

The new committee has 15 members. The president is Sultan Ahmed, the vice-president is Kayes, the general secretary is Manzarul, and Anis holds the responsibility of librarian. Everyone currently working here is providing tireless service through voluntary labour.

Kabir said a new committee has been formed, and he hopes it can now maintain the old atmosphere in a new way. He said the previous committee members had ignored things a lot and hadn't fixed anything properly.

Expressing his sense of duty, librarian Anis said, "Shimanto Gronthagar is not just a library — it is part of Old Dhaka's heritage. When it shut down due to theft and neglect, it felt really bad. Now, seeing the new books and organised shelves feels good. Our only wish is for readers to pick up books again."

But reopening the library does not solve the question of how it will pay for its future. The committee is now looking for a more sustainable source of income.

Manzarul said, "We have plans to build a few shops at the front. The rent income from those shops will be used to cover the library's regular expenses." Besides this, he said, there are plans to formally request book donations from the National Book Centre, the Bengal Foundation, and the Liberation War Museum to further expand the collection.

On 1 September, Shimanto Gronthagar reopened after nearly a year. Elderly readers, local civil society members and book-loving teenagers gathered at the inauguration, bringing new life to the newly painted shelves.

The management board has been surprised by the response from young people. Manzarul said, "One thing that genuinely surprises me is that many students from the madrasas around us are now coming here and reading books. Seeing all kinds of young people drawn to the library by books like this is truly a wonderful sight."

The library will remain closed one day a week but open to readers on the other days. It also welcomes good-quality book donations through librarian Anis Rahman at 01923849779.

The new generation's return offers a glimpse of the library's old vibrancy. But the real test is whether the doors can remain open. Founded in 1951 with just 50 books, Shimanto Gronthagar will truly be reborn when it once again becomes a regular place for reading, learning and cultural life.
Author: Mohsin Islam Tanvir

Title: Ship sinks in Indonesia, 130 still missing
Content:
A passenger ship that had lost contact in Indonesia's Java Sea has sunk, the country's National Search and Rescue Agency said today (13 September), with around 130 people still unaccounted for.

Around 110 people have been rescued and at least one person has died, according to the latest available figures.

The Chinese Consulate General in Surabaya confirmed to Xinhua that there were no Chinese nationals aboard the ship, citing information verified with relevant authorities of the Surabaya city government.

The passenger ship, Virgo Transport 8, was carrying 243 people when it lost contact at around 2:00 a.m. local time on Sunday after encountering bad weather, according to the search and rescue agency.

The vessel had departed from Surabaya in East Java province on Saturday and was heading to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province.

The cause of the accident remains unclear. Indonesian search and rescue authorities have deployed personnel, ships and a helicopter to waters near the vessel's last known position to conduct search and rescue operations.

Indonesia, an archipelagic country with around 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries and other forms of sea transportation to connect its islands and facilitate travel. Maritime accidents occur from time to time due to factors including weather conditions, sea conditions and vessel safety.

Title: Trump says he would be OK with China building cars in US
Content:
President Donald Trump said on Friday (11 September) he would not oppose Chinese automakers building ​cars in the United States despite widespread opposition from US lawmakers ‌and car companies.

"If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I'd be okay with that," Trump said in an interview on the Fox ​News program "The Ingraham Angle."

"Japan does it, but they hire our people. The ​big thing is they hire our people," he said.

He added that ⁠he does not want Chinese automakers to build cars in Mexico and ship ​them to the United States. "I'm not knocking Chinese cars," Trump said.

US automakers have ​urged Trump, who is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington in two weeks, not to agree to allow Chinese automakers access to the US market.

On Wednesday, US Senator ​Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, said there were "rumors that Trump is planning ​to allow Chinese cars to be sold in the US, as part of a larger deal ‌he's ⁠putting together. That would be a strategic mistake."

Trump called Slotkin's statement a "total phony rumor" and said he had kept Chinese vehicles out of the United States.

A regulation imposed by former President Joe Biden's administration in early 2025 effectively bans all ​Chinese automakers from ​selling or building ⁠passenger vehicles in the US Washington also maintains more than 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.

Last week, a group representing ​nearly all major automakers urged Congress to quickly pass legislation ​permanently barring ⁠Chinese vehicles from the US market.

The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents General Motors, Ford, Toyota, Volkswagen, Hyundai, Honda, Stellantis and others, called for passage of the ⁠bill by ​the end of December.

"Right now, Chinese automakers are ​dumping subsidized vehicles with connected software and hardware around the world," the group's CEO, John Bozzella, ​said in a letter to congressional leaders.

Title: Jubo League leader among 8 placed on 4-day remand over Uttarkhan sabotage plot
Content:
A Dhaka court has placed eight people, including a banned Bangladesh Jubo League leader, on four-day remand in a case filed over an alleged plot to carry out sabotage in the capital's Uttarkhan area.

Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Sarah Farzana Haque passed the order today (13 September) following a remand petition by the investigation officer.

Public prosecutor Harun-or-Rashid confirmed the matter. The accused are Mohammad Mazharul Islam alias Raihan, 32, joint general secretary of Ward 45 Jubo League; Mohammad Rakib, 23; Mohammad Tanvir Khan, 26; Mohammad Abdur Rahman, 40; Mohammad Sifat, 20; Mohammad Mahfuzur Rahman, 24; Mohammad Ashik Mia, 23; and Mohammad Bakul Ahmed alias Raju, 24. Earlier, Uttarkhan Police Sub-Inspector Mohammad Rafiqul Islam, also the investigation officer in the case, produced the accused before the court and sought five days' remand for each.

The investigation officer said the accused needed to be interrogated to uncover the circumstances of the case, identify and arrest other accomplices and determine the identities and whereabouts of those allegedly behind the planned sabotage. After hearing both sides, the court granted four days' remand for each accused.

The defence lawyer, Mostafizur Rahman Talukder Dipu, sought cancellation of the remand.

The prosecution opposed the plea. According to the case statement, several members of a banned organisation gathered inside an auto-rickshaw garage in the Puranpara area of Uttarkhan on yesterday (12 September) night and were allegedly planning activities aimed at disrupting public peace and carrying out sabotage.

Acting on a tip-off, police conducted a raid at the garage and arrested the eight suspects. Police said another 25-30 unidentified people fled after sensing the presence of law enforcement. Sub-Inspector Mohammad Zahid Hossain of Uttarkhan Police Station filed the case under the Special Powers Act 1974.

Title: Missing Chhatra Dal leader's body recovered from Padma
Content:
The body of a Chattra Dal leader, who went missing after a bulkhead hit a pillar of Hardinge Bridge in Pabna's Ishwardi, was recovered from the Padma River around 35 hours later.

His body was recovered from the river near Char-Kurulia Akater Ghat in Lakshmikunda Union around 10:30am today (13 September), said Bheramara Upazila Nirbahi Officer Amirul Arafat and Bheramara Police Station Officer-in-Charge Zayedur Rahman.

The deceased was identified as Rakibuzzaman Rocky, 30, president of the Shailkupa municipal unit of Chattra Dal in Jhenaidah.

According to police, the bulkhead carrying 123 tourists reached Hardinge Bridge around 9:10pm on Friday (11 September), when strong currents pushed the rear of the vessel into Pillar No. 4 of the bridge.

Rocky, along with two other passengers, Liton and Wahab, fell into the river and went missing. Liton and Wahab were later rescued, but Rocky remained missing.

The group had travelled from Katla Garighat in Shailkupa to visit the Solaiman Shah shrine in Bheramara. The accident occurred while they were returning after visiting the shrine.

After Rocky went missing, the Bheramara upazila administration launched a search operation. Fire service teams from Ishwardi and Bheramara, along with river police, conducted searches in the Padma.

After nearly a day of searching, rescuers recovered Rocky's body from the river near Char-Kurulia Akater Ghat today.

The body was being prepared to be handed over to his family after completion of the necessary legal procedures.

Title: Xi proposes BRICS AI open-source zone to deepen Global South cooperation
Content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping today (13 September) proposed a BRICS AI Open Source Zone and a special economic zone partnership as part of a series of initiatives aimed at deepening cooperation among the expanded grouping of emerging economies.

Speaking at the closing session of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Xi said China would take the lead in establishing the BRICS AI Open Source Zone to promote cooperation on large language models, AI training and the development of an open AI ecosystem.

He also proposed a BRICS Special Economic Zone partnership and said China would host a BRICS Service Trade Forum next year to boost trade and investment ties among member countries.

Xi said the success of the "Greater BRICS Initiative" depends on laying a solid foundation for pragmatic cooperation, according to Xinhua.

"Greater BRICS countries should further cooperate, maintain the stability of industrial and supply chains and cultivate an integrated market," Xi told the summit.

BRICS has expanded beyond its original members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – to include Iran, Indonesia, Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates.

The grouping, founded nearly two decades ago, has sought to increase the influence of emerging economies and promote an alternative to a global order long dominated by the United States and other Western powers.

BRICS also has 10 partner countries across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East, further expanding its reach across the Global South.

Title: The real AI threat is losing control
Content:
A massive military supercomputer named AM (Aggressive Menace) is given total control over World War III. AM becomes trapped in its own rigid programming and develops a deep, algorithmic hatred for its creators. It wipes out humanity, leaving only five survivors whom it keeps alive eternally to torture inside its endless subterranean complex.

This is the plot of the famous 1967 post-apocalyptic short story by American writer Harlan Ellison 'I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream'. This is perhaps the most grotesque post-apocalyptic dystopian piece of literature regarding technology going rogue and wiping us out.

And this is precisely why when Jacob Coxon, a researcher who spent his prime helping to build the technology that may define this century at both OpenAI and Anthropic, said, "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade…This is not a marketing stunt… I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger", it began to blare alarm bells all over the world.

And when some of the prominent AI-researchers did not shun Coxon, instead expressed similar concerns, it was time to go in the full-panic mode. Who wouldn't be terrified when the CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei warned that within 6–12 months, AI agent swarms could potentially take over the entire internet with a persistent botnet, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed his statement?

Therefore, the question is no longer merely whether AI will take jobs, spread deepfakes or occasionally invent a court judgment. Those days are gone. It is now whether humanity is becoming Frankenstein and creating a technology it may eventually be unable to control.

When AI acts on its own

Current chatbots are not conscious. They do not secretly feel anger, fear or ambition. When Google engineer Blake Lemoine claimed in 2022 that LaMDA was sentient, Google and most AI researchers rejected his interpretation. Fluent language can imitate a mind without containing one. But consciousness is not necessary for catastrophe.

Research has shown that the Houthis in Yemen have used Claude to guide missiles toward Saudi Arabia. Russian operators have used it to run nearly an entire espionage operation, handling everything from phishing and setup to data theft against Ukrainian, European and diplomatic targets, including drone makers. Chinese operators who did not know Arabic used it to find out Uyghur dissents spread across Syria.

This is where Coxon's warning becomes more unsettling than the familiar "killer robot" caricature. His central concern is recursive self-improvement where an AI capable of conducting AI research, writing better code, designing experiments and improving the next generation of systems. Once machines begin accelerating the work required to build more capable machines, human institutions may struggle to understand, let alone supervise, the rate of change.

Coxon's central concern is recursive self-improvement where an AI capable of conducting AI research, writing better code, designing experiments and improving the next generation of systems. Once machines begin accelerating the work required to build more capable machines, human institutions may struggle to understand, let alone supervise, the rate of change.

Coxon told the BBC that researchers were "genuinely frightened", with some believing dangerous capabilities could emerge within two years. Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger went further, estimating a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade and acknowledging that researchers still lack a reliable solution to aligning superintelligence with human interests.

No government would approve a bridge with a 10% probability of collapse. No airline would fly an aircraft with a 10% chance of killing everyone aboard. Yet the most powerful corporations on Earth are racing to construct systems whose internal workings their own researchers admit they cannot fully explain.

The alarm is coming from the AI industry itself

Coxon is hardly a lone doomsday prophet. He is probably the lowest-profile one.

In 2023, more than 350 executives and researchers—including OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief executive Demis Hassabis, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei, and AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio—signed a one-sentence declaration, "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."

Hinton had already resigned from Google so he could speak more freely about the technology's dangers. More recently, Amodei has called for AI development to be slowed, independently monitored and subjected to enforceable international controls—a proposal reportedly supported in principle by Altman and Elon Musk.

In AI safety circles, P(doom) is the subjective probability assigned to AI causing human extinction or irreversible disempowerment, with a major survey of AI researchers finding a mean estimate of 14.4% and a median of 5%.

Individual expert estimates align exactly with the provided data, as Roman Yampolskiy predicts a 99.9% chance of AI-driven human extinction, Paul Christiano places his estimate at 50%, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei estimates the risk between 10% and 25%. Furthermore, Turing Award laureates Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton assign probabilities of roughly 20% and 10% to 20%.

Is the apocalypse also a sales pitch?

The sceptics have a serious case too.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has called the idea that AI will end humanity "complete nonsense". Meta's Yann LeCun argues that extinction narratives anthropomorphise software, treating mathematical optimisation as though it automatically produces a creature hungry for domination.

Others see regulatory capture. If Anthropic and OpenAI persuade governments that only giant, heavily regulated laboratories can safely build advanced AI, smaller competitors and open-source developers could be squeezed out. Doom, under this interpretation, becomes product marketing: our machines are so powerful that only we can be trusted with them.

Researchers including Timnit Gebru and Andrew Ng also warn that spectacular extinction stories can distract from harms already here—discrimination, surveillance, labour displacement, deepfakes, energy consumption and confidently fabricated information.

These criticisms matter. AI companies should not be allowed to write regulations that conveniently entrench their dominance. Nor should speculative catastrophe make today's victims invisible.

Let us go back to the short story once again. The story ends as an anguished, despairing narrator states that he has no mouth, yet he must scream. We still have our mouths, so why not start screaming about AI regulation and safety now?
Author: Shadique Mahbub Islam

Title: Dengue: 6 more deaths, 1,561 hospitalised in 24 hours
Content:
Six more people have died from dengue while 1,561 new patients were hospitalised across Bangladesh in the 24 hours to today (13 September), taking the country's dengue death toll to 149 this year.

The latest figures were released by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) through its Health Emergency Operation Centre and Control Room.

Of the six deaths recorded during the latest 24-hour period, two were reported in Chattogram Division, two in Khulna Division, and one each in Dhaka and Mymensingh divisions.

Meanwhile, 1,394 dengue patients were discharged from hospitals during the period, taking the total number of recoveries this year to 48,093.

The cumulative number of dengue cases reported nationwide has now reached 51,837, according to DGHS data.

Title: Journalist killed in Faridpur road accident
Content:
A journalist was killed and another person was injured in a head-on collision between a bus and a motorcycle in Bhanga upazila of Faridpur today (13 September).

The accident occurred around noon in the Munsurabad area on the Dhaka-Khulna highway, police said.

The deceased was identified as Kazi Ashraf, Lohagara upazila correspondent for Daily Bhorer Darpan. The injured person, identified as Anik, was travelling on the motorcycle with him.

According to police, Ashraf and Anik were travelling towards Dhaka from Narail on a motorcycle. When they reached the Munsurabad bus stand area, a Dola Paribahan bus coming from the opposite direction collided head-on with the motorcycle, leaving both riders critically injured.

Both were critically injured in the accident.

Highway police rescued and took them to Bhanga Upazila Health Complex. As Ashraf's condition deteriorated, he was transferred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital where doctors declared him dead.

Police said legal proceedings in connection with the accident are underway.

Title: BRICS without Bangladesh: Principled stand or opportunity lost?
Content:
'They saw it through a plurilateral prism when we saw a bilateral slight'

M Humayun Kabir, former ambassador

BRICS is a plurilateral organisation. It is where a country such as Bangladesh has, in effect, been invited under a degree of pressure that this term comes into use — plurilateral. And my sense is that it is precisely in this bilateral-cum-plurilateral space that some of our difficulty lies. Take the fact that India invited our head of government as the chair of BIMSTEC.

The BIMSTEC chair, after all, may at any given time be Bangladesh, as it may be under SAARC. So our head of government was invited in that capacity, under the BIMSTEC-chair designation. From their side, technically, that is how they regarded our Prime Minister within the context of that conference or summit.

From our side, we took the view that they had invited the BIMSTEC chair, i.e. the office-holder, and not our Prime Minister as such. That is how we framed it where our Prime Minister was concerned. And it is because the framing on the two sides was somewhat different that, to my mind, this confusion arose and it is out of that confusion that things ended up as they did.

Now, had we gone, what might have come of it? There is something new taking shape there, though the final outcome I have not yet seen. What they are seeking is to deepen cooperation and, in that connection, to bring about a degree of digital-currency alignment, while increasing the use of each country's own currency.

In other words, if you do business in India, you may do it in the Indian currency; in China, in the Chinese currency. So they are attempting to build an alternative economic, or financial, structure. For a country like ours—one that works with everyone and carries a certain exposure, with trade and commerce running to all 11 of these member states—this matters.

In that situation, were we able to plug into this financial network, or something of the kind, our leverage would rise somewhat. I would then no longer have to worry that, having taken a nuclear power plant from Russia, we might be hit with American sanctions, because if my trade with Russia is conducted in taka or in roubles, sanctions imposed through the dollar lose much of their bite.

Then there is the point that was made about resolving matters through dialogue and diplomacy. For Bangladesh this holds especially true, because as a relatively small country, we always carry this kind of security concern.

In that light, if a general principle takes hold that everyone wishes to settle disputes through dialogue and diplomacy, and accepts as much, then there is an advantage in it for us.

And the third point is that the heads of state and government of 11 countries were present there. Our presence, therefore, could have created the opportunity to interact, and to share our thoughts and priorities, and so on. That carries a diplomatic value of its own. But since we were not there, we did not get that opportunity.

So, in that respect, attending would have been the better course. Even so, we tried to send a message: that we now have a spine — that we will not simply go wherever, and however, you wish. The requisite level of dignity and honour must be extended to us; only then do we wish to engage. That is the message that went out from our side.

Yes, in terms of the message, 'we are strong', we did genuinely demonstrate that Bangladesh is no longer the docile, compliant Bangladesh of old. That message has been delivered. The question now is how much we gained in material terms, and that remains to be seen.

And it seems to me that the Indians viewed the matter through a multilateral, or plurilateral, prism, whereas we viewed it from a bilateral angle. That mismatch bred the confusion.

M Humayun Kabir is a former ambassador and President and CEO of the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute (BEI).

'Not going now is temporary, joining BRICS ought to be our top priority'

Maj General (Rtd) Fazle Elahi Akbar, security expert

For Bangladesh, increasing cooperation and dialogue with the BRICS countries is very important, because for all these years our focus has been India-centric — we sat within a South Asia-centric frame. We were never especially serious about multilateralism; even with the OIC our engagement was minimal. Our day-to-day affairs — the economy, diplomacy, even national security, trade and transit — everything was South Asia-centric.

Because we remained South Asia-centric and India-centric for so long, India came to take us almost entirely for granted; and it reached the point where we were gradually losing our sovereign autonomy. From that perspective, we needed to break out of it. We are trying to do so now — but merely breaking out is not enough unless we open other windows. BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation are exactly the windows we ought to jump into; and, if required, the OIC platform is very much a format to work through as well.

The more windows we have, the less the pressure from any one bloc or any one country. This, in fact, is how smaller countries survive — they keep their options open and stay in charge of their own course. They do not allow themselves to be sucked into a single black hole; and we were in that black hole for the last 16 years, under the previous fascist regime. So joining BRICS is now vitally important.

As to why we did not go to Delhi — why the invitation was not accepted — I think our state minister for foreign affairs has explained it amply. He was invited as the chair of BIMSTEC, not as Prime Minister, of course; and they also attached certain conditions. Those conditions we know: the return of the fascist leader who is in exile there, having been legally convicted, and likewise the killers of Hadi, who have also been in hiding. This has, in truth, been the pattern for a very long time — anyone wanted in Bangladesh takes shelter there. We have an extradition treaty, and even that has not been reciprocated, whereas in the past, even under the fascist regime, we complied on more than one occasion, several times over, to return their wanted persons into their custody.

Not going now is a temporary matter. But diplomatically, and for Bangladesh's foreign policy, joining BRICS and the SCO ought to be our top priority. We know that even in Hasina's day — in the time of fascism — the government of Bangladesh had applied; and despite our good relations with our neighbour, it was India that vetoed our entry. So we must now make the endeavour once again — to join BRICS, and the SCO as well. If not directly, then we must first become an observer and then, step by step, move into full membership, because this opens avenues to a new economic bloc and new opportunities for trade, for exchange, for technology, for everything.

Both these organisations are, in effect, Russia- and China-dominated; and in a changed, globalised world, this is what we should be looking towards — rather than remaining wholly India-centric, or centred on any single power.

Maj Gen (retd) Fazle Elahi Akbar is Chairman of the Foundation for Strategic and Development Studies (FSDS).

'BRICS is a separate matter, Bangladesh should have gone'

Dr Dilara Choudhury, academic

BRICS is a multilateral organisation. It has many members — around 11 countries, I believe — and these countries cooperate on trade, investment and economic matters. There is no security-pact dimension to it at all.

So the strain over Hasina — set that aside; that is a bilateral problem with India. What is the reason for staying away on India's account? This is not a bilateral issue; it is not a quarrel with India. Declining a bilateral visit to India because of the ongoing tension is one thing — but BRICS is an entirely separate matter. BRICS is a multilateral organisation, and I believe Bangladesh ought to have attended.

For Bangladesh, joining all these multilateral organisations is vital, because the country's economic development depends on trade and investment, and multilateral forums are precisely where that is advanced. So why did we not go? I see no justification for staying away simply because of the strain with India.

In the world now taking shape — as the American-led order gradually declines — bodies of this kind are especially important for the Global South, for what we call the Global Development Initiative. We will need cooperation with these countries on a range of economic issues, so we ought to join the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

Why? Because Bangladesh has been making this mistake from the very start. We never joined ASEAN — and we certainly should have, from the beginning. Now we cannot get into ASEAN at all. Our foreign policy was so India-centric that we simply assumed India was our friend, that India would solve all our problems, that staying close to India would deliver us enormous development. That India-centric mindset led us into many mistakes in the past. Now an opportunity has come — so why on earth would we let it slip?

Dr Dilara Choudhury served as a Professor and Chair of the Department of Government and Politics at Jahangirnagar University.

'It is just as well the PM did not go, but the road must stay open'

Dr Parvez Karim Abbasi, academic

There is no point pretending, or telling ourselves, that everything in the Bangladesh-India relationship is sweet and harmonious. From day one after this new elected government took office, there have been push-ins across the West Bengal border, and that many Awami League leaders now in India, convicted absconders before our own courts, have been running all manner of propaganda. Most recently, around 5 August, there were Sheikh Hasina's remarks and the publicity given to them at the Foreign Correspondents' Club. Naturally, then, there is a trust deficit between the two governments. There is the issue of border killings, and a lingering question over the renewal of the water treaty.

So the question is whether the Prime Minister ought to have gone. The event has already taken place, so we can discuss it academically. My personal view is that, for a multilateral event convened at very short notice, and with so many outstanding problems, it is just as well that he did not go. It is not as though Bangladesh is saying we have broken off all contact with India. In future, once adequate diplomatic preparation and homework have been done, a visit between the two heads of government can certainly take place; that road must be kept open, because India is our neighbour and the two countries are, in many respects, interdependent.

But one question does remain. It is perfectly fine for the Prime Minister not to go — yet many countries sent their foreign ministers. Our own foreign minister is a seasoned diplomat; had he gone, there would have been a great deal of engagement to be had. Where else would you find so large a forum? BRICS has a concentrated focus on the Global South. In such a setting we might have met President Xi Jinping, or Vladimir Putin — Russia, after all, is our second-largest lender, for the Rooppur nuclear plant. There is South Africa, home to many Bangladeshi expatriates; Anwar Ibrahim; the Indonesian president; the UAE crown prince; and, in Saudi Arabia, our own foreign minister. There were opportunities for a great many side meetings.

And since we hold the BIMSTEC chair, the responsibility to raise our standing in global forums falls on Bangladesh. Many are asking what Bangladesh gained by not going. One gain could be the signal it sends to India: that, since we now speak of "Bangladesh First," when we do engage, our self-respect must remain intact, and we should go only in a conducive, enabling and friendly environment, with the groundwork for our outstanding issues laid down in advance.

On the other hand, we are living through an unstable period. The United States — the sole superpower — is gradually facing challenges on many fronts: economically, in trade, in investment, in technology, even in military capability. No one is entirely certain which way the global trend will turn; for the next 10 to 20 years there will be a transition, a period of global instability. At such a time Bangladesh ought to hedge and pursue multiple engagements.

We talk of bilateral free-trade agreements and of entering regional ones, yet ASEAN has closed its door to us. LDC graduation will come in another two years, and we will then lose the duty-free, quota-free access we now enjoy. We must secure our energy supplies, move towards renewables — for which rare earths are needed — and seek out new export markets. At this summit, at least the groundwork for all this could have begun. So I support the Prime Minister not going: there has not yet been adequate time, there is a trust deficit, and there is unease among the public. But we could still have sent the foreign minister, or a capable state minister.

Dr Parvez Karim Abbasi is an Assistant Professor of Economics at East West University, Dhaka, and Executive Director of the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS).

'Little to gain, little to lose'

Md Tanvir Habib, academic

Bangladesh is not a current member of BRICS; it has been clear for some time that India is unwilling to admit other regional nations as equal members, because that would cut against its idea of control over South Asia.

Given that Bangladesh is not a prospective member, the visit would not have gained the Prime Minister, or the country, a great deal to begin with — beyond showing his face and mingling with a number of global leaders. So I do not think the decision carries major implications for Bangladesh. In bilateral terms, the Prime Minister has already made his maiden visits to Malaysia and to China; on the China front the relationship is strong, and he enjoys a good working relationship with the United States and others. Diplomacy is multi-pronged and multi-tiered, and that too will have factored into his calculation of whether joining, or not joining, BRICS carries any real consequence. Had some BRICS members been keen to see Bangladesh join, that might have made a difference — but Bangladesh already has good relations, on its own account, with the likes of Iran and Saudi Arabia.

BRICS has become interesting of late, in that it wants — with Russian assistance — to build a de-dollarised system. So the Prime Minister's staying away is, in a sense, a signal: that Bangladesh is not, at this moment, eager to enter arrangements that are geopolitically contentious. It is the same caution we saw over the Mecca Pact discussions earlier; Bangladesh is following a similarly careful path.

Certainly, attending the summit would have given him the chance to speak to the Indian political leadership and to other global leaders, and it is the bilateral meetings on the sidelines of such events that tend to be the real avenues for a diplomatic breakthrough. With the Indians, it might well have produced one. But before any breakthrough, Bangladesh had to convey its own requirements to India — and those requirements not being met was, I think, a key reason the Prime Minister chose not to go in the first place.

As for the other countries, I do not foresee any significant degradation. We have very good bilateral relations right across the group. With Russia, ties are not at any low ebb — they remain structured and continue in a routine manner. With China, the relationship is moving to a much higher plane, in bilateral trust and in trade, with Xi Jinping speaking of a more cultural, more civilisational approach. With the United States we have a historically good relationship, and with Europe a strong working one. The government has recently signed trade and framework agreements with South Korea, Japan and Australia, and work with the European Union is ongoing. So with every actor, inside BRICS and beyond it, Bangladesh has robust bilateral relations; the summit will not significantly affect them.

And I think every one of these countries would understand why the Prime Minister did not go — because he cannot visit unless something is forthcoming for him. His diplomatic success required a measure of compromise from the Indians, and the absence of that is the major reason he stayed away.

Md Tanvir Habib is an Assistant Professor at the Department of International Relations at the University of Dhaka.

Title: No alternative to boosting police cyber capacity: IGP
Content:
There is no alternative to strengthening the skills and capabilities of police personnel to combat cybercrime, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md Ali Hossain Fakir said today (13 September).

"Criminals are misusing technology to commit cyber fraud, online financial crimes, data theft, hacking, online harassment and digital extortion," he said while inaugurating a Training of Trainers course on cybercrime case investigation at Police Staff College Bangladesh in Mirpur.

The IGP said emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, deepfakes, encrypted communication and cloud computing are creating new challenges for law enforcement agencies alongside new opportunities.

He said policing methods need to evolve to address the growing threat of cybercrime, making stronger investigative capabilities essential for modern law enforcement.

Addressing the participating officers, Ali Hossain Fakir said the course would help them develop both technical and training skills.

"The knowledge and skills gained through the training must be shared with other investigators. If you effectively train other investigators, the number of cybercrime case investigators in the police force will increase many times over," he said.

The IGP also called for regular training programmes of this kind and for training materials and modules to be updated regularly.

Police Staff College Bangladesh organised the 10-day course at the initiative of the Training Branch of Police Headquarters.

A total of 332 police officers will participate in the training course in phases. They will later train field-level investigators handling cybercrime cases.

Title: President urges stronger Bangladesh-Pakistan trade and education ties
Content:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir today (13 September) called for stronger cooperation between Bangladesh and Pakistan in trade, investment, air connectivity, education, training and other areas of mutual interest.

He made the call when Pakistan High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haider paid a courtesy call on the president at Bangabhaban.

During the meeting, the high commissioner reiterated an invitation from Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari for Mirza Fakhrul to visit Pakistan. The president thanked him for the invitation and invited his Pakistani counterpart to visit Bangladesh at a convenient time.

The president said Pakistan is an important partner of Bangladesh in various sectors and that expanding bilateral trade and economic activities would benefit people in both countries.

He stressed the need to increase contacts between businesses and entrepreneurs and explore new trade opportunities.

Mirza Fakhrul said Pakistani ready-made garments, particularly women's clothing, are popular in Bangladesh. He called for exploring opportunities to import Pakistani garments, cotton yarn and other products while working towards a more balanced trade relationship.

The Pakistani high commissioner said a trade fair featuring Pakistani products would be held in Dhaka in October and invited Bangladesh to organise a similar fair in Pakistan featuring Bangladeshi products.

He also said Pakistani entrepreneurs were interested in joint ventures to manufacture footballs and other sports equipment.

Referring to the resumption of direct air connectivity between Dhaka and Karachi this year, Imran Haider said the service was helping boost bilateral trade, medical tourism and people-to-people contacts. He stressed the need to increase the number of flights.

The high commissioner praised the quality of Bangladeshi tea and called for increasing tea exports to Pakistan by taking advantage of the existing duty-free facility in the Pakistani market.

The president said there was also significant potential to increase exports of Bangladeshi ceramics, betel leaves, agricultural products, pharmaceuticals and other quality goods to Pakistan.

He stressed the need for closer communication between relevant authorities and business communities in both countries to realise these opportunities.

Imran Haider said Pakistan attaches great importance to its relations with Bangladesh and is working to strengthen bilateral trade, investment and cooperation.

The president also emphasised expanding training exchanges between members of the two countries' armed forces and civil administrations, as well as opportunities for higher education in science, engineering, technology and medicine.

The high commissioner sought the president's cooperation in carrying out his diplomatic responsibilities in Bangladesh.

Mirza Fakhrul assured him of full cooperation and expressed hope that increased trade, education, culture, training and people-to-people contacts would make bilateral relations more productive and multifaceted.

Senior officials from the President's Office, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and relevant government agencies were present at the meeting.

Title: We have not been vindictive, nor do we want to be: Law minister
Content:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said the government has not acted vindictively and has no intention of doing so, while stressing the need for impartial policing and accountability.

"We will continue working under the prime minister's guidance to ensure good governance for the people of Bangladesh," he said at an exchange meeting at the Satkhira deputy commissioner's office at 10am today (13 September).

The meeting discussed law and order, corruption, drug control, good governance and accountability in the district.

The minister said the police force had previously been turned into a partisan institution and that the government had to restore officers' morale and confidence after August 2024.

"The police force had been turned into a partisan force. After August 2024, we had to restore their morale and courage. They are now trying to work impartially and are continuing to do so," he said.

On politically motivated cases, the minister said police had previously acted as complainants in cases intended to harass political opponents.

"In the past, police used to be the complainants in politically motivated harassment cases. Since 5 August, there has not been a single example of police filing such a politically motivated case as complainants," he said.

He added that police could not refuse to accept a case filed by an individual, but would examine its merits.

"But if an individual files a case, police cannot refuse to accept it. Police will examine the matter. We have now reached this balance. There are no more false or fabricated cases like before," he said.

On drug control, Asaduzzaman said narcotics were entering Bangladesh from neighbouring countries and warned that the issue could not be addressed by focusing only on domestic offenders.

"It is not only a handful of people in our country who are involved in drugs; consignments of narcotics are also coming from neighbouring countries," he said.

He also called for action against both financial and intellectual forms of corruption. "Corruption takes two forms — financial and intellectual. We have to stop both," he said.

The minister said the government was taking a similar stance against political criminalisation.

"Just as we are speaking out against drugs, we are also speaking out against political criminalisation.

We do not want to tolerate any form of political criminality," he said.

Title: Maulana Faruqi murder case: Charge framing set for 25 October
Content:
A Dhaka court has set 25 October for the hearing on the framing of charges against the accused in the murder case of Islami Front leader and television presenter Nurul Islam Faruqi.

Dhaka Ninth Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge Mahmudul Islam fixed the date today (13 September) after defence lawyers sought more time to prepare for the hearing.

Abdul Karim, bench assistant of the court, confirmed the matter.

Earlier, on 5 November 2024, CID Additional Superintendent of Police KM Abul Kashem, also the case's investigation officer, submitted a charge sheet against seven people and recommended the discharge of 12 others.

The charge-sheeted accused are Hadisur Rahman alias Sagar, Abdullah Al Tasnim Nahid, Rafiqul Islam Fardin, Abu Raihan Mahmud Abdul Hadi, Mahmud Ibn Bashar and Ratan Chowdhury alias Engineer Ripon alias Rakibul Islam Riaz.

Bashar and Rafiqul are absconding, and arrest warrants have been issued against them. Hadisur is in jail, while the other three accused are out on bail.

According to the case documents, a group of men rang the doorbell of Faruqi's residence at around 7pm on 27 August 2014.

Two men entered the house and sat with Faruqi in the drawing room, followed by six or seven others.

When Faruqi's cousin Maruf Hossain went inside to bring chairs, he returned to find the attackers holding a pistol and a machete to Faruqi's head.

The attackers then tied up those inside the house and hacked Faruqi to death, according to the case documents.

His son Faisal Faruqi later filed a murder case with Sher-e-Bangla Nagar Police Station against eight to 10 unidentified people.

Faruqi presented Channel i's Islamic programmes Kafela and Shantir Pothe, as well as My TV's live programme Sotyer Sondhane.

He was also international secretary of Ahle Sunnat Wal Jamaat Bangladesh and khatib of the Supreme Court Jame Mosque.

Title: Putul's appointment a 'shame' for international organisations: Humaiun Kobir
Content:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir has described the appointment of recently resigned Saima Wazed Putul to a senior position at the World Health Organization (WHO) as "very unfortunate", alleging that she lacked the qualifications, experience and expertise required for such a high-level post.

"It was not a surprise. Someone without any credible qualification, any credible expertise, just because she happens to be the daughter of (former PM) so-and-so, was given the appointment," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs questioning the appointment.

The state minister described the appointment of Putul, daughter of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, as regional director for Southeast Asia as a "shame" for international organisations and stressed the need for greater seriousness and scrutiny in selecting people for senior positions.

"You need people who can lead the organisation. We need to be very serious about these appointments," Kobir said.

The state minister said Bangladesh would support a candidate with appropriate qualifications in future, mentioning a candidate from the Maldives who, he said, has a good track record and strong credentials.

"We hope that in the near future the organisation will be led by competent people," he said.

He said international organisations should not appoint individuals simply because they are connected to a particular political family or regime.

"People should not be appointed simply on the grounds of being connected to a family or a regime," he said, adding that such organisations have important institutional responsibilities and their leadership should have the necessary expertise and credentials.

Referring to the WHO, Kobir said the organisation is highly important and therefore requires people with appropriate professional expertise to lead it.

"If you put any kind of unqualified people in those positions, the outcome for the region and the world is not going to be good," he said.

The state minister also referred to a candidate from the Maldives, saying he hoped that a person with stronger credentials would be selected for the position in the future.

Kobir said that if irregularities or corruption were involved in appointments, such matters would eventually come to light.

He reiterated that the credibility, experience and expertise of candidates should be carefully examined before making appointments to senior positions in international organisations.

"Someone without credible qualifications, experience and expertise should not be appointed to such a high-level position," he said.

He said allegations of corruption, manipulation and concealment of information surrounding such appointments would eventually come to light. "The smell of corruption can never be suppressed; it will eventually come out," Kobir said.

Referring to the WHO, Kobir said the organisation plays a crucial role in global public health, particularly recalling its importance during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Asked how many countries the government is working with to recover the huge amount of money allegedly siphoned out of Bangladesh, Kobir said the government is working with international partners to bring back laundered assets and funds.

"We are working with international partners to recover the assets and money that have been siphoned out," he said.

He said Bangladesh has already established a partnership with the United Kingdom in this regard.

The government is also in discussions with countries that have legal and forensic expertise to help trace and recover the assets, he said.

"We are determined to bring back the people's stolen money and assets through legal and diplomatic processes," Kobir said.

He said the recovered assets should be used for the welfare of people rather than ending up in the pockets of individuals.
