Title: Electrical, electronics exports hit record growth amid rising EU compliance hurdles
Content:
Bangladesh's electrical and electronics exports are gaining momentum, with shipments of electrical products rising nearly 24% in FY2025-26, even as manufacturers seek to keep pace with increasingly demanding sustainability, traceability, and product-compliance requirements in the European Union.

According to the latest Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data, exports of electrical products increased 23.82% from $166.52 million a year earlier, reaching a record $206.19 million.

The category was the largest earner among engineering products, surpassing bicycles, which earned $151.04 million, up 29.71%.

Engineering exports overall rose 21.77% to $652.15 million, underscoring the growing contribution of electrical and electronics products to Bangladesh's export diversification.

The growth comes as the European Union introduces new sustainability requirements through its Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) and Digital Product Passport (DPP) framework.

The ESPR entered into force in July 2024, introducing requirements for DPPs and product durability, as well as a ban on destroying certain unsold goods.

The ESPR does not immediately require every electronic product to carry a DPP. Instead, product-specific requirements are being introduced through delegated acts. Where applicable, manufacturers will need to provide information on materials, components, environmental characteristics, durability and repairability.

For Bangladesh, this could prove challenging as manufacturers remain dependent on imported components and raw materials, making supply-chain traceability more difficult.

Industry races to prepare

Mohammad Ali, senior vice-president of the Bangladesh Electrical Merchandise Manufacturers Association (Bemma), said the association was preparing its members through workshops covering product origin, warranties, after-sales service, repairability, and documentation.

"We are already working on a product basis, product origin, product warranty, and after-sales service – whether a product is repairable or not," he said.

But the sector still lacks adequate testing infrastructure, Ali said.

Bemma has approached the commerce and industries ministries several times for support in establishing facilities capable of testing electrical products against European and other Western-market standards.

"For the electrical sector, we think there should be an individual common facility centre," he said.

Such a facility could particularly benefit smaller manufacturers that are beginning to explore export markets.

Imported inputs pose traceability challenge

Supply-chain traceability remains another hurdle, particularly because many manufacturers source components and raw materials from China and Vietnam.

"Most of the raw materials we are importing are from China or Vietnam. In that case, it is actually totally difficult to identify the carbon footprint," Ali said.

Bemma members that have traditionally focused on the domestic market face a steeper learning curve as they move towards exports, he said.

Walton says it can adapt

For leading exporter Walton, adapting to changing international standards is not new.

Syed Al Imran, executive director of Walton Hi-Tech Industries, said the company had repeatedly upgraded its systems as overseas requirements changed, citing the transition from manual registration to the digital Registered Exporter (REX) system and changes in European energy-efficiency ratings.

"When A+++ changed to A, B, C, D and E, Walton instantly upgraded," Al Imran said.

He attributed the company's ability to respond quickly partly to its vertical integration, with Walton manufacturing many of its own parts and components.

Another advantage is Walton's NUSDAT-UTS laboratory, which provides testing and certification services, including CB certificates, he said.

Walton previously had to send refrigerators to India for testing, but NUSDAT-UTS reports are now accepted for the relevant Indian star-rating process, eliminating the need to send products abroad, Al Imran said.

When new requirements emerge, Walton can work with NUSDAT-UTS and partner laboratories to identify necessary upgrades and implement them, he added.

Vision prepares for European entry

PRAN-RFL Group's Vision Electronics is also preparing to enter the European market.

The company currently exports across South Asia, Southeast Asia, Oceania and Africa, while Europe remains a strategic target.

For refrigerators and air conditioners, Vision is redesigning its product architecture to meet European quality, safety and eco-design requirements. It has already secured G-Mark certification for its air-conditioner line for the Middle East.

The company is integrating ERP systems to track raw-material origins, chemical compliance and sub-assembly batches. It is also digitising bills of materials and working with consultants to measure Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions at its Habiganj and Danga industrial parks.

Its R&D team is moving towards modular PCB designs and quick-release compressor and fan-motor mounts to facilitate repairs and component replacement.

Vision is also replacing some non-recyclable composite plastics with single-grade polymers such as ABS and HIPS, while planning for the long-term availability of key spare parts.

Policy support needed

Bemma says stronger government support is needed to help the broader industry compete internationally.

Ali called for incentives, back-to-back letters of credit and duty relief on imported raw materials, similar to support mechanisms available to the garment sector.

"If we get this kind of government backup in the electrical sector, I think electrical and electronics can be the most promising sector over the next 10 years, even more promising than RMG," he said.

The senior vice-president also urged the commerce, industries and finance ministries to hold sector-specific discussions with electrical manufacturers.

A more immediate regulatory deadline concerns batteries. Under the EU Batteries Regulation, an electronic battery passport will be mandatory from 18 February 2027 for electric-vehicle batteries, industrial batteries above 2kWh and light means of transport batteries placed on the EU market.

For Bangladesh's rapidly expanding electrical and electronics industry, the challenge is moving beyond producing competitive goods to being able to prove how they are made, tested, sourced and repaired.

Bangladesh currently exports a range of consumer electronics and appliances, including televisions, refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners, as well as electrical equipment such as power transformers, electric cables and insulated wires, switches, sockets, circuit breakers and LED lighting solutions.

The export basket also includes rechargeable batteries, transistors and semiconductor devices, along with eco-friendly bicycles and other light mechanical components.

With electrical exports growing at a double-digit rate, manufacturers that build these capabilities early could be better positioned to turn the sector's export growth into a sustained foothold in major global markets.

Title: Ten banks hold over 72% of Tk6 lakh cr defaulted loans
Content:
Just 10 of the country's 61 banks accounted for more than 72% of the banking sector's total non-performing loans (NPLs), commonly known as defaulted loans, at the end of June.

According to the latest data from the Bangladesh Bank, total NPLs in the banking sector stood at Tk6,06,555 crore at the end of June, equivalent to 32.78% of total defaulted loans. In other words, nearly Tk33 out of every Tk100 lent by banks was classified as non-performing.

NPLs stood at Tk5,88,704 crore at the end of March, meaning defaulted loans increased by around Tk17,851 crore in three months.

The 10 weak banks had around Tk4,39,527 crore in NPLs at the end of June. This means nearly three-quarters of the banking sector's NPLs were concentrated in just one-sixth of its banks.

The figures show that the banking sector's crisis has not affected all lenders equally. Rather, a handful of banks have become particularly vulnerable after years of irregularities, weak credit management, lending to influential borrowers, inadequate monitoring of loan utilisation and failures in recovery.

The quality of assets at these banks has deteriorated rapidly, particularly as a portion of large corporate loans has remained unpaid for years. Many loans have eventually become classified as non-performing even after being rescheduled or restructured, suggesting that measures to keep loan classifications apparently under control have failed to resolve the underlying problems.

Asset quality deteriorates sharply

The Bangladesh Bank's latest assessment also shows a significant deterioration in the quality of bank assets.

According to the central bank's Financial Stability Report 2025, the NPL ratio in the banking sector rose to 30.60% at the end of December 2025 from 20.20% a year earlier.

The volume of defaulted loans increased further during the first six months of this year, surpassing Tk6 lakh crore by June. The surge is putting additional pressure on banks' capital, provisioning requirements and profitability.

The Bangladesh Bank has already taken several measures to reduce NPLs, including strengthening loan recovery, tightening supervision of credit management and assessing the quality of banks' assets.

It is also identifying weak banks and taking steps towards their reform, merger and restructuring.

The World Bank has also identified weaknesses in Bangladesh's banking sector as a major economic risk. In a report published in June, the multilateral lender said weak corporate governance, regulatory weaknesses and related-party lending had placed significant pressure on the banking sector.

The World Bank said the NPL ratio in Bangladesh's banking sector stood at 32.6% at the end of March 2026, compared with a South Asian average of 7.9%.

The banking sector represents around 90% of the assets of Bangladesh's overall financial sector, according to the World Bank. As a result, weakness in banks' financial positions affects not only depositors and lenders but also investment, business activity, employment and overall economic growth.

Ten banks account for most defaulted loans

Private-sector Islami Bank had the highest volume of NPLs at Tk98,914 crore at the end of June, equivalent to 52.15% of its total loans.

A large portion of the bank's defaulted loans is associated with S Alam Group. The group took control of the bank in 2017, and a large portion of the loans taken by the group had become non-performing by the time the Awami League government fell in 2024.

State-owned Janata Bank had the second-highest volume of NPLs at Tk75,728 crore, representing 75.05% of its total loans.

Beximco Group, associated with former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's adviser Salman F Rahman, is among the bank's largest defaulters. S Alam Group and AnonTex are also major defaulters.

The merged banks are in the worst position in terms of their NPL ratios. First Security Islami Bank had the highest ratio at 97.08%, followed by Union Bank at 96.78%, Social Islami Bank at 78.15% and Exim Bank at 70.81%.

Major defaulters at these banks include S Alam Group, Beximco, Nassa Group and Sikder Group, among several other groups.

National Bank had an NPL ratio of 65.74%, while the ratios at IFIC Bank and AB Bank stood at 63.38% and 56.40%, respectively.

State-owned Agrani Bank had an NPL ratio of 43.98%. Its major defaulters include Judge Bhuiyan Group, Zakia Group, Muhib Steel and Ship Recycling, Moon Group and several other companies.

A Bangladesh Bank executive director told The Business Standard that the crisis could not be resolved simply by rescheduling or restructuring loans again.

"The actual condition of long-overdue loans must be determined, action must be taken against those responsible, and effective measures must be taken for speedy recovery," he said.

The official also stressed the need to assess borrowers' repayment capacity before extending new loans, monitor the use of loan proceeds and strengthen risk controls for large borrowers.

Otherwise, the executive director warned, the crisis in a handful of banks could gradually create greater pressure across the entire banking system.

Title: Money gets cheaper, yet takers are hard to get
Content:
Money is getting cheaper in Bangladesh, but the falling cost of credit reflects a sluggish economy rather than a recovery.

Interest rates have steadily declined as banks accumulate vast excess liquidity amid weak credit demand. Simultaneously, Bangladesh Bank has shifted towards an easier monetary stance by cutting its benchmark policy rate, placing further downward pressure on money-market yields.

Healthy commercial banks have trimmed both lending and deposit rates by 1-2 percentage points in recent months. This comes as private-sector credit growth dropped to 4.47% in June – the lowest level in 33 years. Average deposit rates at most institutions now hover between 7% and 8%, while lending rates range from 10% to 11%. With minimal credit demand from businesses, banks have piled into government securities, driving yields on all Treasury bills and bonds down into single digits.

By June 2026, total excess liquidity in the banking sector surged by 39.40% year-on-year to exceed Tk4 lakh crore. The foreign-exchange market shows a similar imbalance: robust dollar inflows and weak import demand have created upward pressure on the taka. To prevent sharp currency appreciation and protect exporters and remitters, the central bank resumed dollar purchases from commercial banks on 1 September, buying $50 million at Tk122.75 – well above market remittance rates of Tk122.30-122.60. Gross foreign-exchange reserves subsequently rose by nearly $5 billion over the year, reaching $36.33 billion by 3 September.

This rate decline occurs against a fragile macroeconomic backdrop marked by sluggish growth, persistent inflation, and high unemployment, raising fears of stagflation. Although inflation eased to 8.26% in August, it remains comfortably above the government's 7.5% target for FY27. Because prices were already elevated last year, this ongoing inflation compounds a high baseline, keeping consumer prices uncomfortably high.

In response, Bangladesh Bank is injecting liquidity via stimulus measures and planning further monetary easing to reignite investment. However, economists and bankers warn that injecting liquidity without addressing structural bottlenecks will fail to revive real demand and could aggravate inflation.

Why is Bangladesh Bank cutting rates? In July, Bangladesh Bank lowered its policy rate by 50 basis points to 9.5% to spur private investment. This marked a clear departure from the tight monetary stance maintained since 2022, during which the policy rate was gradually raised from 5% to 10% and kept there for nearly two years from October 2024.

"Our earlier assumption was that raising the policy rate would make money expensive, reduce liquidity, and curb inflation," a senior Bangladesh Bank executive said on condition of anonymity. "However, that mechanism failed in our context. Despite keeping the rate high for two years, inflation remained stubborn."

The official added that elevated interest rates instead drove up corporate financing and production costs, which firms passed directly to consumers. "We are now testing a supply-side strategy: lower the policy rate to reduce production and import costs. If supply expands and unit costs fall, prices should moderate."

Easier money risks fueling inflation Md Ezazul Islam, Director General of the Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management, argues that lower interest rates are a symptom of economic paralysis. "Economic activity remains constrained by gas and electricity shortages, the lingering aftershocks of recent political instability, and global uncertainty," Islam noted.

While deposit growth has remained steady, banks cannot generate matching credit due to absent loan demand. "Banks naturally redirect excess funds into government Treasury bills and bonds. With heavy government borrowing and intense competition among banks for these safe assets, yields drop. That is basic market dynamics," Islam said, adding that the trend will persist until private credit demand rebounds.

Islam cautioned that monetary easing without productive capacity risks worsening inflation. "Job creation and investment are primarily fiscal responsibilities. If the government wants to stimulate the economy, it must deploy fiscal tools through the budget – such as tax relief, infrastructure spending, and securing energy supplies – rather than over-relying on central bank liquidity."

Structural hurdles mute credit demand Despite lower borrowing costs, credit demand shows no sign of recovery. City Bank, one of the country's prominent private lenders, recorded just 7%-8% credit growth over the first nine months of the year – half its historical average – despite double-digit deposit growth.

A senior executive at the bank noted that expected credit demand failed to materialise even after post-election political uncertainty subsided. "Even when we offer competitive rates to large corporate clients, many refuse to borrow due to persistent gas shortages," the executive said. Consequently, City Bank redirected surplus liquidity into government debt and deployed over Tk 2,000 crore into the central bank's stimulus fund.

The executive also cast doubt on the official 4.47% private-sector credit growth figure for June. "Real growth is likely negative; much of that figure reflects forced loans and accrued interest on existing facilities."

He noted that the central bank's Tk60,000 crore stimulus package equals roughly 3% of total bank loans. Fully implementing it would only push credit growth to 7%-8% – far below the 15%-16% required to support the government's 6.5% GDP growth target for FY27. "Furthermore, banks will not take the risk of lending to distressed or insolvent businesses simply because money is cheap," he added.

Certainty over cheap money Tareq Refat Ullah Khan, managing director of BRAC Bank, emphasised that falling rates stem directly from surplus liquidity rather than intentional economic stimulus. "When credit growth halts, money builds up. Lowering rates alone cannot create demand if the wider business environment remains unsupportive."

BRAC Bank has lowered corporate lending rates to 11%-12% (with select prime clients receiving 9%-10%), while SME rates have dropped to 14%-15% and retail rates to 11%-12%. Deposit rates across sound banks have settled around 8%-9%. Distressed banks continue offering 11%-12% on deposits solely to maintain liquidity, rather than to finance new lending.

Abul Kashem Md Shirin, former managing director of Dutch-Bangla Bank, observed that major industrial borrowers are holding back expansion plans due to broader uncertainty. "When liquidity is abundant and credit demand falls, rates drop naturally. Bangladesh Bank spent years trying to force interest rates down through directives, but market forces are finally driving the adjustment automatically – which is precisely how a market economy ought to function."

Title: ‘Some members of my own team have disowned me’: Badhan drops bombshell after landing in Dhaka
Content:
Actress Azmeri Haque Badhan returned to Bangladesh this morning after allegedly being attacked and harassed during her visit to Italy for the Venice International Film Festival.

Speaking to journalists at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, Badhan said she believed those behind the alleged attack were ultimately putting themselves at risk through their actions.

“I feel that those who carried out the attack are creating problems for themselves. The attackers think they will get away with it, but this time they physically assaulted me. It was not simply a matter of abusing me from a distance, chanting slogans or throwing water at me. They laid hands on me. This brutality must stop. I feel that they are actually making their own position unsafe,” she said.

Badhan also said the incident had tarnished Bangladesh’s image abroad. “Bangladeshi expatriates behaved brutally towards me and attacked me in a despicable manner. Because of this, our country’s image was tarnished on foreign soil. Foreigners may think that we are a nation constantly fighting among ourselves — that wherever someone goes, they are attacked. That is simply unacceptable,” she said.

Badhan alleged that she was targeted because of her active role in the July-August 2024 student-led mass uprising. She claimed that some of those involved in the attack identified themselves as supporters of the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned, and the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League.

Addressing Awami League supporters, Badhan urged them not to become “blind followers”.

“You can love your party and support it, but please don’t become blind followers. If you are held accountable today, your families will suffer,” she said.

Referring to party leaders abroad, she added, “Those who are provoking you through audio and video messages from abroad do not live the same kind of life as you do. You work hard, earning money through your sweat and sending it back to Bangladesh. Please don’t do this. This is my request to you. What you have done is completely wrong.”

Badhan also addressed the party’s leadership, urging them to reconsider the direction of their future politics.

“My only request to the leaders is this: you are a major political party. Your activities may have been suspended temporarily, but you will engage in politics in the future. You are already drawing up a roadmap for what kind of politics you will pursue. Please do not create a roadmap that you will have to be ashamed of in the future,” she said.

During the interaction, Badhan also made allegations concerning members of her own team. While noting that director Rubaiyat Hossain had supported her, Badhan claimed that some members of the team had “disowned” her following the incident.

She also said she had been dropped from the Toronto International Film Festival, without elaborating on the circumstances. However, Badhan said her co-stars Sunerah Binte Kamal and Zaineen Chowdhury Karim, as well as Karim’s mother, had stood by her.

Badhan travelled to Italy as part of the team of Rubaiyat Hossain’s “The Difficult Bride”, which had its world premiere at the Venice International Film Festival on September 6.

Following the premiere, Badhan went to a local park with members of her family, where she alleged that she was physically assaulted and harassed.

Title: Celine Dion returns to stage after six years
Content:
Celine Dion returned to the stage in Paris on Saturday for her first full concert in more than six years, opening her 2026 residency at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre.

The 58-year-old Canadian singer began with her 1998 French-language song “On ne change pas”, but paused moments into the performance as she became tearful. She wiped her eyes, took a breath and continued after the audience applauded.

“I had promised myself not to cry. I don’t keep my promises. But I’m so happy to see you all. I missed you. I’m going to sing like you without crying,” Dion told the audience.

The concert was Dion’s first full show since March 2020. She stopped performing after being diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder, in 2022.

The Paris residency consists of 16 performances between September 12 and October 17. Dion’s official website announced the engagement in March, describing the September shows as her return to live performance.

Saturday’s set included some of Dion’s best-known songs, including “My Heart Will Go On” and “All By Myself”. She performed 25 songs over a little more than two hours.

Dion had returned to the public stage before Saturday’s concert, performing “Hymne à l’amour” at the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics in 2024. The Paris residency, however, marks her return to a full concert programme.

Speaking to the audience during the show, Dion said: “I want to sing for you, to sing about life.”
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Israeli minister threatens to revoke citizenship of 'NAZA' filmmakers over Gaza documentary
Content:
Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar has threatened to seek the revocation of the Israeli citizenship of Oscar-winning filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accusing them of “treason against the state” following the success of their latest documentary, "NAZA", at the Venice Film Festival.

Zohar made the remarks on X yesterday, a day after "NAZA" won the Special Jury Prize at the festival. The 80-minute documentary also received a 25-minute standing ovation, reportedly setting a festival record.

הזכייה של הסרט הנבזי נז״א בפסטיבל ונציה מזעזעת. השנאה העצמית היוקדת של היוצרים שמוכנים לפגוע במולדתם כדי לקבל מחיאות כפיים מהאנטישמים בעולם בלתי נתפסת ומהווה בגידה במדינה. זו בדיוק הסיבה שהובלתי את הרפורמה החשובה בקולנוע כדי שאזרחי ישראל לא ישלמו יותר מכיסם על הפגיעה בחיילי צה״ל ובמדינת ישראל. כשר התרבות, אפעל מיידית לשלול את האזרחות הישראלית של היוצרים השפלים הללו בגין בגידה במדינה.

“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X. He also accused the filmmakers of being willing to “harm their homeland” in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world.

Produced by The Guardian, "NAZA" takes its title from an acronym reportedly used by Israeli intelligence to refer to the estimated number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike on Gaza.

Israeli law allows citizenship to be revoked under certain circumstances, although the measure is rarely used. In 2022, the Supreme Court upheld the state’s authority to strip individuals of their nationality if they had failed to demonstrate “loyalty”, including through acts of espionage or treason. The law was expanded in 2023 to cover people convicted of “terrorism”.

The procedure requires the interior minister to submit a request for citizenship revocation, followed by approval from the justice minister and judicial validation.

The documentary features interviews with 24 Israeli military and intelligence whistleblowers, who describe AI-powered targeting systems allegedly used in Israeli bombardments of Gaza. One source claims that approval was given to kill 500 NAZA in an operation targeting a single Hamas member.

The film has drawn further criticism from other Israeli ministers, while Abraham and Szor are already known for their 2024 documentary "No Other Land", which won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature in 2025. The film examines Israeli settler violence and the displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Following the world premiere of "No Other Land" in 2024, Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Nusraat Faria exits Raihan Khan’s ‘Tribunal’
Content:
Actress Nusraat Faria has decided to step away from the upcoming courtroom drama “Tribunal”, directed by Raihan Khan.

The film is inspired by a real case under Bangladesh’s Women and Children Repression Prevention Act. Faria had joined the project last year and was set to play a barrister. However, she has now confirmed that she will no longer be part of the film.

“Raihan Khan is someone very close to me. We have spoken about it. I was supposed to play a lawyer in the film, but I am not doing it anymore,” Faria said.

“I have heard that there are some internal issues with the film. Because of this, it is no longer possible for me to remain involved with the project,” she added.

Faria also said that filming for her scenes had not yet begun. Most of the film had already been shot, but her scenes were still pending as they primarily involved courtroom sequences.

“I have heard that they have shot a large portion of the film, but my parts were still left. Since my scenes are courtroom-based, I had not started shooting them. Now it is no longer possible for me to continue with the film,” she said.

Earlier, Raihan Khan had said that around 65 per cent of “Tribunal” had been completed. The filmmaker had initially planned to finish the remaining shooting and post-production and release the film during Eid-ul-Fitr. However, production was delayed, with reports citing actress Tania Brishty’s illness as one of the factors affecting the schedule.

The film features Tariq Anam Khan, Moushumi Hamid, Tania Brishty, Saira Akhter Jahan and others. Earlier reports had also identified Faria as playing a barrister who would represent the accused in the case.

Meanwhile, Faria is nearing completion of her work on the web film “Lapatta”, directed by Mehedi Hassan. Recent reports said only a song sequence remained to be filmed, with the project expected to premiere on iScreen in October.

The actress has also recently signed another film, “Lojja”, in which she will share the screen with Azmeri Haque Badhan. Directed by M H Khokon and jointly produced by Impress Telefilm and Jaaz Multimedia, the film is scheduled to begin shooting on September 20.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Pori Moni reunites with filmmaker Gias Uddin Selim after four years
Content:
Actor Pori Moni is reuniting with filmmaker Gias Uddin Selim after four years for a new web film titled “Separation”.

Pori Moni has often referred to Selim as her mentor. In previous interviews, the actress has said that it was while working in his film “Swapnajaal” that she learnt how to internalise a character and translate it onto the screen.

The two last worked together in the 2022 film “Gunin”. The project also marked a significant chapter in Pori Moni’s personal life, as she entered into a relationship with her co-star Sarifula Razz during the production. The relationship ended two years ago.

Shooting for “Separation” has already begun in the capital’s 300 Feet area. However, details about the story and Pori Moni’s character have yet to be revealed. Both the director and the actor have refrained from discussing the project ahead of an official announcement.

According to reports, the web film also stars Imtiaz Barshon and Sharlin Farzana, while actor Nirab Hossain will appear in a special role.

“Separation” is set to be released on the OTT platform iScreen.

Pori Moni was most recently seen on the big screen in “Felubakshi”, which marked her Tollywood debut in January 2025. The film also starred Soham Chakraborty and Madhumita Sarcar. Her most recent OTT appearance was in Anam Biswas’ web series “Rongila Kitab”.

The actor is also awaiting the release of “Dodur Golpo”, directed by Reza Ghatak and produced with a government grant.

Pori Moni has also signed on for Shamsul Huda’s “Golap” and Leesa Gazi’s “Shasti”. She will star opposite Nirab Hossain in “Golap”, while “Shasti” will feature her alongside Chanchal Chowdhury.
Author: Arts & Entertainment Desk

Title: Before AI revived the ’80s, what made Dhallywood’s golden era iconic?
Content:
For the past few days, social media has been awash with an ’80s-inspired trend. From hairstyles and outfits to vintage poses, many have used AI-generated images to recreate the look of the decade. Today’s generation calls it “vintage cool”. And if these looks really are inspired by the cinema of that era, perhaps it is time to revisit the films of the ’80s. The 1980s were a golden chapter in Bangladeshi cinema. Alongside mainstream commercial films, the decade also saw the emergence of alternative cinema. Commercial, folk and action films flourished, while realistic and literary adaptations also found their place on screen.

The decade belonged to stars such as Nayak Raj Razzak, Shabana, Babita, Kabori, Alamgir, Sohel Rana, Zafar Iqbal, Rozina, Wasim, Ilias Kanchan, Olivia, Bulbul Ahmed, Sucharita, Anju Ghosh and Rubel. At the same time, filmmakers such as Abdullah Al Mamun, Amjad Hossain and Syed Salahuddin Zaki were shaping a different kind of cinema, featuring actors including Afzal Hossain, Humayun Faridi, Raisul Islam Asad and Suborna Mustafa.

The decade began with several significant releases. Abdullah Al Mamun’s “Sakhi Tumi Kar” (1980), starring Raj Razzak, Shabana and Farooque, explored a love triangle, while Amjad Hossain’s “Koshai” (1980), featuring Alamgir, Babita and Rozina, went on to win National Film Awards.

Syed Salahuddin Zaki’s “Ghuddi” (1980) marked Suborna Mustafa’s film debut alongside Raisul Islam Asad and Tariq Anam Khan. Considered a modern film for its time, it also introduced audiences to the timeless song “Abar Elo Je Shondhya”, written and composed by Happy Akhand and Lucky Akhand. Abdullah Al Mamun’s “Ekhoni Shomoy” (1980), starring Babita, Uzzal and Abul Khair, earned him the National Film Award for Best Director.

The following years brought an equally memorable run of films. Amjad Hossain’s “Jonmo Theke Jolchhi” (1981) starred Bulbul Ahmed, Babita, Anwara, Prabir Mitra and Sumita Devi. In 1982, Chashi Nazrul Islam adapted Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay’s “Devdas”, with Bulbul Ahmed in the title role, Kabori as Parvati and Anwara as Chandramukhi.

That same year saw the release of “Boro Bhalo Lok Chhilo”, “Dui Poysar Alta" and "Rajanigandha”. Amjad Hossain’s “Dui Poysar Alta”, starring Shabana, Raj Razzak, Nuton and Anwara, won National Film Awards in four categories.

In 1983, “Notun Bou”, directed by Abdul Latif Bachchu, brought Babita opposite Afzal Hossain, with Raisul Islam Asad and Suborna Mustafa also in the cast. A year later came Amjad Hossain’s “Bhat De”, starring Shabana, Alamgir, Rajib and Anwar Hossain, with child actor Ankhi Alamgir. The film won nine National Film Awards and is known as the first Bangladeshi film screened at the Cannes Film Festival. “Noyoner Alo”, directed by Belal Ahmed, also became a popular release that year, featuring Zafar Iqbal, Kajori and Suborna Mustafa.

The mid-’80s brought more memorable titles. “Tin Kanya” (1985), directed by Shibli Sadiq, featured Suchanda, Babita and Champa as three sisters in real life. “Premik”, released the same year, paired the stylish Zafar Iqbal with Babita, alongside Anjana and Nuton.

In 1986, Shahidul Islam Khokon’s “Laraku” introduced Rubel as a leading man and helped establish a new trend of action and karate-based films in Bangladesh. “Usila”, starring Shabana, Uzzal, Zafar Iqbal, Diti and Sunetra, was another notable release.

The latter half of the decade continued the run of popular and critically recognised films. “Opekkha” (1987), directed by Dilip Biswas, featured Alamgir, Shabana, Zafar Iqbal and Sucharita. Abdullah Al Mamun’s “Dui Jibon” (1988), starring Bulbul Ahmed, Kabori, Afzal Hossain and Diti, won National Film Awards in six categories. Shibli Sadiq’s “Bheja Chokh”, featuring Ilias Kanchan and Champa, was another popular release that year.

Then came 1989’s “Beder Meye Josna”, directed by Tozammel Haque Bokul and starring Ilias Kanchan and Anju Ghosh. It went on to become one of the biggest commercial successes in the history of Bangladeshi cinema.

The decade also gave audiences films such as Azizur Rahman’s “Chhutir Ghonta”, Badal Rahman’s “Emiler Goenda Bahini”, Raj Razzak’s “Obhijan”, Sheikh Niamat Ali’s “Dahan”, and literary adaptations including “Parineeta”, “Rajlakshmi Srikanta” and ‘Shubhada”.

Looking back at ’80s cinema, however, means revisiting more than just films. It means returning to an entire era — its stars’ clothes and hairstyles, memorable dialogue, songs and colourful film posters. Together, they created a distinctive visual and cultural identity. That nostalgia remains alive even today. So, beneath the sheen of today’s “vintage cool” lies something familiar: the colours, textures, music and stories of the golden age of Bangladeshi cinema.
Author: Zahid Akbar Zahid Akbar

Title: Sheikh Rabiul Haque’s 80-year creative journey being celebrated
Content:
A week-long art exhibition celebrating the 80-year creative journey of writer, painter, singer and entrepreneur Sheikh Rabiul Haque was inaugurated yesterday at the National Art Gallery of Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.

Renowned painter Rafiqun Nabi attended the inauguration as the chief guest. Painter Jyotsna Mahbuba, Kamrul Islam, general secretary of the Bangiya Sahitya Sanskriti Sangsad, and other cultural personalities were also present.

The exhibition, being held at Gallery 7 on the third floor of the National Art Gallery, will remain open until September 18.

A cultural programme and discussion on Haque’s multifaceted creative journey will be held on September 15 at the National Art Gallery Auditorium. The event will explore his contributions to art and culture across his long career.

Title: BRAC Institute of Languages and The Daily Star redefine English Education for youth
Content:
In an educational landscape often dominated by rote memorisation and rigid textbook formats, a collaborative initiative between the BRAC Institute of Languages (BIL) and The Daily Star's English in "Schools (EIS) initiative" is redefining how young learners engage with language. Through the compilation and adaptation of Learn English for Success: Climb Higher (Class VI-VIII) and Learn English for Success: Climb Higher (Class IX-X) , this partnership stands as a beacon of fresh, dynamic, and deeply interactive learning for students.

Originally conceived to provide school students with accessible opportunities for additional English language practice through the pages of The Daily Star, these materials have moved beyond their original newspaper format. They have now been carefully adapted and compiled into classroom resources for both teachers and learners.

Even though the original newspaper-based initiative has concluded, its legacy endures. The rich collection of learning materials remains remarkably relevant, offering educators practical, engaging, and interactive content that integrates seamlessly into modern English language classrooms. By connecting journalism with classroom teaching, the initiative champions a learner-centred approach that encourages active engagement with language.

Senior figures at BRAC University, notably Advisor Lady Syeda Sarwat Abed and Director of the BRAC Institute of Languages Professor Shaila Sultana, envision that this publication will inspire renewed enthusiasm for innovative methods in language teaching. Above all, the initiative underscores the lasting value of student-centred, engaging resources that encourage young minds to see language not as a burdensome task, but as an engaging pathway to exploration.

Rifah Tashfia Islam is a postgraduate student at North South University and an intern at Star Books and Literature. A writer and dreamer, she is often found chasing stories and romanticising ordinary moments.
Author: Rifah Tashfia Islam Rifah Tashfia Islam

Title: Finding home, identity, and art in ‘Parsa’s Pithas’
Content:
How do you stay connected to your own culture and roots while living thousands of miles away from home? This is the question at the heart of Sumaiya Matin’s debut children’s book Parsa’s Pithas. Set in Canada, the book tells the heartwarming story of a seven-year-old girl named Parsa who, through making pithas with her mother, is able to learn more about her Bangali roots and traditions while also gaining more confidence in her ability to express herself through her art.

The book opens with the young protagonist frustrated at her inability to draw the “perfect” sky. In dire need of a distraction, Parsa decides to take a break from her school art project to instead help her mother make nakshi pakon pithas for the Bangla New Year. However, as the two begin to make the pithas, Parsa’s frustration returns when she realises that she cannot make pithas as smoothly and intricately as her mother. First struggling to make the right consistency of dough, and then betrayed by the breaking of a toothpick, Parsa struggles with a question that every artist has asked themselves at least once —does art have to be perfect in order to be good?

For Parsa, the answer to this question is found in her mother’s stories about the Bangladeshi women who first made nakshi pakon pithas. Learning about the girls in Bangladesh who made art with whatever they had—rice flower, sticks, stones, and thorns of date palm trees—inspires Parsa to jump over the hurdle of perfectionism and focus her energy and creativity in expressing herself in her own unique way rather than trying to replicate what others are doing.

It is in this intertwining of cultural lessons with a story of a young girl persevering and learning not to give up that Parsa’s Pithas achieves immaculately what every good children’s book sets out to do—act as “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” for children around the world.

First introduced by children’s literature scholar, Rudine Sims Bishop, the concept of “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” is a metaphor for the different ways in which children can see themselves and the world around them in children’s books. Mirrors signify children seeing their own experiences reflected in the books they read, windows symbolise children learning about different cultures through books, and sliding glass doors refer to children using their imaginations to enter experiences that are different from their own. Bishop argues that all three of these reading experiences are essential to the development of a growing child. What makes Parsa’s Pithas so remarkable is that it is able to do all three of these things at the exact same time.

Written primarily with Bangladeshi diaspora children in mind, the book puts to pages an experience that is not often represented in books or media. Though there are an abundance of Bangladeshi children’s books with representation of Bangladeshi characters, we seldom see books made specifically for children who are learning to navigate their Bangladeshi roots and identity while living away from Bangladesh. Acting as a mirror, the story of Parsa and her mother keeping Bangali traditions alive by celebrating Bangla New Year all the way in Canada allows children of the Bangladeshi diaspora to finally see their own unique experiences and struggles be represented on paper.

Acting as a window, Parsa’s Pithas being a book that is written in English and available on the international market, offers many children, both in Bangladesh and outside, an insight into the Bangali culture and its traditions. The stories of Bangladeshi women told to Parsa by her mother in the book, combined with the vibrant and colourful illustrations by Nesba Yousef, act as the perfect introduction to Bangladeshi history. Furthermore, by framing the cultural lessons within the narrative of a young girl struggling with her artistic expression, the book is able to introduce Bangladeshi culture and values not as something that is unfamiliar and distant, but rather as something that everyone can learn from and incorporate into their own lives.

Lastly, it is in this invitation to participate, that the book shines the brightest. Going a step further than just introducing Bangladeshi culture to readers, with a full recipe for nakshi pakon pithas and an activities section, the book invites readers not only to learn, but fully immerse themselves in the culture they just read about.

It is here also that Matin’s message of embracing uniqueness over trying to replicate things perfectly comes in full clutch. For children in the diaspora, taking part in their culture may not always look the same as what it does for children living in Bangladesh. Many of them may be working with different tools, ingredients, and circumstances. However, as Parsa learns, just because something is different does not mean it is any less meaningful or beautiful in its own right. Afterall, sometimes to keep a culture alive is to be brave and resourceful enough to make it your own.

Shanjida Nowshin Chowdhury is a lecturer in the Department of English and Modern Languages at North South University.
Author: S Shanjida Nowshin Chowdhury Shanjida Nowshin Chowdhury

Title: Out of the archives, into the feed
Content:
Open Instagram or TikTok for 10 minutes and you will likely run into him: a nervous Prague insurance clerk, dead for a century now, staring out from a grainy black-and-white photo with a quote about cages and birds stamped across it. Beside him sits a brooding Russian novelist who once faced a firing squad and lived to write about it afterward.

Franz Kafka and Fyodor Dostoevsky—two of literature’s heaviest names—are thriving unexpectedly on apps built mostly for dance trends and comedy skits.

It shouldn’t work on paper. These are writers obsessed with guilt, confusing systems, and deep self-doubt—hardly algorithm-friendly material. Yet here we are, watching teenagers highlight The Brothers Karamazov (1880) between class notes and skincare reviews. What explains this sudden revival of century-old books among young people online?

‘Burnout’ plays a huge part in this trend. This generation didn’t inherit simple, inspiring stories where the hero wins and everything turns out fine. Instead, they inherited constant traffic jams, rising heat and pollution, endless coaching classes, hyper-competitive exams, and a job market where people who were promised high salaries after studying BBA 10 years ago now face modest pay in Motijheel or Gulshan and are treated like they can be replaced at any moment.

Kafka never wrote heroic adventure stories. He wrote about regular people stuck in absurd, stressful situations they couldn’t escape. In his most famous story, “The Metamorphosis” (1915), a man named Gregor Samsa wakes up turned into a giant bug. His main worry isn’t his terrifying new body; it is how he will explain being late to work to his boss.

That is the real tragedy of the story. And somehow, it hits harder for an exhausted 22-year-old today than any big action quest could. The story was never really about turning into a bug—it was about how soul-crushing it feels to give your life away to a job that doesn’t care about you.

“I am a cage, in search of a bird.”

Dostoevsky hits a different note. Where Kafka suffers quietly, Dostoevsky explodes with emotion. His short story “White Nights” (1848), about a lonely dreamer wandering the streets of St. Petersburg, has become an unlikely hit for people feeling overwhelmed by their own thoughts. His lines get placed over slow piano music and blurry city footage, and somehow, it keeps working.

“I am a dreamer; I have so little real life that I look upon such moments as this as a dream…”

There is a strange reality worth thinking about here. This is the most digitally connected generation in history, yet surveys constantly show record levels of loneliness. Everyone is easy to reach through text and social apps, but very few people actually feel understood.

The overwhelming guilt, overthinking, and deep loneliness in Dostoevsky’s stories no longer feel like old, distant fiction from Russia. They read like entries from a private diary written yesterday. They give young readers permission to feel things deeply in a culture that often tells people to stay detached.

Meme culture deserves plenty of credit for this revival too. Classic literature usually comes wrapped in dust and serious classroom rules, which keeps everyday readers at a distance. The internet strips that seriousness away without much ceremony.

On social media, Kafka becomes “that anxious guy who hated his job and had huge issues with his dad.” Dostoevsky becomes “the guy who replays one single awkward conversation in his head for six years straight.”

It’s funny, but it’s also remarkably accurate. Internet humour makes these intimidating writers feel like old friends. Someone laughs at a joke about a man turning into a bug, gets curious, opens the book, and suddenly finds themselves deep in a story that speaks directly to their own inner thoughts. The joke acts as a welcoming front door to complex literature.

Visual style plays a big role as well—perhaps bigger than most people like to admit. The Dark Academia online trend—tweed jackets, candlelight, rainy library windows, and worn-out paperbacks—adopted Kafka and Dostoevsky as unofficial faces of the movement.

Sharing a photo of a coffee-stained copy of Crime and Punishment (1866) alongside a warm drink isn’t always just about the plot of the book. Sometimes it’s a quiet signal to the world that says: I want to slow down, and I care about deeper things than just short video clips.

Kafka’s private love letters help explain the appeal too. Letters to Milena (1952) is full of short, emotional lines that easily fit into video captions. Lines like “I am yours, even if I am not with you” look completely natural written over a moody picture online today. They offer a level of romantic vulnerability that feels refreshing in a world of quick online chats and ghosting.

Is some of this just for show? Probably. Does that make it fake? Not necessarily. It is completely possible to use literature as an online style choice and still be deeply moved by the words inside the book once you actually read them.

What stands out most is that neither writer offers easy comfort or fake happy endings. Gregor Samsa dies forgotten by his own family. Dostoevsky’s dreamer ends up more alone than when his story began. Nothing about either writer fits neatly into a social media feed built on beauty filters and forced happiness.

So, why do these century-old writers matter so much to young readers right now? In a culture, like ours, where family expectations, academic pressure, and the fast pace of city life leave very little room to feel uncertain, Kafka and Dostoevsky offer something rare: real validation. When we feel overwhelmed by high demands, strict societal goals, or the quiet loneliness of a crowded city, these books do not sell us fake comfort or easy answers. Instead, they gently remind us that feeling lost, overthinking, and searching for who you are isn’t a personal failure—it is a timeless human experience that people have been trying to make sense of for over a hundred years.

Rania Fatema Tui is a writer and master of making simple tasks complicated. Powered by iced coffee and last-minute panic, she spends 10% of her time typing, 90% staring at a blank screen, and re-reading text messages five times before sending them.
Author: R Rania Fatema Tui Rania Fatema Tui

Title: Kobitabela: a soulful afternoon
Content:
On Friday, September 5, 2026, a small crowd gathered beneath the bright summer sky, drawn together by their shared passion for poetry. Organised by Intersectional Network Bangladesh (INB) in collaboration with Circle of Sorts (CoS), Kobitabela—a poetry reading event—was hosted at the Garden Bistro, Uttara. Initiated by Asif Ahmed, guardian of CoS, Nahid Kabir, owner of Garden Bistro, and Kashfia Nahreen, founder of INB, this programme aspires to bring people together and to foster community spaces through literary events.

The programme commenced with a round of introductions, moderated by Kashfia Nahreen. 12 poets from diverse backgrounds read their expressive poems, some penned in Bangla, some in English, others blending both languages. One performer accompanied their poem on the ukulele while singing the verse. The performances underscored the significance of expanding the boundaries of traditional verse, prompting listeners to ponder the definition of poetry itself.

The concluding open-mic segment extended the programme, drawing several audience members to read their works. Two poets collaborated on an impromptu duet, captivating the audience with their verse. The evening created a space where students and professionals alike could step away from the demands of everyday life and find comfort through their shared love for creative expression.

Kashfia Nahreen is a passionate reader and writer who can be found exploring various arts and crafts while cuddling with her cats. She can be reached @the.k.atelier on instagram.
Author: K Kashfia Nahreen Kashfia Nahreen

Title: Two nights that lit Azimpur
Content:
In the Azimpur government colony of the 1970s, two occasions—Ashura and ShabeBarat—turned familiar lanes into processional corridors and classrooms of companionship.

In the government colony blocks of Azimpur, the 1970s felt like a long conversation that picked up each afternoon where we had left off the day before. We belonged not only to our own flats but to shared stairwells and open courtyards, to verandas with gossip flowing like tea, and to a playground that doubled as parliament, theatre and auditorium.

Ashura arrived with the hush of a story you don’t interrupt. The Hussaini Dalan complex lay roughly two kilometres from our colony, near enough for curiosity to tug at our sleeves. In the days leading up to the tenth of Muharram, we sometimes walked over in small groups to watch preparations: the measured fixing of banners and standards, the careful laying out of routes, the way elders explained, in low voices, the meaning of what was to come. It was a lesson given without a classroom. Even the silence of the workers felt like part of a longer recitation.

On the day itself, a grand mourning procession would emerge from Hussaini Dalan and move through the city streets. We stationed ourselves at the Salimullah Orphanage intersection, where, year after year, the procession seemed to collect and release the city’s breath. To secure a view we formed a small wedge at the front of the crowd—half strategy, half bravado—leaning forward as if those few inches would let us better understand grief carried across centuries. Chests beat in rhythm, eyes glistened, and yet the atmosphere felt protective rather than frightening, the way adults will form an invisible ring around children in a sudden rain.

If the procession supplied our solemn awe, the fair supplied our giddy hunger. The long road between the Azimpur bus stand and the graveyard would wake up like a travelling caravan, the ‘official’ oneday fair stretching, quite naturally, into a week and peaking on Ashura. It was a child’s university: you learned to bargain for toy pistols and tin cars, to press your eye to a bioscope’s small window and gasp at a parade of painted frames, to feel important holding a plastic binocular that made the world nearer by stubborn faith alone. The dhol beat from a few stalls at once as if sound itself were a banner; clay dolls sat in patient rows, their eyes permanently surprised; and a creaking nagordola—our modest Ferris wheel—climbed and descended like a lesson in bravery. Father gave me five taka and with that money I bought a bioscope and a tin car. How happy I was!

We returned home from the fair carrying a mathematics of delight. If I saved two taka on toy money here, could I add a packet of muri-murki there? If I skipped the binocular for now, would the stall still be open tomorrow? These negotiations felt like a first apprenticeship in adulthood, though our parents pretended not to notice, smiling at the way we reported our victories with straight faces. The colony community absorbed the energy of the day: khallamas compared prices as if they were recounting cricket scores; uncles developed brisk opinions about bioscope morals; neighbours tried the nagordola to show the younger ones that fear is a muscle that improves with use.

If Ashura took us into a history of courage and loss, ShabeBarat returned us to the night as a neighbour. In our colony it had a robust presence—part supplication, part streettheatre of generosity. Every home cooked halwas and sweets; ricerotis stacked high on trays seemed to multiply, as if the house itself had become a small bakery. Before the call to Magribh, families began a gentle choreography of distribution: plates travelling to the next flat and the next; portions set aside for those who slept outside our gates or simply needed the comfort of a soft, sweet bite. The flavour of the night was mercy.

But if you ask what we children looked forward to most, the answer is shamelessly simple: we were allowed to stay out all night. In groups that reshuffled like playing cards, we visited almost every mosque within walking distance, including, with a certain pride, the old Shahi Masjid of Chawkbazar. Our piety, I admit, was often a cover for adda—long conversations that circled the same topics and somehow never grew dull: the speed of a leftarm bowler, the possibility of a new cassette deck, the mystery of a classmate’s smile. We lit candles and tarabati sparklers that scribbled light on the air, our laughter briefly drowning out the night birds.

Our vigil had a ritual ending. Just before dawn we would make our way to the Tin Gambuj mosque—some three hundred metres from home—to offer Fajr. But what drew us there, alongside prayer, was an older comfort: warm tehari served on daora woven from dried jackfruit leaves. The first bite felt like a promise kept. We ate not only with our mouths but with our shoulders and eyes, borrowing warmth from each other under a sky that was just beginning to colour. By the time we emerged, the alleys were narrower, the hush clean, and the permission of the night had become a memory we could carry into algebra and homework.

Looking back, I realise how elegantly these two nights taught us about companionship. Ashura asked us to witness another community’s wound with sincerity and respect; ShabeBarat asked us to enact generosity until it felt like habit. Both made room for us, children of many flats and a few religions, to belong to a city larger than our block. The lessons were practical rather than preachy. Hold your ground at the intersection, but do not shove. Stand aside so an elder can see. Share your lanterns. Give your last halwa without counting.

We sometimes say that those days were simpler, as if simplicity were a property of the calendar. They were not. Grownups still flinched at newspaper headlines, and budgets were still a kind of puzzle. But the colony’s distances were small enough for hope to travel fast. A call from one staircase would be heard in the next; a rumour of trouble would fetch a father in sandals and a mother with a shawl around her shoulders; a plan for a midnight mosqueround would produce, from somewhere, an extra sweater for a younger cousin who insisted he was not cold.

I still picture the Hussaini Dalan preparations in the hush of late afternoon, the banners catching the smallest breeze. I still hear the bioscopeman calling out a story in a voice that had absorbed a hundred other stories. I still see the slow carousel of the nagordola tipped against the sky. On ShabeBarat I still taste a spoonful of halwa platehopped from one kitchen to the next and feel the soft warmth of tehari on daora after Fajr. When memory lines up these images like frames in a projector, the throughline is easy to read: religious in nature, secular in spirit, these occasions took private devotion and turned it into public companionship.

Azimpur taught us that a neighbourhood can be a syllabus. Ashura showed us how a people remember—out loud, together, and with beauty that does not hide pain. ShabeBarat showed us how a people feed—quietly, door to door, until nobody feels left out of the night. In the morning after, when we washed our faces and headed to school, we carried the residue of those lessons like a second skin. They have not rubbed off. Even now, all these years later, I still find myself glancing up when the air changes, as if a procession might turn the corner or a lanternline might suddenly appear, and the colony of our childhood might, for a moment, come back into view.

Ahmed Ahsanuzzaman is professor of English at Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB). He can be reached at: ahsanuzzaman@iub.edu.bd.
