Title: Your complete map to Bangladesh’s most iconic Mughal mosques
Content:
Our country is blessed with beautiful mosques. Be it the Sultanate era mosques or the modern marvels, Bangladesh is dotted with these awe-inspiring places of worship that span many centuries. Among them, Mughal mosques are indeed an interesting chapter of our heritage.

In this holy month of Ramadan, Star Lifestyle presents to you a map of Bangladesh's prominent Mughal mosques — your essential list of mosques from this era that you should definitely visit.

We invite you to see this map, which took us about a month to create, and we invite you to visit these age-old buildings.

Along with the map, this article will give an idea about our research journey, providing you with more insights than just names and geography.

Mughal mosques combine to form a rich time capsule, but which timeframe are we really looking into?

According to the book Mosque Architecture in Bangladesh, by Dr Abu Sayeed M Ahmed and Syed Zakir Hossain, Bengal was "conquered by Mughal rulers" in 1576. So, that is the beginning.

On the other hand, we can cut off the Mughal era at 1757 if we are very strict — an obvious year, due to the Empire's collapse surrounding the Battle of Palashi that was led by Nawab Sirajuddaula against the British.

Of course, the timeframe is up for debate. To exemplify, it can be stretched to 1857, and rightly so, because there was resistance to the "new" British East India Company regime. Nazly Chowdhury and Babu Ahmed wrote in Mughal Monuments of Bangladesh, "In 1857, the Sepoy Revolt broke out but was soon suppressed by iron hands... and the rule of the Mughals in India was finally ended."

Neither the beginning nor the end of the Mughal era happened overnight.

Given this context, even though we kept in mind the 1576-1757 time period, we prioritised those mosques that are the most Mughal-inclined in terms of architecture, reputation, etc., hence allowing flexibility for a few mosques that were likely established after the 1757 milestone.

We will spare you the technicalities and details, leaving them for architects and historians. It is best to visit the mosques in person to appreciate it. And now, you have the map to guide you there!

Three-domed structures are common, although variations regarding the number of domes can also be easily found. Facades are decorative. Four corner turrets (or small towers) reinforce elegance. Inside, cusped arches, floral motifs, and views of the domes above your head will strike a chord in your heart!

However, it is saddening that many mosques of that era underwent mindless paintjobs, addition of tiles, extensions, etc. in modern times. Where such cases were severe, we dropped them out of our list.

In some cases, old structures have more or less been completely replaced by modern ones. For such mosques, the only major Mughal connection is in the collective memory of locals, history books, or the dates on the signboards. We have not included those buildings in our map as well.

Furthermore, there are several mosques that locals believe to be Mughal, but that fact cannot be ascertained from inscriptions (or lack thereof), architecture, or books of history. We have dropped most of those as well.

Therefore, this map indicates the most prominent ones that are worth visiting for the budding history buff.

You may be furious to see that very few number of mosques from the Dhaka district have made it to our map. Well, control your rage, and look at the disclaimer at the bottom of the map: Old Dhaka is home to so many magnificent Mughal-era mosques that it was not possible for us to fit them all: Haji Khwaja Shahbaz Mosque, Khan Muhammad Mirdha Mosque, Khwaja Ambar Mosque, and Begum Bazar Mosque are some of the names that have every right to be included in the map, and being history buffs ourselves, our hearts ached for this compromise.

Dhaka division posed another head-scratcher. This one had to do with the Mymensingh division. Curiously enough, this division is empty in our map! After consulting credible sources, we believe that Mymensingh's prominent mosques that are irrefutably Mughal in style, architecture, date, etc. are from the so-called "Greater Mymensingh" region, which includes places like Kishoreganj and Tangail; but in present times, they officially fall under Dhaka division!

Overcoming the many challenges throughout this journey, we have finally come up with this map. We hope it encourages you to visit the mosques and stir up conversations about the rich heritage the Mughals have left us.

Sources: Mosque Architecture in Bangladesh by Dr Abu Sayeed M Ahmed and Syed Zakir Hossain; Mughal Monuments of Bangladesh by Nazly Chowdhury and Babu Ahmed; Mosques of Bangladesh by Nymphea Publication; Banglapedia; Bangladesh government websites; UNESCO's Tentative List of "Mughal Mosques in Bangladesh".

Special thanks to Sazzadur Rasheed, architect, academician, and admin of Save the Heritages of Bangladesh for providing valuable inputs to our project. We are also grateful to The Daily Star's Habiganj and Moulvibazar correspondent Mintu Deshwara, and Sheikh Nasir, Sylhet photographer for their help in our research.
Author: M M H Haider J Jawwad Sami Neogi A Ashif Ahmed Rudro M H Haider , Jawwad Sami Neogi , and Ashif Ahmed Rudro

Title: How one family keeps the 'Tepa Putul' tradition alive
Content:
Rag dolls made from tattered saris and handmade clay dolls called tepa putul were once the few tangible belongings young girls in rural Bangladesh ever had.

Silt and clay collected from riverbeds, along with scraps found around their homesteads, were the materials village children used to craft their own toys. They kept them with utmost care in shoeboxes or rusted tin containers.

But these are stories of once upon a time. Today, the face of toys has changed, and with it, the fate of traditional toys and crafts.

With imported culture flooding the market and the aggressive rise of plastic products, even village shelves are now filled with mass-produced items.

These seemingly insignificant clay dolls, tepa putul, once found across pastoral Bangladesh, along with other artisanal items, have now become part of our lost craft heritage.

I met Subodh Kumar Pal, a tepa putul artisan, at an upmarket fair in Dhaka last year. Since then, I have followed his work, and he eventually took me to his village, Boshontopur Palpara in Rajshahi.

I am fascinated by heritage and folk keepsakes, and tepa putul is one cultural legacy I want to hold on to. Crafted by pressing raw clay with fingertips, dried in the sun, and then fired, tepa putul derives its name from the Bengali words tepa (pressing) and putul (doll), a nod to its simple finger-moulding process.

Figures of a mother and child, brides and grooms, farming families, or deities make up these rustic dolls. Unpainted and adorned only with ornamental clay markings, they are fine specimens of Bengal's folk artistry.

These crafts are not only cultural markers but also vital to the livelihoods of artisan communities.

Subodh's small family -- his son Shojib Kumar Pal and wife Bijli Rani Pal -- is the only one in Rajshahi still making tepa putul.

There are other potter families in the village, but each specialises in a different traditional craft. His neighbour, for instance, only makes Shoker er Hari or Hobby pots, decorative vessels used to store food or carry sweets during weddings and rituals.

Subodh, however, carries the torch for clay dolls. Bijli Rani has been making traditional clay dolls for 18 years and insists the craft requires a joyful mind.

"To do this kind of work, your mind must be in a good place. If the heart is heavy, the work won't turn out well. You must keep yourself happy," she says.

Her journey into mrit shilpo, the art of clay crafts, was shaped by her husband's family. Her father was a doll maker as well, though her mother never practised the craft. Bijli embraced it after marriage, continuing a fragile lineage of artisans.

An intricate doll can take two to three days to finish, while smaller ones are often made in batches of eight or ten over two days.

"The dolls that require painstaking work are priced at Tk 100 to Tk 400 depending on size, and Tk 3,000 to Tk 5,000 for the large ones. But profits are limited. People don't want to pay much for these delicate items. Only collectors who value heritage pay their true worth. Most prefer cheaper products," Subodh says.

In Rajshahi, only one family continues the craft; in Tangail, Somodarani Pal keeps it alive; in Kishoreganj, Sunil Pal does the same. Bijli says only a handful of artisans remain, though perhaps some practise quietly elsewhere. The tradition is on the verge of disappearance.

HAND-CRAFTING THEIR SURVIVAL PLAN

Sales in Subodh's village are modest, so the family relies on fairs in Dhaka, Sylhet, and government-sponsored exhibitions.

"I am gearing up for Independence Day, the Zainul Mela, and other fairs in Dhaka this December. These events are essential for our survival," he says.

Bijli and Subodh express deep gratitude to the organisers of the Zainul Mela and the Charukala (Fine Arts) authorities, who offer food, lodging, respect, and excellent sales opportunities – almost a lifeline for niche crafts.

"They value us the most. Without such fairs, our craft would have gone extinct years ago," they say.

"If Charukala stops including clay dolls in their fairs, we will lose everything," Bijli warns.

The challenges facing mrit shilpo are many. The widespread use of plastic for household items has eroded the market for clay products. Cooking pots, bowls, plates, and even matir chari – large clay tubs used for feeding cattle – have all been replaced by plastic alternatives.

Clay items are becoming rare, and their value is diminishing.

The financial strain on artisans remains a pressing issue. It takes almost three days of labour to complete one large doll. Every step is done by hand – moulding, polishing, finishing, and designing – and even collecting raw clay requires effort. River silt, once freely available, now requires payment to collect.

Most potters work independently, stocking items for yearly fairs, which remain their primary income source. Commissioned orders are rare. This raises the hard questions: how do they manage daily expenses, or pay helpers?

"The truth is, if I don't work, I don't eat. Courier services refuse to take responsibility for fragile clay items, which limits distribution and our income," Subodh says.

Clay crafts require time and artistic freedom. Electric wheels may help with larger items like pitchers or tubs, but they cannot replace the artisan's touch. Delicate work still relies entirely on hand finishing and creative insight.

Tepa putul is more than craftwork; it is a heritage skill passed down through generations. Subodh showed me an archetype of the first tepa putul made by his great-great-grandfather. The red-fired clay figure had only a pressed outline and simple dots for eyes. Over generations, intricate designs were added, shaping the doll we recognise today.

Subodh believes his son will eventually add his own creativity to this age-old tradition.

The story of Subodh and Bijli is emblematic of Bangladesh's endangered mrit shilpo. Their words reflect resilience and vulnerability. They reveal a devotion to craft despite low margins, cultural neglect, and systemic obstacles.

This tradition is sustained by festivals, a fragile network of artisans, and the stubborn persistence of those who refuse to let crafts like tepa putul vanish.

It is a way of life rooted in joy, patience, and heritage. Unfortunately, its future is threatened by rapid urbanisation and the social turmoil of the present.
Author: Raffat Binte Rashid Raffat Binte Rashid

Title: Two loudest voices in 2026 Ballon d’Or race
Content:
The 70th edition of the Ballon d’Or will be staged in London for the first time on October 26, in tribute to Stanley Matthews, the winner of the very first award. Seventy years after Matthews became the inaugural winner, the football world is again asking the same question: who is going to win the coveted prize?

London is preparing for a night of football history, but there is already plenty of noise before the lights come on.

The 30-man shortlist is packed with familiar giants. Harry Kane, Erling Haaland, Lionel Messi, Jude Bellingham, Ousmane Dembele, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal are all in the conversation. But curiously, two voices have been louder than the rest in recent interviews.

And neither appears particularly interested in letting someone else make the argument for them.

At 19, Yamal has already developed the confidence of someone who knows exactly where he wants to go. After helping Barcelona retain La Liga and Spain become world champions this summer, the young winger believes his season deserves the game's biggest individual prize.

“For me, Mbappe and me, we're the two best players in the world,” Yamal said.

Then he went one step further.

He believes he deserves the Ballon d’Or because of what he has won.

It is a bold statement, but perhaps that is what makes Yamal so fascinating. He is no longer talking like a teenager happy simply to be included among football's elite. He is talking like someone who expects to belong at the very top.

Mbappé, meanwhile, has built his case on a different foundation.

Real Madrid did not win a major trophy. France's World Cup campaign ended in a semi-final defeat by Spain. Yet Mbappe's individual numbers are difficult to overlook.

He scored 25 goals in La Liga and 15 in the Champions League before taking his World Cup tally to 22, making him the tournament's all-time leading scorer. And there is a particularly interesting detail to that record: he took it from Lionel Messi, a player many consider one of the greatest ever alongside Cristiano Ronaldo.

For Mbappe, that matters.

He argues that the Ballon d’Or is an individual award and should recognise players who do extraordinary things, even when their teams do not collect the biggest trophies.

“I believe I can win it this year,” he said.

And when asked whether anyone was better than him this season, his answer was even more direct. “There was no player better than me.”

So here is the curious part.

Yamal's argument is essentially: look at what I won.

Mbappe's is: look at what I did.

Both are compelling. Both are confident. And both leave the voters with a difficult choice.

Because the shortlist is hardly short of alternatives.

Kane scored 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country and helped Bayern Munich secure a treble. Haaland scored 58 in 64 games. Messi produced 75 goal contributions in 49 matches for Inter Miami and Argentina. Dembele, last year's winner, still has a claim after Paris Saint-Germain retained the Champions League.

And yet, somehow, the conversation keeps circling back to the 19-year-old and the 27-year-old.

Maybe because this is about more than one award.

For years, Messi and Ronaldo defined football's great individual rivalry. Now, could Yamal and Mbappé be preparing to write the next chapter?

On October 26, London will provide the answer to one question: who wins the 2026 Ballon d’Or?

It may also hint at something much bigger -- whether the future of football belongs to the fearless teenager from Barcelona, the superstar from Madrid, or someone else waiting quietly to steal the spotlight.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Man United left looking back in anger after derby defeat
Content:
For Noel Gallagher, Old Trafford was a place to celebrate on Sunday. For Manchester United fans, though, it was another afternoon to look back in anger.

The Oasis frontman watched from the Manchester City end as his boyhood club beat United 1-0 in the derby, joining the travelling supporters in performing the Poznan after the final whistle. For Sir Jim Ratcliffe, watching from the directors' box, the scene could hardly have been further from the vision he had when he agreed in December 2023 to spend £1.25 billion for a minority stake in United.

The intention was to restore one of English football's biggest clubs to its former glories. Nearly three years on, United are still searching for the green shoots of that recovery.

The 199th Manchester derby offered an uncomfortable snapshot of their current predicament. United had almost 70 minutes to find a way past a City side reduced to 10 men, yet they struggled to create enough to turn their numerical advantage into a result.

Two efforts did hit the crossbar, Marcus Rashford's free-kick and Kobbie Mainoo's late attempt, but those moments masked an otherwise blunt attacking display. United generated just 0.04 expected goals on target (xGOT) between the seventh and 95th minutes, underlining how little they troubled Gianluigi Donnarumma and the Manchester City defence.

Their clearest opening came in stoppage time, when Bruno Fernandes slipped Bryan Mbeumo into the box, only for Donnarumma to make the save.

Erling Haaland's controversial 60th-minute winner was decisive, but the deeper concern was what happened around it.

The goal should not have stood, with Pro Ref acknowledging the offside error, but there was also a familiar defensive failing in the build-up. Patrick Dorgu followed the ball across the pitch after a miscued header, ending up on the opposite side and leaving Lisandro Martinez facing a two-against-one at the back post. Haaland was able to exploit the space.

Even had the goal been ruled out, however, the larger question would have remained: why could United not break down a 10-man City side for almost 70 minutes?

Their passing lacked the speed and precision required to open up a deep defence, while their attacking movement became increasingly static as City dropped back. United had possession and a numerical advantage, but struggled to turn either into sustained pressure or clear chances.

The contrast in the two squads only made that more striking.

Joshua Zirkzee, a player United had been trying to sell during the summer, was brought on with seven minutes remaining. His most notable contribution was an overhit cross.

City, meanwhile, had Iliman Ndiaye, a £65 million summer signing, who had already made a decisive contribution before the final whistle. Ndiaye won possession after Dorgu's miscued header failed to reach Harry Maguire, starting the move that led to Haaland's winner.

Ndiaye may not maintain that level throughout the season, just as Zirkzee can still have a positive influence at United. But the wider point is difficult to ignore: City have been able to strengthen their squad with targeted additions, while United's work in the transfer window left Michael Carrick with fewer solutions.

The midfield offered another telling contrast. City's pairing of Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez cost a combined £241 million, while United's midfield pivot was assembled for £35 million, the value of Youri Tielemans' release clause, alongside academy graduate Mainoo.

Yet Mainoo arguably had the better of Anderson in several moments, including the tackle that helped set up Rashford's effort against the side-netting. The academy graduate's performance also underlined the curious nature of United's recent recruitment decisions, given that the club were previously open to offers for him at a fraction of the value attached to City's midfielders.

Sunday's derby therefore highlighted more than a difference in spending. It exposed a difference in squad depth, recruitment strategy and the number of solutions available when a game takes an unexpected turn.

United spent £148 million during the summer, yet still appeared short of answers when City went down to 10 men.

And the problems extend well beyond the pitch.

Before the derby even began, United supporters had made their feelings clear. Thousands protested outside Old Trafford, while inside the stadium The Red Army displayed a banner reading: "The way you treat us is a disgrace."

The protests were aimed at the club's ownership and its treatment of match-going supporters, with anger intensified by United's investigation into ticket sharing. The club has said 685 fan accounts were banned, while a further 464 were sanctioned or warned.

The relationship between supporters and the ownership has been deteriorating against a backdrop of severe financial pressure. United's latest accounts showed an overall debt of £1.3 billion, including outstanding transfer fees. The club has also refinanced £314 million of bonds at a higher interest rate and borrowed a further £92.4 million.

For Ratcliffe, the timing could hardly be more uncomfortable.

When chief executive Omar Berrada spoke to staff in September 2024, the stated ambition was for United to win the Premier League title in 2028.

That target now looks increasingly distant.

United have four points from their opening four league games, matching their worst start to a Premier League season since 1992-93. It is also exactly the same points tally they had after four games last season under Ruben Amorim.

Michael Carrick deserves credit for the turnaround that followed his arrival midway through last season, when he helped United secure a third-place finish and Champions League qualification.

But Sunday showed the limits of how far that improvement can carry them without a deeper transformation.

"We haven't got as many points as we would have liked at this point, for sure," Carrick said afterwards. "There's no getting away from that."

There is also no getting away from the larger question facing United.

They have changed managers, restructured their football operation and spent heavily on players. Yet against 10-man City, with Old Trafford demanding answers, they still looked like a team short of both solutions and certainty.

For Noel Gallagher and the blue half of Manchester, the derby was another reason to sing. For the red half, it was another reminder that the road back to the top remains considerably longer than the club hoped.
Author: Tanvir Ahmed Pranto Tanvir Ahmed Pranto

Title: 50% match fee fine and 11-point deduction: Pakistan hit with double WTC blow
Content:
Pakistan have been hit with a pair of sanctions for maintaining a slow over-rate during the third and final ICC World Test Championship contest against England in Birmingham.

Pakistan were ruled to be 11 overs shorts of the target after time allowances were taken into consideration during the Edgbaston Test that England won by eight wickets, with the team fined 50 percent of their match fee as a result and receiving an 11-point deduction in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle.

Ranjan Madugalle of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel of Match Referees imposed the sanction, after on-field umpires Paul Reiffel and Chris Gaffaney, third umpire Allahudien Palekar and fourth umpire Russell Warren levelled the charge.

It means Pakistan lose ground at the bottom of the World Test Championship standings as a result, with the side now sitting in ninth place with a 4.63 points percentage.

In accordance with Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which relates to minimum over-rate offences, players are fined five per cent of their match fee for each over their team fails to bowl within the allotted time, with the maximum penalty capped at 50 percent of the match fee.

In addition, as per Article 16.11.2 of the ICC World Test Championship playing conditions, a side is penalised one point for each over short. Consequently, 11 World Test Championship points have been deducted from Pakistan’s points total.

Pakistan are scheduled to play their next World Test Championship series in November, when they host fellow Asian side Sri Lanka for a two-match Test series in Rawalpindi and Lahore.

First Test: England won by an innings and 103 runs

Second Test: England won by 194 runs

Third Test: England won by eight wickets
Author: ICC

Title: Another day, another Cavan Sullivan show
Content:
Cavan Sullivan is making the extraordinary look routine.

The 16-year-old produced another sensational performance on Monday, scoring twice and setting up another as Philadelphia Union thrashed San Diego FC 5-0 to extend their remarkable surge and strengthen the case for his first United States men's national team call-up.

Sullivan opened the scoring just before half-time with the kind of finish that has become his trademark. The teenager raced into the box to meet Indiana Vassilev's low cross before flicking the ball with his backheel, sending it inside the far post.

CAVAN SULLIVAN BACKHEEL?! 😲 The 16-year-old gives @PhilaUnion the lead in San Diego just before halftime! pic.twitter.com/oSvyKnvfRp

And he wasn’t done there.

In the 62nd minute, Sullivan collected Vassilev's pass and drilled a finish past Duran Ferree from a tight angle for his first MLS brace.

Now he's nutmegged the keeper 😳 Cavan Sullivan gets his brace in style for @PhilaUnion ! pic.twitter.com/IjinRebcch

CAVAN SULLIVAN BRACE.

Less than six minutes later, he showed another side of his game. Carrying the ball infield, Sullivan slowed the move before slipping a perfectly weighted pass through the San Diego defence to help create Philadelphia's third.

“First brace, it was pretty cool,” Sullivan told Apple TV. “I'm really happy to score those ones, but, like I said, three points matters the most.”

Sullivan's opening goal was perhaps the night's signature moment.

“I just remember darting in the box,” he said.

“He lifted his head up, so I knew it wasn't a blind ball. He saw me. We sort of made eye contact.”

“It felt perfect. He just found my back foot and I sort of just, yeah, like you said, back-heeled it. It was really special.”

Sullivan's latest display comes after a remarkable run of form since MLS resumed following the World Cup break.

He had already equalled Freddy Adu's record for the most MLS goal contributions by a player aged 16 or younger with 10, before moving beyond that mark with his goal against CF Montreal last weekend. MLS credited him with becoming the youngest player in league history to record a goal contribution in five consecutive matches.

Cavan Sullivan has been unstoppable. pic.twitter.com/p6kRE7L4Fd

Then came the Cincinnati demolition, when Sullivan supplied three assists in Philadelphia's 5-0 win. That extended his goal-contribution streak to six MLS matches and underlined how rapidly his influence has grown.

Now he has added his first MLS brace and another assist in San Diego.

The backheel made the headlines, but the greater significance may be that Sullivan is increasingly controlling matches rather than simply producing isolated moments of brilliance.

That brings the USMNT into the conversation. Mauricio Pochettino is preparing for a new four-year cycle towards the 2030 World Cup and has spoken openly about using the next camp to introduce younger players. US Soccer says the 26-man squad will be announced on September 17, ahead of friendlies against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada.

Sullivan is now one of the names generating the most interest.

There is no need to rush a 16-year-old into senior international football simply because of a few spectacular weeks. But Sullivan is making the argument harder to ignore with every match.

He is scoring. He is creating. And increasingly, he is deciding games. For now, Philadelphia remains the priority.

But with Pochettino's first 2030-cycle squad approaching, Sullivan has given the USMNT coach a very difficult name to leave off the conversation.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Zverev hails mother's unwavering belief after US Open triumph
Content:
Family was at the heart of Alexander Zverev's U.S. Open triumph on Monday as the German saluted the members of his inner circle and paid a heartfelt tribute to his mother for refusing to let diabetes define his future.

The top seed beat American Ben Shelton 6-3 7-6(2) 5-7 6-2 at Flushing Meadows to finish a spectacular year at the Grand Slams in which he proved his doubters wrong by going from perennial nearly man to two-time major champion.

Shortly after his victory, Zverev reserved special praise for his mother Irina, a former professional tennis player, and credited her with ensuring type 1 diabetes never limited his ambitions in life.

"When your 4-year-old son is diagnosed with diabetes and doctors in the office tell you that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to say 'my son will be whatever he wants to be'," Zverev said.

"'If he wants to be a tennis player, he'll be a tennis player. If he wants to do something else, he'll do something else, but this illness will not define us'.

Zverev gave an emotional speech after winning the U.S. Open about his mom and how she helped him achieve his dreams despite struggling with diabetes “I wanna thank one more person who’s never actually watching my matches but is the most important person in my tennis life and in… pic.twitter.com/xDIRIuvMf2

"I'm happy that we worked through it and we're doing the things that we're doing now. My mother is the most important and strongest person I know because it takes an unbelievably strong woman to do what she did."

The 29-year-old thanked his team, which includes his father Alexander Zverev Sr and his brother Mischa, for their hard work that had delivered him another Grand Slam trophy to add to his Olympic gold medal from the Tokyo Games five years ago.

"We went almost 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now we've won two in a span of three months," Zverev said.

"I think God has seen how hard we've worked, how much we've suffered, how much pain we went through and I think that 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before."
Author: Reuters, New York

Title: 6 wins from 6: Barca can set a new record in their next match
Content:
Barcelona's 2026-27 season could hardly have started in more impressive fashion.

Hansi Flick's side have made a perfect beginning to their competitive campaign, winning all six of their opening matches and creating an atmosphere of growing confidence around the club.

Five of those victories have come in LaLiga, against Elche, Athletic Club, Rayo Vallecano, Valencia and Levante, while the Champions League campaign also began with a win over Feyenoord. Six games, six victories and a 100 percent record have put Barça firmly at the top of the early-season conversation.

The perfect start has also placed Flick's team alongside some of the most successful sides in Barcelona history. Only three previous Barça teams had won their first six competitive matches of a season. The first came almost a century ago, in 1929/30, when James Bellamy's team opened the campaign with six straight victories. In 1960/61, Ljubisa Brocic's side matched the achievement, winning their first four league games before completing the run with victories in both legs of their European Cup tie against Belgian club Lierse.

More than 50 years later, Ernesto Valverde's Barcelona repeated the feat in 2018/19. That particular run was notable because the six victories came across three competitions. Barça began with a Spanish Super Cup victory over Sevilla, followed that with four consecutive LaLiga wins and then defeated PSV 4-0 in the Champions League. Yet all three historic teams eventually failed to win their seventh competitive match.

The 1929-30 side were held by Athletic Club at Les Corts, while the 1960-61 team lost to Atletico Madrid at the Metropolitano. Valverde's 2018-19 Barcelona were stopped by Girona, who earned a 2-2 draw at Camp Nou. Now Flick's team have an opportunity to go one step further and create a new record.

Their latest victory, a hard-fought 4-2 win over Levante in Valencia, showed both the quality and imperfections of the current side. Lamine Yamal was once again decisive, scoring twice, while Xavi Espart and Karim Adeyemi also found the net. The result maintained Barça's perfect league record, with five wins from five and a three-point advantage over Real Madrid.

However, the match also exposed some defensive weaknesses. Barcelona looked comfortable for long periods, but Levante fought back late in the game through goals from Ivan Romero and Roger Brugue, making the final stages unnecessarily tense. Flick admitted afterwards that it was not Barcelona's best performance, particularly in the second half, but he was satisfied with the result and insisted that the team must continue improving.

Rodri's assured presence in midfield and captain Raphinha's relentless running were also important to the victory. Together with Yamal's attacking brilliance, they helped Barcelona overcome a difficult spell and preserve their winning streak.

Now the challenge is clear. Racing Santander stand between Barça and history [1.30am, Bangladesh time, Thursday]. Victory would make it seven consecutive competitive wins to start the season, taking Flick's team beyond every previous Barcelona side that achieved six. The numbers are already impressive, the football is producing results and the belief is growing. For this Barcelona team, the message is simple: just keep on winning.
Author: Agencies

Title: Referee body admits 'error' for Haaland goal in Manchester derby
Content:
Professional Game Referees (Pro Ref) admitted Sunday that the decision to allow Erling Haaland's winner in Manchester City's 1-0 victory over Manchester United was an "error of judgment".

With City down to 10 men after Phil Foden's dismissal for kicking Bruno Fernandes, Haaland netted on the hour mark with a close-range finish from Josko Gvardiol's cross.

The goal was initially disallowed for offside against Haaland but VAR eventually overturned that decision, even though City midfielder Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position and attempted to reach the ball before the Norwegian forward.

Fernandez did not touch the ball so the goal was given, allowing Haaland to celebrate his ninth league strike in Manchester derbies.

Premier League Match Centre posted on social media after the goal to say the VAR "determined that Haaland was in an onside position" and "deemed that while in an offside position, Fernandez didn't play the ball".

However, Pro Ref later on Sunday came out to say that the VAR "did not recognise the likely impact" of the Argentine midfielder's position and "should have recommended an on-field review".

"Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgment. A review of the incident will take place," the statement added.

After the match, United manager Michael Carrick said it was "worrying" that a team of officials had come to the conclusion that Haaland's goal should stand.

Lisandro Martinez was the United defender at the centre of the controversy.

The Argentine said he was clearly impacted by the presence of his international teammate Fernandez and branded the City goal an "injustice".

"I went to him because he was in front of me. That's why Haaland was free at the back," Martinez told Sky Sports.

"Five or six people (officials) doing this kind of mistake in the Premier League is unacceptable.

"We have to go home with this injustice."
Author: AFP, London

Title: India women follow men’s team’s lead, refuse Asia Cup trophy from Naqvi
Content:
India’s unprecedented eighth Women’s Asia Cup title triumph ended in familiar scenes on Sunday night, as the Harmanpreet Kaur-led side refused to receive the trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) president Mohsin Naqvi during the post-match presentation in Dubai.

The presentation ceremony was delayed by nearly 50 minutes after India defeated Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final. Naqvi, who is also the chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board and Pakistan’s interior minister, was present at the ceremony.

Sri Lanka’s players and coaching staff were presented with their runners-up medals before captain Chamari Athapaththu received the runners-up cheque from Naqvi. The ceremony was then abruptly brought to an end, with India’s players neither receiving their tournament medals nor collecting the Asia Cup trophy.

The episode closely mirrored last year’s men’s Asia Cup final at the same venue, when India also declined to accept the trophy from Naqvi.

India’s women’s team instead held its own brief medal presentation while waiting for the official ceremony. Fielding coach Munish Bali presented the best-fielder medal, while BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia handed the award to Nandani Sharma. BCCI vice-president Rajeev Shukla was also present.

The decision came against the backdrop of strained cricketing relations between India and Pakistan following heightened cross-border tensions in May 2025. Since then, Indian teams have avoided handshakes with Pakistan players and officials.

India women’s head coach Amol Muzumdar said the team fully supported the BCCI’s position.

“That stand has been taken by the BCCI and we stand by it. For us, this tournament is over. We are the champions, and that’s good enough. It was on the big board that India are the champions of the Asia Cup 2026,” Muzumdar said.

“This tournament is officially over for us. We are happy that we are the champions and we look forward to the Asian Games.”

Asked when India would receive the trophy or whether the situation could change, Muzumdar said there had been no update.

“No news as yet. So, I cannot answer that,” he said.

Muzumdar was also asked whether the developments surrounding India-Pakistan cricket and trophy presentations could affect the spirit of sportsmanship.

“The stand has been taken by the BCCI and we are united and standing by it. Absolutely,” he said.

“For us, this tournament is officially over. The fact that we are champions, we are really glad and I am really proud of every single person in this unit, including the support staff and the players.”

The controversy came after India had produced a dominant performance in the final, posting 184 before restricting Sri Lanka to secure a 72-run victory.

Captain Harmanpreet Kaur praised her side for maintaining the standards they had set throughout the tournament, particularly on Dubai’s slow pitches.
Author: Agencies

Title: 'Less about the result': Bangladesh seek credibility against DPR Korea
Content:
Although the 20th Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games officially open on September 19, Bangladesh’s campaign begins today, with the women’s football team taking on three-time champions DPR Korea at Nagai Stadium.

Bangladesh, who qualified automatically as participants in the 2026 AFC Women’s Asian Cup, are the lowest-ranked side in the 12-team competition at 107th in the FIFA rankings, 96 places below DPR Korea.

The women in red and green have had a solid build-up for their second Asian Games appearance, combining home training with a 10-day camp in China that included two practice matches.

But British coach Peter Butler is keeping expectations grounded, particularly after Bangladesh suffered a 5-0 defeat to the same opponents at the AFC Women’s Asian Cup in Australia in March.

“We’re playing against a Korean team blessed with really good players. They are well-funded and well-resourced. We played them last time at the Asian Cup and lost 5-0. We didn’t play particularly well, but it was a great learning experience for our young players,” Butler said yesterday.

“For us, it is less about the result and more about credibility. We have to be realistic and pragmatic about what we expect. We want to give a good account of ourselves, put in a positive performance and show what we can do.”

Butler will demand greater defensive organisation against a DPR Korea side that repeatedly exposed Bangladesh’s backline in March, despite being held scoreless in the first half.

“Our plan? We don’t have a real specific plan, but it’s to give a good account of ourselves and be honest with ourselves. Nobody gives us a cat in hell’s chance or any hope of winning, and that may be the case. But it’s all about learning, credibility, and putting in a positive shift and a positive performance tomorrow,” Butler concluded.
Author: Sports Reporter
