Title: This year I deserve Ballon d'Or: Lamine Yamal
Content:
Lamine Yamal believes he and Kylian Mbappe are the two best players in the world and said he deserves to win the 2026 Ballon d'Or after a trophy-laden year with Barcelona and Spain.

"For me, Mbappe and me, we're the two best players in the world," the 19-year-old Barcelona winger said in an interview on Movistar Plus, excerpts of which were published on Sunday.

"I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I've won," he added.

Yamal helped Barcelona retain La Liga before becoming a world champion with Spain this summer, strengthening his claim for the game's most prestigious individual award.

He had struck a more measured tone at a press conference last Tuesday, saying he believed he had a chance after an "incredible" season but would not beg for votes.

Mbappe, meanwhile, has also made his case for the award in recent days.

The France captain finished as top scorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup, although Real Madrid failed to win a major trophy.

Yamal's Barcelona and Spain teammate Ousmane Dembele, last year's winner, believes the award should remain with a Paris Saint-Germain player after the French club retained the Champions League.

Bayern Munich striker and England international Harry Kane is also among the favourites to win the award, which will be issued in London on October 26.
Author: AFP, Barcelona

Title: Ronaldo condemns ‘unacceptable’ chants about Diogo Jota, calls for lifetime bans
Content:
Cristiano Ronaldo said on Sunday that fans who appeared to make chants referencing former teammate Diogo Jota at Ruben Neves during a Saudi Pro League match should be banned from football stadiums for life.

The chants occurred on Saturday during a fixture between Al-Taawoun and Neves' side Al-Hilal in Buraidah, Saudi Arabia.

Jota died on July 3, 2025, in a car crash in Zamora, northwestern Spain, along with his brother Andre Silva. A close friend of Jota, Neves was a pallbearer at his funeral.

Footage filmed from the stands during the match and circulated on social media appeared to show supporters chanting 'Jota'.

The shouts attracted the attention of Neves, who pointed to his eye and then up to the sky in response.

Passing through the mixed zone after the game, Neves commented, "I hope they don't go to pray afterwards."

In response to an Instagram post showing the footage, Ronaldo commented from his personal account.

"The league must take action and punish this kind of fan behaviour," said Ronaldo.

"This is no longer football, and there have to be limits. People who behave like this should never be allowed to enter a stadium again."

The game finished 6-0 to Al-Hilal, with Neves playing 75 minutes before being substituted.

Al-Hilal Club Company announced in a statement on its website on Sunday that it had filed a complaint with the Saudi Arabian Football Federation relating to the incident. The Saudi Pro League club were "confident" that measures would be taken to "protect the integrity of sporting competition from offensive practices."

"The Company expressed its absolute rejection of such actions targeting players or their families, or intended to cause personal offence," said Al-Hilal's statement.

Later on Sunday, Al-Taawoun also released a statement, which strongly condemned the offensive chants.

"Such conduct is completely unacceptable and does not represent Al-Taawoun, its supporters or the values for which its terraces are known."

Al-Taawoun added that it would "take all necessary measures in coordination with the relevant authorities to prevent a recurrence and hold offenders accountable."

The Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF) and the Saudi Pro League (SPL) also condemned the supporters' behaviour on Sunday.

In a joint statement, SAFF and the SPL said the conduct of some fans during the match was "inconsistent with the values of Saudi football and the principles of sportsmanship."

The governing bodies added that exploiting personal tragedies "for the purpose of abuse or provocation is unacceptable behaviour that has no place in Saudi football."

SAFF said the relevant committees had identified the conduct in question and would take the necessary action in accordance with applicable regulations and procedures, with the outcome to be announced once the process is completed.
Author: Reuters

Title: Zverev beats Shelton to win US Open title
Content:
Alexander Zverev beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (7/2), 5-7, 6-2 to win the US Open on Sunday, expunging the memory of a bitter Flushing Meadows defeat with his second Grand Slam title.

The top-seeded German, who was within two points of the US Open crown in 2020 but fell in five agonizing sets to Dominic Thiem, added the trophy to the French Open title he captured this year.

He denied Shelton's bid to become the first US man in 23 years to lift a Grand Slam trophy.

The 23-year-old Shelton was one month shy of his first birthday when Andy Roddick hoisted the 2003 US Open trophy in the last major triumph for a US man.

Hopes were high that Shelton could end the drought after his epic five-set quarter-final victory over defending champion Carlos Alcaraz, and a come-from-behind win over compatriot Frances Tiafoe in the semi-finals.

But Zverev's all-court excellence proved too much for Shelton, despite the support of a star-studded Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd trying to will the American to victory.

With their backing, Shelton surged in the third set, eliminating the errors that Zverev had ruthlessly exploited.

Serving to extend the set, Zverev fell behind 0-40. Shelton fired long on his first set point but on the second Zverev's forehand volley went wide. Shelton had his first break of the match and they were headed to a fourth set.

Zverev responded immediately, running Shelton ragged through a 24-shot rally until Shelton sailed a backhand wide to drop his serve in the opening game of the fourth set.

Even with a break in hand, Zverev was feeling the tension, from a determined Shelton and the hostile crowd.

At 30-30 in the fourth game, he received a time violation warning as he prepared to serve, but shook it off and won the game with a crisp crosscourt backhand that put him up 3-1.

He rolled home, lifting his arms in triumph after Shelton fired a serve return long on match point and finally receiving his own huge cheer from the crowd.
Author: AFP, New York

Title: Cricketers embrace coaching culture
Content:
Coaching is gaining traction in Bangladesh cricket, with active players increasingly eager to understand the game from a different perspective. Their growing interest in coaching education is a sign of a maturing cricket culture, where understanding the game and its nuances is becoming as important as playing it.

The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) began a Level 1 coaching course on Saturday, bringing together current domestic cricketers, recently retired players and other members of the cricket fraternity. Former national team star Mahmudullah Riyad is among the participants, while prominent coaches Mohammad Salahuddin, Sohel Islam and Naveed Nawaz are leading the sessions.

The BCB selected 33 participants from those who submitted their CVs, with players such as Rony Talukder and national team analyst Shaon Jahan also taking part. BCB officials said many participants were interested in pursuing coaching, while the five-day course was also designed to help players develop a better understanding of the game during their playing careers.

Fundamentals, biomechanics, planning and programming, and skill acquisition are among the key areas covered in the course.

“This Level 1 course consists entirely of players, including current, first-class, national team, and ex-players,” coach Sohel Islam, one of the instructors, told The Daily Star on Sunday.

“Previously, they did not participate in such large groups. It is a very positive sign for Bangladesh that big players are showing interest and stepping into coaching. Along with the [playing] experience they already have, this course will help them in coaching and has the potential to be valuable for the country,” he added.

The BCB has already conducted Level 3 and Level 2 coaching courses this year.

In England, many first-class cricketers undertake Level 1 coaching courses, a practice Sohel believes can contribute to players’ personal growth and help them assist teammates.

“Not sure if it is mandatory in England, but it helps with cricketers’ personal growth and it also equips them to assist other players within their teams,” he said.

While former players moving into coaching is not a new phenomenon, the interest shown by active cricketers reflects a broader shift in Bangladesh cricket. Players are increasingly recognising the value of understanding not just how to execute a skill, but also why it works, how to develop it and how to help others improve.

“When we came into coaching, the professionalism surrounding it currently was not there. Today, coaching is a respected and established profession worldwide. It offers a solid career path with better financial prospects than before, which naturally attracts more players to consider it,” Sohel said.

Pacer Kamrul Islam Rabbi, who was undergoing National Cricket League practice in Barishal, travelled to Mirpur to attend the course.

“In England we see this helping players to mature even during U-19 days,” Rabbi said. “It’s a BCB programme and they run them quite regularly. For me, even if I want to affiliate myself with any sector of sports, not just coaching, I need to know these things since I will be playing cricket for another three-four years. The renowned coaches of the country are taking the course and there is a lot to learn.”

For Rabbi, the course is not merely preparation for life after cricket, but an opportunity to understand the game more deeply while he is still playing.

“I want to undertake Level 2 and 3 as well. I will gradually start them and this is the first step. Since Level 1 delves into the process of developing young players step-by-step, I feel it was valuable to start the course now,” he said.

As more players embrace coaching education, the benefits could extend beyond their individual careers. A stronger understanding of technique, planning and player development can eventually enrich the next generation of cricketers, making the growing coaching culture a promising sign for the future of Bangladesh cricket.
Author: A Abdullah Al Mehdi Abdullah Al Mehdi

Title: India crush Sri Lanka to win eighth Women's Asia Cup title
Content:
Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana laid the foundation with a record opening stand before India’s spin attack completed the job as they beat Sri Lanka by 72 runs at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Sunday to win their eighth Women’s Asia Cup title and fourth in the T20 format.

Shafali smashed 68 off 39 balls and Mandhana struck 59 off 39 as the pair added 129 for the first wicket, the highest partnership for any wicket in Women’s T20 Asia Cup history. Their assault helped India post 183-5.

Sri Lanka struggled to build momentum in the chase despite India putting down five catches. Deepti Sharma took 3-19 and Shree Charani 4-20 as the Indian spinners kept the Lankans under pressure throughout.

Chamari Athapaththu top-scored with 36, but Sri Lanka were eventually bundled out for 111. India now lead Sri Lanka 6-1 in Asia Cup final meetings.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Tigers begin Asian Games camp, hope to get ‘adequate’ preparation
Content:
Bangladesh began their Asian Games preparation camp on Sunday, returning to T20 cricket for the first time since their full series in Zimbabwe in July. With concerns over the facilities in Japan, adequate preparation is the priority as the Tigers prepare to depart for the tournament on September 24, ahead of their opening match in the quarterfinals on September 28.

At least half of the squad, including skipper Litton Das, Najmul Hossain Shanto and Mustafizur Rahman, were present as the Tigers began their preparations. The team are still awaiting the arrival of players who recently featured in the ‘A’ team’s tour of South Africa. National team head coach Phil Simmons attended the session, while Mohammad Salahuddin, head coach for the Asian Games tournament, conducted the preparations.

“We may not have access to adequate facilities in Japan, so we have to make the most of what is available here and complete as much of our preparation as possible before leaving. We are structuring our practice sessions accordingly,” a member of the team management informed.

The Tigers will also play two practice games in Mirpur on September 21 and 23.

Bangladesh clinched the gold medal at the 2010 Asian Games in Guangzhou, China, and the feat remains their only gold medal at the Asian Games to date. The last time they appeared in the event, the Tigers won bronze by beating Pakistan by six wickets. This time, they are once again aiming for gold, having named a strong outfit featuring several senior national team players.

“The goal is to definitely go for gold medal. Given that we have not played T20 cricket for quite some time, the goal in terms of preparation is to get into T20 rhythm,” a member of the coaching staff said.

It is understood that a drop-in wicket is likely to be used during the tournament. The Tigers’ main concern will be regaining their batting rhythm after a lengthy break from the format, and batting will be given priority as the tournament approaches. Mustafizur was the only bowler to bowl at the two centre wickets during the batting session.

“We practiced on the [two] centre wickets and slabs were also used. Everyone got a chance to bat on the two centre wickets,” the coaching staff said as preparations kicked into gear for another gold-medal bid.
Author: Sports Reporter

Title: Ferran Torres fires PSG to first win of Ligue 1 season
Content:
Ferran Torres was on target as champions Paris Saint-Germain finally got their Ligue 1 campaign up and running with a 1-0 win at Brest on Sunday.

Prior to their trip to Brittany, Luis Enrique's double Champions League-winning side had managed just two points from their opening three matches in an uncharacteristically sluggish start to the league season.

They began their quest to win a third consecutive Champions League title by thrashing Slovan Bratislava 6-1 on Wednesday and four days later they are now off the mark domestically thanks to new signing Torres.

The close-season arrival from Barcelona, who scored the winning goal for Spain in the World Cup final this summer, netted a hat-trick midweek and followed it up with a sumptuous early strike at Brest's Stade Francis-Le Ble.

Torres, 26, now has six goals in five outings in all competitions for PSG.

The result sent the Parisians up to seventh in the league table, with an identical record to their hosts, who had been unbeaten heading into the encounter.

Ahead of kick-off, Brest paid tribute to their former coach Eric Roy, who died in June aged 58 after suffering from pancreatic cancer.

PSG got the crucial breakthrough in the fifth minute when Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele flicked a backheel into the path of the onrushing Torres.

The Spaniard strode onto the ball just outside the 'D' and caressed it into the bottom corner beyond the dive of goalkeeper Egil Selvik.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia then went close to doubling PSG's lead in an entertaining first half.

It was not all good news for PSG in the opening period, however, as Morocco captain and right-back Achraf Hakimi limped off just before half-time to be replaced by midfielder Fabian Ruiz.

Brest came within a whisker of equalising five minutes after the interval when Nuno Mendes carelessly played the ball across for Kamory Doumbia, but the forward saw his effort rebound off the post when he had only goalkeeper Matvey Safonov to beat.

The hosts then turned into their own net two minutes later but the goal was disallowed for a push by Warren Zaire-Emery, which forced the error.

Safonov was the hero for PSG late on as he got down quickly to fingertip a Pathe Mboup effort past his far post as Luis Enrique's side held on for the victory.

Earlier, Ethan Mbappe redeemed himself after his Champions League red card in midweek by scoring a late goal in a 2-0 win over Troyes which sent Lille top of Ligue 1.

Mbappe, the younger brother of France and Real Madrid star Kylian, was sent off in Wednesday's 3-2 home loss to Real Betis in Europe for elbowing an opponent.

The 19-year-old put that incident behind him, though, as he came off the bench against Troyes to seal victory in stoppage time, after the hosts had taken a first-half lead through Portuguese full-back Tiago Santos.

Mbappe celebrated his first goal since December in subdued fashion by apologising to supporters for his red card, but the strike lifted Lille above Monaco and Rennes on goal difference at the top of the table.

Lille have taken 10 points from a possible 12 under new coach Davide Ancelotti, the son of Brazil boss Carlo Ancelotti.

Last season's surprise title challengers, Lens, have found the going tougher this season in Ligue 1.

A 3-2 Champions League win on Thursday at Slavia Prague and victory over PSG in the French Champions' Trophy last month stand in juxtaposition to a difficult early domestic campaign.

They now have just four points from as many outings following a 2-2 draw away to newly-promoted Le Mans on Sunday, which leaves them in ninth.
Author: AFP, Paris

Title: VAR controversy rocks Manchester derby: Why Haaland’s goal stood and Foden saw red
Content:
Manchester City won the 199th Manchester derby 1-0 at Old Trafford on Sunday despite playing with 10 men for most of the match, but the game was overshadowed by two major VAR controversies involving Phil Foden’s red card and Erling Haaland’s winning goal.

Both decisions were based on the precise wording of the International Football Association Board (IFAB) Laws of the Game. However, they also raised questions about how those laws are applied to situations that can look very different in real time.

The first major incident came in the 23rd minute. Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes tangled with Foden and bundled the England international heavily to the ground before remaining over him aggressively.

Foden reacted while lying on his back, kicking both legs upwards and catching Fernandes in the midriff with his studs.

Referee Michael Oliver immediately showed Foden a straight red card. His explanation over the match communications system was: “Red card Phil Foden -- kick out into the body of Bruno.”

VAR quickly reviewed the incident and agreed with the decision.

“That looks like a clear red card to me. Looks to be a secondary movement. Confirming the red card for Manchester City No.47,” the VAR said.

The key phrase used was “secondary movement.” Under IFAB Law 12, violent conduct is when a player uses or attempts to use excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball. In refereeing terms, a secondary movement can separate an accidental or involuntary movement from a deliberate act of retaliation.

Foden’s initial movement came as he fell to the ground. But once that movement had stopped, his kick was considered a separate action. The ball was not being contested, the challenge was over and his studs made contact with Fernandes’ body. That meant VAR had little room to overturn the decision. Under the strict interpretation of the law, the red card was justified.

However, City’s frustration was that Fernandes was not punished for his role in starting the confrontation. In modern refereeing, the player who starts an incident can escape punishment if their initial action is judged careless or reckless rather than violent, while the player who retaliates can often receive the heavier punishment, which has been one of the criticisms of VAR in recent times.

The bigger controversy came around the hour mark when Haaland scored the winner.

City sent the ball into the United penalty area, where Enzo Fernandez made a diving attempt to head it. He missed, and Haaland pounced. The assistant referee initially flagged Haaland for offside, but VAR overturned the decision.

Semi-automated offside technology showed that Haaland was marginally onside, with the trailing boot of a recovering defender keeping him level.

The question, then, was whether Fernandez had interfered with play. Fernandez was in an offside position when he attempted to head the ball, but simply being offside does not mean a player has committed an offence under IFAB Law 11.

An offside player can be penalised if they interfere with an opponent by challenging for the ball, clearly attempting to play a nearby ball in a way that affects an opponent, or making an obvious action that affects an opponent’s ability to play the ball.

Fernandez’s diving attempt appeared to meet the second and third conditions. He tried to play a nearby ball, and his movement caused defender Lisandro Martinez to react. Behind him, Martinez had to adjust his position, change his stride and prepare for Fernandez’s movement before trying to clear the ball.

However, VAR took a narrower view. Fernandez did not touch the ball, make contact with Martinez or block the goalkeeper’s line of sight. Officials therefore decided that Martinez was still able to play the ball and that Fernandez had not interfered enough to be penalised.

The official explanation was: “VAR checked the referee’s call of no goal for offside -- and determined that Haaland was in an onside position and recommended that the goal was awarded. The VAR also deemed that while in an offside position, Fernandez didn’t play the ball.”

VAR's decision to overturn the assistant referee's call drew criticism from former Manchester United defender Gary Neville, who was working as a co-commentator for Sky Sports.

“I'm going to need the offside rule explained to me because it's lost me,” Neville said during the broadcast. “I think when they look back at this, they will recognise they got it wrong.”

Neville’s argument was that the decision did not take into account how defenders actually react in these situations.

A defender cannot simply ignore a player making a diving attempt at a ball. The attacker’s movement can force the defender to shift his weight, change his position and adjust his timing, even if there is no physical contact.

Martinez, who was directly involved in the incident, was also unhappy with the decision.

“Every season, they come to explain their rules and then they make that kind of mistake,” the Argentine said after the match. “It's an injustice.”

Under the strict interpretation of the IFAB laws, both decisions can be explained.

Foden’s kick was considered a clear act of violent conduct because it was a separate, deliberate movement towards Fernandes after the initial collision had ended.

Fernandez, meanwhile, was in an offside position but was judged not to have interfered with Martinez enough to meet the threshold under Law 11.

The laws are designed to give officials clear technical standards, but football is also played through instinct, movement and split-second reactions.

In Foden’s case, VAR focused on the final kick rather than the confrontation that preceded it. In Haaland’s goal, it focused on whether Fernandez physically crossed the threshold for interference rather than how his movement affected Martinez’s attempt to defend.

The Manchester derby therefore offered another example of the tension between the technical wording of football’s laws and the way the game is experienced on the pitch.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Haaland fires 10-man Man City to memorable win over Man Utd
Content:
Erling Haaland fired 10-man Manchester City to a memorable 1-0 victory over Manchester United despite Phil Foden's first-half red card to extend a perfect start to Enzo Maresca's reign.

Foden kicked out at United captain Bruno Fernandes on 23 minutes to give the visitors a mountain to climb.

But a new-look City were up to the challenge as the near £250 million ($340 million) midfield pairing of Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez proved their worth.

Haaland's winner was laced with controversy as Fernandez was deemed not to be interfering with play when he attempted to head in before the ball reached the Norwegian.

Defeat compounds a miserable Premier League start for United as they are already eight points adrift of City and defending champions Arsenal.

By contrast, victory was a huge statement for Maresca to quell fears of a major drop-off from City following Pep Guardiola's trophy-laden decade in charge.

A fervent pre-match atmosphere was fuelled just as much by United fans' anger towards their own club as it was by the usual animosity between the supporters.

A crackdown on ticket touting in recent months has resulted in widespread condemnation from supporters' groups after many innocent people faced the threat of sanction.

A normal array of banners and flags in the Stretford End was replaced by just one bearing the message: "The way you treat us is a disgrace."

The visitors had made the better start in the opening quarter but looked to have been completely undone by Foden's ill discipline.

City will argue Fernandes should also have seen red as he fouled Foden and then kicked him in the back.

But there was little case for Foden's defence as he retaliated by throwing both legs up into Fernandes's midriff.

Kobbie Mainoo blocked Rayan Cherki's goalbound effort before Youri Tielemans nearly sliced Antoine Semenyo's cross into his own net as City continued to be the more threatening.

Marcus Rashford was inches away from his first United goal since December 2024 when his free-kick came crashing back off the post with United's best effort before the break.

The woodwork came to City's rescue again just after half-time when Mainoo curled onto the post from distance and the ball rebounded kindly into Gianluigi Donnarumma's grasp.

But the City sucker punch arrived on the hour mark.

Haaland adjusted his body brilliantly to sweep in Josko Gvardiol's deflected cross.

A VAR review deemed Haaland was onside and that Fernandez was not interfering as he stooped to try and head in himself.

City came close to landing the telling blow when Fernandez's effort was turned onto the post by Senne Lammens.

Haaland also should have had a second when he got onto Fernandez's wicked low free-kick delivery.

City, though, were not made to pay for failing to add a second as United lacked the composure and quality to make the man advantage count until the final minute of stoppage time.

Fernandes's reverse ball perfectly picked out Bryan Mbeumo but he was denied by a fine save from Donnarumma.

Maresca scampered down the touchline in delight at full-time.

After a battle for the title went down to the final week of last season, Arsenal and City look a class apart from the competition once more.

Both are locked on 12 points with Chelsea, Liverpool and United already cut adrift.
Author: AFP, Manchester

Title: Yamal brace helps Barcelona beat Levante
Content:
Lamine Yamal scored twice as Barcelona continued their perfect start to the season with a hard-fought 4-2 LaLiga victory over Levante in Valencia on Sunday.

Xavi Espart and Karim Adeyemi were also on target for Barcelona, who are alone at the top of the LaLiga table with five wins from five, three points ahead of Real Madrid.

Barcelona went ahead after five minutes when a slick one-touch move ended with 19-year-old Espart firing home from the edge of the box via a slight deflection for his first senior goal.

Barcelona continued to dominate possession and doubled their advantage in the 19th minute. Raphinha controlled Fermin Lopez's through ball expertly and picked out an unmarked Lamine in the centre of the box for an easy finish.

Levante rallied after their early struggles, applying some pressure of their own,and despite failing to create a clear opening, ended the half with six attempts to Barcelona's three.

A limping Gerard Martin was targeted by Levante's forwards, and withdrawn by Barcelona manager Hansi Flick at halftime,replaced by Andreas Christensen.

Barcelona struck when Aissa Mandi conceded a penalty for a foul on Lamine 42 seconds after the restart. The winger converted the spot kick to complete his third double in as many LaLiga matches and puncture Levante's growing belief that they could fight their way back into the contest.

Levante came close on the hour when Victor Garcia beat goalkeeper Joan Garcia, but a partial block by Pau Cubarsi and Christensen's goal-line clearance combined to keep his effort out.

An errant pass from Espart in the 79th minute allowed Levante to pull one back, with forward Ivan Romero rounding Joan Garcia before passing the ball into the net.

Nine minutes later, Roger Brugue burst through multiple Barcelona challenges to reduce the deficit to one goal as what looked like a comfortable Barcelona win threatened to turn into a heroic Levante comeback.

Yet Adeyemi's mazy run and smart finish in the 93rd minute ended the hosts' hopes of a draw. The home crowd nevertheless showed their appreciation for the fighting spirit shown by their side, chanting 'Levante' as the German celebrated his goal.

Despite their late wobble, Barcelona secured a sixth successive win in all competitions, with Rodri's assured midfield display and captain Raphinha's relentless running central to their success.
Author: Reuters, Valencia

Title: Can Ronaldo crown his career with Asian Champions League glory?
Content:
Cristiano Ronaldo will have a last crack at winning the Asian Champions League when the continent's top club competition begins on Monday, with big-spending Saudi teams set to dominate.

The 41-year-old former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus superstar said in August that it was "probably my last year in football".

The Portuguese attacker has nearly won it all during his club career, including five UEFA Champions League crowns.

But the Asian Champions League has so far eluded the five-time Ballon d'Or winner.

His Al Nassr side go into the latest continental campaign under a new coach in former Tottenham manager Ange Postecoglou, who was sacked by Spurs in June 2025 despite taking them to Europa League glory.

Along with Ronaldo, the Riyadh-based outfit have proven international attacking quality in Kingsley Coman, Sadio Mane and Ronaldo's Portugal team-mate Joao Felix.

Al Nassr are second in the Saudi Pro League after six matches, behind Al Hilal only on goal difference.

The skipper Ronaldo has been in good form, scoring three times in five league games.

Simone Inzaghi's Al Hilal present a major obstacle in Ronaldo's bid to win the AFC Champions League for the first time.

Al Hilal were major spenders in the recent transfer window, snapping up Aston Villa's England striker Ollie Watkins and Brazil winger Gabriel Martinelli from Arsenal for a combined $150 million.

The format of the Asian Champions League is heavily skewed in favour of teams from Saudi Arabia, which is spending vast fortunes on football and will host the 2034 World Cup.

Since the 2024-2025 season the competition was rebranded as the Champions League Elite and the quarter-finals, semis and final are held in a centralised location in Saudi Arabia.

Al Ahli made the most of home advantage by winning the title in 2025 and 2026.

An Al Ahli side with England's Ivan Toney in attack beat Japan's Machida Zelvia 1-0 in extra time in April's final on home turf in Jeddah.

Al Nassr, Al Ahli and Al Hilal will be joined in this year's competition by Al Ittihad and Al Qadsiah, making it a bumper five Saudi sides among the 32 teams.

As in recent years, the competition is divided equally into two leagues of East and West.

Each side will play four matches at home and four away.

The biggest threat to the Saudi stranglehold will likely come from Japan -- teams from Asia's strongest footballing nation have reached the final in each of the last four editions.

There are also five J. League teams, prime among them reigning domestic champions Kashima Antlers.

Former Kashima star Yasushi Endo admitted the Saudi teams would be hard to beat.

"It's difficult for Japanese teams to be champions these days given the financial strength of teams in the West who can invest heavily in players that traditionally play in strong European leagues," he said.

"With the tournament being played in a centralised format in the West, it also makes things extra difficult.

"We cannot underplay the importance of having large fan support."
Author: AFP, Hong Kong

Title: Bangladesh finish fifth, remain hopeful of World Cup chance
Content:
Bangladesh’s U-20 women’s team ended their Junior Asia Cup campaign on a winning note, beating Malaysia 2-1 in the fifth-place play-off in Hukunbir City, China, today to secure fifth place and keep alive their hopes of reaching next year’s Junior World Cup.

After a goalless first half, captain Sharika Rimon broke the deadlock in the 31st minute, converting a penalty stroke to put Bangladesh 1-0 ahead.

Bangladesh doubled their advantage five minutes into the fourth period when Kona Akter scored from a field goal in the 50th minute.

Malaysia pulled one back through Irdina Jeffrey in the 59th minute, but Bangladesh held on to secure the victory and finish fifth in the tournament.

The result could yet prove significant for Bangladesh’s hopes of making the Junior World Cup for the first time. Their direct route to next year’s tournament ended in the quarterfinals, where they lost 2-0 to Japan. Bangladesh needed to reach at least the semi-finals to secure direct qualification.

However, a route to the World Cup remains open if next year’s Women’s Junior World Cup is held in India.

Under the qualification rules, if the host nation secures a World Cup place through its continental qualification route, an additional team from the same continent gets the opportunity to qualify.

As Bangladesh finished fifth in the Junior Asia Cup, they would be in line for that place.

Coach Zahid Hossain Raju said, “Officials of the Asian Hockey Federation and people from several other teams have told us that we have a chance of playing in the World Cup if we finish fifth. We should be able to confirm the matter within a few days.”

Bangladesh had made a dominant start to the tournament, sweeping aside all four opponents in the group stage. They beat Chinese Taipei 7-0, Pakistan 5-1, Kazakhstan 4-0 and Hong Kong 6-0 before the quarter-final defeat to Japan.

The fifth-place victory over Malaysia ensured Bangladesh finished the campaign with five wins from six matches, having scored 26 goals and conceded just five across the tournament.
Author: Star Sports Desk

Title: Japan end Bangladesh’s unbeaten run, World Cup dream
Content:
Bangladesh’s hopes of securing a place in the FIH Women’s Junior World Cup were dashed on Thursday as the women in red and green suffered a 2-0 defeat to Japan in the quarterfinals of the Women’s Junior Asia Cup in China.

Bangladesh will now play a fifth-sixth place-deciding match against either Malaysia or South Korea. The top four teams in the tournament will qualify for the next edition of the Women’s Junior World Cup.

The women in red and green entered the quarterfinals as unbeaten champions of the Challenger Pool, having won all four of their matches. But they fell short against Japan, who finished third in the Elite Pool, in the teams’ maiden meeting at this level.

Arif Ali’s charges fought hard against a strong Japanese side and kept them at bay until Yoshino Hirai converted a penalty stroke in the 26th minute to give Japan the lead.

Bangladesh pushed for an equaliser but could not break down Japan, who sealed the victory in the 47th minute when Momoka Suzuki scored from open play.

Despite missing out on the semifinals and, with it, a maiden Junior World Cup ticket, head coach Arif Ali took pride in his side’s performance against Japan and looked forward to producing a strong result in their fifth-sixth place-deciding match.
Author: Star Sports Report

Title: New No. 1 Rybakina sets up Gauff semi; Zverev rolls through
Content:
Elena Rybakina ended Zheng Qinwen's spirited US Open run on Wednesday, guaranteeing her rise to world No. 1 as she booked a semi-final showdown with Coco Gauff.

Rybakina beat Zheng 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 and is assured of ending Aryna Sabalenka's reign atop the standings -- even if the Belarusian wins a third straight title.

"It's just a number right now," Rybakina said. "It's a different achievement ... but mostly you think about the titles in the end of the day."

Therefore the 27-year-old Kazakh star will be focused on Gauff, who saved two match points in a 2-6, 7-6 (9/7), 6-2 victory over Russian 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva, the fifth-ranked reigning French Open champion from Russia.

Sabalenka will play third-seeded Jessica Pegula in Thursday night's semi-finals -- the first time since 1975 at the US Open that the top four women all made it to the penultimate round.

Top-seeded Alexander Zverev completed the men's semi-final lineup, cruising past Botic van de Zandschulp 6-2, 7-5, 6-1.

Gauff made it by the skin of her teeth, struggling early and saving two match points in the tiebreaker.

She rallied with some inspiration from Frances Tiafoe's come-from-behind five-set victory over Alex Michelsen.

"I just had to reset," Gauff said. "Honestly, I was thinking about Frances Tiafoe and how he came back. I was just trying to leave the court without regrets."

Rybakina, the first Kazakh player to reach number one, is chasing a third Grand Slam title after winning the Australian Open in January -- four years after winning Wimbledon.

"I feel like you will appreciate and think about it even more when you finish your career," she said of the ranking. "Like now, you still need to keep on going."

Reigning Olympic champion Zheng, a former world number four ranked 121 after missing about eight months due to elbow surgery, went through qualifying and won seven matches in New York, including comeback wins over six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek and former Australian Open winner Madison Keys

She rocked Rybakina early behind fierce serve and a variety of shots, effectively neutralizing the Kazakh's power until a slight dip allowed Rybakina to seize control in the second set.

In a close third Zheng missed a chance to break in the third game. Rybakina broke her in the next and rocketed to victory.

"I got lot of chances in the third set, but I didn't took it," Zheng said. "That was a bit pity for me to lose this match, but obviously I could take positive things from US Open this year."

Zverev rolls through

Zverev was largely untroubled against Dutch veteran van de Zandschulp, who upset Carlos Alcaraz in the second round two years ago and beat sixth-seeded Australian Alex de Minaur in the second round last week.

The reigning French Open champion won the last five games of the opening set to go one set up after just 37 minutes, and saved a set point in the penultimate game of the second before breaking van de Zandschulp to pocket the set.

He ran away with it in the third to give himself another early night in a tournament that saw him labor into the early hours of the morning in first- and second-round five-setters.

Zverev will face veteran Karen Khachanov for a place in Sunday's final.

Khachanov advanced when Belgian Alexander Blockx retired from their quarter-final with the Russian leading 6-2, 7-5, 3-2.

"I saw really that he was suffering all over his body," Khachanov said of 21-year-old Blockx, who had already been on the verge of retiring from his fourth-round win over Francisco Cerundolo with a rib injury.

On Wednesday he played with one thigh wrapped and had medical timeouts for treatment on one foot and pain in his lower back that hindered him much of the match.

"I think today my body just gave up," Blockx said. "I think I finally understand how physical the slams are."
Author: AFP, New York

Title: Meet Purna, the new generation’s keeper of Old Dhaka
Content:
At a time when the past can feels increasingly distant, Maliha Masharat Hossain Purna is bringing old Dhaka’s colours, stories, and traditions to a new generation.

My impression of Generation Z is that they move through the world with a cultural and historical amnesia. Their online culture, behaviours, and values are constantly refreshing and prioritising what’s trending or visually striking. In that rhythm, yesterday’s post is already forgotten, last year’s event feels ancient, and national history that is decades or centuries old barely registers.

Patriotism or cultural heritage doesn’t anchor them the way it did for older generations. Raised on smartphones and high‑speed internet, how else could they be?

Yet when I came across Purna in an Instagram reel, I felt the exact opposite.

At 23, Maliha Masharat Hossain Purna stands out for her devotion to Dhaka’s old soul. She is an influencer, and in her reels, the lanes and locales are not just about nostalgia; they are living textures carrying the essence of Dhaka in the 1900s.

She carries a vintage heart, weaving velvet dreams much like her grandmother once did, recreating era-based looks in today’s street‑side chic. The illusion of vintage touches sealed the look: her hair tied into a braid with silk tassels in riotous colour swinging past the hip, her outfit defined by the loose shalwar, a short, straight kurti, and a dupatta. Flat leather sandals, bangles stacked high, long jhumkas brushing the neck — practical yet ornate, folk yet regal, echoing the rhythm of pre‑Partition streets and festivals.

The jewellery, bangles, tassels — even the garments — are handmade or thrifted, sometimes bought for Tk 30 from Shahbagh.

Shankhari Bazar was her first canvas, where she wandered without a plan, taking in the street’s pulse, and claimed it as her own.

Puja items stacked in corners, brassware glinting in shopfronts, rudraksha beads strung like quiet prayers, shola crowns waiting for festivals — all of that, some say, is like “a piece of Kolkata,” but she shrugs off the cliché, insisting it belongs to Bangladesh’s own Bengali culture, a weave of Hindu and Muslim traditions.

Her creative journey began at home. Purna’s mother, who stitches all her clothes by hand, is her first collaborator. From her, she inherited not only garments but memories — like the tassel her grandmother once wore, which Purna researched and re‑imagined, improvising her vintage look that feels both personal and historical.

She replicated wedding zari, which were basically shimmery metallic ribbons of gold or silver that were popular in weddings, especially in the 1970s, reminiscent of her parents’ marriage; used her grandmother’s fan to evoke vintage moods; and wore jewellery passed down through generations.

She has a collector’s instinct; these objects are not props but vessels of memory.

Her presentation style is deliberately cinematic. She chooses Hindi songs from that era, and when I saw her walking to one in that attire, I was thrilled to feel that the baton of old‑world charm has been successfully handed down to Gen Z.

Her reels are not made for virality; she films for herself, sending drafts to her mother before posting. And with the internet now flooded by 1947 Partition stories, especially those revisiting Bengal’s fashion before independence, her reel found a perfectly timed boost.

She insists that if even one young person chooses to love Dhaka in this way, its history, colours, and vibrancy will endure. In her thrifted rings, rooftop setups, and insistence on talking to strangers, she embodies a rare kind of generational defiance.

This thoughtful gesture about my Dhaka — and that too from someone this young — makes me believe the city’s mosaic of colours and stories will linger for a few more decades through young Dhakaites like Purna.

For her, connecting with people is as important as curating looks. She delights in conversations with tea sellers and strangers, and asks for a candid photo to capture the moment.

She wants highlights of other places too — Banglabazar, vinyl and cassette shops, hand‑painted signboard makers. She wants to show people what still exists, what is fading, and what deserves recognition.

Her plans to explore Dhaka through documenting overlooked corners of culture are ambitious yet grounded. At 23, she is determined to collect, preserve, and re‑imagine the city’s memory, making Dhaka look like a visual poem, where nostalgia and dreams blur into one.
Author: R RBR RBR

Title: Weavers and the human cost of Tangail tant
Content:
A Tangail saree can pass through many hands before it reaches the buyer who eventually unfolds it across a shop counter. There is yarn to source, a design to choose, a loom to prepare, a trader to finance the production, another to take it to market, and finally a retailer who gives the finished product its price tag. But behind that finished saree is an industry where the hands doing the weaving often earn the least.

The problem cannot be understood through wages alone.

Zaidur Rahman, a Liaison Officer working with the weaving sector, describes a production system in which many marginal weavers lack sufficient capital to operate independently.

They need money before a saree can even be woven: to buy yarn, prepare the loom, pay for production and support the household while waiting for the finished fabric to be sold.

Government-backed loans are available to some weavers, but the amount may not always cover their needs. As a result, some turn simultaneously to institutional loans and traditional mahajans.

The mahajan is a complicated figure in this economy. He can provide capital, yarn, designs, orders and, crucially, a route to market. But financial dependence can also mean the weaver has little bargaining power over the price of his labour.

Rahman explains that some mahajans finance production on the condition that the finished cloth is supplied back to them at predetermined rates. For a cash-strapped weaver, refusing may not be realistic.

Working capital becomes particularly important because weaving money does not return immediately. Rahman describes the problem as needing capital in three places at once.

One portion is required for yarn. Another is already tied up in the fabric being produced on the loom. A third can remain trapped in finished goods until those goods are actually sold and payment comes back.

If the sale is delayed, the cycle stalls. Without cash in hand, the weaver cannot buy the next batch of yarn or keep another loom working.

Transport and market access can make that delay worse.

Rahman says changes in trading routes and the greater dependence on sea transport for some goods have increased pressure on smaller businesses because capital remains locked away for longer. Small producers do not have the financial cushion of larger companies.

Raw-material costs add another burden. Imported yarn remains important to parts of the sector, while good-quality local yarn is not always sufficiently available to small handloom producers.

Rahman says a system through which weavers' associations once imported yarn via the Handloom Board stopped around 2021 following irregularities. He believes a properly regulated version should return because easier access to yarn could reduce production costs.

In Pathrail, Rahman says one weavers' association has 365 members. Of them, 93 have received approximately Tk 1.3 crore in loans collectively since 2019.

Applicants approach the authorities through their association, undergo verification, and their eligibility is reviewed at the upazila level before recommendations are made.

Such financing matters. But credit alone cannot solve an industry in which production costs are rising while some workers remain at the bottom of the value chain.

Loans can keep a loom moving. They cannot guarantee that weaving will become financially attractive enough for someone's son or daughter to choose it as a career.

Asked what he wants from the government, Tomol Chandra Das, handloom craftsman from Pathrail union, does not speak in the language of policy, subsidies or supply chains.

“We want to live well,” he says. “We want to be able to eat properly.”

The debate around Tangail saree often focuses on heritage, GI recognition, authenticity and the threat of power looms. All of these matters, but heritage ultimately depends on people being able to make a living from preserving it. The danger, then, is not simply that cheaper machine-made sarees will compete with handloom ones. It is that one day consumers may still ask for an authentic handwoven Tangail saree, only to discover that too few hands remain willing to weave it.
Author: A Ayman Anika Ayman Anika

Title: Visiting Falkland Islands: Where Penguins Roam Free
Content:
For a Bangladeshi traveller, reaching the Falklands is not easy. The islands lie in the South Atlantic, roughly 480 kilometres from mainland South America, more specifically Argentina. The archipelago consists of two principal islands, East Falkland and West Falkland, along with hundreds of smaller islands. Stanley, on East Falkland, is the capital and main population centre.

The distance is only part of the challenge.

Regular access is limited, flights are expensive, and the islands are far removed from the world's major travel routes. Scheduled air links include services connecting the Falklands with South America, while flights from the United Kingdom operate from RAF Brize Norton. Cruise and expedition ships provide another important way of reaching the islands.

For ordinary visitors, the Falklands has their own immigration requirements.

My own arrival was different because I was travelling as part of an expedition cruise. I was initially concerned because I did not have a UK visa and had very little time to arrange one specifically for the Falklands.

Oceanwide Expeditions, the Dutch expedition company operating our voyage, assured us that the necessary landing arrangements would be handled through the ship's authorities. We submitted our passports to the ship's authorities and received them back after leaving the British territory. We also received Falkland Islands immigration stamps in our passports — an unexpected and memorable souvenir of the journey.

The moment we boarded MV Hondius in Ushuaia, we knew the Falklands were our first major destination. As the ship began sailing south, our excitement grew. We passed through the Beagle Channel, the spectacular waterway at the southern tip of South America that connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans through the waterways around Tierra del Fuego.

Soon we were sailing into the majestic South Atlantic. The deep blue water of the southern ocean was overwhelming. For a while, the vast horizon and the ship moving through endless water reminded me of the great movie Titanic. But there was no drama—only an immense ocean, a sense of freedom and the feeling that we were moving farther away from the familiar world.

The islands are home to only a few thousand people. Life is shaped by remoteness, fishing, farming and tourism. Sheep farming has traditionally been important, while commercial fishing is a major pillar of the modern economy.

Tourism, particularly expedition and cruise tourism, has also become increasingly important. For me, one of the most fascinating questions was why people choose to live in such a remote place. Yet after seeing the island communities, I began to understand that remoteness does not necessarily mean isolation from a meaningful life. For the people who live there, the Falklands is simply home.

The political story remains impossible to ignore.

Argentina claims sovereignty over the islands and calls them Islas Malvinas, while Britain administers them as a British Overseas Territory. The 1982 war remains central to the history of both countries. In a 2013 referendum, Falkland Islanders overwhelmingly voted to retain their existing status as a British Overseas Territory. The dispute continues, but during my journey I found myself much more interested in the human and natural story of the islands.

Our Zodiac took us from Hondius towards Carcass Island. As soon as we reached the shore, I stepped onto Falkland soil. The sandy beach gave way to tussock grass and marshy ground, and the air smelled of sea, grass and peat.

And then I saw my first wild penguins.

Magellanic penguins waddled along the beach and around their burrows. Seeing them in their natural environment was completely different from seeing penguins in a zoo or on a screen. They were curious, energetic and entirely unbothered by our presence.

Carcass Island offered much more. We saw Steamer ducks, geese and other birds, while sheep grazed across the landscape. We walked several kilometres towards a small settlement, where residents welcomed visitors with tea and homemade pastries. Sitting there, surrounded by the quiet landscape of a remote South Atlantic island, felt almost unreal.

And there was another first for me. On Carcass Island, we also encountered King penguins for the first time. They were fewer in number than the Magellanic penguins, but their striking appearance immediately caught our attention. Seeing a King penguin in the wild was one of the most memorable moments of the expedition.

After returning to Hondius for lunch, we headed towards Saunders Island. If Carcass Island introduced me to the Falklands, Saunders showed me just how extraordinary its wildlife could be.

We walked along the coast among Gentoo penguins sitting on nests and guarding their chicks. Magellanic penguins appeared around their burrows, while Rockhopper penguins hopped energetically between rocks. Then we reached a colony of black-browed albatrosses.

The albatrosses were magnificent, too. Their enormous wings, elegant appearance and perfectly formed nests made them one of the most impressive sights of the expedition. We watched them carefully from a safe distance, following the instructions of the expedition guides so that we did not disturb the birds.

The beaches and hills around Saunders were filled with life: penguins, gulls, oyster catchers, skuas, caracaras, Steamer ducks and sheep. It was a powerful reminder that the Falklands is not simply a place defined by a war or a sovereignty dispute. It is also a remarkable wildlife destination.

Eventually, we sailed towards Stanley, the capital. In many ways, it felt like a tiny piece of Britain transplanted into the South Atlantic. The familiar red telephone box, post boxes, British-style streets, pubs, cafés and shops created an atmosphere that felt strangely familiar despite being thousands of kilometres from London.

We explored Stanley by hop-on hop-off bus, seeing the town and its surroundings. We visited the Falkland Islands Museum, explored shops and cafés, and took in the atmosphere of a small capital at the edge of the world. We also bought dry food and snacks from a local supermarket for the next stages of our expedition.

That simple supermarket visit became part of the adventure. We were preparing to continue across the South Atlantic, into the Southern Ocean and eventually towards the Antarctic Peninsula before returning to Ushuaia. With every mile south, the world around us would become more remote.

When we finally left Stanley, I looked back at the islands and thought about how my relationship with the Falklands had changed. I had first known it as a name in history books, then as the site of a devastating war, a continuing political dispute and a famous football rivalry. Now I had seen another Falklands—the Falklands of people, farms, fishing boats, supermarkets, penguins, albatrosses and endless blue ocean.

For years, I wondered why anyone would choose to live so far from the regular world. After visiting, I realised that perhaps the better question is not why they stay, but what makes a place feel like home.

For the rest of us, the Falklands may be one of the most remote destinations on Earth. For the people who live there, it is simply home. And for me, it was a dream finally fulfilled.

The writer is a Mass Communication and Journalism graduate from the University of Dhaka, a travel enthusiast, filmmaker, and tourism entrepreneur.
Author: N Nilay Kumar Biswas Nilay Kumar Biswas

Title: Why are we so afraid of being disliked?
Content:
We all want to be liked. It feels good when people appreciate our choices, understand our jokes, praise our work, or simply enjoy having us around. But somewhere between wanting to be liked and needing to be liked, the line can quietly disappear.

The need for approval can influence what we wear, what we post, whom we spend time with, what opinions we express, and even what opportunities we accept. We may say “yes” when we mean “no”, remain silent when something bothers us, or constantly wonder, “What will they think?”

Wanting connection is human. However, when being liked becomes a condition for feeling good about ourselves, it can become exhausting.

The desire to fit in often begins harmlessly. We adjust ourselves to the people around us because belonging matters. In school, university, workplaces, friendships, and families, being accepted can feel like proof that we are doing something right.

The problem starts when fitting in requires us to repeatedly edit ourselves.

We may laugh at jokes we do not find funny, agree with opinions we do not share, or hide interests because they seem “uncool”. Social media can intensify this pressure. Likes, comments, views, and reactions can turn approval into something measurable.

Eventually, we can become so focused on how others perceive us that we lose touch with how we perceive ourselves.

Validation is not inherently bad. Encouragement from friends, recognition at work, or appreciation from family can make us feel valued. External validation becomes unhealthy when it becomes the primary source of our self-worth.

When our mood depends on someone’s response, a delayed reply can feel like rejection. When a post receives fewer likes, we may question its worth and, eventually, our own.

The truth is that approval is unstable. People change their minds. Their preferences change. Their expectations differ. Trying to satisfy everyone is therefore an impossible task.

A useful question is: “If nobody could see this decision, would I still make the same choice?”

The answer can reveal how much of our life is being shaped by other people’s opinions.

One of the simplest ways to step away from approval-seeking is to learn the uncomfortable art of saying no.

“No” does not automatically mean rude, selfish, or uncaring. It can simply mean that your time, energy, money, or emotional capacity has limits.

We often over-explain our boundaries because we fear disappointing people. But a respectful “I can’t take this on right now” can be enough.

At first, saying no may feel uncomfortable. That discomfort does not necessarily mean you have done something wrong. Sometimes it simply means you are doing something unfamiliar.

You do not have to make everyone happy to be a good person.

Breaking the need to be liked does not mean becoming indifferent to others. It means learning to separate being considerate from being controlled by approval.

Start small. Wear something you genuinely like. Express an honest opinion respectfully. Spend time doing something without posting it. Decide without conducting a mental survey of everyone’s reactions.

Most importantly, notice the moments when you automatically ask, “Will they like this?” and replace the question with, “Do I like this? Does this feel right for me? Does it align with what I value?”

With practice, the need to fit in begins to loosen.

Every hour spent worrying about someone’s opinion is an hour not spent building your own life.

Instead of constantly monitoring how you are being perceived, redirect that attention towards things you can control: your work, relationships, creativity, health, learning, and personal goals.

Not everyone will like you. Some people will misunderstand you. Others may disagree with your choices. That is not necessarily a problem to solve.

A meaningful life cannot be built entirely around being universally approved of.

Perhaps the real freedom is not reaching a point where nobody’s opinion matters, but reaching a point where your own opinion of yourself matters enough. Because fitting in may give us acceptance for a moment. Knowing who we are gives us somewhere to stand.
Author: F Farhana Faiza Farhana Faiza

Title: Are we raising a generation that doesn’t read?
Content:
Book reading losing popularity has been one of the biggest tragedies of the tech era. Ever since the advent of social media and, consequently, smartphones, more and more youth have replaced the familiar comfort of pages with brightly lit screens, and it has come with its penalties.

Consistently falling reading and comprehension scores in younger students suggest that the habit of reading as a hobby has taken a major hit in recent times. Some experts have gone so far as to suggest that each new generation is proving worse than its predecessor when it comes to literacy, with Gen Alpha as the newest, and possibly the worst readers of their time.

“Each new grade I teach has fewer and fewer readers,” shares Maria Mahmud, a Grade V teacher at a popular English Medium school. “Children simply do not have the appetite for reading, and this hits hard because reading was one of the highlights of our school life and continues to be such a joy now.”

A study by UCLA raises further concerns by finding a plausible relationship between children’s cell phone ownership and their ability to read. Published in Behavioural Sciences and discussed in a university press release, the popular research has found that elementary school students who owned cell phones generally performed worse on reading comprehension tests than classmates who did not own devices.

Mir Adiba Awlad, Teacher Librarian at a prominent IB school, shares her own experience on the subject.

“I see the attraction of screens every day. A screen can capture a child’s attention almost instantly. It is bright, fast, interactive and always ready with something new. Sometimes, even getting children to settle for story time can feel like a challenge when they are used to the constant stimulation of digital content, when they can feel the excitement of scrolling up and down with just a flick of their fingertip!”

Notably, the above-mentioned study suggested that weaker reading performance was associated with owning a phone for a period of time, not with the proximity of a device during examination. This was not about momentary distraction, but about prolonged exposure and what it does to a young brain.

Maria agrees and explains why this rings true.

“Children use ‘chat speak’ on social media, and this spills over to their copies. This language is quick, short and often disregards grammatical rules, owing to the informality of the whole thing. Continuously communicating in language that is designed to capture attention for shorter spans of time does not do any favours to young, impressionable minds.”

According to Maria, this affects their quality of work across the curriculum. “A child that can read well will not only ace grammar and vocabulary but will also comprehend better. This will put them far ahead of a student that struggles to read and understand basic instructions.”

As a suggestion post the UCLA study, most experts felt that delaying phone ownership for as long as possible was the best course of action; introducing smartphones too early could interfere with children’s ability to develop strong reading habits and understand written material.

Of course, this study does not definitively demonstrate that owning a phone directly causes poor reading performance or reduced comprehension for written material, but it does imply a strong correlation between the two factors, corroborating previous warnings from neuroscientists about declining academic performance among young phone users, with some even suggesting that Gen Z may be the first modern generation to perform worse than its preceding generation on standardised academic tests.

As worries about literacy rise and book reading once again, Adiba offers a glimmer of hope.

“Young minds are malleable. If we can introduce the youngest students to the wonder of books, it can be powerful”

Adiba worries when reading becomes something children do only when there is nothing else to do. “That's why I believe our responsibility is not simply to tell children, 'Read more'". We need to help them discover why reading is enjoyable in the first place.”

Reading habits developed in the early years can become groundwork for a lifetime.

“When a child learns that a library is a place where they can choose, explore, wonder and find something that speaks to them, reading stops feeling like another task. It becomes something personal.”

Screens are here, and they are not going anywhere, anytime soon. So perhaps the question is not, "Can books compete with screens?" Perhaps the better question is: Are we giving children enough opportunities to discover the magic of books for themselves?
Author: M Munira Fidai Munira Fidai

Title: Aydha Mehnaz launches avari, an independent advisory group to support creative businesses
Content:
Aydha Mehnaz launches avari, an independent advisory group to support creative businesses. Headquartered in New York City at 161 Water Street, avari will make strategic advisory one of its primary missions, working with established organisations and emerging creatives globally.

‘In Sanskrit, the word ‘avari’ is derived from the concept of being unbounded, a shapeshifter. That’s exactly what we would imagine avari to be — a consistent partner that helps brands and organisations evolve into their next step.’ Team avari thrives on cultural fluency.

‘In the context of Bangladesh, we have supported designers and organisations behind the scenes with workshops, brand strategy, shows, leading conversations to orchestrate local and international campaigns, and our relationships across the board have been instrumental to their development.’

Mehnaz, in this new advisory role, brings more than a decade of experience in leading high-stakes brand strategy for fashion, luxury and lifestyle brands at a global scale. With the formal launch of avari, she signals the intention of opening a chapter in Paris, alongside strengthening avari’s presence in Dhaka.

‘We continue to work with storied luxury houses who have amazing brand legacies. Via avari, I genuinely look forward to applying that acquired knowledge independently at various scales and for projects that we are truly passionate about.’

Title: Beyond the festival stage: Identity in modern Bangladesh
Content:
Bangladesh is home to numerous communities, each with its own history, customs and ways of understanding the world. Despite this diversity, many people know little about their everyday lives, contemporary concerns or cultural contributions. Their traditions are admired from a distance, but their voices are not always heard with the same attention.

For cultural activist Tuku Talukder and designer Tenzing Chakma, preservation does not mean keeping culture trapped in the past. It means creating the conditions for it to remain visible, respected and relevant. Their reflections reveal a culture negotiating tourism, social media, changing lifestyles, disappearing languages and commercial fashion, while continuing to assert its place within contemporary Bangladesh.

Indigenous cultures often receive public attention during festivals such as Biju or around the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples, observed on 9 August. For the rest of the year, however, their languages, foods, social practices, ecological knowledge and contemporary experiences rarely receive the same visibility.

Talukder believes this gap is partly the result of insufficient institutional support.

“There is a lack of government patronage and positive promotion,” she shares. “If there were active efforts to nurture these communities and their traditions, people would certainly know more.”

She argues that indigenous culture is too often reduced to songs, dances, and colourful performances. Although these are important forms of cultural expression, they represent only part of a much wider reality. Community structures, relationships with nature, traditional knowledge, food habits, languages and values are equally significant.

Representation becomes shallow when people are invited to perform but are not given space to explain their identities, concerns and aspirations in their own words.

“Promotion should not happen only on Indigenous Day or during festivals like Biju,” Talukder clarifies. “It needs to be year-round and inspirational.”

Food reveals how prejudice can gradually change.

Talukder remembers how her local dishes were once treated negatively by outsiders. Foods associated with indigenous communities were sometimes mocked because their ingredients, smells, or preparation methods were unfamiliar.

Today, visitors to the Hill Tracts are more willing to try such dishes. Young indigenous creators also use social media to talk about foods they may once have felt embarrassed to mention publicly.

“So, what if people talk?” Talukder asks. “They talk because they don’t know.”

This shift matters because cultural loss does not always begin with the disappearance of an object or practice. Sometimes it begins when people are made to feel ashamed of their own language, clothing, food or customs.

A larger culture inevitably influences a smaller one, Talukder observes. At one point, indigenous women sometimes avoided wearing the pinon because outsiders considered it unusual. Some adopted sarees in public spaces to avoid unwanted attention.

Now, the pinon is being embraced again, particularly by younger generations. Social media has helped turn what was once treated as “different” into a visible expression of pride.

However, digital visibility remains uneven. Poor mobile connectivity in many villages prevents residents from participating fully in online cultural promotion. Those living closest to traditional practices may have the least access to the platforms where these cultures are discussed.

For designer Tenzing Chakma, indigenous textiles provide another record of cultural memory.

“The idea comes entirely from nature, from colourful nature,” he says. “Most indigenous clothing is vibrant because the concepts come from the changing colours of the seasons. The patterns are a traditional part of our identity.”

The colours and motifs of textiles such as the pinon-hadi are not merely decorative. They reflect landscapes, seasons, inherited skills and the visual language of a community.

According to Chakma, traditional textiles once relied mainly on a limited palette that included red, black, blue and yellow. Over time, the range of colours and variations expanded as lifestyles, environments and consumer preferences changed.

For him, this evolution does not necessarily weaken tradition. Culture can adapt while retaining its roots.

Chakma’s years of working with artisans also taught him that the value of weaving lies in its process.

“Patience!” he says. “You must have the patience to understand the craft.”

From artisans, he learned the names of different parts of the weaving process, the discipline required to produce a textile and the influence of seasons. The rainy season, for instance, can create difficulties for weaving.

He is especially interested in reviving original cotton thread produced directly from cotton plants, as well as natural dyes. Before chemical dyes became common, colours came from natural materials. Returning to those processes would be valuable, he says, though it would also be expensive and time-consuming.

Talukder is particularly concerned about traditions and languages that are gradually disappearing. Preservation, she argues, requires accountable institutions and consistent community involvement rather than occasional cultural programmes.

Younger generations also need reasons to feel proud of their heritage. Social media can help, but digital content alone cannot preserve a language, craft or cultural practice. Families, schools, community organisations, cultural institutions and policymakers all have roles to play.

Chakma remains hopeful about the interest shown by Gen Z. Young people are wearing indigenous-inspired clothing, creating videos and presenting cultural identity with greater confidence.

His advice to them extends beyond fashion.

“Respect each other’s culture,” he says. “If we respect one another, we can learn from each other.”

That respect begins with curiosity, but it must lead to something deeper: listening to indigenous voices, learning the meanings behind traditions, crediting cultural creators and recognising communities as active participants in modern Bangladesh.

Indigenous cultures do not need to remain frozen to survive. They need space to develop without losing ownership of their stories. Their future depends not only on preservation, but on whether the wider society is prepared to understand them as living, changing and equal cultures.
