Prime Bank PLC has signed an agreement with Bangladesh Bank to participate in the central bank’s Tk 5,000 crore working capital refinance fund for the cottage, micro, small and medium enterprise (CMSME) sector.

The fund aims to provide working capital financing to eligible CMSMEs at affordable interest rates and on easier terms, according to a press release.

Md Jobdul Islam, director of the SME and Special Programmes Department of Bangladesh Bank, and M Nazeem A Choudhury, additional managing director of Prime Bank PLC, signed the agreement at the central bank’s headquarters in Motijheel, Dhaka recently.

Md Anisur Rahman, deputy governor of Bangladesh Bank, attended the signing ceremony as the chief guest. Nahid Rahman, executive director, and Shahanaj Parveen, additional director of Bangladesh Bank, were also present.

The refinance fund was established under Bangladesh Bank’s Tk 60,000 crore stimulus package to provide working capital loans or investment to CMSMEs, helping them operate their production, service and business activities at full capacity.

Eligible CMSMEs facing working capital shortages will have access to financing at interest rates of up to 9 percent.

Prime Bank said its participation would further expand access to affordable working capital financing, helping CMSMEs strengthen operations, increase production capacity, sustain growth and generate employment.

Nahid Rahman, executive director of Bangladesh Bank, and Shahanaj Parveen, additional director, were also present at the event.
Author: Star Business Desk

Title: NRBC Bank launches training programme for management trainee officers
Content:
NRBC Bank PLC yesterday launched a 40-day foundation training programme for its management trainee officers (MTOs) at its Human Resources Training & Development Centre in Dhaka.

A total of 40 MTOs are participating in the comprehensive training programme, which is designed to prepare the next generation of banking leaders. Md Touhidul Alam Khan, managing director and chief executive officer of the bank, inaugurated the training programme as the chief guest, according to a press release.

In his speech, Touhidul said professionalism, integrity and the ability to adapt to changing circumstances are essential for bankers in an evolving financial environment.

He advised the trainees to prioritise customers’ needs, continuously enhance their knowledge and apply what they learn through training in their day-to-day work.

He also said that for new banking professionals, knowing banking rules and regulations alone is not enough. Effective communication with customers, responsible conduct and the ability to make decisions in changing circumstances are equally important.

Fahmida Chowdhury, head of the training centre, presided over the programme.

Among others, Md Shaheen Howlader, deputy managing director and chief business officer of the bank, and Faisal Ahmed, chief human resources officer, were also present at the inaugural ceremony.
Author: Star Business Desk

Title: FinExcel appoints Selim Barkat as chairman
Content:
Financial Excellence Ltd (FinExcel) has appointed Selim Barkat as chairman of the company.

Selim brings nearly four decades of leadership experience in banking and financial services in Bangladesh and the United States. His areas of expertise include strategic leadership, corporate governance, risk management, transaction banking, treasury and capital markets, according to a press release. Most recently, he served as regional general manager of Habib Bank Limited (HBL) for Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and the Maldives. In the role, he helped drive the bank’s strategic transformation in the South Asia region.

Earlier, he held senior positions at Citibank and Citigroup in Bangladesh and New York. He was involved in global business management and later worked as a portfolio banker covering credit and counterparty-risk portfolios for investment banks, broker-dealers, financial market intermediaries and the North American insurance industry.

He also played a key role in establishing Citibank, National Association’s first branch in Bangladesh.

As chairman, Barkat will bring his international banking experience, strategic vision and focus on risk management and corporate governance to FinExcel.

He holds an MBA in Finance from the Institute of Business Administration (IBA), University of Dhaka. He also served as an adjunct faculty member at Rutgers Business School, Rutgers University, USA.
Author: Star Business Desk

Title: Shimanto Bank plans IPO by 2028
Content:
Shimanto Bank PLC plans to go for an initial public offering (IPO) by 2028, subject to an evaluation of the bank’s overall financial situation.

Maj Gen Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui, director general of Border Guard Bangladesh and chairman of the bank, said this at the bank’s 10th annual general meeting (AGM), held recently at the BGB headquarters in Peelkhana, Dhaka.

In his welcome speech, Ashrafuzzaman highlighted some of the actions taken and progress made by Shimanto Bank PLC on decisions aimed at the welfare of members of Border Guard Bangladesh.

The bank’s operating profit increased by 6.08 percent in 2025, while its assets increased to Tk 4,149.91 crore, registering growth of 25.70 percent. Loans and investments increased by 23.37 percent and 41.08 percent, respectively, he said while presiding over the meeting, according to a press release.

Deposits stood at Tk 3,276.12 crore, representing growth of 29.21 percent over the same period. The bank’s capital adequacy ratio stood at 25.07 percent, against the regulatory minimum requirement of 12.5 percent. He informed the shareholders about initiatives to introduce an “Islamic Banking Window” and “Agent Banking”.

Md Nurul Azim, managing director and CEO of the bank, said its paid-up capital had increased to Tk 525 crore from Tk 400 crore in 2016.

He assured the shareholders that the bank would remain committed to achieving its goals. Hossain Suman, company secretary of the bank, moderated the AGM.

The shareholders approved the directors’ report, auditor’s report and other major issues placed before the meeting.
Author: Star Business Desk

Title: 13 officials face BB action for deposit incentive irregularity
Content:
Bangladesh Bank has ordered Bangladesh Commerce Bank to take the highest administrative action against 13 officials for allegedly receiving Tk 4 crore from the bank’s funds in the name of incentives under a deposit mobilisation campaign.

Through a letter to the managing director of the bank on August 25, the banking regulator also directed the lender to take legal action over the irregular withdrawal of the money and recover the funds.

The central bank took the decision after a special inspection of Bangladesh Commerce Bank’s head office and principal branch following allegations of misappropriation of Tk 5 crore belonging to depositors.

Contacted, Arief Hossain Khan, executive director and spokesperson of Bangladesh Bank, told The Daily Star that there is no scope for providing any incentive for collecting deposits.

“What happened at the bank was that it collected deposits at a lower rate but showed a higher rate and took the difference as a cash incentive,” said the spokesperson, adding that this is against the policy.

According to the inspection report, Tk 4 crore was deposited into the personal accounts of 13 officials on June 4, 2026, as “incentives” for collecting deposits under the bank’s “Ujjibon” deposit campaign.

The payment was not approved by the bank’s board of directors, the report said.

The 13 officials included eight from the head office, four from the principal branch and one from the bank’s Dilkusha branch.

The money was subsequently withdrawn in cash through 14 cheques over two days.

Nine cheques were used to withdraw Tk 3.04 crore on June 4 this year, while five cheques were used to withdraw Tk 96 lakh on June 7, according to the inspection findings.

The cash was withdrawn by Md Delwar Hossain, senior executive vice president and head of the treasury department of Bangladesh Commerce Bank, and Md Hamidur Rahman, senior principal officer and personal secretary to the managing director.

The two officials reportedly left the principal branch with the cash in the bank’s vehicle after each withdrawal.

Bangladesh Bank has instructed the bank to dismiss Delwar Hossain and Hamidur Rahman. The directive is separate from any previous orders issued against them.

The central bank has also ordered the bank to take the highest administrative action against the other 11 officials involved and inform it of the measures taken within a month.

The other officials are First Assistant Vice President (FAVP) Yusuf Siddiq Ullah, AVP Saleh Ahmed, Officer Sarwar, FAVP Sujon Das, AVP Tasnuba Majumder, AVP Ahsan Habib, Principal Officer Adnan Ash Shafique, FAVP Monirul Haque, Senior Officer (SO) Rifat-ul Mursalin, Officer Saifur Rahman and SO Shahinur Rahman.

During the inspection, the officials were asked to explain the transactions in their accounts.

Except for Saleh Ahmed, who was on leave due to illness, the officials told the inspection team that they had handed over their signed cheques to the marketing department on the advice of the bank’s management, the BB report showed.

“They said the money was intended to cover expenses such as transportation, hospitality and gifts related to bringing in deposits under the bank’s 2026 deposit campaign.”

The managing director told the inspection team that the bank had secured a Tk 100 crore deposit from Gazipur City Corporation through the Ujjibon campaign at an interest rate of 2.5 percent, according to the report.

He claimed that additional expenses were incurred for business development and hospitality to bring in the deposit, taking the effective cost of the deposit to 6.5 percent.

As the interest rate on a one-year fixed deposit was around 11.5 percent, the bank would save about 5 percentage points through the arrangement, he informed the inspection team, according to the BB report.

The Daily Star tried to reach Md Obaidul Hoque, managing director of the bank, for comment over the phone and through WhatsApp text messages, but he did not respond to the phone calls or messages until the report was filed.

Bangladesh Bank, however, found that the expenses were improperly routed through the personal bank accounts of 13 officials and paid as incentives without approval from the board.
Author: Star Business Report

Title: 7,896 customers withdraw Tk 327 crore on second day
Content:
Some 7,896 customers of the five merged banks withdrew Tk 327 crore on the second day of fund disbursement, officials of Sammilito Islami Bank said.

The bank, formed last year through the merger of five troubled Islamic banks—First Security Islami, Global Islami, Union, Exim and Social Islami—started repaying depositors on September 7.

Depositors of the five had been struggling to withdraw their money for more than two years and staged protests demanding the return of their deposits.

In addition, around 12,000 new customers applied to withdraw Tk 331 crore today, the officials said.

Abedur Rahman Sikder, managing director and chief executive officer of Sammilito Islami Bank, told The Daily Star that around 19,000 customers had applied to withdraw more than Tk 1,000 crore, but they had withdrawn only a small portion of the amount because they have confidence in the bank.

On August 25, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman announced that individual depositors would be allowed to withdraw the principal amount of their deposits according to their needs from September 1.

Following the announcement, Sammilito Islami began accepting applications from customers and continued the process.

Bangladesh Bank provided Tk 5,000 crore on Sunday to facilitate payments to customers of the five banks.

Sikder said the bank had contacted all customers who had applied to withdraw money and asked them to come to their respective branches.

“Not everyone came to withdraw their money,” he said.
Author: Star Business Report

Title: Regent Chairman Shahed arrested again in money laundering case
Content:
Regent Hospital Chairman Mohammad Shahed Karim has been formally shown arrested in a money laundering case involving allegations of acquiring assets worth Tk7,187,265 beyond known sources of income.

Judge Mohammad Abdullah Al Mamun of Dhaka Special Judge Court-5 on Monday passed the order following a petition filed by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC).

ACC lawyer Delwar Jahan Rumi confirmed the matter.

On the same day, Shahed’s lawyer Dabir Uddin sought bail, but the court did not hear the petition.

According to case records, ACC Deputy Director Md Farid Ahmed Patwary filed the first information report (FIR) on March 7, 2021.

Following an investigation, ACC Assistant Director and investigating officer Mohammad Ziyatul Islam submitted a charge sheet to the court on January 10, 2024, against Shahed and his wife, Sadia Arbi.

According to the charge sheet, Sadia Arbi declared movable and immovable assets worth Tk61.30 lakh in an asset statement submitted to the ACC on December 28, 2020.

However, the investigation found assets worth Tk7,623,625 in her name, indicating that she had concealed assets worth Tk1,493,625.

Including family expenses of Tk1.80 lakh, her total assets were valued at Tk7,823,625. Her income tax records, however, showed earned income of only Tk4.50 lakh.

The investigation therefore found Tk7,353,625 in movable and immovable assets beyond her declared income and outside her known sources of income, according to the charge sheet.

Investigators also found that Sadia had no reliable independent source of income. Shahed allegedly assisted her in acquiring the assets by transferring, converting and concealing funds obtained through illegal and corrupt means in her name.

The ACC subsequently sought to frame charges against the couple under Sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, Section 4(2) of the Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2012, and Section 109 of the Penal Code.

Shahed is also a convict in several cases involving forgery and fraud and faces warrants in cases involving arms possession and cheque dishonour, among others.

After serving a lengthy period in prison, he was recently arrested again under a complaint register (CR) warrant.

He was subsequently sent to jail under a warrant enforcing a one-year prison sentence and a fine for loan default and cheque dishonour in a case involving Mercantile Co-operative Bank.

Shahed remains in custody due to the sentences and warrants pending against him in various cases.
Author: Tribune Report

Title: State minister: Shyamoli TB Hospital to become national TB institute
Content:
The 250-bed TB Hospital in Dhaka’s Shyamoli will soon be upgraded to the National Institute and Hospital for Tuberculosis Control, said Primary and Mass Education State Minister and hospital management committee Chairman Bobby Hajjaj.

He said the upgrade would expand facilities for tuberculosis diagnosis, treatment, research and training while strengthening the hospital’s overall capacity.

“Necessary initiatives have been taken to develop the hospital into a modern, integrated and effective institution for tuberculosis control,” he said.

Bobby Hajjaj made the comments as the chief guest at a meeting of the hospital management committee at the hospital’s conference room on Monday.

The state minister said steps would be taken to fill vacant posts for doctors, officials and employees as soon as possible.

Addressing the manpower shortage was essential to improve the quality of services and make the hospital’s operations more effective, he said, adding that the necessary measures would be taken in consultation with the Ministry of Health.

He also said an initiative would be taken to construct a new 500-bed building to expand the hospital’s services and capacity.

Bobby Hajjaj instructed the relevant authorities to remove encroachments from the footpath in front of the hospital to ensure unobstructed movement for patients and the public.

During his visit, the state minister inspected different wards and spoke with patients, attendants, doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers about the hospital’s services and challenges.

He also sought updates on cleanliness, medicine supplies and other facilities and instructed officials to take necessary measures to improve the hospital’s overall services.

“Every patient who comes to a government hospital for treatment must be treated with humanity and responsibility. The hospital authorities must give the highest priority to ensuring that patients do not face any kind of suffering or inconvenience,” Bobby Hajjaj said.

The meeting was chaired by Dr Ayesha Akter, member secretary of the hospital management committee and deputy director of the hospital.

Officials from the Ministry of Health, Directorate General of Health Services and Department of Social Services, members of the hospital management committee, health reporters, doctors, officials and employees of the hospital attended the meeting.
Author: Tribune Report

Title: Around 20 million children gets measles vaccines in five months
Content:
The government has administered measles vaccines to 19,771,720 children across the country in five months under ongoing measles-rubella vaccination programme.

This figure exceeded the initial target of vaccination by about 10%.

When the country witnessed a measles outbreak at the end of March this year, the government swiftly launched an emergency vaccination program on April 5, covering 30 upazilas in 18 districts, in the first phase.

The second phase of vaccination began on April 12 in four major city corporations (Dhaka South, Dhaka North, Barisal, and Mymensingh), and in the final third phase, the ongoing nationwide measles-rubella vaccination drive commenced on April 20, said officials at the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).

However, due to the persisting measles outbreak, the government is set to launch another massive vaccination campaign starting on September 26 to prevent the disease.

Initially, the officials said the programme aimed to vaccinate about 18 million children nationwide. But the vaccination coverage surpassed the target due to various government initiatives.

According to data from the DGHS, the government's target was to vaccinate 18,015,064 children against measles and rubella. But, as of September 13, a total of 19,771,720 children received the vaccine.

Data obtained from the integrated control centre for the measles-rubella vaccine shows that 1,110,698 children received the measles-rubella vaccine in Barisal division, while 4,841,924 in Chittagong division, 4,919,913 in Dhaka division, 1,695,779 in Khulna division, 1,530,916 in Mymensingh division, 2,213,197 in Rajshahi division, 20,73,488 in Rangpur division and 1,385,805 in Sylhet division.

Among the city corporation areas, 44,119 children were administered with the vaccine in Barisal city, while 336,870 in Chittagong city, 48,643 in Comilla city, 557,688 in Dhaka north city, 418,972 in Dhaka south city, 206,927 in Gazipur city, 83,697 in Narayanganj city, 96,792 in Khulna city, 62,305 in Mymensingh city, 63,059 in Rajshah city, 82,253 in Rangpur city and 72,349 in Sylhet city.

DGHS Additional Director General Professor Dr Zahid Raihan told BSS that vaccinating children is an ongoing process.

However, he said the announcement to administer measles vaccines to children on a massive scale across the country starting September 26 is an intensified effort by the government.

The primary objective of this programme is to ensure that no child is left unvaccinated, he added.
Author: BSS

Title: Verdict in case against Quader, Arafat, 5 others Tuesday
Content:
The International Crimes Tribunal is set to deliver its verdict on Tuesday against seven accused, including Awami League General Secretary Obaidul Quader, former state minister for information and broadcasting Mohammad Ali Arafat, and five others in a case involving alleged crimes against humanity committed during the July mass uprising in 2024.

A three-member bench of International Crimes Tribunal-2, headed by Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, fixed the date on Monday.

The other members of the bench are Judge Md Manzurul Bashid and Judge Nur Mohammad Shahriar Kabir.

Prosecutors Gazi MH Tamim, Faruk Ahmed and other members of the prosecution team were present at the tribunal.

The tribunal had earlier kept the case reserved for judgment after hearing closing arguments from both the prosecution and defence. Tribunal-2 passed the order on August 17.

State-appointed lawyers M Hasan Imam and Ishrat Jahan represented the accused, while prosecutors Mizanul Islam and Gazi MH Tamim represented the prosecution.

Besides Obaidul Quader and Mohammad Ali Arafat, the other accused are Awami League Joint General Secretary AFM Bahauddin Nasim, Jubo League President Sheikh Fazle Shams Parash, and General Secretary Mainul Hossain Khan Nikhil, Chhatra League President Saddam Hossain and General Secretary Wali Asif Enan.

All seven accused are absconding.

On January 22, Tribunal-2 ordered the trial to begin after framing charges against the seven accused. The tribunal took cognisance of the formal charges the prosecution submitted on December 18, 2025.

The prosecution began presenting its closing arguments on August 4.

According to the prosecution, the accused jointly issued directives and made provocative and inciting statements to suppress the July-August movement.

They allegedly held several meetings to plan violence and called on party activists to take to the streets and put up resistance.

The prosecution further alleged that the accused were involved in armed attacks, harsh repression and efforts to control the media in some areas.

It said their actions resulted in killings, attempted killings and widespread violence across the country, which constitute crimes against humanity.
Author: Tribune Report

Title: Family alleges medical negligence in infant’s death at Dhaka hospital
Content:
The family of a nine-month-old infant has alleged that medical negligence led to the child’s death at Padma General Hospital in the capital.

A relative raised the allegation during a Facebook Live session late Sunday night, claiming that no doctor was available when the child’s condition deteriorated in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU).

The hospital, however, denied the allegation, saying the child died of cardiac arrest.

The relatives said nine-month-old Ayan Abdullah was admitted to Padma General Hospital on September 1.

The child’s mother alleged that when his condition worsened while he was receiving treatment in the PICU, repeated attempts to call a doctor went unanswered.

“If a child dies right now—if their breathing stops—what happens to them? The child had developed complications beforehand. My allegation is that this occurred precisely because of negligence in duty,” she said.

The relatives also alleged that no doctor was available near their ward.

“There were no doctors in the vicinity of our ward. We went to the doctors’ room nearby. There are several doctors’ rooms; we checked those too. There wasn’t a doctor anywhere. There wasn’t even a doctor from the NICU present,” they said.

Dr Nazmul Haque, a medical officer at the hospital, said the child died of cardiac arrest. He said the child had remained stable until around 8pm but stopped breathing around 9pm.

Dr Md Atiqul Islam, a consultant at the hospital, said he was informed about the situation during the night.

“I asked if my presence was required, but the hospital told me it wasn’t anything serious,” he said.

Zahirul Islam Anik, an administrative officer at Padma General Hospital, said the allegation could be checked through CCTV footage.

“Whether a doctor was present or not can be verified by checking the CCTV footage. We will investigate the matter. We have doctors and nurses on duty 24 hours a day,” he said.

He denied the allegation of medical negligence.
Author: Tribune Report

Title: Rain likely in parts of country
Content:
Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) on Monday forecasted rain in different parts of the country in next 24 hours commencing 9am.

"Light to moderate rain or thundershowers accompanied by temporary gusty wind is likely to occur at a few places over Rangpur, Rajshahi and Chittagong divisions and at one or two places over Dhaka, Mymensingh, Khulna, Barisal and Sylhet divisions," said a Met Office bulletin in the morning.

Besides, it said, moderately heavy to heavy falls may occur at places over the country.

Day and night temperatures may remain nearly unchanged over the country.

The highest temperature on Sunday was recorded at 35.5°C in Feni and Ramgati, while Monday's minimum temperature is 23.8°C in Bandarban.

In the last 24 hours (till 6am on Monday), the highest 48 millimetre rainfall occurred in Rajarhat.

The sun sets at 6:04pm on Monday and rises at 5:45am on Tuesday in Dhaka.
Author: BSS

Title: BSF shooting victim’s body handed over along Thakurgaon border
Content:
The body of a Bangladeshi national who was shot dead by the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) has been handed over to Border Guard Bangladesh through the Thakurgaon border.

The deceased was Asadul Haque, 38, son of Abdul Wazed of South Indrail village in Pirganj upazila.

Lieutenant Colonel Abdullah Al Moin, commander of Dinajpur 42 Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), said the BGB held a flag meeting with the BSF to facilitate the repatriation of Asadul's body.

The flag meeting was held at the zero line of the Chanderhat border on Sunday afternoon, with representatives of the Dinajpur 42 BGB and the Indian BSF.

During the meeting, the two sides discussed the prompt repatriation of Asadul's body.

Following legal formalities, the BSF handed over the body to the BGB at around 10pm on Sunday, he said.

Meanwhile, two other Bangladeshi nationals, Mostakim and Sri Uda, who survived the shooting, remain in Indian custody.

They were charged under India's Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, and several sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

They were later produced before the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate in Raiganj in India, which ordered that they be held in judicial custody for 14 days.

Mostakim, son of Ahed Ali, and Sri Uda, son of Narayan, are both from North Indrail village in the same upazila.

According to local residents and BGB sources, several Bangladeshi youths entered Indian territory near border pillar No. 333, under the jurisdiction of the Chanderhat Border Outpost (BOP), in the early hours of Saturday.

At that time, a patrol team of the BSF's 63 Chakshibananda camp in India's North Dinajpur district opened fire on them.

Asadul, Mostakim and Sri Uda were injured in the firing.

BSF personnel later rescued them and took them to Kaliaganj State General Hospital in North Dinajpurwhere Asadul died.
Author: Zakir Mostafiz Milu

Title: India women refuse Asia Cup trophy from top Pakistan official after title triumph
Content:
India’s women refused to collect the Asia Cup trophy from Pakistan Cricket Board chief Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday after beating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final to claim a record-extending eighth continental title.

The decision echoed the stance taken by India’s men’s team after winning last year’s Asia Cup, when they also declined to receive the trophy from Naqvi, who is Pakistan’s interior minister as well as chairman of the country’s cricket board and president of the Asian Cricket Council.

India’s players instead celebrated their title without taking part in the formal trophy presentation, as tensions between the two nuclear-armed neighbours again spilled into a major cricketing event.

“That stand has been taken by BCCI (Indian cricket board), and we stand by it,” India coach Amol Muzumdar told reporters.

“We are the champions, that's good enough.”

The presentation ceremony was delayed by nearly 50 minutes before Naqvi handed medals to the Sri Lankan runners-up. The ceremony then ended abruptly, with India’s players presenting medals to each other in the presence of BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia and vice-president Rajeev Shukla.

On the field, India had little trouble securing their eighth Asia Cup crown.

After winning the toss, India posted 183-5, powered by a spectacular opening partnership between Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma. Mandhana scored 59 and Verma smashed 68 as the pair added 129 runs in 12.5 overs.

Sri Lanka’s chase began positively, with captain Chamari Athapaththu making 36 and sharing a 58-run partnership with Vishmi Gunaratne, who scored 20.

But Sri Lanka collapsed from 62-1, losing its last nine wickets for just 49 runs. India spinner Shree Charani finished with 4-20 as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 111 from the final ball.

India’s emphatic victory secured the title, but their refusal to accept the trophy from Naqvi became the defining moment of the post-match ceremony.
Author: Agencies

Title: Badhan: Those who attacked me are inviting trouble for themselves
Content:
Actress Azmeri Haque Badhan said on Monday that those who attacked and harassed her in Italy were “inviting trouble for themselves” and called for an end to their “barbaric” behaviour.

“Those carrying out the attacks are, I think, inviting trouble for themselves. Their barbaric behaviour must stop,” Badhon told reporters at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport after returning to Bangladesh from Italy.

Badhon travelled to Italy to attend the Venice Film Festival, where she alleged that a group of expatriate Bangladeshis attacked and harassed her.

“They laid hands on me. I think by doing this, the attackers are making themselves unsafe. What happened in Italy was unfortunate. It has tarnished our image on foreign soil,” she said.

Addressing those who attacked her, Badhon said they might be acting out of loyalty to a political party, but warned that party leaders would not stand by their families if they faced difficulties.

“You are doing this out of love for your party, but when your families suffer, the party leaders will not be there. They are living comfortably and sending video messages,” she said.

Badhan also praised the Italian police for their response, saying she was provided with 24-hour security after the incident and received cooperation from local police and relevant authorities during her stay.

On the night of September 7, Badhan alleged that a group of expatriate Bangladeshis harassed and attacked her while she was staying with family members in Mestre, Italy.

A video of the incident later circulated widely on social media. Various reports said water and soft drinks were thrown at her and that she was physically assaulted.

The video showed several people engaged in a heated exchange with Badhon. She later filed a complaint with the local police, who began analysing video and CCTV footage to identify those involved.

The incident triggered widespread concern over Badhan’s safety in both Bangladesh and Italy. The Bangladesh Embassy and Consulate in Italy said they would provide her with legal and other assistance.

The Bangladesh government also expressed concern and said it would raise the matter strongly with Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Author: Tribune Report

Title: Putin urges global youth to change the world together at Ekaterinburg festival
Content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has called on young people from around the world to work together to build what he described as a “new, open and just world”, in a televised address marking the opening of the International Festival of Youth in Ekaterinburg.

Addressing around 10,000 young participants representing 191 countries on Sunday, Putin said every nation should have the freedom to determine its own path while enjoying equal access to resources and technology.

“We want every person to remain human and for their fate be determined by things other than nationality, a wallet packed with money, status or background,” Putin said.

“If you share these aspirations, let’s change the world together,” he added, inviting young people to participate in projects in Russia while encouraging them to pursue similar initiatives in their own countries.

Putin welcomed participants to Ekaterinburg, describing the Urals city as a place “where Europe and Asia meet” and highlighting its historic role in Russia’s industrial and intellectual development.

He also referred to the Russian word “mir”, which can mean both “peace” and “world”, saying the dual meaning reflects the character of Russia’s multi-ethnic society.

The festival, running from September 13 to 17, has brought together 5,000 Russian citizens and 5,000 international participants, including 1,000 teenagers aged between 14 and 17.

According to the Federal Agency for Youth Affairs (Rosmolodezh), more than 113,000 applications were submitted from around the world.

Organisers said international applications exceeded those from Russia for the first time in the history of the festival movement, by around 32,000 applications.
Author: Shaikh Shahrukh

Title: Dhaka air 6th worst in world Monday morning
Content:
The air quality in Dhaka turned 'unhealthy' on Monday morning, compared with Sunday's 'unhealthy for sensitive groups' level.

Dhaka ranked 6th on the list of cities with the worst air quality in the world this morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 160 at 8:35am.

The air quality was classified as ‘unhealthy’, meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.

Singapore topped the list with an AQI score of 169, followed by Malaysia’s Kuala Lumpur with 167 and Indonesia’s Jakarta with 165.

Earlier on Sunday morning, Dhaka ranked 11th among the world’s cities with the worst air quality, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 108 at 9:15 am.

According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as “unhealthy for sensitive groups”, posing health risks to children, older adults, and people with heart or lung diseases, while the general public is mostly unaffected.

An AQI reading of 101 to 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, while 151 to 200 is classified as ‘unhealthy’. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered ‘very unhealthy’, and anything above 301 is categorized as ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.

The AQI provides a daily indication of air quality by measuring the level of pollution and its potential impact on human health.

In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants—particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.

Dhaka has long faced serious air pollution problems, with air quality generally deteriorating during the winter months and improving during the monsoon season.

The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to around 7 million deaths worldwide every year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.
Author: UNB

Title: Can the RMG sector maintain its position in the global apparel market?
Content:
Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry stands at a critical juncture. The sector generates over 80% of the country’s export earnings while supporting millions of livelihoods. However, global competitiveness now extends beyond cost, quality, and delivery to include sustainability, transparency, responsible business practices, and credible environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance.

The key question is whether Bangladesh can move beyond a compliance-driven mindset and leverage sustainability practices and reporting as strategic tools to strengthen its position in the global apparel market.

The RMG sector transformed significantly after the 2013 Rana Plaza tragedy, which exposed critical weaknesses in workplace safety, labour compliance, and factory governance. In response, the industry adopted widespread reforms supported by global initiatives, regulatory authorities, and international buyers.

These reforms led to significant improvements in workplace safety, structural integrity, labour standards, and environmental management. Bangladesh now hosts the world’s largest number of LEED-certified green garment factories. Many manufacturers have also adopted energy-efficient technologies, wastewater treatment, water recycling, and renewable energy systems, demonstrating the sector’s growing commitment to sustainable manufacturing.

Despite these achievements, Bangladesh operates in an increasingly competitive global apparel market. Increasing competition from Vietnam, India, and Turkey highlights the need to strengthen competitiveness beyond low-cost production. Future success will depend on sustainability performance, innovation, supply-chain transparency, and resilience rather than price alone.

Global sustainability transformation requires organizations to integrate sustainability practices with credible sustainability reporting through a structured five-step roadmap. The process begins with assessment and governance, where organizations identify material ESG risks using double materiality and align priorities with the UN SDGs.

Next, sustainability is embedded into operations through carbon measurement, Scope 3 emissions management, renewable energy, circular production, labour rights, and supply chain traceability.

These practices respond to evolving global regulations. The roadmap then focuses on performance monitoring using measurable ESG indicators and science-based climate targets (SBTi). Finally, organizations disclose sustainability performance through frameworks such as GRI and SASB supported by external assurance.

Together, sustainability practices and reporting enhance accountability, market access, investor confidence, and the long-term competitiveness of Bangladesh’s RMG sector.

Over the past two decades, sustainability has become a core requirement in global apparel supply chains. International brands increasingly require compliance with standards on labour rights, occupational safety, environmental management, and responsible sourcing.

Frameworks such as GRI, the Higg Index, and ZDHC have accelerated the adoption of cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, resource-efficient production, and stronger monitoring systems across factories. Industry leaders increasingly recognize that long-term competitiveness depends not only on compliance but also on embedding sustainability into core business strategy.

A key pillar of this transformation is sustainability reporting. Leading Bangladeshi manufacturers have begun publishing sustainability and ESG reports using internationally recognized frameworks. These early adopters reflect growing alignment with global expectations and increasing institutional maturity across the sector.

Sustainability reporting strengthens buyer confidence, improves operational efficiency, supports access to green finance, and enhances risk management. It also enables manufacturers to benchmark performance and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.

However, progress remains uneven across the industry. While large exporters are increasingly adopting structured reporting, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) still lack the technical expertise, financial resources, and data management systems needed for comprehensive reporting.

As a result, they continue to rely on fragmented disclosures driven by buyer audits, certifications, and compliance requirements.

This gap reduces transparency, limits comparability, and raises concerns about data reliability across the value chain.

Although sustainability reporting is not yet mandatory for all manufacturers, it is expected to become a formal requirement by 2027 as global regulatory frameworks evolve.

Bridging this gap will require coordinated efforts to strengthen technical capacity, improve digital infrastructure, and expand access to affordable green finance.

Despite significant progress, several structural challenges continue to limit the full sustainability transformation of Bangladesh’s RMG industry.

One major challenge is the sector’s continued reliance on fossil-fuel-based energy systems, which restricts large-scale emissions reduction. Although some factories have adopted renewable energy solutions, the national energy structure remains carbon intensive.

Access to green finance is another key constraint, especially for SMEs investing in cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, and digital reporting systems. High initial costs often delay sustainability investments despite their long-term benefits.

Environmental management practices also vary across the sector. While leading factories use advanced wastewater treatment and chemical management systems, many production clusters still face challenges in textile waste management and circular economy adoption.

Labour-related challenges also remain, including wages, worker representation, skills development, and human rights due diligence. Manufacturers must also navigate complex buyer requirements, certification schemes, and regulatory frameworks, which can increase audit fatigue and compliance costs.

To remain globally competitive, Bangladesh’s RMG sector must move beyond compliance-driven sustainability and establish sustainability as a core business strategy.

This requires stronger governance, improved reporting systems, and integration of ESG priorities into corporate decision-making, risk management, and investment planning.

Wider adoption of global reporting frameworks, independent assurance mechanisms, and digital traceability solutions will be essential to improve transparency, credibility, and data quality across the value chain.

At the same time, an inclusive sustainability transition will require targeted support for SMEs through technical assistance, capacity building, and access to affordable green finance.

Collaboration among manufacturers, global brands, policy-makers, financial institutions, development partners, and academic institutions will be critical to overcome barriers and accelerate industry-wide transformation.

Bangladesh’s RMG industry has demonstrated its ability to adapt by improving workplace safety, strengthening compliance systems, and advancing sustainable factory practices.

However, the next stage of competitiveness will depend on transforming sustainability from a set of operational initiatives into a measurable and strategic advantage.

As global apparel sourcing increasingly prioritizes carbon performance, resource efficiency, transparency, human rights, and accountability, cost competitiveness alone will no longer be sufficient.

The central challenge now for Bangladesh is to institutionalize credible sustainability reporting and ensure that responsible practices are embedded throughout the industry.

By doing so, Bangladesh can strengthen buyer confidence, secure long-term market access, and maintain its position as a global apparel leader.

Mohammad Rabiul Kabir is an associate professor at Stamford University, Bangladesh, and a sustainability and ESG professional.
Author: Mohammad Rabiul Kabir

Title: Towards stronger ties with France
Content:
At a time when the Bangladesh economy is experiencing a particularly challenging period, it is more important than ever to strengthen our diplomatic relations with nations.

To that end, the visit of the French Senate delegation and their expressed interest in deeper political engagement with Bangladesh is an important moment, and one that Dhaka should seize with clarity and ambition.

France, beyond being a major European power, is also a strategic actor in global security, climate diplomacy, and development cooperation. Strengthening ties with Paris serves Bangladesh’s long‑term interests, especially as we navigate our economic and social challenges in a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

The senators’ remarks signal that France sees Bangladesh as more than a development partner and views it as a country with growing regional influence and a role to play in Indo‑Pacific dynamics.

This recognition matters and opens the door to more robust cooperation in areas where France has deep expertise: defense modernization, renewable energy, climate expertise, digital governance, and higher education.

Bangladesh, for its part, has every reason to welcome this interest. France has been a consistent supporter of Bangladesh, be it the climate agenda, infrastructure development, or being a growing market for Bangladeshi goods.

With Bangladesh eventually needing to shed its LDC tag, stronger political engagement with France can help diversify partnerships, expand trade opportunities, and strengthen diplomatic leverage in the entirety of Europe.

Bangladesh, for its part, must articulate clear priorities, from technology transfer and green energy investment to cultural exchanges. Engagement must also move beyond courtesy visits and translate into structured dialogue, joint initiatives, and long‑term agreements.

Bangladesh has the opportunity to deepen a relationship built on mutual respect and shared global concerns with a major European nation. We must not squander it. Stronger ties with Paris will not only enhance Bangladesh’s international standing but also support its aspirations for sustainable development, climate resilience, and eventually, a more prosperous future.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: Getting serious about dengue prevention
Content:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s inauguration of the three‑month nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign is a reminder once again that Bangladesh cannot afford complacency when it comes to the disease.

Dengue continues to claim lives while hospitals remain strained, and the next three months are considered the highest‑risk period. The PM’s message is clear and one that ought to have been heeded years ago: Dengue cannot be controlled by mosquito‑killing drives alone; it requires public awareness, daily vigilance, and collective responsibility.

The campaign’s emphasis on keeping surroundings clean and removing stagnant water every day reflects the core truth of dengue prevention. Aedes mosquitoes breed in small, overlooked pockets of water -- flowerpots, rooftop corners, discarded containers, construction sites, and household drains.

No city corporation, no ministry, and no volunteer force can eliminate these breeding grounds without active participation from residents.

The PM’s call for coordinated field‑level activities involving local administrations, volunteers, students, and community groups recognizes that dengue prevention must be woven into everyday life.

Around 25,000 volunteers have reportedly already joined the campaign, and this sort of intent shown is the kind of energy we need to turn this campaign into a success.

Yet, while weekly visits to homes and establishments will help identify breeding sites and raise awareness, their efforts will only succeed if households respond -- by cleaning regularly, checking rooftops and balconies, clearing drains, and refusing to let water accumulate.

The PM’s directive to intensify awareness campaigns across television, mass media, and social media underscores the urgency of changing public behaviour, not just public policy.

We have continued to struggle with dengue because prevention has often been reactive, triggered only after outbreaks worsen. This campaign must mark a shift toward proactive, sustained action.

Dengue is preventable. Bangladesh must prove that it can prevent it.
Author: Tribune Editorial

Title: The non-residential Bangladeshi: Reform or ruin?
Content:
There is an old, unwritten law: You can take a Bangladeshi out of the country, but you can rarely extract the country from the Bangladeshi.

When a person steps off a flight at Heathrow or JFK, a silent internal split occurs.

The passport changes, the currency in the wallet shifts, but the underlying psychological software -- that intricate, centuries-old wiring shaped by deltaic floods, agrarian survivalism, and localized territoriality -- remains intact.

This raises an uncomfortable, introspective question: Does life abroad genuinely elevate the non-resident Bangladeshi (NRB) psyche, or does it merely provide a grander, more lucrative stage for domestic vices?

There is a comforting, widely peddled myth popular in living rooms across Dhaka and Chittagong: That the average Bangladeshi, notoriously prone to skipping queues and bribing their way out of trouble back home, magically transforms into a law-abiding saint the moment they step foot into a Western nation.

The argument usually points to the omnipresent "rule of law" -- the strict speed cameras, the unbribable police, the automated tax audits, and the certainty of punishment.

In Bangladesh, institutional fragility turns law into an optional menu of suggestions; abroad, it is assumed, the sheer weight of enforcement forces instant moral reform.

Yet, public record reveals a far more complicated psychological reality. The rule of law certainly creates external compliance, but it does not automatically erase decades of ingrained survival instincts.

For a significant cohort, the presence of a structured, trusting system does not inspire civic duty -- it merely changes the nature of the game.

Where law back home is evaded through brute influence or financial bribes, abroad it is often tested through administrative loophole-hunting, calculated anonymity, and systemic arbitrage.

To trace the psychological shifts of the diaspora, one must look at the historical trail left in the press and legal archives.

The migration waves of the 1980s and 1990s -- particularly to the United Kingdom and Southern Europe -- brought not just workforce muscle, but also the instinctual survival mechanisms of the homeland.

In the late 1980s and through the 1990s, British media periodically highlighted complex welfare and housing benefit scams originating out of East London’s Tower Hamlets -- a hub heavily settled by Sylheti families.

What local authorities framed as sophisticated "social security fraud" was often, at its core, the psychological extension of shonchoy (survival hoarding) and system-gaming honed in a home country where state institutions were meant to be bypassed, not trusted.

By the mid-2010s, investigative operations in Europe laid bare even stranger phenomena: Operations where Bangladeshi migrants holding Italian passports were flying into London on day trips to lodge fraudulent welfare claims before flying back out.

In Australia, immigration reports over the decades have quietly documented cash-in-hand wage undercutting, pseudo-marriages for permanent residency, and localized rental "hot-bedding" schemes run by established diaspora landlords exploiting newly arrived countrymen.

To the foreign observer, these act as felonies or administrative crimes.

But to an introspective Bangladeshi, they are recognizable reflexes.

The rule of law deters blatant chaos, but it cannot prevent the scarcity-driven impulse to extract maximum resources with minimal exposure.

When we look into the mirror, we see ancestral traits that refused to dissolve in foreign waters.

Take the stereotypical Noakhali ethos: Fiercely hardworking, notoriously tight-knit, possessing an innate commercial shrewdness, and an uncompromising loyalty to the clan.

When transported to London’s Brick Lane, New York’s Jackson Heights, or Sydney’s Lakemba, this trait morphs into an enclave mentality.

It creates vibrant business ecosystems, but it can also create isolated echo chambers where Western civil code is treated as an external inconvenience, and the primary moral obligation remains owed strictly to one's immediate lineage back home.

Conversely, consider the Barisal archetype: Deeply opinionated, intellectually pugnacious, and harbouring an ingrained skepticism toward formal authority -- a product of living in a riverine landscape where land itself shifts overnight.

Overseas, this manifests as a refusal to quietly assimilate.

It can express itself as political factionalism -- where Bangladeshi political rivalries are absurdly re-enacted in municipal hall meetings -- or as an instinctive urge to find the hidden loophole in any structured bureaucracy.

Yet, to characterize the NRB experience solely through its missteps is to miss a profound psychological evolution.

Migration is a pressure cooker. While the weak points of the psyche can rupture into criminality under stress, its strengths -- when paired with actual rule of law -- can crystallize into extraordinary global achievement.

For those who genuinely allow the structural stability of foreign nations to alter their internal compass, the transformation is real:

For these individuals, living abroad broke the chain of scarcity mindsets.

It replaced the anxiety of bluffing through life with genuine mastery, allowing the inherent warmth, hospitality, and intelligence of the Bangladeshi character to shine through without the corrupting friction of institutional decay.

Does the non-resident Bangladeshi change for the better or the worse? The truth is that migration acts as a magnifier, not an automatic moral cleanser.

The presence of the rule of law creates a fork in the road rather than a guaranteed transformation.

If a person departs Bangladesh viewing rules merely as obstacles to dodge, foreign soil simply provides a more stable, lucrative infrastructure to game.

The bad gets worse because the safety nets of wealthy nations offer higher stakes to exploit.

However, if a person uses the predictability of foreign law to shed the hyper-vigilance required to survive back home, the Bangladeshi psyche undergoes a remarkable transformation.

The raw energy used for survival converts into an unmatched work ethic. The clannish loyalty expands into genuine civic responsibility.

The NRB remains forever caught between two worlds: Carrying the river's chaos in their blood, while deciding whether to respect or exploit the paved, orderly streets of the world.

Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.
Author: Wafiur Rahman

Title: Government primary schools in Dhaka face enrolment decline
Content:
On a school day, rows of empty benches outnumbered students at Swamibag Government Primary School in Dhaka, where only a few children were present during scheduled class hours.

At around 10am, three children were seen sitting in one classroom without a teacher. By around 1pm, the few students who remained had left, saying classes were over.

On another day, five students were present. However, government records show that the school has 58 students and 5 teachers.

The contrast between official records and what is visible inside classrooms is not limited to one school.

Over three days, Dhaka Tribune visited several government primary schools in Dhaka’s Sutrapur area, including Government Colony Primary, Swamibag Primary, Bongobashi Government Primary, Muslim Government and Narinda primary schools, at different times between 10am and noon.

Photo: Asiful Islam Rifat/Dhaka Tribune

The visits found classrooms with very few students, aging infrastructure, stagnant water, unclean surroundings, and limited space for children to play.

The gap between official data and ground reality extends to several other government primary schools in the area, including Bangla Bazar, Bongobashi, Muslim and Wari Mohila Somity primary schools.

Sutrapur Thana has 48 government primary schools, 322 working teachers, and 8,274 enrolled students.

Data shows low enrolment at several institutions. Muslim Government Primary School has 23 enrolled students for 4 teachers, Bongobashi Government Primary School lists 26 students for 3 teachers, Nobendro Boshak Lane Government Primary School has 32 students; and Narinda Mohila Somity Government Primary School reports 40 students.

However, the figures do not tell the whole story.

At Swamibag Government Primary School, official records list 58 students and five working teachers against six approved posts. Government data also shows that the school has nine classrooms, three toilets and a safe drinking water source.

During two separate visits, however, only three and five students, respectively, were seen at the school. Some classrooms were covered in dust, while waterlogging made parts of the school unsuitable for classes.

Addressing the discrepancy, Samina Yasmin, headteacher of Swamibag Government Primary School, said: “We have continuously informed the senior authorities about the structural issues at the school. They are well aware of the issue. Our teachers repeatedly encourage students to attend school and communicate with parents, but many children attend for a few days before becoming irregular again.”

She defended the teaching staff while acknowledging the attendance problems.

“We take classes regularly. But when there are no students, what classes can we take?” she added.

Kishori Rani Biswas, headteacher of Bongobashi Government Primary School, said: “Since I joined the school, I have tried my best to improve the situation. Currently, 33 students are enrolled here. We are continuously working to gradually increase the number of students.”

The problem is not limited to attendance. Plaster on the entrance walls was peeling off, revealing damp and weathered brickwork. The narrow passage leading inside was littered with debris and stagnant water.

Broken bricks, rubbish and stagnant water were visible in different areas of the premises. Moss had accumulated along parts of the boundary wall and in narrow spaces behind classrooms.

Classrooms were covered in dust and contained only a few broken benches and a fractured wallboard.

A significant portion of the school premises was waterlogged, with dark, dirty rainwater standing for extended periods. The stagnant water was accompanied by mosquitoes.

The surroundings of school equipment also appeared poorly maintained.

Similar problems were observed at Government Colony Primary School and most of the other schools visited in the area. In several places, aging buildings, limited open space and poor cleanliness were visible.

For many families, government primary schools remain an affordable option. But parents interviewed during the field visits said low cost alone was no longer enough to convince them to choose these schools.

Subhan Rahman, a guardian of two children, said the facilities and classroom environment were not satisfactory.

“The facilities are not very good. Classes are also not always held properly. That is why many people are not interested in sending their children here,” he said.

Farida Yasmin pointed to another problem, describing a cycle in which declining attendance further weakens the school environment.

“Classes are not always held regularly, and the infrastructure is also unsatisfactory. Besides, it creates a cycle. There are fewer students, so there is less activity in the classroom. Again, because the environment is not good, new students do not come,” she said.

Sharmin Sultana, a resident of the area, has not sent either of her two children to a government primary school. Instead, both attend a private institution.

For her, the decision was not simply about academic considerations.

“The school has transport and other facilities, which is important for working mothers. I don’t have to worry about taking my children to and from school,” she said.

“Private institutions follow a more up-to-date curriculum and provide greater individual attention to students,” she added.

Highlighting the systemic nature of the issue, educationist Prof Dr Manzoor Ahmed said affluent and middle-class urban families have long shifted away from government primary institutions.

Emphasizing that physical access alone cannot sustain enrollment without quality and safety, he said: “Dilapidated infrastructure, teacher shortage, security concerns, teaching methods, lack of play areas, and the absence of individualized learning support are driving parents away from government primary schools.”

Commenting on the structural deficiencies, Nahida Sultana, assistant thana education officer (ATEO) of Sutrapur, told Dhaka Tribune: “We are aware of the infrastructural issues in several schools under our jurisdiction. We have documented these concerns and submitted requests for necessary allocations to the higher authorities. Once funds are sanctioned, renovation and infrastructure improvement works will begin.”

She acknowledged administrative shortages, saying: “Some of the schools lack headteachers and assistant headteachers.”

She added: “Although student numbers are low due to parental reluctance, we are actively working to raise awareness among them. We are conducting cluster-based monitoring and submit weekly reports. If any teacher is found negligent in performing their classroom duties upon investigation, strict action will be taken.”

At a recent press conference, State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj said monitoring should not rely only on administrative reports and paperwork but should be based on actual results. On the declining attendance of students, Bobby Hajjaj told Dhaka Tribune: “We are trying to understand and meet the needs of parents and students and take measures accordingly. Government facilities are meant for the people. Our effort will be to understand what people want and find ways to meet those needs. If we fail to meet their needs, government primary schools will eventually be closed."

Asked about the government’s plans for the schools’ infrastructure, he said: “Yes, I am aware of the condition of the buildings. We are working to modernize these buildings, and hopefully, the work will begin by the end of this year or early next year.”

Educationists say government primary schools remain one of the few affordable avenues for formal education for many low-income families in Dhaka. If these institutions continue to lose students while private alternatives expand, the issue could affect access to affordable and equitable education in the capital.
Author: Asiful Islam Rifat

Title: The RYZE of Bangladesh’s first AI Hub
Content:
Artificial Intelligence has become deeply entwined within education, the arts, wellbeing, and everyday life. Consequently, access to different AI tools has become a daily requirement and an important part of the user experience. However, using multiple platforms simultaneously can be a hassle; switching between apps, managing separate subscriptions, and dealing with international payments.

Banglalink took the step towards simplifying AI access, bringing together multiple leading Artificial Intelligence models within its AI-powered digital lifestyle brand, RYZE. Incorporating ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Claude and Gemini within one interface, RYZE’s aim is to simplify access to advanced AI tools for everyday users, students, and professionals.

The RYZE AI Hub was initially soft launched in January this year during a freshers’ orientation programme at BRAC University by Banglalink’s CEO, Johan Buse. It was officially launched in April, marking its wider availability and giving users the chance to select models suited to different tasks, whether writing, research or other activities.

The focus on practical skills and employability has also brought international recognition. RYZE received the AI Innovation Award at the Global Conference on AI Leadership and Flagship Prestige Awards 2026 for its contribution to advancing AI solutions aimed at improving young people's skills and employability. The recognition came within the same year as the AI Hub’s commercial launch.

RYZE’s access model is also different from quintessential subscription approaches. Users get access to premium AI models by purchasing tokens and using them according to requirements rather than taking separate monthly subscriptions. The hassle of payment through dollar endorsed credit card is also removed as users are allowed to pay via local mobile financial services. Moreover, RYZE is not limited to users of one mobile network; it is a telco-agnostic platform that can be accessed by users across networks.

Users receive free 10,000 tokens upon signing up and do so each month for basic use. Additional tokens are available upon purchasing RYZE’s In-App Packs- Core, Pro, Max and Ultra. These packs offer 100,000, 210,000, 575,000, and 1,250,000 tokens respectively, each valid for 30 days.

For users in Bangladesh, the payment mechanism is another practical consideration, reflective of Banglalink’s commitment to care.

Access to many international digital services can be complicated by the need for an internationally enabled credit or debit card. Along with traditional payment methods, RYZE also allows users to purchase tokens through local mobile financial services such as bKash or Nagad.

As AI becomes increasingly relevant to learning and professional life, the evolution of platforms like RYZE suggests that the next question for Bangladesh may not simply be whether people can use AI, but how easily they can access the tools they need.
Author: Press Release

Title: PM for reducing import dependence by boosting farm production
Content:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday stressed the need to reduce Bangladesh’s dependence on imports of agricultural and food products by increasing domestic production of crops that can be grown in the country.

He also asked officials of the Ministry of Agriculture to take effective measures to boost the production of locally viable agricultural commodities, while ensuring food security and making farming more productive and profitable, said a release issued by the PM’s Press Wing.

The prime minister gave the directives at a meeting with officials of the ministry at its conference room in the Bangladesh Secretariat in the afternoon.

He directed officials to focus not only on increasing agricultural productivity but also on reducing farmers’ production costs and ensuring fair prices for their produce.

“We must gradually reduce our dependence on imports of agricultural and food products that can be produced domestically. To this end, we need to put greater emphasis on increasing domestic production by quickly taking research findings, improved varieties, modern technologies, irrigation facilities and mechanization to farmers,” Tarique Rahman said.

Earlier, the prime minister walked from his office to the agriculture ministry and took the stairs instead of using the lift to reach the ministry’s conference room.

At the meeting, officials presented the overall situation of the agriculture sector, ongoing activities of the ministry and its plans.

The ministry informed the meeting that mustard production has increased significantly as part of efforts to reduce dependence on imported edible oil.

Mustard production rose from 8.24 lakh tonnes in 2021-22 to 15.34 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 and 15.41 lakh tonnes in 2025-26.

The meeting was also informed of initiatives to increase onion production and storage capacity. “Measures include introducing air-flow technology for onion storage at farmers’ level and expanding summer onion varieties.”

The ministry is also working to expand climate-resilient crop varieties tolerant to salinity, drought and waterlogging at the field level.

Highlighting progress in agricultural research, officials said a total of 1,090 crop varieties have so far been developed, including 155 rice varieties.

More than 1,000 agricultural technologies have also been developed, according to the presentation.

The meeting stressed greater emphasis on agricultural mechanization to reduce labour and production costs while increasing productivity.

The government is working to increase domestic production of agricultural machinery and make equipment such as combine harvesters, reapers and rice transplanters available to farmers at affordable prices.

The expansion of solar-powered irrigation was also discussed. There are currently 2,617 solar irrigation systems in the country, and expanding renewable energy-based irrigation could help reduce farmers’ irrigation costs and dependence on conventional fuels, officials said.

The meeting also reviewed the Farmers’ Card program aimed at ensuring direct delivery of government support to farmers.

The agriculture ministry has set a target of bringing 43 lakh farmers under the card program in the 2026-27 fiscal year. Preparations are underway to distribute cards to around 1.10 lakh farmers in the first phase, the meeting was informed.

The meeting also discussed canal excavation, tree plantation, and storage and marketing of farm produce.
Author: UNB

Title: Ten rescued after boat capsizes in Padma, including 20-day-old baby
Content:
A 20-day-old baby was among 12 people swept into the Padma River after a boat capsized in Chapainawabganj on Saturday, with 10 Bangladeshis later rescued by India's Border Security Force (BSF) and one person still missing.

The boat capsized around 5:30pm while travelling from Bakherali to Johurpur Belpara in Chapainawabganj Sadar as the river became rough. The baby, Tanisha, was travelling in her mother Tania Khatun's arms when the boat sank and all 12 people on board fell into the water.

Photo: Dhaka Tribune

Md Wasim, 23, managed to swim to the shore, while the remaining 11 passengers went missing.

Amid the strong current and storm, the passengers tried to stay afloat by holding onto the boat’s wooden floor, sacks, floating pieces of wood, paddles and other objects.

Tania Khatun held Tanisha tightly, but at one point the strong current pulled the baby from her arms. Tania later found Tanisha underwater and held her tightly again.

Tanisha’s maternal grandfather Ibrahim also swam while holding the baby above the water with one hand.

After floating in the water for around 1 hour and 20 minutes, the current carried them towards Indian waters. BSF members spotted 10 Bangladeshis, including Tanisha, and went to rescue them in a speedboat before taking them to the riverbank.

At the time of the rescue, 20-day-old Tanisha was almost unresponsive after swallowing water while being held by her mother. BSF members quickly took her to a local medical centre, where doctors examined her and said she was healthy.

The incident occurred while the group was travelling from Bakherali in Chapainawabganj Sadar to Johurpur Belpara. Tanisha is the daughter of Md Sohel and Tania Khatun of Johurpur Belpara in Sadar upazila.

Shariful Islam, subedar of the Bakher Ali Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) camp, said rescuers told him that Tania had been holding Tanisha tightly after the boat sank.

He said: “They floated by holding onto the boat’s rice husk, paddle and wooden floor. At one point, the strong current pulled the child from her mother’s hand and she sank into the water. Later, Tania Khatun found her and held her tightly again.”

Shahidul Islam, company commander of Faridpur Border Outpost (BOP), said Tanisha’s maternal grandfather knew how to swim, while the women stayed afloat by holding onto the boat’s wooden floor, paddles and sacks.

He said: “They remained floating in the water for more than an hour.”

Rabiul Islam Rabu, member of Ward 8 of Narayanpur Union Parishad, said Tania initially held Tanisha tightly, but the strong current and storm caused the baby to slip from her arms and sink.

He said Tania later found Tanisha and held her above the water with her legs. Seeing the baby in distress, her grandfather Ibrahim held her above the water with 1 hand while swimming to survive.

Rabiul Islam Rabu said they remained in the water for around 1 hour and 20 minutes before BSF members rescued them.

Shyamalal Mondal, a resident of Taranagar in Lalbagh police station area of Murshidabad district, was present on the Indian side when the BSF rescued the Bangladeshis.

He said BSF members rescued the Bangladeshis and took them to the riverbank. He added that 20-day-old Tanisha was almost unresponsive at the time and that BSF members immediately took her to a local medical center, where doctors said she was healthy.

Lieutenant Colonel Kazi Mostafizur Rahman, commander of BGB’s 53 Battalion, said members of the BSF’s 71 Battalion Khandua Camp rescued the Bangladeshis with a speedboat on Saturday night.

He said the BSF handed over the 10 rescued Bangladeshis to the BGB that night, after which the BGB released them into the custody of their relatives.

Kazi Mostafizur Rahman said 9 of the 10 rescued Bangladeshis, including Tanisha, returned home that night in healthy condition.

At around 5pm on Saturday, a motorized boat carrying 12 passengers left Alimnagar Ghat in the Bakherali area for Johurpurtek village. The boat sank in the Padma River on the way.

At around 5:50pm, the company commander of the 71 Battalion BSF’s Khandua Camp informed the BGB about the boat sinking. He said the BSF had rescued 10 Bangladeshis alive, including 4 men, 3 women and 3 children.

The Chapainawabganj Battalion, 53 BGB, then took steps to bring them back to Bangladesh. At 9:55pm, a company commander-level flag meeting was held between the commander of Faridpur BOP and the commander of the Khandua BSF Camp.

Following the meeting, the 10 rescued Bangladeshis were brought back to Bangladesh. They were later handed over to their close relative, Md Ismail Hossain, in the presence of local public representatives.

The BGB said all the rescued people were in good health.

The rescued people were Md Russell, 26; Md Ibrahim, 50; Sowdagar, 40; Md Ibrahim, 60; Sakhina, 45; Nilufta, 35; Tania, 22, and her 20-day-old daughter; Sanaullah, 9; and Al Amin, 9.

All of them are from Johurpur (Bokaripara) village in Chapainawabganj.

Meanwhile, Md Mostafa, 60, son of late Altab Hossain, from the same village, remains missing. Search and rescue operations are continuing to locate him.
Author: Dulal Abdullah

Title: Regent Hospital chairman Shahed shown arrested again in corruption case
Content:
Regent Hospital Chairman Mohammad Shahed Karim has been shown arrested in a case filed by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) over allegations of acquiring illegal assets and money laundering.

Judge Mohammad Abdullah Al Mamun of Dhaka Special Judge Court-5 passed the order today (14 September) following an application submitted by the ACC, ACC lawyer Delwar Jahan Rumi confirmed.

ACC Deputy Director Md Farid Ahmed Patwari filed the case on 7 March 2021.

Following an investigation, ACC Assistant Director and investigation officer Mohammad Ziatul Islam submitted a charge sheet against Mohammad Shahed and his wife, Mrs Sadia Arbi, on 10 January 2024.

According to the charge sheet, Sadia Arbi declared assets worth Tk61.30 lakh, including movable and immovable properties, in a wealth statement submitted to the ACC on 28 December 2020.

However, verification and investigation found assets worth Tk76.23 lakh in her name. The charge sheet said she concealed information about assets worth Tk14.93 lakh and provided false information.

Including Tk1.80 lakh in family expenses, the total value of Sadia Arbi's acquired assets stood at Tk78.23 lakh. However, her income tax records showed an income of Tk4.50 lakh.

As a result, assets worth Tk73.53 lakh were found to be outside her income tax records and disproportionate to her known sources of income, according to the charge sheet.

It also said Sadia Arbi had no reliable independent source of income. Her husband, Mohammad Shahed, allegedly provided direct assistance in acquiring assets in her name by transferring, converting and concealing money earned through illegal and corrupt means.

The ACC sought the framing of charges against the couple under Sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, Section 4(2) of the Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2012, and Section 109 of the Penal Code.

Shahed is a convicted accused in several fraud and cheating cases. Several warrants, including those related to an arms case and cheque dishonour cases, are also pending against him in different courts.

After being released following a long period in jail, he was recently arrested again on a Complaint Register (C.R.) warrant.

He was later shown arrested and sent to jail in a loan default and cheque dishonour case filed by Mercantile Co-operative Bank, following a warrant related to a one-year prison sentence and a fine.

He is currently in jail.

Title: SP suspended after testing positive in drug test
Content:
The government has temporarily suspended Superintendent of Police (SP) AFM Nizam from service after he tested positive in a drug test.

The Police-1 branch of the Public Security Division under the Ministry of Home Affairs issued a gazette notification in this regard. Dated 10 September, the notification was uploaded to the ministry's website today (14 September).

According to the notification, SP AFM Nizam was attached to the office of the Deputy Inspector General of police of the Rangpur Range. He left Police Headquarters on 8 January to attend the ongoing DSCSC-2026 course in Mirpur.

During the course, he fell ill on 7 June and was sent to the Combined Military Hospital in Dhaka Cantonment for treatment.

As part of medical examinations conducted on the advice of specialist doctors, he underwent a drug test. The test returned positive for benzodiazepines and amphetamine/methamphetamine.

The notification said the matter was contrary to the discipline of the DSCSC course.

Under these circumstances, AFM Nizam was temporarily suspended from government service on 31 August under Rule 12(1) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018.

The notification further stated that he would receive a subsistence allowance in accordance with the rules during the period of suspension.

Issued in the public interest, the order takes immediate effect.
