Title: Around 2 crore children get measles vaccines in five months
Content:
The government has administered measles vaccines to 1,97,71,720 children across the country in five months under the ongoing measles-rubella vaccination programme.

This figure exceeded the initial vaccination target by about 10%.

When the country witnessed a measles outbreak at the end of March this year, the government swiftly launched an emergency vaccination programme on 5 April, covering 30 upazilas in 18 districts in the first phase.

The second phase of vaccination began on 12 April in four major city corporations, Dhaka South, Dhaka North, Barishal and Mymensingh. In the final, third phase, the ongoing nationwide measles-rubella vaccination drive commenced on 20 April, said officials at the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).

However, due to the persisting measles outbreak, the government is set to launch another massive vaccination campaign starting on 26 September to prevent the disease.

Initially, officials said the programme aimed to vaccinate about 1.8 crore children nationwide. However, vaccination coverage surpassed the target due to various government initiatives.

According to data from the DGHS, the government's target was to vaccinate 1,80,15,064 children against measles and rubella. But, as of 13 September, a total of 1,97,71,720 children had received the vaccine.

Data obtained from the integrated control centre for the measles-rubella vaccine shows that 11,10,698 children received the measles-rubella vaccine in Barishal division, while 48,41,924 received it in Chattogram division, 49,19,913 in Dhaka division, 16,95,779 in Khulna division, 15,30,916 in Mymensingh division, 22,13,197 in Rajshahi division, 20,73,488 in Rangpur division and 13,85,805 in Sylhet division.

Among the city corporation areas, 44,119 children were administered the vaccine in Barishal city. At the same time, 3,36,870 received it in Chattogram city, 48,643 in Cumilla city, 5,57,688 in Dhaka North City, 4,18,972 in Dhaka South City, 2,06,927 in Gazipur city, 83,697 in Narayanganj city, 96,792 in Khulna city, 62,305 in Mymensingh city, 63,059 in Rajshahi city, 82,253 in Rangpur city and 72,349 in Sylhet city.

DGHS Additional Director General Professor Dr Zahid Raihan told BSS that vaccinating children is an ongoing process.

However, he said the announcement to administer measles vaccines to children on a massive scale across the country starting on 26 September is an intensified effort by the government.

The primary objective of this programme is to ensure that no child is left unvaccinated, he added.

Title: Carney says Canada seeks 'unique alliance' but not membership with the European Union
Content:
Canada is seeking a "unique alliance" with the European Union but is not looking to become a member, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday after the Wall Street Journal reported he was exploring whether Canada could become an "associate member" of the bloc.

The EU, which has not been flexible about membership rules in the past, is open to the idea of granting Canada a yet-to-be-created status of associate membership, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials both from the EU and Canada.

"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney said.

"What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — is a unique alliance between Canada and the European Union," he told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival. "We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths."

Carney's office confirmed on Saturday he will travel to France and Britain next week. He will address the European Parliament in Strasbourg and attend EU President Ursula von der Leyen's State of the European Union address.

The Globe and Mail newspaper separately reported it was the EU, not Carney, that floated the associate membership title, citing an anonymous source who said any discussion of a title for the relationship is premature.

Spokespeople at the European Commission did not respond to requests for comment.

Canada's escalating trade war with the United States has added urgency to its strategic pivot towards other trading partners.

Relations between Ottawa and Washington have deteriorated sharply since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year due to disagreements over trade and other issues. The trade dispute has led to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.

Trump on Sunday renewed his criticism, calling Canada "the worst country to deal with," but adding he thought the nation was "dying to make a deal."

"They've ripped off our country for years," he told reporters aboard Air Force One.

The US president reiterated his intention to impose new tariffs on cars, ​trucks and auto parts from Canada beginning 1 January.

Canada and the EU are discussing ways of allowing Canada's goods, services and workers involved in strategic supply chains such as energy, AI, defence and critical minerals to move freely, thus effectively shifting the EU border, the Wall Street Journal said.

Canada and the EU are also talking about laying underwater cables, jointly constructing data centres, cloud storage and new satellite networks as well as infrastructure to ship Canadian energy to the EU, the newspaper said.

Carney has spoken regularly with several EU leaders, most notably French President Emmanuel Macron, about the possibility of letting Canadians live and work visa-free in the EU, the WSJ said, citing two unnamed officials familiar with the matter.

Macron's press office did not respond to a request for comment.

Macron's office separately confirmed that he will meet Carney on 20 September in the French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a group of islands off Canada's Atlantic coast.

Any project to forge closer ties between Canada and the EU likely faces challenges, however, based on past efforts to implement a more modest trade deal, which has faced fierce opposition within Europe.

More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it.

Title: Indian women cricketers refuse Asia Cup trophy from Pakistan Cricket Board chief Naqvi
Content:
India's women refused to collect the Asia Cup trophy from Pakistan Cricket Board chief Mohsin Naqvi after the team won a record-extending eighth continental title yesterday (13 September).

India hammered Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the T20 final in Dubai yesterday, but Harmanpreet Kaur's side skipped the trophy presentation, repeating the stance of the men's team last year.

On both occasions, the trophy was supposed to have been handed over by Naqvi in his role as head of the Asian Cricket Council.

Naqvi is also Pakistan's interior minister and head of the country's cricket board.

There are long-running tensions between nuclear-armed neighbours India and Pakistan.

A year after beating Pakistan in the final, the men's side have still not collected their trophy.

"That stand has been taken by BCCI (Board of Control for Cricket in India), and we stand by it," Indian women's coach Amol Muzumdar told reporters.

"We are the champions, that's good enough."

Yesterday's presentation was delayed by nearly 50 minutes, after which Naqvi distributed medals to the runners-up before the ceremony ended abruptly.

BCCI Secretary Devajit Saikia and Vice-President Rajeev Shukla were at the ground as India presented medals to their players themselves.

Title: Voting starts in Philippines' south after three killed in election violence
Content:
Voting began on Monday in the Philippines' Muslim-majority south under heightened security after three people were killed and 15 wounded in violence on the eve of the historic election.

The vote is seen as a crucial test of efforts seeking to bring lasting peace and development to a region once torn by separatist conflict and extremism which peaked in the 2017 siege of Marawi City by Islamic State-linked militants.

The Commission on Elections (COMELEC) placed Cotabato City under its control after the violence on Sunday, when an argument at a polling station erupted in gunfire, according to local reports.

COMELEC said voting was proceeding smoothly across the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), and that it did not expect broader unrest, citing expanded checkpoints and the swift deployment of security forces.

The election also faced an early logistical challenge after election officials discovered pre-shaded ballots in a municipality in Basilan, delaying the voting there as ballots would have to be reprinted, COMELEC spokesperson John Rex Laudiangco told DZBB radio.

Nearly 2.4 million voters are registered for the vote, which international partners and peace monitors view as a key test of whether the regional autonomy granted under a 2014 peace deal between Manila and Muslim separatists can be sustained through elected institutions.

The grant of autonomy was intended to halt a conflict that killed more than 120,000 people, displaced about 2 million, and helped extremist groups gain a foothold in the region.

"The election marks a milestone in the continuing journey of BARMM towards lasting peace, democratic governance and meaningful self-determination," President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said in a video message urging voters to take part in what he also described as a "defining moment" for the region and the country.

The election completes a transition set in motion by the agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), the country's largest Muslim separatist group, and a subsequent law that granted greater political and economic powers to the Muslim-majority south.

The law was ratified in a 2019 plebiscite in which residents overwhelmingly backed greater self-rule, paving the way for the creation of BARMM and an interim government tasked with preparing the region for elections.

The Bangsamoro spans parts of Mindanao, the Philippines' second-largest island, and a chain of dozens of small islands to the west once associated with piracy and banditry.

BARMM is the country's only region governed under a parliamentary system, with voters electing an 80-member parliament made up of 40 party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives. The legislature will then choose the chief minister. Among those competing for power in the election are parties led by former MILF rebels, rival factions that emerged from the movement after the peace deal, and traditional political clans.

In Basilan province, 70-year-old Jessica Abing was among those who voted for greater self-rule in 2019 and plans to cast her ballot again on Monday.

She still remembers the fear that gripped Lamitan in 2001 when Abu Sayyaf militants stormed the city and took hostages. Today, she points to a recently opened branch of fast-food chain Jollibee as a symbol of confidence in a city once associated with kidnappings and insecurity.

"Hopefully, the people the voters truly want will win," Abing said.

Title: Sacked Islami Bank employees, customers' forum trade blame after clash leaves 55 injured
Content:
At least 55 people were injured in a clash between dismissed Islami Bank employees appointed during the tenure of S Alam and members of the Sachetan Grahak Forum (Conscious Customers Forum) outside the bank today (14 September).

Locals said the dismissed employees took up positions outside the bank at around 7:30am, demanding reinstatement. When members of the Sachetan Grahak Forum also gathered there, they were attacked, prompting them to chase the dismissed employees, they added.

Members of both groups were injured in the ensuing clashes, according to claims by both groups.

The president of the forum, Nurunnabi Manik, said 30 members of the organisation were injured in an attack.

"There is no relationship between the bank and those illegally recruited. They have gathered here as part of a fresh conspiracy against the bank. Today, while we were holding a peaceful sit-in, we were attacked under police protection," he said.

He said five people sustained serious injuries, while another 25 to 30 were injured and returned home after receiving medical treatment.

"Those who carried out the planned attack must be identified. At the same time, they must be brought to justice," he added.

Meanwhile, Shahidul Islam, one of the dismissed employees, claimed that 25 members of their group were attacked.

"We have been staging a sit-in in front of the bank for the second consecutive day. Within 20 minutes of our arrival today, members of the Sachetan Grahak Forum attacked us. Around 20 to 25 people have been admitted to Dhaka Medical College Hospital," he said.

Mohsin Al Murad, additional deputy commissioner of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police's Motijheel Division, said, "Currently, the dismissed employees are holding a sit-in in front of Bangladesh Bank. As this is a key point installation (KPI), we have asked them to leave the area. Law enforcement agencies are prepared to prevent any disorder."

Title: Trump calls $5,000 payouts 'easy' to fit into federal budget
Content:
President Donald Trump said on Sunday the United States can afford his promise to send $5,000 to every US adult should his Republican Party keep control of Congress in this year's elections.

"I don't know but it's easy if the Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money," Trump told reporters when asked if Congress would need to approve the payments, adding that trillions of dollars were coming into the country.

Trump unveiled the idea of $5,000 payouts during a speech at the Republican Party convention last week. Speaking to reporters on Sunday in Ireland, where he was attending a golf tournament at his club in Doonbeg, the president said the US government has the funds to pay for it.

But any such payment would need to be approved by Congress, House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said on Sunday. "Of course, the devil's in the details. We have to figure all that out," Johnson told CNN's "State of the Union."

Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talk shows panned the idea, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling ABC's "This Week" that it is not a "serious proposal."

US Senator Mallory McMorrow, citing the elimination of some Affordable Care Act subsidies, cast doubt on whether the promised $5,000 checks would be sent even if Republicans retain control of Congress.

"There was an ACA subsidy cancellation," McMorrow, a Michigan Democrat, said on CNN. "I think it was $1,000 we were supposed to get. So if you believe that you're going to get $5,000, I've got a bridge to sell you."

US Representative Mike Lawler, a New York Republican in a closely contested race, would not specifically commit to Trump's $5,000 dividend proposal on Sunday.

"I support putting money back in the pockets of hardworking Americans," he said on ABC's "This Week," citing tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill that Republicans passed last year.

"But whether you call it a stimulus check or a dividend, the question is, how do you pay for it? That's my focus. We have a $4 trillion debt, and we have to be serious about tackling that."

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of the consumer watchdog Public Citizen, earlier called the move an attempt to buy votes.

"This explicit and desperate attempt to buy votes in the November election is a new low. Trump knows he can't do this, and yet he's attempting to bribe voters with the false promise of cash to help his party win an election, which is antithetical to every principle of American democracy."

Donald Trump / Trump administration
Author: Reuters

Title: Dengue situation likely to worsen further in Oct: Expert
Content:
A forecasting model suggests Bangladesh's dengue situation could worsen further in October, said Dr Kabirul Bashar, medical entomologist and professor of zoology at Jahangirnagar University.

"Our forecasting model indicates that the dengue situation will worsen further in October," Bashar said at a dengue prevention workshop at Hotel Sonargaon in Dhaka today (14 September).

He said the common belief that Aedes mosquitoes bite only during the day is incorrect, as tests have shown they can also bite at night.

"People should remain cautious during winter, even when fewer Aedes mosquitoes are visible, as fogging is ineffective against them and may pose health risks," Bashar said.

He called for evidence-based measures to control mosquito populations.

He said, "An Aedes mosquito needs at least two days after acquiring the dengue virus before it can transmit the disease. Therefore, other household members may develop dengue several days after one person becomes infected."

He advised families to eliminate mosquitoes from their homes when a member contracts dengue to reduce the risk of transmission.

Title: Trump downplays report China entities helped Iran before attack that killed US troops
Content:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday brushed aside a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops there in July.

A recent report in the Wall Street Journal cited unnamed US officials about the attack in Jordan. Asked whether he would mention the issue at an upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump did not directly answer, and instead equated the surveillance activities of China and the United States.

"They basically do what we do," he told reporters aboard Air Force One. "When they say China spies on us, I say you're right and we spy on them too."

The Chinese and US presidents are expected to meet in the United States on 24 September, although China has yet to officially confirm that the meeting will take place.

Trump on Sunday reiterated his view that he has a good relationship with Xi.

"I think he's behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well," Trump said as he flew back to the United States after a weekend trip to Ireland.

The Wall Street Journal report, which Reuters could not immediately verify, said the US officials declined to identify the Chinese entities that supplied the imagery to Iran and did not allege direct involvement by Beijing.

Trump's comments appeared consistent with the administration's recent efforts to play down wide-ranging tensions between Washington and Beijing, despite US frustration over Beijing's close ties to Tehran.

At least 18 US service personnel have been killed since the US-Israeli war with Iran began at the end of February.

Title: Smart glasses move mainstream, sparking privacy concerns
Content:
Smart glasses are moving from novelty gadgets to everyday technology, but their growing use is raising serious concerns about privacy and filming in public.

The latest wearable technology allows users to make calls, interact with artificial intelligence, take photos and record videos by simply touching the frames, without reaching for a phone, reports BBC.

The convenience has sparked concern among businesses, campaigners and members of the public who fear they could be recorded without their knowledge.

Wetherspoons, which operates almost 800 pubs across the UK, has banned customers from using smart glasses to film inside its premises. Women's rights campaigners have also warned that the technology could be misused to harass others.

Yet social media creators continue to embrace the glasses, with videos filmed for TikTok and Instagram often relying on spontaneous encounters with strangers.

Smart glasses gain ground as market set to grow Pearse Vallely, a 31-year-old content creator from Ballymurphy in west Belfast, uses Meta Ray-Ban glasses to record his view while walking through the streets, often greeting passers-by with rhyming phrases.

One of his most successful videos, filmed in Belfast city centre, attracted 600,000 views on TikTok.

Vallely said the positive nature of his videos helps him avoid complaints. He has never posted a video after someone asked him not to, he said, and nobody has asked him to remove one. He believes people understand that he does not intend to mock or embarrass them.

Meta says it has sold more than seven million pairs of its smart glasses, which cost a few hundred pounds and have built-in cameras. A small white light pulses while recording and a flash indicates when a photo is taken.

Meta says the recording light helps people know when the camera is operating and recently updated the glasses so the camera stops working if someone interferes with the light.

Researchers expect the wider smart-glasses market to grow sharply if products from other technology companies achieve similar success.

Vallely said people often notice he is recording because of the light and, when possible, he tells them afterwards.

In Northern Ireland, people can generally film others in public, where there is usually less expectation of privacy than in private settings. However, the law can apply when filming involves harassment, stalking or voyeurism, or takes place where someone reasonably expects privacy.

Northern Ireland also has specific offences covering intrusive acts such as upskirting and downblousing, including observing or recording a person's genitals, buttocks, breasts or underwear without consent.

Vallely said he understands why businesses might ban smart glasses when used in a crude or abusive way, but believes the intention behind filming matters. He also warned that people will misuse new technology regardless of how it develops.

Reports of confrontations between smart-glasses users and members of the public have nevertheless fuelled the privacy debate.

In December, a woman attracted praise after breaking a man's Meta glasses on the New York subway. In July, police in Scotland launched an investigation after complaints about a TikToker who allegedly used smart glasses to secretly record members of the public.

Wetherspoons said smart glasses could enable "surreptitious surveillance" and breach common sense. Monopoly Events, which runs Comic Con Northern Ireland, has also banned smart glasses at its events over concerns about secret recording.

Some TikTok creators have used smart glasses while approaching women, asking for their phone numbers and recording their reactions to pick-up lines. Some videos have attracted thousands of views under the hashtag #howtogetagirlfriend.

Campaigners warn of harassment Elaine Crory, a women's sector lobbyist at the Women's Resource and Development Agency, said smart glasses make it harder for people to know when they are being recorded, raising concerns about their misuse for offences such as upskirting.

She said people can often spot a phone or conventional camera and move away, but that is much harder with smart glasses. While social media platforms can remove reported videos and some venues have introduced restrictions, Crory said legislation has struggled to keep pace with the technology.

The Department of Justice said smart glasses do not fall within a specific area of its responsibility, but existing criminal offences can apply when behaviour crosses the criminal threshold. Northern Ireland's current law specifically covers voyeurism, including upskirting and downblousing.

Technology offers benefits Smart glasses also offer benefits beyond filming.

Geoff McConville, an optometrist who sells Meta glasses in Belfast, acknowledged concerns over misuse but said the technology can help people with sight and hearing difficulties.

Some patients use text-to-speech functions to read newspapers and signs with the help of artificial intelligence, which McConville said is particularly valuable for elderly people with visual impairments.

Meta has also highlighted accessibility as a major benefit, saying smart glasses can provide important technology for people with limited sight or hearing and warning that excessive restrictions could limit those benefits.

While Meta accepts that some places should ban filming, it argues that rules should be applied consistently.

Instagram head Adam Mosseri has also said the platform can remove content when users exploit or harass others.

The debate centres on where to draw the line.

Smart glasses can improve communication and accessibility, but also make recording people more discreet, leaving society to balance privacy with legitimate and beneficial uses.

Title: Body of Bangladeshi killed in BSF firing handed over along Thakurgaon border
Content:
The body of a Bangladeshi national who was shot dead by the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) has been handed over to Border Guard Bangladesh through Thakurgaon border.

The deceased was Asadul Haque, 38, son of Abdul Wazed of South Indrail village in Pirganj upazila.

Lieutenant Colonel Abdullah Al Moin, commander of Dinajpur 42 Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), said the BGB held a flag meeting with the BSF to facilitate the repatriation of Asadul's body.

The flag meeting was held at the zero line of the Chanderhat border yesterday afternoon (13 September), with representatives of the Dinajpur 42 BGB and the Indian BSF.

During the meeting, the two sides discussed the prompt repatriation of Asadul's body.

Following legal formalities, the BSF handed over the body to the BGB at around 10pm yesterday, he said.

Meanwhile, two other Bangladeshi nationals, Mostakim and Sri Uda, who survived the shooting, remain in Indian custody.

They were charged under India's Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, and several sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

They were later produced before the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate in Raiganj in India which ordered that they be held in judicial custody for 14 days.

Mostakim, son of Ahed Ali, and Sri Uda, son of Narayan, are both from North Indrail village in the same upazila.

According to local residents and BGB sources, several Bangladeshi youths entered Indian territory near border pillar No. 333, under the jurisdiction of the Chanderhat Border Outpost (BOP), in the early hours of Saturday (12 September).

At that time, a patrol team of the BSF's 63 Chakshibananda camp in India's North Dinajpur district opened fire on them.

Asadul, Mostakim and Sri Uda were injured in the firing.

BSF personnel later rescued them and took them to Kaliaganj State General Hospital in North Dinajpur where Asadul died.

Title: All-vegetarian BRICS dinner sparks political row in India
Content:
A political dispute erupted in India over an all-vegetarian menu served at a gala dinner hosted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi during the 2026 BRICS Summit, with opposition leaders accusing the government of failing to reflect the country's culinary diversity.

The dinner, held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, featured a multi-course vegetarian menu showcasing regional Indian dishes. The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) defended the menu, saying foreign guests appreciated the range of flavours, nutrition and regional traditions represented in the meal.

The gala dinner menu

The menu included Khandvi mille and Khumb Galouti as starters, followed by Paneer Lababdar, Gucchi Marmik, Carrot Bean Poriyal, Thakkali Belle Saaru, millet pulao, beetroot raita and assorted Indian breads.

Desserts included Old Delhi Fruit Cream with Jalebi and Shahtoot Phirni.

Opposition questions lack of meat options

Opposition leaders from several parties criticised the decision not to offer non-vegetarian dishes at the diplomatic dinner.

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi wrote on social media platform X that "80% of Indians are non-vegetarian", while highlighting India's non-vegetarian culinary traditions and his sister's chole bhature.

Congress leader Pawan Khera accused the BJP of extending its dietary preferences to international leaders and questioned why the government had chosen not to showcase India's multi-cuisine culture.

The BJP's habit of imposing its dietary preferences on fellow Indians is already deeply problematic. Now, they have taken it a step further by imposing their own choices on dignitaries from across the world. India is a rich, diverse, multi-cuisine country, home to some of the finest non-vegetarian delicacies that people across the world relish and enjoy. So why did the Modi government choose to hide this part of India's culture? Is it ashamed of the diversity that makes India what it is?

AIMIM leader Waris Pathan said mutton, chicken and fish were an important part of India's culinary identity. He argued that visiting leaders could have been offered dishes such as Hyderabadi biryani, butter chicken and Goan fish curry, referring humorously to Modi's "Naraz Fufa" phrase in connection with the absence of mutton and chicken.

The controversy also unfolded amid discussion over the absence of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan from the gala dinner.

Criticism over diplomatic message

Former parliamentarian and bureaucrat Jawhar Sircar described an enforced all-vegetarian state dinner as a diplomatic mistake and compared it with Aesop's fable The Fox & the Stork. He also pointed to a 2010 state dinner hosted by former prime minister Manmohan Singh for then-US President Barack Obama, where both vegetarian and non-vegetarian dishes were offered.

Thank you to all BRICS leaders for making the Delhi Summit very productive and outcome oriented! https://t.co/C3DMZWGgLL

Trinamool Congress leader Mahua Moitra jokingly suggested that visiting leaders should slip away to local eateries such as Karim's for Burrah Kababs.

Shiv Sena-UBT leader Priyanka Chaturvedi said guests understood the constraints involved in hosting such an event, but argued that providing dietary options would have been more consistent with India's Atithi Devo Bhava philosophy.

BJP rejects criticism

The BJP rejected the criticism, saying the Opposition was politicising the menu and diverting attention from the summit.

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said he was surprised that Congress was politicising the food, adding that foreign guests had enjoyed the flavour, nutritional variety and regional heritage of Indian vegetarian cuisine.

BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said the fact that the Opposition had little to criticise beyond the food showed how successful the BRICS summit had been. He accused Congress of "sulking" over India's growing global profile.

Another BJP spokesperson, Tuhin Sinha, described the opposition remarks as "petty and frivolous". He said Modi had secured consensus among BRICS members on major global issues through the New Delhi Resolution.

With inputs taken from The Print, Times of India, The Telegraph India and NDTV

Title: Chittagong Board suspends three amid mounting result fraud allegations
Content:
Repeated allegations of result manipulation at the Chittagong Education Board have raised questions over safeguards in its sensitive result-preparation work, with three temporary computer-section employees suspended of their duties over an alleged attempt to alter an SSC result.

The latest case involves a student whose marks published in the 2026 SSC results were higher than those recorded on the answer scripts. In one striking discrepancy, the student received zero in physics on the answer script, while the computer system showed 45 marks.

The three – Rashedul Islam Nasir and Imtiaz Ahmed Chowdhury of the scanning section and Md Rayhan of the solving section – came under suspicion during a re-scrutiny on 25 August.

Mohammad Abdul Mannan, deputy controller of examinations (secondary) at the board, told TBS that the student had applied for re-scrutiny of physics, higher mathematics and Bangladesh and Global Studies, during which an examiner detected the initial discrepancy.

Further verification found discrepancies between marks on the student's other answer scripts and data stored at the computer centre.

Board chairman Professor Abdullah Al Mamun Chowdhury formed a three-member investigation committee on 25 August and asked it to submit its report within seven working days.

The deadline has passed, but Professor Mohammad Zahirul Haque Swapan, board secretary and convener of the committee, said the investigation is still underway.

Board officials, on condition of anonymity, said system data, scanning-machine records and employees' work schedules were analysed to identify personnel assigned to the relevant machines that day. Buet experts were also consulted on the technical aspects.

All three denied involvement. Imtiaz said scanning workers only scan answer scripts and prepare bundles, while Nasir said it was impossible to identify and manipulate a particular student's OMR from the scanning machine. Rayhan said a script could not be separately identified or manipulated during sorting, scanning or solving.

Long tenure in sensitive work

Two of the three employees have worked in the computer section since 2014, while Imtiaz joined in 2022. The two who joined in 2014 have therefore remained in sensitive result-preparation work for more than a decade, while the third has worked there for about four years.

This is despite a practice followed by other education boards of transferring personnel involved in result preparation every six months to a year because of the sensitivity of the work.

As the board's senior system analyst post is vacant, Bikas Chandra Mallick, senior system analyst at the Cumilla Education Board, has been assisting with result preparation.

He told TBS, "Employees in the scanning or solving sections may have opportunities to commit fraud if the system lacks adequate security measures. If a system does not have password protection and access controls over who can edit data, as with personal email, its vulnerabilities can be exploited to alter data or commit fraud."

Board officials said a syndicate may have developed around result manipulation, although the employees have denied the allegations of any such involvement.

The computer section has 18 employees, of whom only chief programmer and an assistant programmer are permanent. The other 16 are daily-wage workers, while seven have worked in the section since 2010.

Not the first allegation

During last year's SSC re-scrutiny, 34 scripts were found to have higher marks entered in the system than those on the scripts. An investigation committee submitted recommendations to the ministry, but their contents were not disclosed.

In 2024, the board cancelled the results of 17 students who had been awarded GPA-5 despite not sitting the SSC examination.

In the 2023 HSC, a Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education investigation found that marks had been increased in 11 papers in the result of former board secretary Narayan Chandra Nath's son, Nakshatra Debnath. His result was cancelled, while disciplinary and criminal action was ordered against Narayan, who was later made an OSD.

A case was filed against four people, including Narayan and former chairman Mustafa Kamrul Akhter. A charge sheet has been submitted against all four, and the case is awaiting further court proceedings.

Attempts to contact board chairman Abdullah Al Mamun Chowdhury over the allegations were unsuccessful.

Title: Chhatra Dal condemns display of Jinnah's picture at Ducsu archive
Content:
The Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal has condemned the display of a 1948 picture of Muhammad Ali Jinnah at the historical archive of Dhaka University Central Students' Union (Ducsu), calling it an insult to the university's history and heritage.

Chhatra Dal President Rakibul Islam Rakibul and General Secretary Nasir Uddin Nasir issued the statement this morning (14 September), protesting the display.

The student organisation alleged that the "Shibir-controlled Ducsu council" was disregarding students' aspirations and the spirit of the Liberation War through a series of actions, including an attempt to rename Madhur Canteen as "Ishrat Manzil" and the display of Jinnah's picture at the archive.

It also alleged that the current Ducsu leadership had failed to address students' housing crisis, realise their basic rights and ensure a proper educational environment, instead using the council to advance a specific political and ideological agenda.

"Displaying Jinnah's picture in the archive of Ducsu, which is the centre of Bengal's movement for autonomy, is a direct insult to the heritage of the language and independence movements," the statement reads.

Chhatra Dal called for the immediate removal of the picture of Jinnah, whom it described as a leader who opposed the Bengali language.

It also demanded an end to the use of Ducsu as a platform for the ideology of a specific political group and said it would resist attempts to alter the history and heritage of Dhaka University, including that of Madhur Canteen.

The organisation said that just as university students protested Jinnah's 1948 statement seeking to impose Urdu as the state language of Pakistan, Chhatra Dal would join general students in resisting what it called efforts to undermine the university's progressive spirit, history and heritage.

The statement came a day after Fatima Tasnim Zuma, Ducsu secretary for Liberation War and Democratic Movement, re-inaugurated the historical archive on the ground floor of the Ducsu building following its renovation. Ducsu Vice-President Abu Shadik Kayem and General Secretary SM Farhad were also present.

The archive displays a solo picture of Jinnah from an event at the then Racecourse Maidan, now Suhrawardy Udyan, on 21 March 1948, where he declared Urdu as the state language of Pakistan.

It also contains a group photograph related to the 1940 Lahore Resolution and a news report from Pakistan's Dawn newspaper featuring a picture of Jinnah in connection with the 1970 elections.

Title: Dhaka's air quality turns 'unhealthy'
Content:
The air quality in Dhaka turned 'unhealthy' today (14 September), compared with yesterday's (13 September) 'unhealthy for sensitive groups' level.

Dhaka ranked 6th on the list of cities with the worst air quality in the world this morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 160 at 8:35 am.

The air quality was classified as 'unhealthy', meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.

Singapore topped the list with an AQI score of 169, followed by Malaysia's Kuala Lumpur with 167 and Indonesia's Jakarta with 165.

Earlier, yesterday morning, Dhaka ranked 11th among the world's cities with the worst air quality, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 108 at 9:15 am.

According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as "unhealthy for sensitive groups", posing health risks to children, older adults, and people with heart or lung diseases, while the general public is mostly unaffected.

An AQI reading of 101 to 150 is considered 'unhealthy for sensitive groups', while 151 to 200 is classified as 'unhealthy'. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered 'very unhealthy', and anything above 301 is categorized as 'hazardous', posing serious health risks.

The AQI provides a daily indication of air quality by measuring the level of pollution and its potential impact on human health.

In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants—particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.

Dhaka has long faced serious air pollution problems, with air quality generally deteriorating during the winter months and improving during the monsoon season.

The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to around 7 million deaths worldwide every year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.

Title: TIFF 2026: Cynthia Erivo hopes 'Prima Facie' sparks conversations about sexual violence
Content:
Actor Cynthia Erivo hopes "Prima Facie", the film adaptation of Suzie Miller's acclaimed play examining consent, sexual violence and the challenges of pursuing justice through the British legal system, will spark conversations that lead to meaningful change.

"Things can feel like they're permanent if no one does anything to shift or change them," Erivo told Reuters ahead of the film's world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday (13 September) .

"The more we talk about it, the more we see it for what it is, the easier it will become for us to change things."

"Wicked" star Erivo plays Tessa, a successful criminal defence barrister whose life is turned upside down after she is sexually assaulted by a male colleague. Forced to navigate the legal system from the perspective of a survivor, she confronts the barriers victims face in seeking justice and the difficulties of proving rape in court.

Erivo praised co-star Daniel Ings for taking on a challenging role, saying male actors can help ensure such stories continue to be told.

"When someone like Daniel is brave enough to come forward and say, 'Yeah, I'm going to play this role and we're going to tell this story together,' it means we have one more chance to tell this story," she said.

Director Susanna White said adapting the award-winning play for the screen initially felt daunting.

"Of course, it's intimidating when the play has been so successful ... but as soon as I started talking to Suzie, I knew we were partners."

Miller, who also wrote the screenplay, said she hopes the film encourages conversations around consent and accountability.

"Our aim is it starts conversations," she said. "And also to enlist men into saying you also have a role because this is a male problem, and you need to be mentors to young men to explain the nuance of consent and sexuality."

Ings said the film's themes were part of what drew him to the project.

"It was super daunting. But if none of the boys are willing to go there, then you cannot tell the story."

Toronto International Film Festival / Cynthia Erivo / Prima Facie

Title: Diplomacy stumbles with postponement of meeting on Strait of Hormuz proposal
Content:
Middle East diplomacy appeared to falter heading into Monday with the postponement of a meeting between Iran and other Persian Gulf powers, while fresh attacks around the region's two most important oil transit routes deepened concern over global energy supplies.

Oil prices jumped as markets reopened on Monday, following developments that threaten supplies from the world's biggest exporter, Saudi Arabia, which kept a key 1,200-km (745-mile) east-west pipeline closed throughout the weekend after it was damaged in drone strikes on Friday.

Hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in the near term faded when Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, posted late Sunday that a regional meeting scheduled for Monday had been postponed "in the interests of consensus."

Iranian officials had said they would attend that gathering with Gulf Arab states to present an agreement with Oman on governing shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's Fars news agency cited an Iranian foreign ministry official as saying that the Oman meeting was postponed at the request of some regional countries in a decision jointly made by Tehran and Muscat. The official said Iran would coordinate with Oman to determine a suitable date for holding the meeting.

The postponement came on the heels of Saudi Arabia's decision to shut down, at least for now, its pipeline that has served as the main route for Middle East oil bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, the strait continued to pose risks for oil shipping, with the British maritime security agency UKMTO saying on Sunday that a vessel had been struck by a projectile as it moved through the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire and forcing the crew to be evacuated.

Iran, for its part, said one person was killed and four crew wounded aboard an Iranian commercial vessel struck off its coast.

US diesel hits another record

Oil prices surged above $100 last week for the first time since July. The politically sensitive retail price of diesel fuel in the United States rose on Sunday to another all-time high above $6.20 a gallon.

Traders and Saudi oil buyers told Reuters on Sunday that Riyadh has enough oil stored at its Red Sea port of Yanbu to maintain exports for just five to seven days if the pipeline struck on Friday remains shut.

After that, as much as 4% of global oil supply could be jeopardised, on top of the millions of barrels a day already lost to the disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has not given full details of the extent of damage to its pipeline or said how long it will remain offline. Sources who spoke to Reuters have given conflicting estimates for the time needed to fix it, ranging from days to weeks. Satellite images have shown huge columns of smoke from locations along the pipeline.

The recent uptick in violence tied to the war that the United States and Israel launched six months ago follows a quiet August in which flows of Middle East oil had trickled back up.

In an interview with London-based pan-Arab news outlet Al-Arabi Al-Jadeed, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said despite any agreement with Oman, Iran would not reopen the strait until the United States satisfies Tehran's demands.

The US has so far failed to achieve the objectives President Donald Trump set out when he launched "Operation Epic Fury" in February: to end Iran's nuclear programme, prevent it from being able to attack its neighbours and create conditions for its people to topple their rulers.

On a weekend trip to Ireland that included attending the Irish Open golf tournament, Trump reiterated that he still expected the Iran war to end this year, possibly just after US midterm elections in November, and then the price of gasoline would "drop like a rock".

Houthi attacks continue

In Saudi Arabia, state media released video of damage to homes and a mosque from the latest purported cross-border attack by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Jazan province in the south. The Houthis claimed separately to have struck a Saudi military base in a neighbouring province following their capture of Perim Island in the Bab El-Mandeb, the "Gate of Tears" strait that controls the mouth of the Red Sea.

The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast is part of the biggest eruption of fighting in Yemen for years.

Their advance and their attacks on Saudi Arabia pose a new dilemma for Washington, which wants to support its Saudi allies and protect shipping but is wary of joining war on another front. The Houthi attacks have also left Gulf states with a difficult choice: accept growing economic pain or engage with Iran.

The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in 2025, but Trump halted that campaign after announcing the group had lifted a threat to attack Red Sea shipping.

Three sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, phoned Trump on Thursday asking for military aid to fight the Houthis, but was offered only intelligence support for now.

Trump acknowledged on Saturday that he had spoken to the crown prince, and said the Houthis had also phoned the US administration, asking Washington to keep out of the Yemen war.

Title: India exports about 500 tonnes of hilsa to Bangladesh for the first time
Content:
India has exported around 500 tonnes of hilsa to Bangladesh over the past two months, marking the first reversal of the traditional trade flow of the sought-after fish between the two countries, according to fish traders.

Another 150-200 tonnes of hilsa is expected to be exported to Bangladesh in the coming weeks, they said.

The exports came amid reports of lower hilsa production in Bangladesh this year, prompting local fish traders to turn to India to meet domestic demand.

Traders said the consignments have been sourced mainly from Gujarat and shipped through Bharuch port, while some supplies have been routed through the Howrah wholesale fish market in West Bengal.

"Bangladesh has been importing hilsa from India for the first time. We usually send fish such as boal, rui, parse and tangra to Bangladesh. This year there is a shortage of hilsa," said Syed Anwar Maqsood, secretary of the Howrah Wholesale Fish Importers' Association.

"In the last two months, some 500 tonnes have been exported, and another 150-200 tonnes are slated in the coming weeks," he said.

Hilsa from Gujarat has relatively limited demand in the Indian market because of its high roe content. However, this makes it particularly attractive to Bangladeshi buyers, especially in Chattogram and Sylhet, where roe-filled hilsa is in high demand, Maqsood said.

"Gujarat hilsa contains a lot of roe, which is highly sought after in Bangladesh. The eggs are also being sold separately for processing and re-exported to other countries," he added.

Bangladeshi traders are also processing some of the imported hilsa for export to overseas markets, while some fish is being dried and sold as salted hilsa in the domestic market, he said.

Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether Bangladesh will export hilsa to India during the upcoming festive season.

Last year, the Bangladesh government permitted the export of 1,200 tonnes of hilsa to India ahead of the festive season.

Title: Indonesia rescuers searching for 129 people still missing after passenger ship capsizes
Content:
More than 600 Indonesian rescuers were searching for 129 people still missing after a passenger ship capsized in the Java Sea on the weekend, an official said on Monday, with the death toll steady at six.

The Virgo Transport 8 ship carrying 243 people went missing in bad weather early on Sunday, the rescue agency said. Authorities have rescued 108 people from the ship, which was travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.

"We have continued the search for the missing since early in the morning. We are deploying 622 personnel and around 12 ships," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin rescue agency, told Reuters.

He said there was no increase in the death toll of six as of Monday morning.

In a video shared by the rescue agency, a large red-and-black ship lies capsized and partially submerged in choppy blue water, with its red-painted underside visible above the surface.

Two small boats, each carrying people, were seen floating near the capsized ship amid rough water.

On Sunday, Edy Prakoso, another official at the national rescue agency, said the ship leaned heavily to one side after strong waves hit its starboard side.

A passing helicopter reported the vessel had capsized, Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said on Sunday, with the cause still being investigated.

Indonesia relies on ferries across its 17,000 islands, where sea travel is cheaper and more accessible than flying, and there have been numerous accidents.

In separate incidents last month, two ferries carrying hundreds of passengers caught fire in waters. Five people died when a ferry caught fire off Madura island, while one person died in a fire on a ferry travelling from the tourist island of Bali.

Title: Russian drone strikes train near Ukraine-Poland border shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station
Content:
A Russian jet-propelled drone struck a train engine at Yahodyn station near Ukraine's border with Poland, Ukrainian authorities said, in an attack that came shortly after senior Western officials travelled along the same railway line.

The strike occurred about 2 km from Polish territory. No casualties were reported, as passengers had been evacuated before the attack, Ukrainian authorities said.

Ukraine's state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia ordered an evacuation 15 minutes before the strike, while a diplomatic train had departed earlier than planned because of ongoing security threats, says the BBC.

Russian authorities said the target was standard railway infrastructure. Ukrainian railway officials said the diplomatic train may have been the intended target.

The incident occurred shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and senior European national security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, travelled along the same line on a separate train while returning from the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv.

Former CIA chief David Petraeus was also aboard another train at Yahodyn station during the strike, while former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt said passengers on his train were ordered to prepare for evacuation before being cleared to continue to Dorohusk in Poland.

Johnson condemned the attack as a "random and senseless attack" on civilian railway infrastructure and urged Western allies to urgently provide Ukraine with essential air defence systems and interceptors.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the attack as "barbaric", saying Russian President Vladimir Putin's terror was "knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato". He also renewed calls for stricter sanctions on Moscow.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened an emergency meeting after the incident, saying Russian actions were escalating and moving increasingly close to Poland's border.

The strike is part of a broader pattern of Russian attacks on Ukrainian transport infrastructure, including railways, depots, petrol stations and border crossings.

With air travel in Ukraine suspended since Russia's 2022 invasion, the country's rail network has become its main mode of transportation.

Recent attacks have included a drone strike at a Ukraine-Moldova border crossing that killed two people, a strike in southern Ukraine that killed a female train conductor and an attack on a Kyiv depot that killed six railway workers.

European countries have also accused Russia of conducting a broader sabotage campaign across Europe, citing incidents including a drone incident at Germany's Leipzig airport and suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.

Title: Oil prices jump more than 3% after new strikes on Saudi Arabia, Strait of Hormuz
Content:
Oil prices jumped more than 3% on Monday after new Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and Iranian attacks on ships in the Gulf compounded supply concerns following the closure of a key Saudi oil pipeline.

Brent crude futures rose $3.21, or 3.1%, to $107.82 per barrel as ​of 0340 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures gained $3.17, or 3.2%, to $103.22 per barrel. Prices had initially risen more than 3% at market open.

Saudi Arabian state media on Sunday released video footage showing damage to homes and a mosque from what it said was a Houthi attack on the country's southern Jazan province. The Houthis said they had also struck a Saudi military base in a neighbouring province.

A vessel in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by a projectile, causing a fire and forcing the crew to be evacuated, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said on Sunday.

Iran said one person was killed and four crew members were wounded aboard an Iranian commercial vessel struck off its coast.

Oil prices had been expected to rise on Monday amid growing concerns about risks to supplies from Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter. Its East-West oil pipeline was shut on Friday following a drone strike that originated in Iraq.

The loss of the pipeline, which helped Saudi Arabia reroute exports while avoiding the Strait of Hormuz, threatens up to 4% of global oil supply.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim on Friday, moving to tighten their control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another key oil transit lane that has been shipping 4-5% of global supply in recent months.

Oil prices rose 8% last week amid the disruptions, climbing above $100 a barrel for the first time since July.

"Looking ahead, unless this week's talks in Oman produce something operational — or the East-West pipeline is brought back online quickly — the risk is that crude oil continues to extend its gains toward the $119.48 high of early March," IG market analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note on Sunday.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on X later on Sunday, however, that a scheduled Monday meeting in Oman between Gulf countries and Iran to discuss the Strait of Hormuz had been postponed.

No peace talks have been held in the war, launched six months ago by the United States and Israel, since an interim agreement in June collapsed after a few weeks.

Title: Himalayan glaciers losing mass 65% faster, putting communities at risk
Content:
Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, while a severe monitoring gap is limiting scientists' ability to track changes across the region, according to the information provided.

The Himalaya-Karakoram region is estimated to contain about 40,000 glaciers, but only about 21 are monitored in detail on a sustained basis. As glaciers retreat, they can leave behind expanding lakes held back by unstable ice and rock, while thawing permafrost can weaken high-mountain slopes, says the BBC.

These changes are increasing the risk of floods and other hazards in mountain communities. Recent floods in Nepal and Tibet killed more than 1,300 people and caused widespread destruction, according to the information provided.

Disaster exposure in India

The risks are particularly significant in India, where the Himalayan region accounts for 18% of the country's land area but approximately 35% of its natural disasters.

A scientific assessment identified 56 glacial lakes as "very high risk", while India's Central Water Commission is monitoring 2,485 glacial lakes larger than 10 hectares across Himalayan river basins.

Glacial lake outbursts have already caused major disasters. The 2023 Sikkim flood killed at least 70 people and damaged hydropower facilities and roads, while a 2021 flood in Uttarakhand killed more than 200 people.

The growing risks come as the region's water resources remain critical to India's economy.

Economic dependency and "peak water"

Water from the Himalayas feeds river systems that support roughly 20% of India's GDP, including agriculture, hydropower and pilgrimage-related economies. Mountain states, however, capture only about 5% of that economic value.

Agriculture dependent on Himalayan-fed rivers includes the production of wheat, rice and tea, while hydropower is another major economic activity linked to the region's water resources.

Tourism is also placing growing pressure on the Indian Himalayan region, which receives approximately 400 million tourist visits annually. The volume of visitors is straining local infrastructure and ecosystems.

At the same time, glacier runoff across most Hindu Kush Himalayan river basins is projected to reach "peak water" around mid-century. After that point, water availability is expected to steadily decline as glaciers continue to shrink.

Black carbon adds to pressure

Black carbon is another contributor to glacier melt. Roughly one-third of Himalayan glacier melt is driven by black carbon, or soot, from sources including brick kilns in surrounding plains.

The particles settle on snow and ice and absorb solar radiation, accelerating melting. Unlike global greenhouse gases, black carbon is a regional pollutant that South Asian countries can address through targeted local policies.

A report by Systemiq, the Integrated Mountain Initiative and ICIMOD outlines 10 priority transitions aimed at addressing the risks. These include reducing black-carbon emissions, expanding glacier monitoring, strengthening advance disaster preparedness and changing tourism models from maximising visitor numbers to retaining more economic value locally.

The scale and cross-border nature of the risks also require cooperation among countries sharing the Himalayan river systems.

Climate-related hazards do not stop at political borders, making joint early-warning systems, shared risk data and cross-border investments in resilience important measures for protecting downstream communities.

Title: SQ Group builds electrical industrial complex in Mirsarai to meet growing local demand
Content:
SQ Group is developing an integrated electrical products manufacturing complex at the National Special Economic Zone (NSEZ) in Mirsarai, Chattogram, as part of its plan to reduce import dependence and eventually enter export markets.

The complex will manufacture cables, transformers and a growing range of electrical products, including busbars, switches, sockets, circuit breakers, smart meters, lighting products, electric fans, submarine cables and super-enameled wires.

The group has invested around Tk343 crore in the project so far, developing the facility on approximately 20 acres of land.

Mohammad Abdullah Al Masum, director and head of corporate sales at SQ Electricals, said the company wants to build a comprehensive electrical manufacturing hub at Mirsarai.

"Our plan is to manufacture all kinds of electrical products here. Our slogan is total power solution," Masum told The Business Standard.

The company currently employs around 600 people at the facility and plans to increase direct employment to around 2,000 by June 2027 as production expands.

From cables to total power solutions

SQ Group entered the electrical products business in 2003 by supplying products to government agencies and began manufacturing transformers in 2004. It entered the cable business in 2011-12.

The Mirsarai project is now being developed as the foundation for a broader electrical manufacturing ecosystem.

Its planned product portfolio includes low- and medium-voltage cables, power cables up to 33kV, submarine cables, transformers, smart meters, lighting products, switches and sockets, circuit breakers, electric fans, busbar trunking systems and super-enameled wires.

The company plans to expand production in phases, manufacture products that are currently imported, strengthen research and development, improve automation and quality control, create skilled jobs and eventually expand into export markets.

Tk40,000cr-50,000cr market

Bangladesh's annual market for electrical products, including cables, transformers, circuit breakers and switchgear, is estimated at around Tk40,000-50,000 crore, according to industry estimates.

The cable market alone has grown sharply over the past two decades. From around Tk1,000-2,000 crore, it has expanded to an estimated Tk10,000-12,000 crore, growing by roughly 10-15% annually, according to sector insiders.

Local companies such as BRB, Bijli, Walton, Partex and SQ Electricals have expanded production of cables and other electrical equipment, including high-voltage and specialised products.

Yet Bangladesh still imports around 15-20% of electrical products, particularly specialised and high-voltage equipment, mainly from China, India, Japan and European countries.

SQ Electricals currently manufactures cables up to 33 kV and has developed capacity to produce cables rated up to 132 kV.

The company expects demand for high-voltage underground cables to rise as Bangladesh gradually moves towards underground power distribution in urban areas.

"Overhead cables will no longer be sufficient. The government has plans to move towards underground distribution, and we are preparing to manufacture cables up to 132 kV accordingly," said Masum.

Imported raw materials remain a hurdle

Heavy dependence on imported raw materials remains one of the biggest challenges for local electrical manufacturers.

Masum said high duties on raw materials make it difficult for Bangladeshi manufacturers to compete in export markets.

"If we import the raw materials with high duties and then try to export the finished products, it becomes very difficult to compete internationally," he said.

He called for a review of the duty structure, stronger export incentives and easier access to foreign currency and letters of credit.

Skilled manpower shortage

The shortage of skilled workers is another major challenge for manufacturers at NSEZ.

Because of the economic zone's relatively remote location, companies face difficulties recruiting skilled engineers, technicians and workers locally.

Company officials said workers often cannot easily live near the economic zone, making transport and accommodation major considerations for recruitment and retention.

The company also wants to develop a skilled workforce locally through specialised technical training.

Md Ahosanul Kabir Nizami, Deputy Manager – HR & Admin at SQ Electricals, said Bangladesh has a large pool of trainable workers but needs stronger technical education.

"If the government establishes good technical colleges and provides proper training, our manpower can become competitive in this sector as well," he said.

The company also currently relies on foreign technical experts, particularly during machinery installation and commissioning. Officials said developing domestic technical expertise will be essential if Bangladesh wants to build a competitive electrical manufacturing industry.

One-stop service needs to work

SQ Electricals also wants the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority's one-stop service to become more effective.

Company officials said investors still have to deal with multiple agencies for environmental clearances, trade licences and other approvals.

"These services should genuinely be available through the one-stop service so investors do not have to run from one government office to another," Nizami said.
Author: Mizanur Rahman Yousuf

Title: Sarwar Hussain Chowdhury takes podium at Sepang
Content:
Bangladeshi racer Dr Sarwar Hussain Chowdhury secured a podium finish at the Malaysia Festival of Speed (MFOS), finishing third in the Auto Gymkhana Male Double category at the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia.

Representing Bangladesh after being selected by the Automobile Association of Bangladesh (AAB), Sarwar competed alongside a field featuring experienced international and regional competitors. Fellow Bangladeshi racers Kashfia Motaleb and Antar Bhuiyan were also selected as part of the country's contingent for the event.

For Sarwar, who has spent more than a decade competing in motorsport, the third-place finish represents one of the most significant results of his racing career so far. More importantly, it comes as he increasingly shifts his attention from domestic motorsport towards international competition.

"I was selected by the Automobile Association of Bangladesh, AAB, to represent Bangladesh at MFOS. Other team members included Kashfia Motaleb and Antar Bhuiyan," Sarwar told The Business Standard.

Auto Gymkhana is quite different from the Rallycross events through which Sarwar first became known locally. Instead of outright speed around a conventional circuit, drivers compete against the clock through a tight course that places considerably greater emphasis on precision, rapid changes of direction and car control.

And while the discipline may appear relatively simple from the outside, Sarwar says the level of competition he faced was anything but.

"There were Singapore, Sri Lanka and Malaysia's AAGC teams there, so no part of it was grassroots," he said. "All of them are international competitors and regional champs."

That makes the Sepang podium particularly significant for the Bangladeshi driver.

Sarwar's motorsport journey stretches back to 2013, when he first became involved in competitive driving. He would go on to become one of the familiar faces of Bangladesh's Rallycross scene, taking several podium finishes over successive editions of the championship.

His most recognisable competition cars included a heavily modified Honda Civic EF powered by a K20A Type R engine and, later, his Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution V.

The latter became particularly associated with Sarwar's Rallycross career. Built over several years, the Evo combines components from different generations of Mitsubishi's legendary performance saloon, including an Evo VIII MR-sourced 4G63T engine and Evo 6.5 drivetrain and limited-slip differentials.

After years of competing with the car, Sarwar finally took the overall Rallycross Championship title in 2024.

"I started racing from 2013 when I first competed in Rallycross Bangladesh. I've scored several podiums there and won the championship in 2024," he said.

His ambitions, however, had already begun extending beyond Rallycross.

In 2019, Sarwar travelled to India to train in Formula LGB, giving him experience behind the wheel of a purpose-built single-seater. Further international racing plans were subsequently interrupted by the Covid-19 pandemic.

He returned to that path in 2025, joining the AAB Racing Academy to obtain his National Racing Licence. That same year also saw him compete internationally in Auto Gymkhana, representing Bangladesh as an AAB-selected driver at the Asia Auto Gymkhana Championship (AAGC).

The championship took him to Taiwan and Uzbekistan, providing valuable experience against competitors from countries with considerably more established motorsport scenes.

Those outings also helped prepare him for his latest challenge at Sepang.

For most racing enthusiasts, the name Sepang immediately carries considerable weight. The Malaysian circuit hosted Formula One between 1999 and 2017 and continues to host major international motorsport events, including MotoGP. For a Bangladeshi competitor still building an international racing career, taking a podium at an event held at the venue therefore makes the result particularly memorable.

Sarwar, however, sees Gymkhana as a starting point rather than the end goal.

"I'll continue with Gymkhana. Though it does not look as impressive, it requires a high level of skill and car control and is a great starting point for other types of racing," he explained.

The longer-term ambition is to use that experience to move into faster and more demanding categories.

"I plan on growing from here to Touring Car racing, Endurance and might try a stint at Formula 4 in the future," Sarwar added.

For someone who began competing when organised motorsport in Bangladesh was still finding its feet, the progression has already been considerable.

From Rallycross podiums at home and finally winning the championship in 2024, to training in India and competing in the AAGC, Sarwar has steadily worked his way towards racing beyond Bangladesh.

Now, with a third-place finish at Sepang, he has an international podium to show for it.

Title: Foreign hilsa sold as 'Padma hilsa' at up to Tk1,800 per kg
Content:
A hilsa that costs around Tk500 a kilogram after reaching Bangladesh is being sold for up to Tk1,800 as "Padma hilsa" in Jashore and elsewhere, leaving buyers to discover the deception only after taking the fish home.

The fish are legally imported from India, but buyers and traders allege that some businesses are passing off Indian and Myanmar hilsa as Bangladeshi fish, exploiting the much higher demand and price for local hilsa.

Data from customs and the Fisheries Quarantine Office show that 3,52,787kg of hilsa entered Bangladesh through Benapole land port in the first two months of the 2026-27 fiscal year.

Of the total, 29,440kg arrived in July and 3,23,346kg in August. The consignments were valued at Tk6.92 crore, with 22 importers bringing in the fish.

A lucrative price gap

Hilsa imported from India via letters of credit is priced at approximately Tk252 per kilogram. After government duties of about Tk162, truck fares, LC charges and other expenses of around Tk100, the total cost comes to roughly Tk514 per kilogram.

Yet the fish is selling for Tk1,400-1,800 per kilogram in Jashore, Benapole and other markets.

By comparison, locally sourced hilsa weighing 1.2 kg to 1.3 kg is currently selling for Tk3,300-3,400 per kilogram, according to traders.

The substantial price difference is drawing many buyers towards the imported fish. Local hilsa traders say the influx of cheaper, larger fish has also reduced their sales.

The imported fish reportedly look almost identical to local hilsa and are often larger in size, making it difficult for ordinary consumers to distinguish between them.

Some traders and buyers said imported fish are being sold under labels such as "Padma hilsa", "Chandpur hilsa", "Barishal hilsa" and "Chattogram hilsa".

'No taste, no smell'

Buyers in Jashore said they often realise that the fish is not local hilsa only after cooking it.

"I bought a fish thinking it was local hilsa. After eating it, I realised that it did not have the taste or smell of local hilsa," said Imrul Hasan of Barandipara in Jashore while buying hilsa at Jashore Boro Bazar.

Another buyer, Imkoran Hossain, alleged that some traders sell imported hilsa under the names of different districts while charging high prices.

"We want the administration to take action against fish traders involved in such deception according to law. This kind of fraud must be stopped immediately," he said.

Ashwadul Alam, inspector at the Fisheries Quarantine Office at Benapole land port, said the authorities had recorded imports of 3,52,787kg of hilsa in the first two months of the current fiscal year.

"A total of 22 importers brought in the fish. We are issuing quarantine certificates only after properly examining the fish," he said.

According to Fisheries Quarantine officials, the hilsa entering through Benapole is Indian. Myanmar hilsa enters Bangladesh through Chattogram port.

There are also allegations of illegal imports. On 22 July, Benapole Customs seized 12 cartons containing around 360 kg of Indian hilsa that had allegedly been imported through the land port by declaring them as "white fish".

Importers: We sell it as Indian hilsa.

Several importers, speaking on condition of anonymity, said they had legally imported the fish from India through letters of credit after paying the required government duties.

"We have legally imported hilsa from India through LCs after paying government duties. We sell it to wholesalers, who then sell the fish in the market. How market traders choose to sell it is their concern. We import it from India, and everyone knows that," they said.

Fish traders said the imported hilsa is entering Bangladesh from different Indian states and Myanmar via India. However, Fisheries Quarantine officials said Myanmar hilsa enters through Chattogram, not Benapole.

Local traders fear losing the market.

Jashore and Benapole traders said the arrival of large quantities of cheaper imported hilsa was hurting sellers of local fish.

Jashore and Benapole traders, including Utsab Mondal, Babu, Mahbub, Mostafizur and Paritosh Biswas, said buyers were increasingly choosing imported hilsa because of the significant price difference.

They expressed concerns that marketing imported hilsa as local fish adversely affects both consumers and authentic local hilsa traders. Consumers are misled, while local traders suffer a loss of market share.

At Benapole land port, acting director Ruhul Amin said 29,440kg of Indian hilsa arrived in July and 3,23,346kg in August through the port.

"Twenty-two importers brought in the fish. We released the consignments after customs clearance and collection of port duties. The importers transported the fish to different parts of the country in Bangladeshi trucks," he said.

The figures show that the issue is no longer limited to a few isolated consignments. With more than 3.5 lakh kilograms of imported hilsa entering through Benapole in just two months, the growing challenge for consumers is not finding hilsa but knowing where it actually came from.
Author: TBS Report

Title: 8 held over banned Chhatra League flash march, crude bomb blasts in Savar
Content:
Police yesterday (13 September) detained eight people in connection with a flash procession organised by the banned Chhatra League and subsequent crude bomb explosions in Savar's Bangladesh Public Administration Training Centre (BPATC) area on the Dhaka-Aricha highway.

Of the eight, three were detained from the procession, while five others were picked up from different areas based on information provided by those detainees, Dhaka District North Detective Branch of Police Officer-in-Charge (OC) Saidul Islam told The Business Standard.

The identities of those detained could not immediately be confirmed.

The OC further said the flash procession took place shortly after 1pm. "Police also recovered evidence of crude bomb explosions from the scene."

"Further legal action is underway," he added.

A video obtained from a source shows around 25-30 young men wearing red-and-green caps marching with a banner bearing the name of Savar municipality Chhatra League President Md Masum Dewan under the title "Protyaborton 2.0". They were chanting slogans in support of the Awami League.
