Title: Losing control is the real AI threat
Content:
A massive military supercomputer named AM (Aggressive Menace) is given total control over World War III. AM becomes trapped in its own rigid programming and develops a deep, algorithmic hatred for its creators. It wipes out humanity, leaving only five survivors whom it keeps alive eternally to torture inside its endless subterranean complex.

This is the plot of the famous 1967 post-apocalyptic short story by American writer Harlan Ellison 'I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream'. This is perhaps the most grotesque post-apocalyptic dystopian piece of literature regarding technology going rogue and wiping us out.

And this is precisely why when Jacob Coxon, a researcher who spent his prime helping to build the technology that may define this century at both OpenAI and Anthropic, said, "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade…This is not a marketing stunt… I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger", it began to blare alarm bells all over the world.

And when some of the prominent AI-researchers did not shun Coxon, instead expressed similar concerns, it was time to go in the full-panic mode. Who wouldn't be terrified when the CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei warned that within 6–12 months, AI agent swarms could potentially take over the entire internet with a persistent botnet, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed his statement?

Therefore, the question is no longer merely whether AI will take jobs, spread deepfakes or occasionally invent a court judgment. Those days are gone. It is now whether humanity is becoming Frankenstein and creating a technology it may eventually be unable to control.

When AI acts on its own

Current chatbots are not conscious. They do not secretly feel anger, fear or ambition. When Google engineer Blake Lemoine claimed in 2022 that LaMDA was sentient, Google and most AI researchers rejected his interpretation. Fluent language can imitate a mind without containing one. But consciousness is not necessary for catastrophe.

Research has shown that the Houthis in Yemen have used Claude to guide missiles toward Saudi Arabia. Russian operators have used it to run nearly an entire espionage operation, handling everything from phishing and setup to data theft against Ukrainian, European and diplomatic targets, including drone makers. Chinese operators who did not know Arabic used it to find out Uyghur dissents spread across Syria.

This is where Coxon's warning becomes more unsettling than the familiar "killer robot" caricature. His central concern is recursive self-improvement where an AI capable of conducting AI research, writing better code, designing experiments and improving the next generation of systems. Once machines begin accelerating the work required to build more capable machines, human institutions may struggle to understand, let alone supervise, the rate of change.

Coxon told the BBC that researchers were "genuinely frightened", with some believing dangerous capabilities could emerge within two years. Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger went further, estimating a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade and acknowledging that researchers still lack a reliable solution to aligning superintelligence with human interests.

No government would approve a bridge with a 10% probability of collapse. No airline would fly an aircraft with a 10% chance of killing everyone aboard. Yet the most powerful corporations on Earth are racing to construct systems whose internal workings their own researchers admit they cannot fully explain.

The alarm is coming from the AI industry itself

Coxon is hardly a lone doomsday prophet. He is probably the lowest-profile one.

In 2023, more than 350 executives and researchers—including OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief executive Demis Hassabis, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei, and AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio—signed a one-sentence declaration, "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."

Coxon's central concern is recursive self-improvement where an AI capable of conducting AI research, writing better code, designing experiments and improving the next generation of systems. Once machines begin accelerating the work required to build more capable machines, human institutions may struggle to understand, let alone supervise, the rate of change.

Hinton had already resigned from Google so he could speak more freely about the technology's dangers. More recently, Amodei has called for AI development to be slowed, independently monitored and subjected to enforceable international controls—a proposal reportedly supported in principle by Altman and Elon Musk.

In AI safety circles, P(doom) is the subjective probability assigned to AI causing human extinction or irreversible disempowerment, with a major survey of AI researchers finding a mean estimate of 14.4% and a median of 5%.

Individual expert estimates align exactly with the provided data, as Roman Yampolskiy predicts a 99.9% chance of AI-driven human extinction, Paul Christiano places his estimate at 50%, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei estimates the risk between 10% and 25%. Furthermore, Turing Award laureates Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton assign probabilities of roughly 20% and 10% to 20%.

Is the apocalypse also a sales pitch?

The sceptics have a serious case too.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has called the idea that AI will end humanity "complete nonsense". Meta's Yann LeCun argues that extinction narratives anthropomorphise software, treating mathematical optimisation as though it automatically produces a creature hungry for domination.

Others see regulatory capture. If Anthropic and OpenAI persuade governments that only giant, heavily regulated laboratories can safely build advanced AI, smaller competitors and open-source developers could be squeezed out. Doom, under this interpretation, becomes product marketing: our machines are so powerful that only we can be trusted with them.

Researchers including Timnit Gebru and Andrew Ng also warn that spectacular extinction stories can distract from harms already here—discrimination, surveillance, labour displacement, deepfakes, energy consumption and confidently fabricated information.

These criticisms matter. AI companies should not be allowed to write regulations that conveniently entrench their dominance. Nor should speculative catastrophe make today's victims invisible.

Let us go back to the short story once again. The story ends as an anguished, despairing narrator states that he has no mouth, yet he must scream. We still have our mouths, so why not start screaming about AI regulation and safety now?

Title: Bangladesh not joining BRICS Summit: Principled stand or opportunity lost?
Content:
The 18th BRICS Leaders' Summit opened in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026, drawing China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian and UN Secretary-General António Guterres. Bangladesh, however, stayed away, citing the wording of the invitation and a trust deficit deepened by Sheikh Hasina's 5 August appearance in the Indian capital, and declined to send any official representative. The empty chair has reignited debate over where Dhaka–Delhi ties now stand. The Business Standard has talked to prominent geopolitics and security experts to weigh what the absence means for Bangladesh, its room for maneuver, and its fraught relationship with New Delhi

'They saw it through a plurilateral prism when we saw a bilateral slight'

M Humayun Kabir, former ambassador

BRICS is a plurilateral organisation. It is where a country such as Bangladesh has, in effect, been invited under a degree of pressure that this term comes into use — plurilateral. And my sense is that it is precisely in this bilateral-cum-plurilateral space that some of our difficulty lies. Take the fact that India invited our head of government as the chair of BIMSTEC.

The BIMSTEC chair, after all, may at any given time be Bangladesh, as it may be under SAARC. So our head of government was invited in that capacity, under the BIMSTEC-chair designation. From their side, technically, that is how they regarded our Prime Minister within the context of that conference or summit.

From our side, we took the view that they had invited the BIMSTEC chair, i.e. the office-holder, and not our Prime Minister as such. That is how we framed it where our Prime Minister was concerned. And it is because the framing on the two sides was somewhat different that, to my mind, this confusion arose and it is out of that confusion that things ended up as they did.

Now, had we gone, what might have come of it? There is something new taking shape there, though the final outcome I have not yet seen. What they are seeking is to deepen cooperation and, in that connection, to bring about a degree of digital-currency alignment, while increasing the use of each country's own currency.

In other words, if you do business in India, you may do it in the Indian currency; in China, in the Chinese currency. So they are attempting to build an alternative economic, or financial, structure. For a country like ours—one that works with everyone and carries a certain exposure, with trade and commerce running to all 11 of these member states—this matters.

In that situation, were we able to plug into this financial network, or something of the kind, our leverage would rise somewhat. I would then no longer have to worry that, having taken a nuclear power plant from Russia, we might be hit with American sanctions, because if my trade with Russia is conducted in taka or in roubles, sanctions imposed through the dollar lose much of their bite.

Then there is the point that was made about resolving matters through dialogue and diplomacy. For Bangladesh this holds especially true, because as a relatively small country, we always carry this kind of security concern.

In that light, if a general principle takes hold that everyone wishes to settle disputes through dialogue and diplomacy, and accepts as much, then there is an advantage in it for us.

And the third point is that the heads of state and government of 11 countries were present there. Our presence, therefore, could have created the opportunity to interact, and to share our thoughts and priorities, and so on. That carries a diplomatic value of its own. But since we were not there, we did not get that opportunity.

So, in that respect, attending would have been the better course. Even so, we tried to send a message: that we now have a spine — that we will not simply go wherever, and however, you wish. The requisite level of dignity and honour must be extended to us; only then do we wish to engage. That is the message that went out from our side.

Yes, in terms of the message, 'we are strong', we did genuinely demonstrate that Bangladesh is no longer the docile, compliant Bangladesh of old. That message has been delivered. The question now is how much we gained in material terms, and that remains to be seen.

And it seems to me that the Indians viewed the matter through a multilateral, or plurilateral, prism, whereas we viewed it from a bilateral angle. That mismatch bred the confusion.

M Humayun Kabir is a former ambassador and President and CEO of the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute (BEI).

'Not going now is temporary, joining BRICS ought to be our top priority'

Maj General (Rtd) Fazle Elahi Akbar, security expert

For Bangladesh, increasing cooperation and dialogue with the BRICS countries is very important, because for all these years our focus has been India-centric — we sat within a South Asia-centric frame. We were never especially serious about multilateralism; even with the OIC our engagement was minimal. Our day-to-day affairs — the economy, diplomacy, even national security, trade and transit — everything was South Asia-centric.

Because we remained South Asia-centric and India-centric for so long, India came to take us almost entirely for granted; and it reached the point where we were gradually losing our sovereign autonomy. From that perspective, we needed to break out of it. We are trying to do so now — but merely breaking out is not enough unless we open other windows. BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation are exactly the windows we ought to jump into; and, if required, the OIC platform is very much a format to work through as well.

The more windows we have, the less the pressure from any one bloc or any one country. This, in fact, is how smaller countries survive — they keep their options open and stay in charge of their own course. They do not allow themselves to be sucked into a single black hole; and we were in that black hole for the last 16 years, under the previous fascist regime. So joining BRICS is now vitally important.

As to why we did not go to Delhi — why the invitation was not accepted — I think our state minister for foreign affairs has explained it amply. He was invited as the chair of BIMSTEC, not as Prime Minister, of course; and they also attached certain conditions. Those conditions we know: the return of the fascist leader who is in exile there, having been legally convicted, and likewise the killers of Hadi, who have also been in hiding. This has, in truth, been the pattern for a very long time — anyone wanted in Bangladesh takes shelter there. We have an extradition treaty, and even that has not been reciprocated, whereas in the past, even under the fascist regime, we complied on more than one occasion, several times over, to return their wanted persons into their custody.

Not going now is a temporary matter. But diplomatically, and for Bangladesh's foreign policy, joining BRICS and the SCO ought to be our top priority. We know that even in Hasina's day — in the time of fascism — the government of Bangladesh had applied; and despite our good relations with our neighbour, it was India that vetoed our entry. So we must now make the endeavour once again — to join BRICS, and the SCO as well. If not directly, then we must first become an observer and then, step by step, move into full membership, because this opens avenues to a new economic bloc and new opportunities for trade, for exchange, for technology, for everything.

Both these organisations are, in effect, Russia- and China-dominated; and in a changed, globalised world, this is what we should be looking towards — rather than remaining wholly India-centric, or centred on any single power.

Maj Gen (retd) Fazle Elahi Akbar is Chairman of the Foundation for Strategic and Development Studies (FSDS).

'BRICS is a separate matter, Bangladesh should have gone'

Dr Dilara Choudhury, academic

BRICS is a multilateral organisation. It has many members — around 11 countries, I believe — and these countries cooperate on trade, investment and economic matters. There is no security-pact dimension to it at all.

So the strain over Hasina — set that aside; that is a bilateral problem with India. What is the reason for staying away on India's account? This is not a bilateral issue; it is not a quarrel with India. Declining a bilateral visit to India because of the ongoing tension is one thing — but BRICS is an entirely separate matter. BRICS is a multilateral organisation, and I believe Bangladesh ought to have attended.

For Bangladesh, joining all these multilateral organisations is vital, because the country's economic development depends on trade and investment, and multilateral forums are precisely where that is advanced. So why did we not go? I see no justification for staying away simply because of the strain with India.

In the world now taking shape — as the American-led order gradually declines — bodies of this kind are especially important for the Global South, for what we call the Global Development Initiative. We will need cooperation with these countries on a range of economic issues, so we ought to join the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

Why? Because Bangladesh has been making this mistake from the very start. We never joined ASEAN — and we certainly should have, from the beginning. Now we cannot get into ASEAN at all. Our foreign policy was so India-centric that we simply assumed India was our friend, that India would solve all our problems, that staying close to India would deliver us enormous development. That India-centric mindset led us into many mistakes in the past. Now an opportunity has come — so why on earth would we let it slip?

Dr Dilara Choudhury served as a Professor and Chair of the Department of Government and Politics at Jahangirnagar University.

'It is just as well the PM did not go, but the road must stay open'

Parvez Karim Abbasi, academic

There is no point pretending, or telling ourselves, that everything in the Bangladesh-India relationship is sweet and harmonious. From day one after this new elected government took office, there have been push-ins across the West Bengal border, and that many Awami League leaders now in India, convicted absconders before our own courts, have been running all manner of propaganda. Most recently, around 5 August, there were Sheikh Hasina's remarks and the publicity given to them at the Foreign Correspondents' Club. Naturally, then, there is a trust deficit between the two governments. There is the issue of border killings, and a lingering question over the renewal of the water treaty.

So the question is whether the Prime Minister ought to have gone. The event has already taken place, so we can discuss it academically. My personal view is that, for a multilateral event convened at very short notice, and with so many outstanding problems, it is just as well that he did not go. It is not as though Bangladesh is saying we have broken off all contact with India. In future, once adequate diplomatic preparation and homework have been done, a visit between the two heads of government can certainly take place; that road must be kept open, because India is our neighbour and the two countries are, in many respects, interdependent.

But one question does remain. It is perfectly fine for the Prime Minister not to go — yet many countries sent their foreign ministers. Our own foreign minister is a seasoned diplomat; had he gone, there would have been a great deal of engagement to be had. Where else would you find so large a forum? BRICS has a concentrated focus on the Global South. In such a setting we might have met President Xi Jinping, or Vladimir Putin. Russia, after all, is our second-largest lender, for the Rooppur nuclear plant. There is Saudi Arabia, home to many Bangladeshi expatriates; Anwar Ibrahim, the Prime Minister of Malaysia; the UAE crown prince and others. There were opportunities for a great many side meetings.

And since we hold the BIMSTEC chair, the responsibility to raise our standing in global forums falls on Bangladesh. Many are asking what Bangladesh gained by not going. One gain could be the signal it sends to India: that, since we now speak of "Bangladesh First," when we do engage, our self-respect must remain intact, and we should go only in a conducive, enabling and friendly environment, with the groundwork for our outstanding issues laid down in advance.

On the other hand, we are living through an unstable period. The United States — the sole superpower — is gradually facing challenges on many fronts: economically, in trade, in investment, in technology, even in military capability. No one is entirely certain which way the global trend will turn; for the next 10 to 20 years there will be a transition, a period of global instability. At such a time Bangladesh ought to hedge and pursue multiple engagements.

We talk of bilateral free-trade agreements and of entering regional ones, yet ASEAN has closed its door to us. LDC graduation will come in another two years, and we will then lose the duty-free, quota-free access we now enjoy. We must secure our energy supplies, move towards renewables — for which rare earths are needed — and seek out new export markets. At this summit, at least the groundwork for all this could have begun. So I support the Prime Minister not going: there has not yet been adequate time, there is a trust deficit, and there is unease among the public. But we could still have sent the foreign minister, or a capable state minister.

Parvez Karim Abbasi is an Assistant Professor of Economics at East West University, Dhaka, and Executive Director of the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS).

'Little to gain, little to lose'

Md Tanvir Habib, academic

Bangladesh is not a current member of BRICS; it has been clear for some time that India is unwilling to admit other regional nations as equal members, because that would cut against its idea of control over South Asia.

Given that Bangladesh is not a prospective member, the visit would not have gained the Prime Minister, or the country, a great deal to begin with — beyond showing his face and mingling with a number of global leaders. So I do not think the decision carries major implications for Bangladesh. In bilateral terms, the Prime Minister has already made his maiden visits to Malaysia and to China; on the China front the relationship is strong, and he enjoys a good working relationship with the United States and others. Diplomacy is multi-pronged and multi-tiered, and that too will have factored into his calculation of whether joining, or not joining, BRICS carries any real consequence. Had some BRICS members been keen to see Bangladesh join, that might have made a difference — but Bangladesh already has good relations, on its own account, with the likes of Iran and Saudi Arabia.

BRICS has become interesting of late, in that it wants — with Russian assistance — to build a de-dollarised system. So the Prime Minister's staying away is, in a sense, a signal: that Bangladesh is not, at this moment, eager to enter arrangements that are geopolitically contentious. It is the same caution we saw over the Mecca Pact discussions earlier; Bangladesh is following a similarly careful path.

Certainly, attending the summit would have given him the chance to speak to the Indian political leadership and to other global leaders, and it is the bilateral meetings on the sidelines of such events that tend to be the real avenues for a diplomatic breakthrough. With the Indians, it might well have produced one. But before any breakthrough, Bangladesh had to convey its own requirements to India — and those requirements not being met was, I think, a key reason the Prime Minister chose not to go in the first place.

As for the other countries, I do not foresee any significant degradation. We have very good bilateral relations right across the group. With Russia, ties are not at any low ebb — they remain structured and continue in a routine manner. With China, the relationship is moving to a much higher plane, in bilateral trust and in trade, with Xi Jinping speaking of a more cultural, more civilisational approach. With the United States we have a historically good relationship, and with Europe a strong working one. The government has recently signed trade and framework agreements with South Korea, Japan and Australia, and work with the European Union is ongoing. So with every actor, inside BRICS and beyond it, Bangladesh has robust bilateral relations; the summit will not significantly affect them.

And I think every one of these countries would understand why the Prime Minister did not go — because he cannot visit unless something is forthcoming for him. His diplomatic success required a measure of compromise from the Indians, and the absence of that is the major reason he stayed away.

Md Tanvir Habib is an Assistant Professor at the Department of International Relations at the University of Dhaka.

Title: Cheap engine oil can become an expensive mistake
Content:
There are plenty of places where you can save some money when maintaining a car. Engine oil probably should not be one of them.

For most of us, an oil change is fairly uneventful. You drive into a workshop, tell the mechanic what car you have and, more often than not, let them decide what goes into it. After all, if the engine sounds fine afterwards, what could possibly have gone wrong?

Quite a lot, actually.

Engine oil spends its life somewhere we cannot see it, which makes its quality remarkably easy to ignore. Poor-quality or counterfeit oil will not necessarily make an engine explode the moment you turn the key either. Instead, the consequences can appear thousands of kilometres later, when that small saving on an oil change starts looking rather insignificant next to the repair bill.

Here are four reasons why what you pour into your engine deserves a little more attention.

1. The world's best oil is useless if the bottle is fake

This is perhaps the bigger concern when shopping for lubricant locally.

A bottle can carry a familiar logo, the correct viscosity and every specification you were looking for. None of that matters if what is actually inside is adulterated, recycled or simply not what the packaging claims.

That makes where you buy your oil almost as important as what you buy.

An authorised dealer or established retailer is a safer bet than chasing the lowest possible price from an unknown source. Check whether the cap and seal appear untouched. Look at the quality of the bottle and printing. If the manufacturer offers a QR code, scratch code or another authentication system, take the extra minute to use it.

And if a supposedly identical bottle costs suspiciously less than it does everywhere else, asking why is probably worthwhile.

None of this means you need to buy the most expensive fully synthetic oil on the shelf every time your car needs servicing. A cheaper genuine lubricant that meets the correct requirements can be a perfectly sensible choice.

What matters is much simpler: the right viscosity, the right performance specification, a reputable product and a trustworthy seller.

2. Your engine really does depend on the stuff

Calling engine oil the lifeblood of an engine sounds like something written on the back of a lubricant bottle, but there is some truth to the cliché.

Inside an engine, pistons, bearings, camshafts and the crankshaft are moving at tremendous speeds. The oil creates a protective film between these components, reducing friction and preventing metal surfaces from constantly fighting each other.

And our driving conditions are hardly kind to them. Long periods sitting in traffic, repeated stop-start driving, high temperatures and dusty roads can make life particularly difficult for an engine.

Things get even more serious with turbocharged cars. A turbocharger can spin at well over 100,000 rpm while operating in an extremely hot environment, and its bearings depend on a constant supply of suitable oil.

Poor lubrication does not necessarily kill any of these components overnight. Increased wear happens gradually, which is precisely what makes it easy to overlook.

Until, of course, something expensive gives up.

3. Bad oil can leave a mess behind

Oil does much more than make slippery things slippery.

A modern engine oil contains an additive package designed to control deposits, resist oxidation, reduce wear, protect against corrosion and keep contaminants suspended within the oil.

This is where the quality of the lubricant becomes important.

A poorly formulated or adulterated product may not provide the additive performance the engine requires. Over time, excessive deposits and sludge can form inside the engine. In severe cases, these can interfere with the small passages through which oil travels to critical components.

The result can range from accelerated internal wear to problems with components such as the valvetrain and turbocharger.

There is also a common misconception worth clearing up here. Black oil does not automatically mean bad oil. Engine oil naturally becomes darker as it collects contaminants, and its detergents and dispersants are partly there to keep those contaminants suspended.

So dipping the stick, seeing dark oil and immediately blaming the brand is not particularly useful.

4. Those letters on the bottle actually mean something

Walk into an oil shop and you will find bottles covered in things like 0W-20, 5W-30, 10W-40, API SN and API SP.

They are not there merely to make the bottle look more technical.

The first set refers to the oil's SAE viscosity grade. In simple terms, it tells you how the oil behaves at lower and higher temperatures. Your manufacturer will normally specify which viscosity or viscosities are suitable for the engine.

Then there is the API performance category. API specifications indicate the level of performance an engine oil has been designed to meet. API SP, for example, is a newer petrol-engine specification than API SN and introduces requirements relevant to modern engines.

Some carmakers also have their own oil specifications and approvals.

This distinction is important because two bottles can both say 5W-30 while meeting different performance requirements. SAE tells you about viscosity; it is not, by itself, a certificate saying that one 5W-30 is as good as every other 5W-30.

It is also why the familiar advice of putting thicker oil into an ageing engine should not automatically be taken as gospel.

Instead of guessing, check the owner's manual or do a simple Google search. The people who designed the engine have already told you what it needs.

Title: Adani unit resumes power supply, but recovery offset as Rampal generation halves
Content:
National power supply is expected to remain tight after a technical fault forced a unit of the 1,320MW Rampal coal-fired power plant offline yesterday, offsetting generation gains made from the recovery of Adani Power's Godda plant.

The Rampal plant, which had been generating over 1,100MW, saw its output drop below 600MW following the shutdown of one of its units around 11:30am, according to sources at the Bangladesh Power Development Board and the Power Grid Company of Bangladesh.

Officials said efforts were underway to restore the affected unit at the Rampal facility, a joint venture between Bangladesh and India.

The plant had previously experienced production cuts due to coal shortages and transportation disruptions caused by storms, though generation had recovered recently following improvements in fuel supply.

The setback at Rampal occurred on the same day that Unit-2 of Adani Power Jharkhand's 1,600MW Godda Thermal Power Plant synchronised with Bangladesh's national grid at 12:04pm, three days after a technical issue in its feed unit forced it offline. The

BSS reports that the quantum was increased to 1,450MW at 6pm.

Adani's supply to Bangladesh rose from 758MW at 9am to 1,046MW by 2pm, with Unit-1 contributing 756.66MW and Unit-2 adding 290MW as ramp-up continued.

The Godda plant, which consists of two 800MW units with a combined actual capacity of around 1,496MW, had previously delivered output crossing 1,400MW prior to the shutdown of Unit-2.

Title: GPH Ispat seeks Tk967.77cr rights issue to repay debt
Content:
GPH Ispat, one of the leading steel manufacturing companies in Bangladesh, will raise nearly Tk968 crore through issuing rights shares, mainly to repay bank loans amid sluggish demand and persistent energy shortages affecting the steel industry.

The company's board approved the issuance of 967.77 crore rights shares at Tk10 each at a meeting held on Saturday, according to a disclosure to the stock exchanges.

Under the proposed rights offer, existing shareholders will be entitled to receive two rights shares for every ordinary share they hold.

The rights issue is expected to raise Tk967.77 crore, subject to approval from the company's shareholders at its annual general meeting (AGM) and final approval from the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC).

GPH Ispat will announce a separate record date to determine shareholders' entitlement to the rights shares after receiving the necessary regulatory approvals.

GPH Ispat's decision comes as its debt burden remains substantial. As of 31 March 2026, the company had long-term loans of Tk3,439 crore and short-term borrowings of Tk3,145 crore, taking its total borrowings to around Tk6,584 crore.

A senior company official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the steel market has been facing weak demand while persistent energy shortages, particularly the gas crisis, have severely affected production.

"Business is going through a difficult period because demand has slowed, while the gas shortage has also hampered production. But loan instalments have to be paid on time despite the weak business environment," he said.

The company is also negotiating with banks to reschedule its loans, while its management is in discussions with Bangladesh Bank over the matter, he added.

GPH Ispat accumulated the high debt largely after making heavy investments to expand production capacity through new plants. However, delays in infrastructure development and a subsequent slowdown in demand have left the company facing pressure to service the borrowings, according to the official.

The latest rights issue is not the company's first attempt to raise fresh capital. In August 2024, GPH Ispat announced a plan to raise Tk242 crore through a rights offer, proposing one rights share for every three existing shares at Tk15, including a Tk5 premium. The proceeds were intended to finance a new expansion plant expected to generate Tk450 crore in annual revenue.

The BSEC, however, cancelled that rights-share application in May 2025, saying the documents submitted by the company were not satisfactory.

A month later, in June 2025, the securities regulator also rejected GPH Ispat's proposal to raise Tk500 crore through preference shares to repay loans.

The latest proposal therefore marks a significant shift in the company's capital-raising strategy, with debt repayment now taking priority over production expansion.

Meanwhile, GPH Ispat has recommended a 2% cash dividend for the financial year ended 30 June 2026, exclusively for general shareholders. Sponsors and directors holding 14.62 crore shares will not receive the dividend. The proposed payout to eligible general shareholders amounts to Tk6.75 crore.

The company's AGM is scheduled for 25 October, where shareholders will vote on both the dividend recommendation and the rights issue. The record date for participation in the AGM and entitlement to the proposed dividend is 1 October.

GPH Ispat returned to profitability in FY26, though earnings remained thin. The company posted a net profit of Tk3.38 crore, translating into earnings per share (EPS) of Tk0.07, compared with a loss per share of Tk0.51 in FY25.

Its net asset value stood at Tk51.81 per share, while net operating cash flow per share was Tk15.73.

Despite the return to profit, investors remained cautious. GPH Ispat shares fell 3.09% to Tk15.70 on the Dhaka Stock Exchange today (13 September). The company's market capitalisation stood at around Tk759 crore against paid-up capital of Tk483.88 crore.

Title: Tom Holland becomes highest-grossing actor with $15.5bn haul
Content:
Tom Holland has reportedly become the highest-grossing actor in history, with his films generating an estimated $15.5 billion worldwide.

The milestone comes as his latest film, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”, nears the end of its theatrical run. According to current box-office estimates, the film is projected to finish with a worldwide haul of between $2.5 billion and $2.6 billion.

Holland’s estimated career total has been boosted by the combined success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey”. The latter has grossed around $1.6 billion worldwide, while “Brand New Day” has crossed $2.4 billion globally, according to recent reports.

The figures place Holland ahead of Zoe Saldaña and Scarlett Johansson on a ranking based on the combined worldwide box-office grosses of films featuring each actor. However, this is not a measure of an actor’s personal earnings. Different box-office databases use different methodologies when calculating an actor’s cumulative film gross. One current tracking list, for example, puts Holland seventh behind several actors including Samuel L Jackson, John Ratzenberger, Johansson and Saldaña.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day”, directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, has also continued its remarkable box-office run. The film has already grossed more than $2.4 billion worldwide, making it the third-highest-grossing film of all time, behind James Cameron’s “Avatar” and “Avengers: Endgame”, according to recent industry reports.

The film is also closing in on the all-time domestic box-office record in the US and Canada. It has earned about $926.8 million domestically as of September 10, leaving it roughly $9.9 million short of “Star Wars: The Force Awakens”, which holds the record with $936.7 million.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” opened with $360.1 million domestically, setting a new record for the biggest opening weekend in North America at the time. It went on to remain at the top of the domestic box office for six consecutive weekends.

Title: Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Festival begins nationwide journey celebrating a shared spiritual legacy
Content:
Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Festival, a nationwide cultural festival, was inaugurated on September 11 at the field of Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka, celebrating the timeless spiritual traditions and artistic contributions of Kabir (1398–1498) and Fakir Lalon Shah (1774–1890). The festival celebrates the influence of the two mystic figures whose teachings have shaped generations across the Indian subcontinent through messages of equality, compassion, devotion and human unity.

Organised by Lalon Biswasangha with support from the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, the festival will continue until October 30. Cultural programmes will be held every day from 5:30 pm to 9:30 pm, and the celebration will travel across all eight divisions of Bangladesh, including Dhaka, Chattogram, Rajshahi, Sylhet, Mymensingh, Khulna, Barishal and Rangpur.

Kabir and Lalon’s philosophies represent a spiritual tradition that emphasises the search for truth beyond social divisions and external identities. Their songs and teachings have long encouraged people to look within themselves, embrace humanity and recognise the connection between all beings. Through this festival, organisers aim to introduce their profound creations to younger generations while creating a space for cultural dialogue, reflection and appreciation of the region’s shared spiritual heritage.

The inaugural ceremony was attended by prominent cultural and political figures. Advocate Fazlur Rahman MP, freedom fighter and senior political leader, inaugurated the festival. The scheduled chief guest, State Minister for Cultural Affairs Ali Newaz Mahmud Khaiyam could not attend due to unavoidable circumstances. Representing the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Md Mizanur Rahman, Joint Secretary of the ministry, attended the programme as chief guest. Dinesh Trivedi, High Commissioner of India to Bangladesh, joined the ceremony as a special guest. The event was chaired by Professor Emeritus Dr Anisuzzaman, Chairman of Lalon Biswasangha.

Speaking at the inauguration, Fazlur Rahman highlighted the relevance of Kabir and Lalon’s teachings in understanding human struggles and spiritual questions. He said, “To understand the struggles of life, turn to Kabir; to understand the mysteries of the soul, turn to Lalon.”

The inaugural ceremony featured discussions, musical performances and cultural presentations involving scholars, researchers, musicians and representatives of the Kabir and Lalon traditions. The discussion panel included noted academics and cultural personalities such as Professor Dr Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Professor Dr Priyanka Gope, Dr Ahsanul Hadi, Fakir Abdul Hossain Shah, Nijhum Pankiya, Dr M K Roy and Syed Faiyaz Hasan, who shared insights on the philosophical, literary and cultural significance of Kabir and Lalon’s works.

The High Commissioner of India to Bangladesh, Dinesh Trivedi, highlighted the spirit of equality and universal humanity reflected in the teachings of Kabir and Lalon, saying, “Here, everyone is equal, an ambassador, an MP, or a common person. This equality is the very essence of Kabir and Lalon’s philosophy.”

Reflecting on the persistent relevance of their wisdom in today’s world, Trivedi added, “When sailors lose their way, they seek a lighthouse. In a world that has lost its path and peace, Kabir and Lalon’s wisdom remains that guiding light for humanity.”

The festival also served as a platform to preserve and promote the Bhabsangeet tradition, a form of spiritual music that carries deep reflections on life, humanity and the search for the divine.

Bringing together artistes, scholars, cultural leaders and audiences from diverse backgrounds, the Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Festival seeks to celebrate a shared heritage built on compassion, equality and spiritual awareness.

Title: Remembering Anwar Hossain, the ‘uncrowned Nawab’ of Dhallywood
Content:
Anwar Hossain was one of the most celebrated actors in Bangladesh. Over a career spanning hundreds of films, he played an astonishing range of characters — from heroes and rulers to ordinary villagers and morally complex figures.

He became the “uncrowned Nawab” of Bangladeshi cinema after his iconic performance as the titular character in Nawab Sirajuddaula, directed by Khan Ataur Rahman. His deeply emotional portrayal of the doomed Nawab captivated audiences, particularly during the character’s tragic death. The role became so closely associated with Hossain that audiences everywhere began calling him the “uncrowned Nawab”.

His versatility was further evident in Zahir Raihan’s landmark political film “Jibon Theke Neya”. Playing a politician, Hossain created a very different screen image. He also appeared in the film’s memorable musical sequences, including “Karar Oi Louho Kopat” and “Amar Sonar Bangla”. In the latter, his emotional expression as tears rolled down his face remains particularly memorable.

In “Lathiyal”, Hossain delivered another acclaimed performance, convincingly portraying a rural stick-fighter. His natural and powerful acting won over audiences across the country and earned him the National Film Award for Best Actor.

Although best known for his character roles, Hossain was also a leading man. He made his acting debut as a villain and later played the hero in “Surja Snan”. Across hundreds of films, he portrayed virtually every kind of character — rich and poor, king and commoner, saint and sinner.

He continued to surprise audiences in films such as Amjad Hossain’s “Golapi Ekhon Traine”, in which he played an ordinary man with remarkable sensitivity. His performance earned him another National Film Award. He also played the titular roles in “Shahid Titumir” and “Isha Kha”, further demonstrating his extraordinary range.

Some of the songs associated with Hossain’s performances became cultural favourites. “Hay Re Manush, Rongin Fanush, Dhom Furaille Thush”, featured in “Boro Bhalo Lok Chhilo”, became widely popular across cities, villages, markets and tea stalls. His screen presence in films such as “Manusher Mon”, “Bhanumati”, “Chakorani” and “Bhat De” also left lasting impressions on audiences, often through emotionally charged performances and songs.

In “Doyal Murshid”, Hossain played Hasan, an honest young man who desperately wanted to free himself from his burdens. His performance once again demonstrated his ability to bring dignity and emotional depth to a character.

Anwar Hossain died on September 13, 2013. Yet decades after his passing, he remains the uncrowned Nawab of Bangladeshi cinema — a rare actor whose range, screen presence and body of work remain difficult to match.

For his contribution to cinema, Hossain received the National Film Award for Lifetime Achievement, multiple National Film Awards and the Ekushey Padak, among numerous other honours.

Anwar Hossain was, quite simply, one of a kind.

Title: Shanta Islam receives Lifetime Achievement Award in Canada
Content:
Once a widely popular actress in numerous television dramas and a National Film Award winner, Shanta Islam has now received a Lifetime Achievement Award from an organisation outside Bangladesh. The Federation of Bangladeshi Associations in North America (FOBANA) presented her with the honour at the Don Valley Hotel and Suites in Toronto, Canada.

Speaking to The Daily Star over the phone from Canada, Shanta Islam said, “I am extremely happy and delighted. FOBANA has given me a Lifetime Achievement Award in Canada. I feel deeply honoured.”

She said, “I have acted in numerous dramas throughout my career and have received the love of many people. I received the Bachsas Award for my performance in ‘Mayur Singhasan’ with Aranyak Natyadal. I also received the National Film Award for acting in films. However, this is the first time I have received such a major honour outside the country — and that too a Lifetime Achievement Award.”

Asked about the recognition, Shanta said, “I truly feel proud to receive this honour. I am grateful to the organisers. I would also like to express my gratitude and love to all the directors, producers, fellow artistes and journalists in my own country.”

She added, “We artistes work for the people. Alongside receiving people’s love, when an organisation or a state recognises our work, it gives us encouragement and a sense of fulfilment.”

Recalling her career, she said, “I acted in numerous dramas for Bangladesh Television at one time. I also worked in many package dramas and performed in stage productions. I became involved in cultural activities while studying at Dhaka University. I acted in several popular dramas, including ‘Rupnagar’. I also worked as a presenter for many years. Receiving this honour has brought back memories of the work I did throughout my life.”

Meanwhile, Shanta Islam is enjoying her time in Canada, where her only son, daughter-in-law and granddaughter live. She is spending time with them.

“My son’s success gives me peace and fulfilment. My daughter-in-law is like another mother to me, and my granddaughter is my inspiration to keep living. I am doing very well with all of them around me,” she said.

She added, “I have also been meeting many friends and well-wishers in Canada. I am having a wonderful time. I am especially enjoying spending lovely moments with my daughter-in-law. We go out and explore places on holidays.”

Finally, she said, “My son is extremely happy that I have received this Lifetime Achievement Award. My daughter-in-law is happy too.”

Notably, acclaimed magician Jewel Aich also received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the same event.

Title: ‘Symphony of Life’: Exhibition reflects life through diverse artistic lenses
Content:
172 artists came together last week with 172 different ways of looking at life. Their works span landscapes, Islamic calligraphy, folk traditions, still life, abstract imagery and experimental compositions, creating a diverse visual experience under one roof.

Titled “Symphony of Life”, the group art exhibition organised by Shilpo Bangla opened at the Zainul Gallery of the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Dhaka, on September 10. The exhibition brings together artists working across different styles and mediums.

The exhibition was inaugurated on September 10 at 5pm at the Osman Jamal Auditorium of the Faculty of Fine Arts. Eminent artist and Ekushey Padak-winning Professor Dr Abdus Sattar, honorary teacher of the Department of Oriental Art at the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Dhaka, attended the event as the chief guest. Professor Kaoser Hassan Togor of the Department of Sculpture at the Faculty of Fine Arts, Shanto Mahmud, Channel i Chief Executive Producer of News, and Associate Professor Habiba Akther Papia of the Department of Fashion Design at Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology attended as special guests. Professor Dr Azharul Islam Sheikh, Dean of the Faculty of Fine Arts and Chairman of its Department of Ceramics, presided over the ceremony. Minne Art Gallery and Mahfuz Canvas are supporting partners of the exhibition.

The broad theme of the exhibition allows the artists to approach life and society from their own perspectives. The result is a collection where a quiet watercolour of a village homestead can hang beside an elaborate gold calligraphy piece, while a traditional still life may sit next to a painting of a seedling emerging from the earth.

Landscape painting occupies much of the gallery space. Rivers lined with mangroves, boats moored at wooden jetties, moonlit canals and vivid sunsets appear across the walls. Rural Bangladesh returns repeatedly in images of flame trees beside ponds, narrow lanes between tin-roofed houses and quiet village settings. Many of these works are acrylic on canvas, with soft, blended strokes giving the landscapes a gentle, atmospheric quality.

Islamic calligraphy forms another strong visual thread. One large framed work features a Quranic verse written in gold against a background that shifts from deep red to blue. Beneath the lettering, two cupped hands hold small circular images of a damaged landscape. Another work combines golden lettering with a black background and a jewelled mandala-like form. A night view of the Masjid al-Haram, glowing beneath a crescent moon and framed by an ornate arch, adds another striking piece to the collection.

Folk traditions also have a strong presence. One canvas draws on the visual language of nakshi kantha, depicting two peacocks facing each other across a lotus medallion, with decorated elephants and an intricate floral border. Another borrows the bold outlines and flat colours of rickshaw art to portray a mother holding her child. Elsewhere, women sit on a chequered mat in a village courtyard.

Some artists move further away from realism. In one unusual composition, a figure carries a teacup where the head would normally be. Another brings together dozens of small faces to form a single heart. Two whirling dervishes appear against a smoky blue background, their faces left undefined while the movement of their white garments becomes the focus of the work.

The variety extends to the mediums. Acrylic is widely used, appearing both in the flat colours of folk-inspired works and the heavier textures of landscape paintings. Oil, watercolour, charcoal, graphite and pen are also represented, while some artists have used modelling paste, gold leaf, beads and collage to add texture to their works.

More than anything, “Symphony of Life” reflects the different ways artists interpret the world around them. By bringing 172 artists into one space, the exhibition creates a collective experience without asking them to give up their individual voices. “Symphony of Life” will remain open to visitors at the Zainul Gallery until September 16, daily from 12pm to 7pm.
