Title: A family: The beating heart of Bangladesh table tennis
Content:
Walking into the training hall at Dhaka’s Shaheed Tajuddin Ahmad Indoor Stadium during a national session, one hears a rhythmic, high-tempo syncopation: the sharp clack-clack of celluloid balls striking blue wooden tables.

A close look at the line of tables reveals a rare statistical anomaly: four top spots on the Bangladesh women’s table tennis roster belong to a single family tree.

Two sisters and two cousins -- five-time champion Sonam Sultana Soma, former junior champion Nowrin Sultana Mahi, former national champion Sadia Rahman Mou, and former junior runner-up Samanta Hossain Tushi -- form the core of an unprecedented national sports dynasty. All except Mou are set to represent Bangladesh at the upcoming Asian Games in Japan.

Having played in the 2019 SAFF Games in Nepal, 2021 Asian Championships in Qatar, and 2025 Islamic Solidarity Games in Turkey, sisters Soma and Mahi eagerly await receiving their cousin Tushi into the senior squad. Tushi previously earned her stripes on the international youth circuit during the South Asian Youth Table Tennis Championships.

This family is the beating heart of the national team. Five-time champion Saleha Parvin, Mou, former junior champion Sumiya Hossain Oishi, who is the elder sister of Tushi, and doubles champion Akhi Akhter Synthi have all been central to the senior and junior sides since Soma and Saleha first joined the national team fold at the 2010 SA Games in Dhaka.

Their journey began in a modest compound in Narail municipality, where sport was a central pillar of daily life. Inspired by former paddler and younger uncle Ismail Hossain, Saleha and Soma fell deeply in love with table tennis at Narail Table Tennis Club.

Younger sisters and cousins soon followed, stepping from district competitions in Narail onto the national stage to define the country's circuit.

In Dhaka, they train at an in-house family academy run by national coach Mohammad Ali, who happens to be Soma’s husband. Living together gives them constant access to elite sparring partners to refine side-spin serves and backhand counter-loops. Daily tactical discussions allow them to channel sibling rivalry into their ultimate accelerator.

“I am just providing them with proper guidance on how to improve their game, remain calm, and react effectively during matches,” coach Mohammad Ali told The Daily Star.

“Even though they are cousins, they play with complete dedication in competition -- one will even burst into tears after losing to another.”

Soma shared, “It is a wonderful feeling to see sister after sister join the national squad. It has been made possible by our shared passion and love for table tennis, as we played purely for the joy of the game.

“We also cherish every moment together after matches, as everyone is otherwise busy with their respective routines.”

Mahi, who is 14 years younger than Soma, said, “It is impossible to express in words what it feels like when we, as sisters, represent Bangladesh internationally. Carrying the national flag was beyond anything we imagined when we first picked up the rackets.”

Tushi, meanwhile, is ecstatic to play as the youngest family member on the senior squad. While navigating local facility limitations, their path is sustained by vital off-table backing. Year-round support from Bangladesh Ansar and VDP -- providing monthly salaries, allowances, and international airfare -- remains the foundation enabling this sisterhood to make sports history.

As the sharp echoes of celluloid against wood fade into the daily grind of preparation, Narail’s smashing sisters remain focused on the horizon. Beyond the titles and medals lies an enduring legacy: a family bound by blood, fueled by fierce devotion, ready to carry Bangladesh’s colours proudly once more.
Author: A Anisur Rahman Anisur Rahman

Title: Japan shatter Bangladesh’s Hockey Junior World Cup dream
Content:
Bangladesh’s hopes of qualifying for the FIH Hockey Junior World Cup for the second successive time were dashed as Japan handed the men in red and green a heavy 6-2 defeat in the place-deciding match of the AHF Hockey Junior Asia Cup in China today.

The defeat means Bangladesh will now face Chinese Taipei in the seventh-place play-off, with only the top six teams from the tournament securing tickets to the next Junior World Cup.

Having qualified for the 2025 edition of the Junior World Cup after finishing fifth in the AHF Men’s Junior Asia Cup, Bangladesh had no alternative but to beat Japan today to keep their World Cup hopes alive.

However, despite making a promising start, Bangladesh were badly let down by their finishing as Japan gradually took control of the contest.

Bangladesh enjoyed the early possession but conceded against the run of play in the second minute when an unmarked Seia Yamada found the net from open play.

The men in red and green responded positively and created an opportunity to level the score, but missed an open-net chance. Japan were also wasteful, with Yunosuke Sone squandering a penalty stroke.

Sone, however, made amends in the 29th minute, converting another penalty stroke to double Japan’s advantage. Shota Hanayama then made it 3-0 with a field goal on the stroke of half-time.

Japan continued to dominate after the change of ends, extending their lead to 4-0 in the 36th minute as Rintaro Sakai converted a penalty stroke.

Sakai struck again in the 41st minute to put Japan firmly in command.

Bangladesh finally found a way back when Mohammad Mehedi converted a penalty stroke in the 41st minute, but their hopes of a comeback were quickly extinguished as Japan restored their five-goal cushion with their sixth in the 45th minute.

Bangladesh created a number of chances in the final two quarters but could only reduce the deficit once more, with Munna Islam converting a penalty corner in the 50th minute.

Title: Tangail taant: A classic saree for every weekday
Content:
On a weekday morning, Tasfia Mumtarin is not thinking about making a fashion statement. She is thinking about Dhaka traffic. The dancer and sales executive at an automobile company has meetings ahead, several hours at her desk, perhaps a client visit, and dance practice later in the evening. Her question is simple: could a saree realistically survive all of that?

“I would wear sarees more often if I stopped thinking that wearing one meant I had to dress up,” explains Mumtarin. “If I can wear a cotton saree with a comfortable blouse, flats, a big work bag and almost no jewellery, then it becomes clothing rather than an occasion.”

That distinction may be precisely what the Tangail saree needs.

For a textile so deeply connected to Bengal’s clothing history, the Tangail saree increasingly finds itself in a curious position. We bring it out for Pahela Baishakh, Puja, weddings, office celebrations, and cultural programmes. Yet, the saree that could be one of the most practical pieces in a Bangladeshi wardrobe often waits patiently for an “occasion.”

Perhaps, the more interesting question is not how to preserve the Tangail saree, but how to wear it again.

There is little about traditional Tangail that inherently demands ceremony.

Tangail sarees are known for their fine texture, local motifs and detailed weaving, and can be made using cotton, silk or jute.

In 2025, UNESCO inscribed the traditional saree weaving art of Tangail on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising a weaving tradition sustained across generations of Basak and Jhola communities.

However, cultural importance does not mean a garment needs to become precious to the point of impracticality.

In fact, some of the qualities associated with taant make it especially appropriate for Bangladesh. Lightweight cotton, breathability and relatively uncomplicated care have long made handloom sarees suitable for humid weather and regular use

Fashion director and stylist Sonia Yeasmin Isha points first to accessibility.

“First of all, Tangail sarees are reasonably priced. They are affordable for almost everyone,” she remarks. There is, of course, enormous variation within the category. Everyday cotton Tangails coexist with elaborate, highly valuable pieces. A weaver from Tangail Saree Kutir Ltd. explains that Tangail should not be automatically equated with inexpensive casual wear.

“There are many expensive Tangail sarees. Some cost more than Tk 1,00,000,” he says. “These sarees can easily be worn at weddings or any kind of party.”

That range may actually be one of Tangail’s greatest strengths. It does not have to choose between the everyday and the extraordinary. The same weaving tradition can occupy both spaces.

Ask many young women why they do not wear sarees regularly and the answers are predictable: too difficult to drape, too formal, too much fabric, difficult for commuting, uncomfortable for a full working day.

Some of these concerns are genuine. Others have as much to do with how we have learned to style a saree as with the garment itself.

We often construct a complete ritual around it. A matching blouse must be made. Jewellery needs to be chosen. The anchal needs to behave. The pleats must be exact. Hair and makeup suddenly require attention.

By the time the look is complete, what began as six yards of cotton has turned into an event.

Isha proposes treating Tangail much more freely. “It can be paired with almost anything and styled in many different ways,” she says.

For office wear, she suggests a blazer over the saree. A shirt can be knotted and worn as a blouse. In winter, a high-neck or black turtleneck can replace the conventional blouse, with a belt or jacket added if desired.

Even a familiar Tangail can therefore behave differently depending on what surrounds it. That may be particularly relevant for younger wearers who do not necessarily want to look “traditional” simply because they are wearing a traditional textile.

There is another habit worth questioning: the Bangladeshi tendency to save clothes.

The beautiful saree remains folded because it is “too good” for work. Another is reserved for an invitation that never quite matches it. Years later, a wardrobe can contain perfectly wearable handloom sarees that have appeared in public only twice.

For Nafisa Raidah, a communications professional, repeat wear would make sarees much more appealing.

“If I buy a Tangail saree, I want to know I can wear it to work on Monday, to lunch with friends a month later, and then to a family dinner with different accessories,” she shares. “I don't want every saree to have one fixed identity.”

It is a useful way of thinking about sustainability too. Sustainable fashion is not only about what something is made from. It is also about whether we actually wear what we own.

An everyday Tangail does not require five separate sarees for five looks. One muted saree might be paired with a white shirt for work, a sleeveless blouse and silver jewellery for dinner, a contrasting cotton blouse for daytime, and a jacket during winter.

The repeat is not a styling failure. The repeat is the point.

One practical complaint about new cotton Tangail sarees is that they can initially feel crisp or slightly voluminous.

Isha acknowledges this. “Many people avoid Tangail sarees because the fabric can feel slightly stiff or puffy,” she clarifies. “However, after a few washes, it usually becomes much softer.”

That is an important everyday detail because we often judge handloom clothing straight from the shop rather than considering how natural fabrics change with use.

A saree that softens over time develops familiarity. It becomes easier to pleat, easier to move in and less intimidating. In that sense, an often-worn Tangail may actually become more useful than one permanently preserved in pristine condition.

For a workday, practical choices matter too: secure the pleats with pins, keep the pallu manageable, choose shoes that allow walking, avoid unnecessarily heavy jewellery and select a blouse that lets the arms move freely.

A saree does not have to be worn as though one is perpetually arriving at a reception.

Tangail also lends itself naturally to restrained dressing.

Isha notes the variety within its visual language. Some sarees have broad, striking borders; others have narrow ones, while some place greater emphasis on motifs across the body. “In most Tangail sarees, however, the border is one of the main attractions,” she elaborates.

For someone beginning an everyday saree wardrobe, that means the textile can supply its own decoration.

A strong border hardly needs a statement necklace. A saree with small motifs can work with a plain blouse. Black, white, beige, indigo and other versatile blouse colours can remove the pressure to tailor something new for every saree.

The goal is not to make Tangail resemble Western clothing to call it contemporary. It is to remove unnecessary rules around how it must be worn.

The saree does not need rescuing. It needs wearing

The Tangail saree has already demonstrated an extraordinary ability to adapt. Weavers have long responded to changing tastes through new colours, designs and motifs. Historical reporting from Tangail likewise shows artisans producing both casual handloom sarees and more expensive versions while adapting designs to contemporary demand.

Its relevance therefore does not have to depend on nostalgia. Nor does honouring craftsmanship require keeping it behind glass.

UNESCO recognition understandably places renewed attention on Tangail’s weaving knowledge, communities and cultural importance. Bangladesh also lists Tangail saree as a registered geographical indication product. Perhaps, one of the most meaningful forms of this appreciation happens far away from exhibitions and ceremonies. It is when someone reaches into the wardrobe before work and chooses a Tangail.

Isha believes younger wearers are already drawn towards cotton and softer, more comfortable fabrics. What remains is to show them the possibilities. “We now need to introduce Tangail sarees to a wider audience,” she says. “People should be shown that these sarees can be worn in many different ways and styled in a variety of contemporary looks.”

For generations, Tangail's looms have produced extraordinary clothing. Perhaps the next chapter is wonderfully ordinary.

Title: What inspires Gen Z’s funky hair colours?
Content:
Want a trick to spot Gen Z in a crowd? Just take a look around. If your eyes catch flashes of lavender or burgundy, cherry red, electric blue, or any other funky hue splashed across someone’s hair, you’ve got it.

A flash of lavender at a coffee shop, ombre green and black curls on a university campus, or perhaps cherry red bangs peeking out from under a bandana! Colourful hair has become one of Gen Z’s favourite ways to express themselves, and they are nailing it effortlessly. In a world where trends come and go overnight, vibrant hair remains one of the generation’s boldest forms of self-expression.

“I usually colour my hair when I feel sad or down,” said Nabila Tabassum, a university student. “I always go for electric blue because somehow I feel that blue represents my personality and aesthetics.”

For this generation, hair colour means more than what it looks like. They paint their hair not just to look cool but to let you know their personality.

Some dye it impulsively; some do it after a breakup. Others simply wake up one morning and decide black or brown isn’t cutting it anymore. Whatever the reason, one thing is clear: this generation is not afraid to wear its personality, quite literally on its head.

Muntaha Rahi, an artist, still remembers the first time she dyed her hair red. “I felt powerful, to be honest.” She added, “It gave me an incredible sense of confidence.”

For Rahi, experimenting with hair colour is not just about changing her appearance; it’s about how it makes her feel. “Once you discover the power of hair colour, you might keep changing the shades, but you will probably never want to go back to plain black,” she expressed with a laugh.

It’s hard to scroll through social media without watching a dramatic hair transformation video. One minute, someone’s showing off their natural brunette locks; the next, they are rocking icy silver or bubble-gum pink. Before you know it, you are wondering if maybe burgundy highlights would not be such a bad idea after all.

“I’ve definitely been influenced," stated Sabit Ahmed, a 26-year-old university student. “It was very impulsive. I was watching hair transformation videos, and then I felt like I had to paint my hair blue.”

Social media may spark the idea, but K-pop often seals the deal. With every comeback, idols seem to debut a new hair colour: platinum blond one month, mint green the next, followed by cherry red or ash grey.

Fans do not really copy the exact look, but they do borrow the confidence to experiment.

Western musicians and influencers have embraced the same playful approach, treating hair colour like an accessory that changes with the mood, the season or even the playlist.

Yet for many young people, colouring their hair goes beyond keeping up with trends. Sometimes, it’s less about the colour itself and more about how it makes them feel.

In Bangladesh, this hair colour revolution is quietly gaining momentum too. From university campuses to trendy cafes, these places are becoming showcases for ash grey, wine red, deep violet, copper orange and peekaboo highlights.

And of course, colourful hair comes with its own set of responsibilities. Sulphate-free shampoos become your bestie, maintaining a hair care routine becomes a regular thing, and you will probably learn more about hair masks than you ever expected. However, ask anyone rocking cobalt blue curls, and they will probably tell you it is worth every faded towel and every extra minute in the shower.

Because at the end of the day, funky hair is not just about following the trend. It’s a feeling that stays with you.
Author: S Sabrin Zawad Ritu Sabrin Zawad Ritu

Title: How to style corsets with sarees for every occasion
Content:
Corsets were invented in the early sixteenth century to attain an hourglass shape by cinching the waist into submission! The earliest corsets were made by inserting wooden panels and whalebone into silk or layered linen bodices, and were worn by aristocratic men and women to attain better posture and structure. From being a marker of status to attaining a desired body silhouette, corsets have transformed from being an undergarment to being an essential element of an upper-class Victorian woman’s wardrobe, then eventually being discarded for their rigidity and impracticality.

Corsets of yore were demonised by women forced to wear and endure them; their accounts have been immortalised in literature and various accounts of that time as being extremely restrictive. Fainting was a regular occurrence as blood circulation was severely limited, and bruises and wounds were commonplace from ‘tightlacing’ the corsets, well, too tightly!

Modern corsets are anything but; appealing, stylish and elegant, they look and feel fabulous and fierce!

A saree, traditional as it is, when worn with a corset is a match made in sartorial heaven! A refreshingly modern way to pair two ancient pieces together to fantastic effect. In the Western world, corsets have always been a great reference point for legendary designers such as Jean Paul Gaultier, whose entire repertoire is based on it. Worn with pants, skirts, on top of shirts and even dresses, corsets are highly versatile. However, wearing corsets with sarees and lehenga is remarkably stylish and unique too. Not for the faint of heart, sarees worn with corsets make a fantastic statement and are a mark of a true-blue fashionista.

When planning to wear a corset with a saree, keep the occasion in mind. A slinky sheer georgette number with a black lace corset will look fabulous for your next cocktail night.

Pick a lovely floral one for the next ladies’ lunch; contrasting colours also look lovely. For a chic dinner at your friend’s new penthouse apartment, pick an elegant corset with pearls and pull up your hair in a sleek bun. And that’s not all. Traditional sarees look drop-dead gorgeous when worn with a corset too!

Pair your Kanjeevaram with a sheer, detailed corset and kundan jewellery and wow everyone at your cousin’s wedding!

Title: Summer makeup tips for a long-lasting look
Content:
Every year as summer returns, so does the challenge of doing long-lasting makeup. Along with the high temperatures and humidity, the search for the right products and techniques to have a durable makeup look becomes a part of our everyday struggles.

To make that search a little easier, we have curated a short guide containing some simple ways to ensure your makeup stays on longer during the heat.

Almost all long-lasting makeup guides begin by stating the importance of skin prep before doing makeup, and rightfully so.

As we all know, the biggest hurdle in having makeup last longer during hot days is sweat. The skin’s pre-condition before any makeup products are applied is a major contributing factor to sweating. Rubbing ice cubes or spraying some cold water on the face and letting it dry out is a great way to soothe the skin before the main show begins.

According to experts, for a long-lasting makeup look during summer, primers are non-negotiable.

They are always applied before foundation or any other product and are formulated to fill the pores of the skin and help control oil. Regardless of the skin type, primers are highly recommended as they help the other makeup products “grip” onto the skin. For dry skin, liquid-based primers containing hyaluronic acid can be a good choice.

While “glowy” makeup looks and creamy formulas have become more popular recently, in summer they can be the biggest enemy of makeup.

Swapping cream-based foundations and blush for powdered products and a matte makeup look is the ideal solution for humid weather. The powder also helps limit sweating by absorbing moisture.

Though the heat and humidity force many people to opt for more minimalist makeup looks, makeup artists often encourage using this opportunity to maximise on eye makeup instead.

Even if areas of the face such as the T-zone are at risk of excess sweat and oil, the eyelids and their nearby regions are at less of a disadvantage. Matte eyeshadow and waterproof eye-makeup products are the way to go during such weather.

Products and formulas aside, the techniques of applying and blending the makeup are also crucial in ensuring it stays on longer.

Instead of smearing or strongly blending the products against the skin, tapping it gently using brushes or a makeup sponge is highly advised. It is widely believed that relaxed skin is less likely to sweat profusely during and immediately after applying the makeup.

Another non-negotiable product for makeup during summer is setting spray or setting powder. They are a must to ensure all the products are locked in and remain intact for as long as possible. This is usually the final step in the makeup routine, and the product must be applied generously for it to work.

Most of these products are widely available and offer a great variety of brands to choose from. Some small changes to the regular makeup routine, replacement of certain products and adjusting to some new techniques can make a big difference in ensuring your makeup stays put longer during this heat.

Title: Rising from the ashes: Ahmed Tuhin Reza and Tanzila Elma return with renewed purpose
Content:
A fashion house’s return can mean more than reopening its doors. For House of Ahmed, it became an opportunity to rebuild with a clearer sense of identity and to make a stronger case for what contemporary luxury from Bangladesh can look like.

On 21 August, House of Ahmed marked the beginning of its Chapter 2 with the grand launch of its new space on the entire Level 6 of Ventura Mall in Gulshan. The evening brought together members of the fashion industry, media, clients and supporters, while the space itself offered a visual introduction to the brand’s renewed direction.

The launch followed a major setback caused by a fire that disrupted the brand’s operations. For Reza, however, the return was not about recreating what existed before. According to Tanzila Elma, Co-Founder, House of Ahmed, around 24,000 fresh red roses were used across the event space, from the backdrop to the welcoming area.

Inside the store, House of Ahmed’s signature zardozi craftsmanship appeared in installations inspired by Bangladesh. Ahsan Manzil, Lalbagh Fort, a handmade map of Bangladesh, a Dhaka rickshaw and a sewing machine were recreated through intricate zardozi work.

Another display celebrated Nakshi Kantha, Benarosi, Muslin and Jamdani, centred around the shapla motif. References to the Sundarbans, a Cox’s Bazar sampan, Jessore’s date palm and Barishal’s palki further connected the interiors to different parts of the country.

The overall concept and ideation for the space came from Ahmed Tuhin Reza and Tanzila Elma, while Saimul Karim of Eskay Décor was responsible for translating that vision into the final interior design with meticulous attention to detail.

With Chapter 2, House of Ahmed’s return was therefore not simply a reopening, but a renewed statement of ambition, craftsmanship and confidence in Made in Bangladesh luxury.

House of Ahmed’s Chapter 2 launch was also a showcase of the house’s design language in motion. Guests from Bangladesh’s entertainment, fashion and creative industries arrived in House of Ahmed ensembles, offering different interpretations of the brand’s approach to contemporary luxury.

Rehan wore a black premium silk ensemble paired with a maroon-and-mint katan jacket. The colour combination and construction were designed around his personality, looking a sharp but individual character.

Zayed Khan opted for an all-black look, pairing a premium silk open jacket with a black silk panjabi and statement box pants. Heavy zardozi work added depth and richness to the monochrome ensemble.

Shoumik Ahmed wore black on black, with full sleeves covered in heavy zardozi work. White three-dimensional embroidery at the shoulders created a striking contrast and looked its defining detail.

Nusraat Faria stepped out in an electric-blue pure organza saree, paired with a Benarasi katan blouse. The saturated colour and contrast of sheer organza against structured katan gave the look a distinctly contemporary finish.

Tangia Zaman Methila

Tangia Zaman Methila wore a dark navy-blue saree embellished with House of Ahmed’s signature motifs. The design incorporated the house’s logo and its signature shapla motif, turning the saree into a direct expression of the brand’s identity.

Reflecting her association with more traditional aesthetics, Toma Mirza wore onion-pink Mirpur Benarasi katan. A multicoloured blouse with zardozi detailing brought additional texture and colour to the traditional silhouette.

Masuma Rahman Nabila

Masuma Rahman Nabila appeared in striped silk organza in a soft rose-gold tone, finished with an onion-wine border. The restrained palette allowed the fabric and its subtle contrasts to take centre stage.

Peya Jannatul chose a coffee-brown Benarasi salwar kameez with an organza dupatta. Intricate work around the neckline created the focal point of the otherwise understated, tonal ensemble.

Azra Mahmood wore an emerald-green saree featuring intricate badla work, paired with a raw-silk katan blouse. The rich jewel tone and metallic detailing looked a formal, polished finish.

Ahmed Tuhin Reza wore one of House of Ahmed’s signature shades, royal blue, in a silk-fusion jacket layered over a short panjabi and paired with box pants. The silhouette balanced traditional menswear references with the house’s contemporary vocabulary.

Tanzila Elma complemented the brand’s signature palette in a black Anarkali detailed with electric-blue and gold zardozi work. Together, Elma and Reza incorporated House of Ahmed’s signature colours into their own looks for the Chapter 2 launch.

Karim wore a black Bangla-style ensemble with sleeves inspired by the doors of House of Ahmed, creating a direct connection between what he wore and the space he helped bring to life.

Title: Giving children a voice through fashion
Content:
Bangladesh Street Kids Aid uses skateboarding to connect with street-involved and underprivileged children. It also links them to education, medical and hygiene support. The children of BSKA have found confidence, discipline and a powerful form of self-expression through skateboarding. For a special Star Lifestyle project, that spirit became the starting point of a collaboration with three creative professionals who approached the children not simply as subjects of a photoshoot, but as individuals with their own stories and identities.

For Sara Hossain, Director of Craftsman Footwear & Accessories Ltd, designing shoes for the children began with an image that stayed with her. She had seen photographs of girls skateboarding in sarees during Pahela Baishakh, moving with a confidence that challenged familiar ideas about how girls should dress or occupy public space.

“To me, it felt like a rainbow in a cloudy sky,” Hossain recalls. “When they are in motion, they look like a flock of butterflies.”

That sense of movement, colour and freedom shaped the footwear she created for the Star Lifestyle photoshoot. Bright mustard, green, magenta and contrasting combinations were chosen with the children’s ages and energy in mind.

“Being a girl in Bangladesh is difficult,” she says. “Doing something out of the norm is even harder.”

For the BSKA children, that philosophy resulted in shoes designed not to tone down their energy, but to keep up with it.

I saw a couple of videos of the children on social media and fell in love with the statement of freedom and self-expression they demonstrated,” recalls Sharmin Rahman, creative director and designer.

For the photoshoot, Rahman decided the clothes should begin with the children themselves. She wrote to them and asked them to draw whatever they liked. Those drawings became the visual language of the 11 outfits.

Rather than refining the drawings into conventional motifs, Rahman preserved their uneven lines, spontaneous colours and individual character.

“I thought these children are extraordinary and they should be presented as who they are and in their true spirit,” she explains. “They should hold their heads high when they are wearing something they created themselves.”

The project reflects Rahman’s broader design philosophy. Before thinking about silhouette or decoration, she considers who a garment is made for, its purpose and the story it should portray. For her, responsible fashion extends beyond sustainable fabric to the use of local materials, techniques, artisans and community capabilities.

Khalid Mahmood Khan and the Kay Kraft team helped turn the creative language of the outfits into wearable garments.

“We felt connected to the concept when Sharmin Rahman shared the idea in her very own way,” says Khan, Entrepreneur, Kay Kraft.

Each outfit was designed around an individual child’s artwork, making the project closer to made-to-order work.

“Usually, Kay Kraft does ready-to-wear products. This collection was like individual samples for the children, with their own drawings incorporated in individual pieces,” Khan explains.

Preserving the individuality of those drawings required extra attention.

“From a production point of view, it needs a bit more effort and care to keep individuality and uniqueness,” he says.

The team approached the work enthusiastically, knowing the children would eventually see their own drawings transformed into garments. Khan credits Rahman for developing the concept and guiding its execution, while noting that the project also aligned naturally with Kay Kraft’s broader mindset.

For him, however, the most rewarding part was emotional rather than technical.

“We know that the children will be happy and more spirited, inspired wearing this,” Khan says. “We wanted to be a part of their happiness.”

Title: The hidden language we speak through jewellery
Content:
Long before jewellery became a fashion statement, it was a way of saying something without uttering a word. Across cultures and centuries, people have worn different kinds of jewellery made from gold, silver, iron, or beads to communicate who they are, where they belong, and what they value.

If we think about that for a moment, some of the oldest known jewellery, tiny shell beads discovered in Morocco, dates back more than 140,000 years. That indicates humans were making and wearing ornaments long before agriculture, cities, or even writing!

From an anthropological perspective, this tells us that jewellery was never simply about looking beautiful; it was an early form of symbolic communication.

What makes this even more fascinating is that jewellery was completely unnecessary for survival if we think logically. Someone had to find a shell, make a hole in it and carefully turn it into something wearable. And why make that effort? Simply because humans have always attached meaning to objects, using material things to express identity and enhance social connections.

Across many African societies, jewellery has functioned as a visible social language. Take beadwork, for example, which can communicate age, marital status, social position and ethnic identity.

Among the Maasai of Kenya and Tanzania, the colours or stones indicate wealth or ethnic identity, while certain materials, motifs and arrangements of beads carry special meanings; in parts of West Africa, gold jewellery has historically been associated with status, authority, and wealth.

These things may look decorative to outsiders but can work almost like a social code within the community.

We can find a similar idea among the indigenous communities of Bangladesh, although each group has its own traditions. This includes communities such as the Chakma, Marma, Garo, and Santal. Ornaments made from beads, silver, coins and locally available materials have been part of cultural identity forever.

In Mongolia, traditional jewellery has also conveyed information about the wearer’s identity and social status. Silver ornaments and pieces of coral, turquoise and other stones have been incorporated into elaborate headdresses, earrings, necklaces and clothing decorations, with styles diverse among different Mongolian groups.

Different types of colour or stones indicate wealth or ethnic identity, while certain materials and motifs were also associated with protection and spiritual beliefs.

East Asia offers another fascinating example. Traditional Chinese jade has historically been connected with virtues, protection and social status, while Korean norigae ornaments conveyed symbolic and aesthetic meanings.

In Japan, kanzashi hair ornaments could indicate the wearer’s age, social setting and occasion. The object itself signified meaning, but cultural knowledge is also important to understand.

Across Bangladesh, we see this communication take another shape in everyday life. We often see gold ornaments, bangles and especially nose rings have long been associated with marriage. The meaning depends not only on how they look but also on who wears them and what occasion they are worn for.

And lastly, there is the jewellery we choose simply because it feels like us. We might wear silver. It suits our attire, colourful beads because they reflect our personality, or a handmade statement. After all, we want something unique.

Even without knowing the cultural history behind it, our ornament choice tells people something about how we see ourselves. That is why naming jewellery merely an accessory feels incomplete.

The materials of the jewellery have changed, from shell and bones to gold and silver, gemstones and beads, but the tendency remains remarkably familiar: we decorate ourselves to communicate about ourselves.

Title: Syed Saymun Haque Nayim on reimagining denim fabric
Content:
Denim is usually associated with structure and durability, and familiar garments such as jeans, jackets, and shirts. A saree, on the other hand, depends on movement. Its fabric must fold, fall and respond naturally to the body. Bringing the two together required Syed Saymun Haque Nayim to reconsider not only the silhouette, but also the type of fabric he used.

The fashion design student at BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology is currently exploring denim through The Royal Fade, a collection that combines contemporary silhouettes with visual references from Rajasthan. At the centre of the project is a denim saree made with Tencel denim, chosen for its lighter weight, comfort and ability to drape more fluidly than conventional denim.

“I wanted to take the various denim fabrics available and modernise them a bit,” Nayim shares. “We usually see standard items being made, like regular denim pants, denim shirts and other fits such as barrel, cargo and baggy.”

Rather than repeating those established forms, he wanted to discover whether denim could take on a more ceremonial and culturally layered identity.

“I wanted to bring this into a different silhouette to make it more interesting,” he explains, “something no one in Bangladesh has done with denim yet.”

The denim saree was not simply a traditional garment recreated in a heavier fabric. Nayim conducted both local and international trend research and then studied the market to identify a material that would support the saree’s movement.

“I had to do market research for the specific fabric and materials I needed for the saree,” he says. “I used Tencel denim, which is very suitable because it drapes well, can be worn as a saree, and is a lightweight, comfortable fabric.”

His process demonstrates the balance required between innovation and wearability. An experimental silhouette may look convincing on paper, but it only succeeds as clothing when the material responds properly to the body.

The saree became part of The Royal Fade, inspired by Rajasthan’s architecture, vibrant colours, traditional prints and elaborate embellishment traditions.

“I used heavy embellishments because I was inspired by the architecture of Rajasthan, their vibrant colours, and embellishment techniques like mirror work and Zardosi,” Nayim says. “My prints were also taken from Rajasthani prints.”

The collection brings together references such as Bandhani, Leheriya, ghagras, turbans and ornate surface decoration alongside contemporary denim forms. Denim introduces associations of youth, practicality and rebellion, while the Rajasthani elements bring grandeur, colour and craftsmanship.

“That was the purpose behind choosing denim, to give it a different look,” he says. “Instead of following the usual path everyone takes, I wanted to include my own unique touch and create a collection.”

Nayim’s current practice also reflects the expanding role of technology in fashion design. He uses Adobe Illustrator to digitise inspiration, prepare silhouettes and experiment with motif placement.

He explains that a designer inspired by a tree might traditionally begin by sketching it with a pencil, developing the image into a motif and then applying it to a garment.

“But now is the generation of AI, so we are adapting to AI very well,” he clarifies. “I can take my inspiration and digitise it.”

He has also explored NewArc, an AI-supported fashion tool used to generate preliminary ideas through written prompts.

“We can get an idea by writing a prompt there,” Nayim explains. “Then there is patternmaking. What we used to do by hand, we can now do through computer-based methods. It is very accurate, and the measurements come out perfectly.”

Yet, he does not believe technology can replace every stage of fashion.

“There are some things that have been done traditionally from the beginning which technology cannot replace,” he explains, pointing to traditional handicrafts and embellishment techniques. “You cannot get the same finish with machinery.”

Draping, in particular, still requires direct engagement with fabric.

“Draping obviously has to be done by yourself,” he asserts. “In pattern software, draping does not come out as beautifully as it does manually.”

For Nayim, technology is therefore not a substitute for craftsmanship. It is a tool that can support speed, accuracy and visualisation, while handwork continues to provide texture, character and finish.

Nayim’s interest in design began in class five, when he won first place in a district-level art competition organised by Lifebuoy in Madaripur.

“My father influenced me a lot,” he recalls. “He said that since I am good at art, I should study fashion designing or fine arts.”

His mother, sister and wider family also encouraged him. Acclaimed Bangladeshi designer Lipi Khandaker belongs to his family, and seeing her work on television helped him imagine fashion as a profession. Later, the work of Sabyasachi Mukherjee, Gaurav Gupta, and Manish Malhotra expanded his creative references.

Nayim now plans to develop his work under the brand name House of Inaya. At present, he mainly uses the platform to share his projects rather than operate commercially.

“I have not started working commercially in that way yet,” he remarks. “But hopefully, I will very soon.”

His denim saree offers an early indication of that future. It asks denim to move differently, carry cultural ornamentation and enter a silhouette rarely associated with it. Through The Royal Fade, Nayim is building a practice grounded in research, technical learning and a willingness to take familiar materials somewhere unexpected.

Nayim’s exploration of Rajasthan extends beyond the denim saree into jackets, sherwanis and coordinated separates, with each garment translating a different aspect of the region’s visual heritage.

The embroidered jacket combines patchwork, Shisha mirror work, paisley and floral embroidery, while red fringes create movement and a contemporary edge. Its defining feature is the large elephant motif placed across the back.

“Historically, elephants were associated with Rajput kings and royal processions,” Nayim explains. “They were used during royal ceremonies, festivals and palace celebrations, making them one of Rajasthan’s strongest cultural symbols.”

He chose the back because it offered “the largest uninterrupted surface,” allowing the elephant to become the garment’s central statement.

The sherwani takes inspiration from Ajrakh, known for its intricate geometric and floral patterns. Nayim recreated the surface through laser printing rather than traditional block printing, describing the result as a blend of “traditional craftsmanship with modern technology.” Embroidery inspired by Hawa Mahal and Amber Fort appears near the lower front, while the deep blue palette references Jodhpur, the Blue City. Layered gold jewellery further strengthens the royal character of the look.

The dhoti skirt and blouse ensemble offers a softer, more fluid interpretation. The skirt draws from traditional Indian draping and Rajasthani block-print traditions, while the blouse uses oxidised metal ornamentation, beads, sequins and stones to evoke the elaborate jewellery worn by Rajasthani women.

“I wanted the blouse itself to appear like a piece of jewellery,” Nayim says.

Together, the pieces show how one cultural source can take multiple forms. The jacket carries symbolism, the sherwani becomes a canvas for architecture, and the skirt and blouse reinterpret textile and jewellery traditions through contemporary silhouettes.

Title: When handloom fabrics meets androgynous styling
Content:
In our collective consciousness, handloom fabrics have been associated with our strong identity since time immemorial. They powerfully represented our cultural heritage and traditions through local weaves. To that end, traditional attire such as sarees, salwar kameezes, kurtas, panjabis and such became the perfect foil for this representation.

Perhaps not always! Fashion by nature is dynamic. Fluid and alive, it must always push boundaries, break old and established rules, and make way for the new. That’s what makes fashion remarkable, meaningful as opposed to being frivolous because dressing well is anything but.

Power dressing can be addictive. Walking into a room and letting your presence speak without uttering a word is truly remarkable. To that end, women who embrace androgynous fashion are on a league of their own. They never give a damn about what others think; they dress for themselves.

Legendary fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent viewed androgyny as a way for women to feel empowered and confident in a patriarchal world. When a woman wore a suit, rather than appearing masculine, her feminine mystique and allure heightened, Laurent remarked.

It was groundbreaking in every sense of the word, especially during the ‘60s when the hyper-feminine ideal was celebrated, and women wore cinched dresses and skirts. Laurent’s models strutted in boxy pantsuits and tuxedo jackets, celebrating progressive femininity that defied gender stereotypes and preconceived beliefs.

Speaking of stereotypes, androgynous dressing, predominantly inspired by menswear, has been crafted with suiting and shirting materials like wool, silk, leather, and such. But why should it always be so? Why not craft a boxy jacket from handloom indigenous fabric such as khaadi? Imagine a striped pantsuit but made of khaadi instead!

Androgynous styling is not limited — fluid, alive and breathing, it takes on so many forms just like its wearer. So, why not style a khaadi or striped taant saree with a short jacket and a shirt? A chic little tie will be a touch masculine; maybe you could borrow your significant other’s one? And a cool belt will pull it all together, the perfect finishing touch!

How will we get through life without our favourite wide-legged trousers? Style it with a boxy blazer! The idea is to give a traditional masculine silhouette a fresh new twist by adding your own personal touch. A khaadi blazer worn with a crisp white shirt will look fantastic, and when accessorised with a bowtie made of brocade or silk, what could be more chic? Black boots will make you stand taller among your set, making cool Fall evenings magical.

And that’s the beauty of fashion. Alive, accepting and fluid, she is always open to all that’s new and makes it her own.

Androgynous styles crafted from quintessentially Bangladeshi handloom fabrics would seem like a lofty dream, but what a transcendental concept it is. And it’s time for you to make it your own!

Title: How costume and jewellery became storytellers of Patar Bashori
Content:
The ancient corridors of Panam Nagar have witnessed centuries of history, but this time with Coke Studio Bangla Season 4’s newest release, Patar Bashori , those old walls seem to sing once again.

As you watched the music video unfold, it became clear that the story was not being told through every stitch, every piece of jewellery, and every carefully crafted visual detail. Filmed in the beauty of Panam Nagar, Patar Bashori brings the abandoned city back to life through a story of love, memory, and history that continues to echo.

The story follows a young man who, while wandering near the forgotten palace, unknowingly resurrects the spirit of a princess who has waited centuries for the melody only he could sing. Their worlds collide for a fleeting moment before she disappears again, leaving behind nothing but longing.

What immediately caught my attention was how naturally the visual language mixed with the narrative. The concept, costumes, and jewellery are giving an extension of the characters themselves, which are carrying emotions in a way that words often fail to express.

For costume designer Aniqa Zaheen, the foundation of the visual storytelling began with one of Bengal’s most beloved tragic romances.

“We wanted to tell a love story of longing that travels farther than words, so we took inspiration from Mahuyar Pala, the famous tragic love story of Mohu and Nodh from Mymensingh Gitika,” she shared.

The essence moulded the entire wardrobe that allows the costumes to reflect not just history, but also the feeling of unfinished love. Instead of replicating a particular historical period, the creative team created an imagined royal world inspired by different eras.

“When director Samiur Rahman briefed me on the production design, it became clearer that we wanted to create a reference rather than follow one,” Zaheen explained.

She further added, "We created an ancient realm filled with colours and visual poetry.”

Muslin, silk, and velvet materials were used as the foundation of the wardrobe, while the silhouettes stayed unmistakably rooted in Coke Studio Bangla’s own artistic resemblance. Every fabric, cut and colour silently showed the story, allowing viewers to experience the emotion and the craftsmanship behind it.

Sunidhi Nayak’s costume becomes the emotional centrepiece of the production. “Her lehenga tells the love story of Mohuyar Pala, as I mentioned before, and it took nearly 300 hours of hand embroidery to complete,” Zaheen revealed.

Every little stitch was completed locally, reinforcing the team’s commitment to showcasing Bangladeshi craftsmanship while filming in Sonargaon’s historic Panam Nagar. The two lead characters also reflected the story through their contrasting looks.

“Sunidhi represents the lost princess, and Ishaan is a time traveller from the present who is wearing a cropped jacket with red strings connecting him to the ancient realm,” Zaheen said. She also mentioned that symbolism in costume is something that should be felt rather than translated.

The subtle contrast quietly reminds the viewers that even though the characters belong to different timelines, they remain intertwined by something far deeper than time itself.

The jewellery follows that same philosophy where it is not competing for attention but enriching the story with quiet symbolism. The jewellery designer Tanwy Kabir, the founder of the heritage-inspired brand Canvas , believes that heritage should feel alive rather than trapped behind museum glass.

“The brief was to create jewellery rooted in heritage while relevant to today’s audience. I wanted to preserve the soul of tradition instead of recreating historical ornaments exactly as they once were,” she described.

Drawing inspiration from Panam City’s architecture and traditional Bangali craftsmanship, she reimagined known motifs through a modern lens. Peacock figures, Benaroshi weaving patterns, rose motifs and architectural details all found their way into this project.

“Rather than replicating traditional ornaments, I reinterpreted these elements into lightweight, refined pieces that could move naturally with the performer while preserving the essence of Bangladeshi heritage,” she said.

One detail which beautifully ties the jewellery to its surroundings is the colour palette. The collection embraces deep reds, greens, and black and hints of blue to mirror the song’s mysterious vibe.

“The meenakari colours were inspired by the stained-glass windows of Panam Nagar, allowing architecture itself to become part of the jewellery’s storytelling,” Kabir shared.

Among all the creations, one piece holds a specific significance. “Without a doubt, the Twin Peacock hansuli represents the spirit of Patar Bashori. It brings together the traditional hasuli silhouette, peacock motifs, lotus details and handcrafted textures into one contemporary piece that honours our heritage,” she explained.

The design perfectly reflects the project’s bigger vision of allowing tradition to evolve without losing its soul.

Maybe that is what makes the song Patar Bashori linger long after the final notes fade. Beyond its heavenly melody lies an extraordinary collaboration between music, costume, jewellery and architecture. Each element carries equal weight in telling the story of Patar Bashori.

Title: A celebration of silver jewellery
Content:
A soft curtain of mist settled over the horizon. It was nearly dusk but not quite; Aparajita let out a content sigh as she leisurely witnessed the slow burn of day giving way to night from her balcony. Soon it will be time for a much-awaited music festival that has been in the works for months. Folk music artists from all over the country are coming together on one stage, and Aparajita is the chief organiser.

It’s a big night, and all eyes are going to be on her. Keeping that in mind, Aparajita chose a slinky green number that made her golden skin glisten and brown eyes pop. That aside, it’s her choice of tribal silver jewellery that truly stole the show!

An ardent lover of traditional tribal silver pieces, Aparajita has been a passionate collector for years. Scouring antique shops in Dhaka New Market, Tantibazar silver market, flea markets in Turkey, and vintage stores in neighbouring countries, she has steadily added unique pieces to her collection that are one of a kind.

A woman of discerning taste, Aparajita chooses silver pieces that are more than just jewellery. They tell a story — of her life, her choices, her past, present and future. Her collection is remarkable, from an evil eye amulet armlet from Tibet meant to ward off bad luck to a Chinese silver filigree bracelet worn by noblewomen for fertility to a headpiece with coins and charms worn on the forehead by Baloch women in Pakistan.

Generic things do not interest her at all. Her travels take her to far-flung, exotic destinations from where she finds lovely heritage pieces as well as personal ones that appeal only to collectors.

For tonight she chose a silver kaan bala worn by women of Chittagong hill tracts, and a fantastic choker with blue and pink meenakari worn by Banjaran women of Rajasthan.

On her arms she wore chunky ghungroo bangles from Lucknow, and a large statement ring from Nepal.

A wild, wanton beauty enamoured her person, her silver jewels making her shine like a true star!

Purchasing silver: What buyers need to know

Tantibazar’s name carries its past. Once associated with weavers, the area evolved as Bengal’s textile economy declined. Historical accounts trace how gold and silver entered the region through trade tied to Muslin and silk. When that system weakened, many weaving families transitioned into jewellery-making.

Buying silver jewellery in Tantibazar, like all other jewellery hubs of the city, requires attention to detail.

When asked about the silver’s current general price per bhori, a silversmith replied, “Tk 5000 or more.” But this is not a fixed number. “There are categories here.”

Purity is the first distinction.

“Hallmarked silver carries a slightly higher price tag, often Tk 130 to 150 higher” than regular rates. Lower-purity silver contains alloys, which reduce both price and durability. “The ones that have alloys, the price decreases step by step.”

Appearance is another factor. “Silver is naturally white. It will turn black after you use it for a while,” he explains. “Tarnishing is not a flaw. It is a natural reaction.”

Making charges adds another layer. These are rarely fixed. They depend on design complexity, labour, and negotiation. In a market like Tantibazar, where pricing is fluid, it responds to conversation as much as calculation!
