Title: A day trip from Dhaka: 5 places to discover in Munshiganj
Content:
Just a few hours’ drive from Dhaka’s urban tangle, Munshiganj presents itself as a significant piece of Bengal's history. This unassuming district, formerly known as Bikrampur, once thrived as the capital of kingdoms, and still bears the signs. So, if you are looking to experience the rich heritage of Bengal, Munshiganj can easily be your next pick.

Imagine arriving at a riverside fort built more than 350 years ago, where Mughal soldiers once waited (and perhaps prayed not to see any) for enemy boats to appear on the horizon.

Idrakpur Fort at Munshiganj still stands with its weathered brick ramparts that echo stories of Mughal ambition and warfare. Its battle days are long gone; even the waterbody beside it has dried up. However, step through its arched gateways and the past seems to stir. While running your eyes along the timeworn brickwork, it is easy to imagine boats cutting through the river as soldiers kept watch from the fort.

In the golden hour, when sunlight spills across the aged, rustic walls, shadows gather beneath the arches, and the nearby pond glows beyond the monument; every corner offers a new frame, maybe even a glimpse into the centuries that came before.

Tucked away in the old town of Munshiganj, Baba Adam's Mosque might not really entice you the moment you hear its name. But built in 1483 during the Sultanate era, this modest structure predates the Mughals, making it one of the oldest surviving mosques in Bangladesh and a rare, tangible link to a nearly forgotten chapter of Bengal's Islamic architecture.

When you step inside, you are met with a sense of peaceful seclusion. There is a stunning ceiling adorned with six intricately designed domes. The graceful curves and terracotta detailing showcase craftsmanship that has withstood over five centuries of monsoons and changing empires. Legends associate the mosque with a Sufi saint, whose story has become intertwined with this site.

At first glance, this structure may not seem extraordinary at all. It stretches just 53 meters long and features a pointed central arch flanked by two smaller arches. It consists of worn bricks, sturdy octagonal pilasters, and craftsmanship that reflects a bygone era.

You might consider taking a ride through the water beneath the crossing, allowing the boat to carry you toward this historical structure. As you glide past, look up to appreciate the central arch overhead, a view that can easily be underestimated from the shore, yet is surprisingly exhilarating when you are directly underneath it.

What makes this bridge truly fascinating is that it was never intended to be an imperial showpiece. Instead, it served a practical purpose, connecting communities and facilitating daily life across the waterways of Mughal Bengal. Now, it feels surreal to stand over a canal that once rippled beneath the feet of generations of people.

Standing side by side on a single raised masonry platform in the picturesque village of Sonarang, the Twin Temples rise like monuments from folklore, their soaring towers reflected in the moat that wraps around three sides of the ground beneath them. These structures wear their age with striking grace; their walls bear elaborate plaster ornamentation, and the smaller temple features rows of snake heads coiling around every side.

Locals will tell you, partially joking, that the sikharas hide secret treasure chambers guarded by serpents so numerous they could "devour the whole country" if ever released.

Whether you come for the architecture, the eerie story, or simply the sight of two temples mirrored in still water, Sonarang has a way of pulling you in and refusing to let go until you have wandered around it at least twice with a camera in hand.

In the serene village of Nateshwar in Tongibari, an entire Buddhist city has been buried beneath the soil for nearly a thousand years. This ancient city features pyramid-shaped stupas, wide ceremonial walkways, prayer halls, and mandaps, which archaeologists have only begun to uncover since excavations started around 2010.

Walking through the excavated grounds today, amid the eight-sided stupas and the faint outlines of ancient homes, feels like eavesdropping on a civilisation that traded, worshipped, and constructed in brick and clay long before modern cities came into existence, standing here, watching this thousand-year-old city slowly re-emerge from the earth, it is hard not to feel as though you are witnessing history being rewritten in real time.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: A guide to post-travel recovery: Coming home after the adventure
Content:
For those who are fluent in travel and have been trotting from one place to another, have you ever noticed the difference between travelling in your younger years and travelling now? If the answer is yes, then it is safe to presume that you might have felt like taking some time off between your travel and getting back to your daily routine.

Millennials called it post-travel depression; the younger crowd of today rebranded it as post-travel recovery. While it is true that we millennials only gave a term to the problem without seeking an answer for it, the new-age travellers had the bluntness to actually address the issue. Unbeknownst to me, I had already gone through the process of travel recovery after my last adventure.

First, let’s zero in on the symptoms of post-travel depression you face after a trip. Right after you land or reach the bus station back home, a wave of anxiety sprinkled with a pinch of emptiness falls on you. The idea of going back to work and facing your boss is nothing less than hearing fingernails scratching the blackboard. During every tea or smoke break, you question your life decisions while reminiscing about your fond experiences.

If you are resonating with the paragraphs above, then the following suggestions are for you!

Planning the timeline of your trips is the first mountain you must climb. Most people usually plan their trips according to the number of leave days they can manage. If you somehow get four days off, you travel for four days. If it is five, you try to squeeze every bit of travelling out of those five days. I used to do the same.

The problem starts when your bus reaches Dhaka at 6 in the morning, and you have office at 9.

At that point, whatever peace you managed to collect from the mountains, sea or wherever you travelled to disappears somewhere between Gabtoli and Karwan Bazar.

So, if possible, keep one day empty after coming back. I know that sounds almost criminal when you have limited annual leave, especially in Bangladesh, where getting a decent stretch of leave itself can sometimes feel like negotiating a peace treaty. But that one day makes a massive difference.

Do not make plans for it either.

Come home. Take a shower. Sleep. Unpack whenever you feel like it. Eat normal home food. Lie around. Go through the pictures. Maybe meet no one. Basically, allow yourself to become boring again.

This was something I did after my last trip without even realising that people now have a term for it.

Another thing that helps is fixing your sleep before going back to work. Trips have a way of destroying whatever sleep cycle you had. You stay awake talking until 3 AM, wake up at 6 AM to catch a sunrise, spend eight hours on a bus and somehow convince yourself that this is fun. It is fun, of course. Until Monday arrives.

If you are coming back from somewhere far, particularly after a long overnight bus journey, do not underestimate how physically tired you actually are. Sometimes what feels like sadness is simply exhaustion mixed with the sudden realisation that tomorrow you have countless unread emails.

There is another trick I have started appreciating. Do not immediately start hating your regular life.

This sounds obvious, but after a good trip, everything at home suddenly feels dull. The road you were travelling through two days ago had mountains on both sides. Now you are staring at the same traffic signal in Mohakhali for 25 minutes. It is not exactly a fair comparison.

Instead, bring something back with you from the trip. And I do not mean a fridge magnet.

Maybe start walking more because you enjoyed walking there. Maybe keep your phone away for an hour in the evening because you realised how little you needed it during the trip. Cook something you ate there. Call the people you travelled with. Go through the photos together and laugh at the ones that will never make it to Instagram.

Most importantly, give the trip an ending.

For me, that is probably what post-travel recovery really is. It is not about getting over a place or forcing yourself to be happy about returning to work. It is simply giving your mind enough time to understand that the trip is over and normal life has started again.

And normal life is not necessarily the enemy.

It is also the thing that eventually pays for the next trip.
Author: K Tanzeel Zaman K Tanzeel Zaman

Title: Bangladesh to Antarctica: Planning the journey to the end of the world
Content:
Some places exist in the imagination long before they exist on a map of one's own journey. For years, Antarctica was one such place for me: a distant world of ice, silence, and immense wilderness that seemed almost impossible to reach. Making a dream a reality, however, was not a matter of simply booking a flight. An Antarctic expedition requires months of preparation, careful financial planning, multiple international connections, visas, specialised clothing and a willingness to accept that, once the journey begins, nature — not the traveller — sets the schedule.

The journey began in Ushuaia, Argentina. There is no direct route, and the journey normally involves a long-haul flight from Dhaka to Buenos Aires through an international transit hub such as Istanbul, Doha or Addis Ababa, followed by a domestic flight to Ushuaia.

For us, preparations began nearly a year earlier. The first challenge was deciding which expedition to take. Antarctica can be visited through a range of operators and itineraries, from relatively short voyages to extended expeditions covering several destinations across the Southern Ocean.

The choice of operator matters, but the itinerary matters just as much. A traveller interested only in seeing Antarctica may choose a shorter Antarctic Peninsula expedition. Those looking for a broader experience can choose longer voyages incorporating the Falkland Islands and South Georgia.

Antarctica is expensive before you even see the ice

Antarctica is among the world's most expensive travel destinations, largely because reaching it requires specialised expedition vessels, complex logistics and access to one of the most remote environments on Earth.

Expedition fares can begin at around $8,000, while longer itineraries and higher cabin categories can push the cost considerably higher.

But the advertised expedition fare is only the beginning.

For a Bangladeshi traveller, the actual budget must also account for flights to Argentina, domestic flights, visas, hotels, travel insurance, meals before and after the expedition, local transportation, thermal clothing, waterproof gear and other equipment. The total expenditure can reach around Tk 15–25 lakh or more per person! Longer voyages that include the Falkland Islands and South Georgia naturally cost more than shorter Antarctic Peninsula trips.

Argentina is a key part of the journey because Ushuaia serves as the gateway for many Antarctic expeditions. Visa requirements, supporting documents, financial records, accommodation information and travel plans all need to be considered carefully.

The Argentine Embassy in Dhaka is working and issues tourist visas to Bangladeshi citizens.

To start the process, applicants need to send an email to the Consular Section explaining why they want to visit Argentina. The embassy will then reply with the next steps and required documents. The visa process must be initiated by the traveller personally; no agency can apply for the visa on behalf of the applicant, although agencies can provide guidance and help with preparing the documents.

Visa arrangements should ideally be planned alongside the expedition booking rather than afterwards.

Flights require similar attention. It is unwise to schedule for arrival in Ushuaia just hours before an expedition departure. A missed connection or delayed flight could mean missing a ship that cannot wait for a passenger.

The Antarctic expedition season normally begins in late October or November and continues until March, during the Southern Hemisphere’s summer. Each month offers a different experience.

November is ideal for pristine snow, dramatic sea ice and seeing penguins returning to their breeding grounds and beginning courtship. December brings longer daylight, retreating sea ice and the first penguin chicks, while wildlife activity increases across the region.

January and February are my recommended months for a first Antarctic expedition, particularly for those who want to see penguin chicks and experience relatively favourable conditions.

By late February and March, the number of whales increases significantly, making this one of the best periods for whale watching, while penguin chicks become older and begin preparing to leave the colonies.

Thermal base layers, insulating clothing, waterproof outerwear, gloves, warm socks, a hat and suitable waterproof footwear are essential. Waterproof protection becomes particularly important.

Photography equipment needs its own preparation. Cameras and lenses must be protected from water, spray and cold, while batteries can drain faster in low temperatures.

The expedition operator's equipment list should always be checked before buying specialised gear. Some operators provide certain items, while others expect passengers to bring their own.

Physical preparation is also important, although Antarctica does not require an athlete's fitness level. Travellers should be comfortable walking on uneven ground, climbing into and out of Zodiac boats and spending time outdoors in cold and windy conditions.

A shorter voyage focused on the Antarctic Peninsula can provide an unforgettable introduction to the continent at a comparatively lower cost. But a longer voyage can offer something much more comprehensive.

Our 20-day expedition showed the difference clearly.

The Falkland Islands offered rugged coastlines and remarkable birdlife. South Georgia brought enormous concentrations of penguins and seals. Antarctica delivered the vast ice landscapes, glaciers, mountains and iconic polar wildlife.

The additional time was expensive, but it transformed the journey from a visit to Antarctica into a much broader exploration of the Southern Ocean.

There is no easy way to make a visit more affordable. But it is not an ordinary tourist destination.

The journey is demanding precisely because the destination is so remote.

After travelling for days across oceans, standing among icebergs and penguins creates a feeling that is difficult to replicate anywhere else. Modern life seems to disappear. There are no crowded streets, familiar sounds or constant digital distractions—only mountains, ice, ocean, wind and wildlife.

For anyone in Bangladesh dreaming of making the journey, the most important advice is simple: start planning early. Research the expedition operators. Compare itineraries. Calculate the entire cost rather than just the cruise fare. Begin visa preparations well in advance. Allow flexibility in your flights. Invest in proper clothing and insurance. And be prepared to accept that Antarctica will always have the final word.
Author: N Nilay Kumar Biswas Nilay Kumar Biswas

Title: Budget-friendly getaways your parents will love
Content:
At some point in life, even the most adventurous spirits find themselves having to slow down to prioritise their families. The trips they planned to take get postponed in between holding hands to school every day, staying up through fevers, and working late to save just enough for a secure future, and before they know it, time slips away.

Here is a guide with spot-on insights that would help you plan the perfect getaway for your favourite grown-ups without breaking a sweat, whether you tag along with them or not.

When it comes to budget-friendly, slow-paced vacations, Cox’s Bazar tops the list without a doubt. If you have been working a few years to save up for a trip within Bangladesh, this is one of the best places to start.

People with graceful salt-and-pepper hair do not want an itinerary packed with breathtaking adventures. Instead, they seek a tranquil spot where they can sit quietly by the beach (perhaps reminiscing about their honeymoon) and watch the waves as long as they want, feeling the sand and water cascading beneath their feet.

Reaching Cox’s Bazar is relatively hassle-free as well. You can book them flights for a quicker journey, or you can opt for the train and book a cabin if they hate the highway traffic but want to enjoy the scenic view. The food options are excellent. Whether they crave daal-bhaat or want to try the range of seafood, Cox’s Bazar has it all.

Bandarban is like the slightly adventurous child, yet it knows how to please the parents. If your folks are in their mid-fifties, they might not mind a little walk, but then again, they would not be glad if you arranged an episode of Man vs. Wild. So, places like Nilgiri, Meghla, and surrounding viewpoints are the finest, as they can be reached by transport through the hills, winding roads, and clouds hanging over the lush green landscape.

The food holds up its end too, from steaming bowls of bamboo-cooked dishes to familiar Bangladeshi favourites made with fresh, local ingredients.

Travelling from Dhaka to Bandarban typically takes seven to nine hours. Night buses, particularly sleeper coaches, provide a convenient option as they can travel overnight and arrive in the morning.

Got a promotion and want to plan something international? Put Nepal on the list.

The ancient maze-like streets of Kathmandu, the Annapurna Mountain Range visible from Pokhara, the massive Buddha stupa, surrounded by the temples adorned with prayer flags, create a sense of calm that people often miss amid the hustle and bustle of Dhaka.

The country will allow you to build a trip around the comfort of your Ma and Baba that includes scenic drives, peaceful lakeside evenings, beautiful hotels, cosy cafes, temples, and mouth-watering momos.

Thailand is an obvious name in this list, even if it asks for a slightly bigger budget. However, it offers stunning beaches, shopping malls, and not to mention delicious food. Your parents would love to go sightseeing in the morning, find a nice café in the afternoon, and hop the markets at night, as relaxing as it can get. If Bangkok feels like a city with its volume pumped up to maximum, then opt for Chiang Mai. Nestled in northern Thailand, it has a slower and more peaceful rhythm, surrounded by beautiful waterfalls, gardens, and breathtaking mountain viewpoints.

If your parents grimace at the mention of health checkups, this is your time to shoot your shot. The country has several internationally recognised hospitals with comprehensive health-screening packages, so you can schedule a routine check-up for them, get basic tests done, and have a doctor consultation during the stay. It is very sneaky, but effective.

Before you narrow your eyes at Turkey because you feel it is expensive and question its position on the list, then lo and behold, it is not exactly.

While the per-day cost here can vary depending on your chosen level of luxury, Turkey is considered one of the most “worth every penny” countries in Europe.

Turkish food certainly deserves a shout-out. The charred, juicy lamb kebabs, and gozleme stuffed with cheese definitely have to be on your menu. However, just when you think you are done, baklava appears on the table. Crisp golden layers soaked in syrup and topped with nuts make you feel there is a separate room dedicated to desserts. Another interesting aspect of Turkey is its chocolate boutiques. You can sample the chocolates for free and choose your favourites (spoiler alert: you might want to grab them all!).

If any of your parents is not into food that much and rather enjoys the historical relics, you need to take them to visit the Blue Mosque.

Topkapi Palace has to be on the list as well. It was the administrative centre of the Ottoman Empire for 400 years and was also the home of the sultans.
Author: K K T Humaira K T Humaira

Title: Salahuddin Sumon and stories a map cannot tell
Content:
Before travel reels took over our screens, the bug of exploring the world had already bitten me. During long, chaotic commutes across Dhaka, I often daydreamed about telling stories from my travels through a camera.

A decade later, much has changed, including me. However, daydreaming remains my refuge. I have travelled quite a bit over the years, sure, but never made an honest attempt to tell the stories I wanted to share.

One evening after work, I visited my parents. After the usual pleasantries, they returned to their seats and resumed watching television.

Naturally, I asked what they were watching.

“We’ve been watching Salahuddin Sumon’s travel vlogs,” my mother replied gleefully. “He was a journalist before he started telling stories about places he finds interesting.”

Their excitement encouraged me to sit down and watch. It did not take long to realise that Sumon was doing what I had been longing to do for years.

When I finally spoke to Sumon, I expected us to begin with Antarctica, the Amazon, or one of those forgotten corners of Bangladesh that most of us know only after he points a camera at it. Instead, we began with time, or the lack of it!

In television journalism, he told me, seven days of reporting might eventually become a story of two minutes. On his own channel, that wall is gone. Yet, freedom does not mean throwing everything at the audience.

“I do not want to waste even one second of a viewer’s time by including something that does not need to be there,” he said.

That line stayed with me. Sumon might have forty minutes of material and still cut it to thirty. He looks at his work as a creator, then sits in what he calls the viewer’s chair. The old newsroom instinct remains, even without the stopwatch.

It also explains why people like my parents remain invested. He does not simply show them a road, an old building, or a grave. He gives the place a human face.

When Sumon planned to combine travel with history, a colleague warned that nobody would watch. His work on the descendants of Mir Jafar proved otherwise. Dates can feel distant, even when they belong to our own past. Put a living person connected to that history on camera and the old story comes close. Not simpler, necessarily, but alive.

Fame has made natural moments harder to capture.

Once, Sumon could enter a village unknown, and people behaved normally. Now his arrival can become an event. Recognition feels good to him as a person, he said, but “from the perspective of a creator, however, it can feel unfortunate”.

So, he does not announce where he is going or call a crowd in advance. He does not want to create excitement first and present it as reality.

There is adventure in his stories, of course, but he does not perform fearlessness. In the Amazon, animal calls once frightened him enough to phone his travelling companion Niloy and ask him to come over.

“On another night, our guide took us out in a small boat. We could see what looked like countless fireflies. But the guide corrected us by pointing out that those were reflected eyes of crocodiles. Sitting in such a small boat, I kept thinking that a crocodile could overturn it,” he said plainly.

The Drake Passage was kinder than expected. Then, in Brazil, his iPhone was stolen along with footage from Antarctica and a day in the Amazon.

“It was a nightmare. To go through that ordeal and capture the famous Drake Passage, gone,” he said.

Our conversation became more uncomfortable when it turned towards Bangladesh.

During the Antarctica expedition, a German passenger asked how people from a poor country like ours could afford to be there. Instead of anger, Sumon considered the limited picture many foreigners carry of us. He does not deny our poverty, nor accept it as the only honest image.

“I am not ashamed that my country has less money. Poverty itself is not shameful. I explained that Bangladesh is not economically equal to the world’s wealthiest countries. However, that is not the whole picture. We have land that produces food, abundant water, fish and agriculture. Some wealthier countries have money but very little capacity to produce their own food. Prosperity can be understood from more than one angle,” he said.

He was sharper about Bangladeshis who misuse tourist visas. Their actions, he argued, place suspicion on everybody holding the same passport.

He expressed his dismay, “What embarrasses me is behaviour that damages the reputation of every Bangladeshi traveller.

“Some people enter another country on a tourist visa and then disappear or overstay.

Immigration officers consequently look at all of us with suspicion. They may assume that a Bangladeshi visitor has no intention of returning home. That is humiliating.”

It is uncomfortable to hear, but a national image is shaped by how we behave when nobody back home is watching.

Sumon is equally uneasy about his own influence.

A palm-lined road in Niamatpur, Naogaon, became a tourist attraction after his video. Years later, stalls had started to cover the view people came to see. He understands why locals want to earn, but unmanaged attention can consume a place.

Creators can warn people, he said, but local authorities must decide where shops go, how waste is handled, and what must remain protected. The answer included his responsibility without casting him as a saviour.

The same caution guides the sponsors he accepts. He avoids promotions involving overseas recruitment, student placement, certain real-estate schemes, and health products where a trusted face might lead someone into serious trouble.

“Trust matters more than the size of the fee,” he said.

It sounds obvious. In practice, especially in our corner of the internet, it is a position that costs money.

Near the end, Sumon spoke about Indonesia’s remote islands. His curiosity remains attached to people, history and how life continues somewhere unfamiliar.

The interview did not magically turn me into the storyteller I have spent years imagining during Dhaka traffic. However, it made my excuses feel smaller.

Sumon reminded me that a story is not hiding at the farthest edge of the map. It begins when we notice the people inside a place and care about what remains after the camera leaves.

Title: What to eat when you have dengue: Three stages of recovery
Content:
Dengue, a mosquito-borne infectious disease, is caused by the virus DENV. Symptoms typically begin 3 to 14 days after infection and may include high fever, headache, vomiting, muscle pain and joint ache, and a characteristic skin rash. At the onset of the symptoms, it is vital to boost the patient's immunity by giving him/her food that is loaded with essential nutrients and vitamins.

In Stage 1 nutritional treatment of the patient, liquid food is recommended, as it is comparatively more easily tolerated than solid food. Frequent intake of fluids, in small portions, can help to replace the fluids lost, and also bring down body temperature.

As patients start to recover from dengue, Stage 2 nutritional treatment may commence in the form of easily digestible foods, like gooey khichuri, curd and rice, porridge, boiled potatoes, boiled vegetables like papaya, pumpkin, green peas, etc.

One can use lemon juice or herbs to enhance the flavour.

Along with the soft diet, drinking plenty of fluids like fresh juice, soups, and coconut water is necessary. This helps to maintain the water and electrolyte balance of the body. Fruits help too — ripe banana, ripe papaya, and watermelon.

And finally, Stage 3 involves returning to a normal, nutritious diet following recovery from dengue.

Keeping one hydrated by replenishing lost water

Dengue fever generally results in severe dehydration. Coconut water is immensely beneficial to fight this; it is a rehydrating drink and is loaded with electrolytes and vital nutrients. Lemon water is a very good source of vitamin C; it detoxifies the body. In many cases, ginger water is also suggested, since it helps to fight nausea that many dengue patients experience. Sometimes, oral rehydration solution (ORS) is suggested to hydrate the body. It supplies vital potassium to the body.

Boosting the platelet count

Broccoli is an excellent source of Vitamin K, which helps to regenerate blood platelets. If there's a sharp decline in the platelet count, then broccoli should be included in the daily diet. It is rich in antioxidants and minerals.

Spinach is a rich source of iron, vitamin K, potassium and phytonutrients that strengthen the immune system. It is also an effective way to increase the platelet count.

Pomegranate — the bright red wonder fruit is rich in essential nutrients and minerals that provide the body with required energy and reduce the feeling of exhaustion and fatigue. Being a rich source of iron, pomegranate stands out as quite beneficial for maintaining/increasing blood count.

Papaya leaf is not very popular in our diet, but it has healing properties. Rich in enzymes like papain and chymopapain, it aids in digestion, prevents bloating and other digestive disorders. Many researchers have found that papaya leaves play a crucial role in fighting dengue, especially by improving the platelet count. Replacing cow's milk with goat milk is also considered beneficial.

Turmeric is an antiseptic and metabolism booster. Consumption of turmeric with milk helps in faster recovery from dengue fever. Fenugreek, known as methi, helps induce sleep and acts like a mild tranquiliser that aids in easing pain. It is also known to stabilise high fever.

Black grape is a fruit rich in antioxidants and helpful for blood formation. Guava is effective in increasing platelet count.

Beetroot soup contains a very high amount of water, vitamins (B9, Vitamin C), and minerals (manganese, potassium, iron); these are very helpful in increasing the RBC count. Tomato soup is also rich in vitamin C and potassium.

Oily, spicy and fried foods, along with processed foods, must be avoided at all costs. They can cause acid to accumulate in the stomach, lower the pH level, which may lead to ulcers and damage the walls of the intestine.

Caffeinated beverages — as they rapidly increase the heart rate, cause fatigue and muscle breakdown. They also dehydrate our body.

Title: The foods that may help your body fight inflammation
Content:
We have done keto, paleo, and intermittent fasting. We have sworn by them and given up on them in turn. However, the diet in question here is less about losing weight and more about reducing inflammation. Here’s why —

Chronic inflammation in the body is a central driver of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and other illnesses. Thankfully, certain diets endorsed by the movers and shakers of the research world can help the gut microbiome mediate better between the food we eat and inflammation, reducing the risk of non-communicable diseases and even responding better to cancer treatments.

Research shows that diets that incorporate fruits such as apples and avocados, carrots and leafy green vegetables, whole grains, oily fish, olive oil, and moderate dairy are consistently tied to lower inflammation, a reduced risk of non-communicable diseases and even mental health disorders.

Interestingly, the diet described is very close to the Mediterranean diet, which includes variants such as DASH and MIND that offer still more benefits for blood pressure and brain health.

However, there is a snag in the stocking. One must be mindful of not only what is being eaten, but how much of it is eaten, how it is being prepared, and what it is being combined with. Experts suggest at least 50 grams of fibre-rich food per day, paired with proper hydration. That might look like a cup of black beans, a cup of raspberries, and a medium apple with skin.

Now, let’s talk combinations. Research suggests that nutrients work differently when consumed together and in different food matrices: tomatoes, for example, work better at reducing inflammation when paired with avocadoes and cheese; a baked potato is best friends with your immunity, whereas a French fry is possibly one of the worst things to ever happen to it.

Diets that are high in ultra-processed foods, red meat, and saturated fats lead the partaker to far greater risks of heart attacks, cancer, depression, and death than other types of foods. By literal calculation, that would mean that each 100-gram increase in such foods raises C-reactive protein (one of the bad guys) by almost 4 per cent.

Fibre, on the flipside, is linked to better responses in cancer treatments, with an additional 5 grams daily lowering progression or the risk of death by nearly 30 per cent. Fermented foods are even better for the body, boosting microbiome diversity in the gut to alleviate suffering of a serious nature.

While research will shed more light on the best food combinations to enable the best environment for our bodies, evidence thus far supports a fibre-rich diet with both hands up, backs whole foods as opposed to supplements and also gives a major thumbs down to processed food.
Author: M Munira Fidai Munira Fidai

Title: Pregnancy after 35: Separating facts from fear
Content:
More women today are choosing to start or grow their families later in life. Whether it’s because of higher education, career goals, financial stability, or simply waiting for the right time, pregnancy after 35 has become increasingly common. Yet, despite advances in healthcare, many women still find themselves met with a term that can sound intimidating: advanced maternal age.

While the phrase may raise concerns, experts stress that it is not a diagnosis but simply a medical classification used to ensure mothers receive appropriate care and monitoring throughout their pregnancy.

Dr Aklima Zakaria Zinan, is an Assistant Professor, Gynaecology and Obstetrics, at Bangladesh Medical College Hospital.

She says, “As we women age, we go through multitudes of changes in our body. As such, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists have set the benchmark for advanced maternal age pregnancy to be from 35 onwards.”

Any pregnancy at the age of 35 or above is considered a pregnancy at advanced maternal age. Pregnancy after the age of 45, previously referred to as a “ geriatric pregnancy,” is now more appropriately described as a pregnancy at very “advanced maternal age.” The shift in terminology reflects a more respectful and medically accurate approach while acknowledging that many women are having healthy pregnancies later in life.

Age, however, does bring about natural biological changes. As the quality and number of a woman’s eggs decline over time, the chances of certain pregnancy-related complications gradually increase. This is why doctors recommend closer monitoring rather than assuming something will go wrong.

One of the most significant concerns is miscarriage. The risk naturally rises after the age of 35, and according to Zinan, it increases dramatically after the age of 45, when the miscarriage rate can reach as high as 53 per cent.

Other complications that may occur more frequently include pregnancy diabetes or gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), high blood pressure during pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), where the baby is smaller than expected for its gestational age, and premature birth.

These conditions do not affect every woman over 35, but they are common enough that healthcare providers recommend more frequent antenatal check-ups and screenings.

Still, advanced maternal age should not be viewed as a prediction of an unhealthy pregnancy.

Many women in their late 30s and early 40s go on to have uncomplicated pregnancies and deliver healthy babies. Overall health, existing medical conditions, access to prenatal care, and lifestyle choices often play just as important a role as age itself.

Preparing the body before conception can make a meaningful difference, particularly when it comes to nutrition.

Dr Zinan emphasises that maintaining a balanced diet is one of the most important steps women can take before and during pregnancy.

A diet rich in protein, healthy fats, fruits, and vegetables provides essential nutrients for both mother and baby. At the same time, she advises reducing sugar intake, not only from sweets but also from sugary drinks, and limiting frequent consumption of “junk food,” which can increase the risk of complications such as gestational diabetes.

Lifestyle habits extend beyond what’s on the plate.

Sleep, for example, is often overlooked despite its significant role in maternal health. Pregnancy can already make restful sleep difficult, and women in their late 30s or 40s, especially those balancing demanding careers and family responsibilities, may struggle even more with maintaining a regular sleep routine.

“Often easy, pregnancy-friendly exercise or even a 30-minute walk can help to relax the body and mind, ensuring a good night’s sleep,” says Dr Zinan.

She adds that regular physical activity during pregnancy offers benefits beyond better rest. It supports healthy blood circulation to the baby, may lower the risk of developing high blood pressure, and can even increase the chances of having a vaginal delivery, provided there are no medical contradictions.

Mental well-being is equally important. The emotional pressures surrounding pregnancy after 35, from societal expectations to fears about the so-called “biological clock,” can leave many women feeling anxious before they even conceive. Managing stress through adequate rest, light physical activity, supportive relationships, and regular communication with healthcare providers can contribute to a healthier pregnancy experience.

Women planning to conceive after 35 should also schedule a preconception consultation with a gynaecologist. This allows doctors to evaluate their overall health, identify any underlying medical conditions, and discuss necessary investigations before pregnancy.

Vaccinations are another important part of preparation. Rather than recommending the same vaccines for every woman, Dr Aklima Zakaria Zinan explains that vaccination plans should be tailored to individual needs. Depending on a woman’s medical history, immunity, and test results, a gynaecologist may recommend specific vaccines before conception to help protect both mother and baby during pregnancy.

Ultimately, advanced maternal age is not a reason to lose hope. It is a reminder to approach pregnancy with informed planning, healthy lifestyle choices, and regular medical care. With today’s medical advancements and early prenatal monitoring, women over 35 have more support than ever before in navigating pregnancy safely.

Growing older may change the journey to motherhood, but it does not diminish the possibility of a healthy pregnancy or a healthy baby. With the right care and guidance, age becomes just one part of the story but never the whole story.

Title: Why psychological safety at work matters more than ever
Content:
By all accounts, the COVID-19 pandemic changed us. Even as life has largely returned to normal, many of us continue to carry the invisible after-effects of an experience that was, in many ways, unprecedented. We collectively lived through uncertainty, isolation and fear. While some have emerged relatively unscathed, others continue to navigate lingering anxiety, burnout, and mental health challenges that have become woven into the fabric of everyday life.

I’m not a psychologist, nor do I claim expertise in clinical mental health. My perspective comes from working in organisational culture and development, where much of my work involves observing how people experience workplaces, teams, leadership and change. Over the years, and particularly since the pandemic, I have noticed one theme emerge repeatedly: people perform at their best when they feel psychologically safe.

The concept of psychological safety is no longer a niche conversation reserved for wellbeing specialists. Across the world, health and safety legislation is evolving to recognise that employee wellbeing extends far beyond physical hazards. Organisations are increasingly being called upon to create environments where people feel supported, respected, and able to bring their authentic selves to work.

This shift matters because work occupies a significant portion of our lives. The quality of our workplace experiences inevitably influences our families, relationships, communities, and overall sense of well-being.

For leaders, people professionals, and anyone who has the ability to influence workplace culture, the question becomes: what can we do today to help create safer, healthier environments for the people around us?

From my observations and experience, a few practical approaches stand out.

Most workplaces have fire wardens and first aid officers. These roles exist because we recognise that emergencies can happen unexpectedly and that immediate support matters.

Why should mental health be any different? Training a group of employees as Mental Health First Aid responders can provide an invaluable first point of contact for colleagues who may be struggling. These individuals are not therapists, nor are they expected to solve complex problems. Rather, they serve as trusted people who can recognise signs of distress, listen without judgement, and guide colleagues towards appropriate support services.

In a city like Dhaka, where daily life often comes with significant pressures, from traffic congestion to economic demands and family responsibilities, the need for accessible support within workplaces is perhaps more relevant than ever.

Many of us grew up in communities where support was readily available.

There was always a neighbour to visit, a local tea stall where conversations unfolded naturally, or a familiar face who noticed when something was not quite right. While modern urban living has brought countless opportunities, it has also introduced a level of isolation that previous generations rarely experienced.

Today, despite being more connected digitally, many people report feeling profoundly alone.

Workplaces have an opportunity to help bridge this gap by creating peer support networks. These do not need to consist of trained professionals. Instead, they can be groups of trusted colleagues who volunteer to be confidential listeners and sources of encouragement.

One of the unique benefits of workplace peer support is context. Colleagues often understand the pressures, challenges, and dynamics contributing to someone's stress. Sometimes, having a compassionate person who understands your environment can make all the difference between feeling overwhelmed and feeling supported.

One of the hidden costs of modern city living is the gradual erosion of community.

In our pursuit of independence, efficiency, and productivity, we sometimes overlook a fundamental truth: human beings are wired for connection. Throughout history, our survival depended on belonging to groups.

Yet, many of us now move between home and work in relative isolation. Even within households, technology and busy schedules can create invisible walls.

This is where workplaces can play a surprisingly powerful role.

Family days, team lunches, cultural celebrations, volunteer activities, and social gatherings may sometimes be dismissed as "nice-to-have" initiatives. In reality, they can serve a much deeper purpose. They help foster belonging and remind people that they are part of something larger than themselves.

For those team members who have relocated or migrated to Dhaka for work, away from family or support networks, these connections can be particularly meaningful.

You may work within a large multinational organisation, but every team has the potential to become a small community. Leaders who intentionally create opportunities for connection often discover that trust, collaboration, and well-being improve alongside performance.

Physical health has long been part of workplace conversations. Mental well-being deserves the same level of openness.

We live in a world that rarely slows down. Many of us spend our days indoors, disconnected from nature, juggling competing demands with little opportunity to pause and reset. Under these conditions, proactively looking after our mental health becomes essential.

Education remains one of the most effective tools available. Organisations can invite mental health professionals to facilitate workshops, provide wellbeing resources, and encourage conversations that challenge outdated stigmas.

Just as importantly, leaders can model vulnerability by speaking openly about stress management, self-care, and seeking support when needed.

The more normal these conversations become, the easier it becomes for people to reach out before challenges escalate into crises.

One of the most rewarding aspects of working in people-focused professions is recognising that our impact rarely stops with the individual sitting in front of us.

When we support one employee, we often support their family. When we help create a healthier workplace, we contribute to a healthier community.

The effects may not always be visible immediately. They rarely make headlines and often go unnoticed. Yet, every colleague who feels heard, every employee who receives support during a difficult period, and every team that experiences a greater sense of belonging creates a ripple effect that extends far beyond office walls.

The next time you open the news and find yourself overwhelmed by another troubling headline, feeling as though there is little you can do to change the world around you, remember that meaningful change is often built through small, consistent acts of care.

Creating a psychologically safe workplace may not earn you a gallantry medal, and there may never be public recognition for the effort. But you can sleep a little better at night knowing that you have done your bit. In ways both seen and unseen, you have helped make someone's day, someone's family, and perhaps even someone's future a little better.

And sometimes, that is exactly how the world changes.
Author: N Naaz Fahmida Naaz Fahmida

Title: Your favourite snacks may be loaded with hidden salt
Content:
We often think of salt simply as the ingredient that brings life to our meals. However, reducing salt in our diet is one of the most vital steps we can take for our long-term health.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), globally, high salt intake is a major health risk, linked to nearly 1.7 million deaths every year.

Most of us do not realise how much salt we are actually eating. It is not just the pinch we add to our rice. It is the hidden sodium in almost everything we buy from the grocery store.

To help us understand these risks, Dr Chowdhury Tasneem Hasin, Chief Clinical Dietitian and HOD of the Dietetics and Nutrition department at the Continental Hospital PLC, clarified firmly that a healthy adult should strictly stay within the 4–5-gram range of salt daily.

This balance is crucial for maintaining a healthy heart and stable blood pressure. However, for those already battling high blood pressure, the rules change significantly.

"For hypertensive patients, the intake should be even lower, bringing it down to 2 to 2.5 grams daily," Dr Hasin suggested hopefully. She believes that even small reductions in the kitchen can lead to massive improvements in heart health over time.

The modern diet relies heavily on processed convenience. These products are often marketed as quick fixes, but they carry a heavy sodium price tag.

This leaves no room for salt in our regular meals, like lentils or curry. Dr Hasin pointed out the deceptive nature of the snacks we crave.

She advised urgently that it is vital to read the nutritional labelling on every packet. Many consumers buy these items without ever checking the salt content listed in fine print.

Regrettably, she also mentioned that many local manufacturers in Bangladesh do not follow strict labelling standards. This makes it incredibly difficult for a common person to track their intake. We often eat hidden salt without even knowing it exists in our favourite sweet biscuits or bread.

The risk is no longer confined to the elderly. A new wave of health issues is crashing into young adults aged between 25 and 35. This age group is the primary consumer of street food and processed snacks.

Young adults are appreciating processed foods more than traditional meals. This shift in palette is leading to uncontrolled hypertension in people who should be at their physical peak. The biological impact is far more complex than just feeling thirsty.

When sodium levels in the blood rise too high, the kidneys work overtime. This constant pressure leads to long-term organ damage. Dr Hasin explained scientifically that sodium and potassium work like a seesaw in the body.

When one goes up, the other usually goes down. A high-salt diet forces potassium levels to drop. This is a disaster for heart rhythm and muscle function.

Even people with no history of kidney problems can face issues if their salt intake remains high. "The damage is often silent," Dr Hasin clarified seriously. It shows no symptoms until the kidneys are already struggling to function. By then, the road to recovery is long and difficult.

We cannot eliminate salt entirely, but we must learn to regulate it. In this case, we must happily return to our traditional roots. Instead of just obsessing over oats and avocados, which are not readily available for the masses, we must invest in our cheap and homemade deshi food items like chira, homemade muri, murki, etc.

Homemade treats are far safer than anything in a shiny plastic packet.

These options allow us to control exactly how much salt we add to our food. In the kitchen, there are many ways to make food pop without using a salt shaker.

"Using lemon, yoghurt, a bit of vinegar or even tamarind can enhance the taste of your curry," encouraged Dr Hasin. These ingredients provide a sharp flavour that satisfies the tongue. By using these alternatives, we can reduce sodium while still enjoying delicious meals. Small, mindful steps today can save thousands of lives from the silent threat of salt.

Title: Can too much AC make you sick? What you should know
Content:
In Bangladesh, air conditioning often feels less like a luxury and more like survival. During extreme heat, it can make homes, offices, and classrooms bearable. But spending long hours in air-conditioned spaces can also create a different set of problems. The issue is not that AC is harmful by itself. The issue is how it changes the air around us and how we use it.

Air conditioners cool rooms by removing heat and moisture from the air. That is exactly why they feel effective in humid weather. But when the air becomes too dry, the body notices. Low humidity can irritate the eyes, dry out the nose and throat, and make skin feel tight, itchy, or rough. The same dry air can also worsen conditions like eczema, allergies, and sinus irritation.

This is why some people who spend hours in AC rooms complain of burning eyes, scratchy throats, or skin irritation, even when they are technically “comfortable.”

Another common complaint linked to long AC exposure is headache. Part of that may come from dehydration. People often drink less water in cooler rooms because they do not feel sweaty or thirsty, but the body can still lose fluid. Dehydration itself is a well-established cause of headache, fatigue, and dizziness. Dry indoor air can make that worse.

That means the office headache or late-night heaviness you blame on work might sometimes be tied to cold, dry indoor air and not enough water.

For people with asthma, sinus issues, or other respiratory sensitivities, AC can be tricky. Dry air can irritate the airways and make breathing feel more difficult. If filters are dirty or maintenance is poor, air-conditioning systems may also circulate dust, allergens, or mould-related irritants. Low humidity itself can trigger sore throat, cough, and sinus discomfort.

So, the problem is not simply “cold air.” It is the combination of dryness, poor ventilation, and indoor air quality.

One of the most uncomfortable parts of AC use in Bangladesh is the constant shift between outdoor heat and heavily cooled indoor spaces. When the temperature difference is too extreme, the body has to keep adjusting. That can leave people feeling sluggish or drained, especially if they move in and out repeatedly throughout the day. Heat-related illness is still a risk outdoors, but overcooling indoors does not help the body adapt smoothly either.

The practical solution is moderation. Keep the room cool, not freezing. Drink water even if you do not feel thirsty. Use moisturiser if your skin is drying out, and artificial tears if your eyes feel irritated. Clean filters regularly and allow some fresh air circulation when possible. If indoor air feels too dry, adding controlled humidity may help, though too much moisture can encourage mould and worsen allergies.

Air conditioning is useful, especially in intense heat. But when used without attention to hydration, humidity, and maintenance, it can quietly make the body feel worse. The goal is not to avoid AC. It is to use it in a way that cools the room without drying out everything else.

Title: Why renaming PCOS to PMOS matters more than we think
Content:
PCOS is having a rebrand. After a long global consultation process involving clinicians, researchers, and patients, experts recommended a new name: polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS.

The old name, PCOS, often misled people. Many of us grew up believing ovarian cysts were the main reason for this condition, when in reality, not every person with PCOS actually develops cysts in their ovaries.

This one change of word completely shifted how millions of people understand their own bodies.

Countless individuals spent years undiagnosed, confused, and dismissed, as scans did not show cysts. The term “cystic” nailed down the conversation to one symptom, while the main condition has always been far deeper and more complex. For years, conversation about PCOS also ended up to “just take birth control” and you are good to go. The seriousness of this condition did not receive the attention it needed, and women have been suffering without a proper cure.

The new name finally acknowledges the actual problem is deeply connected to our metabolism instead of just our ovaries. “Polyendocrine” acknowledges that multiple hormone systems are involved. “Metabolic” brings attention to insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk. “Ovarian” remains relevant because ovarian dysfunction is still central to many cases.

In bodies affected with PMOS, insulin resistance plays a big role, and for many people, it silently impacts how the body processes energy and regulates hormones. This is why people with PMOS experience symptoms like exhaustion, sudden weight gain, cravings, acne, irregular cycles, facial hair, and hair thinning – all these things together.

People might think, “How can a single letter be that revolutionary,” right? Yes, it can. Maybe it does not magically solve the condition, but now it changes the way we feel and talk about it. It encourages us to start understanding it instead of treating it as a reproductive issue.

PMOS is one of the biggest rebrands of modern medicine in women’s health. Sometimes changing one letter can change an entire perspective.

With a new change, it will reduce the conversation about periods and fertility and focus more on full-body metabolic conditions.

Title: How to protect children from Dhaka’s scorching summer heat
Content:
To call this summer “hot” would be an understatement. Relentlessly oppressive, it seems to be leaving even the kings and the queens of hydration among us gasping for respite. Children, at this time, are particularly vulnerable and require unrelenting supervision and care. It is common knowledge that children do not like drinking water. So, here are a few steps to help them fight dehydration in summer.

Give your child plenty of water breaks to ensure they remain hydrated throughout the day. Time-stamped bottles are a good way to ensure they are drinking enough fluid to replace what is lost to sweat. Keeping a count of bottles or glasses is another way to make sure children are drinking enough.

The healthiest drink, of course, is plain water as it ensures solid, pure hydration. Water can also be infused with fruit wedges to add flavour without introducing processed sugar into the body. The next best bet, especially for those who are okay with lactose, is cold milk. It not only hydrates but is also a rich source of calcium, fortifying children’s teeth and bones. Fruit juices and powdered drinks are full of sugar, the former still being the healthier option of the two, especially if consumed quickly.

Choosing food with high water content is also a good idea. Watermelon and oranges, and vegetables such as iceberg lettuce, celery, tomatoes, zucchini, spinach and cucumbers all have a lot of water in them, hydrating the body through digestion.

While humidity has no chill at any time of day this summer, the actual heat of the sun is not equally harsh throughout the day. Therefore, it’s fair to allow children to stretch their legs in the mornings and in the very late afternoons, provided they wear hats, use sunscreens, and drink well during this time. The humidity can suck out moisture and drain your child, especially if they are very young and very active. Keep children indoors between 10:30 AM and 4:00 PM to avoid heat exhaustion and heat stroke.

Tight and dark-coloured clothes are a big no-no for the sort of stuffy weather Dhaka is experiencing. When not in school, children should be kept in light coloured, loose cotton clothes. This ensures that sweat does not stick to their bodies long enough for them to catch summer colds. Sudden changes in temperature should be avoided, such as stepping into a cold, air-conditioned room after being out in the heat for a long time. Similarly, instead of having them jump into the shower as soon as they step in, allow them to cool off naturally first.

Daily baths with lukewarm to lightly cool water are good for the little ones to wash off the sweat and grime of the day. It not only helps to relax them but also keeps away the germs they accumulate through the day that can cause itchiness and sweat allergies.

Dark coloured urine, headaches, dizziness, confusion, heat intolerance or chills, nausea, looking pale or clammy, rapid heart rate and/or rapid shallow breathing, a lack of appetite (especially with a sugar craving), and elevated body temperature are all signs that your child may be experiencing heat exhaustion.

Take them to a cool place and offer slow, continuous sips of water. Make them comfortable by allowing them to lie down with their feet up. If possible, give them a bath with lukewarm water, or, in the very least, give them a cool compress under the fan. This should be enough for their body temperature to come down, but if none of this works, it is best to take them to the ER for a consultation.
Author: M Munira Fidai Munira Fidai

Title: Stop these daily habits that quietly damage your mental health
Content:
For the longest time, to anyone seeking guidance for their mental well-being, it has been the norm to hand them a list of things they should do. But what if, for once, instead of looking at things we should do, we look at things we should not do?

The purpose of discussing all of this is simple: instead of looking into the addition of new habits and practices into our lives, why not first look towards changing what’s always been there and modify the elements of our daily lives, things which are subconsciously harming our mental health more than we realise.

Social media apps have increased our ability to stay aware of distressing news and alarming information, but sometimes we find ourselves caught in a cycle of viewing such negative content. We become victims of “doom scrolling”, which is the habit of continuously viewing negative and disturbing content on social media, despite the unwanted emotions that are caused by this, which they ignore.

Many apps like Instagram have algorithms, which ensure the new content popping up on your screens is similar to what you regularly view, often leading to an overload of such news.

While compulsive scrolling causes its victims to be stuck in a loop of negative emotions such as sorrow, fear, anxiety and even rage, it is especially harmful when done before bedtime. Watching disturbing content before sleep leaves a lasting effect on our mind throughout the next day; the information churns in our brain for a long time during sleep, often leading to nightmares as well.

Emotions aside, scrolling in general takes away time from our lives, leaving us with poor sleep schedules and rushed routines. The lack of proper sleep itself can cause anxiety and stress, which only gets worse for people who have been binging on negative news, leaving them in a state of panic and, if too severe, depression.

It is often said that emotions make us human. If that is true, we must never feel shame in addressing them, especially the unpleasant ones. One of the biggest enemies of our mental well-being is “bottled up emotions”.

For a vast majority of people, especially teenagers and young adults caught up in their ever-so-busy lives, ignoring feelings such as loneliness and guilt seems like the easier solution than addressing them. It may seem that ignoring emotions will help us forget about them, but the bottled-up feelings always creep into our subconscious and leave us in a state of constant confusion and discomfort.

It is essential to acknowledge that feelings, no matter what kind, are natural. Being honest with ourselves and acknowledging those feelings, so that we may take the required steps to deal with them, is the correct course of action.

As we grow older, the only other thing increasing as notably as our age is the workload. For different people, work can mean different things, but the key idea is that our responsibilities increase when the workload is on the rise.

This demands more attention to work, but in doing so, we must never lose ourselves. It is very easy to fall prey to the habit of overworking, especially when more work often means more physical benefits like promotions or raises.

Overworking not only strips us of time we could have spent behind ourselves doing something to soothe our mind, but additional work always brings about added stress with it, especially when the mind realises work is non-stop, it begins to associate work with all sorts of unpleasant feelings, making the whole working experience distressing.

When work is something we have to spend most of our week doing, it is very harmful for our mental health if our brain starts to associate this with negativity. It not only makes it harder to concentrate but also leaves our minds in an unpleasant state most of the time, all of which prevents our mental well-being.

The people we regularly interact with have a very important role in our mental health, which is why it’s crucial not to surround ourselves with negative people. People who are seemingly toxic, constantly pessimistic or always have something unpleasant to say to us are not ideal company.

While we aim to surround ourselves with people who have our best intentions at heart, sometimes certain people may express themselves in ways that are harmful to our mental health. Such as always having a fault to point out, starting every conversation with an accusation instead of praise or consolation and expecting us to remain a version of ourselves that they have envisioned, instead of acknowledging us for the unique individuals we are.

These individuals, irrespective of what their true intentions might be, carry negative energy into our lives and can often make someone feel “drained” if their piling expectations from us become overwhelming and ignorant of our true situation in life.

We must try as much as possible to distance ourselves from such individuals and instead surround ourselves with people who make us feel heard and valued, in front of whom we can be our true selves without guilt.

Title: Food & Recipes
The versatile appeal of focaccia bread
Content:
Focaccia is one of those breads that looks impressive but begins with a very simple dough. Crisp and golden at the edges, soft and airy inside, and generously coated with olive oil, it works just as well beside a meal as it does on its own with tea, dips or a light spread.

This version uses bread flour for structure, olive oil for richness, and a simple topping of cherry tomatoes and rosemary. The final olive oil and water brush helps keep the surface moist while encouraging that characteristic golden crust. The key is to give the dough enough time to rise and to handle it gently so the air developed during fermentation is not lost.

150g water, lukewarm

Cherry tomatoes, halved

Olive oil, as needed

A little salt, optional

For the olive oil and water brush —

1 tablespoon olive oil

Pour the lukewarm water into a large mixing bowl. Add the sugar and yeast and stir gently. Leave it for about 5 to 10 minutes, until the mixture begins to look slightly foamy.

The water should be warm rather than hot, as very hot water can damage the yeast.

Add the bread flour and salt to the yeast mixture. Mix until the ingredients begin to come together into a rough dough. Pour in the olive oil and continue mixing until it is incorporated. Transfer the dough to a lightly floured or lightly oiled work surface. Knead for around 8 to 10 minutes, until the dough becomes smoother and more elastic. The dough may feel slightly sticky. Avoid adding too much extra flour, as a softer dough helps produce a lighter focaccia.

Lightly oil a clean bowl and place the dough inside. Turn it once so that the surface is lightly coated with oil. Cover the bowl with a clean kitchen towel or plastic wrap and leave it in a warm place for approximately 1 to 1½ hours, or until the dough has roughly doubled in size. Rising time may vary depending on room temperature.

Prepare the baking tray

Generously brush a baking tray or small rectangular baking pan with olive oil. Once the dough has risen, gently transfer it to the prepared tray. Do not aggressively punch out all the air. Using lightly oiled fingers, carefully stretch the dough towards the edges of the pan. If it keeps springing back, leave it to rest for 10 minutes before stretching it again.

Cover the tray loosely and allow the dough to rise again for around 30 to 45 minutes. By this stage, it should look visibly puffier and softer.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Mix 1 tablespoon olive oil with 1 tablespoon water to make the brushing mixture. Using your fingertips, press deeply into the risen dough to create the characteristic focaccia dimples. Be firm enough to create indentations, but avoid tearing through the dough. Brush or drizzle the olive oil and water mixture generously across the surface. Arrange the halved cherry tomatoes over the dough, pressing them in slightly. Scatter rosemary over the top. Finish with another drizzle of olive oil and, if desired, a small amount of salt.

Bake the focaccia in the preheated oven for approximately 20 to 25 minutes, or until the top is golden and the edges are nicely browned. Ovens vary, so begin checking towards the end of the baking time.

Once removed from the oven, brush the hot focaccia lightly with a little additional olive oil for extra flavour and a softer, glossy surface. Allow it to cool in the tray for around 5 to 10 minutes before transferring it to a cooling rack or serving board.

Serve the focaccia warm or at room temperature. It can be eaten on its own, paired with tomato or basil-based dips, served alongside soups and salads, or sliced horizontally to make sandwiches. For the best texture, enjoy it fresh on the day it is baked. If reheating, warm it briefly in the oven rather than the microwave to help restore its crisp exterior.

Title: Mungdi brings hill cuisine to Dhaka
Content:
A bowl of Mungdi does not rely on thick gravy or an abundance of spices. Handmade rice noodles sit in a light chicken-stock broth, accompanied by egg, chicken, fish or prawns. The broth remains delicate, the ingredients recognisable and the flavours closer to the natural character of the food.

For many diners in Dhaka, however, even the name is unfamiliar. Tara Bikash Tripura, owner of Mungdi Restaurant, is working to change that by introducing traditional foods from the hilly regions to a wider audience.

“Mungdi is one of our traditional soup items,” he explains. “The broth is very light and does not contain many spices. It has a natural flavour that comes from chicken stock.”

According to Tripura, the restaurant serves five variations: Egg Mungdi, Chicken Mungdi, Fish Mungdi, Prawn Mungdi, and Special Mungdi. The broth remains largely the same, while the main accompaniment changes. Egg Mungdi contains a whole egg, while Chicken Mungdi is served with sliced chicken.

Each bowl also contains handmade rice noodles brought from the hilly regions. For Tripura, sourcing these ingredients helps maintain a connection between the food served in Dhaka and the places where the recipes are traditionally prepared.

Before opening Mungdi Restaurant, Tara Bikash Tripura worked for a company for around eight to 10 years. During that period, he continued thinking about establishing a restaurant of his own.

“I always had a passion for opening a restaurant,” he recalls, adding, “I had been planning it for a long time. After eight to 10 years of preparation and planning, I finally opened this place on June 15 last year.”

The beginning was difficult. As a new establishment serving unfamiliar food, the restaurant struggled to find workers and earn customers’ confidence.

“People did not trust us at first,” he recounts. “So, I started it myself along with some of my cousins. Three or four of us managed everything together.”

Gradually, customers began discovering the restaurant and learning about its menu. “Now we are in a much better position than before,” Tripura elaborates. “People are becoming familiar with our traditional food. Our customers are satisfied, and that makes me very happy.”

Although the restaurant is named after the soup, the menu includes several other traditional preparations.

One is Toja Morich Bhorta, made with boiled vegetables and chilli mash. Dried fish, onion and a little lemon are added, and the dish is eaten by mixing it with rice.

The menu also includes Chicken Laksa, made with steamed chicken, lemon and chilli.

“The chicken is steamed and then prepared with lemon and chilli,” Tripura explains. “It is a sour and spicy, salad-style item. People really enjoy it as a snack.”

Together, these dishes show the range of flavours and techniques found in the food traditions of the hilly regions. Steaming, boiling, mashing and lightly seasoning ingredients allow the natural taste of vegetables, herbs, bamboo shoots, fish and meat to remain prominent.

Running the restaurant involves more than preparing food. Tripura and his team must also explain the dishes to customers who may never have heard their names.

“At first, people ask, ‘What is this?’ because they have not even heard the names,” he says. “We have to present it to them very politely and explain what it is.”

There is always some uncertainty when a new customer tastes the food. “We feel a little anxious about whether they will like it, since they are not accustomed to these flavours,” he admits.

Positive feedback, therefore, carries particular significance.

“When a customer says the food is good, it feels like a great achievement for us,” he says. “It means we are successfully reviving something that was being lost.”

Tripura remembers a time when these dishes were more common in Khagrachari, where he once lived. He believes the growing popularity of fast food is gradually pushing traditional foods out of everyday life.

“With the rise of various fast-food items in Bangladesh, our traditional food and culture are on the verge of fading away,” he remarks.

The disappearance of a dish can also mean the loss of knowledge about local plants, ingredients and preparation methods. Preserving indigenous food therefore requires more than documenting recipes. The dishes must continue to be cooked, served and taught, while the communities behind them receive proper recognition.

“I hope more people start doing this so our heritage and culture can survive,” Tripura says.

Mungdi offers a reminder that Bangladesh’s culinary identity extends far beyond its most familiar dishes. In one light bowl of broth and handmade rice noodles lies a story of migration, entrepreneurship and cultural preservation.

Each time Tripura explains an unfamiliar dish to a customer, another traditional name enters Dhaka’s food vocabulary. Each bowl served becomes a small but meaningful act of keeping that heritage alive.
