Title: Bangladesh must assess risks before joining Mecca Defence Alliance: Experts
Content:
Bangladesh should assess the proposed Mecca Defence Alliance's structure, obligations and impact on strategic autonomy and ties with India, the US and China before joining, experts said. The alliance could offer defence and economic opportunities, but Dhaka must examine its compatibility with foreign policy and international obligations, they said.

The observations were presented at a roundtable titled "Significance of Mecca Defence Alliance & Options for Bangladesh", organised by the Centre for Strategic and Development Studies (CSDS) and chaired by former ambassador Maj Gen (retd) AMSA Ameen.

Professor Shahab Enam Khan of Jahangirnagar University said Bangladesh should consider the Myanmar situation, including Pakistan's potential role in Rohingya repatriation and its growing defence ties with Myanmar.

"Bangladesh needs a regional partner to keep the OIC channel active. Pakistan could be an important partner in this regard," he said.

China's role in the Bangladesh-Myanmar context also requires Dhaka to balance ties with Washington and Beijing, Shahab said. Changing relations among Saudi Arabia, the Gulf countries, Iran and Türkiye could create diplomatic challenges, while ties with Saudi Arabia, other Gulf states and Qatar remain important, particularly because Bangladesh depends heavily on Qatar for natural gas imports.

He also stressed defence modernisation and diversification, saying these had become more important after 2024. Myanmar's move to establish a nuclear power plant was another concern, he added.

Former ambassador Mahbub Uz Zaman said the pact had so far developed as a joint defence arrangement among three countries, with a key provision treating an armed attack on one member as an attack on all three.

"If Bangladesh joins the agreement, it needs to know under what circumstances it could be required to use force and what kind of international obligations this could create," he said.

Mahbub said membership could affect Bangladesh's "strategic autonomy" and balanced ties with India, the US and China. The pact should also be assessed against Article 25 of the Bangladesh Constitution and relevant principles of the UN Charter, he said.

Professor Shahiduzzaman, a retired international relations professor at Dhaka University, said uncertainty remained over the pact's future structure and sustainability.

Bangladesh should wait for a formal proposal, he said, adding that expansion was unlikely to make significant progress in the next few months. Its future would also depend on relations among Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Türkiye and Iran.

Lt Gen (retd) Aminul Karim said the pact should not be compared directly with Nato because its organisational structure remains unclear. However, Türkiye's military technology, Pakistan's military capabilities and Saudi Arabia's financial resources could benefit Bangladesh's defence and economy.

He called for stronger defence capabilities and credible deterrence, particularly a stronger air force and air defence system, while maintaining good relations with India. Greater defence capability would strengthen Bangladesh's position in talks with India based on sovereign equality, he said.

Former Pakistani senator Mushahid Hussain Sayed, joining virtually, called the alliance a "significant and historic initiative" that could offer Muslim countries a new strategic alternative.

Bangladesh should remain focused on South Asia, he said, while stronger Bangladesh-Pakistan ties and cooperation among Bangladesh, Pakistan and China could help create regional balance.
Author: TBS Report

Title: Larry Ellison cancels plan to sell Oracle stock worth up to $7.5 billion
Content:
Oracle said yesterday (12 September) that its co-founder and executive chairman Larry Ellison had cancelled a plan to sell up to 50 million Oracle shares, worth about $7.5 billion at Friday's (11 September) closing price.

Oracle had disclosed in a regulatory filing Friday (11 September) that Ellison had adopted the trading plan on 22 June 2026, and that it was scheduled to expire on 24 October 2026.

"No Oracle stock was sold under that plan, and he has no other plans to sell any of his Oracle stock," Oracle said yesterday (12 September).

Oracle's stock has taken a beating this year amid growing investor concerns over soaring capital expenditure that has pressured its free cash flow.

The shares are down nearly 23% year to date and were more than 18% below their closing level on 18 June, the last trading day before Ellison adopted the plan.

Oracle did not give a reason for the cancellation of Ellison's trading plan.

Ellison, 82, served as Oracle's CEO until 2014 and is the company's largest shareholder, owning over 38% of the company, according to LSEG data.

Earlier in the week, Oracle had reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street estimates and a smaller cash burn than expected, easing some concerns about its debt-fuelled spending spree and leading to a jump in the shares on Friday.

However, its stock later reversed course as analysts said a recovery in cash flow remained some way off.

The firm also announced that restructuring costs, part of a plan that includes job cuts, will rise by about $700 million.

Oracle / Larry Ellison

Title: Jahangirnagar University team wins DIMFF-UNHCR mobile filmmaking workshop
Content:
A team from Jahangirnagar University has won a month-long mobile filmmaking workshop organised by the Dhaka International Mobile Film Festival (DIMFF) in collaboration with UNHCR, with the closing ceremony held at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB) Permanent Campus on 11 September.

The workshop focused on filmmaking and refugee experiences under the theme "Forced to Flee", with participants receiving training in colour grading and other filmmaking techniques, according to a press release.

Participants also learned about the experiences of refugees and UNHCR's work in supporting refugee communities before producing short films based on the workshop theme.

Five teams were shortlisted from 20 participating universities, including the University of Dhaka, ULAB, North South University, Jahangirnagar University and Daffodil International University. The jury selected "MANOB" from Jahangirnagar University as the winning team.

The closing ceremony featured remarks from Professor Dr Sumon Rahman, dean of the School of Social Sciences and head of the Department of Media Studies and Journalism at ULAB, and Mir Wadud Islam, instructor and co-adviser of DIMFF 2027.

Representing UNHCR Bangladesh, Kevin Lindblom, associate external relations officer, highlighted the role of storytelling in building awareness and understanding of refugee experiences.

Jury members Md Hafizuddin Munna and Ishtiyak Ahmad Zihad also shared their observations on the participating films and encouraged young filmmakers to use storytelling to highlight issues and experiences around them.

The winning team said the workshop helped its members discover new skills and explore creative ways of telling stories through filmmaking.

Certificates were distributed among participants at the ceremony in recognition of their involvement in the workshop. As the winning prize, UNHCR will provide the MANOB team with a day-long tour of a Rohingya refugee camp.

The ceremony concluded with a vote of thanks from Syeda Sadia Mehjabin, senior lecturer and adviser of DIMFF 2027. Organisers said the workshop reflected DIMFF's aim of empowering young filmmakers to use mobile technology as a tool for storytelling and communication.

Title: Adani power supply rises as Godda plant's Unit-2 synchronised with national grid after 3 days
Content:
Unit-2 of the Godda Thermal Power Plant, owned by Adani Power Jharkhand Ltd, in India's Jharkhand, synchronised with Bangladesh's national grid at 12:04pm today (13 September), three days after it went offline following a technical problem in its feed unit.

With the synchronisation, power supply is expected to increase, creating some breathing space to manage severe load shedding sweeping across the country, Md Zahurul Islam, member (production) of the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB), confirmed to The Business Standard.

The unit will take several hours to reach its optimal generation capacity, officials said.

At 9am, power supply from Adani was recorded at 758MW, according to Power Grid Bangladesh.

Adani has been supplying around 750-760MW since Thursday (10 September), when Unit-2 was shut down following a technical problem with its feed unit. The supply rose to 846MW at 1pm, Power Grid Bangladesh said.

Later, Adani, through its PR agency, said power supply had risen to 1,046MW as of 2pm, with Unit-1 supplying 756.66MW and Unit-2 290MW.

In a short message sent to TBS through its PR agency earlier today, Adani Power said Unit-2 was successfully lit up at 5:17am, ahead of schedule, with synchronisation expected by 11:30am.

Before the unit went offline at around 1am on Thursday, Adani was supplying around 1,430MW to Bangladesh.

A feed unit, also known as a boiler feed pump, in the main water supply system of Unit-2 had developed a fault, forcing the generating unit to shut down.

The boiler feed pump is a critical component of a thermal power plant, as it continuously pumps high-pressure water into the steam boiler. Any malfunction can disrupt boiler operations and trigger an automatic shutdown as a safety measure.

The latest technical disruption follows a series of supply interruptions at the Adani plant in recent weeks.

The plant had earlier reduced generation due to severe congestion on the railway network, which disrupted coal transportation to the Godda plant in India.

Adani Power said restrictions on coal transportation and loading had affected coal availability, prompting it to optimise generation and prioritise supply during evening peak hours.

Adani Power's Godda plant has two units, each with an installed capacity of 800MW. Its combined actual generation capacity, however, is around 1,496MW.

Title: TIFF 2026: K-pop superstar Lisa sparks fan frenzy at documentary premiere
Content:
K-pop star Lisa was met by piercing screams from fans as she walked the red carpet at ​the Toronto International Film Festival for the premiere of her ‌new documentary, "Always Lalisa."

Lisa rose to fame as a member of the K-pop girl group Blackpink, and the film follows a year in her life after ​taking a break from the band to embark on ​a solo career.

"I just tried to find new things — like ⁠what can I do more than this?" she told Reuters ​in an interview after the Friday premiere.

The star, whose full name ​is Lalisa Manobal, said she initially thought a year would be long enough, but is still trying to figure out what she loves and her next challenge.

"Always Lalisa" ​captures her triumphs and setbacks between 2024 and 2025, documenting ​the release of her debut solo album "Alter Ego," her acting debut in HBO's ‌hit ⁠series "The White Lotus" and preparations to perform on her own before huge crowds at the Coachella music festival.

The documentary was directed by Sue Kim, an executive producer on Apple TV's 2024 documentary ​series "K-Pop Idols."

"This is ​this incredible opportunity ⁠to get to know someone who we're only ever given a very specific image of because ​of the music system that she comes from. ​We get ⁠to have this unprecedented access, proximity and exposure to her ... It's not the world of K-pop," Kim told Reuters.

After Lisa's return to ⁠the ​group, Blackpink in February made a return ​with the mini-album "DEADLINE," their first release in more than three years.

"Always Lalisa" opens in cinemas on ​12 October.

Title: The Pentagon is using polygraphs to hunt leakers, but the tests are more theatre than fact
Content:
Atlanta, In August 2026, government investigators subjected roughly 50 military officers and civilian employees on the Joint Staff to polygraph tests as part of an inquiry into press leaks about the Iran war and depleted US munitions, according to The New York Times.

The newspaper described the scope of the investigation as unprecedented in the modern military.

This is not the first time the Trump administration has used polygraphs in this way; in 2025, it directed that a wave of tests be administered across the executive branch to expose minor leaks.

As someone who has taken roughly a dozen polygraphs during my 27-year career with the CIA, I am wary of how the process is understood – and of the certainty its use can appear to convey.

Polygraphs carry an ominous, almost mythological reputation among Americans. The more familiar and unofficial term – lie detector tests – likely fuels that perception. Television crime dramas have done their part, too, often portraying the device as an oracle for uncovering the truth when conventional methods fail.

In those portrayals, the polygraph is not merely a tool – it's a window into the soul.

Among those entering government service, especially in national security, the greater anxiety is not the background check but passing the polygraph. My advice is always the same: Don't lie. It's the best – and perhaps only – guidance for a process that most assessments have concluded is a more subjective interpretation than empirical science.

Why the polygraph persists

Polygraphs are "pseudo-scientific" in that they measure physiological responses such as heart rate, blood pressure and perspiration. The assumption is that liars betray themselves through spikes in those signals. But this presumes a kind of psychological transparency that simply doesn't hold up. A person might sweat and tremble simply from fear, anger or frustration – not deceit.

There also are no specific physiological reactions associated with lying. The National Academy of Sciences in 2003, and the American Psychological Association in a 2004 review, concluded that the polygraph rests more on theatre than fact. A 2019 assessment reached the same conclusion.

Accordingly, polygraph results are not generally admissible in US courts. Only a handful of states – such as Georgia, Arizona and California – permit their use even under limited conditions. And they typically require that both parties agree to admission and a judge to approve it. Unconditional admissibility remains the exception, not the rule.

And yet, inside many national security agencies, polygraphs remain central to the clearance process – a fact I observed firsthand during my time overseeing personnel vetting and analytic hiring within the intelligence community.

While not treated as conclusive, polygraph results often serve as a filter. A candidate's visible discomfort – or the examiner's subjective judgment that a response seems evasive – can stall or end the hiring process.

For instance, I know that government agencies have halted clearances after an examiner flagged elevated reactions to questions about past drug use or foreign contacts, even when no disqualifying behaviour was ultimately documented.

In some cases, an examiner's suggestion that a chart shows an anomaly has led otherwise strong applicants to volunteer details they hadn't planned to share – such as minor security infractions, undeclared relationships, or casual drug use from decades earlier – that, while not disqualifying on their own, reshape how their trustworthiness is perceived.

The polygraph's power lies in creating the conditions under which deception is confessed.

A predictable pattern

No administration has been immune to the impulse to investigate leaks. The reflex is bipartisan and familiar: An embarrassing disclosure appears in the press – contradicting official statements or exposing internal dissent – and the White House vows to identify and punish the source. Polygraphs are often part of this ritual.

During his first term, Trump intensified efforts to expose internal dissent and media leaks. Department guidelines were revised to make it easier for agencies to obtain journalists' phone and email records, and polygraphs were reportedly used to pressure officials suspected of talking to the press. That trend has continued – and, since 2025, escalated.

Policies at the Pentagon now restrict unescorted press access, revoke office space for major outlets and favour ideologically aligned networks. The line between legitimate leak prevention and the surveillance or sidelining of critical press coverage has grown increasingly blurred.

At agencies such as the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI, polygraphs reportedly have been used frequently – and more punitively – to identify internal dissenters. Even "cold cases," such as the leak of the Supreme Court's Dobbs opinion ahead of its overturning of Roe v. Wade, were reopened, despite prior investigations yielding no definitive source.

Government reaction varies

Not all leaks are treated the same. Disclosures that align with official narratives or offer strategic advantage may be quietly tolerated, even if unauthorised. Others, especially those that embarrass senior officials or reveal dysfunction, are more likely to prompt formal investigation.

In 2003, for example, the leak of CIA officer Valerie Plame's identity – widely seen as retaliation for her husband's criticism of the Iraq War – triggered a federal investigation.

The disclosure embarrassed senior officials, led to White House aide Scooter Libby's conviction for perjury, later commuted, and drew intense political scrutiny.

Leaks involving classified material draw the sharpest response when they challenge presidential authority or expose internal disputes. That was the case in 2010 with Chelsea Manning, whose disclosure of diplomatic cables and battlefield reports embarrassed senior officials and sparked global backlash. Government reaction often depends less on what was disclosed than on who disclosed it – and to what effect.

A narrow set of disclosures, such as those involving espionage or operational compromise, elicit broad consensus as grounds for prosecution. But most leaks fall outside that category. Most investigations fade quietly. The public rarely learns what became of them. Occasionally, there is a vague resignation, but direct accountability is rare.

What the future holds

The Pentagon polygraph campaign is not likely to eliminate leaks to the press. But it may have a chilling effect that discourages internal candour while diverting investigative energy away from core security priorities.

Even if such campaigns succeed in reducing unauthorised disclosures, they may come at the cost of institutional resilience. Historically, aggressive internal enforcement has been associated with declining morale and reduced information flow – factors that can hinder adaptation to complex threats.

Some researchers have suggested that artificial intelligence may eventually offer reliable tools for detecting deception but caution that the technology is nowhere near operational readiness.

For now, institutions will have to contend with the tools they have – imperfect, imprecise and more performative than predictive.

Title: Neon Nights on reinventing pop and retro hits: 'Sweet spot is when someone hears something they haven’t heard before'
Content:
From strangers to band mates, Neon Nights has been through a musical journey worth talking about. Comprising Lian Khuptong on drums, Jael Syuhlo and Asherie Zonunmawi on vocals, Joshua Constantine on guitar, Daniel Hatzaw on bass, and Lian Suanlal Guite on piano, the band is set to perform at The Piano Man, Safdarjung, New Delhi this Saturday.

They are best known for their lively renditions of the biggest pop hits from around the world and that is just what they will showcase this weekend in the capital.

HT talked to the band about what journey so far has been like and what they are most excited about for the upcoming performance.

You describe Neon Nights as a bunch of "misfits turned music maestros". Who are the misfits in the band, and how did you all end up making music together?

Honestly, all of us. We come from pretty different musical spaces. Some of us grew up on rock and retro, others are more into pop, soul and newer music. So when we first got into a room together, there wasn't some grand plan to create a particular "sound". We were just playing songs we liked and seeing what happened. And a lot happened.

Someone would change a groove, somebody else would throw in a harmony that wasn't there, and suddenly a song we'd all heard a hundred times felt new again. We kept coming back to that. So yes, the misfit part is still accurate. "Music maestros" is probably us getting slightly carried away.

You've said you put a fresh spin on everything from current pop hits to retro classics. What makes a song worth reworking for Neon Nights, and is there a song you've completely transformed?

Usually it starts with a song that all of us genuinely want to play. That matters. If we're bored playing it, the audience is going to feel that too. Then we ask ourselves: what can we do with this that the original doesn't already do?

Sometimes it's a different groove. Sometimes we make it heavier, strip it down, change the vocal arrangement or take a very polished pop track and make it sound like five or six people actually playing together in a room. We particularly enjoy taking newer songs and giving them an older live-band feel. That contrast is fun.

There are a couple in the 12 September set where you'll recognise the song almost immediately, but what happens after that isn't quite what you expect. We'd rather not ruin those before the show.

The band launched only in 2024. What has surprised you most about going from garage jams to performing at a venue like The Piano Man?

How quickly it stopped feeling like "just a jam". At first, you're thinking about very basic things. Did everyone learn the song? Is that transition clean? Who forgot the ending this time?

Then you start playing in front of people and your whole way of looking at the music changes. You notice which moments make people sing, which songs make a room go quiet and listen, and which ones suddenly get everyone out of their seats. That part has probably surprised us the most.

Playing The Piano Man is special because people there really listen. You can't hide behind volume or production. If the music works, they'll give you everything. If it doesn't, you know pretty quickly. That's exciting. Also mildly terrifying. In a good way.

When you're playing a mix of familiar Western hits, how do you balance giving audiences the songs they came to hear with putting your own stamp on them?

We never want somebody to hear their favourite song and think, "What have these guys done to it?" There are certain things you don't mess with. A chorus that everyone wants to sing. A melody people have known for years. Sometimes even a tiny guitar part that people are waiting to hear without realising it.

We keep those moments. Then we play around with everything surrounding them — the groove, harmonies, dynamics, solos, intros, endings and the way one song moves into another. That's where Neon Nights comes in.

For us, the sweet spot is when someone knows every word of the song but still hears something they haven't heard before.

You're performing at The Piano Man in Delhi this weekend. What can people expect from a Neon Nights gig that they might not get from simply listening to the original versions of these songs? Which song are you most excited about performing?

The unpredictability. You know exactly what happens when you press play on a recording. Live, we don't always know what's going to happen either.

If the room starts singing, we might leave space for them. A solo can run a little longer. We might suddenly pull everything down to just the vocal and one instrument, then come back in full force. Songs also bleed into each other in ways you won't find on the original records.

And we jump around a lot. One minute you're somewhere in the '80s or '90s, a few minutes later you're singing something that came out much more recently. That's what we love about the show. It feels alive.

As for the song we're most excited to play? Ask us again after September 12. It's usually the one where the crowd ends up louder than the band. But if we had to pick one, then I would say "The Chain" by Fleetwood Mac.
Author: Hindustan Times

Title: Tension outside Islami Bank as sacked employees demand reinstatement, customers push back
Content:
Dismissed Islami Bank officials appointed during S Alam's tenure and customers under the banner of Sachetan Grahak Forum (Conscious Customers Forum) held counter sit-ins in front of the bank's head office in Motijheel today (13 September), with both sides making competing demands.

The dismissed officials from the Chattogram region were demanding reinstatement, while several hundred customers were protesting against what they described as the "conspiracy of S Alam's looters".

Both groups began their programmes in front of Islami Bank Tower around 9am and left the area around 12:50pm.

Face-off between customers and dismissed staff

Sachetan Grahak Forum opposed the dismissed employees' demand for reinstatement and called for the bank's normal operations to continue and action to be taken against irregularities.

Shamim Hasnain, vice-president of the forum, said they took position in front of the bank at night after learning that the dismissed employees planned to hold a programme there.

"During S Alam's tenure, many were appointed through irregularities and forged certificates. After 5 August 2024, the bank took initiatives to verify the certificates of these appointments. There was also an initiative to retain qualified candidates through examinations. But they did not take part in the exam," he said.

"Now they are creating chaos in front of the bank demanding their jobs back. The Grahak Forum will not accept such chaos in front of the bank," Shamim said.

Meanwhile, Anwar, one of the dismissed employees, said they had been living a "subhuman existence" since losing their jobs.

Claiming that the bank's new board of directors formed after 5 August 2024 dismissed them, he said, "We will not return home until we get our jobs back. We will return home only with our jobs back."

Regarding allegations that some employees were appointed using forged certificates, Anwar said, "Let Bangladesh Bank investigate and submit a report. If our appointments are proven illegal, we will return all the money earned from the job."

"Action can be taken against those who have issues against them. But there is no meaning in dismissing everyone together like this," he said.

The rival programmes created a tense situation in front of the Islami Bank head office in Motijheel.

Title: ‘I resign as CM’: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke takes dig at MP govt in satirical letter
Content:
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Sunday took a dig at the Madhya Pradesh government, sharing a satirical resignation letter as the state's chief minister.

This comes a day after Dipke was allegedly heckled by some influencers in Balaghat, where he had gone to meet the parents of tribal children who had died due to an infection.

"I hereby resign as the Chief Minister of MP with immediate effect. I thank Hon'ble PM @narendramodi ji for giving me the opportunity to serve the people of MP, an opportunity in which I have clearly failed," Dipke wrote on X while sharing the fake letter that looked close to authentic.

I hereby resign as the Chief Minister of MP with immediate effect. I thank Hon'ble PM @narendramodi ji for giving me the opportunity to serve the people of MP, an opportunity in which I have clearly failed. @GovernorMP https://t.co/BVhfJDIf5n

In the satirical letter, Dipke discussed what he called the "failures" of the state government, taking a dig at chief minister Mohan Yadav and his colleagues over the Sagar hooch tragedy and the Balaghat infection deaths, among other issues.

CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka reacted to Dipke's post, joking that he was "running away" from responsibility.

Dipke heckled in Balaghat

Abhijeet Dipke visited Adori, Korka and Bondari villages in MP's Balaghat on Saturday to meet the families of tribal children who allegedly died due to infectious diseases and to gather information about local healthcare facilities.

A viral video showed a woman 'influencer' sticking a mic in Dipke's face as he was driving away in a car, and asking him if he had come there to "do politics on corpses" and why he was visiting the area so late. Dipke was heard saying he apologised for visiting the area late.

The woman was also heard saying, "A good road has been constructed here. Can't you see it?" As the situation escalated, CJP workers accompanying Dipke put him in another car and took him away. While the CJP founder left, the woman was heard saying, "he ran away, he ran away."

Local journalists said they were surprised to see this group of social media influencers from outside turn up in the remote village and wondered whether they had been sent by someone to disrupt the CJP founder's visit.

The Madhya Pradesh high court recently sought a response from the state government over the deaths of more than 30 children in the region.

The HC issued notices to the state Health Department, the Women and Child Development Department, the Balaghat collector, and others while hearing a PIL alleging that children were not receiving adequate treatment and that around 400 children were being treated at a hospital with a capacity of 50 beds.

A report prepared by the petitioner alleged widespread filth in the area and claimed that these conditions were causing infections and that children continued to die from diseases.

A tragedy was reported from the Banda area of Sagar district after several people allegedly fell ill following the consumption of spurious liquor. 16 people lost their lives in the tragedy, and so far, 19 accused have been arrested in the case.

A medical treatment involving fomepizole, an antidote used in suspected toxic alcohol poisoning, has also emerged as a crucial intervention in the treatment of several patients. According to officials, the drug has helped save the lives of more than 30 people so far.

Fomepizole is used as an antidote in cases of poisoning involving toxic alcohols such as methanol. Its use can help prevent the formation of toxic metabolites and is an important part of treatment when methanol poisoning is suspected.

Abhijeet Dipke / Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)
Author: Hindustan Times

Title: French senators eye stronger political engagement with Bangladesh
Content:
A delegation of three French senators today (13 September) met State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam at her office and discussed issues and ways to further strengthen political engagement between Bangladesh and France.

Senators Guillaume Chevrollier, Pierre-Alain Roiron and Olivier Henno arrived in Dhaka yesterday night (12 September) on a three-day official visit.

Ambassador of France to Bangladesh Jean-Marc Séré-Charlet and Head of the Political Wing of the Embassy Christian Bec accompanied the senators during their meeting with the state minister.

They are part of the French-Southeast Asia and Bangladesh Senate Friendship Group, and the visit is particularly meaningful as it is the first political-level visit from France since the new democratically elected government took office in Bangladesh, said the French Embassy in Dhaka.

They will discuss strengthening political and parliamentary ties, exchange perspectives with their Bangladeshi counterparts and explore new areas of cooperation between the two countries.

The French Senate (Sénat) is the upper chamber of the French Parliament, alongside the National Assembly.

The senators are scheduled to meet Speaker of Parliament Hafiz Uddin Ahmad and hold discussions with various Bangladeshi interlocutors.

Their programme also includes visits to places associated with French development cooperation, museums, and meetings with members of the French community in Dhaka, as well as engagements with representatives of the business community.

Title: HC dismisses writ challenging ban on Awami League’s activities
Content:
The High Court has dismissed as not pressed a writ petition challenging the legality of the government notification banning all activities of the Awami League and its affiliated, associated and like-minded organisations.

The High Court bench of Justice JBM Hassan and Justice Aziz Ahmed Bhuiyan passed the order today (13 September).

Earlier, Md Al Amin, a resident of Munshiganj, filed the writ petition on 7 September. Advocate Yunus Ali represented the petitioner.

The petition sought a rule asking the authorities to explain why the notification issued on 12 May 2025 should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority.

The petitioner also sought a stay on the operation of the 12 May notification while the rule, if issued, remained pending.

The Public Security Division of the Ministry of Home Affairs issued the notification on 12 May last year, banning all activities of the ousted Awami League and its affiliated, associated and like-minded organisations until the completion of trials of their leaders and activists in the International Crimes Tribunal.

According to the notification, these activities included publications, campaigns through the media, online platforms and social media, processions, meetings, rallies and conferences.

Title: Bahrain rejects proposed Gulf-Iran summit until ties restored
Content:
Bahrain has declined to attend a proposed Gulf summit with Iran in Oman to discuss maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz, saying it would not participate until diplomatic relations between Manama and Tehran are restored.

The Bahraini Foreign Ministry rejected what it described as a "policy of appeasement" or "overlooking attacks", citing recent strikes on an ammonia tank in Bahrain and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as evidence that economic and civilian infrastructure remained under threat, says Arab News.

Bahrain said lasting regional stability required four conditions: an end to all attacks; international accountability and compensation for damages; respect for state sovereignty and a ban on using another country's territory as a launchpad for attacks; and the resolution of outstanding disputes through legal channels.

On the Strait of Hormuz, Bahrain said the waterway must remain open without "discrimination, fees or permits". It said maritime traffic should be governed by the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and principles endorsed by the International Maritime Organization.

Oman is set to host a meeting involving Gulf foreign ministers, Iran and Iraq to discuss maritime traffic through the strategically important waterway.

A senior Iranian official said no signed agreement was expected from Monday's meeting. Iran has continued to seek an arrangement that would allow it to collect transit fees from ships passing through the strait, an idea Oman rejects.

Title: Two-day 'Nazrul Dance Festival 2026' underway at BSA
Content:
A two-day "Nazrul Dance Festival 2026", organised by Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy as part of the Nazrul Barsha celebrations, is underway at the academy, featuring dance performances inspired by the works and philosophy of National Poet Kazi Nazrul Islam.

The festival, which began yesterday (12 September), will conclude today (13 September), with the final day's programme starting at 6:30pm at the National Music and Dance Centre Auditorium.

Different dance groups are presenting performances based on Nazrul's songs and creative works, exploring themes of rebellion, love, equality, humanity and beauty.

The festival aims to explore Nazrul's multifaceted creative world through dance and present his spirit of humanism, communal harmony and resistance in contemporary dance language.

Culture Affairs Secretary Yasmin Begum, who presided over the inaugural session on Saturday, said Nazrul always stood beside oppressed and helpless people and sought to revitalise society through his works. "We want to remember him in this way through various forms of art," she said.

Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy Director General, poet Sheikh Rezauddin Ahmed (Rezauddin Stalin), in his welcome address, said Nazrul occupies a significant place in the tradition of classical music and that the festival was organised around dance based on his songs.

"Love and separation of the people of Bengal find expression through rhythm and dance. Rhythm is present at every stage of life. Dance influences our lives and expands our imaginative world," he said.

Ekushey Padak-winning dancer and dance researcher Amanul Haque, the keynote speaker, said the themes of Nazrul's humanism and rebellion could be conveyed through dance.

"We want to embrace his thoughts and philosophy in our hearts and express them through dance," he said.

On the first day, Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy presented "Shankashunyo Lakkho Konthe" at the beginning of the second segment of the programme. Naim Khan Dance Company performed "Amar Kaifiyat", while Nrityayatan, Mymensingh, presented "O Bhai Khati Sonar Cheye Khati", choreographed by Md Nazmul Haque.

Other participating groups included Spondon, Bhabna, Nrityalok Cultural Centre, Bangladesh Academy of Fine Arts and Kayashram.

Dance groups from different parts of the country also took part in the festival, including Swapnik Nritya Bikash of Madaripur, Anjali Nrityangan Academy, Artisty, Sadhana, Nrityayan, Nabodoot Cultural Academy of Kishoreganj, Diksha, Tapasya, Nandan Kalakendra, Nrityomi of Mymensingh, Paraspara, Nrityakkho, Nrityasur, Swapnachura Cultural Academy, Gurukul Cultural Centre, Zinia Nrityakala Academy, Bakul Nrityalay and Nrityam Nrityashilan Kendra.

The academy hopes the festival will create a creative dialogue between Nazrul's diverse body of work and dance, encouraging new productions that explore his songs, rhythms, ideas, love, rebellion, equality and humanity through contemporary dance.

The festival is open to all.

Title: Padma water level starts falling in Chapainawabganj
Content:
The water level of the Padma River in Chapainawabganj fell by 6 centimetres in the 24 hours leading up to 6am today (13 September), but the overall flood situation in the district has not improved significantly.

Low-lying areas of five unions in Sadar and Shibganj upazilas remain inundated, leaving several thousand people affected by the flooding.

Meanwhile, water levels in the district's other two major rivers, the Mahananda and the Punarbhaba, rose further.

According to data from the Chapainawabganj office of the Bangladesh Water Development Board (WDB), the Padma water level fell by 6 centimetres over the past 24 hours and was flowing 32 centimetres below the danger level as of this morning.

The Mahananda rose by 3 centimetres and was flowing 1.02 metres below the danger level, while the Punarbhaba rose by 4 centimetres and was flowing 1.98 metres below the danger level.

WDB Executive Engineer SM Ahsan Habib said the flood situation is expected to start improving after remaining at the current level for another three days.

Earlier, some low-lying areas in Narayanpur and Alatuli unions of Sadar upazila and Panka, Durlabhpur and Ujirpur unions of Shibganj upazila were inundated due to the rise in water levels of the three rivers following an onrush of water from the upstream, leaving around 4,350 families waterlogged.

Title: Chinese technologies help drive global mining industry's green transition
Content:
Green technologies, intelligent equipment and smart mining solutions showcased at the 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition are highlighting China's growing role in the global mining industry's shift toward greener and more sustainable practices.

The conference and exhibition, held in north China's Tianjin Municipality from Thursday to Saturday (10-12 September), featured autonomous mining trucks, real-time data systems and advanced mineral processing equipment aimed at improving efficiency while reducing energy use and environmental impacts.

At the Xinhai Mining booth, a sand-table model demonstrated a smart green mine, with a central control screen displaying real-time data on ore hoisting, equipment loads, tailings pond levels and personnel locations.

"Staff can monitor and control the mineral processing plant remotely from a computer screen," said Zhang Yunlong, chairman of Shandong Xinhai Mining Group Co. Ltd.

The company's whole-process smart mining solution has been used in more than 100 countries and regions. Zhang cited a gold mine project in Zimbabwe with a daily processing capacity of 500 tonnes, where a clean-energy supply system covering 100,000 square metres has reduced costs by about 75 percent compared with diesel-based power generation.

A new large magnetic separator also attracted attention at the exhibition. Without changing processing capacity or beneficiation requirements, the technology reduces equipment size by about 50 percent and operating energy consumption by around 30 percent, while improving beneficiation indicators by about 20 percent.

Beneficiation involves a series of processes through which raw ore is converted into a concentrated product with greater economic value.

Li Chaopeng, deputy general manager of LONGi Magnet Co. Ltd., said the equipment has been deployed in more than 70 countries and regions, most recently at an iron ore project in Brazil.

"Our equipment uses less energy, recovers more resources from tailings and reduces iron ore waste, better meeting the mining industry's demand for automated and intelligent development," Li said.

The approach has drawn attention from mining professionals outside China.

"When I speak to many of our Chinese clients, they take sustainability very seriously. They have very strong sustainability standards," said Andrew Thake, an Australian mining industry practitioner and divisional director at Beacon Events & Exhibitions.

He said China's green mining practices, developed over more than a decade, provide useful examples for pursuing sustainable development under different resource conditions and levels of economic development.

China has established institutional, standards and evaluation systems for green mining and has promoted technologies including backfill mining, comprehensive use of solid waste and clean-energy substitution in mining areas.

Chinese mining companies are also applying these practices through overseas projects.

Zijin Mining, for example, has developed green mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo based on China's ecological civilization practices. Its green mine in Serbia has also contributed to improved environmental management in mining areas.

"I appreciate the efforts China has made in green development and environmental restoration," said Patricia, a Zimbabwean geospatial analyst. "I have followed some of the environmental restoration projects that have been carried out in China and I think they have been done quite well."

Dmitry Tetenkin, deputy minister of natural resources and environment of the Russian Federation, described green and intelligent industrial development as an urgent priority for the mining sector.

"Digital technologies, innovations, rational use of resources and reduction of environmental burden are no longer issues of the distant future, but necessary conditions for the modern mining industry," he said. "Technological progress must work simultaneously for production efficiency and responsible attitude to the environment."

China's green mining approach also extends to ecological research and conservation.

Under the International Big Scientific Plan on Resources and Environmental Effects of Global Karst Dynamic Systems, China has worked with several countries on resource and environmental surveys, carbon-cycle research and ecological protection in karst regions. The efforts have gradually contributed to a global karst monitoring network and explored ways to balance resource development with ecological protection.

In Tanzania, a Chinese technical assistance project at the Ngorongoro Lengai geopark has helped improve infrastructure and promote the integrated development of geological research and tourism.

Orkotete Lesongoyo, a resident of a village at the foot of Mount Lengai, became a local geological guide after receiving training organized by the geopark. He now introduces visitors from around the world to the geological features of the Lengai volcano.

"This project has raised the international profile and influence of Tanzania's tourism resources and created new livelihoods for surrounding residents," said Ren Junping, director of the Southern Africa Geological Survey Cooperation Center at the Tianjin Center of the China Geological Survey.

From green mining and environmental restoration to community development, Chinese practices are providing practical examples for the global mining industry's green transformation, Ren said.

The transition toward green and low-carbon development has become a key direction for high-quality growth in the global mining industry.

The Tianjin Declaration on Green Development of the Mining Industry, issued at the conference, called on countries, international organisations and other stakeholders to accelerate the industry's transition toward green and low-carbon development and contribute to global sustainable development.

Mohamed Noorain, CEO of Kossel Sudan mining enterprises, said China's technologies, standards and management experience in green mine development offer valuable lessons.

He expressed hope for stronger exchanges and cooperation between China and other countries, including Sudan, in green mining so that more environmentally friendly technologies and practices can be implemented and contribute to sustainable development in the sector.

Title: Redmin Industries holds annual partner summit ‘Redmin Horizon’ in Dhaka
Content:
Redmin Industries Limited, a manufacturer of chemicals and industrial raw materials, held its annual partner summit, "Redmin Horizon", in Dhaka on Saturday (12 September), bringing together distributors from across Bangladesh and senior company officials.

The day-long event took place at the Dhaka Regency Hotel, according to a press release.

Redmin Industries Chairman SM Nurul Alam Rezvi; Managing Director SM Monjurul Alam Ovee; Directors Raisa Sigma Hima and Rifah Tasnia Swarna; and Chief Business Officer Md Zahurul Haque attended the summit.

Guests were honoured with awards in various categories, while singer Sabrina Ehsan Porshi performed at the event.

Speaking at the summit, SM Monjurul Alam Ovee highlighted innovation, product quality and technical support as central to the company's operations.

"The core driving force of Redmin is innovation and the production of quality products. With the support of our Research and Development (R&D), Product Development, and Technical Support teams, we are able to provide fast, reliable, and cost-effective solutions to complex production challenges," he said.

"Redmin is a reflection of our commitment to developing smarter, safer, and more environmentally friendly products to ensure a modern standard of living for our customers. We believe that through this initiative, we will take another step forward in the industrial sector as a diversified industrial group," he added.

Established in 2022, Redmin Industries operates as a manufacturer, supplier and distributor. Its product portfolio includes chemicals, adhesives, thinners, printing and packaging inks, hot melt glue, hygiene glue, toys, baby products and agricultural products, alongside industrial and commercial solutions.

The company said one of its principal objectives was to develop a more advanced, technology-driven and self-reliant chemical and industrial solutions sector in Bangladesh while contributing to economic growth.

Its priorities include reducing dependence on imports through domestic production of quality and innovative products, creating industrial opportunities and generating direct and indirect employment.

Title: Eritrea accuses UAE of pursuing ‘port imperialism’ across Africa
Content:
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh has accused the United Arab Emirates of pursuing what he called "port imperialism" across Africa, saying Abu Dhabi's investments in maritime facilities have strategic political motives beyond commercial interests.

In an interview with Middle East Eye, Saleh said the UAE was seeking to establish a wider strategic presence through its involvement in ports and other maritime infrastructure.

UAE-backed port operators DP World and AD Ports hold stakes in maritime facilities in countries including Egypt, Tanzania, Somaliland and Puntland. The expansion has faced resistance in parts of the region.

Djibouti cancelled a concession held by DP World in 2018, while Sudan called off a $6 billion agreement for a Red Sea port in 2022, citing UAE support for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

Eritrea has also rejected UAE involvement in its ports. It declined a proposal for DP World to manage its ports and rejected a 2016 UAE request to establish a joint UAE-Israel military base on an island in the Dahlak Archipelago.

Relations between Eritrea and Ethiopia have also deteriorated following the breakdown of their tactical alliance during the Tigray civil war. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has pressed for access to the Red Sea while receiving weapons and drone support from the UAE.

Eritrea has become increasingly wary of cooperation between the UAE and Israel in Somaliland and Ethiopia. It subsequently decided to end diplomatic relations with Israel, according to the source, citing concerns about external powers establishing strategic strongholds in the region.

The two countries have also taken opposing positions in Sudan's war. The UAE has been accused of supporting the RSF, while Eritrea has hosted Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.

Eritrea has aligned itself with Egypt, Turkey and Saudi Arabia in opposing RSF control, reflecting wider competition among regional powers over influence in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea.

Title: BSF hands over 10 rescued Bangladeshis to BGB after Padma boat capsize
Content:
India's Border Security Force (BSF) has handed over 10 Bangladeshis to Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) following their rescue from the Padma River after a boat carrying 12 passengers capsized in Chapainawabganj Sadar upazila yesterday (12 September).

They were handed over to BGB around 10:00pm yesterday at the Faridpur border following a company commander-level flag meeting between the two border forces.

Lieutenant Colonel Kazi Mustafizur Rahman, commanding officer of 53 BGB Battalion, said members of Khandua BSF Camp rescued the 10 Bangladeshis from the Padma after the boat capsized and informed BGB of the incident.

Following the flag meeting, BSF formally handed over the rescued Bangladeshis to BGB, which later reunited them with their relatives in the presence of local public representatives.

The rescued Bangladeshis were identified as Russel, 26, Ibrahim, 50, Sawdagar, 40, Ibrahim, 60, Sakhina, 45, Nilufa, 35, Tania, 22, her 20-day-old infant, Sanaullah, 9, and Al Amin, 9. All are residents of Jahurpur Bokripara in Narayanpur union under Sadar upazila.

Earlier, around 5:00pm on yesterday, the boat carrying the 12 passengers left Bakherali Ghat for Jahurpur.

About 20 minutes into the journey, the boat capsized amid strong winds and strong currents, according to police and locals.

Patrolling BSF personnel from Khandua Camp rescued 10 passengers alive and took them into Indian territory.

Another passenger, identified as Wasim, 25, managed to swim back to Bangladeshi territory, while Mostafa, 60, remained missing.

Police and Fire Service personnel rushed to the scene after receiving the news, while BSF subsequently notified BGB of the rescue.

Title: Maya Ride: Ride-sharing for women, by women
Content:
One day, Jannatul Ferdous was discussing with her husband Fahad Chowdhury about how uncomfortable it is for women to navigate Dhaka's busy roads. Every day, thousands of women do so, for work, study and business. Packed buses can mean unwanted touching or harassment, while travelling in CNGs or on ride-sharing motorbikes can also leave women uneasy.

Jannatul wondered what if there were a ride-sharing service operated by women, exclusively for female passengers?

Fahad took the idea seriously. Together, they launched 'Maya Ride', a women-focused ride-sharing platform designed to make travel more comfortable and secure. The service connects female passengers with female riders, offering women an alternative to navigating Dhaka's often uncomfortable transport system.

"Since I have been working in data marketing for eight years, I thought I would run an experiment," Fahad says. That small experiment gradually grew into a platform.

Both of the couple grew up in Dhaka. Fahad completed his O Levels and A Levels before moving to London for higher education. He earned a bachelor's degree in Computer Science and a master's degree in Data Science from Queen Mary University of London. Jannatul, meanwhile, is studying for an LLB at London South Bank University.

However, they did not start the initiative with a business dream in mind. Rather, they wanted to do something alongside their studies that could generate some income while, more importantly, benefiting people.

"I often saw women in Dhaka feeling uncomfortable sitting on motorcycles with male riders. I used to think that I probably wouldn't feel comfortable either if I were in that situation. That thought really stayed with me," Jannatul says.

70 female riders and counting

Maya Ride launched its website and Facebook page in mid-April 2026. Soon after, female motorcycle riders began expressing interest in joining the platform. Starting with four riders, the network grew to around 70 within four months, though about 30 are currently active.

Women who owned cars also came forward spontaneously, expressing interest in providing car rides. Around 25 female car drivers are now connected with Maya Ride, with four to five regularly providing rides.

Before launching Maya Ride, both Fahad and Jannatul were concerned about how people would respond to their initiative. Dhaka already has established ride-sharing services such as Uber and Pathao. Why would a woman choose a new platform instead of these popular services?

But the response from both riders and passengers surprised them. Within just four months, more than 300 motorcycle rides had been completed. Customers have also shown considerable interest. In one case, a customer used Maya Ride more than 22 times during the early days of the platform. Some have used it even more frequently.

'I can travel without worrying'

Nuzhat Tabassum, a resident of Shyamoli, has used Maya Ride's services more than 30 times. She has been commuting regularly to her office in Gulshan-1 since 2023. Although she owns a car, she cannot always use it. Her commute became particularly difficult during periods of fuel shortages.

At different times, she had to rely on buses, CNGs or conventional ride-sharing services, which often came with their own set of problems. Finding a CNG during busy hours was difficult, while long traffic jams were another challenge. She also had to consider her safety and comfort when travelling with male riders.

One day, a colleague at her office told her about Maya Ride. After having a positive experience on her first ride, Nuzhat began using the service regularly. For her, the biggest source of comfort was having a woman in the driver's seat. It made her feel both more comfortable and safer.

"It is true that the cost is somewhat higher than Pathao or Uber. But considering how safe I feel here and how I can travel without worrying, I would say the extra cost is worth it," she says.

"I often saw women in Dhaka feeling uncomfortable sitting on motorcycles with male riders. I used to think that I probably wouldn't feel comfortable either if I were in that situation. That thought really stayed with me."

Jannatul explained that the platform still does not have as many drivers as it needs. The existing pool of riders is not yet large enough. As a result, riders sometimes have to travel deep into different parts of Dhaka to pick up a particular passenger. At times, they also have to come from quite far away to provide a service, which naturally increases the cost.

However, they want to lower fares, which requires more female drivers. For now, she considers increasing the number of riders their biggest challenge. They believe a larger pool of drivers would not only lower fares but also double their customer base.

Fahad said Maya Ride verifies key details before approving drivers, prioritising passenger safety. Applicants register through the website and provide their NID details, driving licence, photograph, vehicle or motorcycle registration number and contact information. Those with little driving experience or newly obtained licences are not approved immediately, with the platform prioritising riders with at least one to two years of experience.

As many female passengers are not comfortable travelling by motorcycle, Maya Ride introduced a car service, mainly through weekly and monthly subscriptions. Cars can carry either one passenger or three to four women, who are picked up from a designated nearby point.

The service offers two packages: the 'Pick-up Point' package and the 'Door-to-Door' package. The monthly cost of the Pick-up Point package is approximately Tk7,300, while the Door-to-Door package costs Tk9,200. The same monthly rate applies regardless of where within Dhaka city the passenger travels from.

Under the Pick-up Point package, several passengers wait at a convenient location, making it relatively easier for a driver to pick everyone up. The Door-to-Door service, on the other hand, offers pick-up and drop-off directly at the passenger's doorstep.

All Maya Ride services are essentially based on pre-booking. Since the platform currently has a shortage of car drivers, customers who want to use the car service need to make a booking several days in advance.

For motorcycle rides, passengers can book by 10pm the night before. Their request is shared in the riders' group, and an available rider is assigned and informed. Both parties receive each other's phone numbers, and the rider arrives at the designated location at the scheduled time.

Motorcycle rides have no weekly or monthly packages. Passengers pay the rider in cash after the trip, with the fare determined in advance through Maya Ride's website fare calculator, which estimates the cost based on the distance between the pick-up and destination points.

Not every working parent can drop their child off at school or pick them up afterwards. At the same time, many parents may not feel comfortable entrusting their child to a stranger. This concern led to Maya Ride's new initiative, Maya Kids, a transportation service for school-going children.

The entire process is arranged through pre-booking. There is even an option for a family member to accompany the child during the journey. This allows the family to keep track of the child.

Jannatul said one of the main aims of Maya Kids is to reduce parents' worries about their children's school commute amid their busy schedules. So far, Maya Kids has around seven customers.

Breaking into a male-dominated space

The journey has not always been easy for Fahad and Jannatul. They have faced rider shortages, while some drivers have left midway. Others faced discouraging comments and ridicule after joining, making many women initially hesitant to take up the work.

Jannatul, however, continued encouraging them and explaining the potential of the opportunity. Many eventually gained the confidence to ignore the criticism and continue.

That is what the couple wanted: to make women more comfortable with ride-sharing as a profession. Maya Ride currently takes a 10% commission from riders' earnings.

The service mainly operates through its website, but Fahad is developing an app to make it more organised. The app will maintain separate records for customers and riders and provide complete information about each ride. Fahad hopes to launch it within three months, making the service more efficient and convenient for customers.

Jannatul said Maya Ride is not only about passenger safety but also about creating employment opportunities for women. Women who own cars or motorcycles can use their vehicles and skills to earn an income. She believes many are also motivated by a desire to help other women.

"Women are working with the intention of helping other women. Isn't that a beautiful thing?" Fahad says.

Title: South Korea's expanded espionage law takes effect amid push to protect chip technology
Content:
South Korea's expanded espionage law takes effect on Sunday, broadening espionage offences beyond acts involving North Korea to include all foreign countries as Seoul seeks to protect key technologies amid intensifying competition in semiconductors and other strategic industries.

Here are more details:

• The National Assembly passed the revised Criminal Act on 26 February after years of criticism that existing laws were ill-suited to punish technology and industrial espionage involving non-North Korean actors.

• The amendment creates a new offence covering espionage for a foreign country or equivalent organisation, carrying a minimum sentence of three years in prison. Existing provisions for espionage benefiting an "enemy state" remain in place.

• Under the previous law, espionage charges generally applied only to acts benefiting North Korea, forcing prosecutors in many cases involving foreign governments or companies to rely on other industrial technology or trade-secret laws.

• The National Intelligence Service welcomed the amendment when it was passed, saying it would strengthen South Korea's ability to prevent leaks of strategic technologies such as semiconductors, displays, batteries and AI.

• Legal and security experts cited the change as closing a longstanding loophole that often left advanced industrial technology leak cases subject to lighter penalties, with supporters arguing it will strengthen deterrence against industrial espionage.

• The amendment was promulgated on 12 March and takes effect after a six-month grace period on 13 September.

• The change follows high-profile technology leak cases, including the indictment last year of five former Samsung Electronics employees accused of transferring key dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chip technology to Chinese memory maker CXMT. Samsung and CXMT did not comment at the time.

• Asked whether the law, which does not specify any country, could be seen as targeting Beijing, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China requires its enterprises to conduct international cooperation in accordance with international rules and laws. "At the same time, to this end, we believe that all countries should safeguard the normal investment and business activities of enterprises and provide a fair, just, and non-discriminatory business environment," Mao told a regular news briefing on Friday.
Author: Reuters

Title: AI, robotics, technical education being added to textbooks for grades 6-10: Mahdi
Content:
Prime Minister's Education and Primary and Mass Education Adviser Mahdi Amin has said the government is bringing about major changes in the country's education system to develop world-class skilled human resources and prepare a technology-driven future generation.

"From the next academic year, modern subjects such as artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, machine learning and cybersecurity are being given special priority in textbooks for grades six to ten. At the same time, technical education is being institutionally integrated with mainstream education and made compulsory for all students," he said.

He made the remarks while speaking at a plenary session of the 'Bangladesh Innovation Fair 2026', organised by the Ministry of Science and Technology at Novo Theatre in the capital yesterday (12 September).

Mahdi, who is also the Prime Minister's Office spokesperson, said the government is giving the highest priority to STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) education to keep pace with the rapidly changing, technology-driven global landscape.

"The prime minister has given direct instructions to give equal priority to STEM education not only at the secondary and higher secondary levels but also at the tertiary level," he said.

Outlining the curriculum reforms, he said necessary changes are underway at every stage from primary to higher education to address the limitations of theoretical education and reduce the gap between book-based learning and practical application.

He said two new subjects, 'Sports' and 'Culture', will be introduced in the fourth grade at the primary level from the next academic year.

Meanwhile, 'Learning with Happiness' will be introduced in the sixth grade to help students develop interpersonal and transferable skills needed in real life.

The adviser said technical education is currently not compulsory for all students.

However, it will be introduced in the sixth grade from the next academic year, with completion gradually becoming compulsory for students from grades six to ten in schools across the country.

"The government's objective is to integrate technical education with mainstream education, without treating it as a 'taboo', as in developed countries," he said.

Emphasising the need to link higher education with real-life demands, Mahdi Amin said work is underway to determine how technical and vocational education can be integrated into the curricula of around 2,500 institutions affiliated with the National University.

Praising the calibre of Bangladeshi youth by international standards, he said young Bangladeshis are working with distinction on the global stage and, given appropriate resources and platforms, are capable of succeeding worldwide.

The government wants to prevent 'brain drain' and turn it into 'brain circulation', he said.

In this regard, the government plans to build a strong industry-academia ecosystem by utilising endowment and CSR funds and the experience of Bangladeshi alumni, as is done at world-class universities.

It also plans to involve Bangladeshi experts working abroad in curriculum and industrial development through special fellowships.

The seminar, titled 'STEM for a Future-Ready Bangladesh: Building the Backbone of the Innovative Economy', was moderated by Science and Technology Ministry Secretary Md Anwar Hossain.

National University Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr ASM Amanullah, Unesco Dhaka Office Chief of Education S Kyung Ko, senior official of a leading telecommunications company Tanvir Mohammad, Independent University, Bangladesh Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr M Tamim, among others, also participated in the discussion.

Title: 'This is the test': All eyes on US Fed to tackle high inflation
Content:
The US Federal Reserve goes into a key rate-setting meeting this week with markets expecting policymakers to pull the trigger on a rate hike to tackle persistently high inflation, while analysts say central bank chief Kevin Warsh's credibility is on the line.

The world's largest economy has been dealing with years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of US President Donald Trump's war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.

The Fed has held rates steady since January, choosing to wait to gauge the effects of energy price shocks and to let the tariffs' effects on prices ripple through the economy.

In recent weeks, however, several Fed policymakers, including Warsh himself, have hinted that if inflation does not show clear signs of slowing, the central bank will have to act by raising interest rates.

On Friday (11 September), new data on consumer inflation for August showed it remaining steady at 3.4%, no change from the month before, but still well above the Fed's long-term 2% target.

Market expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike on Wednesday (16 September) surged in the wake of the data, with the probability at more than 85% according to CME's FedWatch tool.

The Fed last raised rates three years ago, when it was fighting surging inflation in the wake of the pandemic. They currently stand between 3.50% and 3.75%.

Trump has railed against the Fed over interest rates since taking office for his second term, launching unprecedented attacks on the central bank's independence as he demands lower rates to spur economic activity.

The US president launched a criminal probe against previous Fed chair Jerome Powell, is attempting to fire another Fed governor, and has even threatened to cut trade ties with certain countries if the Fed raises rates.

Warsh was appointed by Trump and analysts say this is his first real test since taking office: Will the Fed raise rates to combat inflation, or hold steady in line with what the White House prefers?

"This is the test. This is what comes with that job, and now he has to decide how to handle it," said David Wessel, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

"He's either going to completely disappoint the markets, or he runs the risk that he's going to start to anger Donald Trump."

The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee, with its 12 voting members, will announce its decision after a two-day meeting on Wednesday at 2 pm (1800 GMT).

"It's quite likely that the Fed will raise interest rates next week," said Claudia Sahm, chief economist at investment firm New Century Advisors who previously worked at the Fed.

But "it's not a done deal," she cautioned in comments to AFP. "This is a difficult decision for them to make."

Raising interest rates would increase borrowing costs across the board for the US economy, acting as a brake on further investment and consumption activity.

Sahm warned such a move was "not a magic wand and it is a costly medicine."

She said the Fed could still hold rates steady rather than administer that medicine, but it would have to explain its decision clearly to markets.

"If they surprise markets and they can't explain why they're surprising markets, then Wednesday (16 September) afternoon will be pretty messy," she said.

Since taking office, Warsh has changed the way the Fed communicates about its decisions, advocating for less transparency into the process as he thinks it locks policymakers into courses of action that may need to be adjusted.

Investors have had mixed reactions to the cut in what is known as "forward guidance", with analysts saying it has introduced more uncertainty into how financial markets price in inflation and interest rate expectations.

Warsh has advocated in the past for lower interest rates due to expected productivity gains from AI technology, but in recent weeks he has doubled down on the Fed's mandate to bring inflation down.

"There's always been this doubt about whether Kevin Warsh is going to be like his predecessors and do what's right for the economy, even if it's politically inconvenient," said Wessel of Brookings.

"If he raises rates now and Trump goes ballistic, he will have established his credibility as an independent Fed chair for the rest of his term."

Donald Trump / Kevin Warsh / US Federal Reserve

Title: Baghdad confirms attack on Saudi pipeline came from Iraq
Content:
Saudi Arabia has said it will not retaliate and wants Iraq to "take the necessary measures." Baghdad is under pressure from the United States to rein in Iran-backed militias

Iraq's government confirmed on Saturday that Friday night attacks on a key Saudi oil pipeline had been launched from Iraqi territory.

Saudi Arabia said that it shut down the pipeline on Friday, calling it a "precautionary measure" over a drone attack that occurred the previous day.

Riyadh said that it would not retaliate, stressing that it wanted to give Baghdad "an opportunity to take the necessary measures."

The Iraqi government dismissed the military commander and police chief in Maysan province, on the Iranian border, which has long been viewed as an area where Iran-backed Shiite militias operate.

Iraq also closed the main border crossing in Maysan.

Who is behind the attacks on the Saudi pipeline?

No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks.

The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an alliance of Iran-backed Iraqi militias, denied any involvement.

The militias are formally part of Iraq's security forces, but some of the groups occasionally act independently.

US President Donald Trump said Saturday that Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack, while also seemingly downplaying the US and Saudi Arabia's conflict with the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia that controls swathes of Yemen.

"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."

The Houthis and some of the Iraqi Shiite armed groups are part of what Tehran dubs the "Axis of Resistance," a group of Iran-backed militias in the Middle East that oppose the United States and Israel.

The Yemeni armed group has imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia since July and seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday. Thousands of people have fled the city.

The Houthis on Thursday also captured the island of Perim, after a weeklong offensive that has culminated in solidifying their hold of strategic points on the Bab el-Mandeb strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.

The Houthis have previously targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, citing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza amid Israel's offensive in the territory.

But the movement has said that maritime traffic remains safe for all shipping companies, except for Saudi vessels.

Iraq under pressure to disband Iran-backed militias

Iraq has been under pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned Shiite armed groups, as some of the militias have hit US-linked targets in the region since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28.

While Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for their disarmament, several militias have said they will not comply with the order.

The deadline coincides with the date set for the withdrawal of the remaining US-led coalition forces from Iraq.

One of the most influential militias, Kataib Hezbollah, has heavily criticised the disarmament plan and called for guarantees that US forces would never return and measures would be implemented to rid Iraq of US influence on political or economic decision-making.

Author: Deutsche Welle

Title: Hungary PM Magyar says to scrap Orban-era restriction on gay adoption
Content:
Hungary's government will change legislation passed in 2020 by Viktor Orban's former government that had effectively banned gay adoption, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Saturday.

Adoption in Hungary, a European Union member state, by gay and lesbian couples was possible until late 2020 if one partner applied as a single person.

Under the law passed by Orban's right-wing Fidesz party in 2020, single people had to have their adoption requests approved by the family affairs minister, which has amounted to an effective ban.

Magyar ousted Orban after 16 years in a landslide election win in April. Changing the system of adoption would be a significant measure to restore LGBTQ rights.

"We can state unequivocally that we will change this system: it should not be the minister, a politician ... who makes the decision in such cases, but rather professionals capable of determining the conditions under which a given young child can achieve ... a life that allows them to become a happy and harmonious member of society," Magyar told a briefing, in reply to a question.

Orban, who cast himself as a defender of what he called Christian values from Western liberalism, passed laws ending the change of gender in personal documents, effectively halting adoption by same-sex couples and banning materials in schools seen as promoting homosexuality or gender transition.

The erosion of LGBTQ+ rights had a traumatic effect on the community.

Orban's government violated European law with rules prohibiting or restricting access to LGBTQ content, which stigmatise and marginalise gay and trans people, the European Court of Justice ruled in April, just before the election.

Hungary has never allowed gay marriage but still recognises civil unions.
